0.title: Jeremiah: The Weeping Prophet
0.overview:
The message. Jeremiah is the book of a man sent to tell his own nation that it was finished, and of the God who would not let that be the last word. For forty years Jeremiah warned Judah that because they had forsaken the LORD, “the fountain of living waters” (2:13), he would bring Babylon against them, and that no temple, treaty or prophet of easy peace could save them. They would not listen, and every word came true. Yet in the ruins God promised what judgment could never produce: a righteous King from David’s line, and a new covenant in which he would write his law on their hearts and say, “I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more” (31:34). The God who tears down also builds and plants, and the building has the last word.

Background: the prophet. Jeremiah was a priest’s son from Anathoth, a village a few miles north-east of Jerusalem (1:1). God called him in the thirteenth year of King Josiah, about 627 BC, while he was “only a youth” (1:6), promising, “I am with you to deliver you” (1:8). He was forbidden to marry (16:2), so that his lonely life became a sign of the coming ruin. He was put in the stocks (20:2), tried for his life (chapter 26), arrested as a deserter (37:13) and lowered into a muddy cistern (38:6). After the city fell he was taken to Egypt against his will (43:6–7), and there the record ends. More than any other prophet he lets us see inside: he argues with God, curses the day he was born, and tries to stop preaching, but the word is “a burning fire shut up in my bones” (20:9).

When and where. Jeremiah lived through the end of a world. Assyria, which had destroyed the northern kingdom a century earlier, collapsed; Nineveh fell in 612 BC. Josiah’s great reform, after the Book of the Law was found in 622 BC, never reached the people’s hearts (3:10), and in 609 BC he was killed in battle by Pharaoh Neco. Judah’s last kings followed fast: Shallum (Jehoahaz), deported after three months (22:11–12); Jehoiakim, who burned Jeremiah’s scroll column by column (36:23); Coniah (Jehoiachin), taken to Babylon in 597 BC (22:24–26); and Zedekiah, who consulted Jeremiah in secret and never dared obey him (38:14–23). In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish (46:2), and Judah’s kings tried to survive by playing Egypt against Babylon. Jeremiah said the real danger was the LORD they had abandoned, and Babylon the rod in his hand. Jerusalem and its temple were burned in 586 BC (587 on some reckonings). The nations would serve Babylon “seventy years” (25:11); Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 BC, the first exiles went home about 538 BC, and Daniel read the number in Jeremiah’s book and prayed (Daniel 9:2).

The kind of writing. Jeremiah is prophecy: poetry and sermons, acted parables (a ruined loincloth, a smashed flask, an ox’s yoke), the prophet’s anguished prayers, and long stretches of story. It is not in date order, so watch the kings named at the head of each section. Its warnings carry a condition: if a nation “turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster” (18:8). Its promises of return to the land, of Israel and Judah reunited and David’s throne restored, are read in this commentary, with the New Testament, as fulfilled in Christ and his one people and completed in the new creation.

How the book makes its case. The call comes first [1]: “to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant” (1:10), four words of demolition and two of building, and the building words last. Then the case against Judah [2–25]: the temple sermon against trusting “these deceptive words” (7:4), and the diagnosis beneath it all: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?” (17:9). Then the prophet in conflict [26–29]: tried for his life, opposed by the false prophet Hananiah, writing to the exiles to settle in Babylon. At the centre stands the Book of Consolation [30–33], with the new covenant (31:31–34) and a field bought at Anathoth while Babylon besieged the city (chapter 32). Then the story of the end [34–45]: the burned scroll rewritten, the siege and fall, and the flight to Egypt. The oracles against the nations follow [46–51], ending with Babylon itself, “the hammer of the whole earth”, broken (50:23). An appendix [52] retells the fall and ends with Jehoiachin, David’s heir, released from prison to eat at the king’s table every day of his life (52:31–34): a small light left burning for David’s house.

How did the book come to be? The book itself tells us. Jeremiah dictated to Baruch his scribe, and when Jehoiakim burned the scroll, a second was written, “And many similar words were added to them” (36:32). “Thus far are the words of Jeremiah” (51:64) marks the end of his words; chapter 52, matching the end of 2 Kings, was added after about 561 BC. Many modern scholars hold that the book grew over a long time and that its prose sermons are largely the work of later editors in the exile. The ancient Greek translation is also about an eighth shorter and places the oracles against the nations mid-book, and both forms were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. This commentary’s view is that the book is Jeremiah’s own message, gathered by him and Baruch, its prose and poetry alike carrying his voice and fitting his times; that the Hebrew text our Bibles follow is most likely the fuller edition they completed; and that the message is the same in both.

Where it leads: to Christ. Jeremiah leads to Christ first by the need it exposes. Even Josiah’s reform could not change the heart; the people could no more cure themselves than “the Ethiopian change his skin” (13:23). Only a new covenant would do: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (31:33). On the night he was betrayed Jesus said, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews quotes Jeremiah’s promise in full to show that it has come (Hebrews 8:8–12). It leads by promise: God will “raise up for David a righteous Branch”, whose name is “The LORD is our righteousness” (23:5–6). And it leads by pattern. Jeremiah was “like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter” (11:19); he wept over his city, preached against its temple and was condemned by its priests, and some took Jesus for “Jeremiah or one of the prophets” (Matthew 16:14). Jesus too called the temple “a den of robbers” (Matthew 21:13; Jeremiah 7:11) and wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). Matthew heard Rachel weeping (31:15) in Bethlehem’s grief (Matthew 2:17–18). But Jeremiah could only announce the new covenant. Jesus made it, in his own blood.

For us. Jeremiah is for anyone tempted to trust religion instead of God; for anyone who must keep speaking unpopular truth and sees little fruit, since faithfulness is measured by obedience, not results; and for believers living as exiles, told to “seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile” (29:7). The famous promise of 29:11 was spoken to a whole people, many of whom would die in Babylon, not as a pledge of an easy life; but for everyone in Christ, God’s plans run through the ruins to “a future and a hope”. So let the believer boast in this, “that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth” (9:24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Man and His Times
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book opens by setting Jeremiah in history, so that we read everything that follows as God’s word spoken into real events. He is a priest’s son from Anathoth, a village outside the capital (v. 1). The word of the LORD came to him in the thirteenth year of Josiah, about 627 BC, while reform was gathering pace (v. 2), and it kept coming through the reign of Jehoiakim to the end of Zedekiah’s, when Jerusalem went into captivity (v. 3). That last phrase tells how forty years of faithful preaching ended: in the ruin of the city he loved.
verseByVerse.theology: God's word comes to a real man, in named years, under named kings: the message of this book is anchored in history.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, to whom the word of the LORD came in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign. It came also in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, and until the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, the son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the captivity of Jerusalem in the fifth month.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the words of a real man in real history: a country priest’s son whom God sent to speak for forty years to a capital that would not listen, until it fell.

The words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah. A priest’s son from Anathoth, a village within sight of Jerusalem, not a member of the temple establishment in the capital. Anathoth was the town to which Solomon had banished the priest Abiathar (1 Kings 2:26), and Jeremiah’s family may well have been of that line, priests long kept at a distance from the Jerusalem temple. He is an outsider, and he will spend his life telling the capital what it does not want to hear.

In the days of Josiah. The date matters. Josiah was the last good king of Judah, who “did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in all the way of David his father” (2 Kings 22:2). Jeremiah’s ministry begins as a national reform gathers pace: Josiah had begun purging the idols the year before (2 Chronicles 34:3), and the great reform came five years later (2 Kings 22:3). He is called in the best years, and he will watch them end.

Until the captivity of Jerusalem. The last phrase tells how forty years of preaching went. Under Jehoiakim Babylon had already closed in (2 Kings 24:1). The thirteenth year of Josiah is about 627 BC; the fifth month of Zedekiah’s eleventh year is the summer of 587 BC (some reckon 586), when the Babylonians burned the temple and the city (2 Kings 25:8–9).

Faithfulness, not results. Judged by results, Jeremiah failed. Judged by faithfulness, he is one of the great men of the Bible. Those are not the same measure, and confusing them has wrecked more ministries and more Christians than open sin has.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah prophesied for about forty years, from about 627 BC to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 and beyond. Anathoth was a priests’ town about 3 miles north-east of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Before I Formed You in the Womb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s call rests on his own choice, not on Jeremiah’s fitness, and God supplies everything the call requires. Before Jeremiah was born God formed, knew, consecrated and appointed him a prophet to the nations (vv. 4–5). Jeremiah protests that he cannot speak and is only a youth (v. 6). God forbids the excuse, tells him where he will go and what he will say, and meets the real problem, fear, with his presence: “I am with you to deliver you” (vv. 7–8). Then he touches Jeremiah’s mouth, puts his words in it, and sets him over nations with a word that tears down and builds (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: The call rests on God's prior choice, God's presence and God's words, not on the prophet's ability.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God chose, knew and set Jeremiah apart for his work before he was born, so his calling rested entirely on God and not on anything in him. From here the narrator’s voice becomes the prophet’s own: “the word of the LORD came to me.”

Before I formed you in the womb. Four verbs, and God is the subject of every one: he formed, he knew, he consecrated, he appointed. All four happened before Jeremiah had done anything at all, before he had any character to commend him or any failure to disqualify him.

I knew you. More than knowing facts about him: knowing him personally and setting his love on him. Before there was a person to know, God knew him. “Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them” (Psalm 139:16).

Others called from the womb. Paul spoke of God “who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace” (Galatians 1:15), and John the Baptist was to be “filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother’s womb” (Luke 1:15). Above all, Isaiah’s servant says, “The LORD called me from the womb” (Isaiah 49:1), and that Servant is Jesus.

What follows for us. God deals with unborn children as persons he knows, names and has purposes for. And your significance is not something you are building. It was settled before you existed, by God, and no failure of yours can overturn it.

A calling needs a Caller. Our culture usually means by vocation something inward: find your passion and go after it. A calling you invent for yourself has nobody behind it, and when it goes wrong, as Jeremiah’s ministry would by every outward measure, it can only tell you that you chose badly. Os Guinness argued in The Call that the very word assumes a Caller: you cannot be called by no one. Verse 5 puts the Caller first. Before Jeremiah had a passion, a gift or a single sermon, God knew him and appointed him. That lifts two burdens our culture lays on the young: the pressure to manufacture a meaningful life from scratch, and the fear that one wrong turn will waste it. And the One who calls goes with those he calls, which is the whole point of verse 8. Jesus told his friends, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16), and he does not drop those he has chosen.

What about a child who dies before birth? Parents who have lost a pregnancy often come to this verse with an ache, and it speaks to them gently. A child carried for a few weeks and never held was known by the God who formed it, and is not forgotten. Scripture does not tell us all we would like about such little ones, but it gives ground for hope: when his infant son died, David said, “I shall go to him, but he will not return to me” (2 Samuel 12:23), and the Westminster Confession of Faith and the 1689 London Baptist Confession both teach that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ. Such a child may be entrusted to the Judge of all the earth, who will do right (Genesis 18:25), and whose Son took little children in his arms (Mark 10:16). A miscarriage is a sorrow, not a sin, and no mother should hear this verse as blame.

Does “before I formed you in the womb I knew you” mean souls exist before their bodies? No. It means God chose and set Jeremiah apart before his life began; the knowing is God’s, not the soul’s. It speaks first of Jeremiah’s unique call as a prophet, but it rests on a truth that holds for all God’s people: “he chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). And it shows that God knows and forms each person in the womb (Psalm 139:13–16).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah meets God’s call with dismay, pleading that he cannot speak and is too young, and both objections only show that the work will have to depend on God.

Ah, Lord GOD! A cry, not a greeting. The objection comes in two parts: I cannot do this, and I am too young to be taken seriously.

I do not know how to speak. Both objections are probably true, and that is the point. Moses said the same at the burning bush (Exodus 4:10), and God’s answer was not a compliment about his hidden potential but a question, “Who has made man’s mouth?”, and a promise: “I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak” (Exodus 4:11–12).

Not self-esteem but God. In these calls God never says, You are better than you think. He says, I will be with you. Confidence for service does not come from a higher estimate of yourself; it comes from a higher estimate of God.

For I am only a youth. Youth is no disqualification in Scripture. Paul told a young minister, “Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity” (1 Timothy 4:12).

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to me, "Do not say, 'I am only a youth'; for to all to whom I send you, you shall go, and whatever I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God refuses Jeremiah’s excuse, takes charge of where he goes and what he says, and answers his fear with his own presence.

Do not say, ‘I am only a youth.’ God does not argue with the objection; he forbids it. Then he replaces the two halves of Jeremiah’s excuse with two commands that put the responsibility where it belongs: where you go is not your decision, and what you say is not your decision either. That is a hard word and a liberating one: no freedom to choose the audience or edit the message, and no burden of inventing something worth saying.

Do not be afraid of them. God names the real problem. It is not inability; it is fear. Jeremiah will be beaten, put in the stocks, thrown into a cistern and accused of treason, so the fear is not irrational. The remedy is not a promise that they will listen, or that he will be liked. It is a presence: “I am with you.”

For I am with you to deliver you. The risen Christ left the same word with his church when he sent it into the world: “And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20), a presence he keeps by the Spirit he gives. Paul heard it in Corinth when he was afraid: “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you” (Acts 18:9–10). Is there a conversation you are avoiding because of what the person might say back? The promise is the same for you: he goes with you into it, and he has already forgiven the times you stayed silent.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD put out his hand and touched my mouth. And the LORD said to me, "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. See, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself supplies the words Jeremiah lacks, and those words carry God’s authority over whole nations, first to tear down and then to build.

The LORD put out his hand and touched my mouth. The objection was about a mouth, so God touches his mouth. Isaiah’s lips were touched with a coal from the altar to deal with his guilt (Isaiah 6:7); here the touch is a commission, and the words themselves are put into his mouth.

Sweet and bitter. Ezekiel was made to eat a scroll (Ezekiel 3:1–3), and John ate a little scroll that was “sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter” (Revelation 10:10). That is Jeremiah’s life in a sentence: the word of God is sweet to receive and bitter to carry.

Over nations and over kingdoms. A village boy is set over nations and kingdoms, not with an army but with a message. The empires of his day would have laughed. They are gone, and his words are still being read.

To pluck up and to break down. Six verbs: four tear down, two build. That is the proportion of this book, and it is honest about what the word of God must do in a place that has gone wrong. You cannot plant in ground that has not been cleared. Paul describes his ministry the same way, with weapons that “have divine power to destroy strongholds” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5).

To build and to plant. But the two building verbs are not an afterthought. Later God takes them up again: “so I will watch over them to build and to plant” (31:28). The book that begins with demolition has a new covenant at its centre (31:31–34).

The prophet like Moses. “I have put my words in your mouth” and “whatever I command you, you shall speak” (v. 7) echo God’s promise to Moses of a coming prophet: “I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him” (Deuteronomy 18:18). Jeremiah stands in that line, but the promise is finally kept in Jesus (Acts 3:22), in whom the tearing down and the building up meet: he bore the judgment, and he builds his church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — Two Visions: the Almond and the Boiling Pot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two visions show Jeremiah that God’s word will certainly be done, and what that will mean for Judah. The first is an almond branch, the “watching” tree: God is watching over his word to perform it, so neither warning nor promise will fail (vv. 11–12). The second is a boiling pot tipped from the north: disaster is about to pour over the land (vv. 13–14). God himself is summoning the northern kingdoms to set their thrones at Jerusalem’s gates (v. 15), and he names the reason, so that no one will call it chance: his people have forsaken him and bowed down to the works of their own hands (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: God watches over his word to do it, and the first thing it will do here is bring an army from the north.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Jeremiah, what do you see?" And I said, "I see an almond branch." Then the LORD said to me, "You have seen well, for I am watching over my word to perform it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The almond branch tells Jeremiah that God is wide awake over everything he has said and will certainly bring it to pass.

Jeremiah, what do you see? The first vision is almost domestic, a branch in blossom such as anyone might notice on a walk: God is teaching him to read ordinary things.

I see an almond branch. The answer turns on a play on words English cannot carry: the Hebrew word for almond sounds like the word for watching. The almond is the first tree in the land to blossom, flowering in late winter while everything else still looks dead, which is probably why its name sounds like “the wakeful one”. Jeremiah sees an almond branch, and God says, I am the watching God, and what I am watching over is my word.

I am watching over my word to perform it. That is the sentence to hold for the next fifty-one chapters. Not one syllable of what God says in this book will fall to the ground unattended. “So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose” (Isaiah 55:11). “Has he said, and will he not do it?” (Numbers 23:19).

For prophet and nation. It cuts both ways, which is exactly why it is here. For a prophet who will preach for forty years and see almost no response, it means his labour is not wasted. For a nation that has heard the warnings and shrugged, it means the warnings are not empty words. And for us it means the promises are not empty either: “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).
verseByVerse.note: Wordplay: “almond” (shaqed) sounds like “watching” (shoqed) (ESV note). The almond is among the first trees to blossom in spring.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me a second time, saying, "What do you see?" And I said, "I see a boiling pot, facing away from the north." Then the LORD said to me, "Out of the north disaster shall be let loose upon all the inhabitants of the land. For behold, I am calling all the tribes of the kingdoms of the north, declares the LORD, and they shall come, and every one shall set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, against all its walls all around and against all the cities of Judah. And I will declare my judgments against them, for all their evil in forsaking me. They have made offerings to other gods and worshiped the works of their own hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The boiling pot shows disaster about to pour over Judah from the north, and God says plainly that he is the one summoning it, because his people have forsaken him for gods they made.

I see a boiling pot, facing away from the north. A cooking pot at the boil, tilted so that what is inside is about to pour out southwards over Judah.

Out of the north. Babylon lay to the east, but the desert was in between, so its armies marched round and came down from the north; that was the road every invader took. Within Jeremiah’s lifetime Nebuchadnezzar’s armies would come down it.

I am calling all the tribes of the kingdoms of the north. The one doing it is God: “I am calling.” Babylon thought it was pursuing its own ambitions; it was being summoned. The thrones set in the gateway are the picture of a conquered city, with foreign officials sitting where Judah’s elders used to give judgment.

For all their evil in forsaking me. The reason is given plainly, so that no one can call the disaster meaningless. It is not bad luck, nor merely the politics of empires. It is “forsaking me”, and the shape that forsaking took: worshipping “the works of their own hands”. They made something, then bowed to it. Every generation does, and only the objects change.

Does God do evil? The Hebrew word can mean “evil” or “disaster”. God brings calamity as judgment on sin (Isaiah 45:7), but he never does moral evil or tempts anyone to it (James 1:13). The disaster from the north was the just punishment of a people who had forsaken him.

Uncertain wording. “Facing away from the north” renders a compressed Hebrew phrase, literally “its face from the face of the north”. Translations differ over whether the pot is tilted away from the north or towards the south, or is tipping over from the northern side. The point is the same in every reading: the pot is about to spill, and its contents will pour from the north over Judah, as v. 14 explains.
verseByVerse.note: The kingdoms of the north turn out to be Babylon and its allies (25:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–19 — An Iron Pillar and Bronze Walls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God does not remove the opposition Jeremiah will face; he makes Jeremiah strong enough to stand in it. The prophet must get ready and speak everything he is commanded, for to fear the crowd more than God would break him (v. 17). God makes him a fortified city, an iron pillar and bronze walls against kings, officials, priests and people alike (v. 18). They will fight against him, but they will not prevail, because the LORD is with him to deliver him (v. 19). The chapter ends where the call began, with the promise of God’s presence (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not promise the prophet an easy audience; he promises to make him able to stand and to keep him through it.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, dress yourself for work; arise, and say to them everything that I command you. Do not be dismayed by them, lest I dismay you before them. And I, behold, I make you this day a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls, against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands Jeremiah to get ready and speak without flinching, and makes him strong enough to stand alone against every power in the land.

Dress yourself for work. Literally, gird up your loins: gather the long robe, tie it at the waist, get ready to move. It is the posture of a man about to run or to fight.

Lest I dismay you before them. A warning with a sting in it. Fear of the audience is not a small weakness to be indulged in a preacher; it is the thing that will break him in public. If he will not fear God more than the crowd, God will let the crowd frighten him. The cure for the fear of people is not courage summoned from inside but the fear of God, which crowds out every lesser fear, and it is God who gives it.

A fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls. Three images, all defensive and immovable. God does not remove the opposition; he lists exactly who it will be: the palace, the officials, the clergy and the public. Instead of removing them, he makes the man able to stand. Ezekiel received the same kind of hardening (Ezekiel 3:8–9). God gives what the calling requires, and he gives it to the person who has just said he cannot do it.

Strength for cowards. Every Christian who has kept quiet out of fear has a better word than a scolding. The one who never once flinched from the Father’s word went to the cross for cowards, and his Spirit makes the fearful bold.
verseByVerse.note: The same picture of readiness is used in Job 38:3 and 1 Peter 1:13.

verseByVerse.quote: They will fight against you, but they shall not prevail against you, for I am with you, declares the LORD, to deliver you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not promise that Jeremiah will escape attack, but that his enemies will never finally overcome him, because God is with him.

They shall not prevail against you. The chapter ends with its promise, worded with great care. God says plainly that they will fight him. What he promises is that they shall not prevail.

What the promise covers. Read Jeremiah’s life to see. He was put in the stocks, left to sink in a muddy cistern, imprisoned, accused of desertion, ignored by a king who burned his scroll, and finally carried off to Egypt. He was not protected from any of it. He was preserved through all of it, and the word he carried outlived every one of his opponents.

The same promise to the church. Jesus said of his church, “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18), and told his disciples, “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

Not delivered, so that we would be. There is one prophet to whom this promise was not kept in that form. Jeremiah wept over Jerusalem and was preserved; Christ wept over the same city (Luke 19:41) and was handed over to it. He had the words of God in his mouth as no prophet ever had, speaking only what his Father gave him (John 12:49), and when they fought against him he did not call for deliverance. He was the prophet Moses promised (Acts 3:22), and he was not delivered, so that we would be.

1.title: The Call of Jeremiah: I Am Watching Over My Word
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens the book. Before a single sermon we learn who Jeremiah was, how long he preached and how it ended (vv. 1–3), and then how God called him: the commission he will lean on when the whole nation turns against him.

The message. The word Jeremiah carries is God’s, not his, and God will see it done. God chose him before he was born, put his own words in his mouth and promised to stand with him; and God is awake over his word, so the judgment he announces will come, and so will the rebuilding he promises.

Why it was said. Jeremiah was called in Josiah’s reign, when reform was in the air, but he would preach for forty years to a nation that would not listen, and watch it fall to Babylon (see the introduction). He needed to know from the first day that both the message and its outcome were God’s business.

How the chapter makes its case. A heading sets the man in his times (vv. 1–3). Then the call: God formed, knew, consecrated and appointed him before birth (vv. 4–5). Jeremiah pleads his youth, and God answers with a command and a presence: “I am with you to deliver you” (vv. 6–8). God touches his mouth and sets him over nations, to tear down and to build (vv. 9–10). Two visions follow: an almond branch, for God is watching over his word (vv. 11–12), and a boiling pot tipped from the north, the invasion God will summon because his people have forsaken him (vv. 13–16). Last, God makes the prophet a fortified city: they will fight him, and not prevail (vv. 17–19).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ chiefly by pattern, and by the character of God. Jeremiah is a prophet with God’s words in his mouth, as Moses was promised (Deuteronomy 18:18), opposed on every side and preserved by God’s presence. In Christ the pattern is complete: he spoke only what the Father gave him (John 12:49), and the same city fought him. But Jeremiah was delivered, and Jesus was handed over, so that we would be delivered. And the God who watches over his word kept the greatest promise in this book, the new covenant (31:31–34), in Christ’s blood.

For us. Our worth and calling rest on God’s prior choice, not on our sense of being adequate. Every Christian has some unwelcome word to speak, and the cure for our fear is not a higher view of ourselves but a higher view of the God who goes with us. We are asked to be faithful; the God who watches over his word will see to the results.
1.theology:
God's call rests on his own prior choice, not on the one called (vv. 4-5; Ps 139:16; Gal 1:15), and he deals with the unborn as persons he knows and appoints. Fitness for service is not self-confidence but God's presence and God's words (vv. 6-9; Exod 4:11-12; Matt 28:20).

The word of God does demolishing work before it builds (v. 10; 2 Cor 10:4-5), and the building is promised (31:28). God watches over his word to perform it, so that neither warning nor promise falls to the ground (v. 12; Isa 55:11; Num 23:19).

God governs the nations that punish his people: the invader from the north is summoned by him (v. 15). Fear of man is the prophet's real danger, and the remedy is the fear of God (v. 17). God does not remove opposition but makes his servant able to stand and preserves him through it (vv. 18-19; Matt 16:18). The prophet greater than Jeremiah was not delivered from those who fought him (Acts 3:22; Luke 19:41), so that we would be.
1.examples: Jeremiah's forty years of faithful preaching, ending in national ruin, are a standing rebuke to judging a ministry by its results. And when a calling feels too large, God's answer to "I can't" is never "you are better than you think" but "I am with you".

keyVerse.quote: “Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you, declares the LORD.”
keyVerse.note: Jeremiah’s real problem is not his age or his speech but fear, and God answers it not with a better estimate of Jeremiah but with his own presence. The promise frames the chapter, returning as its last words (v. 19), and it carried Jeremiah through forty years of opposition. It is the same promise the risen Christ gives every church he sends: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

1.reflection:
God knew and appointed Jeremiah before he was born (v. 5). How does it change the way you see your own life, its worth and its purpose, that it rests on God’s choice rather than on what you achieve?

Jeremiah’s objections were honest: he was young and not a speaker (v. 6). God did not argue; he promised his presence (vv. 7–8). What reasons do you give for not speaking or serving where God has put you, and what difference does “I am with you” make to them?

God is “watching over my word to perform it” (v. 12). Which of God’s warnings or promises do you find hardest to believe he will actually keep? How do the cross and the resurrection settle the question?

God did not promise Jeremiah freedom from opposition, only that his enemies would not prevail (v. 19). How should that shape what we expect when we live and speak faithfully, and how does Jesus, who was not delivered from the cross, change the way we hold the promise?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Devotion of Your Youth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before a word of accusation, God remembers the love of Israel’s youth, and the memory makes their forgetting all the more terrible. He recalls how Israel followed him like a young bride into the wilderness and was holy to him, protected like the firstfruits of his harvest (vv. 1–3). Then he asks what wrong their fathers found in him to make them chase worthless gods and become worthless themselves (vv. 4–5). Nobody asked any more where the LORD was, though he had led them through the desert (v. 6). They defiled the good land he gave them, and every kind of leader, priest, teacher, ruler and prophet, failed together (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: The question of verse 5 is a lover's question as well as a judge's: what did I do, that you should leave me?

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me, saying, "Go and proclaim in the hearing of Jerusalem, Thus says the LORD, "I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed me in the wilderness, in a land not sown. Israel was holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of his harvest. All who ate of it incurred guilt; disaster came upon them, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God opens his case against Jerusalem not with an accusation but with a tender memory of Israel’s early love, when they followed him like a young bride and were his own, guarded by him.

Go and proclaim in the hearing of Jerusalem. The first sermon of the book does not open with a charge. It opens with a memory, and it is God’s memory.

I remember the devotion of your youth. He is thinking of the exodus and the wilderness years, and he describes them as a husband describes the early days of a marriage. There was a time when they followed him anywhere, into “a land not sown”, with no crops and no guarantees, simply because he was going that way. That is a remarkable thing for God to say of the wilderness generation, for Exodus and Numbers are full of their grumbling. He remembers the love and does not rehearse the complaints. Grace has a long memory for the good.

The firstfruits of his harvest. The firstfruits were the portion given to God and reserved for him alone; anyone else who ate them was guilty. That is what Israel was to him: set apart, his own, guarded by his jealousy, so that whoever touched them answered for it.

A husband’s memory. Hear the tone before a word of accusation. This is not a landlord evicting a tenant but a husband remembering a honeymoon, and it is about to become one of the saddest chapters in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, O house of Jacob, and all the clans of the house of Israel. Thus says the LORD: "What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me, and went after worthlessness, and became worthless? They did not say, 'Where is the LORD who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us in the wilderness, in a land of deserts and pits, in a land of drought and deep darkness, in a land that none passes through, where no man dwells?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God asks what fault their fathers ever found in him to justify leaving him, and the answer is none: they chased worthless things, became worthless, and simply stopped asking where he was.

All the clans of the house of Israel. Jeremiah stands in Jerusalem, but the summons goes to the whole house of Jacob, the northern tribes included, a century after Assyria scattered them. The whole family was in the wilderness, and the whole family is called to answer.

What wrong did your fathers find in me? The question at the heart of the chapter, and God is the one asking it. Not, what did you gain by leaving, but what fault did you find? He invites them to produce the grievance that justified it. There is none.

Went after worthlessness, and became worthless. The word is the same on both sides: you become what you worship. “Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8). Paul says the same of the human race: they “exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images”, and “their foolish hearts were darkened” (Romans 1:21–23). Worship is never neutral. Whatever you give yourself to is shaping you into its likeness now.

Where is the LORD? The failure was not a decision to reject God but a question they stopped asking. The rescue was still in the history books and had gone out of the conversation. That is how faith is usually lost: not in a crisis of belief, but in a slow silence.

A land of deserts and pits. And see what they had stopped remembering: not a pleasant journey but deserts, pits, drought and deep darkness. Moses had told the same people to remember the God “who brought you water out of the flinty rock” (Deuteronomy 8:15). The worse the road had been, the more there was to be grateful for, and the more complete the forgetting.

verseByVerse.quote: And I brought you into a plentiful land to enjoy its fruits and its good things. But when you came in, you defiled my land and made my heritage an abomination. The priests did not say, 'Where is the LORD?' Those who handle the law did not know me; the shepherds transgressed against me; the prophets prophesied by Baal and went after things that do not profit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave his people a rich land, and they used his gift to forget him, while the very leaders meant to keep them near God led the way out.

I brought you into a plentiful land. God gave them “a land in which you will eat bread without scarcity” (Deuteronomy 8:9), and the gift became the occasion of the forgetting. Prosperity is often harder on faith than poverty, because it removes the daily sense of need.

You defiled my land. The possessives matter: my land, my heritage. God gave them the land and never stopped owning it. What they defiled was not their property but his inheritance. Everything a believer has is held on the same terms.

Four failed leaders. Every group has failed. The priests never asked where God was. The scholars who handle the law did not know its author. The shepherds (the ESV notes the word may be rendered “rulers”) broke the covenant themselves. And the prophets preached another god entirely. When a nation collapses spiritually, it is rarely the people who fall first.

Those who handle the law did not know me. The first failures are failures of knowing. It is entirely possible to handle Scripture professionally, every day, and not know the God who wrote it. The question for anyone who teaches is not how much of the text he has mastered, but whether he still asks where the LORD is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Leaving God is not only wicked but senseless, and the ruin it brings is self-inflicted. No pagan nation trades in its gods, yet Israel has exchanged the living God, its glory, for what cannot help (vv. 9–11). So heaven is called to be appalled at two evils: forsaking the fountain of living waters, and digging broken cisterns that hold no water (vv. 12–13). Israel, God’s son, has become prey; the lions have roared, the land is waste and Egypt has shamed them, and they brought it on themselves by forsaking the God who led them (vv. 14–17). Running to the Nile or the Euphrates for protection will not mend it, because the real lack is the fear of God (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin is never only a rule broken. It is a greater good abandoned for a lesser one, and heaven itself is summoned to be appalled at the exchange.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I still contend with you, declares the LORD, and with your children's children I will contend. For cross to the coasts of Cyprus and see, or send to Kedar and examine with care; see if there has been such a thing. Has a nation changed its gods, even though they are no gods? But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No nation abandons its gods, even false ones, yet Israel has traded the living God, its true glory, for what is worthless, and God, still pleading, takes them to court.

I still contend with you. God brings a lawsuit, and it runs across generations: “with your children’s children I will contend”. A God who is still contending three generations on has not given up on the defendants.

Cross to the coasts of Cyprus and see. The case rests on a survey. Send west to Cyprus, send east to Kedar in the Arabian desert, and ask a simple question: does anyone do this?

Has a nation changed its gods? The survey is almost comic: other nations keep faith with deities that do not exist, while Israel breaks faith with the one who does. Israel traded its glory, the living God himself, its honour and its boast, for something that “does not profit”. It is not only wicked; it is a spectacularly bad deal.

The civilisation that changed its gods. Verse 11 has a modern ring. The modern West may be the first civilisation in history to walk away from the God who shaped it. Many see that as a coming of age; Jeremiah would ask what we exchanged him for. A culture does not stop worshipping when it stops believing; it moves its devotion elsewhere, and what we have made ultimate are mostly good gifts asked to do a god’s work: the self, success, the nation or the cause, romance, health and youth. They have simply been asked to carry a weight they cannot hold, which is why verse 13 calls them broken cisterns. Yet God has not given up on the defendants; he will contend with their children’s children (v. 9). The God the West has walked away from is still pleading with it, and Christ is still the fountain at the end of the empty road.

verseByVerse.quote: Be appalled, O heavens, at this; be shocked, be utterly desolate, declares the LORD, for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin is two evils at once: leaving God, the free and endless spring of life, and toiling to make substitutes that cannot hold what they promise.

Be appalled, O heavens, at this. Heaven is called as witness and told to be horrified. Sin has become so normal on earth that the proper horror has to come from heaven.

The fountain of living waters. The first evil is leaving. God is a spring: moving, fresh, free, endlessly replenished, asking nothing but a cupped hand. In a hot country that is not poetry; it is life.

Broken cisterns that can hold no water. The second is the substitute. A cistern is a pit cut out of rock to hold rainwater. Cutting one is months of brutal labour, and the water it holds is still and stale at best. These are broken cisterns, cracked, so that the digger is left with a dry hole he spent his strength on.

Never be thirsty again. Jesus stood in the temple and answered this verse directly: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37), and he meant the Spirit whom believers were to receive. To a woman drawing water he said, “whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again” (John 4:14). At the end of the Bible the offer still stands: “To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment” (Revelation 21:6). The fountain is free; only the cisterns cost.

In everyday life. That is the pattern of every sin: a real spring abandoned, and enormous effort spent on a leaking substitute. Nobody works harder than someone trying to get from a career, a relationship, a bottle or an image what only God gives. And the cistern always leaks, which is why it must be dug again next year.
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew usage “living water” is running water from a spring, as opposed to water stored in a tank.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is Israel a slave? Is he a homeborn servant? Why then has he become a prey? The lions have roared against him; they have roared loudly. They have made his land a waste; his cities are in ruins, without inhabitant. Moreover, the men of Memphis and Tahpanhes have shaved the crown of your head. Have you not brought this upon yourself by forsaking the LORD your God, when he led you in the way?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel, God’s own son, has become plunder for the nations, and the ruin is not bad luck: they brought it on themselves by letting go of the God who was leading them.

Is Israel a slave? Israel was God’s son, not anyone’s slave, so why is he being carried off like plunder? The lions are the empires, and their roaring has already begun: towns burned, fields wasted, villages emptied.

The men of Memphis and Tahpanhes. Memphis and Tahpanhes are Egyptian cities, and the shaved crown is the mark of a slave or a mourner. The allies Judah courted have treated her shamefully. Jeremiah’s hearers would probably think of 609 BC, when Pharaoh Neco killed Josiah at Megiddo, deposed his son and put Judah under tribute (2 Kings 23:29–35).

Have you not brought this upon yourself? Verse 17 refuses every comfortable explanation: not the empires, not bad luck, not God’s neglect. They brought it on themselves by forsaking the LORD. Not every sorrow is of this kind, and Scripture never says it is; but there is a kind of pain that is simply our own choices coming back on us, and this was it.

When he led you in the way. The last clause makes it worse. They were not lost when they left. They were being led, as a father leads a small child, and they let go of his hand. Moses had described that wilderness care: “the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went” (Deuteronomy 1:31).

Uncertain wording. “Have shaved” is, as the ESV notes, literally “have grazed”. The Hebrew may picture Egypt grazing Judah bare like a pasture, or it may be a word for breaking, so that the men of Egypt have cracked the skull. Either way the picture is of humiliation at the hands of the power Judah trusted.

verseByVerse.quote: And now what do you gain by going to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile? Or what do you gain by going to Assyria to drink the waters of the Euphrates? Your evil will chastise you, and your apostasy will reprove you. Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to forsake the LORD your God; the fear of me is not in you, declares the Lord GOD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Running to Egypt or Assyria for protection is just another broken cistern; the sin will bring its own punishment, because at the root the people have lost the fear of God.

To drink the waters of the Nile. The water image returns, now as foreign policy. Judah’s politics swung between the two superpowers, drinking first from the Nile and then from the Euphrates, buying protection with tribute and treaties. Every generation has its version: the fear that God is not enough, and the search for a stronger friend.

Your evil will chastise you. God does not need to invent a punishment; the sin brings its own. The psalm shows God doing this as a judgment: “So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels” (Psalm 81:12). Sometimes the severest thing God does is let a person have what he insisted on.

The fear of me is not in you. The verse ends at the root of it all, and every other failure in the chapter grows out of that absence. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7), and a people without it will run to Egypt and Assyria because they are more afraid of the empires than of him. What a person fears most is what he ends up obeying.
verseByVerse.note: The Nile is “Shihor” and the Euphrates “the River” in Hebrew (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — The Choice Vine Gone Wild
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s unfaithfulness is not a lapse but a deep stain, a compulsion and a lie, and only God can deal with it. Freed from slavery, they refused to serve him and bowed to idols on every high hill (v. 20). God planted them a choice vine, and it grew wild (v. 21); no lye or soap can wash out the stain of their guilt (v. 22). They deny it, yet they chase other gods like a camel bolting or a wild donkey in heat, and say it is hopeless to stop (vv. 23–25). Like a thief caught in the act they will be shamed, calling a tree their father and crying to God only when trouble comes (vv. 26–28).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry is both a slavery that cannot be broken by willpower and a stain that cannot be scrubbed out.

verseByVerse.quote: "For long ago I broke your yoke and burst your bonds; but you said, 'I will not serve.' Yes, on every high hill and under every green tree you bowed down like a whore. Yet I planted you a choice vine, wholly of pure seed. How then have you turned degenerate and become a wild vine? Though you wash yourself with lye and use much soap, the stain of your guilt is still before me, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people God freed refused to serve him and bowed to idols instead, his choice vine grew wild, and their guilt is a stain no human scrubbing can remove.

I will not serve. God broke the yoke in Egypt, and the freed slave answered, I will not serve: not him, at least. Then he bowed anyway, on every hill and under every tree, to whatever local shrine was at hand. Nobody serves nothing. The yoke thrown off is always replaced.

I planted you a choice vine. The gardener chose the best stock and planted it himself, and what came up was wild (compare Isaiah 5:1–7). The fault cannot be traced to the seed or the gardener. Jesus would one day say, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1): where Israel failed, he bore the fruit God looked for, and those joined to him bear it too.

Though you wash yourself with lye. Now the image changes to laundry, and it settles the question of self-improvement. Lye and soap were the strongest cleaners available. Scrub as hard as you like: “the stain of your guilt is still before me”. The stain is before him, and that is the problem: what matters is not whether we feel clean but what God sees.

The one open door. This verse leaves only one door open, and the New Testament opens it: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). The stain no effort removes is removed by confession and the blood of Christ, and by nothing else.

Uncertain wording. The opening words can be read two ways. The ESV takes them as God speaking of what he did: “I broke your yoke and burst your bonds” in the exodus. The same Hebrew can also be read as an old form meaning “you broke your yoke”, Israel throwing off God’s rule, and several translations follow that. Either way the next words are Israel’s refusal to serve.

Textual note. The King James Version reads “I will not transgress” here. The Hebrew words for “serve” and “transgress” differ by one similar-looking letter, and the scribes’ marginal reading gave “transgress”; most modern translations, with the Greek Old Testament, read “I will not serve”. Either way, the people’s words were contradicted on every hill.

verseByVerse.quote: How can you say, 'I am not unclean, I have not gone after the Baals'? Look at your way in the valley; know what you have done— a restless young camel running here and there, a wild donkey used to the wilderness, in her heat sniffing the wind! Who can restrain her lust? None who seek her need weary themselves; in her month they will find her. Keep your feet from going unshod and your throat from thirst. But you said, 'It is hopeless, for I have loved foreigners, and after them I will go.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah denies serving other gods, but its conduct shows a compulsive craving it cannot control, and its answer to God’s plea is despair: it is hopeless, I cannot stop.

Look at your way in the valley. The denial is answered with evidence. The valley is most likely the Valley of Hinnom below Jerusalem, where children were burned to Molech (7:31). Do not tell me what you believe; look at what you have done.

A restless young camel running here and there. The images are deliberately undignified: a young camel bolting in every direction, a wild donkey in heat that nobody needs to chase, because she comes to them. Idolatry is not sophisticated. It is compulsive.

Who can restrain her lust? The chapter is honest about addiction. The question expects the answer nobody, certainly not the animal herself. Anyone who has tried to break a habit by willpower alone knows the verse from the inside. The God who broke the yoke in Egypt (v. 20) is the one who breaks this one too, by his Spirit, his word and the help of his people.

It is hopeless. God pleads with them to stop wearing out their shoes and their throats chasing what will not feed them. The reply is the saddest line in the chapter: not defiance but despair. I am too far gone; this is who I am now. Many people are held in something they hate by exactly that sentence, and it is a lie, because the God who is still pleading in this verse has not called it hopeless.

verseByVerse.quote: "As a thief is shamed when caught, so the house of Israel shall be shamed: they, their kings, their officials, their priests, and their prophets, who say to a tree, 'You are my father,' and to a stone, 'You gave me birth.' For they have turned their back to me, and not their face. But in the time of their trouble they say, 'Arise and save us!' But where are your gods that you made for yourself? Let them arise, if they can save you, in your time of trouble; for as many as your cities are your gods, O Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah will be shamed like a thief caught in the act, for it treats its idols as its makers in good times and turns to the God it has ignored only when trouble comes.

As a thief is shamed when caught. A thief’s shame is not remorse for stealing but the shame of being caught. That is the shame coming to Judah, and the list runs from the palace down, much as in verse 8: the failure runs through the whole society.

Religion in good times and bad. Two sentences that between them describe most religion. In good times they say to a tree, “You are my father,” and to a stone, “You gave me birth”: they treat what they have made as if it had made them. In bad times they cry, “Arise and save us!” to the God on whom they have turned their backs.

They have turned their back to me, and not their face. God notices the posture. A wandering child still faces his father; a settled rebel has turned his back. It also shows what repentance is: turning round is all that is required, and it is the one thing they will not do.

Where are your gods that you made for yourself? Call them, God says; see if they stand up. Isaiah put it the same way: “Who fashions a god or casts an idol that is profitable for nothing?” (Isaiah 44:10). There was a god for every town, and not one of them able to move.

In everyday life. The test still works. When the diagnosis comes, or the job goes, or the marriage cracks, you find out very quickly which of the things you serve can stand up and help, and that the God you had turned your back on is still the one who can.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people have forgotten him and refuse to admit any wrong, and that refusal is what he will judge. His discipline taught them nothing, and they killed the prophets he sent (vv. 29–30). He asks whether he has been a barren wilderness to them, that they should call distance from him freedom; a bride never forgets her wedding dress, yet his people have forgotten him days without number (vv. 31–32). Skilled at chasing other loves, with the blood of the innocent poor on their clothes, they still say, “I am innocent” (vv. 33–35). Their restless search for allies will end in shame, for God has rejected every refuge they trust (vv. 36–37).
verseByVerse.theology: The final defence of a guilty people is not argument but denial, and God answers it by bringing them to judgment for the denial itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you contend with me? You have all transgressed against me, declares the LORD. In vain have I struck your children; they took no correction; your own sword devoured your prophets like a ravening lion. And you, O generation, behold the word of the LORD. Have I been a wilderness to Israel, or a land of thick darkness? Why then do my people say, 'We are free, we will come no more to you'? Can a virgin forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? Yet my people have forgotten me days without number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah has ignored God’s discipline and killed his messengers, treats distance from him as freedom, and has forgotten him as no bride would forget her wedding dress.

Why do you contend with me? They are arguing with him, and he asks why. Then two sentences of terrible summary: the discipline achieved nothing, and the messengers sent to explain it were killed. A nation that will neither feel a warning nor hear an explanation has closed both doors.

Have I been a wilderness to Israel? The question of verse 5 returns, sharper. Have I been barren ground to you, the dark place you had to escape? God asks to be shown the evidence for the way he is being treated.

We are free, we will come no more to you. The oldest lie about God: freedom defined as distance from him. It is what the serpent suggested in Eden, and what every generation repeats.

Can a virgin forget her ornaments? A bride does not forget her wedding dress; it is the most precious thing she owns and the day is the biggest of her life. Yet God’s people have forgotten him “days without number”. The charge is not atheism but forgetting, and forgetting does not feel like rebellion. It feels like being busy. God measures it in days: how many have gone by with no thought of him at all?

The Bridegroom who does not forget. Paul uses the same marriage language of the church: he had betrothed the Corinthians to one husband, Christ, and feared they would be led astray (2 Corinthians 11:2–3). The bride who forgot is answered by a Bridegroom who does not forget, who “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). His faithfulness, not hers, holds the marriage.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “we are free” is rare. It probably means to roam at will, like an animal off its tether; older versions guessed “we are lords”. Either way the people are claiming independence from God.

verseByVerse.quote: "How well you direct your course to seek love! So that even to wicked women you have taught your ways. Also on your skirts is found the lifeblood of the guiltless poor; you did not find them breaking in. Yet in spite of all these things you say, 'I am innocent; surely his anger has turned from me.' Behold, I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah is expert at chasing other loves and has the blood of innocent poor people on its clothes, yet it insists it is innocent, and that denial is exactly what God will judge.

How well you direct your course to seek love! Two charges together, and their pairing is the point. They have become so expert at pursuing love in all the wrong places that even wicked women could learn from them, and there is blood on their clothes: the lifeblood of the guiltless poor, people who had done nothing. Idolatry and injustice arrive together, always. A people who will worship anything will eventually sacrifice anyone. The prophets never separate the two, and neither should we.

You did not find them breaking in. Legal language. The law allowed a householder to strike a burglar caught at night: “If a thief is found breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no bloodguilt for him” (Exodus 22:2). The poor who were killed were no burglars, so there was no such excuse for their deaths. They were simply in the way.

I am innocent. With blood on the hem, the claim is innocence, and God names what he will judge: not only the sin, but the denial of it.

The one obstacle. That is a sobering line, and also a hopeful one. The one thing standing between this people and mercy is the sentence they keep repeating. The next chapter shows God pleading for one word of acknowledgement (3:13), the same word the New Testament asks for (1 John 1:8–9). Insisting that we are innocent is the one attitude in which forgiveness cannot be received.

verseByVerse.quote: How much you go about, changing your way! You shall be put to shame by Egypt as you were put to shame by Assyria. From it too you will come away with your hands on your head, for the LORD has rejected those in whom you trust, and you will not prosper by them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s restless search for powerful allies will end in humiliation, because God has rejected every refuge it trusts in place of him.

How much you go about, changing your way! The chapter ends with restless diplomacy: first Assyria, now Egypt, always looking for a better arrangement. Assyria’s shaming lay a century back: King Ahaz had paid the Assyrian king for help, and he “afflicted him instead of strengthening him” (2 Chronicles 28:20).

With your hands on your head. The posture of prisoners and mourners, and the gesture Tamar made when she walked out disgraced (2 Samuel 13:19). A nation that had courted every available power would end with the same gesture: used, and sent away.

The LORD has rejected those in whom you trust. The reason comes last, and it is final. Every refuge that is not God is a refuge God has already rejected. Better to learn that before the crisis than during it.

Looking back on the chapter. Judah kept switching allies because none satisfied: the cistern of verse 13 again, dug in a new place each time. The only fixed point in the chapter is the one they left: the God who remembered the devotion of their youth and was still contending for them.

2.title: Two Evils: The Fountain and the Broken Cisterns
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 called the prophet; chapter 2 is the first sermon he was sent to preach in Jerusalem, and it opens the case against Judah that runs to chapter 25. It is probably among his earliest preaching, from Josiah’s reign.

The message. God is the fountain of living water, and his people have left him to dig cracked tanks that hold nothing. He loved them like a young bride and did them no wrong; they forgot him, ran after gods and allies who could not help, and now insist they are innocent.

Why it was said. Judah looked religious, but the nation’s heart had wandered: shrines on every hill, leaders who did not know God, and a foreign policy swinging between Egypt and Assyria (see the introduction). The people did not think of themselves as apostates at all.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with a memory of Israel’s first love (vv. 1–3), then asks what wrong their fathers found in God, who led them, gave them a land and was forgotten by every leader (vv. 4–8). No nation changes its gods, but Israel has exchanged its glory, and heaven is called to be appalled at the two evils of the forsaken fountain and the broken cisterns (vv. 9–13). The ruin they suffer is self-inflicted, and Egypt and Assyria will not mend it (vv. 14–19). Then a run of images: a freed slave bowing to idols, a vine gone wild, a stain no soap removes, an animal in heat, a thief caught (vv. 20–28). The chapter ends with a bride who has forgotten her husband and a people with blood on their clothes protesting, “I am innocent” (vv. 29–37).

Where it leads. Chiefly by God’s character revealed in Christ, and by the need it exposes. The God who calls himself “the fountain of living waters” (v. 13) stood in the temple and said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). The stain that no lye or soap can remove (v. 22) is washed away only by his blood (1 John 1:7). And the husband forgotten by his bride is answered by the Bridegroom who “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25).

For us. Ask what you are digging: what you are asking a career, a relationship, money or an image to give you that only God gives. The fountain is free and the cisterns are hard work. And the one sentence that keeps a sinner from mercy is “I have not sinned” (v. 35); the way back is to stop saying it and come to Christ to drink.
2.theology:
Sin is defined here in two steps: forsaking God, the fountain of living waters, and constructing substitutes that cannot hold what they promise (v. 13). Christ answers the first half by offering living water freely (John 4:14; 7:37; Rev 21:6).

Worship shapes the worshipper: those who go after worthlessness become worthless (v. 5; Ps 115:8; Rom 1:21-23). Prosperity and forgetfulness, not argument, are how faith is usually lost (vv. 6-7, 32). Leaders fail first (vv. 8, 26).

Sin carries its own punishment (v. 19; Ps 81:12), cannot be washed out by self-improvement (v. 22; 1 John 1:9), and is most dangerous when denied: God judges the claim I have not sinned (v. 35). Idolatry and injustice always travel together (vv. 33-34).
2.examples: The chapter's pictures stay with a reader because they are ordinary: a husband remembering a honeymoon, a man cutting a tank in rock beside a free spring, lye and soap on a stain that is before God and not before us, a bride who could never forget her dress. Each says the same thing from a different side: the fault was never in the God they left, and he is still calling them back.

keyVerse.quote: for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water.
keyVerse.note: This is one of the clearest definitions of sin in Scripture, and the rest of the chapter illustrates it. Sin is two evils, not one: leaving the God who gives life freely, and working hard at substitutes that cannot hold what they promise. Jesus answers it directly, offering himself as the spring of living water to anyone who is thirsty (John 4:14; 7:37).

2.reflection:
God begins not with an accusation but with a memory of Israel’s first love (vv. 2–3). What does it tell you about God that he remembers the devotion of his people and passes over their grumbling? Where has your own first love for him cooled?

“What wrong did your fathers find in me?” (v. 5). If you have drifted from God, what reason would you actually give? How does the cross answer the suspicion that God has held out on us?

Verse 13 contrasts a free spring with broken cisterns that take enormous effort to dig. What cisterns are people around you digging, and which one are you most tempted by? What would it look like to drink from Christ instead this week?

The people say both “It is hopeless” (v. 25) and “I am innocent” (v. 35). Why are despair and self-justification both ways of avoiding God? Which comes more naturally to you, and how does the gospel answer it?
