For we have sinned against the LORD our God, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day, and we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Would You Return to Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God invites his unfaithful people back, even though his own law said the door was shut, but their warm words cannot hide what they are doing. Under the law a divorced wife who had married another could never return to her first husband, yet God asks Judah, after many lovers, whether she will return to him (v. 1). Her shrines are on every bare height; the rains have been withheld, yet she has lost the ability to blush (vv. 2–3). She calls God “My father” and assumes he cannot stay angry for ever, while doing all the evil she can (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: Affectionate words to God alongside unchanged behaviour are not repentance; and yet the impossible invitation to return is the one God makes.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man divorces his wife and she goes from him and becomes another man's wife, will he return to her? Would not that land be greatly polluted? You have played the whore with many lovers; and would you return to me? declares the LORD. Lift up your eyes to the bare heights, and see! Where have you not been ravished? By the waysides you have sat awaiting lovers like an Arab in the wilderness. You have polluted the land with your vile whoredom. Therefore the showers have been withheld, and the spring rain has not come; yet you have the forehead of a whore; you refuse to be ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though God’s own law said an unfaithful wife could never return to her first husband, God invites his adulterous people back, even while they are so hardened in sin that they have forgotten how to blush.

Will he return to her? The chapter opens with a point of law. Under Deuteronomy a man who divorced his wife could not take her back once she had married someone else: “her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after she has been defiled, for that is an abomination before the LORD” (Deuteronomy 24:4). The door is shut by God’s own statute.

And would you return to me? Then, in the same breath, God asks the astonishing question, and everything else in the chapter stands under it. What the law forbids, love offers. God does not pretend the marriage was undamaged or the adultery small (“many lovers” is his own phrase), and still he opens a door the law had bolted. How he can do this without ceasing to be just is the question the whole Bible answers at the cross, where the bridegroom bore the guilt of his unfaithful bride.

Where have you not been ravished? The invitation does not pretend to forget: every hilltop has a shrine, and she has been at all of them. “Like an Arab in the wilderness” pictures a desert raider crouched beside a caravan route, watching the road for whoever comes along. Israel is not a victim ambushed by temptation but the one lying in wait for it.

Therefore the showers have been withheld. The drought was a message, and it was missed. Moses had warned that turning to other gods would make the LORD “shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain” (Deuteronomy 11:16–17). The irony was sharp: Baal was worshipped in Canaan as the god of storm and rain, and it was the LORD who held the showers back.

You have the forehead of a whore. A face that has lost the capacity to blush. Shame is painful, and it is a mercy; a conscience that can still be embarrassed is still alive. The danger point in any life is not doing wrong but reaching the stage of doing it without a flicker of shame.

What it does not mean. The chapter uses divorce law as a picture of God and his people; it is not teaching about when Christians may divorce or remarry, which the New Testament addresses directly (Matthew 19:3–9; 1 Corinthians 7). And it puts God in the place of the wronged husband who still pleads for reconciliation, never the one who walks away.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you not just now called to me, 'My father, you are the friend of my youth— will he be angry forever, will he be indignant to the end?' Behold, you have spoken, but you have done all the evil that you could."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah speaks to God in warm, devout words while doing every evil it can, and fine religious language is no substitute for repentance.

Behold, you have spoken. “My father, you are the friend of my youth”: warm, intimate, theologically correct, and quite compatible with having “done all the evil that you could”. Religious language is not repentance. It is possible to call God Father in one breath and keep every arrangement he hates in the next, and this verse exists to stop us doing it comfortably.

Will he be angry forever? The theology inside their question is true: “He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever” (Psalm 103:9). But they use it as a licence to go on sinning. God will say almost those words himself, “I will not be angry forever” (v. 12), to people who return. The same truth is comfort to the penitent and presumption in the mouth of someone who has done all the evil he could.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Faithless Israel and Treacherous Judah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah has watched what happened to unfaithful Israel and learned nothing, so the call to return goes first to the exiles in the north. In Josiah’s days God points to two sisters: Israel, who played the harlot on every hill and was sent away with a decree of divorce, and Judah, who saw it all and did the same without fear (vv. 6–8). Judah took her sin lightly and came back to God only in pretence, for all the reform of those years (vv. 9–10). So exiled Israel is the more righteous, and Jeremiah must call northward: return, for I am merciful; only acknowledge your guilt (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Watching judgment fall on someone else and learning nothing is worse than the sin that brought it; and the way back is one honest admission.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to me in the days of King Josiah: "Have you seen what she did, that faithless one, Israel, how she went up on every high hill and under every green tree, and there played the whore? And I thought, 'After she has done all this she will return to me,' but she did not return, and her treacherous sister Judah saw it. She saw that for all the adulteries of that faithless one, Israel, I had sent her away with a decree of divorce. Yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but she too went and played the whore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah watched God send her sister Israel into exile for unfaithfulness, and instead of taking warning she went and did exactly the same.

Have you seen what she did? Two sisters. Israel is the northern kingdom, destroyed by Assyria a century before Jeremiah preached; Judah is the southern kingdom, still standing, listening to this sermon.

After she has done all this she will return to me. The language of a patient husband waiting at the window, and it is how God describes his own long-suffering. And “her treacherous sister Judah saw it”: Judah had a front-row seat at her sister’s funeral.

Yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear. She watched the deportations, the ruined towns, the end of a nation, and drew no conclusion at all. There is no education in watching judgment fall on someone else if you have decided in advance that it cannot happen to you.

A decree of divorce. The legal image of verse 1 made concrete. Isaiah uses it of Zion’s own exile, asking, “Where is your mother’s certificate of divorce, with which I sent her away?”, and answering, “for your transgressions your mother was sent away” (Isaiah 50:1). The exile of the north was not God abandoning a faithful wife; it was the consequence of a marriage she had already left.

verseByVerse.quote: Because she took her whoredom lightly, she polluted the land, committing adultery with stone and tree. Yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in pretense, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s return to God under Josiah’s reform was outward only, a pretence, because she never took her sin seriously and her heart never came back.

She took her whoredom lightly. That is how nations and people fall: not by deciding sin is good, but by deciding it is small.

In pretense. This is said in the days of King Josiah, during the great national reform: the idols were smashed, the temple repaired, the Passover kept. It was genuine at the top, and it never reached the heart of the people. A reformation of behaviour without a change of heart is what God calls pretence, and he can tell the difference.

Not with her whole heart. Isaiah describes the same condition: “this people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me” (Isaiah 29:13). This book will later promise the cure God himself supplies: “I will give them a heart to know me”, so that “they shall return to me with their whole heart” (24:7). What Judah could not produce under Josiah, God undertakes to give.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, "Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah. Go, and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, "'Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful, declares the LORD; I will not be angry forever. Only acknowledge your guilt, that you rebelled against the LORD your God and scattered your favors among foreigners under every green tree, and that you have not obeyed my voice, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah, with all her privileges, is more guilty than exiled Israel, yet God sends Jeremiah to call even the scattered north home, asking only that they honestly admit their guilt.

More righteous than treacherous Judah. A shocking verdict. Israel sinned with no warning example in front of her; Judah sinned having watched the consequences, while holding the temple, the law, the priesthood and the promises. The more light, the greater the guilt.

Proclaim these words toward the north. Jeremiah is told to face north, towards a people scattered into Assyria a hundred years before, a lost cause by every reckoning, and preach to them. The reasons given are all about God: “I am merciful”, “I will not be angry forever”. The ground of the invitation is his character, which is the only ground any of us has.

Only acknowledge your guilt. That is the whole requirement. Not restitution first, not cleaning yourself up, not a period of good behaviour to prove you mean it. Say what is true; that is the door. Joel says, “return to me with all your heart”, and “rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2:12–13). Hosea gives the words to use: “Take with you words and return to the LORD” (Hosea 14:2). And John says it to the church: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

How do I acknowledge my guilt? It is simpler than we fear and harder than we like. Be specific. Not “I haven’t been great lately”, but the thing itself: I lied to my manager about the report; I have been cold to my wife for a week. Vague confessions keep the sin and shed only the discomfort. Say it to God without excuses. Leave out the “but” that explains why it was not really your fault. David found relief at exactly that point: “I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity” (Psalm 32:5). Tell the person you wronged. Where someone else was hurt, go to them, say what you did, and put right what can be put right. Tell a trusted Christian friend when a sin keeps returning: “confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16). Then believe the pardon. Do not keep confessing the same forgiven sin as if God had not heard. You come not to an accuser but to a Father, and “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — Shepherds After My Own Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises a homecoming far greater than a return to the old ways: a gathered remnant, true shepherds, and a people united around his presence. He calls his faithless children back because he is still their master, and he will gather them one from a city and two from a family (v. 14). He will give them shepherds after his own heart, who feed them with knowledge (v. 15). The ark of the covenant will not even be missed, because the whole city will be the LORD’s throne, all nations will gather to his presence, and hearts will no longer follow their own evil way (vv. 16–17). Judah and Israel will come home together (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The restoration is small in its beginnings, pastoral in its care, and larger than Israel at its end.

verseByVerse.quote: Return, O faithless children, declares the LORD; for I am your master; I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you to Zion. "'And I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls his faithless people back because they still belong to him, and promises to gather a remnant one by one and to give them shepherds who will feed them with true knowledge.

For I am your master. The ground of the call is a claim. The Hebrew word can also mean “husband”, as the King James Version takes it (“I am married unto you”), and it shares its root with the name Baal, “lord” or “owner”: the LORD claims the title the idol had usurped. They had left, but they had not stopped being his. Their unfaithfulness did not cancel his right to them, and it is that right, not their merit, that lets him call them back.

One from a city and two from a family. The promise is deliberately modest. God is not predicting a national landslide but a remnant, gathered person by person out of places that will not come as a whole. Revival is talked about in national terms; it usually arrives one and two at a time, and God calls that homecoming.

Shepherds after my own heart. Chapter 2 exposed shepherds who “transgressed against me” (2:8). Here is the remedy: not better management but men whose hearts match God’s, and whose work is feeding. The phrase echoes what God said of David, “a man after my heart, who will do all my will” (Acts 13:22). The risen Christ still gives “the shepherds and teachers” to his church (Ephesians 4:11), and behind every faithful one stands the good shepherd himself (John 10:11).

Where Christians differ: how is this return fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. Dispensationalists look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel; they do so out of reverence for God’s promises. This commentary’s view: the promises reach beyond any return to territory, to a new heart, a Davidic King and the nations gathered. They are fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Romans 11:26), and they will be complete in the new creation. This follows the apostles, who read such promises as gathered up in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20; Acts 15:14–17).

verseByVerse.quote: And when you have multiplied and been fruitful in the land, in those days, declares the LORD, they shall no more say, "The ark of the covenant of the LORD." It shall not come to mind or be remembered or missed; it shall not be made again. At that time Jerusalem shall be called the throne of the LORD, and all nations shall gather to it, to the presence of the LORD in Jerusalem, and they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart. In those days the house of Judah shall join the house of Israel, and together they shall come from the land of the north to the land that I gave your fathers for a heritage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day is coming when even the ark will not be missed, because God’s presence will fill his city, the nations will gather to him, and his people’s hearts will be changed.

The ark of the covenant of the LORD. The most sacred object in Israel’s worship, the throne of God’s presence in the holy of holies, will simply not be needed. That is not a downgrade but a promotion. A sign becomes unnecessary when the thing it signified has arrived in person. The ark itself drops out of the record; it was probably lost when Babylon burned the temple in 586 BC, and the temple rebuilt after the exile stood without it.

The throne of the LORD. The whole city becomes the throne room, not one gold box inside one room. All nations gather, not Israel alone. And the heart itself changes: “they shall no more stubbornly follow their own evil heart”, which is what chapter 31 will call the new covenant. The divided kingdoms come home together, the family reunited.

All nations shall gather to it. Isaiah saw the same gathering: “all the nations shall flow to it”, saying, “come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD” (Isaiah 2:2–3). The Word who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14) is the presence the ark only marked, and the last pages of the Bible complete the thought. John sees the holy city and reports, “I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). The box that once marked God’s throne is not missed, because God himself is present without one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — I Will Heal Your Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God grieves over the children he longed to bless, and he promises to heal the faithlessness that took them away. He had hoped to give them the best of lands and hear them call him Father, but they left him like a treacherous wife (vv. 19–20). Now weeping is heard on the same bare heights where they sinned, as they realise they have forgotten the LORD (v. 21). God calls again, “I will heal your faithlessness,” and the people answer: the hills were a delusion, and salvation is in the LORD alone (vv. 22–23). They confess what idolatry has cost them and lie down in their shame, owning the sin of generations (vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.theology: God heals faithlessness rather than merely forgiving it, and the confession that follows is the fruit of that healing, not a way of earning it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I said, How I would set you among my sons, and give you a pleasant land, a heritage most beautiful of all nations. And I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me. Surely, as a treacherous wife leaves her husband, so have you been treacherous to me, O house of Israel, declares the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells of his longing to treat Israel as his own children and hear them call him Father, and of the grief of being left like a husband betrayed.

How I would set you among my sons. God speaking about his own hopes, and it is almost unbearable to read. He wanted to treat them as children, to give them the best land there was, to hear them call him Father.

A grieving God. Scripture is not embarrassed to show God like this. “How can I give you up, O Ephraim?” he says through Hosea; “My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender” (Hosea 11:8). Whatever else the judgment in this book is, it is not the cold act of a God who never wanted anything else. And the longing to be called Father is finally answered in Christ, through whom God sends “the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Galatians 4:6).

As a treacherous wife leaves her husband. The marriage picture again: not a tenant breaking a lease, but a wife walking out. The offence is measured by the intimacy it violated, which is why sin against God is never merely rule-breaking.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice on the bare heights is heard, the weeping and pleading of Israel's sons because they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God. "Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness." "Behold, we come to you, for you are the LORD our God. Truly the hills are a delusion, the orgies on the mountains. Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the hills where they sinned, the people begin to weep, and God answers with the gospel of this chapter, the promise to heal their faithlessness, and they come home confessing that salvation is in the LORD alone.

A voice on the bare heights. The bare heights were the scene of the idolatry in verse 2. Now the same hills carry a different sound: weeping. The place of the sin becomes the place of sorrow over it. And the cause is named in the right order: “they have perverted their way; they have forgotten the LORD their God”. The crooked road is the symptom; the forgetting is the disease.

I will heal your faithlessness. God promises not merely to forgive the faithlessness but to heal it. He treats the disloyalty as a disease in his people, not only a debt against himself, and he undertakes the cure. If the invitation were simply to come back and do better, it would sink the very people it calls, who have already proved they cannot. The God who is wronged will himself restore their ability to love him, and for the Christian reader that healing is the work of the Spirit, who pours God’s love into the heart and makes a faithless people steady (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Romans 5:5).

Behold, we come to you. And they answer. Repentance always includes seeing that what we left God for was worthless: all that noise on the hilltops, and nothing in it. They put their hope in a new place: “Truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel.” Not in the hills or the alliances, but in a person. It is the confession Jonah made from inside the fish, “Salvation belongs to the LORD!” (Jonah 2:9), and it is where every true return ends.

Uncertain wording. The second half of verse 23 is compressed and difficult in Hebrew. “A delusion” is, as the ESV notes, literally “commotion”, and “the orgies on the mountains” renders a phrase that may mean the noisy crowds or the uproar of the hilltop worship. The sense is clear enough: the clamour of the hill shrines promised help and was empty.

verseByVerse.quote: "But from our youth the shameful thing has devoured all for which our fathers labored, their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters. Let us lie down in our shame, and let our dishonor cover us. For we have sinned against the LORD our God, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day, and we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The returning people make a full and honest confession: idolatry has devoured everything they had, and they and their fathers have sinned against the LORD from the beginning.

The shameful thing. A scornful name for Baal, the Hebrew word for shame put where the idol’s name would go (11:13 sets the two side by side). They add up what idolatry took: the livestock, the harvests, the children given to Molech. Sin is finally accounted for not as pleasure but as loss.

Let us lie down in our shame. Set this beside verse 3, “you refuse to be ashamed”. The capacity to blush has come back. In a returning people shame is not despair; it is the sign of a conscience coming back to life.

We and our fathers. They do not minimise: “we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day”, the exact reverse of the people who said “I am innocent” (2:35). This turn comes after the promise to heal, not before it; the kindness makes the confession possible. Nor does the returning life become flawless afterwards. The obedience Israel never gave, Christ gave in his people’s place, and it is counted as theirs (Romans 5:19), so each new failure has the same way back as this one: confession, and the mercy God promised.

3.title: Return, Faithless Israel: I Will Heal Your Faithlessness
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 ended with Judah protesting, “I am innocent” (2:35). Chapter 3 continues the same sermon and the same marriage picture, but now the word that keeps sounding is “return”. Verses 6–18 are dated “in the days of King Josiah”, during his reform.

The message. God invites his unfaithful people back when even his own law said the door was shut. All he asks is that they stop pretending and acknowledge their guilt, and he promises not only to forgive their faithlessness but to heal it. Words of devotion and outward reform are not repentance; a true return comes from the heart, and God himself will make it possible.

Why it was said. Josiah’s reform had cleared the idols away, and Judah felt religious again, but the people had come back to God “in pretense” (v. 10; see the introduction). They had watched the northern kingdom go into exile without learning a thing.

How the chapter makes its case. The law forbids a divorced wife who has remarried to return, yet God asks, “would you return to me?” (v. 1), though Judah cannot blush and her fine words are contradicted by her deeds (vv. 2–5). Then two sisters: Israel, exiled for her unfaithfulness, and Judah, who saw it, did the same and came back only in pretence, so that Israel is the more righteous (vv. 6–11). Jeremiah is sent to call north: return, only acknowledge your guilt (vv. 12–13). God promises a remnant, shepherds after his own heart, a city that is his throne and a reunited people (vv. 14–18). Last, God tells how he longed to be called Father (vv. 19–20), promises, “I will heal your faithlessness”, and the people come home confessing their sin (vv. 21–25).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. How God can take back an unfaithful wife without ceasing to be just is answered at the cross, where Christ bore the guilt of his bride. The promises of this chapter, shepherds after God’s heart, the nations gathered, a presence that makes the ark unnecessary, a healed heart, are kept in the good shepherd (John 10:11), in the gathering of the nations to him, in the Word who “dwelt among us” (John 1:14) and in the Spirit he gives.

For us. Religious words and a tidier life are not the same as coming back to God. The door is open wider than we deserve, and only one thing is required: to name our sin honestly, without excuses. Then believe that the God who forgives also heals, and keep coming back the same way.
3.theology:
The invitation to return goes beyond what the law allows (v. 1; Deut 24:1-4): grace opens a door justice had shut, at a cost only the cross explains. Religious language and partial reform are not repentance (vv. 4-5, 10), and those who know more are more to blame (v. 11).

The one condition of return is honest acknowledgement of guilt (v. 13; Joel 2:12-13; 1 John 1:9).

God gathers a remnant one by one (v. 14), gives shepherds after his own heart (v. 15; Acts 13:22; Eph 4:11), and will make the ark unnecessary because the presence it signified has come (vv. 16-17). God promises to heal faithlessness, not merely pardon it (v. 22), and the confession of vv. 24-25 follows that promise rather than earning it.
3.examples: The chapter's pictures are easy to carry away: a door the law had bolted, opened by love; a face that has forgotten how to blush; Judah in a front-row seat at her sister's funeral, learning nothing. They warn against a reform that is genuine at the top and never reaches the heart, and they steady anyone discouraged when revival comes one from a city and two from a family.

keyVerse.quote: “Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness.”
keyVerse.note: This is the gospel of the chapter. God does not only invite his people back, he promises to cure the very faithlessness that made them leave, treating it as a disease in them and undertaking the cure himself. The people’s confession follows the promise, not the other way round: it is his kindness that makes the return possible, and in Christ, by the Spirit, he keeps the promise.

3.reflection:
The law said a divorced wife who had married another could not go back, yet God asks, “would you return to me?” (v. 1). What does that tell you about God’s grace? How can he welcome sinners back and still be just?

Judah called God “My father” while doing all the evil it could (vv. 4–5), and returned under Josiah “in pretense” (v. 10). How can we tell the difference between religious words or outward reform and real repentance, in ourselves and in a church?

God asks only one thing: “acknowledge your guilt” (v. 13). Why is honest confession so hard for us, and what makes it easier? What would it mean for you to be specific with God, and perhaps with someone you have wronged?

“I will heal your faithlessness” (v. 22). Where do you feel most unable to stay faithful? How does it change things to know that God undertakes not only to forgive you but to heal you?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — If You Return, Return to Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A real return to God means coming back to him, not merely changing the outside. If Israel returns, it must be to the LORD himself: idols put away, no wavering, and his name sworn by in truth, justice and righteousness, and then the nations will find blessing in him, as God promised Abraham (vv. 1–2). Judah must break up the hard, unploughed ground of its heart rather than sow among thorns, and circumcise its heart to the LORD, before his wrath burns like a fire no one can put out (vv. 3–4). The demand is impossible without God, which is why he will promise to do it.
verseByVerse.theology: Real return is to a person, not to a programme, and it reaches the heart or it is not return at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return. If you remove your detestable things from my presence, and do not waver, and if you swear, 'As the LORD lives,' in truth, in justice, and in righteousness, then nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel comes back, it must be to God himself, wholehearted and honest, with the idols gone, and such a return would open God’s blessing to the nations.

To me you should return. Chapter 3 ended with “Behold, we come to you” (3:22); chapter 4 tests it. Not to religion, not to the temple, not to better behaviour: to me. It is possible to reform a life without returning to God, and the two look alike for a while.

And do not waver. The conditions are concrete: remove the idols and do not waver. No half-return, no shrine kept in the garden just in case.

As the LORD lives. The ordinary oath in Israel, said constantly by people serving other gods. God attaches three conditions: in truth, in justice and in righteousness. His name on the lips of someone living a lie is not devotion; it is perjury.

Nations shall bless themselves in him. Look where it leads. If Israel returns honestly, the nations are blessed: God’s promise to Abraham, that all nations would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3), surfacing in a sermon about repentance. A people genuinely right with God becomes a blessing to everyone else.

The gospel beforehand. Paul says Scripture “preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham”, and it is fulfilled when the nations are justified by faith in Abraham’s offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3:8, 16). Israel’s honest return was always meant to open onto that wider blessing, and in Christ it does.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: "Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns. Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts, O men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of the evil of your deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah must let God break up its hardened heart and cut away what stands between it and him, because outward signs of belonging are worthless if the heart is untouched.

Break up your fallow ground. Fallow ground is land left unploughed so long it has hardened over. It is not barren; it is compacted, and seed thrown on it bounces. The command is not to sow harder but to break the ground first. Hosea said it too: “break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).

Sow not among thorns. Many try to sow good seed on a heart unbroken for years: more services, more resolutions, more reading. And clearing what chokes the seed is part of the work, as the parable of the sower says of cares and riches (Mark 4:18–19).

Circumcise yourselves to the LORD. Circumcision was the mark in the body that a man belonged to God’s covenant people, and every man in Judah had it. The mark of belonging is worthless if the heart is untouched.

Who circumcises the heart? A difficulty the whole Bible answers. The people are commanded to circumcise their own hearts, but in Deuteronomy God promises, “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart” (Deuteronomy 30:6), and in this book he will promise to write his law on it (31:33). Both are true: God commands what only he can give, and the command is how people come to ask him for it. Paul completes it: “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter” (Romans 2:29), and it is done in Christ, “a circumcision made without hands” (Colossians 2:11). So the Christian does not break up his own heart by willpower; the Spirit now in him does the ploughing through the word. Where his heart is still hard in places, as it will be, Christ’s own wholehearted obedience is counted as his (Philippians 3:9), and the way back is confession, not despair.

How do I break up hard ground? Fallow ground is usually not one great sin but a corner of life you stopped letting God near. Find the field. Ask where you have grown hard: the subject you change when it comes up in a sermon, the relationship you have quietly written off, the habit you no longer even call sin. Pray, “Search me, O God, and know my heart!” (Psalm 139:23). Turn the soil with the word. Read a passage that speaks to that very area, slowly, and let it say what it says. Name it to God plainly. Hardness thaws in confession, not in vague regret: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). Pull one thorn. Cancel the subscription, make the call, close the tab. Let others in. We are to “exhort one another every day, as long as it is called ‘today,’ that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13). None of this earns a soft heart. It is how you ask for one, from the God who has promised, “I will give you a new heart” (Ezekiel 36:26), and who ploughs gently because his Son was broken for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–18 — The Alarm from the North
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The disaster God threatened is now on its way, and he is the one bringing it, yet even now he calls Jerusalem to be saved. The trumpet sounds and people flee for the walled cities, because God is bringing destruction from the north (vv. 5–6). A lion, a destroyer of nations, has set out; the right response is sackcloth and mourning (vv. 7–8). King, officials, priests and prophets will lose their nerve, and Jeremiah protests that the people have been deceived by promises of peace (vv. 9–10). A scorching wind is coming, not to winnow but to judge (vv. 11–13). Still God pleads, “wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved”, as the besiegers close in, the bitter harvest of the people’s own deeds (vv. 14–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is announced in detail, the false comfort is exposed, and in the middle of the siege the door is still open.

verseByVerse.quote: Declare in Judah, and proclaim in Jerusalem, and say, "Blow the trumpet through the land; cry aloud and say, 'Assemble, and let us go into the fortified cities!' Raise a standard toward Zion, flee for safety, stay not, for I bring disaster from the north, and great destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The alarm sounds for the whole land to flee into the walled cities, because God himself is bringing disaster from the north, just as he warned at Jeremiah’s call.

Blow the trumpet through the land. The tone changes without warning, like an air-raid siren in the middle of a sermon. These were the orders given when an invader crossed the border: families in the open country left their farms for the walled towns, and a standard, a signal pole raised on a height, pointed the refugees towards Zion.

For I bring disaster from the north. The terrible clause in the middle of the panic. The invasion is not an accident of history that God will use. He is bringing it.

The call fulfilled. This is the vision of Jeremiah’s call arriving on schedule. As a young man he had been shown a boiling pot and told, “Out of the north disaster shall be let loose upon all the inhabitants of the land” (1:14). What was a picture then is a trumpet now. God’s warnings have dates attached.

verseByVerse.quote: A lion has gone up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations has set out; he has gone out from his place to make your land a waste; your cities will be ruins without inhabitant. For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the LORD has not turned back from us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The destroyer, like a lion out of its thicket, is already on the move, and the only fitting response is to mourn, because God’s anger has not turned away.

A destroyer of nations has set out. Nebuchadnezzar is never named; he is simply a lion up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations on the march. This is not a threat about what might happen if things do not improve. It has started.

Put on sackcloth, lament and wail. The right response to the news is not a strategy meeting but mourning. There is a kind of trouble that calls for grief before it calls for plans, and a church that has lost the ability to lament will meet such trouble with activity instead.

Has not turned back from us. The pronoun matters. The prophet does not stand outside the verdict pointing; he counts himself among the people under it.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day, declares the LORD, courage shall fail both king and officials. The priests shall be appalled and the prophets astounded." Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD, surely you have utterly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the invasion comes, every leader will lose his nerve, and Jeremiah cries out to God in anguish that the people have been lulled by promises of peace.

Courage shall fail both king and officials. The four groups again: king, officials, priests, prophets, and not one of them will have anything to say. The prophets in particular will be astounded: the men who had been predicting peace will be the most surprised people in the city.

Surely you have utterly deceived this people. Jeremiah’s protest is startling, and the Bible records it without softening it. He hears the message of the official prophets, “It shall be well with you,” and lays the responsibility at God’s door.

Protest as faith. Jeremiah says this to God, not about him behind his back. Honest protest addressed to God is a form of faith; the psalms are full of it.

Does God deceive? Scripture does not teach that God lies. His own answer comes later in the book: he never sent those prophets, who “have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace” (6:14). But the prophet feels something real here: God sometimes judges people by giving them what they insist on. When people insist on comfortable preaching, God may let them have it, and the comfortable preaching becomes part of the judgment. When Ahab wanted only favourable prophets, Micaiah saw heaven’s court decide it, and told the king, “the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets” (1 Kings 22:23). Paul says of those who refuse the truth, “God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false” (2 Thessalonians 2:11). God does not deceive the honest. He hands those who wanted to be deceived over to what they chose, and the sermon you most want to hear may be the most dangerous one available.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, "A hot wind from the bare heights in the desert toward the daughter of my people, not to winnow or cleanse, a wind too full for this comes for me. Now it is I who speak in judgment upon them." Behold, he comes up like clouds; his chariots like the whirlwind; his horses are swifter than eagles— woe to us, for we are ruined!
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is coming is not a gentle breeze that sorts wheat from chaff but a scorching desert wind of judgment, an army so fast that the people cry out that they are ruined.

Not to winnow or cleanse. A farmer wants a light breeze to winnow grain, separating wheat from chaff. What is coming is the desert wind that strips the field bare. This is not corrective discipline any more; it is judgment.

Woe to us, for we are ruined! The voice of the people themselves, seeing it clearly for the first time.

Swifter than eagles. Habakkuk describes the same army: “Their horses are swifter than leopards”, and their horsemen “fly like an eagle swift to devour” (Habakkuk 1:8). Two prophets watching one invasion from different vantage points, and neither sees any way to outrun it.

Uncertain wording. “A wind too full for this comes for me” is a compressed Hebrew phrase. It probably means a wind too strong for winnowing, coming at God’s command (or “from me”). The general sense is clear from the context: this wind does not sift, it destroys.

verseByVerse.quote: O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved. How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you? For a voice declares from Dan and proclaims trouble from Mount Ephraim. Warn the nations that he is coming; announce to Jerusalem, "Besiegers come from a distant land; they shout against the cities of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even with the enemy on the road, God still calls Jerusalem to wash her heart and be saved, while messengers report the invader drawing closer.

That you may be saved. In the middle of the siege report, an invitation. The army is on the road and God is still offering salvation. Mercy runs later into the story than anyone expects.

Wash your heart from evil. The diagnosis again goes to the inside, with a question: how long will wicked thoughts lodge within you? The word suggests a guest who has settled in. Sins that were once visitors become residents, and the difference is how long they were allowed to stay.

You were washed. The call echoes Isaiah’s opening sermon, “Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean; remove the evil of your deeds from before my eyes” (Isaiah 1:16), and like every such command it drives the hearer to the one who can actually do it. Paul writes to converts who had been everything this chapter describes: “But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

From Dan and from Mount Ephraim. Dan is the northern border; Ephraim is the hill country just above Jerusalem. The report is a relay of dispatches as the enemy moves south, and the distance closes between sentences.

Warn the nations. The surrounding peoples are told too. What happens to Jerusalem is not a private family matter; the whole region is meant to learn from it what kind of God the God of Israel is.

verseByVerse.quote: Like keepers of a field are they against her all around, because she has rebelled against me, declares the LORD. Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you. This is your doom, and it is bitter; it has reached your very heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The besiegers surround Jerusalem like watchmen round a field, and God says plainly that the city’s own rebellion has brought this bitter harvest upon it.

Like keepers of a field. Besieging armies ring the city as watchmen sit round a field at harvest: patient, settled, waiting for what is inside to be ready.

Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you. The verdict already given in 2:17. It needs saying plainly, because people will do almost anything to avoid it. Not every disaster is deserved; the book of Job is in the Bible to prevent that conclusion. But some are, and pretending otherwise makes repentance impossible. “It has reached your very heart”, the place the whole chapter has been pointing to.

What one sows. Paul states the principle for the church: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7). The bitterness in Judah’s mouth was the taste of her own harvest.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet who announces the judgment is broken by it, and God explains why it must come. Jeremiah cries out in anguish: his heart pounds, he cannot keep silent, for he hears the trumpet and sees the land laid waste crash upon crash, homes torn down in a moment, and he asks how long it must go on (vv. 19–21). God answers with a diagnosis. His people are foolish children who do not know him; they are clever at doing evil and have no idea how to do good (v. 22). Judgment is grievous, but it is not arbitrary.
verseByVerse.theology: The man who preaches the judgment is broken by it; God's word is never delivered from a safe distance.

verseByVerse.quote: My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly; I cannot keep silent, for I hear the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war. Crash follows hard on crash; the whole land is laid waste. Suddenly my tents are laid waste, my curtains in a moment. How long must I see the standard and hear the sound of the trumpet?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah is torn apart by the disaster he must announce, feeling the ruin of his people as his own, with no trace of satisfaction at being proved right.

My anguish, my anguish! This is why Jeremiah is called the weeping prophet. He is not reading a bulletin; he is doubled over. There is no satisfaction in him at being proved right, no relish in the doom of people who have dismissed him for years.

No relish in judgment. That is the test of anyone who handles the severe parts of Scripture. Hell, judgment and wrath can be preached with a certain enjoyment, and when they are, something has gone badly wrong. The one who tells the truth about judgment should be the one most obviously wounded by it.

My heart is beating wildly. He can feel his own heartbeat; he cannot sit still or stay quiet. He calls the ruined homes my tents, my curtains: these are not other people’s losses to him. And then the cry every sufferer knows: How long?

He wept over it. That anguish points beyond Jeremiah. Six centuries later another man came towards the same city, again under sentence, and “he wept over it, saying, ‘Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace!’” (Luke 19:41–42). The prophet’s breaking heart was a preview of the heart of God made flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: "For my people are foolish; they know me not; they are stupid children; they have no understanding. They are 'wise'—in doing evil! But how to do good they know not."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names the root of the disaster: his people do not know him, and they are experts at evil and helpless at good.

They know me not. God answers the prophet’s How long? with a diagnosis. The problem is not intelligence; it is that they do not know him. Then the bitter irony: they are experts at evil and amateurs at good. Every culture has this shape: brilliant at what harms it, helpless at what would heal it.

Wise as to what is good. Paul’s hope for the Roman church is the precise reversal: “I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil” (Romans 16:19). Judah had it backwards, and the gospel does not simply make people cleverer. It turns their competence the right way round.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — I Looked on the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin unravels creation itself, yet God will not let the judgment go all the way. Four times Jeremiah looks and sees the creation week running backwards: the earth formless and empty, the heavens dark, the mountains shaking, no people and no birds, the fruitful land a desert before God’s anger (vv. 23–26). The whole land will be desolate, and God’s purpose is fixed, yet he will not make a full end (vv. 27–28). Meanwhile the city flees, and, deserted, still paints her face for lovers who want her dead, until she cries out like a woman in her first labour, fainting before murderers (vv. 29–31).
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment is creation running backwards, and even there God sets a limit: not a full end.

verseByVerse.quote: I looked on the earth, and behold, it was without form and void; and to the heavens, and they had no light. I looked on the mountains, and behold, they were quaking, and all the hills moved to and fro. I looked, and behold, there was no man, and all the birds of the air had fled. I looked, and behold, the fruitful land was a desert, and all its cities were laid in ruins before the LORD, before his fierce anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah sees the judgment as creation running backwards, a world returned to emptiness and darkness, because sin does not only spoil a life but unmakes the world God made.

Without form and void. Four times Jeremiah says “I looked”, and what he sees is Genesis played backwards. The first phrase comes from the creation account: “The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep” (Genesis 1:2). Then God said, “Let there be light.” Here the light has gone out.

All the hills moved to and fro. Day three of creation gave dry land; here the land itself is unsteady. “The earth staggers like a drunken man,” says Isaiah of the same day (Isaiah 24:20).

There was no man. Days five and six are undone: the birds gone, and humanity, the crown of the creation week, simply absent.

Sin unmakes the world. This passage is terrifying, and it makes a point no amount of moralising could. Sin is not a private matter between a person and God with no wider consequence. It unmakes the world. Creation itself is dragged down by it, groaning, “subjected to futility” and waiting to be “set free from its bondage to corruption” (Romans 8:20–21).

A new creation. That is why salvation in the Bible is never merely the rescue of souls out of a doomed world. It is new heavens and a new earth, and the same God who spoke the first light will speak again. In Christ he already has: “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17).
verseByVerse.note: The four visions run the creation week in reverse: light, land, people and birds, and last the fruitful land with its cities.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD, "The whole land shall be a desolation; yet I will not make a full end. "For this the earth shall mourn, and the heavens above be dark; for I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole land will be laid waste and God will not change his purpose, yet he sets a limit himself: he will not make a full end.

Yet I will not make a full end. These words keep this book from being despair, and they will be repeated (5:10, 18). However far the judgment goes, God draws a line beyond which it will not go, and he draws it himself. A surviving remnant will come through, and through them the promises will run on.

Days cut short. Jesus says the same of the worst days: “if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short” (Matthew 24:22).

I have not relented. Three verbs of settled intent: spoken, purposed, not relented. Elsewhere God does relent when people turn (18:7–8), which is exactly why this is so grave. The door in verse 14 is open, and the people are not walking through it.

verseByVerse.quote: At the noise of horseman and archer every city takes to flight; they enter thickets; they climb among rocks; all the cities are forsaken, and no man dwells in them. And you, O desolate one, what do you mean that you dress in scarlet, that you adorn yourself with ornaments of gold, that you enlarge your eyes with paint? In vain you beautify yourself. Your lovers despise you; they seek your life. For I heard a cry as of a woman in labor, anguish as of one giving birth to her first child, the cry of the daughter of Zion gasping for breath, stretching out her hands, "Woe is me! I am fainting before murderers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the cities empty before the invader, Jerusalem still dresses up for the allies who now want her dead, until her vanity gives way to the cry of a woman in agony.

In vain you beautify yourself. With the army at the gates the city is doing her make-up: scarlet, gold, painted eyes, still trying to attract the very nations whose armies are coming. The alliances she trusted have turned murderous, and she is still dressing for them. Painting the eyes was what Jezebel did as Jehu rode into Jezreel (2 Kings 9:30), and it did not save her either. People do this: faced with ruin, we reach for the thing that ruined us.

A woman in labor. The chapter ends with the cry of a woman in her first labour: pain that cannot be postponed, and hands stretched out for help. In Scripture that image is not always the end. Labour pains lead somewhere, and Paul uses the same picture for a creation in the pains of childbirth (Romans 8:22). But none of that comfort is offered here. The chapter closes on the cry, and leaves the reader inside it.

4.title: Break Up Your Fallow Ground
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 ended with the people coming home in confession. Chapter 4 tests that return, and then the tone changes: the invasion from the north, first seen as a boiling pot in Jeremiah’s call (1:13–15), is now on the road.

The message. Coming back to God must be real, a return to God himself that reaches the heart, or it is no return at all. Because Judah’s heart has not changed, God is bringing a destroyer from the north, and sin will unmake their world. Yet even as the army closes in, God still calls, “wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved” (v. 14), and he will not make a full end.

Why it was said. Judah had outward reform, and its prophets promised that all would be well (v. 10). Jeremiah had to tell a comfortable people that the danger was real, near and sent by God, because their hearts had never turned (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First the terms of return: to God himself, idols removed, oaths sworn in truth, and then the nations will be blessed (vv. 1–2); break up the hard ground and circumcise your hearts (vv. 3–4). Then the alarm: trumpet, flight, a lion out of his thicket, a scorching wind, every leader’s courage failing (vv. 5–13). Even now Jerusalem is told to wash her heart and be saved (vv. 14–18). The prophet breaks down in anguish, and God names the cause: a people skilled at evil who do not know him (vv. 19–22). In four visions Jeremiah sees creation run backwards (vv. 23–26); God will not make a full end (vv. 27–28), and the painted city cries out like a woman in labour (vv. 29–31).

Where it leads. First by the need it exposes. God commands a circumcised heart, but only he can give one (Deuteronomy 30:6), and he does it in Christ by the Spirit (Colossians 2:11). It leads by promise: an honest return was meant to bring blessing to the nations, the promise to Abraham fulfilled in Christ (Galatians 3:8, 16). And it leads by pattern: Jeremiah’s anguish over the doomed city is a preview of Jesus, who wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). The creation that sin unmakes, Christ will make new.

For us. Religion that has not reached the heart cannot save us, and no amount of new resolutions on hard ground will grow anything. Ask God to break up whatever corner of your life you have closed to him. While the door is open, “that you may be saved” is still being said; and let anyone who speaks of judgment do it with Jeremiah’s tears.
4.theology:
Repentance is return to God himself, not reform of behaviour (v. 1), and it must reach the heart: the command to circumcise the heart (v. 4) is what God elsewhere promises to do (Deut 30:6; Jer 31:33) and does in Christ.

God governs the invading army: he brings the disaster (v. 6). Comfortable preaching can itself be part of judgment (v. 10; 6:14). Mercy is still offered while judgment is arriving (v. 14), and honest protest may be addressed to God (v. 10).

Sin unmakes the world: judgment is creation running backwards (vv. 23-26; Gen 1:2; Rom 8:20-22), so salvation must include a renewed creation. And God limits his own judgment: yet I will not make a full end (v. 27).
4.examples: Some hearts are like ground so hard that good seed simply bounces, and some lives carry the outward mark of belonging to God’s people with nothing beneath it in the heart. Wicked thoughts arrive as visitors and, if they are allowed to stay, become residents. And when ruin comes, people still reach for what ruined them, like a city doing her make-up while the army stands at the gate.

keyVerse.quote: O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved. How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you?
keyVerse.note: Spoken while the army is already on the road, this verse holds the chapter together: the problem is the heart, and mercy is still being offered. It shows how late into judgment God’s invitation runs. The command to wash drives the hearer to the one who can do it, and in Christ believers are told, “you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

4.reflection:
“If you return, O Israel… to me you should return” (v. 1). What is the difference between returning to God himself and simply reforming our behaviour or going back to church? How can we tell which we are doing?

Fallow ground is not barren but hardened (v. 3). Is there a corner of your life you have stopped letting God near? What would it look like to break up that ground this week, and why can we ask God for a new heart with confidence?

Judah’s prophets kept saying, “It shall be well with you” (v. 10). Why do we prefer comfortable preaching, and how can a church make sure it hears the hard words of Scripture as well as the comforting ones?

Jeremiah announced judgment with anguish, not relish (vv. 19–21), and Jesus wept over the same city. How should that shape the way we speak to others about sin and judgment?
