verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Search the Streets for One Just Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God would pardon Jerusalem for a single honest man, and the search through the city finds none. Jeremiah is sent through the streets to look for one person who does justice and seeks truth, but the people swear falsely by God’s name and have made their faces harder than rock (vv. 1–3). He tries the poor, supposing they were never taught, and then the great, who know God’s way, and finds them all alike (vv. 4–5), so the wild beasts wait at the gates (v. 6). God asks, “How can I pardon you?” of a people he fed to the full, who repaid him with false gods and adultery (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: God offers to spare a whole city for one just man, and the search fails.

verseByVerse.quote: Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, look and take note! Search her squares to see if you can find a man, one who does justice and seeks truth, that I may pardon her. Though they say, "As the LORD lives," yet they swear falsely.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God offers to spare the whole city of Jerusalem for one person who does what is right and seeks the truth, and the search turns up no one.

See if you can find a man. One just man, and the whole city pardoned: the terms are extraordinary. Abraham once pleaded with God over Sodom, from fifty righteous down to ten: “For the sake of ten I will not destroy it” (Genesis 18:32). Here God does not wait to be bargained with. He starts at one, and he offers it about his own city, with the temple in it and a king of David’s line on the throne.

Though they say, “As the LORD lives”. Zephaniah, prophesying in the same years, pictured God searching “Jerusalem with lamps” (Zephaniah 1:12), and what the search finds is not a shortage of religion but of honesty. Religious language survives long after religion has died.

The search fails. Ezekiel was given the same errand with the same result: “I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none” (Ezekiel 22:30). The psalm had already said why: “They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one” (Psalm 14:3).

One just man, not spared. The gospel is built on the shape of this verse. God would spare a city for one righteous man. There was none in Jerusalem, so God provided one, and “did not spare his own Son” (Romans 8:32). Because the one just man was not spared, the city of God, his people, is spared. And the Father is still “seeking such people to worship him”, in spirit and truth (John 4:23): the search that failed in Jerusalem ends in those he makes true.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, do not your eyes look for truth? You have struck them down, but they felt no anguish; you have consumed them, but they refused to take correction. They have made their faces harder than rock; they have refused to repent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has disciplined his people again and again, and they have felt nothing and learned nothing; their faces have set like stone. Jeremiah appeals to God’s own character: he is not fooled by the oath formula of verse 2, for “the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

They felt no anguish. Three refusals, and the middle one is the most frightening: struck, and they felt nothing. Pain is a mercy when it makes us stop. Hardness is rarely caused by one great sin; it is built by many small refusals.

They refused to take correction. Amos had watched the same pattern more than a century before, with a refrain after every disaster God sent: “yet you did not return to me” (Amos 4:6). Discipline that is received and not heeded does not soften a heart; it hardens it further.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, "These are only the poor; they have no sense; for they do not know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God. I will go to the great and will speak to them, for they know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God." But they all alike had broken the yoke; they had burst the bonds. Therefore a lion from the forest shall strike them down; a wolf from the desert shall devastate them. A leopard is watching their cities; everyone who goes out of them shall be torn in pieces, because their transgressions are many, their apostasies are great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin is not a problem of poverty or ignorance: the educated and powerful have thrown off God’s yoke just as surely as the poor, so danger now waits at every gate.

These are only the poor. Jeremiah tries a very modern explanation: nobody taught these people. So he goes uptown, to the educated and the powerful, and finds exactly the same thing: “they all alike had broken the yoke”. The well-taught are not less guilty but more.

Doesn’t education make people better? It is an honourable modern hope. Socrates argued that no one does wrong knowingly: show a person the good clearly enough and he will choose it. Jeremiah ran the experiment in Jerusalem, and the great were no better than the poor. Modern history has run it again: of the officials who met at Wannsee in January 1942 to organise the murder of Europe’s Jews, more than half held doctorates. Knowing the good and loving it are different things, and Paul puts the gap in one sentence: “For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing” (Romans 7:19). (On where that evil comes from, see the note on Genesis 3:1–7.) If education could save us, the gospel would be good news only for the clever. Instead it comes to the poor and the great on the same terms, because what we need is not better information but a new heart, and a Saviour who knows the worst about us and loves us still.

A leopard is watching their cities. The worst image of the three: the leopard is not hunting but watching, waiting by the gate for whoever steps outside. Hosea used the same animals and put God himself behind them: “So I am to them like a lion; like a leopard I will lurk beside the way” (Hosea 13:7). The predators are not random. “Because their transgressions are many”, the wild beasts outside the walls are God’s answer to the rebellion inside them.

verseByVerse.quote: "How can I pardon you? Your children have forsaken me and have sworn by those who are no gods. When I fed them to the full, they committed adultery and trooped to the houses of whores. They were well-fed, lusty stallions, each neighing for his neighbor's wife. Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD; and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God asks how he can pardon a people who repaid his generosity with false gods and adultery, and he insists that a just God cannot simply look away.

How can I pardon you? God is looking for a way to forgive, and the way is not in them. The first charge is the root of the rest: they “have sworn by those who are no gods”. A man who breaks faith with God will not long keep faith with his neighbour.

When I fed them to the full. The order matters: God fed them to the full, and then they committed adultery. The generosity came first, and the betrayal was fuelled by it. Moses had predicted exactly this in his last song: “But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked; you grew fat, stout, and sleek; then he forsook God who made him” (Deuteronomy 32:15).

Each neighing for his neighbor’s wife. The image is coarse on purpose, and the object is the woman down the street, whose husband they know. Sin here is not abstract; it has an address.

Shall I not punish them? Asked again in verse 29, the question deserves an honest answer. A God who looked at predatory men, betrayed marriages and abandoned children and did nothing would not be loving; he would be indifferent. Wrath is not the opposite of love; indifference is. “How can I pardon you?” is answered at last not by lowering the standard but at the cross, where God is “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

Uncertain wording. The two Hebrew words behind “well-fed, lusty” (v. 8) are rare and their exact sense uncertain; translations vary between well-fed, lusty and roaming. The picture is plain: pampered animals driven by appetite.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment is coming, as fire and as an invading army, but God himself sets its limit and he will not wipe his people out. The vine is to be stripped of the branches that are not his, yet not destroyed (vv. 10–11). The people say God will do nothing and the prophets are only wind (vv. 12–13), so God makes his word a fire in Jeremiah’s mouth and brings a distant nation of unknown speech to eat up everything they trust (vv. 14–17). Even then he will not make a full end, and he gives the exiles the answer to their question why: as they served foreign gods at home, they will serve foreigners abroad (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Practical atheism, the belief that God will do nothing, is answered by a judgment shaped exactly like the sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "Go up through her vine rows and destroy, but make not a full end; strip away her branches, for they are not the LORD's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends the destroyers into his vineyard, but on a leash: they may strip away the branches that are not his, and they may not make a full end.

Go up through her vine rows. The vineyard of chapter 2 is pruned savagely, and the invaders, who think they are looting, are given limits they know nothing about.

For they are not the LORD’s. The branches stripped off are the ones that were never his. Judgment removes what does not belong; it does not uproot the vine. Jesus, the true vine, describes his Father as the same kind of vinedresser: “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away” (John 15:2).

verseByVerse.quote: For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have been utterly treacherous to me, declares the LORD. They have spoken falsely of the LORD and have said, 'He will do nothing; no disaster will come upon us, nor shall we see sword or famine. The prophets will become wind; the word is not in them. Thus shall it be done to them!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel and Judah have betrayed God by deciding that he will never act: no disaster will come, and the prophets who warn of it are only wind.

He will do nothing. Not “There is no God”, simply that he is not going to act, so his opinion need not affect any decision. It is atheism that keeps its religion. Ask what difference it would make to tomorrow if that sentence were true; for many of us the honest answer is very little.

The same creed in every age. Zephaniah heard it too: “those who say in their hearts, ‘The LORD will not do good, nor will he do ill’” (Zephaniah 1:12). Peter hears its later form in scoffers who ask, “Where is the promise of his coming?” because “all things are continuing as they were” (2 Peter 3:4). Delay is mistaken for absence in every generation; Peter’s answer is that the delay is patience, God “not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9).

The prophets will become wind. In Hebrew one word means both wind and spirit: these preachers, they say, have no Spirit, only air. Jeremiah heard it for forty years, and the answer comes in the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of hosts: "Because you have spoken this word, behold, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the people called God’s word wind, he will make it a fire in Jeremiah’s mouth that burns them up like wood.

My words in your mouth a fire. They called his words wind; God calls them fire. Later Jeremiah will say the word is “a burning fire shut up in my bones” when he tries not to speak it (20:9), and God will ask, “Is not my word like fire, declares the LORD, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?” (23:29).

And this people wood. The word of God does something wherever it lands. A congregation that treats preaching as background noise is not thereby safe from it; Jesus said the word he spoke will judge those who reject it on the last day (John 12:48).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am bringing against you a nation from afar, O house of Israel, declares the LORD. It is an enduring nation; it is an ancient nation, a nation whose language you do not know, nor can you understand what they say. Their quiver is like an open tomb; they are all mighty warriors. They shall eat up your harvest and your food; they shall eat up your sons and your daughters; they shall eat up your flocks and your herds; they shall eat up your vines and your fig trees; your fortified cities in which you trust they shall beat down with the sword."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will bring a distant, ancient and merciless nation, whose language Judah cannot understand, to devour everything it has and everything it trusts.

A nation whose language you do not know. No negotiation, no pleading: soldiers in your streets whose orders you cannot understand. Moses had written it into the covenant almost word for word: “The LORD will bring a nation against you from far away, from the end of the earth, swooping down like the eagle, a nation whose language you do not understand” (Deuteronomy 28:49). Nothing in Jeremiah’s warning was new. Judah had simply stopped believing the old words meant what they said.

Their quiver is like an open tomb. Every arrow in it is a grave already dug.

They shall eat up. Four times, and the list moves from food to children to livelihood to defences: everything a family works for, in order. The last phrase names the real casualty: “your fortified cities in which you trust”. What falls is not only the wall but the thing the heart was leaning on.

verseByVerse.quote: "But even in those days, declares the LORD, I will not make a full end of you. And when your people say, 'Why has the LORD our God done all these things to us?' you shall say to them, 'As you have forsaken me and served foreign gods in your land, so you shall serve foreigners in a land that is not yours.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in the disaster God will not make a full end of his people, and he gives them the reason for it in advance: they served foreign gods at home, so they will serve foreigners abroad.

I will not make a full end of you. The limit of verse 10 is restated: God keeps a remnant in his hand, and will promise the new covenant to the very people he scatters (31:31–34).

Why has the LORD our God done all these things? God writes the exiles’ answer before they ask: the punishment has the shape of the sin, so that its true nature is finally visible. What we choose in place of God, we end up serving.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–31 — Eyes That Do Not See
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people are blind to what even the sea obeys, and their blindness shows in ingratitude, injustice and a love of comfortable lies. The roaring waves turn back at a line of sand because God drew it, yet his people neither fear nor tremble before him (vv. 20–22). They never thank him for the autumn and spring rains, and their sins have kept good things from them (vv. 23–25). Some grow rich by trapping their neighbours like birds and refuse justice to the fatherless and the needy, so God asks again whether he should not punish (vv. 26–29). Worst of all, the prophets lie, the priests follow them, and the people love it (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology: The sea obeys its limits and the people do not; and the lies they are told are the lies they want.

verseByVerse.quote: Declare this in the house of Jacob; proclaim it in Judah: "Hear this, O foolish and senseless people, who have eyes, but see not, who have ears, but hear not. Do you not fear me? declares the LORD. Do you not tremble before me? I placed the sand as the boundary for the sea, a perpetual barrier that it cannot pass; though the waves toss, they cannot prevail; though they roar, they cannot pass over it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people have eyes and ears but will not see or hear, and so they do not fear the God whose line of sand holds back the roaring sea.

Who have eyes, but see not. The eyes and ears work; what fails is the seeing and hearing. It is the condition Isaiah described (Isaiah 6:9–10): not a failure of intelligence but of the will. It can live in disciples too; Jesus asked his own, when they missed what he had just done: “Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember?” (Mark 8:18).

I placed the sand as the boundary for the sea. Watch the Atlantic throw itself at a beach, and notice what stops it: grains of sand, because God drew the line. Israel’s neighbours told stories of gods who had to battle the sea as a monster of chaos (in the Canaanite myths Baal fights Yam, whose name means “Sea”); the LORD does not fight it at all, he simply sets its limit. God reminds Job of the same boundary: “Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed” (Job 38:11). The ocean hears that sentence and stops. Judah had heard far more, and kept going.

The one the sea obeyed. On the lake of Galilee the disciples watched a man rebuke the wind and the waves, and asked the question this verse invites: “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). The God who set the sea its boundary had come among them.

verseByVerse.quote: But this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart; they have turned aside and gone away. They do not say in their hearts, 'Let us fear the LORD our God, who gives the rain in its season, the autumn rain and the spring rain, and keeps for us the weeks appointed for the harvest.' Your iniquities have turned these away, and your sins have kept good from you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stubborn hearts never stop to thank God for the rains and the harvest, and their sins have shut out the very good things he gives.

They do not say in their hearts. What they fail to say is about rain: the autumn rain to soften the ground, the spring rain to swell the grain, the weeks kept for harvest, God’s fingerprints on the ordinary year. Gratitude for weather is a better test of faith than most people expect.

The witness of the rain. Paul used this argument with pagans who had never read a page of Scripture: God “did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons” (Acts 14:17). If the rain testifies to the Gentiles, it testifies all the more to the people who were told who sends it.

Your sins have kept good from you. Not every hardship is caused by sin, and this book will not let us say that it is. But some good things are absent from a life because sin has kept them out, and it takes honesty to consider whether that is the case.

verseByVerse.quote: For wicked men are found among my people; they lurk like fowlers lying in wait. They set a trap; they catch men. Like a cage full of birds, their houses are full of deceit; therefore they have become great and rich; they have grown fat and sleek. They know no bounds in deeds of evil; they judge not with justice the cause of the fatherless, to make it prosper, and they do not defend the rights of the needy. Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD, and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of God’s own people have grown rich by trapping others like birds, and they refuse to take up the cause of the fatherless and the poor; God asks again whether he should not punish such a nation.

They lurk like fowlers lying in wait. Bird-catchers crouch, wait and spring a net, and what these men catch is men, “among my people”. Their houses are like cages full of trapped birds, and that is how the wealth was made. Their prosperity is evidence against them, not a sign of blessing.

The fatherless and the needy. The two groups they refuse are always the same two: people with no one to take their case. God notices who cannot get a hearing, and he counts the failure to defend them as a deed of evil in its own right, not merely an omission.

To make it prosper. Justice for the fatherless was meant to be active: taking up their case until it came out well. That is the God of Israel’s own way with the helpless, who “executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner” (Deuteronomy 10:18). It is the way of Christ, who took up our cause when we had no one to plead it (1 John 2:1). For the Christian the same Spirit who brought him from death to life now moves him to take up such cases, and where he has walked past them, as everyone has, there is forgiveness to come back to and the help of the Spirit to begin again.

Shall I not punish them? The question of verse 9 returns unchanged, now with the evidence assembled.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew behind “they lurk like fowlers lying in wait” is uncertain, but the picture of hunters crouching to trap their prey is clear from the rest of the verse.

verseByVerse.quote: An appalling and horrible thing has happened in the land: the prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule at their direction; my people love to have it so, but what will you do when the end comes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophets lie, the priests rule by them, and the people love it so; but no comfortable religion will help them when the end comes.

An appalling and horrible thing. The blame lands in a surprising place: “my people love to have it so”.

Supply and demand. The false prophets are not an occupying force; they are supplying a demand. A people who want to be told that everything is fine will always find someone to tell them. Paul foresaw people with “itching ears” gathering teachers “to suit their own passions” (2 Timothy 4:3), and it is as true of a person choosing what to read and listen to as of a church choosing its teachers.

What will you do when the end comes? Comfortable religion is judged by what it leaves you holding at the end. One answer will stand: to be found in Christ, “not having a righteousness of my own” (Philippians 3:9).

Uncertain wording. “The priests rule at their direction” is literally “at their hands”. It may mean the priests take their direction from the prophets, as the ESV has it, or that they rule on their own authority alongside them. Either way, prophets and priests are in league.

5.title: Search Her Squares: Find One Just Man
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 2 to 4 laid the charge against Judah and sounded the alarm of an invader from the north. Chapter 5 stays in the streets of Jerusalem, probably still in the years of Josiah or just after, and asks whether there is anyone in the city at all who can stand before God.

The message. God is looking for a reason to pardon, and he cannot find one in his people. He would spare the whole city for one honest man, and there is none, among the poor or among the great. Because they have decided that he “will do nothing”, his word will come on them as fire; yet even in judgment he sets the limit, and will not make a full end.

Why it was said. Judah still swore “As the LORD lives”, still kept the temple and still had prophets, but its life was lies, adultery, fraud and contempt for the poor, and it was sure that disaster could not come (see the introduction). Its preachers told it so, and it loved them for it.

How the chapter makes its case. First the search: run through Jerusalem and find one just man, and the city will be pardoned; the poor fail, the great fail, and God asks, “How can I pardon you?” (vv. 1–9). Then the sentence: a people who say God will do nothing will find his words a fire and a foreign nation eating up all they trust, though he will not make a full end, and the exile will fit the sin (vv. 10–19). Last, the diagnosis: the sea keeps the boundary of sand God set, but his people do not; they never thank him for the rain, they trap the helpless and grow rich, and they love the lies their prophets tell (vv. 20–31).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes and by God’s character revealed in Christ. God would pardon the city for one righteous man, and no such man could be found (v. 1; Psalm 14:3). So God provided him. Jesus Christ is the one man who did justice and sought truth, and because he was not spared (Romans 8:32), all who belong to him are pardoned. The God who searched Jerusalem for a reason to forgive has found it in his Son.

For us. No one is pardoned because of his own honesty, but the search still exposes us: oaths that cost nothing, comfort that forgets the giver of the rain, preachers chosen because they say what we like. Come to Christ, the just man, and in him take up the cause of those who have no one to plead for them.
5.theology:
God offers to pardon a city for one righteous man and finds none (v. 1; Ezek 22:30; Ps 14:3), and the gospel answers that search with the one just man God provided. Sin is not a matter of class or education (vv. 4-5).

God's wrath is the response of love to those who prey on others and betray them, not the opposite of love (vv. 9, 29). His word is fire, never without effect (v. 14; 23:29). Judgment is limited by God himself (vv. 10, 18) and shaped to fit the sin (v. 19).

Creation obeys the boundaries God sets and his people do not (v. 22). False teaching flourishes because people want it (v. 31), and comfortable religion is tested by what it leaves a person holding at the end.
5.examples: The theory that better education would fix the human heart is tested among the educated and powerful, and it fails. He will do nothing is atheism that keeps its religion: God is confessed and then ignored. It is common among people who would never deny God aloud. And false teachers rarely impose themselves: they supply what a people already loves to hear.

keyVerse.quote: Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, look and take note! Search her squares to see if you can find a man, one who does justice and seeks truth, that I may pardon her.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this search. God is not hunting for grounds to condemn but for a reason to pardon, and he would spare a city for one just man. The search fails, as it always fails among sinners, and the gospel answers it: God provided the one just man himself, and pardons for his sake.

5.reflection:
God offers to pardon the whole city for one person who does justice and seeks truth (v. 1). What does that tell you about God? How does Jesus answer the failure of that search?

Jeremiah assumed the poor did wrong for lack of teaching, and then found the great no better (vv. 4–5). Why is it so tempting to think sin is a matter of education or circumstance? What does the gospel say we need instead?

The people’s creed was “He will do nothing” (v. 12). In what ways can Christians live as though that were true while believing the opposite? Where does it show in your own week?

“My people love to have it so” (v. 31). Why do people choose teachers who tell them what they want to hear? How can a church, and each of us, guard against it?

"Pour it out upon the children in the street, and upon the gatherings of young men, also; both husband and wife shall be taken, the elderly and the very aged.<sup>12</sup>Their houses shall be turned over to others, their fields and wives together, for I will stretch out my hand against the inhabitants of the land," declares the LORD.<sup>13</sup>"For from the least to the greatest of them, everyone is greedy for unjust gain; and from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely.<sup>14</sup>They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace.<sup>15</sup>Were they ashamed when they committed abomination?
