But they said, 'We will not pay attention.'<sup>18</sup>Therefore hear, O nations, and know, O congregation, what will happen to them.<sup>19</sup>Hear, O earth; behold, I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices, because they have not paid attention to my words; and as for my law, they have rejected it.<sup>20</sup>What use to me is frankincense that comes from Sheba, or sweet cane from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, nor your sacrifices pleasing to me.<sup>21</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will lay before this people stumbling blocks against which they shall stumble; fathers and sons together, neighbor and friend shall perish.'"<sup>22</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Behold, a people is coming from the north country, a great nation is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth.<sup>23</sup>They lay hold on bow and javelin; they are cruel and have no mercy; the sound of them is like the roaring sea; they ride on horses, set in array as a man for battle, against you, O daughter of Zion!"<sup>24</sup>We have heard the report of it; our hands fall helpless; anguish has taken hold of us, pain as of a woman in labor.<sup>25</sup>Go not out into the field, nor walk on the road, for the enemy has a sword; terror is on every side.<sup>26</sup>O daughter of my people, put on sackcloth, and roll in ashes; make mourning as for an only son, most bitter lamentation, for suddenly the destroyer will come upon us.<sup>27</sup>"I have made you a tester of metals among my people, that you may know and test their ways.<sup>28</sup>They are all stubbornly rebellious, going about with slanders; they are bronze and iron; all of them act corruptly.<sup>29</sup>The bellows blow fiercely; the lead is consumed by the fire; in vain the refining goes on, for the wicked are not removed.<sup>30</sup>Rejected silver they are called, for the LORD has rejected them."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment is already at the walls, and God is the one who has ordered it, yet he is still warning. The alarm is raised from the hills south of the city, and Jeremiah’s own tribe of Benjamin is told to flee (v. 1). Enemy commanders settle round Jerusalem like shepherds round a pasture, so eager that they will attack by night (vv. 2–5). But the orders come from the LORD of hosts: the ramp is raised against a city that keeps its evil fresh as a well keeps its water and is full of oppression (vv. 6–7). Even now God says, “Be warned”, before he turns away in disgust (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The siege is described in detail and the warning is still open: even here God says Be warned, not farewell.

verseByVerse.quote: Flee for safety, O people of Benjamin, from the midst of Jerusalem! Blow the trumpet in Tekoa, and raise a signal on Beth-haccherem, for disaster looms out of the north, and great destruction. The lovely and delicately bred I will destroy, the daughter of Zion. Shepherds with their flocks shall come against her; they shall pitch their tents around her; they shall pasture, each in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The alarm is sounded from the hills: disaster is coming from the north, and the enemy will surround lovely, sheltered Jerusalem like shepherds settling their flocks around a pasture.

Flee for safety, O people of Benjamin. Jeremiah’s own tribe is the first told to run. Tekoa and Beth-haccherem, on the hills south of the city, were beacon stations, working perfectly and carrying bad news. There is a pun as well: “blow the trumpet” is tiqʿu in Hebrew, and it sounds like Tekoa.

Blow the trumpet in Tekoa. Tekoa had a history. It was the home town of Amos, “who was among the shepherds of Tekoa” (Amos 1:1), the herdsman God sent north to warn Israel more than a century earlier; Israel ignored him and was destroyed. Now the beacon on Tekoa’s hill is lit for Judah.

Shepherds with their flocks. The shepherds are enemy commanders and their flocks are armies, each taking his own section of wall the way a shepherd takes his own patch of grass.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 2 is difficult, and the ESV notes another possible rendering: “I have likened the daughter of Zion to the loveliest pasture”, which fits the shepherds of the next verse. Either way the contrast is between what she is, lovely and sheltered, and what is about to happen to her.
verseByVerse.note: Beth-haccherem means “house of the vineyard”; it is usually placed on a hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem.

verseByVerse.quote: "Prepare war against her; arise, and let us attack at noon! Woe to us, for the day declines, for the shadows of evening lengthen! Arise, and let us attack by night and destroy her palaces!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The besiegers urge one another on, eager to attack at noon and, when the light fails, by night, never guessing whose orders they are carrying out.

Let us attack by night. We overhear the soldiers, and their eagerness is chilling: frustrated that the light is going, they will not wait for morning.

Whose orders? They believe they are pursuing their own ambition; the very next verse gives the orders from above: “For thus says the LORD of hosts”. Men who think they are acting entirely on their own account are often carrying out a sentence they know nothing about. And their target is precise, “her palaces”, the grand houses of the people the next verse accuses of oppression.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD of hosts: "Cut down her trees; cast up a siege mound against Jerusalem. This is the city that must be punished; there is nothing but oppression within her. As a well keeps its water fresh, so she keeps fresh her evil; violence and destruction are heard within her; sickness and wounds are ever before me. Be warned, O Jerusalem, lest I turn from you in disgust, lest I make you a desolation, an uninhabited land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is God who orders the siege of a city full of oppression and violence, and even as the ramp goes up he pleads with Jerusalem to take warning before he turns away from her.

Cast up a siege mound against Jerusalem. The orders come from God, not the invading general, and the trees round the city are felled for the ramp. The charge is oppression: not idolatry this time, but the treatment of people. In the prophets, worship and justice are never separated for long.

So she keeps fresh her evil. A good well keeps its water fresh; Jerusalem keeps her evil fresh, constantly replenished. And “sickness and wounds are ever before me”: God is not detached from what the city does to its weak. He is looking at the injuries, continuously.

Be warned, O Jerusalem. After all that, a warning rather than a verdict. The siege ramp is going up and God is still speaking as though it might be stopped. This is the pattern of the book, and it tells us what God is like. It is the same heart that wept over this city six centuries later: “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace!” (Luke 19:42).

Lest I turn from you in disgust. The danger named first is not the ruin but God withdrawing himself; the desolation comes second. Hosea put it in one line: “Woe to them when I depart from them!” (Hosea 9:12).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Peace, Peace, When There Is No Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one will listen, so the judgment will be thorough, and the leaders who should have warned the people have soothed them instead. What is left of Israel will be picked over like a vine gleaned a second time (v. 9). Jeremiah asks whom he can warn, since their ears are closed and God’s word gives them no pleasure (v. 10). He is full of the LORD’s wrath and cannot hold it in, and it will fall on every age and every household (vv. 11–12). Everyone is greedy for gain, and prophet and priest heal the people’s wound lightly, saying “Peace, peace” when there is none (vv. 13–14). They have lost the ability to blush, and they will fall with the rest (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: A wound treated lightly is the classic failure of false religion: comfort offered where surgery is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "They shall glean thoroughly as a vine the remnant of Israel; like a grape gatherer pass your hand again over its branches." To whom shall I speak and give warning, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen; behold, the word of the LORD is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The enemy will strip what is left of Israel as thoroughly as a second gleaning of a vine, because the people have closed their ears and find no pleasure at all in God’s word.

They shall glean thoroughly. Gleaning is the second pass over a vine, the careful hand going back along branches already picked. Applied to an army it means thoroughness: what the first sweep missed, the second will take.

Their ears are uncircumcised. Who is left to talk to? In chapter 4 the problem was uncircumcised hearts; here it is the ears, closed over, so that “they cannot listen”.

They take no pleasure in it. This is the deepest measure of a spiritual condition: not whether a person can argue with the Bible, but whether it gives him any pleasure. A believer’s love for the word waxes and wanes, but total distaste for it ought to be taken seriously. The blessed man is the one whose “delight is in the law of the LORD” (Psalm 1:2), and the psalmist says, “How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Psalm 119:103). Appetite for the word is not a personality trait. It is a sign of life, and it can be asked for. Jesus said his sheep hear his voice (John 10:27); his first mercy to the deaf is ears.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I am full of the wrath of the LORD; I am weary of holding it in. "Pour it out upon the children in the street, and upon the gatherings of young men, also; both husband and wife shall be taken, the elderly and the very aged. Their houses shall be turned over to others, their fields and wives together, for I will stretch out my hand against the inhabitants of the land," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah is so full of God’s anger at the nation that he cannot hold it in, and the coming judgment will sweep up every household, young and old, with homes, fields and wives taken by others.

I am full of the wrath of the LORD. Jeremiah, who wept in chapter 4, is here full of God’s wrath and tired of containing it. A man who feels only anger at a corrupt society has stopped loving it; a man who feels no anger has stopped taking its victims seriously.

I am weary of holding it in. The same exhaustion he will confess in his darkest chapter, where the word is a fire shut up in his bones (20:9). He did not choose this message and could not keep it down.

Both husband and wife shall be taken. The list spares nobody: children, young men, married couples, the elderly. Judgment on a nation lands on the whole household, which is one reason it is so grievous and why God delays it so long. The details are the covenant curses coming true. Moses had warned, “You shall build a house, but you shall not dwell in it” (Deuteronomy 28:30), and the same verse foresaw wives taken by other men, as verse 12 says here.

Can a just God sweep up children in judgment? The whole nation fell under the judgment it had chosen, and a city’s fall strikes the young with the old. God takes no pleasure in it: “he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men” (Lamentations 3:33). And the judgment of each soul’s eternal destiny rests with him who does right (Genesis 18:25).

verseByVerse.quote: "For from the least to the greatest of them, everyone is greedy for unjust gain; and from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely. They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone, from the least to the greatest, is greedy and dishonest, and the religious leaders treat the nation’s deep wound as a scratch, promising peace where there is none.

From the least to the greatest. Two phrases take in everyone: “from the least to the greatest”, and “from prophet to priest”. When the leadership is corrupt there is nowhere left to appeal.

Peace, peace. Verse 14 describes a permanent temptation. The wound is real; the treatment is a clean bandage over an infected cut and a reassuring word. Why heal lightly? Because it is what the patient wants, because the true diagnosis is unbearable to deliver, and because the healer is thanked for it in the short term. Micah heard the same men: “yet they lean on the LORD and say, ‘Is not the LORD in the midst of us? No disaster shall come upon us’” (Micah 3:11).

The wound or the feeling. The test for any preaching, counselling or friendship is whether it deals with the wound or only with the feeling about the wound. A gospel that never mentions sin is a bandage over an infection, and its kindness is an illusion that costs the patient everything.

What peace really is. When we say we are at peace, we usually mean we feel calm, and the false prophets dealt in that kind: a feeling produced by not looking at the wound. Peace in the Bible, shalom, is first a state of affairs, things actually put right, beginning between us and God. You can feel calm while the infection spreads, and you can have real peace while you still hurt. So God’s peace never comes by ignoring the wound. It came by someone taking it: “upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). The prophets of Jerusalem said the injury was slight; the gospel says it was so deep that the Son of God bore it, and that it is truly healed. When you reach for calm, ask not “Do I feel settled?” but “Is the wound dealt with?” Bring Christ the sin you would rather bandage, name it, and rest in the peace he has made (Romans 5:1). See Peace.

Peace and security. Paul saw the same false peace at the end of history: “While people are saying, ‘There is peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman” (1 Thessalonians 5:3). The reassurance sounds kindest just before the disaster falls.

verseByVerse.quote: Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush. Therefore they shall fall among those who fall; at the time that I punish them, they shall be overthrown," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people and their leaders have done shameful things without the least shame, and so they will fall with everyone else when God punishes.

They did not know how to blush. Not that they refused to be ashamed; they had lost the ability. Shame is a nerve ending, and a conscience can lose feeling the way a limb does. The loss is quiet and is usually mistaken for maturity or confidence. Paul describes the end of the same process: people “whose consciences are seared” (1 Timothy 4:2).

They shall fall among those who fall. The sentence is flat. There will be no special category for religious leaders; the men who assured everyone of peace go down with the people they reassured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — Ask for the Ancient Paths
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God offers his people the old road home and the rest it brings, and they flatly refuse it, so no costly worship can turn the judgment aside. He tells them to stand at the crossroads and ask for the ancient paths, where they will find rest for their souls, and they answer, “We will not walk in it” (v. 16). He sets watchmen to sound the trumpet, and they will not listen (v. 17). So the nations and the earth are called to witness the disaster that is the fruit of their own schemes, because they rejected his law (vv. 18–19). Imported incense and burnt offerings will not please him; instead the road they refused will be strewn with stumbling blocks (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: The old way is not nostalgia but the road that leads home, and refusing it is a decision, not an accident.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Stand by the roads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, 'We will not walk in it.' I set watchmen over you, saying, 'Pay attention to the sound of the trumpet!' But they said, 'We will not pay attention.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells his people to stop at the crossroads, ask for the old, proven way he gave them, and walk in it to find rest; they refuse both the way and the watchmen who warn them.

Stand by the roads, and look. Four commands, the cure for everything this chapter has described. Stand: stop moving long enough to think. Look: consider the roads in front of you. Ask: for the old paths, which means asking someone who knows them. Walk: because knowing the way home and standing at the junction are not the same as going.

The ancient paths. Not nostalgia for an older decade, but the ways God gave the people he had brought out of Egypt and made his own, older than the fashion of any era. They were never a ladder up to him but the road home with him, and the promise attached is not success but rest.

Find rest for your souls. Jesus takes this exact phrase and offers it in his own name: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). The ancient path, it turns out, is a person. He walked it without one false step, in the place of people who had said “We will not walk in it”, and his obedience is counted to those who come to him (Romans 5:19). The walking that follows is not by willpower: those who belong to him “walk by the Spirit” (Galatians 5:16), and when they stray the same voice calls them back to the road.

Why does more choice leave us less at rest? Careers, cities, partners, beliefs, even identities are now ours to choose, and keep choosing, and we were promised this would make us free. In some ways it has. But the psychologist Barry Schwartz, in The Paradox of Choice, gathered evidence that beyond a certain point more options leave people more anxious and less satisfied, always wondering about the road not taken. Jeremiah’s word is neither “choose whatever feels right” nor “never choose at all”. It is “ask”: there is a good way, older than our moods, and rest is found by walking in it. That sounds like a loss of freedom until you notice that the one who offers rest came out to the crossroads to fetch us. Rest is not in keeping every option open; it is in belonging to him.

How do I ask for the ancient paths? Take the four verbs into your next real crossroads: a job offer, a move, money, a marriage under strain. Stand. Take an evening to pray before the momentum chooses for you. Look. Write the roads down honestly, with where each is likely to lead in five years. Ask. Open the Scriptures first, since “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105), and then ask an older believer who has walked that way: “Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith” (Hebrews 13:7). Walk. Once the good way is clear, take the first step this week. And when you have wandered, do not stand at the junction despising yourself. The path is a person, who said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), and he walks it with you.

We will not pay attention. The refusal is a decision, not a lack of information. The watchmen are the prophets, and what the people resent is an alarm, which wakes people who would rather sleep on. Hebrews draws the line from this refusal to ours: “See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven” (Hebrews 12:25). The watchmen of Jeremiah’s day spoke for God; the voice now is the Son’s.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore hear, O nations, and know, O congregation, what will happen to them. Hear, O earth; behold, I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices, because they have not paid attention to my words; and as for my law, they have rejected it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls the nations and the whole earth to witness that the coming disaster is simply the harvest of Judah’s own schemes, because it rejected his word and his law.

The fruit of their devices. The nations are called as witnesses, and the sentence is described as what grew from the seed Judah planted. God’s judgment is often the ripening of what people have themselves sown (Galatians 6:7).

As for my law, they have rejected it. Judah was not a people who lacked the law but a people who had it and threw it aside.

verseByVerse.quote: What use to me is frankincense that comes from Sheba, or sweet cane from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, nor your sacrifices pleasing to me. Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will lay before this people stumbling blocks against which they shall stumble; fathers and sons together, neighbor and friend shall perish.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Expensive imported incense and lavish sacrifices are worthless to God from people who refuse to obey him, so he will put stumbling blocks in their way and families will fall together.

Frankincense that comes from Sheba. Frankincense came by caravan from Sheba in south-west Arabia, and fragrant cane, probably from as far as India, went into the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23): the best available, and no use to God. The prophets say this repeatedly (“I have had enough of burnt offerings of rams”, Isaiah 1:11; “I hate, I despise your feasts”, Amos 5:21; “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice”, Hosea 6:6), and it is never an attack on worship as such. It is the refusal to accept worship as a substitute for obedience. Generous giving and faithful attendance can both be ways of trying to buy God off.

The offering God accepts. The one offering that fully pleased God was the obedience of his Son, who came saying, “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7), and offered himself. Our worship is acceptable through him, never in place of obeying.

Stumbling blocks. The road they refused to walk becomes a road they cannot walk. Grace refused long enough turns into obstacles, and whole families go down together.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The refining fire of judgment is coming, and it will only show that God’s people are worthless metal. A cruel, merciless nation is approaching from the far north, roaring like the sea and drawn up for battle against Zion (vv. 22–23). The people hear the news and go limp with fear; the roads are unsafe and terror is on every side, so they are told to mourn as for an only son (vv. 24–26). God has made Jeremiah an assayer of his people, and the test shows bronze and iron, not silver (vv. 27–28). The bellows blow and the lead burns away, but the wicked are not removed, and they are called “rejected silver” (vv. 29–30).
verseByVerse.theology: The metal is tested honestly and fails; only a better refining, and a better price, can save such people.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Behold, a people is coming from the north country, a great nation is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth. They lay hold on bow and javelin; they are cruel and have no mercy; the sound of them is like the roaring sea; they ride on horses, set in array as a man for battle, against you, O daughter of Zion!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great and merciless army is coming from the far north, roaring like the sea and drawn up for battle against Jerusalem.

The sound of them is like the roaring sea. An army heard before it is seen, like surf. “Cruel and have no mercy” is the plain character of ancient warfare, and God is telling his people the truth about what is coming rather than letting them imagine a manageable version.

The same words against Babylon. Near the end of the book the same description is turned on Babylon herself: a people from the north, cruel and without mercy, riding “against you, O daughter of Babylon!” (50:42). The God who sends an army against Zion will in time send one against Zion’s destroyer. No nation God uses to judge others is itself exempt from judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: We have heard the report of it; our hands fall helpless; anguish has taken hold of us, pain as of a woman in labor. Go not out into the field, nor walk on the road, for the enemy has a sword; terror is on every side. O daughter of my people, put on sackcloth, and roll in ashes; make mourning as for an only son, most bitter lamentation, for suddenly the destroyer will come upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the news of the invader the people’s courage collapses; terror is everywhere, and Jerusalem is told to mourn as bitterly as for an only son.

Our hands fall helpless. For the first time the people are not arguing. The bravado of chapter 5 is gone; it took the sound of the army to silence it.

Terror is on every side. The phrase becomes a refrain in this book, and later a nickname thrown at Jeremiah himself (20:10). Here it is simply life under siege: going to the field and walking the road have become impossible.

Put on sackcloth, and roll in ashes. The ordinary signs of mourning, called for in advance.

Mourning as for an only son. The loss of an only son was the end of a family line and every hope with it. Zechariah saw where that mourning would finally be directed: “when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child” (Zechariah 12:10). The grief God prescribes for Jerusalem’s ruin becomes the grief of Jerusalem’s repentance, when it recognises the Son it rejected. John saw that verse fulfilled at the cross (John 19:37).

verseByVerse.quote: "I have made you a tester of metals among my people, that you may know and test their ways. They are all stubbornly rebellious, going about with slanders; they are bronze and iron; all of them act corruptly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has appointed Jeremiah to test his people like an assayer tests metal, and the result is base metal: stubborn rebels, slanderers, corrupt through and through.

A tester of metals. A new picture for the prophet’s work. He is an assayer: the man who takes a sample, heats it and reports what the metal actually is. Preaching tests people. The same word that softens one heart hardens another, and how people react shows what they are.

They are bronze and iron. The sample comes back as base metal: useful, but not the silver this refining was meant to produce.

Going about with slanders. The corruption is not only in the temple and the courts. It is in ordinary conversation, the steady traffic of reputations damaged in the street.

verseByVerse.quote: The bellows blow fiercely; the lead is consumed by the fire; in vain the refining goes on, for the wicked are not removed. Rejected silver they are called, for the LORD has rejected them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fire of disaster has been applied to the limit and has purified nothing, so the people are called rejected silver, because the LORD has rejected them.

In vain the refining goes on. Refiners used lead to draw impurities out of silver. Here the bellows roar, the lead burns away, and nothing pure emerges. The fire is the long series of disasters God has already sent. Suffering refines some people and hardens others, and the difference is not in the fire but in what is put into it.

A refiner who does not fail. Malachi promised a different refiner: “He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver” (Malachi 3:3). Where the fire of disaster could only expose the metal, the Lord who comes to his temple will actually purify it.

Rejected silver. The chapter ends with the assayer’s certificate: metal that failed the test, put aside. That is why the New Testament’s language of redemption lands with such force. Peter tells Christians they were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Rejected silver cannot buy anything. But rejected people can be bought back, by a price that does not come from the furnace at all.

6.title: Peace, Peace, When There Is No Peace
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 6 closes the first great block of Jeremiah’s early preaching (chapters 2 to 6). The invader from the north, first heard in chapter 4, now has Jerusalem surrounded, and the next chapter takes the prophet to the temple gate.

The message. Judgment is at the walls, and God is still warning. His people are wounded to the heart, and their leaders cover the wound with “Peace, peace”; God points them to the old road where they would find rest, and they say, “We will not walk in it.” The fire of trouble has only shown what they are: silver that will not refine.

Why it was said. Judah’s prophets and priests were telling a greedy, oppressive nation that all was well, and the people were content to believe them, offering costly incense in place of obedience (see the introduction). Jeremiah had to make them hear the army before it arrived.

How the chapter makes its case. First the siege: the alarm sounds from the hills, enemy commanders pitch round the city like shepherds round a pasture, and God himself orders the ramp built against a city full of oppression, yet still says, “Be warned” (vv. 1–8). Then the reason no one escapes: their ears are closed, everyone is greedy, and the leaders heal the wound lightly, unable even to blush (vv. 9–15). Then the offer refused: ask for the ancient paths and find rest, and the answer is no, so incense from Sheba will not help (vv. 16–21). Last, the army like the roaring sea, the city mourning as for an only son, and the prophet as an assayer whose verdict is “rejected silver” (vv. 22–30).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes and by promise. The wound no false prophet could heal was healed by the one of whom Isaiah said, “with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5), and he made the peace the false prophets only announced (Romans 5:1). The “rest for your souls” of verse 16 is offered by Jesus in his own name (Matthew 11:29): the ancient path turns out to be a person. And silver the fire could not purify is redeemed with “the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19).

For us. Distrust any word, from a pulpit or from your own heart, that calls a real wound slight. Bring the sin you would rather bandage to Christ and let him deal with it. And at your next crossroads, stand, look, ask and walk: the good way is older than our moods, and he walks it with you.
6.theology:
God directs the armies that punish his people (v. 6), and warns even while the siege ramp rises (v. 8). Spiritual deadness shows itself as an inability to hear and a distaste for God's word (v. 10).

False ministry treats a deep wound lightly and calls it peace (v. 14); true ministry names the wound. The remedy is the old way God gave, and the rest it promises is fulfilled in Christ's invitation (v. 16). Worship offered as a substitute for obedience is rejected (v. 20).

Judgment is often the ripening of what people themselves sowed (v. 19). Suffering refines some and hardens others (vv. 27-29), and those who fail the test are bought back, if at all, by a price that does not come out of the furnace: the blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18-19).
6.examples: A clean bandage over an infected wound, with a reassuring word, is still the most tempting kind of ministry, because everyone thanks the healer for a while. A conscience can lose feeling the way a limb does, and the loss is usually mistaken for confidence. And it is possible to stand at the junction knowing the way home, and still not walk it.

keyVerse.quote: Stand by the roads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, ‘We will not walk in it.’
keyVerse.note: In a chapter of sieges and wounds, this is God’s offer, and its refusal is the tragedy of the book in one line. The way home was known, near and good, and the rest it promised is the rest Jesus offers in his own name (Matthew 11:29). The verse asks every reader the same question: will you walk in it?

6.reflection:
Even with the siege ramp going up, God says, “Be warned, O Jerusalem” (v. 8). What does it tell you about God that he keeps warning when judgment is so close?

The false prophets healed the wound “lightly” with “Peace, peace” (v. 14). Where are you, or the people around you, tempted to treat a real wound lightly? What is the difference between feeling calm and having the peace Christ made?

Verse 10 says the word of the LORD gave the people no pleasure. How is your appetite for God’s word at present? What helps it return?

Take a real decision in front of you and walk it through the four verbs of verse 16: stand, look, ask, walk. Whom could you ask, and what would walking in the good way look like this week?

7.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD:<sup>2</sup>"Stand in the gate of the LORD's house, and proclaim there this word, and say, Hear the word of the LORD, all you men of Judah who enter these gates to worship the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Amend your ways and your deeds, and I will let you dwell in this place.<sup>4</sup>Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.'<sup>5</sup>"For if you truly amend your ways and your deeds, if you truly execute justice one with another,<sup>6</sup>if you do not oppress the sojourner, the fatherless, or the widow, or shed innocent blood in this place, and if you do not go after other gods to your own harm,<sup>7</sup>then I will let you dwell in this place, in the land that I gave of old to your fathers forever.<sup>8</sup>"Behold, you trust in deceptive words to no avail.<sup>9</sup>Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, make offerings to Baal, and go after other gods that you have not known,<sup>10</sup>and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!'—only to go on doing all these abominations?<sup>11</sup>Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I myself have seen it, declares the LORD.<sup>12</sup>Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did to it because of the evil of my people Israel.<sup>13</sup>And now, because you have done all these things, declares the LORD, and when I spoke to you persistently you did not listen, and when I called you, you did not answer,<sup>14</sup>therefore I will do to the house that is called by my name, and in which you trust, and to the place that I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.<sup>15</sup>And I will cast you out of my sight, as I cast out all your kinsmen, all the offspring of Ephraim.<sup>16</sup>"As for you, do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer for them, and do not intercede with me, for I will not hear you.<sup>17</sup>Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?<sup>18</sup>The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven. And they pour out drink offerings to other gods, to provoke me to anger.<sup>19</sup>Is it I whom they provoke? declares the LORD. Is it not themselves, to their own shame?<sup>20</sup>Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, my anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place, upon man and beast, upon the trees of the field and the fruit of the ground; it will burn and not be quenched."<sup>21</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh.<sup>22</sup>For in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices.<sup>23</sup>But this command I gave them: 'Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. And walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.'<sup>24</sup>But they did not obey or incline their ear, but walked in their own counsels and the stubbornness of their evil hearts, and went backward and not forward.<sup>25</sup>From the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have persistently sent all my servants the prophets to them, day after day.<sup>26</sup>Yet they did not listen to me or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck. They did worse than their fathers.<sup>27</sup>"So you shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you. You shall call to them, but they will not answer you.<sup>28</sup>And you shall say to them, 'This is the nation that did not obey the voice of the LORD their God, and did not accept discipline; truth has perished; it is cut off from their lips.<sup>29</sup>"'Cut off your hair and cast it away; raise a lamentation on the bare heights, for the LORD has rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath.'<sup>30</sup>"For the sons of Judah have done evil in my sight, declares the LORD. They have set their detestable things in the house that is called by my name, to defile it.<sup>31</sup>And they have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind.<sup>32</sup>Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it will no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter; for they will bury in Topheth, because there is no room elsewhere.<sup>33</sup>And the dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds of the air, and for the beasts of the earth, and none will frighten them away.<sup>34</sup>And I will silence in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, for the land shall become a waste.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Trusting the temple cannot save a people who will not change their lives. Jeremiah is sent to stand at the gate of the LORD’s house and speak to the crowds on their way in to worship (vv. 1–2). His message is simple: amend your ways and you may stay in the land, but do not trust the chant “the temple of the LORD”, as if God’s house made them safe whatever they did (vv. 3–4). Then God spells out what amendment means: honest justice between neighbours, no oppression of the stranger, the fatherless or the widow, no innocent blood, no other gods (vv. 5–6). Do that, and the land given of old is still theirs (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: A building, however holy, guarantees nothing; God attaches his promise to repentance and to the treatment of the weak.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Stand in the gate of the LORD's house, and proclaim there this word, and say, Hear the word of the LORD, all you men of Judah who enter these gates to worship the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends Jeremiah to the temple gate to preach to the worshippers as they come in.

Stand in the gate of the LORD’s house. Everyone coming through those gates believes he is doing the right thing, and the worship itself is commanded: a harder congregation than pagans.

What it cost. Chapter 26 tells this sermon again and shows what it cost: priests and prophets seized him and said, “You shall die!” (26:8). It adds the instruction that made it so dangerous: “do not hold back a word” (26:2). The easiest way to survive a sermon like this is to leave out the paragraph that will cost you, and Jeremiah was told in advance not to. Chapter 26 also dates it “in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim” (26:1), about 609 BC, just after good King Josiah had been killed at Megiddo, when the reform he had led was already unravelling under his son.
verseByVerse.note: Chapter 26 dates the sermon to the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign (26:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Amend your ways and your deeds, and I will let you dwell in this place. Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the people change how they live, God will let them stay in the land; but repeating that the temple is God’s house will not save them.

Amend your ways and your deeds. The offer is unchanged from chapter 4: change, and you may stay. God is naming a condition, not an unavoidable fate, and the condition is conduct, not ceremony.

The temple of the LORD. Three times, like a slogan at a rally: God lives here, and he will never let this city fall, because his own house is in it. A century earlier God had indeed spared Jerusalem from Assyria in Hezekiah’s day (Isaiah 37:33–35), and the people had turned that mercy into a guarantee. God calls the chant “deceptive words”, though every word of it was true. What made it deceptive was what they did with the truth: used it as a reason to feel safe while living as they pleased.

Our own chants. The easiest error in the world to repeat. A denomination, a confession, a conversion experience, a baptism, a family heritage: all good, and all capable of becoming a chant that shields a person from the question of how he actually lives. Jesus finished the Sermon on the Mount on this note: the man who hears and does not do is building on sand, “and great was the fall of it” (Matthew 7:27).

verseByVerse.quote: "For if you truly amend your ways and your deeds, if you truly execute justice one with another, if you do not oppress the sojourner, the fatherless, or the widow, or shed innocent blood in this place, and if you do not go after other gods to your own harm, then I will let you dwell in this place, in the land that I gave of old to your fathers forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Real change means justice between neighbours, protection for the stranger, the fatherless and the widow, no shedding of innocent blood and no other gods; then God will let his people live in the land he gave them.

If you truly execute justice. The list begins with justice “one with another”: ordinary dealings between neighbours. Then three groups: the sojourner, the immigrant with no family network; the fatherless; the widow. In that society these three had no one to take their case. God names them every time, and makes his continued presence with the nation turn on how they are treated. The word “truly” comes twice, because justice can be done only for show.

Innocent blood, and other gods. Only last comes the matter of other gods. A modern reader expects a religious checklist; God gives a mostly social one, without making devotion to him any less important. He refuses to let the two be separated. A church that is orthodox on Sunday and indifferent to the vulnerable on Monday has failed the half of the test God put first. And idolatry is “to your own harm”: false gods damage the people who serve them.

The land that I gave of old. The land was given before any condition was laid down, and the gift was still on offer to a generation that had done nothing to keep it. That is the order for the Christian reader too. We take up the cause of the stranger and the widow because God first took up ours, and the Spirit he has given turns that mercy outward (Galatians 5:22).

What this looks like. The New Testament carries the concern straight over: “Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27). Deal straight. Justice “one with another” starts with the invoice you send, the reference you write and the tenant you rent to. Learn one name. Get to know one newcomer, the family from overseas at the school gate or the student far from home, and have them round for a meal. Visit. Put the widow from church in your diary, not just your prayers, and the single parent who has not had an evening off in months. Speak up. When someone with no one behind them is pushed aside, be the person who takes their case. We do this not to keep our place with God but because we were the strangers once: “you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). Christ found us with no one to plead for us, and pleaded for us himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — As I Did to Shiloh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will destroy his own house rather than let it shelter people who use it as cover for their sins. The worshippers break the Ten Commandments, then come to the temple saying “We are delivered!” and go out to do it all again (vv. 8–10). They have made God’s house a robbers’ den, the hideout where thieves feel safe, and God has seen it (v. 11). So they are sent to look at Shiloh, where God first set his name and which he gave up to ruin because of Israel’s evil (v. 12). Because they would not listen when he called, he will do the same to this house, and cast them out of his sight as he cast out Ephraim (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology: The place God chose can be destroyed by God: Shiloh is the precedent, and the temple is not exempt.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, you trust in deceptive words to no avail. Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, make offerings to Baal, and go after other gods that you have not known, and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!'—only to go on doing all these abominations?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people break God’s commandments one after another, then come to his house, claim to be safe, and go out to do it all again. Worship has become what keeps the sin going.

Will you steal, murder, commit adultery? The list is the Ten Commandments, laid out like charges in a court. Then they go from the sin straight to the service, saying, “We are delivered!”, and out again to repeat it. The language of rescue is being used as an insurance policy.

Only to go on doing all these abominations. This is the sting. Worship had become the thing that made the sin sustainable. Confession with no intention to stop is not repentance; it is a way of keeping the sin going.

Continue in sin that grace may abound? Paul met the same logic in the church and answered it the same way: “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?” (Romans 6:1–2). Grace used as permission to keep sinning has been misunderstood at the root. The cross that forgives sin is also the death of the old life that loved it.

verseByVerse.quote: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I myself have seen it, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people have turned God’s house into a robbers’ hideout, a place to feel safe after doing wrong, and God has seen it all.

A den of robbers. A den is not where robbers rob. It is the cave they retreat to afterwards, where they feel safe and divide the takings. That is what the temple had become: they did their damage in the city and came here to be secure.

Behold, I myself have seen it. The last clause removes every hiding place: “He who formed the eye, does he not see?” (Psalm 94:9). The worshippers imagined that what happened in the city stayed in the city. God saw both, and how they were connected.

Christ in the temple. Six centuries later Jesus walked into the same courts, overturned the tables and quoted this verse. Mark gives the fuller form: “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers” (Mark 11:17). He joined Isaiah’s promise of what the temple was for (Isaiah 56:7) to Jeremiah’s verdict on what it had become, and, like Jeremiah, he foretold that the building would come down (Mark 13:2). But he did more than repeat Jeremiah: he spoke of his own body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21). The meeting place of God and the nations would no longer be a building but himself.
verseByVerse.note: Luke records the same saying (Luke 19:46).

verseByVerse.quote: Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did to it because of the evil of my people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends the people to look at the ruins of Shiloh, where his name first dwelt, to see what he did to a holy place when his people treated it as a charm.

Go now to my place that was in Shiloh. God sends them on a field trip. Shiloh was where the tabernacle stood for generations before the temple was built. In Eli’s day the ark was carried out of Shiloh into battle as a lucky charm, and “the ark of God was captured” (1 Samuel 4:11). The psalm records the end of it: “He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where he dwelt among mankind” (Psalm 78:60).

Close enough to walk to. The ruins were about twenty miles north. That is what God does to a holy place treated as a lucky charm.
verseByVerse.note: Shiloh had been destroyed, probably by the Philistines after the battle of 1 Samuel 4.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, because you have done all these things, declares the LORD, and when I spoke to you persistently you did not listen, and when I called you, you did not answer, therefore I will do to the house that is called by my name, and in which you trust, and to the place that I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the people ignored God’s persistent call, he will do to the temple they trust in exactly what he did to Shiloh.

In which you trust. Misplaced trust is not protected by being religious trust. If anything it is treated more severely, because it uses God’s own gifts as a shield against him.

When I called you, you did not answer. The history that led here is a conversation that only went one way. Isaiah gives the same reason for the same sentence: “because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen” (Isaiah 65:12). Judgment in Scripture is rarely sudden. It is the end of a long, unanswered call.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will cast you out of my sight, as I cast out all your kinsmen, all the offspring of Ephraim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will drive Judah out of his presence just as he drove out the northern kingdom.

All the offspring of Ephraim. Ephraim is the northern kingdom, gone a century before. Judah had watched it happen (3:8) and concluded that it could not happen to them, because they had the temple. God says the precedent stands.

Cast out of my sight. The phrase has an old shape. The first human beings were sent out of God’s garden: “He drove out the man” (Genesis 3:24). Exile in the Bible is always a small repetition of Eden lost, removal from the place where God had made himself present. That is why the promise of return, when it comes, is always more than a promise of land: it is a promise of God’s presence again, kept at last in the one called “Immanuel (which means, God with us)” (Matthew 1:23).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–20 — Do Not Pray for This People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people have gone so far that even prayer for them is now refused. God tells Jeremiah not to intercede for this nation, because he will not hear (v. 16). Look at what is happening in every street: whole families working together, children gathering wood, fathers lighting the fire and mothers kneading dough, to bake cakes for the queen of heaven and pour drink offerings to other gods (vv. 17–18). Yet the harm falls chiefly on themselves, to their own shame (v. 19), and God’s anger will be poured out on people, animals, trees and crops, a fire that will not be put out (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The forbidding of intercession is deeply solemn, and even it is framed by the fact that sin destroys the sinner first.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer for them, and do not intercede with me, for I will not hear you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God forbids Jeremiah to pray for his people, because their judgment is now settled and God will not listen.

Do not pray for this people. This verse is aimed at the intercessor rather than the guilty. The prohibition comes three times in this book (11:14; 14:11), which suggests Jeremiah kept doing it anyway; in chapter 14 he is still pleading (14:7–9, 19–22).

What does it mean? Not that God has stopped being merciful; the same book will promise a new covenant. It means that a point can be reached where judgment is settled and further pleading will not turn it aside; and God tells his prophet in advance, so that when the city falls Jeremiah will not think his prayers failed.

Sin that leads to death. John writes something in the same territory: “There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that” (1 John 5:16). These are not verses to wield against people we have given up on; nobody can know how another person stands with God. They are warnings about how serious sustained refusal is, and they are rare precisely because the normal command is to pray for everyone.

Should I stop praying for someone hardened? No. Jeremiah received a direct word from God about a nation whose sentence was already fixed; no one today receives such a word about a son, a friend or a country. Our standing command is to pray “for all people” (1 Timothy 2:1), even for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44), and many parents have prayed for years over a child who seemed beyond reach and seen that child come home. And the prophet who was told to stop interceding points to an Intercessor who was never told to stop. Christ prayed for the men who crucified him (Luke 23:34), and “he always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven. And they pour out drink offerings to other gods, to provoke me to anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whole families work together at idolatry: children gather wood, fathers light the fire and mothers bake cakes for the queen of heaven, deliberately provoking God.

The children gather wood. It is a family scene, and that is what makes it terrible: children collecting kindling, fathers at the fire, mothers making the dough. Everyone has a job, and the whole household is at work on idolatry. It is cosy. It is also a very effective way to hand a religion to the next generation.

The queen of heaven returns. Decades later, after the city has burned, the survivors in Egypt will defend this exact practice to Jeremiah’s face: “we will do everything that we have vowed, make offerings to the queen of heaven”, because “then we had plenty of food, and prospered” (44:17). A religion taught round the family fire outlasts even the ruin it caused. That is a warning, and an encouragement: what Christian parents teach at their own table, in prayer and Scripture and the way they speak of Christ, goes as deep (Deuteronomy 6:6–7).

Uncertain wording. Who the queen of heaven was is not certain. She was most likely the Mesopotamian goddess Ishtar, known in Canaan as Astarte, a goddess of love and fertility associated with the evening star; some think of a Canaanite goddess such as Anat. The cakes seem to have been made in her image (44:19), and the rare Hebrew word for them may be borrowed from the language of Babylon.
verseByVerse.note: The “queen of heaven” was probably the Mesopotamian goddess Ishtar (Astarte).

verseByVerse.quote: Is it I whom they provoke? declares the LORD. Is it not themselves, to their own shame? Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, my anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place, upon man and beast, upon the trees of the field and the fruit of the ground; it will burn and not be quenched."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people think they are provoking God, but the harm falls on themselves; and his anger will be poured out on the whole land and everything in it.

Is it I whom they provoke? A question that corrects how we picture God’s anger. The damage of sin falls first on the sinner: “Is it not themselves, to their own shame?” His anger is not wounded pride; it is the response of love to people destroying themselves and their children.

Upon man and beast. The land itself suffers with the people, as in the vision of creation undone in chapter 4. Human sin never harms human beings only; and the creation that groans with us will be set free with the children of God (Romans 8:21).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God wanted from the beginning was not sacrifices but an obedient people, and they have refused him from the start. Let them heap up their offerings and eat the meat themselves, for at the exodus God’s first command was not about sacrifice but “Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people” (vv. 21–23). They went their own way, backward and not forward (v. 24). God sent his prophets day after day for centuries, and each generation was worse (vv. 25–26). Jeremiah too will be ignored, and must tell them that truth has perished from their lips and lament on the hilltops over the generation of God’s wrath (vv. 27–29).
verseByVerse.theology: Sacrifice was never meant to replace obedience, and centuries of persistent preaching have met a stiffened neck.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh. For in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this command I gave them: 'Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. And walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells his people to eat their sacrifices themselves, since what he asked for at the exodus was not offerings but obedience: listen to me, and I will be your God and you my people.

Eat the flesh. The tone is bitterly ironic. In the burnt offering the whole animal was burned to God; in other sacrifices the worshippers ate part of the meat. God says: put them all together and eat the lot yourselves. If the sacrifices mean nothing, they may as well be dinner.

What came first. This is not a denial that God gave the sacrificial law, which would contradict Leviticus, but a statement of what came first and what it was for. The founding word came “in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt”: rescue first, and then not a manual of offerings but a relationship. At Sinai the first words were “if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession” (Exodus 19:5), before a single law of sacrifice was given. The sacrifices were given inside that covenant to serve it, never to replace it.

One voice in the prophets. “To obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22). “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings” (Hosea 6:6). “Bring no more vain offerings”, and instead “learn to do good; seek justice, correct oppression; bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow’s cause” (Isaiah 1:13, 17). “But let justice roll down like waters” (Amos 5:24).

Obedience today. Attendance, giving, service and the right doctrinal words are all good, and all able to be offered instead of obedience. And none of us obeys that voice perfectly either. The one who did was the Son, who could say, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), and his obedience is counted to those who trust him (Romans 5:19). That does not make obedience optional; it makes it the glad answer of people already claimed, with a way back when they fail.

verseByVerse.quote: But they did not obey or incline their ear, but walked in their own counsels and the stubbornness of their evil hearts, and went backward and not forward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of listening, the people followed their own stubborn plans and went backward, not forward.

Backward and not forward. The whole history in four words. There is no standing still in this book: a people either walks in the way it is shown or drifts back from it.

Walked in their own counsels. The alternative to God’s voice is named exactly: not a rival god this time, but their own judgment. Proverbs puts the choice the same way: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5). Every drift backward starts with a person deciding he can find the way without being told.

verseByVerse.quote: From the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have persistently sent all my servants the prophets to them, day after day. Yet they did not listen to me or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck. They did worse than their fathers. "So you shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you. You shall call to them, but they will not answer you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For centuries God sent prophet after prophet, and each generation hardened itself more than the last; now Jeremiah is sent knowing in advance that he too will be ignored.

Persistently, day after day. That is God’s patience measured in messengers: not one warning ignored but a stream of them across generations, each one a mercy. A stiffened neck is the picture of an animal that will not turn its head to the rein. And “they did worse than their fathers”: each generation had the added evidence of what the last had suffered, and went further anyway.

But they will not listen to you. Here is a commission almost no one would accept: preach, and they will not listen. God tells his servant the outcome in advance, and still sends him. Jeremiah is not sent to be effective; he is sent to be faithful. Anyone serving in a hard place, a stagnant church, an indifferent family, is standing where Jeremiah stood, and the work will be judged by the standard given here.

The last messenger. Jesus told this history as a parable: a vineyard owner who sent servant after servant to his tenants, and last of all his son, saying, “They will respect my son” (Matthew 21:37). They killed him. The God who sent prophets “day after day” finally sent the one who was more than a prophet.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall say to them, 'This is the nation that did not obey the voice of the LORD their God, and did not accept discipline; truth has perished; it is cut off from their lips. "'Cut off your hair and cast it away; raise a lamentation on the bare heights, for the LORD has rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah is the nation that would not obey God or accept his correction, and truth has died among them; they are to mourn, for God has rejected the generation under his wrath.

Did not accept discipline. One charge explains the rest. Discipline, Hebrews says, “seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11). The pain was never the problem; the refusal to be trained by it was.

Truth has perished. Not merely that people tell lies, but that truth itself has died out of public life, so that no one expects it in a courtroom, a market or a temple. A society can survive a great deal of wickedness; it cannot survive the death of truth, because nothing can then be repaired.

Cut off your hair and cast it away. Cutting the hair was a public sign of grief (see mourning customs), and the bare heights were the hilltops where the idols were worshipped: hold the funeral at the scene of the sin.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The worst sin of all brings the worst judgment: God’s people have burned their own children, and the valley where they did it will be filled with their dead. They have set idols in the very house called by God’s name, and in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom they built the high places of Topheth to burn their sons and daughters, something God never commanded and that never entered his mind (vv. 30–31). So the valley will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, the dead will be buried there for lack of room elsewhere, and the birds will feed on the bodies unchased (vv. 32–33). The joyful voices of bride and bridegroom will fall silent (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: The valley where children were burned gives its name to the place of judgment, and the sound that ends is the sound of weddings.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the sons of Judah have done evil in my sight, declares the LORD. They have set their detestable things in the house that is called by my name, to defile it. And they have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah has defiled God’s house with idols and burned its own children in the valley of Hinnom, an evil God never commanded and never even conceived.

Their detestable things in the house. The idols are inside the temple now. The building they chanted about had been furnished with the very things that made it uninhabitable for God.

To burn their sons and their daughters. This is the lowest point of the book. In a ravine outside Jerusalem, parents were burning their children as offerings. The law had forbidden it plainly: “You shall not give any of your children to offer them to Molech” (Leviticus 18:21). Kings Ahaz and Manasseh had each burned a son as an offering (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6), and Josiah had defiled Topheth so that no one could do it again (2 Kings 23:10); after his death the fires were evidently lit once more.

Nor did it come into my mind. An almost unbearable phrase. Whatever these people told themselves about pleasing a god, it had no connection with the God who was speaking. Religion cut loose from what God has said does not drift toward kindness. (Did God not foresee it? He knows all things, Psalm 139:4. The phrase means that such a thing never came from him: he never willed it or commanded it, and it is utterly foreign to his heart.)

The Valley of Hinnom. See where this valley leads. The Valley of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom in Hebrew, Gehenna in Greek) became the New Testament word for hell itself; the name of a real ravine where children burned became the name for final judgment, the place Jesus described as one “where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched” (Mark 9:48).

What do we sacrifice our children to? Ask why loving parents in Jerusalem did it. Molech worship was a bargain: give the god what is most precious, and he will secure the harvest, the city, the family’s future. The parents were frightened people trying to buy security. Every idol makes that bargain sooner or later, and it always asks for the children. The father who gives his best years to the company and his leftover evenings to his son is making an offering. So is the parent who needs a child’s results to prove the family a success, or the home where the adults’ freedom always comes first. We do not use fire. We still make our children pay for our gods. The God of the Bible is the opposite. When he asked Abraham for his son, he stopped the knife (see the note on Genesis 22:1–2), and then he did what no idol would ever do: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32) is the one God who gives his child instead of taking ours.
verseByVerse.note: The name Topheth is probably linked to a word for a hearth or fireplace.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it will no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter; for they will bury in Topheth, because there is no room elsewhere. And the dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds of the air, and for the beasts of the earth, and none will frighten them away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The valley where children were sacrificed will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter and filled with Judah’s own dead, left unburied for the birds and beasts.

The Valley of Slaughter. The punishment takes the shape of the crime, as in 5:19. The valley where they killed their children becomes the valley where their own dead are buried, so many that the graveyards overflow into it. The renaming is God’s verdict written on the map. Jeremiah will stand in this valley again, holding a clay flask, and repeat it there (19:6): said twice, in two places, so that nobody could claim to have missed it.

None will frighten them away. To be left unburied was a terrible disgrace in that world (see burial customs), and there will not even be anyone left to wave off the birds. It is the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:26, almost word for word.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will silence in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, for the land shall become a waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will silence every sound of joy in Judah, even the voices of bride and bridegroom, for the land will become a waste.

The voice of the bride. The chapter ends with silence. Of all the sounds God could name as the mark of a living community, he chooses the voices of a bride and bridegroom: the sound of people betting on a future. It is how John describes the fall of Babylon at the end of the Bible: “the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more” (Revelation 18:23).

The voices restored. But this God later promises these same exiles that he will bring back into this ruined land the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride (33:11), because his purpose was never the silence. Jeremiah preached in the temple gate that the house would fall, and it did. And the one who quoted this sermon in the same courts went out and was himself put to death, so that the wedding could be held after all: the Bible ends with “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

7.title: The Temple Sermon: Do Not Trust in Deceptive Words
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 is Jeremiah’s famous temple sermon. Chapter 26 tells the same event from outside, dates it to about 609 BC, just after Josiah was killed, and reports that it nearly cost the prophet his life.

The message. God cannot be kept in a box, not even his own house. Judah believed that because the temple stood in Jerusalem, Jerusalem could not fall, whatever they did on the way in. God says that worship which shelters sin is a lie: he wants changed lives, justice for the weak and an obeying heart, and a holy place treated as a lucky charm will go the way of Shiloh.

Why it was said. Josiah’s reform had cleaned the temple but not the nation’s heart, and under his son the old sins came back while the services went on (see the introduction). The people stole, murdered and worshipped other gods, and then came to the temple chanting that they were safe.

How the chapter makes its case. At the temple gate Jeremiah calls the worshippers to amend their ways and stop trusting the chant “the temple of the LORD”, and spells out what amendment means: justice, care for the stranger, the fatherless and the widow (vv. 1–7). They break the commandments and then shelter in God’s house as robbers in a den, so they are sent to look at the ruins of Shiloh (vv. 8–15). Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for them while whole families bake cakes for the queen of heaven (vv. 16–20). God’s first word at the exodus was not sacrifice but “Obey my voice”, and prophet after prophet went unheard (vv. 21–29). Last, children burned at Topheth, the Valley of Slaughter, and the voices of bride and bridegroom silenced (vv. 30–34).

Where it leads. Chiefly by pattern, and by God’s character revealed in Christ. Six centuries later Jesus stood in the same courts, quoted verse 11, “a den of robbers”, and foretold the temple’s fall as Jeremiah had. Then he spoke of his own body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised (John 2:19–21). The meeting place of God and people is no longer a building but a person. And where the gods of Topheth took parents’ children, the true God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

For us. Ask what you are tempted to chant: a church, a baptism, a heritage, a conversion, true things used as a shield against how you live. Trust Christ himself, not the trappings of religion, and let him turn your worship into obedience, beginning with the stranger, the fatherless and the widow near you.
7.theology:
Religious privilege guarantees nothing: true words about God's house became deceptive words when used as a shield for unrepentance (vv. 4, 8; Matt 7:26-27). God ties his presence to repentance and to justice for the weakest (vv. 5-7), and refuses to let worship and ethics be separated (vv. 9-11).

Shiloh proves that God will destroy a place he chose when it is treated as a lucky charm (vv. 12-15). Sacrifice was given inside the covenant to serve obedience, never to replace it (vv. 21-23). Sin's damage falls first on the sinner (v. 19), and God's wrath is love's response to people destroying themselves and their children.

Prayer for a people can be forbidden when refusal has hardened (v. 16; 1 John 5:16), and faithfulness, not results, is the standard for the messenger (v. 27). Jesus took this sermon up in the same courts and went to his death outside its walls, so that the wedding joy silenced here might be restored (33:11).
7.examples: The hardest congregation is the one already on its way into church, and the most dangerous words are true ones used as a shield. A den is not where the robbery happens but where robbers feel safe afterwards, and any place of worship can become one. And a family with a job each, working together at the fire, can hand on idolatry as warmly as faith.

keyVerse.quote: Do not trust in these deceptive words: ‘This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.’
keyVerse.note: Every word of the chant was true, and that is what makes the verse so searching. True words about God became deceptive when used as a shield for a life that would not change. The verse exposes every religious privilege turned into a lucky charm, and it points to the true temple, Christ himself, in whom alone God meets sinners.

7.reflection:
The people’s slogan, “the temple of the LORD”, was true and yet deceptive (v. 4). What good things, such as a church, a baptism or a Christian upbringing, can we use in the same way? How can you tell when something good has become a shield?

God’s test of amendment begins with justice between neighbours and care for the stranger, the fatherless and the widow (vv. 5–7). Why does he put these first? Who are these people in your own setting?

Jesus quoted verse 11 when he cleared the temple, and spoke of his body as the true temple. How does knowing Christ as the place where we meet God change the way we think about church buildings, services and religious duty?

Verse 31 shows parents giving up their children to a god in the hope of security. In what ways do people today make their children pay for their idols? What does the God who gave his own Son say to that?
