verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gods Judah loved will watch, helpless, as their worshippers’ bones are laid out to rot. When the city falls, the bones of kings, officials, priests, prophets and ordinary people will be dragged from their tombs (v. 1) and spread before the sun, moon and stars they loved, served and worshipped, never to be gathered or buried, like dung on the ground (v. 2). And for those still alive in exile, scattered wherever God has driven them, life will be so bitter that they will prefer death (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The gods they served become the witnesses of their shame, and the living envy the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time, declares the LORD, the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of its officials, the bones of the priests, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the inhabitants of Jerusalem shall be brought out of their tombs. And they shall be spread before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and served, which they have gone after, and which they have sought and worshiped. And they shall not be gathered or buried. They shall be as dung on the surface of the ground. Death shall be preferred to life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family in all the places where I have driven them, declares the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bones of Judah’s leaders and people will be left unburied beneath the stars they worshipped, and the survivors will wish they were dead.

The bones shall be brought out of their tombs. Five times “the bones”, tolling through the sentence: kings, officials, priests, prophets, people. Death has levelled the hierarchy, and the invaders will loot the graves.

Which they have loved and served. Five verbs describe their devotion (loved, served, gone after, sought, worshipped), and then the bones are laid out under those same stars. The gods they gave their lives to will watch them rot, and do nothing, because they were only ever lights in the sky. This worship of the host of heaven had flourished under Manasseh, who built altars for it in the temple courts, and Josiah had torn those altars down (2 Kings 21:5; 23:4–5, 12); the bones under the stars expose a devotion the reform never uprooted.

Idols as audience. Idols do not merely fail to save; they become the audience of the disaster. Whatever a person has given himself to will be standing there at the end, mute.

Death shall be preferred to life. For the survivors, life becomes worse than death: a plain statement of what exile will feel like from inside. John sees the same condition at the end of history: “people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them” (Revelation 9:6). A world that has lost God can lose the will to live. Scripture names that darkness honestly, but it is not the last word: the same book carries God’s promise of “a future and a hope” (29:11).

If you long to die. If that describes how you feel, do not carry it alone. Tell a pastor or biblical counsellor, and see your doctor too; medicine, where needed, is no failure of faith. If you are in danger of harming yourself, call emergency services or a crisis line the same day. The God who heard Elijah say, “It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life” (1 Kings 19:4), answered with food, sleep and his own presence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people are refusing to do what every fallen man and every migrating bird does: come back. Anyone who falls gets up, and anyone who takes a wrong turn goes back, but Judah clings to its deceit, and no one stops to ask, “What have I done?” (vv. 4–6). The stork, the dove, the swallow and the crane keep their seasons, but God’s people do not know his ways (v. 7). They boast that they have the law, yet their scribes have made it a lie, and the wise who reject God’s word have no wisdom left (vv. 8–9). So the old sermon is preached again: greed everywhere, a deep wound healed lightly with “Peace, peace”, and no shame (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology: The instinct to get up after a fall has died, the birds, who keep their seasons, shame them, and even the Scriptures have been turned into a lie.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall say to them, Thus says the LORD: When men fall, do they not rise again? If one turns away, does he not return? Why then has this people turned away in perpetual backsliding? They hold fast to deceit; they refuse to return. I have paid attention and listened, but they have not spoken rightly; no man relents of his evil, saying, 'What have I done?' Everyone turns to his own course, like a horse plunging headlong into battle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People who fall get up again, but God’s people cling to their deceit and never stop to ask, “What have I done?”

When men fall, do they not rise again? Two questions from ordinary life, both expecting yes. A man who trips gets up; a traveller who takes a wrong turning goes back. Nobody lies in the road on principle, and nobody keeps walking the wrong way once he knows.

Perpetual backsliding. “Perpetual” is the sting: not a fall but a way of life; not a wrong turning but a direction. And they are holding tight to the wrong thing: “they hold fast to deceit”, clinging to what is destroying them.

What have I done? God has been listening, leaning in to catch one short sentence, and nobody says it. God is not waiting for a defence or a plan for improvement, but for the question people ask when they finally see their own behaviour from outside.

Two men who asked it. Two men in Luke asked it. The younger son in the far country “came to himself” and rehearsed his sentence: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke 15:17–18). The man at the back of the temple would not look up and prayed, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). Neither offered a defence. Each simply asked, in his own words, “What have I done?”, and each was received.

Like a horse plunging headlong into battle. Instead, everyone goes his own way. A warhorse in a charge cannot be reasoned with, cannot stop and will not turn: a life with speed, direction and no brakes.

verseByVerse.quote: Even the stork in the heavens knows her times, and the turtledove, swallow, and crane keep the time of their coming, but my people know not the rules of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Migrating birds come home on time, but God’s own people do not know his ways and will not return.

Even the stork in the heavens knows her times. Look up. The migrating birds leave and return on time, every year, without instruction. Creatures with no reasoning keep God’s calendar, and people made in his image do not know his ways. Isaiah said it with farm animals: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s crib, but Israel does not know” (Isaiah 1:3).

They keep the time of their coming. The birds come back, which is exactly what Judah would not do: “they refuse to return” (v. 5). A bird obeys the instinct to come home that God built into it. God’s people had his own word calling them home, and ignored it.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that one of the bird names is uncertain, as ancient bird names often are, and that “rules” may be rendered “just decrees”. The point does not depend on it.

verseByVerse.quote: "How can you say, 'We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us'? But behold, the lying pen of the scribes has made it into a lie. The wise men shall be put to shame; they shall be dismayed and taken; behold, they have rejected the word of the LORD, so what wisdom is in them?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah boasts of having God’s law, but its scholars have twisted it into a lie, and those who reject God’s word have no wisdom at all.

The law of the LORD is with us. Perfectly true and completely hollow: Josiah’s reform had rediscovered the book, and owning it had become their proof that all was well.

The lying pen of the scribes. The charge is aimed at the professionals. God does not accuse the scribes of losing the text but of turning it into something false, by the way they explained it, applied it and used it to approve what the nation wanted to do. Verses arranged to bless what God condemns, comfort detached from repentance, technical study that never asks for obedience: the pen is lying while every letter it copies is accurate. Anyone who teaches the Bible should read verse 8 once a year.

Twisted Scriptures. Peter warns of the same thing in the church: there are passages “which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures” (2 Peter 3:16). And Paul names the scribe alongside the wise man: “Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?” (1 Corinthians 1:20). Learning that has walked away from God’s word has not become neutral; it has become foolish, however many qualifications it holds. Jesus told the experts of his day that the Scriptures they searched “bear witness about me”, yet they would not come to him for life (John 5:39–40).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I will give their wives to others and their fields to conquerors, because from the least to the greatest everyone is greedy for unjust gain; from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely. They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace. Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush. Therefore they shall fall among the fallen; when I punish them, they shall be overthrown, says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the whole nation is greedy and its leaders still promise peace, everything will be lost to others and they will fall with the fallen.

The sermon repeated. These verses repeat 6:12–15 almost word for word, and the repetition is the message. The sermon has been preached; nothing has changed; so it is preached again, unaltered. Ezekiel used another image for the same men: prophets who say “‘Peace,’ when there is no peace” and then whitewash the flimsy wall the people have built, so that it looks sound (Ezekiel 13:10).

Saying it twice. A preacher who must say the same thing twice to the same people is not necessarily failing; here it was God’s idea.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — No Grapes on the Vine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God came looking for fruit and found none, and the people, too late, see that they are doomed. There are no grapes on the vine and no figs on the tree; even the leaves have withered, and his gifts are slipping away (v. 13). The people decide to shut themselves into the fortified towns and die, admitting at last that they have sinned, but they looked for peace and found terror (vv. 14–15). The snorting of the enemy’s horses is already heard from Dan in the far north, and the whole land shakes (v. 16). God is sending among them serpents that no charmer can control (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The harvest God looked for is not there, and the remedies people reach for are poison and panic.

verseByVerse.quote: When I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; even the leaves are withered, and what I gave them has passed away from them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God comes to his people for fruit and finds nothing, and the gifts he gave them are slipping away.

No grapes on the vine. God comes to his vineyard at harvest and finds nothing: no grapes, no figs, not even green leaves. And “what I gave them has passed away from them”: judgment often begins not with a blow but with good gifts quietly taken away.

Nothing but leaves. Jesus acted out something very like this verse on the road into Jerusalem, “seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf”, and when he came to it “he found nothing but leaves” (Mark 11:13). He told a parable about the patience that comes before the sentence: an owner who “came seeking fruit on it and found none”, and a vinedresser who pleaded, “Sir, let it alone this year also” (Luke 13:6–8). God’s inspection of his vineyard is never hasty. By Jeremiah’s day it had been going on for centuries.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the Hebrew here is uncertain; the opening words may mean that God gathers them in or that he makes an end of them. The barren vine is unmistakable either way.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do we sit still? Gather together; let us go into the fortified cities and perish there, for the LORD our God has doomed us to perish and has given us poisoned water to drink, because we have sinned against the LORD. We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people at last admit their sin, but instead of turning to God they give up and shut themselves in to die.

Why do we sit still? The people speak, and it is almost repentance. They name the cause correctly, “because we have sinned against the LORD”, and then act on despair rather than on that knowledge. Knowing your sin without hope produces a giving up that looks like humility and is not. The God they have sinned against is the one who still says “return”.

We looked for peace, but no good came. This is what the “Peace, peace” preaching of verse 11 finally delivers. People were promised healing and handed terror. False comfort is not a harmless kindness; there are casualties, and they are the ones who believed it.

Uncertain wording. “Poisoned water” uses a word for a bitter, poisonous plant whose identity is unknown; the sense is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: "The snorting of their horses is heard from Dan; at the sound of the neighing of their stallions the whole land quakes. They come and devour the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it. For behold, I am sending among you serpents, adders that cannot be charmed, and they shall bite you," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The enemy is already in the land, and God is sending serpents that no charmer can tame.

The snorting of their horses is heard from Dan. Sound again before sight: cavalry heard from Dan, the proverbial far north. The enemy is inside the country.

Adders that cannot be charmed. Snake charmers’ whole trade was managing danger, and these serpents cannot be charmed. There is a point at which the techniques that have always worked stop working.

The serpent lifted up. Many Christians have heard an echo here of the wilderness, where God once sent serpents among his rebellious people and then gave the remedy himself: “Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live” (Numbers 21:8). No charm, no technique: a look of trust at what God had provided. Jesus took that scene as a picture of his own death: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). Where no charmer can help, the lifted-up Son still can.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — Is There No Balm in Gilead?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet is heartbroken for a people who have run out of time and have refused the cure that was always available. His joy is gone and his heart is sick (v. 18). The people cry out across the land, “Is the LORD not in Zion?”, still trusting his presence, and God asks why, then, they provoked him with idols (v. 19). “The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved” (v. 20). Jeremiah feels their wound as his own (v. 21), and asks why, when there is balm in Gilead and a physician there, his people have not been healed (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The medicine exists and the doctor is available; what is missing is any willingness to be treated.

verseByVerse.quote: My joy is gone; grief is upon me; my heart is sick within me. Behold, the cry of the daughter of my people from the length and breadth of the land: "Is the LORD not in Zion? Is her King not in her?" "Why have they provoked me to anger with their carved images and with their foreign idols?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah is sick with grief as his people cry that God must still be in Zion, and God asks why, then, they serve idols.

My heart is sick within me. Joy gone, grief arrived, heart sick. He has been preaching this judgment for chapters, and it is making him ill. The man who speaks God’s hardest words is not hard himself.

Is the LORD not in Zion? The belief they have always relied on: he lives here; this cannot happen. God answers with a question: then why the carved images? Their confidence rested on his presence while their affections rested elsewhere. You cannot claim God as your security and treat him as optional.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the Hebrew of the first line of verse 18 is uncertain; what comes through is plain grief.

verseByVerse.quote: "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." For the wound of the daughter of my people is my heart wounded; I mourn, and dismay has taken hold on me. Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people’s time has run out; Jeremiah feels their wound as his own, and asks why, with the remedy close at hand, they are not healed.

The harvest is past. A haunting sentence, and it is the people’s own. The window for gathering has shut, the barns are not full, and winter is coming. Opportunity has a season, in health and relationships as in farming. Paul makes the same point with urgency rather than gloom: “now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). The sentence in Jeremiah is what it sounds like to say it too late.

For the wound of the daughter of my people. Jeremiah does not stand outside their loss: their wound is his wound. That shared wound points past him. Isaiah describes one who does not merely grieve over his people’s injury but carries it: “Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows” (Isaiah 53:4). The prophet’s broken heart is the faint outline beforehand; the Servant who takes the wound into himself is the reality.

Is there no balm in Gilead? Gilead, east of the Jordan, was known for a medicinal resin. Of course there is balm, and a physician. Then why is this patient not healed? The whole book has given the answer: because she will not be treated. The wound has been bandaged lightly by men who called it peace, and the physician who could heal it has been refused.

The physician who came. Jesus said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark 2:17). The one thing that keeps a person from the doctor is the conviction that nothing much is wrong. The African American spiritual answered Jeremiah’s question with a gospel yes: there is a balm in Gilead to make the wounded whole, and it is Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis already pictures traders carrying balm from Gilead down to Egypt (Gen 37:25).

8.title: Is There No Balm in Gilead?
8.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 8 continues straight on from the temple sermon of chapter 7 and its Valley of Slaughter. The prophet’s preaching now turns into lament, and the chapter ends with one of the most famous questions in the Bible, which opens the weeping of chapter 9.

The message. A people can have God’s law, God’s temple and God’s prophet, and still refuse the one thing that would heal them: turning back. Everyone who falls gets up, and even the migrating birds come home, but Judah will not; it clings to its lies, never asks “What have I done?”, and so the cure that was always there goes unused. The harvest passes, and they are not saved.

Why it was said. Judah boasted, “the law of the LORD is with us”, while its scholars bent that law into a lie and its prophets kept promising peace (see the introduction). Disaster was already on the northern horizon, and the people still thought God would never let Zion fall.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with a graveyard: the bones of kings, priests, prophets and people laid out unburied under the stars they worshipped (vv. 1–3). Then the puzzle of a people who will not do what everyone and everything else does: get up, turn back, come home; they hold the Scriptures and make them lie, and preach “Peace, peace” again (vv. 4–12). God comes for fruit and finds none; the people shut themselves in to die, and the enemy’s horses are heard from Dan (vv. 13–17). Last, the prophet’s grief: the harvest is past, his heart is wounded with their wound, and he asks why, with balm in Gilead and a physician there, his people are not healed (vv. 18–22).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by pattern. The answer to Jeremiah’s question is Christ, the physician who came “not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark 2:17), and who did not only grieve over his people’s wound like Jeremiah but carried it: “with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). The serpents no charmer could manage (v. 17) recall the bronze serpent lifted up in the wilderness, which Jesus took as a picture of his cross (John 3:14–15).

For us. The physician is here and the balm is free, and the only thing that keeps anyone from healing is refusing to be treated. Ask the question Judah would not ask, “What have I done?”, and bring the answer to Christ while it is still “the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).
8.theology:
Idols cannot save and end as witnesses of their worshippers' ruin (vv. 1-2). Repentance begins with a question almost no one asks: What have I done? (v. 6). Creation keeps God's order while his people do not (v. 7; Isa 1:3).

Scripture can be turned into a lie by the way it is taught, without a word being altered (v. 8), and comfort preached over an untreated wound destroys those who believe it (vv. 11, 15; Ezek 13:10).

Opportunity has a season, and it can close (v. 20; 2 Cor 6:2). The remedy exists, for there is balm and there is a physician (v. 22), and the barrier is the refusal to be treated (Mark 2:17). The prophet does not stand outside the grief he announces (vv. 18, 21).
8.examples: Whatever a person gives himself to will be standing there at the end, as silent as the stars over the bones of their worshippers. A life can become a warhorse in a charge, all speed and direction with no brakes, and the four words that would stop it, What have I done?, are the ones hardest to say. And a teacher can quote every letter of Scripture accurately and still teach a lie with it.

keyVerse.quote: Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s grief gathers into this question. The remedy existed and the physician was near, so the failure lay not in the cure but in the patient who would not be treated. The gospel answers it: Christ is the physician who came for the sick, and by his own wounds his people are healed.

8.reflection:
God says he listened for one sentence and no one said it: “What have I done?” (v. 6). Why is that question so hard to ask honestly? What happens when we do ask it, as the prodigal son and the tax collector did (Luke 15:18; 18:13)?

The people said, “the law of the LORD is with us”, while their scholars turned it into a lie (v. 8). How can people own and even study the Bible and still make it say what they want? How can we guard against that?

“The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved” (v. 20). What opportunities have a season? How does this verse give urgency to the gospel without driving us to despair?

Jeremiah feels his people’s wound as his own (v. 21), and points beyond himself to the one who carried our wounds. Whose wound do you need to feel as your own this week, and how could you bring them to the Physician?

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!<sup>2</sup>Oh that I had in the desert a travelers' lodging place, that I might leave my people and go away from them! verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Oh That My Head Were Waters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin that refuses to know God tears apart the trust between people, and a faithful prophet both weeps for such people and longs to be free of them. Jeremiah wishes his head were water so that he could weep day and night for the slain (v. 1), then wishes for a desert lodging far from a people who are adulterers and traitors (v. 2). Their tongues are bows, drawn and aimed; falsehood has grown strong; no neighbour or brother can be trusted; lying is a practised skill and sin a wearying labour (vv. 3–5). At the root of it all, named twice, is one refusal: they do not know God (vv. 3, 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet weeps for his people and longs to escape them at once, and the sin he grieves is a collapse of truth between neighbours.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah longs to weep day and night for his people, because the slaughter coming on them is beyond any human grief.

Oh that my head were waters. The verse that made Jeremiah the weeping prophet. In the Hebrew Bible it ends chapter 8, answering the question about the balm of Gilead (8:22): there is no cure, so there are tears.

Day and night. Not a few tears but a head turned to water, eyes become a spring that never runs dry. The grief he feels is too small for what he sees: the slain of “the daughter of my people”, a tender name for the nation.

The same tears. The psalmist knew them: “My eyes shed streams of tears, because people do not keep your law” (Psalm 119:136). Paul knew them for his own nation: “I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart” (Romans 9:2). And on his last approach to Jerusalem, “when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it” (Luke 19:41). Christ stood where Jeremiah stood, looked at the same city, and cried.

Some said Jeremiah. Some took Jesus for Jeremiah (Matthew 16:14), perhaps seeing the same tears, the same word against the temple, the same rejection. But the likeness points one way: Jeremiah wept over a judgment he could only announce; Christ wept over the city and then bore judgment himself.

Our own tears. Do we weep over anything but our own losses? The answer begins not with guilt but with Christ, who wept over people like us. Those who know they have been wept over slowly learn to weep for others.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah 9:1 is 8:23 in the Hebrew numbering, so the Hebrew verse numbers of chapter 9 run one behind the English.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that I had in the desert a travelers' lodging place, that I might leave my people and go away from them! For they are all adulterers, a company of treacherous men. They bend their tongue like a bow; falsehood and not truth has grown strong in the land; for they proceed from evil to evil, and they do not know me, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same breath Jeremiah longs to escape his people, faithless to God and treacherous to one another, because they do not know the LORD.

Oh that I had in the desert a travelers’ lodging place. A bare shelter on a caravan route, anywhere away from these people. Anyone who has loved a difficult family, church or city knows both wishes, often in one day, and Scripture does not tidy the prophet’s feelings into consistency. Yet wanting to leave is not leaving: Jeremiah stayed with his people to the end.

They bend their tongue like a bow. A bow is drawn deliberately, aimed and released to wound at a distance: speech used as a weapon. Falsehood, not truth, has become the strong thing in the land.

They do not know me. The root is named last. Not that they do not know about God; they do not know him, and so they go “from evil to evil”.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of the middle line is compressed, literally “not for truth they have grown strong in the land”; hence the King James Version’s “they are not valiant for the truth upon the earth”. Either way, falsehood is strong and no one stands strong for truth.

verseByVerse.quote: Let everyone beware of his neighbor, and put no trust in any brother, for every brother is a deceiver, and every neighbor goes about as a slanderer. Everyone deceives his neighbor, and no one speaks the truth; they have taught their tongue to speak lies; they weary themselves committing iniquity. Heaping oppression upon oppression, and deceit upon deceit, they refuse to know me, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where God is not known, truth dies even between brothers, and lying becomes a trained and exhausting way of life.

Put no trust in any brother. A standing instruction to trust nobody: not enemies, but the people you live beside and the people you are related to. In Hebrew “every brother is a deceiver” plays on the name Jacob, recalling Esau’s complaint that Jacob had cheated him twice (Genesis 27:36). Jacob’s children have become what their father was before God met him.

When trust goes. Ordinary life runs on trust. When it goes, everything costs more: every agreement needs a lawyer, every relationship a guard.

Micah’s collapse. Micah described the same collapse: “Put no trust in a neighbor; have no confidence in a friend”, for “a man’s enemies are the men of his own house” (Micah 7:5–6). Jesus took up those words for what following him would sometimes cost: “a person’s enemies will be those of his own household” (Matthew 10:36). Where truth has died, even the family stops being a refuge.

They have taught their tongue to speak lies. Trained behaviour, practised until fluent, and piled up, “oppression upon oppression, and deceit upon deceit”, as the strong use falsehood to take from the weak.

They weary themselves committing iniquity. Sin is hard work: remembering what was said to whom, keeping up the version of yourself that each person is shown. The gospel’s offer of rest lands precisely here: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). The invitation does not require the double life to be tidied up first.

They refuse to know me. The second time in four verses. Ignorance of God in this book is not a gap in education but a decision kept up daily, and it is why neighbours cannot trust each other.

Uncertain wording. Verse 6 in the Hebrew as usually printed opens “your dwelling is in the midst of deceit” (so the King James Version); the ESV divides the same letters differently: “Heaping oppression upon oppression”. Either way, deceit is their home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–16 — I Will Refine Them and Test Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ruin coming on Judah is God’s own work, done with grief, and he tells them exactly why. He will refine them, for what else can he do with a people whose words are friendly and whose hearts lie in ambush (vv. 7–9)? He takes up the lament himself for the silent pastures, and Jerusalem will become a heap of ruins where jackals den (vv. 10–11). Who is wise enough to understand? God answers his own question: they forsook his law and followed their stubborn hearts and the Baals their fathers taught them (vv. 12–14). So they will eat bitter food, drink poisoned water and be scattered among strangers (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Even the judgment is refining work, and its cause is stated plainly so that no one need guess.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will refine them and test them, for what else can I do, because of my people? Their tongue is a deadly arrow; it speaks deceitfully; with his mouth each speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he plans an ambush for him. Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD, and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because his people speak peace while planning ambush, God will put them through the fire as a refiner tests metal; nothing else is left to do.

For what else can I do? The refining image returns from chapter 6, where the metal failed the test and was called rejected silver (6:27–30). But listen to the middle of the sentence: “for what else can I do, because of my people?” A parent at the end of the options: astonishing on the lips of God, not weakness but a glimpse of what this costs him. Judgment is what remains after prophets, warnings and mercies have all been refused.

In his heart he plans an ambush. Peace spoken aloud, ambush planned within: friendliness used as cover, more damaging than open hostility because the victim never sees it coming. David knew it: “His speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart” (Psalm 55:21). Its darkest hour came when Judas greeted Jesus and kissed him (Matthew 26:49), and the Lord went on to the cross for traitors.

Shall I not avenge myself? The question of 5:9 and 5:29 once more. A God who watched neighbours ambush one another and shrugged would not be kind.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will take up weeping and wailing for the mountains, and a lamentation for the pastures of the wilderness, because they are laid waste so that no one passes through, and the lowing of cattle is not heard; both the birds of the air and the beasts have fled and are gone. I will make Jerusalem a heap of ruins, a lair of jackals, and I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself laments the emptied land even as he declares that he will turn Jerusalem into a ruin: the judgment is real, and it grieves him.

I will take up weeping and wailing. Now it is God who weeps. Jeremiah wanted a head of waters (v. 1); here the LORD takes up the lament himself, for empty pastures, no cattle lowing, roads with nobody on them, birds and beasts gone, as in Jeremiah’s vision of creation unmade (4:25). Whatever else this judgment is, it is not the act of a God who feels nothing.

A lair of jackals. When people move out, jackals move in: David’s city becomes a den for scavengers.

Textual note. The Hebrew reads “I will take up”; the ancient Greek translation has a command, “take up weeping”, which some translations follow.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is the man so wise that he can understand this? To whom has the mouth of the LORD spoken, that he may declare it? Why is the land ruined and laid waste like a wilderness, so that no one passes through? And the LORD says: "Because they have forsaken my law that I set before them, and have not obeyed my voice or walked in accord with it, but have stubbornly followed their own hearts and have gone after the Baals, as their fathers taught them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why is the land ruined? God answers himself: they abandoned his law for their own stubborn hearts and the Baals.

Who is the man so wise? Asked after every catastrophe, and God does not leave it to guesswork; he answers it plainly. Hosea closes his book the same way: “Whoever is wise, let him understand these things” (Hosea 14:9). Wisdom here is accepting God’s explanation of what has happened.

Because they have forsaken my law. Four verbs of one movement: forsaken, not obeyed, not walked, followed their own hearts. “Stubbornly followed their own hearts” is one of Jeremiah’s great phrases for sin (7:24; 11:8): not ignorance but a heart insisting on its own way.

As their fathers taught them. Idolatry is handed down like a trade, and the chain has to be broken by somebody or it runs on. Parents teach their children what to love, whether they mean to or not.

What it does not mean. God himself explains this disaster by this people’s sin; that does not license us to read every illness or loss as a verdict on the sufferer, which Jesus refused to do (John 9:2–3). What every disaster says to all of us is, “unless you repent, you will all likewise perish” (Luke 13:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will feed this people with bitter food, and give them poisonous water to drink. I will scatter them among the nations whom neither they nor their fathers have known, and I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Judah has poisoned itself with idols, God will feed it the bitterness of exile, scattering the people among strangers.

Bitter food and poisonous water. Literally wormwood and gall, the bitterest plants an Israelite knew. Moses warned of “a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit” (Deuteronomy 29:18), a heart turning to other gods. Judah planted that root, and God lets them eat what grew.

Nations whom neither they nor their fathers have known. Moses’ warning of exile again (Deuteronomy 28:64): strangers, foreign speech, no family memory of the place. “Until I have consumed them” is fearful, yet the book never lets it be the last word: “of you I will not make a full end” (30:11).

The bitter cup. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36), and then drank it. The bitterness his people had earned, he swallowed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Call for the Mourning Women
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A people too numb to weep must be taught to grieve, because the death coming on them is real. God calls for the professional mourning women to come quickly and raise the wail, so that dry eyes may run with tears; the cry of the ruined is already heard from Zion (vv. 17–19). The women are to teach their daughters a lament, because this grief will outlast one generation: death has climbed in at the windows, emptied the streets of children and the squares of young men, and the dead will lie like sheaves that no one gathers (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Grief on this scale needs trained mourners and lessons: a generation must be taught how to mourn.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Consider, and call for the mourning women to come; send for the skillful women to come; let them make haste and raise a wailing over us, that our eyes may run down with tears and our eyelids flow with water. For a sound of wailing is heard from Zion: 'How we are ruined! We are utterly shamed, because we have left the land, because they have cast down our dwellings.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God summons the professional mourners, because his people are too numb to weep on their own, and the ruin they must grieve is as good as done.

Call for the mourning women. Skilled women who led the wailing at a funeral and drew out the grief of a family that could not find it alone (see mourning customs). The purpose is “that our eyes may run down with tears”: a people who need help to cry. Numbness is itself a sign that something is wrong, and there are seasons when a church must teach its people to lament rather than hurry them past it; the lament psalms supply the words.

How we are ruined! The lament is quoted from the far side of the event, exile spoken of in the past tense while the city still stands, so sure is God’s word.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O women, the word of the LORD, and let your ear receive the word of his mouth; teach to your daughters a lament, and each to her neighbor a dirge. For death has come up into our windows; it has entered our palaces, cutting off the children from the streets and the young men from the squares. Speak: "Thus declares the LORD, 'The dead bodies of men shall fall like dung upon the open field, like sheaves after the reaper, and none shall gather them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grief will be so great and so long that mothers must teach their daughters laments, for death will break into every home and leave the dead unburied in the fields.

Teach to your daughters a lament. Mourning becomes a lesson to pass on: grief that will last long enough for the next generation to need the songs.

Death has come up into our windows. Death is a burglar: doors can be barred, but windows were where a thief got in. It takes the children from the streets and the young men from the squares, the very places where a healthy town makes its noise. The silence threatened in 7:34 arrives.

Like sheaves after the reaper. A harvest image turned inside out: the sheaves lie in rows waiting to be gathered, and no one comes. The harvest that was past (8:20) is now a harvest of the dead.

The one who holds the keys. No wall kept death out of Jerusalem, and none keeps it out of ours. But one has gone into death’s house and come out again: “I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18). For those who are his, death still climbs in at the window, but it cannot keep what it takes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — Let Him Who Boasts Boast in This
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When everything else has failed, one boast remains: to know the LORD. Wisdom, might and riches, the three things people have always leaned on, are set aside, and the one boast left is understanding and knowing God, who practises and delights in steadfast love, justice and righteousness (vv. 23–24). Then the warning that guards the promise: God will punish all who bear the mark of belonging only in the body, and Judah stands in the same list as Egypt, Edom, Ammon and Moab, because its heart is uncircumcised (vv. 25–26). To know God is to have a heart he has changed.
verseByVerse.theology: Against a chapter of ruin stands the one thing that lasts: knowing the God who delights in steadfast love, justice and righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom, strength and wealth are nothing to glory in; the one thing worth boasting of is knowing the LORD, who does and delights in steadfast love, justice and righteousness.

Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom. After twenty-two verses of ruin the chapter turns. Three boasts are forbidden, the three things people have always traded on: brains, strength and money. None is condemned as a possession; what is forbidden is resting your identity and confidence there. And all three have just failed: the wise put to shame (8:9), the mighty unable to hold the wall, the rich losing their fields to conquerors (8:10).

That he understands and knows me. The one permitted boast is not an achievement. The people “do not know me” and “refuse to know me” (vv. 3, 6); here is the cure, offered as the one thing to be proud of.

Steadfast love, justice, and righteousness. What is to be known is not raw power but character. Steadfast love (ḥesed) is God’s loyal, covenant-keeping love; justice is right done, especially for the weak; righteousness is a life and a rule that are straight. God delights in these, so his people are to practise them, as those who first received them from him. Micah gives a similar list as a command (Micah 6:8); here it describes God himself.

Boast in the Lord. Paul quotes this verse twice: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31; 2 Corinthians 10:17), to a church taken with clever speakers, strong personalities and money: the same three boasts.

Nothing except the cross. And Paul says who the Lord is in whom we boast. Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and he “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). What the wise, the mighty and the rich of Jerusalem could not supply is given in a crucified Saviour, whose righteousness is counted as ours. So Paul would boast in nothing “except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14).

How do I boast in the Lord? Boasting is what you lean on when you need to feel that you count. If the competence, strength and security were removed, what would be left to say about yourself? Notice your boasts. Listen to what you mention early when meeting someone new, and what you rehearse at 2 a.m. when you feel small. Receive them as gifts. Thank God for each by name, and ask Paul’s question of it: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). Put the knowing first. Guard the time in which you come to know God, in his word and in prayer, as carefully as you guard your work. Practise what he delights in. Show steadfast love, justice and righteousness wherever you have influence. Boast in weakness too. When strength fails, say so, and say who holds you: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). You can let the other boasts go because in Christ you have something better: Paul counted everything “as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8).

This is eternal life. Jesus defined life itself by the same boast: “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Knowing God is not a religious extra on top of a successful life. It is the life, and the only possession death cannot take away.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will punish all those who are circumcised merely in the flesh— Egypt, Judah, Edom, the sons of Ammon, Moab, and all who dwell in the desert who cut the corners of their hair, for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will judge everyone whose belonging to him is only skin-deep, and Judah, circumcised in body but not in heart, will be judged alongside the pagan nations.

Circumcised merely in the flesh. The Hebrew is a deliberate paradox, “circumcised in foreskin”: circumcised, yet uncircumcised. Judah is listed with Egypt, Edom, Ammon, Moab and the desert tribes, several of whom practised circumcision as a custom. Judah had it as the covenant sign, yet at the level that matters they are indistinguishable, because “all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart”.

Circumcision of the heart. The theme of 4:4 and 6:10 reaches its conclusion, and Paul draws the line straight through to the church: “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter” (Romans 2:29). Every outward mark of belonging, whether baptism, membership, a Christian family or church attendance, comes under this warning. The mark is good; it settles nothing about the heart. What the mark cannot do, Christ does: “In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands” (Colossians 2:11).

Uncertain wording. “Who cut the corners of their hair” is literally “clipped at the edge”. It most likely means desert tribes who trimmed the hair at the temples, a custom forbidden to Israel (Leviticus 19:27; compare 25:23; 49:32), though it could mean those living at the desert’s far edges (King James Version: “all that are in the utmost corners”).

9.title: Let Him Who Boasts Boast in This
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 runs straight on from the lament that closed chapter 8, where there was no balm in Gilead (8:20–22); in the Hebrew Bible its first verse is the last verse of chapter 8. The case against Judah (chapters 2–25) continues, and the invader from the north is close.

The message. A people who will not know God cannot be trusted with one another, and will not survive what their lies have built. God grieves over the ruin he must bring. But against all the wreckage he sets the one thing worth boasting of: to know him, the LORD who practises steadfast love, justice and righteousness. Without a heart he has changed, every outward mark of belonging counts for nothing.

Why it was said. Judah leaned on its clever men, soldiers, wealth and covenant sign, while lying had become the ordinary speech of the street (see the introduction). The real disaster was already inside the walls: they did not know God.

How the chapter makes its case. Jeremiah wishes his head were water to weep for the slain, then wishes he could escape such people: tongues bent like bows, no brother safe, a nation that refuses to know God (vv. 1–6). God will refine people who speak peace and plan ambush (vv. 7–9); he laments the emptied land himself and gives the reason plainly: they forsook his law for the Baals (vv. 10–16). Mourning women must teach a numb nation to cry, for death has climbed in at the windows (vv. 17–22). Then the great turn: boast not in wisdom, might or riches, but in knowing the LORD (vv. 23–24), for a circumcised body over an uncircumcised heart puts Judah among the nations (vv. 25–26).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the character of God revealed in Christ. The steadfast love, justice and righteousness God delights in meet at the cross, where he shows himself “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). Paul quotes verse 24 to say that Christ has become our wisdom, righteousness and redemption, so that whoever boasts must boast in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:30–31). By pattern, the prophet’s tears over Jerusalem anticipate Jesus weeping over the same city (Luke 19:41). And by the need it exposes: an uncircumcised heart, which only Christ’s “circumcision made without hands” can change (Colossians 2:11).

For us. Brains, strength and money are still the three great boasts, and each fails in the end. Knowing God through Christ is the one possession nothing can take, and those who know him learn to grieve over sin rather than shrug at it. Ask what you lean on for your worth, and lean on him instead.
9.theology:
Grief over sin is a mark of the faithful, and it is shared by God himself (vv. 1, 10; Ps 119:136; Rom 9:2; Luke 19:41). Refusing to know God (vv. 3, 6) destroys trust between neighbours, and sin is exhausting labour (v. 5).

Judgment is what remains when every mercy has been refused (v. 7), and its cause is stated plainly rather than left to speculation (vv. 12-14). Idolatry is handed down by teaching (v. 14).

The one permitted boast is knowing God, whose delight is in steadfast love, justice and righteousness (vv. 23-24; Mic 6:8), quoted by Paul against boasting in wisdom, power and wealth (1 Cor 1:31; 2 Cor 10:17). Outward marks of belonging to God’s people settle nothing without a circumcised heart (vv. 25-26; 4:4; Rom 2:29).
9.examples: Anyone who has loved a hard family or church will know the wish to weep for people and to be rid of them on the same day. Where speech becomes a bow, drawn and aimed, or friendliness becomes cover for an ambush, trust drains away and ordinary life grows costly. And brains, strength and money are still the three boasts, each of which this chapter watches fail.

keyVerse.quote: Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight, declares the LORD.
keyVerse.note: After a chapter of lies, tears and ruin, this verse names the one thing that survives: knowing God himself, and knowing what he is like. It answers the chapter’s diagnosis that the people “do not know me” (v. 3). Paul quotes it to show that in Christ, who became our wisdom and righteousness, the only boast left is in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:30–31).

9.reflection:
Jeremiah longs both to weep for his people and to get away from them (vv. 1–2). When have you felt both about a family, church or community? What does Jesus weeping over Jerusalem show us about how to hold such people?

Verses 3–8 trace how lying destroys trust between neighbours and even brothers, and twice trace it back to not knowing God. Why does refusing to know God lead to deceit? Where do small dishonesties creep into our own speech?

God sent for mourning women because his people could not weep (vv. 17–18). Why do we find lament so hard, and what might it look like for a church to grieve honestly over sin and loss?

Verses 23–24 forbid boasting in wisdom, might and riches. Which of the three do you lean on most for your sense of worth, and what difference does it make that Christ has become our wisdom and righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30–31)?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Learn Not the Way of the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people must not copy the fears and worship of the nations around them, because the gods those nations serve are nothing. Israel is called to hear what its own God says (v. 1): do not learn the nations’ way or be terrified by omens in the sky, as they are (v. 2). Then the satire: a tree is felled, carved, plated with silver and gold and nailed down so it will not topple (vv. 3–4). Such gods are scarecrows in a vegetable patch, dumb and carried about; they can do neither harm nor good, so there is nothing in them to fear (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The gods of the nations have to be nailed upright and carried home; they can neither harm you nor help you.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word that the LORD speaks to you, O house of Israel. Thus says the LORD: "Learn not the way of the nations, nor be dismayed at the signs of the heavens because the nations are dismayed at them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people must not absorb the beliefs and fears of the culture around them, least of all dread of omens in the sky, because the heavens belong to their God.

Learn not the way of the nations. The danger is imitation: not first their crimes but their way, the assumptions everyone holds unexamined. The example is fear of “the signs of the heavens”: eclipses, comets and planets read as omens. The pagan world lived under the sky in dread, and Babylon, where these people would soon live, was the centre of star-reading.

The remedy for dread. Not more astronomy, but this: the heavens belong to the God who calls Israel his own house (v. 1), so they carry no doom for his people. Every age has its dread, read off charts and headlines, and believers absorb it by breathing the air. The horoscope still offers to read the sky for us; Scripture forbids seeking guidance there (Deuteronomy 18:10–14) and gives instead a Father who knows.

Do not be conformed. Paul says the same in the capital of the pagan world: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2). The pressure is the slow shaping of what feels normal, resisted by a mind the Spirit renews through the word.

Is this a ban on Christmas trees? No. Jeremiah describes a tree carved, plated, nailed upright (vv. 3–4) and then worshipped. A decorated tree that no one worships is not this; the warning is against bowing to anything made by human hands.

verseByVerse.quote: for the customs of the peoples are vanity. A tree from the forest is cut down and worked with an axe by the hands of a craftsman. They decorate it with silver and gold; they fasten it with hammer and nails so that it cannot move.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations’ religion is empty, as the making of an idol shows: a tree cut down, carved, plated and nailed in place so that it will not fall over.

The customs of the peoples are vanity. The word (hebel, famous from Ecclesiastes) means vapour, as the ESV notes: something that looks solid and vanishes.

So that it cannot move. The mockery is simply a description of the process: felled, shaped, plated, and nailed down because otherwise it would topple. Isaiah told the joke at length: half the tree roasts a man’s dinner, and the rest “he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it” (Isaiah 44:17).

verseByVerse.quote: Their idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field, and they cannot speak; they have to be carried, for they cannot walk. Do not be afraid of them, for they cannot do evil, neither is it in them to do good."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Idols are scarecrows: they cannot speak or walk, they can neither hurt nor help, so they are not to be feared.

Like scarecrows in a cucumber field. Upright, human-shaped, dressed, motionless, and frightening only to birds. The psalm adds the sting: “Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8).

They have to be carried. A god you must transport is not a god. The LORD says to his people, “I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save” (Isaiah 46:4). Idols are carried by their worshippers; the living God carries his.

Do not be afraid of them. The point of the passage. Israel was tempted to worship these things partly from fear that they might be real; they can neither hurt nor help. Paul names the real danger: the idol is nothing, but worship offered to it goes to demons (1 Corinthians 10:19–20). The threat is not the idol’s power but what we give it of our hearts.

Uncertain wording. Both words in “scarecrows in a cucumber field” are rare: the first can mean a palm tree or a post, the second a cucumber field or beaten metal (so the King James Version, “upright as the palm tree”). The scarecrow reading fits a figure that cannot speak or walk, and the Letter of Jeremiah, an ancient Jewish writing in the Apocrypha, uses the same image. (The ESV’s “Their idols” is simply “They” in Hebrew.)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–16 — There Is None Like You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Set beside the idols, the LORD is seen for who he is: the only true, living and everlasting God, Maker of all and his people’s own portion. Twice the mockery breaks into worship: none is like the LORD, King of the nations, whom all should fear (vv. 6–7); the idols, however costly their silver, gold and purple, are wood, but the LORD is the true God, the living God, the everlasting King (vv. 8–10). A one-line creed in Aramaic is given for the nations (v. 11), and a hymn praises the Creator who commands storm and wind (vv. 12–13). Idols have no breath and will perish; the God who formed all things is Jacob’s portion, and Israel is his (vv. 14–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The satire turns into a hymn: the maker of the world against the things that had to be made.

verseByVerse.quote: There is none like you, O LORD; you are great, and your name is great in might. Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? For this is your due; for among all the wise ones of the nations and in all their kingdoms there is none like you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beside the idols the LORD has no rival: he is great, the King of every nation, and to fear him is simply to give him his due.

There is none like you, O LORD. In the middle of the satire, worship breaks out. Scripture argues not only by exposing the counterfeit but by showing the real thing, and beside a nailed-down scarecrow the living God needs only to be described.

O King of the nations. Not only of Judah: the peoples bowing to blocks of wood are already his subjects. Who would not fear him? No one should, yet the whole book shows people managing it.

The song of the redeemed. At the end of the Bible the redeemed sing this question as praise: “Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you” (Revelation 15:3–4). What Jeremiah asked as a challenge, heaven sings as a certainty, because the Lamb has bought people from every nation.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament lacks verses 6–8 and 10, and a Dead Sea Scroll fragment shares that shorter form. The Greek Jeremiah is about an eighth shorter than the Hebrew throughout, and many scholars think the book circulated in two editions (see the introduction). Our English Bibles follow the Hebrew, and every truth in these verses stands again in verses 11–16.

verseByVerse.quote: They are both stupid and foolish; the instruction of idols is but wood! Beaten silver is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz. They are the work of the craftsman and of the hands of the goldsmith; their clothing is violet and purple; they are all the work of skilled men. But the LORD is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King. At his wrath the earth quakes, and the nations cannot endure his indignation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
However costly and beautiful, idols are only wood and craftsmanship, but the LORD is the true God, the living God and the everlasting King.

The instruction of idols is but wood! A block of wood has nothing to teach. The costs are listed on purpose: silver from Tarshish, a far western port, probably in Spain; gold from Uphaz; violet and purple cloth; skilled craftsmen. Great investment and real artistry, and the product still has to be carried. Modern idols are also costly and beautifully made; neither has ever been evidence of divinity.

The true God, the living God, the everlasting King. True, against the false; living, against things with no breath; everlasting, against gods that will perish. The three titles describe the whole of conversion: people “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “the instruction of idols is but wood” is terse; it may mean that what idols teach is as lifeless as their wood, or that their “discipline” is no more than a stick. Uphaz is unknown apart from here and Daniel 10:5; it may be another name for Ophir, the famous source of gold.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus shall you say to them: "The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth and from under the heavens."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives his people a one-line answer for the nations, in the nations’ own language: gods who did not make the world will perish from it.

Written in Aramaic. This verse is in Aramaic, the international language the exiles would hear all around them in Babylon: a sentence to say to the nations in their own tongue. It even turns on a pun: the gods who did not make (ʿăbadû) will perish (yēbadû).

The gods who did not make the heavens. The test is creation. A god who did not make the world will not outlast it. The one through whom “all things were made” (John 1:3) passes the test.
verseByVerse.note: It may have been meant as a ready-made reply for the exiles to give their captors.

verseByVerse.quote: It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens. When he utters his voice, there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD made the world by his power, wisdom and understanding, and the storm the nations worshipped is his voice and his servant.

It is he who made the earth. Power, wisdom, understanding, and then weather: thunder is his voice, the wind is kept in storehouses, as if God had a barn for gales. The people were tempted to worship storm gods such as Baal; Jeremiah says the storm runs errands for the LORD.

Even the wind and the sea. When Jesus rebuked a storm, his disciples asked, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). The God who brings the wind from his storehouses was in the boat.

The hymn repeated against Babylon. The same hymn returns almost word for word against Babylon, the great city of astrology and carved gods (51:15–19).

verseByVerse.quote: Every man is stupid and without knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them. They are worthless, a work of delusion; at the time of their punishment they shall perish. Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob, for he is the one who formed all things, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the LORD of hosts is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Idol-makers are put to shame because their gods have no breath and will perish, but the God who formed all things belongs to his people, and they to him.

There is no breath in them. The decisive charge. God breathed into man and he lived; men breathe over their gods and nothing happens.

The true image. Men make images of God and nothing lives in them; God has given the true image of himself, his Son, “the image of the invisible God”, by whom “all things were created” (Colossians 1:15–16). The idol is carried by its makers; the Son “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3). So Paul told the Athenians that “the divine being” is not “an image formed by the art and imagination of man” (Acts 17:29).

The portion of Jacob. The comparison ends with relationship rather than argument. God is Jacob’s portion: the share, what the family actually owns. And the possession runs both ways: Israel is “the tribe of his inheritance”. The idol-worshipper owns an object; the believer is owned by, and owns, a person.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the people trusted what could not save, the judgment is now at the gate. The besieged are told to pick up their bundles, for God is slinging them out of the land so that they will at last feel what they have done (vv. 17–18). The prophet, speaking for the city, takes up the wound he must bear: the tent of the nation is down, its children gone, and no one is left to pitch it again (vv. 19–20). The cause is leaders who never asked God anything, and already the rumour of the army from the north is on the wind (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Exile reduces a household to a bundle and leaves no one to pitch the tent again, and behind it stand shepherds who never asked God anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Gather up your bundle from the ground, O you who dwell under siege! For thus says the LORD: "Behold, I am slinging out the inhabitants of the land at this time, and I will bring distress on them, that they may feel it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The siege is coming, and God himself will fling his people out of the land, so that people who felt nothing will at last feel the weight of their sin.

Gather up your bundle. From hymn to evacuation in one line: a household’s whole life reduced to a refugee’s pack.

That they may feel it. The picture is a sling, stones whirled and flung far away. A people who did not feel the earlier blows (5:3) will feel this one: pain used to bring feeling back.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew says only “that they may find”, without saying what; the ESV takes it as “feel it”, others as “find it so”. Either way the judgment will at last be felt.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe is me because of my hurt! My wound is grievous. But I said, "Truly this is an affliction, and I must bear it." My tent is destroyed, and all my cords are broken; my children have gone from me, and they are not; there is no one to spread my tent again and to set up my curtains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Speaking for the ruined nation, Jeremiah accepts its wound as one that must be borne, while grieving the tent torn down and the children gone.

This is an affliction, and I must bear it. The prophet and the people are hard to separate here, which is the point: he carries their grief as his own (8:21). The response is neither denial nor collapse, but a faith that shoulders what cannot be changed without pretending it is light.

My tent is destroyed. The nation as a tent: poles down, ropes snapped, the children gone, and no one left to put it back up.

The one who bore it. Jeremiah carried his people’s wound in sympathy; Christ carried it in their place: “Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows” (Isaiah 53:4).

verseByVerse.quote: For the shepherds are stupid and do not inquire of the LORD; therefore they have not prospered, and all their flock is scattered. A voice, a rumor! Behold, it comes!— a great commotion out of the north country to make the cities of Judah a desolation, a lair of jackals.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The flock is scattered because its leaders never sought the LORD, and now the rumour of the invader is on the wind.

The shepherds are stupid and do not inquire of the LORD. The nation’s leaders (2:8), charged not with consulting God and disobeying, but with never thinking to ask. Leadership that asks God nothing scatters the people it should gather, at home and in church as much as in a palace.

The Good Shepherd. Chapter 23 answers these shepherds with a promise: God will gather his flock and raise up a righteous Branch for David (23:3–5). Jesus, who did only what he saw the Father doing (John 5:19), is that shepherd, and “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

A voice, a rumor! In a siege the news arrives before the army. Judah’s cities will become “a lair of jackals” (9:11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–25 — The Way of Man Is Not in Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends in prayer: humble trust for God’s people, and justice against their cruel destroyers. Jeremiah confesses what the nation’s collapse has proved, that no one can direct his own steps, and asks the LORD to correct his people in justice and not in an anger that would bring them to nothing (vv. 23–24). Then he asks God to pour out his wrath on the nations that do not know him and have devoured Jacob (v. 25), entrusting vengeance to God rather than taking it into human hands.
verseByVerse.theology: A prophet who has watched a nation steer itself into ruin asks for correction rather than for exemption.

verseByVerse.quote: I know, O LORD, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps. Correct me, O LORD, but in justice; not in your anger, lest you bring me to nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can steer his own life, so the prophet asks God to correct his people, measured by justice rather than by an anger that would destroy them.

The way of man is not in himself. After watching a nation steer itself into catastrophe, the prophet states the lesson as a confession. We choose, plan and walk, yet cannot finally set the course of a life: “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). That is frightening or freeing depending on who holds the map.

The captain of my soul. In the 1870s the poet William Ernest Henley, who had lost a leg to tuberculosis and lay in hospital fighting for the other, wrote a poem that ends, “I am the master of my fate, I am the captain of my soul.” It is brave, and it has become the anthem of the modern self. Jeremiah, having watched a nation try to captain itself, concludes the opposite. No one controls the diagnosis, the market or the phone call at midnight, and a person who must be captain lives in anxiety or denial. The gospel offers something better than control. The one man who could truly have taken charge of his fate prayed, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42), and walked into his enemies’ hands for us. Because he gave up control, we can entrust our souls to him.

Correct me, O LORD, but in justice. He does not ask to be spared correction, only that it be measured, “not in your anger, lest you bring me to nothing”. He has seen what unrestrained judgment looks like.

Discipline for our good. A believer can pray this honestly (Psalm 6:1), and the New Testament gives the answer the prophet could not yet see: God “disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:10). For those in Christ correction is never anger; the anger fell on Christ at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Pour out your wrath on the nations that know you not, and on the peoples that call not on your name, for they have devoured Jacob; they have devoured him and consumed him, and have laid waste his habitation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet asks God to judge the nations that devoured his people, handing vengeance to God instead of taking it.

Pour out your wrath on the nations. A hard prayer, honest about what the invaders did. God used Babylon, and Babylon will answer for how it behaved, as the book’s last chapters show. Being an instrument in God’s hand is no defence for cruelty.

A twin in the Psalter. Psalm 79, lamenting a defiled temple, uses almost the same words (Psalm 79:6–7). When grief has no language of its own, Scripture lends it one.

May a Christian pray like this? Such prayers hand vengeance to God instead of taking it (Romans 12:19) and ask that cruelty not have the last word; it will not, when Christ comes “inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God” (2 Thessalonians 1:8). But the Christian prays under the cross, where Jesus prayed for those killing him (Luke 23:34), beside his command to pray for enemies (Matthew 5:44), knowing that God’s answer to the nations includes mercy: all nations will come and worship (Revelation 15:4).

10.title: Scarecrows in a Cucumber Field
10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 10 is a pause in the storm of the case against Judah (chapters 2–25). After the laments of chapters 8 and 9, Jeremiah turns to the gods Judah was tempted to fear and serve, before the siege returns at verse 17.

The message. The idols of the nations are nothing to fear and nothing to trust: wood that must be carved, plated, nailed down and carried. The LORD alone is the true God, the living God and the everlasting King, who made the world and commands its weather, and he is his people’s own portion. To leave him for them is folly, and when judgment comes the right prayer is to be corrected by him, not left to steer ourselves.

Why it was said. Judah lived among nations who dreaded omens in the sky and filled their shrines with costly images, and Judah had copied them (see the introduction). Soon they would live in Babylon, the capital of star-reading and carved gods, and they needed to know which God was real before they arrived.

How the chapter makes its case. Do not learn the nations’ ways or fear their signs: their gods are trees turned into scarecrows (vv. 1–5). Twice the satire breaks into praise: none is like the King of the nations (vv. 6–7); costly idols are wood, but the LORD is the living God (vv. 8–10). A creed for the exiles follows (v. 11), then a hymn to the Creator who commands the storm, the portion of Jacob (vv. 12–16). Then the siege: pack your bundle, the tent is down, the shepherds never asked God anything (vv. 17–22). Jeremiah ends in prayer: our way is not in ourselves; correct us in justice; let your wrath fall on the nations that devoured Jacob (vv. 23–25).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the character of God revealed in Christ. Men make images with no breath in them; God has given “the image of the invisible God”, his Son, by whom all things were created (Colossians 1:15–16). The question “Who would not fear you, O King of the nations?” is sung by the redeemed of every nation (Revelation 15:3–4). And the confession that no one can direct his own steps meets the one man who could have, and prayed instead, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). For those in Christ, correction is never wrath, because the wrath fell on him.

For us. Our idols are better made than Judah’s, but they still have to be maintained, insured and carried; the living God carries his people. Do not absorb the dread of the age: know who holds the sky, and ask him to correct and lead you.
10.theology:
Idolatry is exposed simply by describing how an idol is made: gods that must be manufactured, fastened upright and carried are neither to be feared nor trusted (vv. 3-5; Ps 115:4-8). Believers absorb the fears of their culture unless taught otherwise (v. 2).

The living God is known as Creator, and creation is the test he gives the nations (vv. 11-13; Rev 4:11). He is his people's portion, and they are his inheritance (v. 16).

Human beings cannot direct their own steps (v. 23; Prov 16:9). The right prayer is for correction in justice, not for exemption (v. 24; Ps 6:1), and for those in Christ discipline is never wrath (Heb 12:10). Nations God uses to judge remain accountable for their cruelty (v. 25).
10.examples: A god that has to be nailed down so it will not topple over is a scarecrow, frightening only to birds, and modern idols, however costly and well made, are no different. The storms people once worshipped run errands for the living God. And leaders to whom it never occurs to ask God anything will scatter the people they were meant to gather.

keyVerse.quote: But the LORD is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King.
keyVerse.note: This is the sentence the chapter is built around. Against idols that are false, lifeless and doomed to perish, the LORD is true, living and everlasting. It describes the turn every conversion makes, in Paul’s words, “from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

10.reflection:
Verse 2 warns against learning “the way of the nations” and fearing what they fear. What fears and assumptions of our culture do Christians absorb without noticing, and how does knowing the God who made the heavens answer them?

Jeremiah mocks gods that must be made, nailed down and carried (vv. 3–5, 9). What are the costly, well-made idols of our day, and what does it take to keep them standing? How is the living God different (Isaiah 46:4)?

The shepherds “do not inquire of the LORD” (v. 21). What would it look like for leaders in our homes, churches and workplaces to ask God before acting? Where are you tempted to plan without praying?

“The way of man is not in himself” (v. 23). Does that feel threatening or freeing to you? How does Jesus’ prayer, “not my will, but yours, be done”, help us pray “Correct me, O LORD” with confidence rather than fear?

So shall you be my people, and I will be your God,<sup>5</sup>that I may confirm the oath that I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as at this day."
