verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Hear the Words of This Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s covenant with Israel stands, and Judah is held to the terms it agreed to. God tells Jeremiah to proclaim the covenant made when he brought Israel out of the iron furnace of Egypt: a curse on whoever does not listen, a call to obey his voice, and the promise that they would be his people and he their God, in the land sworn to their fathers (vv. 1–5). Jeremiah answers, “So be it, LORD”. In the streets he declares that God warned their fathers persistently and they would not listen, so all the covenant’s words, its curses included, came on them (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology: The covenant came with blessing and curse attached, and the prophet says amen to both before preaching either.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Hear the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. You shall say to them, Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Cursed be the man who does not hear the words of this covenant that I commanded your fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, saying, Listen to my voice, and do all that I command you. So shall you be my people, and I will be your God, that I may confirm the oath that I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as at this day." Then I answered, "So be it, LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God reads Judah the covenant it agreed to: rescue first, then obedience, belonging, and a curse on refusal; and Jeremiah says amen to it.

Hear the words of this covenant. The chapter is a covenant lawsuit: God charges his people with breaking their agreement, and begins by reading it aloud. The setting is probably the years after the Book of the Law was found in the temple in 622 BC, when Josiah read it to the people and they pledged themselves to the covenant (2 Kings 22:8; 23:2–3); Jeremiah is sent to press it on the towns. The curse comes from Deuteronomy, where the whole nation said amen to it: “Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them. And all the people shall say, ‘Amen.’” (Deuteronomy 27:26). God is not imposing something new; he is enforcing what they swore.

From the iron furnace. The iron furnace is Egypt, a smelting furnace, the place of heat and slavery from which God dragged them. Rescue came first; then the terms: “Listen to my voice, and do all that I command you.” Obedience is the response to redemption, never the price of it.

So shall you be my people. At the centre is the sentence that runs through the whole Bible, and the reason for a covenant at all. It returns at the heart of the new covenant (31:33) and at the end of Revelation (Revelation 21:3). The relationship is the point; the commandments describe what it looks like.

So be it, LORD. Jeremiah’s reply is literally “Amen”. He stands where Israel stood at the foot of the mountain and agrees to a covenant that carries a curse before he preaches a syllable of it. That is what lets him preach judgment without cruelty: he stands under the same word.

Christ became a curse for us. Paul quotes the same curse: all who rely on keeping the law are under it (Galatians 3:10). Then he gives the way out: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). The covenant Jeremiah preached ended in a curse Judah had sworn to; the new covenant he would announce rests on the one who bore it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, "Proclaim all these words in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem: Hear the words of this covenant and do them. For I solemnly warned your fathers when I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, warning them persistently, even to this day, saying, Obey my voice. Yet they did not obey or incline their ear, but everyone walked in the stubbornness of his evil heart. Therefore I brought upon them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded them to do, but they did not."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s whole history is a refusal to listen, so God has done exactly what the covenant said: its curses have come on them.

Hear the words of this covenant and do them. The covenant is not to be read to the devout in the temple but shouted in the streets of the towns. In this book hearing is never complete until it produces action.

Warning them persistently. The warning has run through the nation’s whole history, so nobody can say the terms were unclear.

All the words of this covenant. God brought on them the very words they had agreed to. The disaster is not an outburst but the covenant honoured. God keeps his word in judgment as faithfully as in blessing, and that is a strange comfort: a God whose warnings hold is a God whose promises hold too.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah has deliberately gone back to its idols, and when disaster comes neither those gods nor last-minute prayers will save it. God exposes a conspiracy: Judah has returned to its forefathers’ sins and other gods, and with Israel has broken his covenant (vv. 9–10). So disaster is coming that they cannot escape. They will cry to God and to the gods they have served, and none will answer, though their gods are as many as their towns and their altars to Baal as many as Jerusalem’s streets (vv. 11–13). Jeremiah is told, for the second time, not to pray for them (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry has become organised, and the gods multiplied for every street cannot answer a single emergency.

verseByVerse.quote: Again the LORD said to me, "A conspiracy exists among the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. They have turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, who refused to hear my words. They have gone after other gods to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant that I made with their fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s return to idols is no slip but an agreed rebellion: a deliberate going back to the sins of its fathers that breaks God’s covenant.

A conspiracy exists. A conspiracy is organised, agreed and quiet: not scattered individuals slipping into sin but a settled arrangement among the men of Judah to go their own way while keeping up appearances. Sin usually becomes respectable by consensus; once everyone who matters does it, it feels less like rebellion than common sense.

They have turned back. Not a new idea but a going back. Josiah’s reform pushed the idols out of sight; when the pressure eased they returned, because the heart had never changed. Reform imposed from above is always this fragile, which is why the promise of chapter 31 is about hearts: a law written within by God himself, the work the New Testament gives to the Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, thus says the LORD, Behold, I am bringing disaster upon them that they cannot escape. Though they cry to me, I will not listen to them. Then the cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go and cry to the gods to whom they make offerings, but they cannot save them in the time of their trouble. For your gods have become as many as your cities, O Judah, and as many as the streets of Jerusalem are the altars you have set up to shame, altars to make offerings to Baal. "Therefore do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer on their behalf, for I will not listen when they call to me in the time of their trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Judah has cried to God in emergencies while serving other gods, he will not hear them when disaster comes, their idols will not save them, and Jeremiah must not plead for them.

Though they cry to me, I will not listen. This is not God refusing a repentant sinner. It is God refusing a nation that has cried out in every emergency for generations while serving other gods in between. Prayer used as a fire extinguisher, by people who want rescue but not God, is not prayer.

They cannot save them. They will try the gods they have been funding all along, and those gods “cannot save them in the time of their trouble”. Every substitute god is fine until there is trouble, and in God’s mercy trouble shows which of the things we serve can act. Idolatry multiplies, a god for every town and an altar on every street, because no single idol ever delivers.

Therefore do not pray for this people. The prohibition of 7:16 returns, and will come a third time (14:11), which suggests Jeremiah kept praying: a man forbidden to intercede who could not stop.

What it does not mean. It is not a licence to write people off; no one but God knows how another person stands with him. It is Scripture’s most solemn warning about the point at which persistent refusal becomes settled, and that it grieved the man commanded to obey it is part of the message.

Can prayer change anything? Yes, and this verse shows it: God does not forbid what makes no difference. Moses prayed and Israel was spared (Exodus 32:11–14); later God says even Moses and Samuel could not turn this judgment (15:1), which shows how settled it had become, not that prayer is useless. God ordains his people’s prayers along with the outcomes, and our part is to pray as he commands.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sacrifices cannot shield a people who love other gods, and the tree God planted, he will burn. God’s beloved has no right in his house after all her vile deeds, and no amount of sacrificial meat can avert her doom (v. 15). God once named her a green olive tree, beautiful with good fruit; now, with the roar of a storm, it will be set ablaze (v. 16). The LORD of hosts who planted it has decreed disaster, because Israel and Judah provoked him with offerings to Baal (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The one who planted the tree is the one who burns it; sacrifice offered by a faithless worshipper buys nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: What right has my beloved in my house, when she has done many vile deeds? Can even sacrificial flesh avert your doom? Can you then exult? The LORD once called you 'a green olive tree, beautiful with good fruit.' But with the roar of a great tempest he will set fire to it, and its branches will be consumed. The LORD of hosts, who planted you, has decreed disaster against you, because of the evil that the house of Israel and the house of Judah have done, provoking me to anger by making offerings to Baal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sacrifices cannot protect a people who love other gods; the beautiful olive tree God planted, he will now burn.

What right has my beloved in my house? The tone is that of a betrayed husband watching his wife arrive at his house with a gift. “My beloved”: the affection has not gone. And the questions are sharp: what business have you here, and do you imagine meat on an altar will cancel this?

Can even sacrificial flesh avert your doom? The whole prophetic tradition answers no. Sacrifice was never a payment that let the worshipper keep the sin. That is the difference between the gospel and religion: religion offers God something so that we may keep the sin we love; the gospel puts that sin to death and gives us God.

A green olive tree. An olive tree lives for centuries and takes years to come into full bearing, and God himself had given Judah that name. Now it is set alight in a storm: not a weed grubbed up, but a beautiful tree burned. And it is “the LORD of hosts, who planted you” who decrees the fire. Everything lost here is his own work, which is why judgment costs God something.

The olive tree in Romans. Paul takes up the picture. Some branches of God’s olive tree were broken off for unbelief, Gentiles were grafted in by faith, and God is able to graft the broken branches in again (Romans 11:17–24). The tree Jeremiah saw burned was not finished: its root held, and in Christ it bears fruit from every nation.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 15 is difficult, and translations differ in detail; some follow the ancient Greek translation in places. But the two questions are clear: what right has she in God’s house, and can sacrifice save her?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — A Gentle Lamb Led to the Slaughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet of the covenant becomes the target of a plot, and he commits his cause to God. God reveals what Jeremiah never suspected: he had been like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter, while men schemed to cut him off and erase his name (vv. 18–19). He appeals to the LORD who judges righteously and tests the heart, and hands his cause to him (v. 20). The plotters are his own townsmen of Anathoth, who say, “Do not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand”; God declares that disaster will fall on them in the year of their punishment (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet's own townsmen want him dead, and the words he uses about himself will be used of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD made it known to me and I knew; then you showed me their deeds. But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. I did not know it was against me they devised schemes, saying, "Let us destroy the tree with its fruit, let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name be remembered no more." But, O LORD of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God shows Jeremiah that his own people are plotting to kill him, and the prophet, like an unsuspecting lamb, hands his cause to the righteous Judge instead of taking revenge.

Like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. The chapter turns from the nation to the man, in the first of the passages usually called Jeremiah’s confessions: his own prayers, complaints and terrors, kept in the book. He had walked among them unsuspecting, like a tame lamb following the man with the rope, and God is the one who tells him.

Let us destroy the tree with its fruit. Their plan has three parts, and the third is the cruellest: destroy the tree with its fruit, so nothing of his work survives; cut him off from the land of the living; and “that his name be remembered no more”, as if he never spoke.

The Lamb who knew. Jeremiah’s words about himself echo, without his knowing it, Isaiah’s picture of the servant of the LORD: “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). It was the passage the Ethiopian was reading when Philip told him it spoke of Jesus (Acts 8:32–35). The prophet was a lamb who did not know; Christ was “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), who knew exactly what was planned and walked into it anyway.

To you have I committed my cause. This last clause governs the rest. He does not organise a defence or repay them; he hands the case over.

Let me see your vengeance upon them. The request troubles Christian readers, and it should be read for what it is: a man refusing to take revenge and asking the righteous Judge to act instead. That is the opposite of personal retaliation, and the same instinct Peter records of Christ, who “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). And the God appealed to “tests the heart and the mind” (compare Psalm 7:9; Revelation 2:23), so Jeremiah invites a judgment that will examine him as well.
verseByVerse.note: “Heart and mind” is literally “kidneys and heart”: the inner feelings and the will.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, and say, "Do not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand"— therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will punish them. The young men shall die by the sword, their sons and their daughters shall die by famine, and none of them shall be left. For I will bring disaster upon the men of Anathoth, the year of their punishment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plotters are Jeremiah’s own townsmen, who threaten to kill him unless he stops prophesying, and God answers that their punishment has a date.

The men of Anathoth. His own village, three miles from Jerusalem, the priestly town where he grew up: the people who taught him, families he knew, probably his own relatives, for chapter 12 says his brothers and his father’s house dealt treacherously with him (12:6). Why priests should turn on a priest’s son is not said. The message was reason enough; some suggest too that Josiah’s reform, which closed the country shrines and brought their priests to Jerusalem (2 Kings 23:8–9), had cost families like theirs, and that Jeremiah was seen as its spokesman.

Do not prophesy, or you will die. Their terms are simple: stop preaching or be killed. Not an argument, a threat.

No prophet in his hometown. It is the oldest pattern in Scripture. “No prophet is acceptable in his hometown”, said Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth, where they then tried to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:24–29). “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11). The hardest audience is usually the one that knew you as a child.

The year of their punishment. God answers the threat against his servant personally, and the sentence softens nothing: there is a date on it.

When family turns against you. Preaching the covenant faithfully made Jeremiah hated in his own village, and God took that hatred as aimed at himself. Anyone who has lost family or friends over obedience to Christ stands in a long line, and the Lord of hosts has noticed.
verseByVerse.note: Abiathar, the priest Solomon banished, had been sent home to Anathoth (1 Kgs 2:26), and Jeremiah's priestly family may have been of his line.

11.title: The Words of This Covenant
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 opens a new stretch of the case against Judah (chapters 11–20), framed by the covenant and by the first of Jeremiah’s “confessions”, his prayers of complaint and trust. It probably looks back to the years after the Book of the Law was found in 622 BC, when Josiah led the nation in renewing the covenant.

The message. God keeps his covenant, in blessing and in curse. He rescued Israel from Egypt and bound himself to them: obey my voice, and you will be my people and I will be your God. Judah said amen, then broke it, conspiring to go back to the old gods, so the curse they agreed to will fall, and neither idols nor sacrifices can stop it. And the prophet who announces it finds the hatred turned on himself, like a lamb led to the slaughter.

Why it was said. Josiah’s reform cleared the idols away, but not from hearts, and once the pressure lifted they came back (see the introduction). Judah went on praying in emergencies and sacrificing at the temple, assuming the covenant protected them regardless.

How the chapter makes its case. God reads the covenant aloud: rescue from the iron furnace, a call to obey, the promise of belonging, and a curse; Jeremiah answers, “So be it, LORD” (vv. 1–5). Their history is one long refusal, and the covenant’s words have come on them (vv. 6–8). Now a conspiracy has taken Judah back to its fathers’ gods; disaster will come, gods as many as their streets will not save them, and Jeremiah must not pray (vv. 9–14). The beloved brings sacrifices that cannot avert her doom, and the olive tree God planted will burn (vv. 15–17). Then a plot is uncovered: Jeremiah’s own townsmen at Anathoth mean to kill him; he commits his cause to God, who sentences them (vv. 18–23).

Where it leads. By covenant, and by pattern. The curse Judah swore to is the curse Christ became for us (Galatians 3:13), so that the covenant’s goal, “you shall be my people, and I will be your God”, is reached in the new covenant in his blood (31:31–34; Luke 22:20). And Jeremiah, “like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter” and rejected by his own town, foreshadows the Lamb of God, rejected at Nazareth and in Jerusalem, who knew what was planned and went to it willingly for us (Isaiah 53:7; John 1:29).

For us. God’s warnings are as reliable as his promises, and religion kept for emergencies is not faith. But for those in Christ the curse has been carried. When faithfulness costs us friends or family, we follow the Lamb, who entrusted himself to the one who judges justly.
11.theology:
The covenant carried blessing and curse, and Judah had said amen to both (vv. 3-5; Deut 27:26). Rescue came before commands: obedience is the response to redemption (v. 4). Judgment here is God keeping his word, not losing his temper (v. 8).

Prayer used as an emergency service by people who serve other gods is not prayer (v. 11), and substitute gods fail precisely when trouble comes (v. 12). Sacrifice never buys permission to keep the sin (v. 15).

Jeremiah's words about himself, a gentle lamb led to the slaughter, fit Christ even more truly than they fit him (v. 19; Isa 53:7; John 1:29). Faced with plots, he commits his cause to the God who tests the heart rather than taking revenge (v. 20), and his own townspeople are his fiercest opponents (vv. 21-23).
11.examples: Sin is usually made respectable by everyone agreeing to it, and reform imposed from above lasts only while the pressure does. Prayer can be used as a fire extinguisher by people who want rescue but not God. And the hardest audience is often the people who knew you as a child; anyone who has paid that price for following Christ stands in Jeremiah's line.

keyVerse.quote: Listen to my voice, and do all that I command you. So shall you be my people, and I will be your God,
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the covenant Jeremiah is sent to proclaim: rescue first, then the call to listen, and at the centre a relationship. Judah broke it, and the curse followed. But God repeats the same promise in the new covenant (31:33), and in Christ, who kept the covenant and bore its curse, it is finally fulfilled.

11.reflection:
God rescued Israel from “the iron furnace” before giving them commands (v. 4). Why does that order matter, and how does it shape the way we think about obedience as Christians?

Judah cried to God in emergencies while serving other gods in between (vv. 11–13). In what ways can we treat God as an emergency service? What do our times of trouble reveal about what we really trust?

Josiah’s reform pushed the idols out of sight, but they came back once the pressure lifted (vv. 9–10). Why does outward reform not last without a changed heart, and what does the new covenant promise instead (31:33)?

Threatened by his own townsmen, Jeremiah committed his cause to God (vv. 19–20), as Jesus “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). How can we do that when people close to us oppose our faith?

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why do all who are treacherous thrive?<sup>2</sup>You plant them, and they take root; they grow and produce fruit; you are near in their mouth and far from their heart.<sup>3</sup>But you, O LORD, know me; you see me, and test my heart toward you. Pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and set them apart for the day of slaughter.<sup>4</sup>How long will the land mourn and the grass of every field wither? For the evil of those who dwell in it the beasts and the birds are swept away, because they said, "He will not see our latter end."<sup>5</sup>"If you have raced with men on foot, and they have wearied you, how will you compete with horses? And if in a safe land you are so trusting, what will you do in the thicket of the Jordan?<sup>6</sup>For even your brothers and the house of your father, even they have dealt treacherously with you; they are in full cry after you; do not believe them, though they speak friendly words to you."<sup>7</sup>"I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my heritage; I have given the beloved of my soul into the hands of her enemies.<sup>8</sup>My heritage has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has lifted up her voice against me; therefore I hate her.<sup>9</sup>Is my heritage to me like a hyena's lair? Are the birds of prey against her all around? Go, assemble all the wild beasts; bring them to devour.<sup>10</sup>Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard; they have trampled down my portion; they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness.<sup>11</sup>They have made it a desolation; desolate, it mourns to me. The whole land is made desolate, but no man lays it to heart.<sup>12</sup>Upon all the bare heights in the desert destroyers have come, for the sword of the LORD devours from one end of the land to the other; no flesh has peace.<sup>13</sup>They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns; they have tired themselves out but profit nothing. They shall be ashamed of their harvests because of the fierce anger of the LORD."<sup>14</sup>Thus says the LORD concerning all my evil neighbors who touch the heritage that I have given my people Israel to inherit: "Behold, I will pluck them up from their land, and I will pluck up the house of Judah from among them.<sup>15</sup>And after I have plucked them up, I will again have compassion on them, and I will bring them again each to his heritage and each to his land.<sup>16</sup>And it shall come to pass, if they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, 'As the LORD lives,' even as they taught my people to swear by Baal, then they shall be built up in the midst of my people.<sup>17</sup>But if any nation will not listen, then I will utterly pluck it up and destroy it, declares the LORD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Why Does the Way of the Wicked Prosper?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A believer may bring God his hardest question, so long as he begins by confessing that God is in the right. Jeremiah concedes, “Righteous are you, O LORD”, and then pleads his case: why do the wicked and treacherous prosper, planted by God and fruitful, with God near in their mouths and far from their hearts (vv. 1–2)? He offers his own heart for God’s testing and asks God to set the wicked apart for judgment (v. 3). Meanwhile the land mourns and its creatures die, because of people who say that God will not see how things end (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet brings his hardest question to God rather than about him, and concedes God's righteousness before arguing.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why do all who are treacherous thrive? You plant them, and they take root; they grow and produce fruit; you are near in their mouth and far from their heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah confesses that God is righteous, and then asks him honestly why the wicked flourish, people God himself has planted though they honour him only with their lips.

Righteous are you, O LORD. This is the second of Jeremiah’s confessions, the private laments in which he pours out his struggle to God. Before he asks anything he settles who is in the right: whatever the answer turns out to be, God is not the defendant. Then he argues anyway, “I would plead my case”, in the language of an advocate laying out a case. The complaint is addressed to God, not circulated behind his back, and that is the difference between lament and cynicism.

Why does the way of the wicked prosper? The oldest question believers ask. Job asked it: “Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power?” (Job 21:7). Habakkuk asked why God would “remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he” (Habakkuk 1:13). And Asaph nearly lost his faith over it until “I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end” (Psalm 73:17).

You plant them. Jeremiah’s version has a personal edge: the wicked in view include the men who have just threatened his life (11:21), and they are doing well. And he does not soften it: their success is not in spite of God but from his hand. That is harder than saying evil men flourish by luck, and it is the truth this book keeps insisting on.

Near in their mouth and far from their heart. This pins the whole problem. God’s name is in their conversation, oaths and worship, and nowhere near the centre of them. What enrages the prophet is not open atheism but a religion that keeps God on the lips and out of the life, and prospers doing it. Jesus found the same in his day, quoting Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew 15:8).

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, know me; you see me, and test my heart toward you. Pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and set them apart for the day of slaughter. How long will the land mourn and the grass of every field wither? For the evil of those who dwell in it the beasts and the birds are swept away, because they said, "He will not see our latter end."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah lays his own heart open to God and asks him to judge the wicked, whose sin is ruining the land and who imagine God will never see how it ends.

But you, O LORD, know me. Having described men whose hearts are far from God, he offers his own for inspection, “test my heart toward you”, the appeal of 11:20. A man who asks God to examine him has given up the right to choose what is found. It is also the only safe ground from which to complain about anyone else, and most of our indignation at others would not survive it.

Pull them out like sheep for the slaughter. The prayer makes modern readers wince: that God set them apart as a shepherd separates animals for the butcher. Two things keep it from mere vindictiveness. He asks God to act rather than acting himself; the prayer is a refusal to take revenge. And these men have plotted murder and will preside over the ruin of a nation; to feel nothing about that is not holiness. The souls under the altar in Revelation ask the same: how long before you judge (Revelation 6:10)?

The vengeance fell on him. Still, Christians read it through a later word. One greater than Jeremiah prayed for those who drove the nails, and the judgment this prayer asks for fell on him instead, for all who trust him.

How long will the land mourn? The damage falls on the land first: dead grass, animals and birds gone. Human sin bends the creation it lives in, as chapter 4 showed. And the root is one sentence they tell themselves: “He will not see our latter end.” Not that God does not exist, but that he will not be watching when the account comes due. It is the creed of 5:12 in other words, and the belief that makes any wickedness possible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–6 — How Will You Compete with Horses?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers his weary servant not with an explanation but with a harder call. If racing men on foot has worn Jeremiah out, how will he race horses? If he stumbles in open country, how will he manage the thickets by the Jordan (v. 5)? The troubles so far are the easy part. And the first of the harder things is already here: his own brothers and his father’s house have betrayed him and are hunting him, so he must not trust their friendly words (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not soothe his servant with easy words; he tells him the race gets harder, warns him about his own family, and stays with him in it.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you have raced with men on foot, and they have wearied you, how will you compete with horses? And if in a safe land you are so trusting, what will you do in the thicket of the Jordan? For even your brothers and the house of your father, even they have dealt treacherously with you; they are in full cry after you; do not believe them, though they speak friendly words to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not explain why the wicked prosper; he tells his weary servant that harder things are coming, his own family among them, and that he must grow strong enough to meet them.

How will you compete with horses? God answers, but not the question. The explanation of why the wicked prosper will wait for a cross and an empty tomb. Instead he asks two questions of his own, bracing rather than comforting. You are out of breath from a footrace, and cavalry is coming. You are unsteady on open ground, and ahead is the thicket of the Jordan, the dense scrub along the river where lions lived.

This is the easy part. Anathoth was only a village; Jerusalem is still to come. Yet inside the questions is a promise: he is not asked to find the strength himself. The one asking said, “I am with you to deliver you” (1:8), and makes prophets into iron pillars (1:18).

Isn’t God supposed to make life easier? Much modern spirituality assumes so: God is there to lower our stress and smooth the road to the life we have already chosen, and when the road gets harder, someone has failed. God’s answer to Jeremiah cuts across it. He does not promise a lighter load; he promises a stronger runner, usually not by removing the trouble but by strengthening the one who carries it, by his Spirit within (Ephesians 3:16). That sounds harsh only if comfort is the highest good, and almost no one, looking back, believes it is. Paul knew that “suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope” (Romans 5:3–4). And God never asks his servants to run a race he has not run himself: “Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). He is not a therapist who keeps us comfortable but a Father making us like his Son, who has run the hardest stretch ahead of us. “Let us run with endurance the race that is set before us” (Hebrews 12:1).

Even your brothers. The first of the harder things: his own family “in full cry after you”, the language of a hunt. Then the cruellest kindness in the chapter: “do not believe them, though they speak friendly words to you”. David knew it: “it is not an enemy who taunts me”, but “my companion, my familiar friend” (Psalm 55:12–13). Of the Lord himself it is written that “not even his brothers believed in him” (John 7:5), and he who knew that loneliness promised those who lose family for his sake a hundredfold household of brothers, sisters and mothers among his people (Mark 10:29–30).

Uncertain wording. Two phrases in verse 5 are uncertain. “If in a safe land you are so trusting” may also mean “if you stumble in a safe land”. And “the thicket of the Jordan” is literally “the pride of the Jordan”, most likely the lush growth along the river where lions lurked (compare 49:19), though the King James Version took it as the river in flood, “the swelling of Jordan”. Either way, worse ground lies ahead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — I Have Forsaken My House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment is God’s own bereavement: he hands over the people he loves because they have turned against him. God has forsaken his house and given “the beloved of my soul” to her enemies, because his heritage has roared against him like a lion; he summons the birds of prey and wild beasts to devour (vv. 7–9). Many shepherds have trampled his vineyard into a desert, and no one takes it to heart (vv. 10–11). The sword of the LORD sweeps the land; the people sow wheat and reap thorns, ashamed of their harvests under his fierce anger (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is God's own bereavement: he calls the people he is handing over the beloved of his soul.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my heritage; I have given the beloved of my soul into the hands of her enemies. My heritage has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has lifted up her voice against me; therefore I hate her. Is my heritage to me like a hyena's lair? Are the birds of prey against her all around? Go, assemble all the wild beasts; bring them to devour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God grieves as he hands over the people he loves, because they have turned on him like a lion; the beloved of his soul is given to her enemies.

I have forsaken my house. The voice changes, and it takes a moment to realise who is speaking. This is God, describing what he is doing, and every line is a wound. My house: the temple. My heritage: the people and land he chose for himself out of all the earth. And then, unbearably, “the beloved of my soul”, handed over to enemies, in the language of a man surrendering his wife to men who will hurt her. Read verse 7 before saying that God is detached from the judgment in this book.

His own beloved Son. It foreshadows a greater giving. God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), into the hands of his enemies, and that time the giving was not judgment on the one given but redemption for the ones who took him.

Therefore I hate her. The relationship has reversed: his own inheritance roars at him like a lion. “Hate” in covenant language is not a mood but a verdict, the formal rejection of a party who has broken the treaty. It sits in the same book as “I have loved you with an everlasting love” (31:3), spoken to the same people.

Go, assemble all the wild beasts. Birds of prey circle and scavengers are called to the carcass at God’s own summons. The armies of Babylon are the beasts, and they come at his whistle.

Uncertain wording. “Like a hyena’s lair” follows the ancient Greek translation. The Hebrew most naturally reads “a speckled bird of prey” (so the King James Version, “as a speckled bird”): a strange bird that the other birds of prey gang up on, which fits the next line. Either way, God’s heritage has become something wild, and the scavengers are gathering.

verseByVerse.quote: Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard; they have trampled down my portion; they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness. They have made it a desolation; desolate, it mourns to me. The whole land is made desolate, but no man lays it to heart. Upon all the bare heights in the desert destroyers have come, for the sword of the LORD devours from one end of the land to the other; no flesh has peace. They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns; they have tired themselves out but profit nothing. They shall be ashamed of their harvests because of the fierce anger of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s leaders have trampled God’s vineyard into a wasteland, the sword of the LORD sweeps the land, and all the people’s labour yields thorns, yet no one takes it to heart.

Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard. Shepherds, that is rulers, did not merely fail to protect the vineyard; they trampled it. Twice God calls it “my portion”, the share he took for himself: it is his loss they have caused. Chapter 23 will bring these shepherds into court.

The beloved son. Jesus told of another vineyard whose tenants beat the owner’s servants; “he had still one other, a beloved son”, and they killed him (Mark 12:1–9). The leaders who trampled God’s vineyard in Jeremiah’s day were followed by leaders who killed his Son, and by that death God made the vineyard his own for ever.

No man lays it to heart. The land mourns to God, and no person does: the fields have more sense of what has happened than the people who farm them. A community can live through catastrophe and not register it, and so can a soul.

The sword of the LORD. Babylon’s blade, and God calls it his own. The invaders are instruments, which is why chapter 25 can turn and judge the instrument.

They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns. Good seed in, thorns out; exhausting labour and nothing to show. It is chapter 2 again: cisterns dug at great cost that hold no water (2:13). Sin never produces what it advertises, and the bill for the labour still arrives.

Textual note. The ESV notes that where the English reads “their harvests”, the Hebrew has “your”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hand that uproots will also replant, and his welcome reaches even the nations that corrupted his people. God will pluck up the evil neighbours who seized Israel’s heritage, and pluck up Judah from among them (v. 14). Then he will have compassion and bring each of them home (v. 15). If those nations diligently learn the ways of God’s people and swear by his name, as once they taught Israel to swear by Baal, they will be built up among his people; any nation that will not listen will be uprooted and destroyed (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The same hand that uproots replants, and the offer of a place among God's people is extended to the very nations that corrupted them.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD concerning all my evil neighbors who touch the heritage that I have given my people Israel to inherit: "Behold, I will pluck them up from their land, and I will pluck up the house of Judah from among them. And after I have plucked them up, I will again have compassion on them, and I will bring them again each to his heritage and each to his land. And it shall come to pass, if they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, 'As the LORD lives,' even as they taught my people to swear by Baal, then they shall be built up in the midst of my people. But if any nation will not listen, then I will utterly pluck it up and destroy it, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will uproot both Judah and the neighbours who plundered it, then replant them in compassion, welcoming even those nations among his people if they learn to trust his name.

All my evil neighbors. The nations who moved in on Israel’s land are called “my evil neighbors”, who touch the heritage that belongs to God. Whatever Judah deserved, those who profited by her fall are not innocent. In Jehoiakim’s reign raiding bands of Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites joined the Chaldeans against Judah (2 Kings 24:2), and Edom later gloated over Jerusalem’s fall (Obadiah 10–14; Psalm 137:7).

I will pluck them up. The same verb falls on both: the neighbours, and “the house of Judah from among them”. Being God’s does not mean being spared.

I will again have compassion on them. Here the chapter turns. Of the six verbs of Jeremiah’s call, four destroy and two build (1:10), and this is the pattern at work: the hand that pulls up will plant again, and “each to his heritage and each to his land” reaches beyond Judah to the nations.

Built up in the midst of my people. Easy to read past. The nations that taught Israel to swear by Baal, the source of the corruption this book has spent twelve chapters describing, are offered a place not on the edge but in the midst of God’s people. The condition is real, “diligently learn the ways of my people”, and the learning now runs the other way.

The gospel’s shape. This is the gospel, centuries early. Paul describes Gentiles as a wild olive shoot “grafted in among the others”, sharing the root’s nourishment, with a warning not to be arrogant towards the natural branches (Romans 11:17–18). James summed up the council in Jerusalem the same way: “God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name” (Acts 15:14).

But if any nation will not listen. The offer is genuine but not automatic; the condition that governs Judah governs the nations too. The chapter that began by questioning God’s fairness ends with him opening his household to his enemies, on the same terms he has offered his own people since chapter 3.

12.title: Why Does the Way of the Wicked Prosper?
12.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 12 runs straight on from the plot at Anathoth (11:18–23). Jeremiah’s complaint, the second of his “confessions”, meets God’s reply, then God’s own lament over his people, and the chapter closes with a surprising promise for the nations. It still belongs to the case against Judah (chapters 2–25).

The message. God is righteous even when the wicked prosper and his servant is worn out, and he answers a hurting prophet not with an explanation but with a harder call. The coming judgment is real, and it costs God what he loves: “the beloved of my soul”. Yet the hand that uproots will plant again, and even the nations that corrupted Israel will be welcomed among God’s people if they learn to swear by his name.

Why it was said. Jeremiah had just learned that his own townsmen, even his family, wanted him dead, while the godless of Judah flourished and said, “He will not see our latter end” (v. 4). The neighbouring nations stood ready to seize whatever Judah lost (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Conceding God’s righteousness first, Jeremiah asks why the treacherous thrive, with God near in their mouths and far from their hearts; he offers his own heart for testing and asks God to judge them (vv. 1–4). God answers with questions: if footraces tire you, how will you race horses? Even your brothers have betrayed you (vv. 5–6). Then God laments: he has given the beloved of his soul to her enemies, shepherds have trampled his vineyard, and the people sow wheat and reap thorns (vv. 7–13). Last, the evil neighbours will be uprooted with Judah, then shown compassion and built up among God’s people if they learn his ways (vv. 14–17).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by promise. The God who gives “the beloved of my soul” into enemy hands is the God who “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). The prophet’s question about the prospering wicked is finally answered at the cross, where God showed both his justice and his mercy, and at Christ’s return. And the promise that the nations will be “built up in the midst of my people” comes true as Gentiles are grafted into God’s olive tree through faith in Christ (Romans 11:17).

For us. Bring God your hardest questions, as Jeremiah did, beginning from his righteousness. Expect him more often to strengthen you than to lighten the load. And remember that the God who opened his household to Israel’s enemies has opened it to us.
12.theology:
Complaint brought to God, with his righteousness conceded first, is an act of faith rather than rebellion (v. 1; Job 21:7; Hab 1:13; Ps 73:17). Religion in name only keeps God in the mouth and far from the heart (v. 2), and the creed that makes any wickedness possible is that God will not see how it ends (v. 4).

God's answer to a weary servant is not to lighten the load but to make him stronger: the race gets harder and he must grow (v. 5; Heb 12:1). Asking God for vengeance is a way of refusing to take it (v. 3).

Judgment costs God: he hands over the beloved of my soul (v. 7), language that reaches its deepest meaning when he gave his own Son into the hands of enemies for our salvation (Romans 8:32). The uprooting is followed by compassion (v. 15), and the nations that corrupted Israel are offered a place among God's people on the same condition of listening (vv. 16-17; Rom 11:17-18; Acts 15:14).
12.examples: Honest lament begins by conceding that God is in the right, and then brings him the question anyway. A believer out of breath from a footrace, with cavalry coming, is not told the race will be easy but that God is with him in it. And the nations that taught Israel to swear by Baal are offered a place in the household, which is the gospel's welcome seen from far off.

keyVerse.quote: If you have raced with men on foot, and they have wearied you, how will you compete with horses? And if in a safe land you are so trusting, what will you do in the thicket of the Jordan?
keyVerse.note: This is God’s answer to Jeremiah’s complaint, and it is not an explanation but a call. The troubles so far are the easy part; harder ground lies ahead, and God means to make his servant equal to it. It holds the chapter’s pastoral heart: God more often strengthens the runner than shortens the race, and his Son has run the hardest stretch ahead of us.

12.reflection:
Jeremiah begins his complaint with “Righteous are you, O LORD” before he asks “Why?” (v. 1). How does that order change a complaint? What questions would you like to bring to God, and how can you bring them in faith?

“You are near in their mouth and far from their heart” (v. 2). How can we tell whether our faith is only on our lips? What helps to bring God from the mouth to the heart?

God answers Jeremiah’s weariness with “how will you compete with horses?” (v. 5). When has God strengthened you through a hard season instead of removing it? How does Christ, who “learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), encourage us to keep running?

The nations that taught Israel to swear by Baal are offered a place “in the midst of my people” (v. 16). What does this show about God’s heart for outsiders, and how should it shape the way our church welcomes people with very different pasts?

13.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD to me, "Go and buy a linen loincloth and put it around your waist, and do not dip it in water."<sup>2</sup>So I bought a loincloth according to the word of the LORD, and put it around my waist.<sup>3</sup>And the word of the LORD came to me a second time,<sup>4</sup>"Take the loincloth that you have bought, which is around your waist, and arise, go to the Euphrates and hide it there in a cleft of the rock."<sup>5</sup>So I went and hid it by the Euphrates, as the LORD commanded me.<sup>6</sup>And after many days the LORD said to me, "Arise, go to the Euphrates, and take from there the loincloth that I commanded you to hide there."<sup>7</sup>Then I went to the Euphrates, and dug, and I took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it. And behold, the loincloth was spoiled; it was good for nothing.<sup>8</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>9</sup>"Thus says the LORD: Even so will I spoil the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem.<sup>10</sup>This evil people, who refuse to hear my words, who stubbornly follow their own heart and have gone after other gods to serve them and worship them, shall be like this loincloth, which is good for nothing.<sup>11</sup>For as the loincloth clings to the waist of a man, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me, declares the LORD, that they might be for me a people, a name, a praise, and a glory, but they would not listen.<sup>12</sup>"You shall speak to them this word: 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, "Every jar shall be filled with wine."' And they will say to you, 'Do we not indeed know that every jar will be filled with wine?'<sup>13</sup>Then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I will fill with drunkenness all the inhabitants of this land: the kings who sit on David's throne, the priests, the prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem.<sup>14</sup>And I will dash them one against another, fathers and sons together, declares the LORD. I will not pity or spare or have compassion, that I should not destroy them.'"<sup>15</sup>Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the LORD has spoken.<sup>16</sup>Give glory to the LORD your God before he brings darkness, before your feet stumble on the twilight mountains, and while you look for light he turns it into gloom and makes it deep darkness.<sup>17</sup>But if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride; my eyes will weep bitterly and run down with tears, because the LORD's flock has been taken captive.<sup>18</sup>Say to the king and the queen mother: "Take a lowly seat, for your beautiful crown has come down from your head."<sup>19</sup>The cities of the Negeb are shut up, with none to open them; all Judah is taken into exile, wholly taken into exile.<sup>20</sup>"Lift up your eyes and see those who come from the north. Where is the flock that was given you, your beautiful flock?<sup>21</sup>What will you say when they set as head over you those whom you yourself have taught to be friends to you? Will not pangs take hold of you like those of a woman in labor?<sup>22</sup>And if you say in your heart, 'Why have these things come upon me?' it is for the greatness of your iniquity that your skirts are lifted up and you suffer violence.<sup>23</sup>Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil.<sup>24</sup>I will scatter you like chaff driven by the wind from the desert.<sup>25</sup>This is your lot, the portion I have measured out to you, declares the LORD, because you have forgotten me and trusted in lies.<sup>26</sup>I myself will lift up your skirts over your face, and your shame will be seen.<sup>27</sup>I have seen your abominations, your adulteries and neighings, your lewd whorings, on the hills in the field. Woe to you, O Jerusalem! How long will it be before you are made clean?"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God made his people to cling to him, and their pride has made them useless to him. Jeremiah buys a linen loincloth, wears it unwashed, and then hides it in a cleft of the rock by the Euphrates, the river of Babylon (vv. 1–5). Many days later he digs it up, ruined and “good for nothing” (vv. 6–7). Then God explains. As a garment clings to a man’s waist, so he bound Israel and Judah to himself, to be his people, his name, his praise and his glory; but they would not listen, followed their own hearts and served other gods, and he will spoil their great pride like that rotten cloth (vv. 8–11). The sign is a sentence, and also a window into what God had wanted.
verseByVerse.theology: God made his people to cling to him as closely as clothing; pride ruined that closeness, like a garment left to rot by a foreign river.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD to me, "Go and buy a linen loincloth and put it around your waist, and do not dip it in water." So I bought a loincloth according to the word of the LORD, and put it around my waist. And the word of the LORD came to me a second time, "Take the loincloth that you have bought, which is around your waist, and arise, go to the Euphrates and hide it there in a cleft of the rock." So I went and hid it by the Euphrates, as the LORD commanded me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Jeremiah to wear a linen loincloth and then bury it far away by the river of Babylon: an acted sermon whose meaning he will learn only afterwards.

Go and buy a linen loincloth. Jeremiah’s preaching becomes theatre. He is to wear the most intimate article of dress there is, against the skin under everything else, and never wash it. Linen was fine stuff, the fabric of priestly garments.

Acted sermons. Prophets were often told to act out their message. It makes the word visible, and costs the messenger his dignity: a man walking round Jerusalem in a garment he may not wash becomes the sermon.

Go to the Euphrates and hide it there. The second instruction is stranger than the first. The Euphrates is the river of Babylon, the direction from which the armies will come and the place to which the people will be carried. He obeys without recorded comment: “So I went and hid it”. God tells him what to do and only later what it means, which is how most obedience works.

Uncertain wording. The place is called Perath, the usual Hebrew name of the Euphrates, as the ESV translates it. But the river was hundreds of miles away, and two return journeys would have taken months. Some think he made them; others that it was a vision; others that the place was Parah, a village a few miles from Anathoth whose name sounds almost the same (Joshua 18:23), chosen because it pointed to the Euphrates and Babylon. Many think the last likeliest, but it cannot be settled, and the meaning is the same either way.
verseByVerse.note: Perath may be the Euphrates or a nearby place (Parah) with the same sounding name.

verseByVerse.quote: And after many days the LORD said to me, "Arise, go to the Euphrates, and take from there the loincloth that I commanded you to hide there." Then I went to the Euphrates, and dug, and I took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it. And behold, the loincloth was spoiled; it was good for nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The garment that was made to be worn is dug up rotten and useless, a picture of what Judah has become.

After many days. The prophet kneels in the mud by a foreign river digging up his own underwear, and lifts it out stained and falling apart.

It was good for nothing. Carry this phrase into the meaning (v. 10). The cloth is not damaged but still usable; it can no longer do the one thing a garment is for.

By the Euphrates. The ruin happened not in Jerusalem but by the river of Babylon. What destroys this people is their long, deliberate burial of themselves among the nations whose gods they wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me: "Thus says the LORD: Even so will I spoil the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem. This evil people, who refuse to hear my words, who stubbornly follow their own heart and have gone after other gods to serve them and worship them, shall be like this loincloth, which is good for nothing. For as the loincloth clings to the waist of a man, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me, declares the LORD, that they might be for me a people, a name, a praise, and a glory, but they would not listen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made his people to cling to him, for his praise and glory; but their pride and their refusal to listen will leave them as useless as the rotten cloth.

I will spoil the pride of Judah. The target is named twice: pride. Not first their idolatry or their injustice, but the self-satisfaction underneath both. The linen was proud, priestly stuff, and God says he will rot it.

Three habits in order. Refusing to hear, following their own heart, going after other gods: the sequence runs the same way every time. Stop listening, and you will be led by your own heart; follow your heart long enough, and it will find you a god.

As the loincloth clings to the waist of a man. Here is the tenderness at the centre of a harsh chapter. The point of the sign is clinging. God made them to be as close to him as clothing is to skin, in contact all day, never apart. Moses said it plainly: “You shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him” (Deuteronomy 10:20). “Hold fast” there and “cling” here are the same Hebrew verb, the one used of a husband holding fast to his wife (Genesis 2:24).

A people, a name, a praise, and a glory. Not servants who merely keep rules, but a people he is pleased to be seen wearing. Paul says the same of the church, which Christ will present to himself “in splendor, without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27). What Judah refused to be, Christ makes his people by washing them himself.

But they would not listen. Clothing that will not stay close to the body ends buried in the mud by a foreign river.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — Every Jar Filled with Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A nation full of its own confidence will be filled instead with a confusion from God that sets its people smashing against one another. God gives Jeremiah a saying so obvious that his hearers will scoff at it: every jar shall be filled with wine (v. 12). Then he turns it on them. They are the jars, and what fills them is drunkenness, from the kings on David’s throne through the priests and prophets to every citizen of Jerusalem (v. 13). Full jars knocked together break, and so will fathers and sons, without pity (v. 14). It is the judgment of being given over to the course a people has chosen.
verseByVerse.theology: A proverb about full jars becomes a picture of a nation staggering and smashed against itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall speak to them this word: 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, "Every jar shall be filled with wine."' And they will say to you, 'Do we not indeed know that every jar will be filled with wine?' Then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I will fill with drunkenness all the inhabitants of this land: the kings who sit on David's throne, the priests, the prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And I will dash them one against another, fathers and sons together, declares the LORD. I will not pity or spare or have compassion, that I should not destroy them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people of Judah, so sure of themselves, will be filled by God with a drunken confusion and smashed against one another like full jars.

Every jar shall be filled with wine. God gives Jeremiah a saying so obvious that the reply is predictable: of course jars get filled with wine; that is what jars are for.

I will fill with drunkenness. The saying turns against them: you are the jars, and what fills you is not wine but drunkenness: confusion, staggering, the loss of judgment that comes over a whole society when God gives it up to its own choices. The list runs from David’s throne down to the ordinary citizen. Nobody is sober.

I will dash them one against another. Full jars knocked together: the sound is of pottery breaking. It is a nation turning on itself, “fathers and sons together”, as Judah’s factions did in its last years while an empire waited outside.

I will not pity or spare. These three verbs of withheld mercy are among the heaviest in the book. They are not God’s final word to this people; chapter 31 is. They are his word to a generation that has used his patience as permission.

The cup he drank. Later God hands Jeremiah “this cup of the wine of wrath” for the nations to drink until they stagger (25:15–16). In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “Remove this cup from me” (Mark 14:36), and then drank it to the bottom, so that all who trust him need never taste it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — Give Glory Before the Darkness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While the light lasts, the proud must humble themselves and give God glory, for the darkness is near. Jeremiah pleads with the people to listen and not be proud, and to honour the LORD their God before he brings darkness on the twilight mountains (vv. 15–16). If they will not, he will weep in secret for their pride, because the LORD’s flock is being led into captivity (v. 17). Then a word for the most powerful people in the land: the king and the queen mother must come down from their thrones, for their crown has fallen and the whole of Judah, as far as the cities of the far south, is going into exile (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: There is a window of light in which glory can still be given to God, and pride is what keeps a people from using it.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the LORD has spoken. Give glory to the LORD your God before he brings darkness, before your feet stumble on the twilight mountains, and while you look for light he turns it into gloom and makes it deep darkness. But if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride; my eyes will weep bitterly and run down with tears, because the LORD's flock has been taken captive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While there is still light, the proud must humble themselves and give God glory; if they will not, the prophet will weep for them in secret.

Hear and give ear; be not proud. After the smashing, an appeal: the pattern of the whole book, the door still open while the sentence is being announced. The appeal rests on a relationship that still stands, “the LORD your God”, and what stands in the way is pride, because giving glory means admitting whose it is.

The twilight mountains. A traveller caught in the hills at dusk knows how fast the light goes and how quickly the ground turns treacherous.

Walk while you have the light. Jesus used the same image of himself in the last days before the cross: “The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12:35). Light is a season, not a permanent condition.

My soul will weep in secret. These tears are shed “in secret”, where nobody would see them. Stern in public and broken in private: that combination marks someone who loves the people he is warning. He weeps “for your pride”, grieving the cause as well as the disaster, and he still calls them “the LORD’s flock” in the sentence that describes their captivity.

verseByVerse.quote: Say to the king and the queen mother: "Take a lowly seat, for your beautiful crown has come down from your head." The cities of the Negeb are shut up, with none to open them; all Judah is taken into exile, wholly taken into exile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the king and the queen mother must come down from their thrones, because their crown is already falling and all Judah is going into exile.

The king and the queen mother. The queen mother held real authority in Judah, and the pairing points to the young king Jehoiachin and his mother Nehushta, carried to Babylon in 597 BC after a reign of three months (2 Kings 24:8, 15; see the kings of Judah).

Take a lowly seat. Court language reversed: come down from the throne and sit low. In God’s telling the crown has already fallen while it is still on the head.

The cities of the Negeb are shut up. The Negeb is the far south, the part of the country furthest from the invasion route, and even there the towns are sealed with nobody to open them. The repetition, “wholly taken into exile”, is the sound of a door closing twice.

The King who came down. Judah’s king is pulled from his throne. Jesus told his hearers to choose the lowly seat themselves, “go and sit in the lowest place” (Luke 14:10), and he did it first: the true son of David laid aside his glory willingly and “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death” (Philippians 2:8), and God has highly exalted him. Pride is made to sit low; humility freely chosen is lifted up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–27 — Can the Ethiopian Change His Skin?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The root of the disaster is a nature that cannot change itself, and only God can make Jerusalem clean. Look north, the leaders are told: where is the flock entrusted to you? The allies you courted will rule you, and if you ask why, the answer is your iniquity (vv. 20–22). Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? No more can people trained in evil do good, and they will be scattered like chaff (vv. 23–24). This is the portion measured out to those who forgot God and trusted lies, and their hidden shame will be exposed (vv. 25–27). The chapter ends on an open question: how long before you are made clean?
verseByVerse.theology: Habit has hardened into nature, so the command to do good cannot be obeyed, and the chapter ends with the question only God can answer.

verseByVerse.quote: "Lift up your eyes and see those who come from the north. Where is the flock that was given you, your beautiful flock? What will you say when they set as head over you those whom you yourself have taught to be friends to you? Will not pangs take hold of you like those of a woman in labor? And if you say in your heart, 'Why have these things come upon me?' it is for the greatness of your iniquity that your skirts are lifted up and you suffer violence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s leaders have lost the flock entrusted to them, the allies they courted will rule them, and the disaster is no mystery: it is the fruit of their sin.

Where is the flock that was given you? The question is put to Jerusalem’s leaders, and it is the one every shepherd dreads. The sheep were “given you”, entrusted, not owned, and they were beautiful. Now look north and count them.

Those entrusted to us. Anyone responsible for others, a pastor, a parent, a teacher, will one day be asked some version of this, and can face it only by leaning on the good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11) and loses none of those the Father has given him (John 6:39).

Those whom you yourself have taught to be friends. The allies Judah cultivated will become her masters. The diplomacy of chapter 2, drinking from the Nile and the Euphrates (2:18), ends with the foreign friends installed as rulers. Every compromise made to win their favour becomes a chain.

Why have these things come upon me? God answers before it is asked, as in 5:19 and 9:12: the catastrophe will be no mystery. The imagery that follows, the public shaming of an adulteress, is deliberately hard to read: the prophets use it because unfaithfulness to God’s covenant is not the breaking of a rule but the betrayal of a marriage.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 21 is compressed and has been read in several ways. The King James Version has “thou hast taught them to be captains, and as chief over thee”; the ESV takes it of those Judah had taught to be her friends being set over her as head. Either way the sense is clear enough: the powers Judah courted will become her rulers.

verseByVerse.quote: Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil. I will scatter you like chaff driven by the wind from the desert.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s sin has become second nature: people trained in evil can no more make themselves good than a leopard can change its spots, and only God can change a heart.

Can the Ethiopian change his skin? The whole book leans on this question, and it has only one answer. The Ethiopian (in Hebrew a Cushite, from the Nile lands south of Egypt) is named only because his dark skin was his own and unchangeable; the verse has sometimes been misused to belittle black Africans, and it never does. Neither skin nor spots is a fault; the point is only that they cannot be changed. Then the application lands: you can do good about as easily as a leopard can rearrange its coat.

You who are accustomed to do evil. Weigh the word “accustomed”. The verse does not say people can do no decent act, but that long practice has turned a habit into a nature. What was once chosen is now automatic, and the will that would have to choose differently is the very thing the choosing has shaped.

It cannot. The New Testament says it flatly: “the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Romans 8:7–8). “The flesh” is human nature without God’s Spirit. And Jesus told a religious man at night, “unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3). Not may not; cannot.

The doorway to hope. This is why moral appeals alone never save anyone. It sounds like despair, but it drives the question to the only one who can answer it. What a leopard cannot do to itself, God can do to a person: “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26), and in this book, a law written on the heart (31:33). For the Christian that promise is kept. The Spirit lives in those who belong to Christ and gives the power to walk in God’s ways (Ezekiel 36:27; Romans 8:4), and when they still fail, it is Christ’s obedience in their place, not their own record, that stands for them before God (Romans 5:19).

An Ethiopian in Acts. There is a quiet postscript. An Ethiopian sits in a chariot reading Isaiah, Philip tells him the good news about Jesus, and he goes on his way rejoicing (Acts 8:32–39). He did not change his skin. God changed his heart.

Two creeds about change. Our culture holds two contradictory beliefs: you can become anyone you want, and you should never be asked to change. Jeremiah overturns both. We cannot change at the root by our own effort, yet we must be changed, because what we are accustomed to is killing us. The gospel holds the two together as no self-help programme can. God receives us as we are: “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). And he will not leave us as we are: “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). We are accepted before we change, and so, for the first time, we can.

Like chaff driven by the wind. Chaff is what is left when the grain is gone: weightless, and the desert wind takes it. The ESV notes that “you” is in Hebrew “them”. Either way the picture is of a people with nothing solid left to hold them down.

Where Christians differ: how unable are fallen people? Arminian Christians agree that no one turns to God by his own power, but hold that God gives all an enabling grace they may accept or resist. Reformed Christians hold that the will, though not forced, follows what the heart loves, so God himself must give the new heart. This commentary’s view: the Reformed reading fits this verse and its New Testament echoes best; turning is God’s gift, yet his call is sincere, and whoever comes to Christ he will never cast out (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: This is your lot, the portion I have measured out to you, declares the LORD, because you have forgotten me and trusted in lies. I myself will lift up your skirts over your face, and your shame will be seen. I have seen your abominations, your adulteries and neighings, your lewd whorings, on the hills in the field. Woe to you, O Jerusalem! How long will it be before you are made clean?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because they forgot God and trusted lies, their hidden shame will be exposed, and the chapter ends asking how long it will be before Jerusalem is made clean.

This is your lot. In chapter 10 the LORD was “the portion of Jacob” (10:16): he was their share. Now their share is exile. A people who would not have God as their portion receive another one, measured out by him.

You have forgotten me and trusted in lies. No one trusts in nothing: when God is forgotten, something false takes his place.

Your shame will be seen. The punishment fits the crime: what was done in secret on the hills will be made public. “I have seen”: the shame was visible to God long before it was visible to anyone else.

Your adulteries and neighings. “Neighings” recalls 5:8, where the men of the city were stallions after their neighbours’ wives. The language is coarse because the behaviour was, and because the prophets refuse to describe sin in terms that make it sound manageable.

How long will it be before you are made clean? The chapter ends on a question and leaves it hanging. After verse 23 the reader knows that the city cannot answer it: a people who cannot do good cannot wash themselves either.

God will wash them. The question waits for God, and he answers it later in the same book: “I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me” (33:8). The one who asks how long is the one who will do the washing, and its cost appears at the far end of the story, when the Lamb of God takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29).

13.title: Can the Ethiopian Change His Skin?
13.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 13 continues the long case against Judah (chapters 2–25). Jeremiah has just learned that his own family and village were plotting against him (11:18–12:6). Now his preaching becomes acted parable.

The message. God made his people to cling to him as closely as a garment clings to the body, to be his praise and his glory, and their pride has rotted that closeness until they are good for nothing. Their sin is no longer a habit they could drop but a second nature: they can no more make themselves good than a leopard can change its spots. Unless God himself washes them, they will never be clean.

Why it was said. Judah was proud of its temple, its royal line from David and its clever alliances (see the introduction). Its young king and the queen mother were about to be carried off (v. 18), and still the people could not believe that disaster would reach them.

How the chapter makes its case. A linen loincloth, hidden by the Euphrates and dug up rotten, shows what pride has done to a people made to cling to God (vv. 1–11). A proverb about full wine jars becomes a sentence of drunken confusion and jars smashed together (vv. 12–14). Then an urgent appeal to give God glory before the darkness falls, while the prophet weeps in secret and the king and queen mother step down (vv. 15–19). Finally the root: the flock is lost, Judah’s allies will rule her, and the Ethiopian cannot change his skin. So the chapter ends asking, “How long will it be before you are made clean?” (vv. 20–27).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the need it exposes. Verse 23 is the plainest statement in the prophets that sinners cannot change themselves, and Jesus says the same: “unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3). The closing question is answered by promise later in this book, “I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me” (33:8), and the promise is kept at the cross, where Christ “gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word” (Ephesians 5:25–26). In Christ God has the people who cling to him that Judah would not be.

For us. Pride rarely looks like rebellion; it looks like competence, respectability and needing nothing. The gospel begins where verse 23 ends: you cannot change your own heart, but Christ receives you as you are and will not leave you as you are. Cling to him, and give him glory while it is still light.
13.theology:
God made his people to cling to him as closely as clothing (v. 11; Deut 10:20), to be his people, his name, his praise and his glory, and pride is what rots that closeness (vv. 9, 15-17).

Verse 23 teaches that sinners cannot heal themselves: habit has become nature, so doing good is beyond them (Rom 8:7-8; John 3:3). That drives them to what only God can give, a new heart and a law written within (Ezek 36:26; Jer 31:33), and the closing question, how long before you are made clean, is answered by God himself (33:8).
13.examples: Jeremiah preaches by wearing an unwashed garment round the city and then digging it, rotten, out of the mud of a foreign river. A traveller on a mountain as the light goes, and a leopard invited to rearrange its spots, are the chapter's pictures of urgency and helplessness: move while you can see, and know that you cannot change yourself.

keyVerse.quote: Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil.
keyVerse.note: This question explains the whole chapter, and much of the book: Judah’s pride and unfaithfulness had become a nature it could not change by itself. It is the need the new covenant answers, when God writes his law on the heart (31:33), and it is why Jesus says that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again (John 3:3).

13.reflection:
God made his people to cling to him “as the loincloth clings to the waist of a man” (v. 11). What does it look like in an ordinary week to cling to God like that? What most often loosens your hold?

Verse 10 traces a sequence: refusing to hear, following our own heart, going after other gods. Where have you seen that sequence at work, in the world or in yourself, and where does it usually begin?

Jeremiah pleads, “Give glory to the LORD your God before he brings darkness” (v. 16), and weeps in secret when they will not listen. How can we warn people we love with both urgency and tears?

Verse 23 says we cannot change ourselves at the root, yet the gospel promises a new heart. How does that free us both from the pressure to reinvent ourselves and from the excuse that we can never change?
