Yet you, O LORD, are in the midst of us, and we are called by your name; do not leave us."<sup>10</sup>Thus says the LORD concerning this people: "They have loved to wander thus; they have not restrained their feet; therefore the LORD does not accept them; now he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins."<sup>11</sup>The LORD said to me: "Do not pray for the welfare of this people.<sup>12</sup>Though they fast, I will not hear their cry, and though they offer burnt offering and grain offering, I will not accept them. But I will consume them by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence."<sup>13</sup>Then I said: "Ah, Lord GOD, behold, the prophets say to them, 'You shall not see the sword, nor shall you have famine, but I will give you assured peace in this place.'"<sup>14</sup>And the LORD said to me: "The prophets are prophesying lies in my name. I did not send them, nor did I command them or speak to them. They are prophesying to you a lying vision, worthless divination, and the deceit of their own minds.<sup>15</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the prophets who prophesy in my name although I did not send them, and who say, 'Sword and famine shall not come upon this land': By sword and famine those prophets shall be consumed.<sup>16</sup>And the people to whom they prophesy shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem, victims of famine and sword, with none to bury them—them, their wives, their sons, and their daughters. For I will pour out their evil upon them.<sup>17</sup>"You shall say to them this word: 'Let my eyes run down with tears night and day, and let them not cease, for the virgin daughter of my people is shattered with a great wound, with a very grievous blow.<sup>18</sup>If I go out into the field, behold, those pierced by the sword! And if I enter the city, behold, the diseases of famine! For both prophet and priest ply their trade through the land and have no knowledge.'"<sup>19</sup>Have you utterly rejected Judah? Does your soul loathe Zion? Why have you struck us down so that there is no healing for us? We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror.<sup>20</sup>We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, and the iniquity of our fathers, for we have sinned against you.<sup>21</sup>Do not spurn us, for your name's sake; do not dishonor your glorious throne; remember and do not break your covenant with us.<sup>22</sup>Are there any among the false gods of the nations that can bring rain? Or can the heavens give showers? Are you not he, O LORD our God? We set our hope on you, for you do all these things.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A drought falls on Judah, and the whole land, from nobles to farmers to wild animals, shows what a people’s sin does to everything around it. The city mourns at its gates, and servants sent for water come back from empty cisterns with empty jars and covered heads (vv. 1–3). The cracked ground shames the farmers; a doe abandons her newborn fawn for lack of grass, and wild donkeys stand panting on the bare heights (vv. 4–6). Drought was a covenant curse, and for a people who had forsaken the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns (2:13), the empty jars preach the sermon they would not hear.
verseByVerse.theology: The land itself preaches: empty vessels, ashamed farmers and animals abandoning their young.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought: "Judah mourns, and her gates languish; her people lament on the ground, and the cry of Jerusalem goes up. Her nobles send their servants for water; they come to the cisterns; they find no water; they return with their vessels empty; they are ashamed and confounded and cover their heads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drought has brought Judah’s public life to a halt, and the empty cisterns show in physical form what the nation chose when it forsook the living God.

Her gates languish. The gates were where a town did its business and held its courts; when they languish, public life has stopped. People sit on the ground, the posture of mourning, and the noise of the city has become one long cry.

They find no water. The scene is written like a short film: the order given, the walk to the cisterns, the search, the empty vessels, the long walk back, and then the faces, “ashamed and confounded”, heads covered. Anyone who has watched a harvest, a business or a body fail knows that instinct to cover the head.

The cisterns. This is the book that defined the nation’s sin as digging “broken cisterns that can hold no water” while abandoning “the fountain of living waters” (2:13). Now they go to their cisterns and find exactly what the picture warned of. Sin’s outcome eventually arrives in physical form, and the empty jar in a servant’s hands is the picture of it.

The drought and the covenant. Drought was not random misfortune in Israel’s understanding. God had tied the land’s rain to the covenant: “the heavens over your head shall be bronze, and the earth under you shall be iron” (Deuteronomy 28:23). A sky that gives nothing was a sermon everyone could feel.

verseByVerse.quote: Because of the ground that is dismayed, since there is no rain on the land, the farmers are ashamed; they cover their heads. Even the doe in the field forsakes her newborn fawn because there is no grass. The wild donkeys stand on the bare heights; they pant for air like jackals; their eyes fail because there is no vegetation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The drought falls on rich and poor, people and animals alike, and the suffering of innocent creatures becomes a mirror held up to a guilty nation.

The farmers are ashamed. Even the ground is “dismayed”. The farmers cover their heads like the nobles’ servants, the two ends of society making the same gesture, because the drought does not consult rank. A farmer whose field fails feels it as failure, though he did not make the weather.

The doe forsakes her newborn fawn. These two pictures are among the most affecting in the book. A doe abandons her newborn, against every instinct she has, because there is nothing to feed it with. Wild donkeys stand on the ridges with heads up, panting, eyes failing.

Creation groans. Scripture insists that human sin damages more than humans. The creation was “subjected to futility” and groans (Romans 8:20–22), and here the groaning is a fawn left in the grass. It waits for the day when it “will be set free from its bondage to corruption” (Romans 8:21), the day Christ makes all things new.

A mirror for the nation. It is also, quietly, an argument. The animals have done nothing wrong and are suffering; the people have done a great deal wrong and are complaining. A doe abandoning her young is a mirror held up to a nation that had sacrificed its own children in the valley of Hinnom (7:31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Act for Your Name's Sake
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A prayer that says the right things cannot replace a life that turns. The people confess that their iniquities testify against them and plead God’s name: you are Israel’s hope and saviour, so why act like a passing stranger or a warrior who cannot save? (vv. 7–9). God answers not their words but their feet: they have loved to wander and have not restrained themselves, so he will not accept them (v. 10). For the third time Jeremiah is told not to pray for this people; fasting and sacrifice will be refused, and sword, famine and pestilence will come (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer is theologically perfect, but the feet, the way the people actually live, have not changed direction, and God answers the feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "Though our iniquities testify against us, act, O LORD, for your name's sake; for our backslidings are many; we have sinned against you. O you hope of Israel, its savior in time of trouble, why should you be like a stranger in the land, like a traveler who turns aside to tarry for a night? Why should you be like a man confused, like a mighty warrior who cannot save? Yet you, O LORD, are in the midst of us, and we are called by your name; do not leave us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people confess their sin and plead with God to act for his own name’s sake, and as a prayer it is very good.

Though our iniquities testify against us. They do not argue that they deserve help. They concede the evidence and appeal to the one ground left: “for your name’s sake”. No prayer stands on firmer ground. Moses used it at Sinai; Asaph used it after the temple was sacked: “Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and atone for our sins, for your name’s sake!” (Psalm 79:9); and Daniel would use it in Babylon: “we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy” (Daniel 9:18).

For your name’s sake. To modern ears this can sound like an appeal to God’s ego, as if he were a celebrity guarding his image. But God’s name is who he has shown himself to be. When he proclaimed it to Moses, it was “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). To pray “for your name’s sake” is to say: be who you said you are.

The glory of self-giving love. Timothy Keller often pointed out that a God who seeks his own glory is not self-centred, because the Father, the Son and the Spirit have always delighted to glorify one another: God’s glory is the glory of self-giving love. That love went all the way when Jesus prayed, “Father, glorify your name” (John 12:28), and then went to the cross, so that John can write, “your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake” (1 John 2:12). Judah’s prayer was refused (v. 10), not because the plea was wrong but because their feet had not turned. So when your own record testifies against you this week, do not reach for a better record. Turn, and plead his name: “Because you are merciful, and you have said so.”

Like a traveler who turns aside. The titles are exactly right: “hope of Israel”, “savior in time of trouble”. And the complaint is vivid: you are behaving like a tourist who stops at an inn, sleeps and is gone in the morning, with no stake in the place. Bolder still, like “a mighty warrior who cannot save”, a soldier who has lost his nerve. They end with the covenant itself, “we are called by your name”, and a plea a child might make: “do not leave us”. Read on its own, the prayer deserves an answer, which is what makes the next verse so unsettling.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “confused” in verse 9 occurs only here in the Old Testament. It probably means taken by surprise or dumbfounded: a warrior caught off guard and unable to act.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD concerning this people: "They have loved to wander thus; they have not restrained their feet; therefore the LORD does not accept them; now he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins." The LORD said to me: "Do not pray for the welfare of this people. Though they fast, I will not hear their cry, and though they offer burnt offering and grain offering, I will not accept them. But I will consume them by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers not their words but their feet: a people who love to wander cannot buy his favour with prayer, fasting and sacrifice, and Jeremiah must stop praying for them.

They have loved to wander thus. God answers the way they actually walk. They loved it, not merely drifted, and restraining their feet, the one thing repentance would have required, was never attempted. Beautiful prayers came out of the same city in which the shrines stayed open.

Words measured against a life. The lesson is not that God is deaf, but that words to God are measured against the direction of a life. This book has already said what God is listening for: one honest “What have I done?” (8:6), and a turning that follows it.

Do not pray for the welfare of this people. This is the third time Jeremiah has been told not to pray for them (7:16; 11:14). Each time it is more specific, and each repetition tells us the prophet had gone on praying.

Though they fast, I will not hear. Fasting, burnt offering and grain offering, the full range of religious response, are refused. Isaiah heard the same: “even though you make many prayers, I will not listen; your hands are full of blood” (Isaiah 1:15).

An Intercessor never silenced. Here the human intercessor is silenced. The gospel gives an Intercessor who never is: Jesus “always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and the Father always hears him (John 11:42).

What these verses do not mean. They are not a general statement that God rejects sinners who come to him; the whole Bible says the opposite, and this book will end with a new covenant. They are about a people using worship to force God’s hand while refusing to change course, and they stop anyone treating prayer as a technique.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Being misled by false teachers does not excuse those who wanted to hear them. Jeremiah pleads that the prophets had promised the people assured peace (v. 13). God answers that he never sent those men: their visions came from their own minds, and the sword they denied will consume them, together with the people who listened (vv. 14–16). Then Jeremiah is given a message of tears to speak: the slain lying in the field, the starving in the city, and prophet and priest carrying on their trade without knowledge (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: False comfort kills both the preacher and the congregation, and God orders the weeping over it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said: "Ah, Lord GOD, behold, the prophets say to them, 'You shall not see the sword, nor shall you have famine, but I will give you assured peace in this place.'" And the LORD said to me: "The prophets are prophesying lies in my name. I did not send them, nor did I command them or speak to them. They are prophesying to you a lying vision, worthless divination, and the deceit of their own minds. Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the prophets who prophesy in my name although I did not send them, and who say, 'Sword and famine shall not come upon this land': By sword and famine those prophets shall be consumed. And the people to whom they prophesy shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem, victims of famine and sword, with none to bury them—them, their wives, their sons, and their daughters. For I will pour out their evil upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah pleads that the people were misled, but God answers that he never sent their prophets, and that preachers and hearers who loved the lie will fall together.

Assured peace in this place. Jeremiah tries one more argument, and a generous one: they were misled. Their preachers promised no war, no hunger, “assured peace”, a phrase with a confident, official ring. It is the plea of a pastor who knows his people are not chiefly wicked but badly taught.

I did not send them. The denial is threefold: not sent, not commanded, not spoken to. Whatever those men were doing, God had no part in it.

The deceit of their own minds. The last phrase names the source. They were saying what they themselves found plausible and agreeable, and calling it the word of the LORD. That is how most false teaching is made: sincere men speaking with no word from God behind them.

By sword and famine those prophets shall be consumed. The sentence fits the crime: the men who said the sword would not come will fall to it. Teachers are judged by the standard they preached.

The people die too. Here is the hard part of the answer. The congregation dies with the preachers. Being deceived is not treated as an acquittal, because they chose men who told them what they wanted: “my people love to have it so” (5:31). Nobody will be able to say at the end that they were only doing what their church told them. But God has not left his people to work it out alone: he gives his word to test teaching by, and his Spirit, who leads believers into the truth (1 John 4:1).

Is sincerity enough? Most people today would say that what matters in religion is not being right but being sincere. It sounds generous, and it guards against arrogance, but we apply that rule nowhere else. In December 1799 George Washington’s doctors, among the most respected in America, treated his throat infection by drawing off a large part of his blood. They were entirely sincere, and he died. Sincerity is a virtue in the doctor; it does nothing to the medicine. The people of Jerusalem sincerely trusted their prophets, and the prophets very likely believed themselves (v. 14). It did not stop the sword. That is no reason to despise sincere people, but it is a reason to care very much about what is true. And here the gospel brings unexpected relief. Our sincerity is always mixed and our faith often weak, so it would be bad news if we were saved by the quality of our believing. We are saved by the one we believe in, who is faithful when we waver: “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall say to them this word: 'Let my eyes run down with tears night and day, and let them not cease, for the virgin daughter of my people is shattered with a great wound, with a very grievous blow. If I go out into the field, behold, those pierced by the sword! And if I enter the city, behold, the diseases of famine! For both prophet and priest ply their trade through the land and have no knowledge.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands his prophet to deliver the message with tears, because a city is dying while its religious professionals carry on as usual.

Let my eyes run down with tears. The weeping is commanded: part of the sermon, not a weakness in the preacher. A man who could announce this dry-eyed would misrepresent God, because God is not dry-eyed. He calls them “the virgin daughter of my people”, the tenderest name he has for them, at the moment of her greatest disgrace.

If I go out into the field. Two doors and no way out: outside the walls the war dead, inside them the starving.

Prophet and priest ply their trade. The last line sets the cause beside the effect: religion carried on as business as usual by men who “have no knowledge” of God, while the bodies pile up outside. The priest still takes the service; the prophet still gives the address.

He wept over the city. Six centuries later another prophet came to the same city: “when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it” (Luke 19:41). The tears Jeremiah was commanded to shed were the tears of God himself, and in Jesus they ran down a human face.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “ply their trade” means to go about, often of traders travelling, and the line is compressed. The ESV takes it of prophet and priest carrying on their business in the land; the King James Version has “go about into a land that they know not”, as if already going into exile. Either way they are busy and ignorant of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Right words in a crisis are not the same as a turned heart. The people pray again, and every phrase is true. They ask whether God has utterly rejected Judah and why the promised healing became terror (v. 19); they confess their own wickedness and their fathers’ (v. 20); they plead his name, his throne and his covenant (v. 21); and they confess that no idol and no sky can send rain, only the LORD (v. 22). Read alone it is a model prayer, and the next chapter refuses it. Yet its plea for the covenant points beyond this generation to the new covenant God would make.
verseByVerse.theology: Every word of the confession is right, and still the answer in the next chapter is no: right words are not yet repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you utterly rejected Judah? Does your soul loathe Zion? Why have you struck us down so that there is no healing for us? We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror. We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, and the iniquity of our fathers, for we have sinned against you. Do not spurn us, for your name's sake; do not dishonor your glorious throne; remember and do not break your covenant with us. Are there any among the false gods of the nations that can bring rain? Or can the heavens give showers? Are you not he, O LORD our God? We set our hope on you, for you do all these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people pray again, confessing their sin and pleading God’s name, throne and covenant; every phrase is true, and yet the next chapter shows that true words are not the same as a turned heart.

Have you utterly rejected Judah? The questions are raw: “Does your soul loathe Zion?” They quote back the promise of healing that was preached to them (8:15) and set it against what actually arrived.

We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD. Here is the confession God asked for in chapter 3, “Only acknowledge your guilt” (3:13): their own wickedness, their fathers’ iniquity, and the direct “we have sinned against you”. The appeal is to God’s name, God’s throne and God’s covenant: three grounds, none of them their own merit.

Do not break your covenant with us. The covenant was broken, but not by God. His answer, given later in this book, is a new covenant (31:31–34), and Jesus took the cup at his last supper and called it “the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). The prayer of verse 21 is finally answered at the cross.

Can the false gods bring rain? The prayer ends with sound theology about the weather. The Baals were rain gods; the whole point of serving them was showers. Now, in a drought, the people say what chapter 10 said: those things are nothing, and rain is yours. Zechariah puts it positively: “Ask rain from the LORD in the season of the spring rain” (Zechariah 10:1).

A faultless prayer refused. The chapter ends with every phrase true, the doctrine exact, the confession explicit, and the first verse of chapter 15 refuses it. That must be read carefully. It does not teach that God turns away a broken heart: “a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 51:17). It teaches that words, even perfect words, are not repentance, and that a nation can learn to say the right things in a crisis while loving to wander (v. 10).

Mercies new every morning. For anyone frightened by this passage, Lamentations, long associated with this same man and written over the ruins, gives the answer: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23).

14.title: The Drought, and Prayers That Are Not Heard
14.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 14 opens a new section, dated by a drought, that runs to the end of chapter 15. After the ruined loincloth and the leopard’s spots (chapter 13), the case against Judah now becomes a conversation: the people pray, the prophet pleads, and God answers.

The message. Words to God are weighed against the direction of a life. Parched by drought, Judah prays prayers that are true in every phrase, but its feet have not turned, and God will not accept fasting and sacrifice from people who love to wander. Nor does being misled excuse them: the prophets of easy peace never spoke for God, and preachers and hearers will fall together. The God who refuses here is not deaf; he will not be managed.

Why it was said. Drought was one of the covenant curses Moses had warned of (Deuteronomy 28:23–24). Judah turned to prayer and fasting while its shrines stayed open and its prophets kept promising peace (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The drought is painted in pictures: servants coming back with empty jars, farmers covering their heads, a doe abandoning her fawn (vv. 1–6). The people pray well, pleading God’s name (vv. 7–9), but God answers that they love to wander and forbids Jeremiah to pray for them (vv. 10–12). Jeremiah pleads that the prophets misled them; God replies that he never sent those prophets, and that they and their hearers will die together (vv. 13–16). The prophet must weep as he speaks (vv. 17–18). Then a second prayer, faultless in confession and doctrine (vv. 19–22), which the next chapter refuses.

Where it leads. By the need it exposes and the covenant it longs for. Judah pleads, “remember and do not break your covenant with us” (v. 21), but the people had broken it themselves, and God’s answer is a new covenant (31:31–34), made in Jesus’ blood (Luke 22:20). Where the human intercessor is silenced (v. 11), Christ “always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). And the plea “for your name’s sake” (vv. 7, 21) is answered at the cross: “your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake” (1 John 2:12).

For us. Prayer is not a technique for managing God in a crisis. Bring him your words, and with them your feet: an honest turning from whatever you love more than him. And take care whom you listen to, because a sincere hearer does not make a lie true.
14.theology:
Creation suffers under human sin (vv. 4-6; Rom 8:20-22). Prayer that appeals to God's name rather than to human merit stands on the firmest ground there is (v. 7; Ps 79:9; Dan 9:18), yet God measures prayers against the direction of a life (v. 10), and worship used to move God while the course of life is unchanged is refused (vv. 11-12).

False prophecy is the deceit of the preacher's own mind; teachers are judged by the standard they preached, and hearers are not acquitted for having been deceived (vv. 14-16). Yet the mercy that outlasts this refusal is sung over the ruins (Lam 3:22-23), and the broken covenant is answered by a new one sealed in Christ's blood (31:31-34; Luke 22:20).
14.examples: The chapter's sharpest picture is the empty jars carried back from the cisterns, in the book that called sin a broken cistern (2:13). Its sharpest warning is the prayer that would score full marks offered by people whose lives have not changed direction, and by preachers who say what they find plausible and call it the word of the LORD.

keyVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD concerning this people: “They have loved to wander thus; they have not restrained their feet; therefore the LORD does not accept them; now he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins.”
keyVerse.note: This is God’s reply to a prayer that said all the right things (vv. 7–9), and it explains the whole chapter: God answers not the words but the feet. It does not mean that God turns away the penitent, but that prayer cannot be used to manage him while the heart keeps wandering. The way back is the turning this people would not make.

14.reflection:
The servants come back from the cisterns with empty jars (v. 3), the very picture of 2:13. Where do people today go to “broken cisterns”, and what does it look like when they come back empty?

The prayer of verses 7–9 is humble and pleads God’s name, yet God answers that the people “have loved to wander” (v. 10). How can we tell the difference between praying the right words and truly turning? What does it mean to bring God our feet as well as our words?

The people were misled by prophets promising peace, but God holds them responsible too (vv. 13–16). Why is sincerity not enough? How can we test what we hear, and what does it mean for us that Jesus “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25)?

Jeremiah was commanded to speak with tears (v. 17), and Jesus wept over the same city. How should hard truths be spoken in our churches and families, and what is lost when they are spoken dry-eyed?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Though Moses and Samuel Stood Before Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some judgment, once fixed, no intercession can turn away. Even if Moses and Samuel, the great intercessors of Israel’s story, stood before God, his heart would not turn toward this generation. Each will go to the fate appointed, sword, famine or captivity, and dogs, birds and beasts will finish the work, because of what Manasseh did in Jerusalem (vv. 1–4). Who will pity Jerusalem? It has kept going backward, and God is weary of relenting. He has winnowed and bereaved his people, multiplied their widows and struck down their young men, and the mother of seven faints as her sun goes down at noon (vv. 5–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The greatest intercessors in Israel's history could not turn this, and the sins of a king two generations back are still working themselves out.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to me, "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people. Send them out of my sight, and let them go! And when they ask you, 'Where shall we go?' you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: "'Those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword; those who are for famine, to famine, and those who are for captivity, to captivity.' I will appoint over them four kinds of destroyers, declares the LORD: the sword to kill, the dogs to tear, and the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth to devour and destroy. And I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, did in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God refuses the people’s prayer: even if Moses and Samuel stood before him, he would not turn toward this generation, whose judgment is now fixed.

Though Moses and Samuel stood before me. This is the answer to the faultless prayer at the end of chapter 14, and it is devastating. Moses and Samuel are the two men in Israel’s story whose prayers most famously turned judgment aside. Moses stood in the breach at Sinai, and “the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people” (Exodus 32:14). Samuel said it would be a sin against God for him to stop praying for Israel (1 Samuel 12:23). The psalm remembers both: “They called to the LORD, and he answered them” (Psalm 99:6).

My heart would not turn toward this people. If those two were standing here making the case, his heart would not turn. The moment for this generation has passed, which explains why Jeremiah has three times been forbidden to pray (7:16; 11:14; 14:11).

Where shall we go? They will ask the practical question people always ask in a crisis. The answer offers no refuge, only a fate assigned to each. Then the “four kinds of destroyers”: on a battlefield the sword kills, and then the dogs, birds and beasts come for the bodies. It is deliberately without dignity, because that is what the end of a siege looks like.

Because of what Manasseh did. Manasseh had been dead for decades. He reigned fifty-five years, filled Jerusalem with idols and innocent blood, and, Chronicles records, repented late in his life (2 Chronicles 33:12–13). Kings does not mention the repentance; it is not denying it but explaining why judgment still came (2 Kings 23:26), while Chronicles shows that even Manasseh could be forgiven. His personal forgiveness did not undo what he had built into the nation, and a generation that kept his ways inherited his judgment.

Forgiven, with consequences. Sin can be forgiven and still leave consequences running through families and institutions for generations. A father restored to God may still watch his children live with what his years of neglect made normal. Grace does not undo the past, but it does not leave him alone in it either: he can pray for them, own what he did, and show them the mercy he has found.

An intercessor greater than Moses. There is one who prays as Moses and Samuel never could, pleading not his own record but his own blood: Christ “is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

Are there people Christians should stop praying for? God forbade Jeremiah to pray for a nation whose judgment was fixed. Christians are commanded to pray for all people (1 Timothy 2:1) and for enemies (Matthew 5:44). John speaks of “sin that leads to death” and does not command prayer for it (1 John 5:16), but we cannot see who is beyond hope, so we keep praying.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem, or who will grieve for you? Who will turn aside to ask about your welfare? You have rejected me, declares the LORD; you keep going backward, so I have stretched out my hand against you and destroyed you— I am weary of relenting. I have winnowed them with a winnowing fork in the gates of the land; I have bereaved them; I have destroyed my people; they did not turn from their ways. I have made their widows more in number than the sand of the seas; I have brought against the mothers of young men a destroyer at noonday; I have made anguish and terror fall upon them suddenly. She who bore seven has grown feeble; she has fainted away; her sun went down while it was yet day; she has been shamed and disgraced. And the rest of them I will give to the sword before their enemies, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem has kept turning its back on God, and he, weary of relenting, has brought a bereavement on the city that no one will stop to pity.

Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem? Three questions about loneliness rather than punishment: who will feel sorry, who will mourn, who will even ask how you are? A city that has become a warning to others finds the neighbours passing by on the other side.

I am weary of relenting. After the charge “you keep going backward” (compare 7:24) comes a phrase to stop at. Relenting is what God has been doing for centuries: every warning not carried out, every disaster postponed, every prophet sent instead of an army. He is not saying that mercy has run out in principle; three chapters later he says that if a nation turns he will relent of the disaster he intended (18:8). He is saying that this generation has treated his patience as leave to go on sinning.

I have destroyed my people. In verse 7 God says “I have” three times, and the third is “I have destroyed my people”. He does not distance himself from what is happening, and he does not stop calling them his. The reason is stated last and plainly: “they did not turn from their ways”. Everything in this book comes back to that sentence.

She who bore seven has grown feeble. The promise to Abraham was descendants like the sand of the sea; now the widows are counted that way. Seven sons was the picture of a blessed mother, and Hannah had sung that “the barren has borne seven” (1 Samuel 2:5). Here the song runs backwards: this mother has lost them all.

Her sun went down while it was yet day. The phrase has comforted and haunted the bereaved ever since, because it names the particular cruelty of losing a child: the light going at noon. Scripture does not hurry past that grief or explain it away; it gives it words, so that those who carry it can bring it to God.

Where Christians differ: does God change his mind? Open theists read “weary of relenting” and similar verses to mean that God changes his plans in response to events he did not know in advance. This commentary’s view: God’s purpose never changes, and Scripture speaks of his relenting in human terms, describing his unchanging way of dealing with people as they turn or refuse to turn (18:7–10). His patience is real, and so is its end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — A Man of Strife and Contention
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The faithful messenger can be crushed by the hatred his message brings, and God answers him. Jeremiah turns to his mother and wishes he had never been born: he is a man of strife to the whole land, cursed by everyone though he has given no one cause (v. 10). God replies that he has worked for his servant’s good and pleaded for him in the time of trouble (v. 11). And no one can break the iron from the north: Judah’s treasures will be plundered, and her people will serve their enemies in a land they do not know (vv. 12–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet wishes he had never been born, and God answers him without apology and without contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and contention to the whole land! I have not lent, nor have I borrowed, yet all of them curse me. The LORD said, "Have I not set you free for their good? Have I not pleaded for you before the enemy in the time of trouble and in the time of distress?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hated by everyone for the message he carries, Jeremiah wishes he had never been born, and God answers him with care rather than contempt.

Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me. Now the prophet breaks. In one of his personal complaints to God he turns to the woman who gave him birth and wishes she had not. Job said it in his ashes: “Let the day perish on which I was born” (Job 3:3).

A man of strife and contention. What he cannot bear is what he has become. He never wanted to be always in a quarrel. A village priest’s son who would have been content to be ignored is the most argued-about man in the country.

I have not lent, nor have I borrowed. The saddest touch. Debt was the usual reason a man was hated in a small society. He has given nobody any ordinary ground for a grudge, and they curse him anyway: he is hated purely for the message. Anyone who has been disliked for their faith rather than for their faults knows the particular loneliness of this verse.

God answers the outburst. God does not rebuke it, and he does not pretend the pain is unreasonable. He replies, and his reply is about his own care: he has been at work for Jeremiah’s good and has pleaded for him when enemies pressed. If you have wished you had never been born, notice that the wish is written down in Scripture, and God answered it with care, not contempt. Do not carry it alone: tell someone you trust and your pastor, and if it has become thoughts of ending your life, get help the same day.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew of verse 11 is uncertain, and translations differ widely; the King James Version, for example, takes it as a promise that it will be well with Jeremiah and that God will make the enemy treat him well. What comes through in every reading is that God answers, and that his answer is about his care for his servant.

verseByVerse.quote: Can one break iron, iron from the north, and bronze? "Your wealth and your treasures I will give as spoil, without price, for all your sins, throughout all your territory. I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can break the iron of Babylon: Judah’s treasures will be plundered without payment, and her people will serve their enemies in a strange land.

Can one break iron? The iron from the north is Babylon, and nobody breaks it, certainly not Judah with its alliances: an answer to every plan of escape the palace has been making.

Without price. No ransom, no tribute paid to buy it back, no compensation: the treasures simply change hands. A nation that trusted its reserves discovers they were never security.

In a land that you do not know. This repeats the sentence of 5:19, and the punishment fits the sin: you served foreign gods at home, so you will serve foreigners abroad. Exile is not random misfortune. They chose foreign masters; now they have them.

Uncertain wording. Verse 12 is compressed, and the King James Version reads it differently: “Shall iron break the northern iron and the steel?” Either way, nothing Judah has can break Babylon. In verse 14 the Hebrew words for “serve” and “pass over” differ by one similar letter; the King James Version has “I will make thee to pass with thine enemies”, while the ESV reads “serve”, as in the almost identical 17:4. Either way the people go into a land they do not know.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Your Words Were Found, and I Ate Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word can be a servant’s greatest joy and still leave him lonely and hurting, and Scripture lets him say so. Jeremiah asks God to remember him, avenge him, and not let him be taken away while God is patient with his persecutors, for he bears reproach for God’s sake (v. 15). God’s words were his food and the delight of his heart (v. 16). Yet they set him apart: he sat alone, filled with indignation, and now his pain will not heal, and he asks whether God has become a deceitful brook, waters that fail (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The same words that were his joy have cost him every friendship, and he tells God that he feels like a dry streambed.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you know; remember me and visit me, and take vengeance for me on my persecutors. In your forbearance take me not away; know that for your sake I bear reproach. Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart, for I am called by your name, O LORD, God of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah asks God to remember him in his suffering for God’s sake, and recalls that God’s words, which brought him this trouble, have been his food and his heart’s delight.

O LORD, you know. His first words are the ones every sufferer needs. He does not ask God to explain. It is enough that God knows.

In your forbearance take me not away. He understands his situation well. God is being patient with his persecutors, and that patience is the very thing endangering the prophet: do not let me be killed while you are slow to judge them.

For your sake I bear reproach. This is the ground of the appeal. A psalm uses the same words (Psalm 69:7), and Paul hears Christ praying that psalm: “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me” (Romans 15:3). Jeremiah bore reproach for God’s sake; Christ bore it in full, and those who suffer for him share it (Hebrews 13:13). That is what makes such suffering bearable.

Your words were found, and I ate them. This lovely sentence about Scripture comes from a man in the middle of a breakdown. “Your words were found” may recall the scroll discovered in the temple in Josiah’s reign, or simply the moment God’s word came to him. “And I ate them”: not admired, studied or filed, but taken in as food and made part of himself. Ezekiel was given a scroll to eat and found it “as sweet as honey” (Ezekiel 3:3). The psalmist said, “How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Psalm 119:103). And Jesus answered the tempter, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).

A joy and the delight of my heart. This is the man who has just wished he had never been born. Both are true at once, and anyone who has walked with God through a hard season knows that they can be.

May a believer pray for vengeance on persecutors? Jeremiah hands his cause to God instead of taking revenge (Romans 12:19). Christians may pray for God’s justice against unrepentant evil, while praying for their persecutors to repent (Matthew 5:44), as Jesus did (Luke 23:34).

verseByVerse.quote: I did not sit in the company of revelers, nor did I rejoice; I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation. Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that was Jeremiah’s joy has also left him alone and in unending pain, and he dares to ask whether God himself has become a stream that fails.

I sat alone. Here is the cost of the previous verse. He did not join the parties: he could not bring himself to, and a man who says what he says is not invited twice. The hand of God is usually spoken of as protection or power; here it is what keeps a man out of the room. Faithfulness is often isolating, and Jeremiah does not pretend otherwise; he tells God he is lonely.

The idol of being liked. Few things frighten us more than being the person nobody invites. Our age has turned approval into something we can count, and many people quietly arrange their lives around not being disliked, keeping their convictions where they will cost nothing. Scripture names the trap: “The fear of man lays a snare” (Proverbs 29:25). Approval is a hard master, because it can be withdrawn at any moment and must be earned again every day. The way out is not to stop needing approval but to receive it from somewhere it cannot be lost. The one who was “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3) had first heard his Father say, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and those who are in him share that verdict. A person who already has God’s delight can afford to sit alone for a while, and even to love the people who left the room.

Like a deceitful brook. Among the sharpest things Jeremiah ever says. In a dry country a wadi, a desert streambed, runs full in the rains and is a bed of stones in summer. Travellers died of thirst walking to one because they remembered water there. Job used the same picture of his friends: “My brothers are treacherous as a torrent-bed” (Job 6:15). Jeremiah uses it of God.

Like waters that fail. The accusation lands exactly where this book began: God had called himself “the fountain of living waters” and the people’s idols broken cisterns (2:13). Now the prophet who preached that sermon asks whether the fountain itself runs dry. Scripture writes it down and keeps it, because the God of the Bible is not fragile, and because believers need to know that someone in the book has felt what they are feeling.

If you are where Jeremiah was. If your pain will not lift and God seems to have run dry, this verse is for you. Feeling abandoned is not proof that you are, and saying so to God is prayer, not unbelief. Depression is often an illness as well as a spiritual trial, so do not carry it alone: tell your pastor and a friend, and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; medicine, if it is needed, is no failure of faith. If you are thinking of ending your life, get help the same day. And remember who hears you: a High Priest who can “sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15), who was himself a man of sorrows, and who does not dry up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–21 — If You Return, I Will Restore You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God restores his discouraged servant by calling him to return, and gives him back the promise he started with. If Jeremiah turns from worthless words and speaks what is precious, he will stand before God again and be his mouth; the people must turn to him, not he to them (v. 19). Then God repeats the words of the prophet’s call: a fortified wall of bronze, enemies who fight but do not prevail, and “I am with you to save you and deliver you” (vv. 20–21). The rebuke comes first, and the same commission follows it.
verseByVerse.theology: God calls his own prophet to repent, and then gives him back his commission with the original promise attached.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD: "If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me. If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth. They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them. And I will make you to this people a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail over you, for I am with you to save you and deliver you, declares the LORD. I will deliver you out of the hand of the wicked, and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls his bitter prophet to return, promises to restore him as his mouth if he speaks what is precious, and gives him back the promise of the bronze wall.

If you return, I will restore you. God does not comfort first; he calls his prophet to repent. The word Jeremiah has been preaching to the nation is now addressed to him. God never rebukes his pain or his tears, but his complaint had gone past lament into accusation, words that called God false. So God treats him as an adult: turn, and you will be restored to your place, standing before me as a servant stands before a king.

You shall be as my mouth. He is to sort his speech. Self-pity and bitterness are worthless; God’s word is precious; and the promise attached is staggering: he will speak for God.

They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them. This is the rule for every minister since. The pressure of an audience is constant, and the temptation is to be shaped by the people you speak to until you are saying what they would have said anyway. That is how the false prophets of chapter 14 were made. The prophet is to change his hearers; they are not to change him.

The one who kept the rule. No servant of God keeps it perfectly. The one who did, who “always” did what pleased the Father (John 8:29), is the one whose faithfulness covers those who fail, and the way back for them is the one offered here: return, and be restored.

A fortified wall of bronze. God gives him back his call in the words of the first chapter (1:18–19): a bronze wall, opposition that does not prevail, “I am with you”. The promise is repeated rather than improved, because it was always sufficient and the man had lost sight of it. And it comes after the rebuke, not instead of it. God’s way with his exhausted servants is neither to ignore their sin nor to withdraw his promise, but to call them back and hand them the same commission again. The risen Christ gives his messengers the same words: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20; compare Acts 18:10).

Back to work. Jeremiah went back to work, and kept at it until the city fell, and after.

15.title: A Deceitful Brook, and the Bronze Wall
15.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 15 completes the drought section that began in 14:1. God now answers the people’s faultless prayer (14:19–22), and then the prophet himself breaks down.

The message. There comes a point when a people’s judgment is fixed, and not even the greatest intercessors could turn it. But the heart of the chapter is the man who must carry that message: hated, lonely, delighting in God’s word and yet accusing God of being a dried-up stream. God does not discard him. He calls him to return, sorts his speech, and gives him back the promise he was given at the start: “I am with you to save you and deliver you” (v. 20).

Why it was said. Jeremiah’s generation had inherited Manasseh’s idolatry and refused every warning (see the introduction). And Jeremiah, cursed by everyone, had reached the end of himself. This is one of his “confessions”, the personal complaints to God scattered through chapters 11 to 20.

How the chapter makes its case. God refuses the prayer: even Moses and Samuel could not turn his heart, and the people are assigned to sword, famine and captivity because of what Manasseh began (vv. 1–4). No one will pity Jerusalem; God is weary of relenting, and mothers of seven sons will faint (vv. 5–9). Jeremiah wishes he had never been born, and God answers with his care and with the iron from the north that cannot be broken (vv. 10–14). God’s words were the prophet’s joy, yet they have left him alone, and he asks whether God is a deceitful brook (vv. 15–18). God calls him back: return, speak what is precious, and be again a bronze wall (vv. 19–21).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. Jeremiah bears reproach for God’s sake (v. 15), words Paul hears on Christ’s lips: “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me” (Romans 15:3). Christ too was “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3). But where Jeremiah wavered and had to be called back, Christ “always” did what pleased the Father (John 8:29), and the God who seemed to Jeremiah a failing brook gives in Christ “a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:14). The intercession that Moses and Samuel could not make for that generation, Christ makes for everyone who comes to God through him.

For us. Faithfulness can be lonely, and Scripture lets God’s servants say so. Bring God your honest complaint; when it turns into accusation, hear his call to return. Then feed again on his words, and take up the same work with the same promise: he is with you.
15.theology:
There is a point at which even the greatest intercessors would not turn God's heart (v. 1), and forgiven sin can still leave consequences running for generations (v. 4). God's long patience is real, and people can take it for granted until it ends (v. 6; compare 18:8).

God's word is food and delight to those who receive it (v. 16), and it can isolate the one who carries it (v. 17). Scripture keeps a prophet's accusation that God may be a brook that fails (v. 18), because faith may speak honestly to God. And God calls his weary servant back from accusation, then restores him with the same promise he was first given (vv. 19-21; 1:18-19).
15.examples: Two of the chapter's pictures stay with a reader: the light going at noon for a mother who has lost her children, and a wadi that runs full in the rains and is a bed of stones in summer. Between them stands a man who ate God's word with joy and lost every invitation because of it.

keyVerse.quote: If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me. If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth. They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the chapter, God’s answer to his prophet’s bitter complaint. He does not ignore the accusation, nor does he cast his servant off: he calls him to return and promises to restore him. The verse shows how God deals with discouraged servants, and it sets the rule for every faithful messenger: change your hearers; do not let them change you.

15.reflection:
God says that even Moses and Samuel could not turn his heart toward this generation (v. 1). What does this teach about the seriousness of persistent sin, and why is it good news that Christ “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25)?

Jeremiah was hated though he had given no one cause (v. 10), and he sat alone because God’s hand was on him (v. 17). Have you ever paid a social price for faithfulness? How does God’s delight in us in Christ free us from the fear of being disliked?

“Your words were found, and I ate them” (v. 16). What would it look like for Scripture to be food for you, and not only information? How can the same person delight in God’s word and still feel that God has run dry?

God answers Jeremiah’s accusation with a call to return, and then gives him back the same promise (vv. 19–21). How can we be honest with God in our pain without letting lament turn into accusation? What helps you return?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah’s own life becomes the sermon, because judgment will silence every part of ordinary life. God forbids him to marry or have children, for the sons and daughters born in Jerusalem will die of disease, sword and famine, unburied and unmourned (vv. 1–4). He may not enter a house of mourning, for God has taken away his peace, steadfast love and mercy, and there will be no one left to comfort the bereaved (vv. 5–7). Nor may he sit at a feast, for God will silence the voice of mirth and the voice of bridegroom and bride, before their eyes and in their own days (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet's private life is confiscated and made into the sermon: no marriage, no funerals, no parties.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "You shall not take a wife, nor shall you have sons or daughters in this place. For thus says the LORD concerning the sons and daughters who are born in this place, and concerning the mothers who bore them and the fathers who fathered them in this land: They shall die of deadly diseases. They shall not be lamented, nor shall they be buried. They shall be as dung on the surface of the ground. They shall perish by the sword and by famine, and their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the air and for the beasts of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God forbids Jeremiah to marry or have children, because the families of Jerusalem are about to perish; his single life becomes a living warning.

You shall not take a wife. In a society where marriage and children were the whole of a man’s future, his security in old age and his name after death, God forbids his prophet both. Jeremiah is to be single and childless, not by preference but by command, and the whole town will see it.

The cost of the calling. He has already lost his village (11:21) and his family (12:6); now he is denied the family he might have made. Ezekiel would face something similar when God took his wife and forbade him to mourn: “Sigh, but not aloud; make no mourning for the dead” (Ezekiel 24:17).

They shall die of deadly diseases. The reason turns the command from cruelty into mercy. Children born in Jerusalem now will die in the siege, unburied and unmourned. God is sparing his servant the sight of his own family starving.

A calling for a crisis. Paul reasoned in the same direction for a different crisis: “the appointed time has grown very short”, so “let those who have wives live as though they had none” (1 Corinthians 7:29). Jesus spoke of those who renounce marriage “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:12), and he himself lived unmarried. Singleness is never second-class in Scripture, and here it is part of the prophet’s message.

For the single and childless. The command was Jeremiah’s alone; it tells no one else to stay unmarried. But for those who are single or childless without having chosen it, he is company: a man with no wife and no children whom God called, kept and used.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah’s unmarried life was itself a sign of coming judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: Do not enter the house of mourning, or go to lament or grieve for them, for I have taken away my peace from this people, my steadfast love and mercy, declares the LORD. Both great and small shall die in this land. They shall not be buried, and no one shall lament for them or cut himself or make himself bald for them. No one shall break bread for the mourner, to comfort him for the dead, nor shall anyone give him the cup of consolation to drink for his father or his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah may not go to funerals, because God has withdrawn his peace, steadfast love and mercy from this generation, and the dead will be too many to mourn.

Do not enter the house of mourning. The second prohibition takes away the ordinary duties of a neighbour. In a village culture, staying away from funerals is a public insult, and it is meant to be noticed and asked about.

My steadfast love and mercy. The reason is the most frightening sentence in the chapter: “I have taken away my peace from this people, my steadfast love and mercy”. Peace, steadfast love and mercy are covenant words, what God had bound himself by promise to show, and now he withdraws them.

The cup of consolation. Every custom of comfort is listed and cancelled: the burial, the lament, the mourning rites, the meal brought to the bereaved, the cup pressed into the hand of a man who has lost his mother. The horror is not only death but the collapse of the community that normally carries people through it: there will be too many dead and too few living to sit with them.

Cut himself or make himself bald. Gashing the body and shaving the head for the dead were rites the law forbade (Leviticus 19:28; Deuteronomy 14:1); the people had adopted them anyway.

Not the last word. The same words return in Lamentations, when the city has fallen: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end” (Lamentations 3:22). What is withdrawn from a generation is not lost from the world. And when the steadfast love of God walked among his people in Jesus, he did what Jeremiah was forbidden to do: he went into the house of mourning, wept with the sisters of Lazarus, and called the dead man out of the tomb (John 11:33–44).

Uncertain wording. The word for “house of mourning” (marzeaḥ) is rare. Elsewhere in the Bible it appears only in Amos 6:7, of the revelry of idle feasters, and outside the Bible it names a kind of banqueting fellowship. Here it seems to mean the gathering and meal that followed a death.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not go into the house of feasting to sit with them, to eat and drink. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will silence in this place, before your eyes and in your days, the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah may not feast either, because God is about to silence every sound of joy in the land, and his absence from the celebrations is a preview.

The house of feasting. No funerals, and now no weddings or celebrations either: he may not sit down and enjoy an evening with his neighbours. He has already said that he sat alone (15:17), and this is the command behind it. A man who tells the truth in such a time finds himself outside both the grief and the gladness of his people.

The voice of the bridegroom. Verse 9 repeats the sentence that closed the temple sermon (7:34), and it is the sound of a civilisation ending: no laughter, and no weddings. He stays away from the feasts now because soon there will be none.

Before your eyes and in your days. There is mercy hidden in the timing: God tells him plainly that he will live to see it, so that when it comes he will not think God has lost control.

The bridegroom’s voice again. Jeremiah himself will later promise that the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride will be heard again in the ruined streets (33:10–11). John the Baptist called himself the friend who rejoices “greatly at the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29), and Jesus began his signs at a wedding (John 2:1–11). In him the silenced feast begins again.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A people that cannot see its sin will be given over to the gods it chose. When they hear all this, the people will ask, bewildered, what their iniquity is (v. 10). God answers through his prophet. Their fathers forsook him for other gods and did not keep his law (v. 11), and they have done worse, each following his own stubborn, evil will and refusing to listen (v. 12). So God will hurl them into a land they have never known, where they will serve other gods day and night, and he will show them no favour (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: A people can be so far gone that they cannot name a single sin, and the sentence simply gives them what they wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when you tell this people all these words, and they say to you, 'Why has the LORD pronounced all this great evil against us? What is our iniquity? What is the sin that we have committed against the LORD our God?' then you shall say to them: 'Because your fathers have forsaken me, declares the LORD, and have gone after other gods and have served and worshiped them, and have forsaken me and have not kept my law, and because you have done worse than your fathers, for behold, every one of you follows his stubborn, evil will, refusing to listen to me. Therefore I will hurl you out of this land into a land that neither you nor your fathers have known, and there you shall serve other gods day and night, for I will show you no favor.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people cannot see what they have done wrong; God names their sin, worse than their fathers’, and gives them the other gods they insisted on.

What is our iniquity? God predicts the reaction, and it is not defiance but blank incomprehension. They genuinely cannot think what they have done. This is the end of the process the whole book has been describing: a conscience that has lost feeling (6:15), a people who never ask “What have I done?” (8:6), religion carried on as a trade (14:18). The result is not a guilty nation pleading for mercy but a puzzled one asking what the fuss is about.

You have done worse than your fathers. The answer covers two generations (compare 7:26). Their upbringing explains a great deal and excuses nothing, because each generation could see where the sin of the last had led. And how it happened is stated exactly: “every one of you follows his stubborn, evil will, refusing to listen”. Not one national decision, but thousands of private ones.

Day and night. The sentence is shaped like the sin, as in 5:19. You wanted other gods; you shall have them day and night, in a country where they are the only ones on offer. God’s severest judgment is often to give people what they insisted on, in quantities they never wanted.

In practice. The cure is to ask their question while it can still be answered. Read Scripture as a mirror rather than a weapon, and ask a friend who knows you well what you have stopped noticing in yourself. Then confess it plainly, because the God who names our sin does so in order to forgive it: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — A New Exodus, and Fishers and Hunters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Beyond the judgment God promises a rescue greater than the exodus, but the judgment must come first. A day is coming when people will swear not by the LORD who brought Israel out of Egypt but by the LORD who brought them back from the north country and every land where he had driven them (vv. 14–15). First, though, he sends for fishers and hunters to catch them on every mountain and in every cleft of the rock, for nothing is hidden from his eyes, and he will repay in full a people who filled his land with the carcasses of their idols (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: Even while announcing the hunt, God promises a rescue that will make the exodus a second-best story.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it shall no longer be said, 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt,' but 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the north country and out of all the countries where he had driven them.' For I will bring them back to their own land that I gave to their fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without warning God promises a rescue so great that it will replace the exodus as the story by which his people swear.

The days are coming. Then, suddenly, hope, on a scale that is easy to miss. The exodus was the foundation of Israel’s identity. Every oath, every feast, every creed began there: the God who brought us out of Egypt.

Out of the north country. God says the rescue he is planning will be so much greater that people will stop swearing by the exodus and start swearing by this. The Red Sea will become the second-best story about him. Isaiah said the same in his own way: “Remember not the former things, nor consider the things of old. Behold, I am doing a new thing” (Isaiah 43:18–19). The saying is repeated later in this book (23:7–8), attached there to the coming of a righteous Branch from David’s line.

A greater exodus. Christians can hardly read it without looking further. There is a rescue that makes even the return from Babylon a rehearsal: a greater exodus, out of a deeper slavery, led by Jesus, who kept the Passover the night before he died to accomplish it, and whose death Luke calls his “departure”, in Greek his exodus (Luke 9:31).

Where Christians differ: how is this return fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. Dispensationalists look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel. Faithful Christians differ on whether a future return to the land is also promised, and those who expect one share the same hope in the same Messiah. This commentary’s view: the promises reach beyond any return to territory, to a new heart, a Davidic King and the nations gathered. They are fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Romans 11:26), and they will be complete in the new creation.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I am sending for many fishers, declares the LORD, and they shall catch them. And afterward I will send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain and every hill, and out of the clefts of the rocks. For my eyes are on all their ways. They are not hidden from me, nor is their iniquity concealed from my eyes. But first I will doubly repay their iniquity and their sin, because they have polluted my land with the carcasses of their detestable idols, and have filled my inheritance with their abominations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the homecoming comes the round-up: God sends fishers and hunters, and no one can hide from him, because his eyes are on all their ways.

I am sending for many fishers. Fishermen drag a net through the water and take everything in it; hunters go after what escaped the net, into the hills and rock crevices where refugees hide. Between them, nobody gets away.

My eyes are on all their ways. No one escapes, not because the hunters are skilful but because God sees. There is no cleft of the rock out of his sight. That fact is terrible here, and it is the same fact that makes him a refuge two verses later.

The carcasses of their detestable idols. The idols are called carcasses, dead things whose presence defiles a place like an unburied body. It is the language of contamination, and the land God calls “my inheritance” has been filled with it.

Fishers of men. Many think Jesus had this image in mind and turned it inside out: “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19). The same picture of people caught in a net serves judgment here and salvation there, and the difference is who is doing the sending and what he does with the catch.

Uncertain wording. “I will doubly repay” does not have to mean twice what they deserved. The Hebrew word for “double” can mean a matching equivalent, and many think it means here the full penalty their sin deserved, as when Isaiah says Jerusalem “has received from the LORD’s hand double for all her sins” (Isaiah 40:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–21 — To You Shall the Nations Come
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the darkest chapter so far the prophet worships, and sees the nations coming to the LORD. He calls God his strength, his stronghold and his refuge in the day of trouble (v. 19). Then he sees the nations arriving from the ends of the earth to confess that their fathers inherited nothing but lies and worthless things, and that gods made by human hands are no gods at all (vv. 19–20). God answers that this time he will make them know his power and his might, and they will know that his name is the LORD (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: In the middle of judgment the prophet sees Gentiles arriving from the ends of the earth to renounce the lies they inherited.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, my strength and my stronghold, my refuge in the day of trouble, to you shall the nations come from the ends of the earth and say: "Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, worthless things in which there is no profit. Can man make for himself gods? Such are not gods!" "Therefore, behold, I will make them know, this once I will make them know my power and my might, and they shall know that my name is the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah answers the announcement of judgment with worship, and sees the nations coming from the ends of the earth to renounce their inherited idols and know the LORD.

My strength and my stronghold. The titles are a soldier’s: “strength”, “stronghold”, “refuge in the day of trouble”. David piled up the same words: “The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer” (Psalm 18:2). The man forbidden to marry, to mourn or to feast still has the LORD himself.

To you shall the nations come. His eyes lift to the horizon and he sees what no one else in the chapter is looking at: not Judah restored, but the nations arriving “from the ends of the earth”. Isaiah saw the same procession: “all the nations shall flow to it” (Isaiah 2:2). It is one of the great surprises of the prophets that the books most full of judgment on Israel are also the books that see the world coming in.

Nothing but lies. Listen to what they say: “Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, worthless things in which there is no profit.” That is a whole conversion in one sentence: the religion they were raised in, named as inherited, as a lie, as worthless. Paul describes both the lie, that people “exchanged the truth about God for a lie” (Romans 1:25), and the turning, “from these vain things to a living God” (Acts 14:15). They have seen for themselves what chapter 10 taught: “Can man make for himself gods?” The question answers itself once it is asked out loud.

Isn’t my faith just where I happened to be born? It is one of the commonest objections, and it deserves respect. Most people hold roughly the religion of their parents, and a sceptic reasonably asks whether a belief that tracks your birthplace can be more than an accident. But look at what these converts do: exactly what the objection asks, examining what they were handed and calling it a lie. And the argument cuts every way. The secular confidence of a modern Western graduate is just as typical of where and when he was born, and how anyone came to a belief does not settle whether it is true. The gospel has always spread against inheritance: its first believers were Jews and pagans who left what their fathers taught, and it now grows fastest where hardly anyone’s grandparents were Christians. Scripture never lets faith be a family heirloom. Those who receive Christ are “born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:13). No one is a Christian by birth; everyone who is one has been born again.

I will make them know. God answers the prayer, and three times he says “know”. The judgment falling on Judah is itself part of how the nations will come to know him. The disaster is not only an ending but an announcement: people who never heard of the LORD will learn his name from what he does with his own people, and above all from what he did with his own Son.

16.title: A Life Made into a Sign
16.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 16 follows the prophet’s crisis and restoration (15:10–21). Recommissioned as a wall of bronze, Jeremiah now learns that his private life is to become part of the message.

The message. God’s judgment on Jerusalem will be so complete that marriage, mourning and feasting will all fall silent, and Jeremiah’s single, solitary life is the advance notice. The people cannot even see what they have done wrong, so God will give them the other gods they wanted. Yet the chapter breaks open with hope: a homecoming greater than the exodus, and the nations coming from the ends of the earth to confess that their fathers inherited lies, and to know the LORD’s name.

Why it was said. The people heard Jeremiah’s warnings with blank incomprehension, asking, “What is our iniquity?” (v. 10). They assumed that life, with its weddings, funerals and feasts, would go on as it always had (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Three prohibitions make the prophet’s life a sign: no wife or children (vv. 1–4), no funerals (vv. 5–7) and no feasts (vv. 8–9), because death will come on such a scale that all three will cease. When the people ask what their sin is, God names it: their fathers forsook him and they have done worse, so they will serve other gods day and night in a strange land (vv. 10–13). Then, abruptly, a new exodus (vv. 14–15), but first the fishers and hunters from whom no one hides (vv. 16–18). The prophet answers with worship and sees the nations coming (vv. 19–21).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. Jeremiah was forbidden weddings and funerals because God had taken away his peace, steadfast love and mercy (v. 5). Jesus went to both: he turned water into wine at a wedding and wept at a graveside before raising the dead, because in him God’s steadfast love had come back to his people. The greater exodus began with the return from Babylon, but on the mountain Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31), and the word is exodus. And the nations of verse 19 are coming still, as people turn “to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

For us. A life can speak as well as words, and for some believers singleness, loss or a costly obedience becomes the testimony. Ask God, and a friend who knows you, what you have stopped noticing in yourself, before you are left asking, “What is our iniquity?” And lift your eyes as Jeremiah did: the God who judges is gathering the nations.
16.theology:
A servant's life may itself be made into the message, at great personal cost (vv. 1-9; Ezek 24:16-18), and singleness can be a calling rather than a deprivation (1 Cor 7:29-31; Matt 19:12). God can withdraw his peace and steadfast love from a generation (v. 5), though his mercies do not fail in themselves (Lam 3:22).

Hardened people lose the ability to name their own sin (v. 10), and judgment often consists of being given what was insisted on (v. 13). Yet God promises a rescue greater than the exodus (vv. 14-15), and he will be known by the nations, who come renouncing their inherited lies (vv. 19-21; Isa 2:2-3).
16.examples: The chapter is full of absences: a man the whole town watches not marrying, a cup of consolation with no one left to hand it over, a guilty people who cannot think of a single thing they have done. Against them stands one great arrival, the nations coming from the ends of the earth and calling the religion they inherited a lie.

keyVerse.quote: O LORD, my strength and my stronghold, my refuge in the day of trouble, to you shall the nations come from the ends of the earth and say: “Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, worthless things in which there is no profit.”
keyVerse.note: In a chapter of silenced weddings, unmourned dead and exile, the prophet who has lost nearly everything turns to God as his refuge and sees the nations coming. The verse holds together the two things the chapter teaches: God is enough for the one who has nothing else, and his judgment on his own people opens the way for the world to come to him.

16.reflection:
God made Jeremiah’s single, solitary life part of his message (vv. 1–9). How can a life, and not only words, speak for God? How should our churches honour those who are single or childless, chosen or not?

The people ask, “What is our iniquity?” (v. 10), unable to see their own sin. What helps us notice sins we have stopped seeing? Who in your life could tell you honestly?

God promises a rescue so great that it will outshine the exodus (vv. 14–15). How does the death and resurrection of Jesus, his “exodus” (Luke 9:31), fulfil and surpass that promise?

The nations say, “Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies” (v. 19). What beliefs have you inherited that you have had to examine? How would you answer someone who says that faith is just a matter of where you were born?
