Your wealth and all your treasures I will give for spoil as the price of your high places for sin throughout all your territory.<sup>4</sup>You shall loosen your hand from your heritage that I gave to you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."<sup>5</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the LORD.<sup>6</sup>He is like a shrub in the desert, and shall not see any good come. Let it come!"<sup>16</sup>I have not run away from being your shepherd, nor have I desired the day of sickness. You know what came out of my lips; it was before your face.<sup>17</sup>Be not a terror to me; you are my refuge in the day of disaster.<sup>18</sup>Let those be put to shame who persecute me, but let me not be put to shame; let them be dismayed, but let me not be dismayed; bring upon them the day of disaster; destroy them with double destruction!<sup>19</sup>Thus said the LORD to me: "Go and stand in the People's Gate, by which the kings of Judah enter and by which they go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem,<sup>20</sup>and say: 'Hear the word of the LORD, you kings of Judah, and all Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, who enter by these gates.<sup>21</sup>Thus says the LORD: Take care for the sake of your lives, and do not bear a burden on the Sabbath day or bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem.<sup>22</sup>And do not carry a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath or do any work, but keep the Sabbath day holy, as I commanded your fathers.<sup>23</sup>Yet they did not listen or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck, that they might not hear and receive instruction.<sup>24</sup>"'But if you listen to me, declares the LORD, and bring in no burden by the gates of this city on the Sabbath day, but keep the Sabbath day holy and do no work on it,<sup>25</sup>then there shall enter by the gates of this city kings and princes who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their officials, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Sin Engraved on the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah’s sin is not on the surface but cut into the heart, and its religion has become a monument to its guilt. The sin is written with an iron pen and a diamond point, engraved on the tablet of the people’s heart, the very place where God’s law belonged, and on the horns of their altars, where atonement was made (v. 1). The children have learned the shrines and the sacred poles beside every green tree, so the sin is passing to the next generation (vv. 2–3). The cost will be everything: the treasures given away as plunder, the inheritance God gave prised out of their hands, and service to enemies in a land they do not know, because God’s anger has been kindled (vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.theology: The record of sin is cut into the very place where God means to write his law.

verseByVerse.quote: "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron; with a point of diamond it is engraved on the tablet of their heart, and on the horns of their altars, while their children remember their altars and their Asherim, beside every green tree and on the high hills, on the mountains in the open country. Your wealth and all your treasures I will give for spoil as the price of your high places for sin throughout all your territory. You shall loosen your hand from your heritage that I gave to you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s sin is engraved, not stained: cut into the people’s hearts and into the altars that should have taken it away, learned by their children, and about to cost them the land God gave them.

Written with a pen of iron. The image is of an inscription cut with the hardest tools available, an iron stylus and a diamond point. Not written in ink, which fades, but engraved, which lasts.

The tablet of their heart. That phrase belongs to the covenant. God wrote his law on tablets of stone and asked for it to be kept on the heart. What is engraved there instead is the record of their sin, so deep that it has become part of them.

The horns of their altars. The second surface is worse. The horns at the altar’s corners were where the blood of the sin offering was smeared, the place of atonement. Their sin is carved into the very furniture of forgiveness. Religion practised without repentance does not remove guilt; it records it.

While their children remember. What the children remember is not the Passover or the law read at the feast, but where the shrines were and what happened there. In any household, children learn most surely from what the adults actually do.

You shall loosen your hand. The sentence of 15:13–14 is repeated with one new phrase, a picture of fingers being prised off something held tight. They will not hand the land over; it will be taken out of their grip.

Toward the new covenant. Hold this verse beside the promise the book is moving toward: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (31:33). The new covenant is not a better set of rules but God writing something new on the same heart. For that, the old record had to be removed, and at the cross it was: Christ took the guilt carved into us, and his Spirit now writes, as Paul puts it, “not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything in a life depends on what the heart leans on. The first portrait begins with a curse: the man who trusts in man, makes flesh his strength and turns his heart from the LORD is like a shrub in the desert, alive but never flourishing, set in a salt land where nothing grows (vv. 5–6). The second begins with a blessing: the man whose trust is the LORD is like a tree planted by water, its roots reaching the stream (vv. 7–8). The heat and the drought come to both; the planted tree does not fear, stays green and keeps bearing fruit. Coming after the drought of chapter 14, the two pictures tell Judah that its real need was never rain but God himself.
verseByVerse.theology: Two lives are told as two plants, and the difference is not circumstance but where the roots go.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the LORD. He is like a shrub in the desert, and shall not see any good come. He shall dwell in the parched places of the wilderness, in an uninhabited salt land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To rest your weight on human strength is to turn your heart away from God, and a life built that way survives without ever flourishing, like scrub in a salt desert.

Cursed is the man who trusts in man. One of the great passages of the book, built as a pair of portraits. The first is defined in three parts: he trusts in man, makes flesh his strength, and his heart turns away from the LORD. The ESV notes that “strength” is in Hebrew “arm”: the muscle you lean on.

Whose heart turns away from the LORD. The three go together. Trusting human resources is not a neutral method that happens to fail; it is a heart turning from God. Whatever we lean on has our heart.

Like a shrub in the desert. The picture is scrub in the Judean wilderness: grey, stunted, only just alive. Such a life does not collapse dramatically; it survives, and never flourishes. “Shall not see any good come” is almost worse than disaster: a life in which nothing good is ever quite noticed.

An uninhabited salt land. Soil where nothing will grow, like the ground around the Dead Sea. Misplaced trust does not only fail to feed you; it ruins the ground for anything else.

What it does not mean. This is not a warning against using doctors, savings or friends. It is about where the weight rests. The question is what you would still have if the arm you are leaning on gave way tomorrow.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh his strength” is literally “flesh his arm” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose trust is the LORD. He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes, for its leaves remain green, and is not anxious in the year of drought, for it does not cease to bear fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The person whose trust is the LORD himself is like a tree planted by a stream: the heat and drought still come, but his roots reach water they cannot dry up, so he goes on without fear and keeps bearing fruit.

Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD. The portrait says it twice on purpose: he “trusts in the LORD”, and his “trust is the LORD”. He is not trusting God to deliver a particular outcome; God himself is what he rests on.

Like a tree planted by water. Psalm 1 has the same tree, “like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season” (Psalm 1:3), but Jeremiah adds the weather, and after chapter 14 we know why. The heat comes; the year of drought arrives. The believer is not exempt from the drought that scorched the whole country; his roots are somewhere it does not reach.

Does not fear when heat comes. In the crisis he does not fear and is not anxious. Anyone who has tried to argue himself out of anxiety knows that this cannot be produced by effort. It is the fruit of where the roots are. And the tree did not plant itself: it is planted, and kept watered by God’s Spirit through his word and prayer. Roots grow slowly, in ordinary weather, long before they are tested.

It does not cease to bear fruit. Not merely surviving, but producing, in the drought year, for other people’s benefit.

The man who trusted perfectly. Christ trusted his Father when every human arm failed him. “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now” (Matthew 27:43) was flung at him on the cross, and God answered by raising him from the dead. Joined to him, you are “rooted and built up in him” (Colossians 2:7), planted in the one who has already come through the worst heat there is.

How do I put my roots down? Trust is not a feeling you summon at 2 a.m.; it is a habit of leaning, formed in ordinary weather. Go to the stream daily. Read a passage of Scripture before you pick up the phone, and pray one of its sentences back to God; that is how roots reach water. Name the arm. When the redundancy rumour starts or the test results are late, ask what you are actually leaning on: the savings, the boss’s good opinion, your own competence. Say it to God, and tell him that he is your trust. Act on it in one decision. Give generously when the budget is tight, or tell the truth when a lie would protect you, because your security does not rest on the outcome. Keep company with the planted. Ask believers who have come through a drought how they were kept.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The reason people trust man rather than God lies in the heart, which deceives its owner, and only God can see through it. The heart is deceitful above all things and desperately sick, and no one can understand it; but the LORD searches it and tests the inner self, and gives each person what his ways deserve (vv. 9–10). A proverb shows the deceit at work: the man who grows rich unjustly is like a partridge sitting on a brood that is not hers, left with nothing in mid-life and exposed as a fool at the end (v. 11). Against all this stands God’s glorious throne, the hope of Israel: those who forsake him, the fountain of living water, are written in the dust (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody can read his own heart; God reads it, and the diagnosis drives us back to the fountain abandoned in chapter 2.

verseByVerse.quote: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it? "I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The human heart deceives above all things, its own owner most of all, and it is sick beyond human cure; but the LORD sees straight through it and judges each person by what his life has produced.

The heart is deceitful above all things. Few sentences explain this book better. The heart in Scripture is not the emotions but the control centre of a person: mind, will and affections together, the part of you that decides. It lies, and its most practised victim is its owner. It is “desperately sick”, beyond the reach of any human cure. The King James Version has “desperately wicked”; the Hebrew word means incurably ill, and both renderings describe the same disease.

Who can understand it? Not you, about yourself. The instrument you would use to examine your heart is the heart, and it is the thing under suspicion. This is why sincerity is no defence: a person can be entirely sincere and entirely deceived, because the deceiver lives inside.

I the LORD search the heart. The question is answered in the next breath, and the answer is God. The ESV notes that “mind” is in Hebrew “kidneys”, the innermost parts. He does not guess at us from the outside; he reads what we cannot read.

Why a new heart is needed. A heart this sick cannot be managed, educated or mended by good resolutions. It has to be replaced, and this book promises exactly that: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (31:33); “I will give you a new heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).

The searcher of hearts. The risen Christ takes these words for himself: “I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you according to your works” (Revelation 2:23). That could be the most frightening sentence imaginable, and for the believer it is the opposite, because the one who reads the heart is the one who died for what he finds there. So the right response is the psalmist’s, and it takes courage: “Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!” (Psalm 139:23).

Does this still describe a Christian? A believer has been given a new heart, yet remaining sin still deceives, which is why Christians do not treat their feelings as the final word about themselves. That cuts both ways. A heart that flatters you cannot be trusted, and neither can a heart that condemns you: “whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (1 John 3:20). Assurance rests on Christ and his promise, not on reading your own heart correctly.

Is judgment by works? Each person’s deeds show what is in the heart, and God judges them truly (Romans 2:6). The one who is saved is saved by grace through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9), but saving faith always bears fruit, which God sees.
verseByVerse.note: “Mind” is literally “kidneys” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Like the partridge that gathers a brood that she did not hatch, so is he who gets riches but not by justice; in the midst of his days they will leave him, and at his end he will be a fool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wealth gained unjustly is like a brood of chicks a bird did not hatch: it runs off in the middle of life and leaves its owner exposed as a fool. The proverb fits the chapter: here is the heart’s deceit at work in how a man gets his money.

Like the partridge. The picture is a bird sitting on eggs that are not hers. The proverb draws on what was commonly said of the partridge; its point is the man, not the bird’s habits. She keeps the eggs warm, defends them, does all the work of a mother, and when they hatch they run off to their own kind. She is left with a bare nest.

They will leave him. So it is with money gained unjustly. The man broods over it, and “in the midst of his days they will leave him”: not at the end, when everyone’s wealth departs, but halfway through, while he still had plans for it.

At his end he will be a fool. The verdict is not only that he is wicked, which he is, but that he is stupid. Jesus told of a rich man planning bigger barns, to whom God said, “Fool! This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:20). Injustice for profit is a bad investment.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “gathers a brood” is rare, and whether it means to hatch or to gather is uncertain. The ESV follows the ancient belief that the partridge sits on other birds’ eggs. Whatever the exact habit, the proverb’s point is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: A glorious throne set on high from the beginning is the place of our sanctuary. O LORD, the hope of Israel, all who forsake you shall be put to shame; those who turn away from you shall be written in the earth, for they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against the deceit of the heart stands the throne of God, the hope of Israel: those who forsake him, the fountain of living water, will have their names written in dust.

A glorious throne set on high. After the desert scrub and the empty nest, worship. The temple is not first a building but a throne room, the place where God has reigned “from the beginning”. Whatever happens to the city, that throne is not vacated.

Written in the earth. Those who turn away from God are written in the earth: their names are scratched in dust, which the next wind or footstep erases. Their sin, by contrast, is engraved with an iron pen (v. 1), while the names of God’s people are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). The ESV notes that where the English has “you”, the Hebrew has “me”: the prophet’s prayer slips into God’s own voice.

The fountain of living water. The chapter reaches back to the book’s first great image: they have forsaken “the fountain of living water” (compare 2:13). Everything in between, the cisterns, the drought, the empty jars, the shrub in the salt land and the tree by the stream, has been about water, and here the source is named again.

Christ the fountain. On the last day of the Feast of Booths Jesus stood in the temple courts and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). The fountain Judah abandoned came to Jerusalem in person.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah turns to God for himself, and his prayer shows how a faithful servant holds on when he is mocked. He asks to be healed and saved by the only one who can, for God is his praise (v. 14). His hearers taunt him, “Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come!”, because the disaster has not yet arrived (v. 15). He protests that he has not run from his task as a shepherd, nor wished for the disaster he announces, and that God heard every word (v. 16). He begs God not to become a terror to him, but to be his refuge, and he hands his persecutors over to God’s judgment (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who asked whether God was a failing brook now asks to be healed, and knows who alone can do it.

verseByVerse.quote: Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my praise. Behold, they say to me, "Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come!" I have not run away from being your shepherd, nor have I desired the day of sickness. You know what came out of my lips; it was before your face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mocked because his warnings have not yet come true, Jeremiah asks God alone to heal and save him, and rests his defence on the fact that God heard every word he spoke.

Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed. The wording shows what he believes about God. He does not say, help me to heal. If God does it, it is done; if God does not, nothing else will.

The wound brought to God. This is the man who asked, “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there?” (8:22), and who accused God of being like a deceitful brook (15:18). Now he brings the wound to the only physician there is. Watch for that movement in a life: from complaint that there is no healing to a request for it.

Where is the word of the LORD? The taunt of people who have heard the warnings for years and watched nothing happen. It is the mockery Peter foresaw for the last days: “Where is the promise of his coming?” (2 Peter 3:4). They take the delay as proof that it will never come, and the challenge has a swagger to it: “Let it come!” Within a few years it came.

I have not run away. He denies two things. He has not run away from shepherding this people, though everything invited it. And he has not desired “the day of sickness”: he has not wanted the disaster he preaches, which is the accusation people always make against the man who warns them.

You know what came out of my lips. His defence is simply that God heard him. A minister’s real record is not his reputation among his hearers but what God heard him say.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of “I have not run away from being your shepherd” is compressed and has been taken in different ways; the King James Version has “I have not hastened from being a pastor to follow thee”. Most translations agree with the ESV’s sense: Jeremiah has stayed at the post God gave him.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not a terror to me; you are my refuge in the day of disaster. Let those be put to shame who persecute me, but let me not be put to shame; let them be dismayed, but let me not be dismayed; bring upon them the day of disaster; destroy them with double destruction!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah asks God not to become a terror to him but to be his refuge in the coming disaster, and he leaves the punishment of his persecutors entirely in God’s hands.

Be not a terror to me. An honest prayer: he asks God not to become the thing he is afraid of. When judgment is falling all around, the hand that sends it is the same hand he is sheltering under, and that is a hard place to stand. Everyone who trusts God through a disaster knows the tension: the God who is my refuge is also the God who permitted the thing I need refuge from. Jeremiah does not resolve it; he prays it.

Fleeing to God from God. We picture a refuge as a place away from the danger, a cellar in a storm. Jeremiah’s refuge is stranger. The storm coming on Jerusalem is God’s own judgment, and the shelter he runs to is God (16:19). That sounds impossible until you stand at the cross. There the storm of God’s judgment against sin fell in full on his own Son, so that for everyone hidden in Christ the one place it cannot reach is God himself: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). That changes what we do when trouble comes. When we suspect God is behind a hard providence, our instinct is to keep our distance from him and shelter in something else: busyness, a screen, a drink, a grievance. Jeremiah shows the other way. Take the fear straight to the God you are afraid of, and say with him, “you are my refuge in the day of disaster”.

Destroy them with double destruction! His prayer for judgment on his enemies returns, sharper than before. Read it as the prayer of a man who has been forbidden to defend himself and has handed the case over (11:20): everything he wants done to his enemies he asks God to do, which means he will do none of it himself.

Praying since Calvary. Christians pray differently since Calvary, where the one who was persecuted prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). But the instinct underneath, to leave the judging to God and say so out loud, is one the New Testament commends: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–27 — The Sabbath at the Gates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Trust in God is not only an inner matter; it shows in public, and God tests it at the city gates on the Sabbath. Jeremiah is sent to stand in the People’s Gate, where the kings come and go, and in every gate of Jerusalem (vv. 19–20). He tells kings and people to carry no loads in or out and do no work on the Sabbath, but keep it holy as God commanded their fathers, who stiffened their necks so as not to hear (vv. 21–23). Then he sets two futures before the city. If they keep the day, David’s kings will ride in, pilgrims will come from every region with thank offerings, and the city will stand forever (vv. 24–26); if not, fire will burn in those same gates and consume the palaces (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole future of the city is hung on one visible, weekly act of trust.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus said the LORD to me: "Go and stand in the People's Gate, by which the kings of Judah enter and by which they go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem, and say: 'Hear the word of the LORD, you kings of Judah, and all Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, who enter by these gates. Thus says the LORD: Take care for the sake of your lives, and do not bear a burden on the Sabbath day or bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem. And do not carry a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath or do any work, but keep the Sabbath day holy, as I commanded your fathers. Yet they did not listen or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck, that they might not hear and receive instruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells the whole city, from the king down, to stop carrying loads through its gates on the Sabbath, because the day was the visible sign that Israel belonged to him and lived by his provision, and their fathers had refused to hear it.

Go and stand in the People’s Gate. The place is chosen for traffic: the gate the royal household uses, then every other gate in the city. Everyone entering will hear it.

Keep the Sabbath day holy. After chapters about idolatry, injustice, false prophets and a deceitful heart, God sends his prophet to talk about carrying loads on a Saturday. It can look trivial until you see what the day was for. The Sabbath was the public sign of the covenant, God’s bond with Israel (Exodus 31:13): a weekly, visible statement that this people belonged to God, that their lives were not their own, and that their provision did not depend on their own unbroken effort. A man who stops trading one day in seven is saying out loud that God feeds him. Bringing a load through the gate on that day was not a technicality but a public refusal of the trust described in verse 7. Nearly two centuries later Nehemiah would shut the same gates against the same traders (Nehemiah 13:15–22).

Yet they did not listen. The verdict on the fathers echoes 7:26, and the wording is telling: they stiffened their necks “that they might not hear”. They did not fail to hear by accident; not hearing was the aim.

A palace in time. Benjamin Franklin advised a young tradesman, “Remember that time is money,” and most of us have absorbed the lesson so well that an unproductive hour feels faintly guilty. Phones make every evening a working evening, and rest is valued chiefly as recovery, so that we can produce more on Monday. The Jewish thinker Abraham Joshua Heschel, in The Sabbath, argued that a technical civilisation is very good at conquering space and very poor at hallowing time, and he called the Sabbath “a palace in time”: a day that is not for getting anything. A person who cannot stop has made his work his saviour; he is quietly convinced that if he stops, everything, including himself, will fall apart. The Sabbath answered that fear every week, and Isaiah put the invitation warmly: “call the Sabbath a delight” (Isaiah 58:13).

Rest grounded in a finished work. The gospel answers that fear at the root. On the day Jesus’ body lay in the tomb, his work finished, the women who loved him did nothing: “On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment” (Luke 23:56). Our rest is grounded in a work already done, and none of it ours.

Where Christians differ: does the Sabbath command bind Christians today? It was the sign of the covenant at Sinai, and the New Testament calls Sabbaths “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17). Many godly Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment, and they keep it with great blessing; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds.

This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), so that no one may bind another’s conscience about days (Romans 14:5). The Lord’s Day is a gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom rather than as a law with rules about work. Faithful Christians differ here, and bear with one another.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But if you listen to me, declares the LORD, and bring in no burden by the gates of this city on the Sabbath day, but keep the Sabbath day holy and do no work on it, then there shall enter by the gates of this city kings and princes who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their officials, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And this city shall be inhabited forever. And people shall come from the cities of Judah and the places around Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, from the Shephelah, from the hill country, and from the Negeb, bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices, grain offerings and frankincense, and bringing thank offerings to the house of the LORD. But if you do not listen to me, to keep the Sabbath day holy, and not to bear a burden and enter by the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, then I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem and shall not be quenched.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two futures run through the same gates: if the city honours God’s day, David’s kings and joyful worshippers will fill it forever; if not, fire will burn in those gates and consume its palaces.

But if you listen to me. If they listen: kings of David’s line riding in, officials, crowds, and a city “inhabited forever”. The promise is enormous, and it hangs on something small enough to see from the street. God often puts the weight of great things on one small, visible act of obedience, because that is where trust can be seen.

Bringing thank offerings. Pilgrims come from every region: Benjamin to the north, the Shephelah foothills to the west, the hill country around the city, and the Negeb desert to the south, the whole land on its way to worship. They bring the full range of offerings, and the list ends with thank offerings, brought not because guilt requires them but because someone is glad. That is the picture of a country put right with God: roads full of people who want to be there.

A fire in its gates. And the other future: fire in the gates, spreading to the palaces, unquenchable. That is exactly what happened when Babylon took the city (52:13).

Christ, lord of the Sabbath. For Christians the Sabbath command comes through Christ, who said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath”, and called himself “lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27–28). Hebrews says that “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God”, entered by resting from our own works as God did from his (Hebrews 4:9–10). The city of David’s kings and glad worshippers that Judah forfeited is the city Christ, David’s son, is gathering now from every nation.

The question for us. The chapter finally asks the question of verses 5 and 7 in a practical form. Is your life arranged to say that God provides, or that everything depends on your unbroken effort? The answer is visible in a diary, which is why God sent a prophet to stand at a gate and watch what people carried through it. No one’s diary answers it perfectly. Christ trusted the Father without a lapse, and his rest is offered to those who have not: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

17.title: The Heart Is Deceitful: Two Trees and a Sabbath
17.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 14 to 16 brought drought, the prophet’s bitter complaints, and the command that Jeremiah must not marry, mourn or feast. Chapter 17 gathers several short pieces that go beneath Judah’s behaviour to its heart, and ends with a sermon at the city gates.

The message. Judah’s trouble is not a few bad habits but a heart with sin carved into it, and a heart so deceitful that no one can read it, let alone cure it. Everything turns on where that heart puts its weight: on man, and it withers like desert scrub; on the LORD, and it flourishes like a tree by a stream, even in drought. Only the God who searches the heart can heal it, and the trust he asks for is meant to be seen, down to what a city carries through its gates on the Sabbath.

Why it was said. Judah still had its temple, sacrifices and king, and leaned on alliances, wealth and its own effort while its heart turned from God (see the introduction). It mocked the warnings that had not yet come true (v. 15).

How the chapter makes its case. First the depth of the problem: sin engraved on the heart and on the very altars of atonement, and the land to be lost for it (vv. 1–4). Then the choice, in two portraits: the man who trusts in man and the man who trusts in the LORD (vv. 5–8). Then the reason the wrong choice is made: the heart deceives, though God searches it, and the man who grows rich unjustly is its fool (vv. 9–13). Jeremiah answers with a prayer to be healed and kept (vv. 14–18). Last, trust is put to a public test at the gates, where keeping the Sabbath or breaking it leads to two futures (vv. 19–27).

Where it leads. First by the need it exposes. A heart this sick cannot be reformed; it must be rewritten, and that is what the new covenant promises (31:33) and the Spirit of Christ does, writing “on tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3). Then by pattern and by God’s character. Jesus is the man who trusted the LORD perfectly when every human arm failed him, the fountain of living water Judah forsook (v. 13; John 7:37), the searcher of hearts (Revelation 2:23), and the lord of the Sabbath who gives the rest it pictured.

For us. Ask what you lean on when the heat comes, and do not trust your heart’s verdict on itself, whether it flatters or condemns. Bring it to the God who searches it and in Christ has provided for all he finds there, and let your trust show in visible choices, beginning with the courage to rest.
17.theology:
Sin is engraved on the heart where God intends to write his law (v. 1), and religion without repentance records guilt rather than removing it. Trust is the dividing line between two lives (vv. 5-8): misplaced trust is a heart turning away, and trust in God bears fruit precisely in the drought.

The heart cannot be read by its owner, only by God (vv. 9-10), which is why it must be replaced, not reformed (31:33). God alone heals and saves (v. 14). The Sabbath was the visible weekly sign that life and provision come from God (vv. 21-27), fulfilled in Christ, lord of the Sabbath, and in the rest that remains for his people (Heb 4:9-10).
17.examples: The chapter works in sharp pictures: sin cut with a diamond point into the horns of the altar, the very furniture of forgiveness; grey scrub in a salt land, alive and never flourishing, beside a tree whose roots reach water the drought cannot touch; a partridge brooding over eggs that run off to someone else. Its last picture is the plainest: a diary that says either that God provides or that everything depends on me.

keyVerse.quote: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?
keyVerse.note: This verse explains the whole chapter and much of the book. It is why Judah trusts man rather than God (v. 5), why its sin is engraved rather than stained (v. 1), and why no reform could save it. Only the God who searches the heart (v. 10) can answer its question, and in the new covenant he answers it by giving a new heart.

17.reflection:
Verses 5–8 describe two people, one leaning on human strength and one whose trust is the LORD. What “arm of flesh” are you most tempted to lean on? What would change if it gave way tomorrow?

The tree by the stream still feels the heat and the drought (v. 8); what is different is where its roots are. How have you seen believers kept through hard years? What helps roots grow in ordinary weather?

If the heart is “deceitful above all things” (v. 9), why is sincerity not enough? How should this shape the way we treat our own feelings, both when they excuse us and when they condemn us?

God sent Jeremiah to the gates to talk about carrying loads on the Sabbath (vv. 19–27). What does the way you use your time say about what you trust? What would it look like for you to receive rest as a gift?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Down to the Potter's House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is the potter and his people are clay in his hands, which means he may reshape them as he chooses, and he does not throw spoiled clay away. God sends Jeremiah down to a potter’s workshop to receive his word there (vv. 1–2). He watches the potter at his wheel; the vessel is spoiled in his hands, so the potter reworks it into another vessel, as seems good to him (vv. 3–4). Then God gives the meaning as a question: can he not do with Israel what this potter has done? Like clay in the potter’s hand, so is Israel in his (vv. 5–6). The picture holds authority and mercy together, and both are needed for what follows.
verseByVerse.theology: God sends his prophet to a workshop to watch a craftsman start again with spoiled clay.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will let you hear my words." So I went down to the potter's house, and there he was working at his wheel. And the vessel he was making of clay was spoiled in the potter's hand, and he reworked it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a pot is spoiled on the wheel, the potter does not throw the clay away but reshapes it as he chooses.

Go down to the potter’s house. God’s word does not always come in a temple or a vision; here the prophet must go down to a workshop to receive it. The ESV notes that “I will let you hear my words” may be rendered “will cause you to hear”: the potter’s shed is the place God has chosen to speak.

There he was working at his wheel. The scene is unhurried: a man at a double wheel, kicking the lower stone, hands wet, shaping the clay on the upper one. Jeremiah watches, and the sermon is the craftsman’s hands. Much of what God teaches is learned by watching ordinary work done well.

He reworked it into another vessel. The pot goes wrong, with a stone in the clay, an uneven wall or a wobble, and the potter does not throw the lump away. He collapses it and makes something else of it, “as it seemed good to the potter to do”.

Two truths at once. The chapter needs both. The potter has complete authority over the clay: the clay does not vote on what it becomes. And the potter does not discard spoiled clay: he reworks it. The God who is about to say terrifying things is first shown as a craftsman who will not throw the clay away.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me: "O house of Israel, can I not do with you as this potter has done? declares the LORD. Behold, like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is in God’s hands as clay is in a potter’s, so he has every right to reshape his people, in judgment or in mercy, and they cannot hold him to the shape they prefer.

Can I not do with you as this potter has done? The interpretation comes as a question about rights. Israel had argued for chapters that God could not really destroy the temple, hand over his own city or do this to his people. The potter’s wheel answers all of it.

We are the clay. Scripture uses the image both ways. Isaiah turns it into prayer: “we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand” (Isaiah 64:8). And he turns it into rebuke: “Shall the potter be regarded as the clay, that the thing made should say of its maker, ‘He did not make me’?” (Isaiah 29:16).

Who gets to say what I am? To modern ears the potter is almost an insult. The deepest conviction of our culture is that no one has the right to define me but me: I am not clay, I am the potter, and my life is a pot I am throwing myself. It sounds like freedom, and there is something noble in refusing shapes others chose for us. But notice what it costs. If I am my own maker, I am also my own guarantor. Every failure is a flaw in the only craftsman there is, and a spoiled pot has no one to rework it. Jeremiah’s picture is more humbling and far kinder. You did not make yourself, so you do not have to hold yourself together. You belong to hands that are skilled, patient and unwilling to throw spoiled clay away.

Remade in Christ. In Christ those hands are at work again: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10). Being shaped by someone who loves you is not the end of freedom; it is the end of having to be your own god. And Paul adds the note that keeps the image from crushing anyone: “we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

What it does not mean. Not that people are inert lumps with no responsibility; the next six verses make that impossible to conclude. The point is that God does not answer to the clay for what he does with it, and that the one who has this freedom reworks spoiled clay.

Where Christians differ: does the potter teach election? Paul takes up the potter in Romans 9:20–21 to show God’s sovereign right over his creatures: “Will what is molded say to its molder, ‘Why have you made me like this?’” (Romans 9:20). Some argue that because Jeremiah’s potter reworks the clay as the nation responds (vv. 7–10), the image cannot teach God’s free choice of those he saves.

This commentary’s view: both are true. Jeremiah speaks of how God deals with nations in history, Paul of his sovereign mercy to individuals, and in both the clay has no right to accuse the potter. And Paul’s argument ends in mercy: the Potter makes “vessels of mercy”, prepared beforehand for glory (Romans 9:23), and in Christ he remakes spoiled clay.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s threats and promises are not fixed forecasts but real calls to respond, and Judah refuses the call. If God announces that he will pluck up and destroy a nation, and it turns from its evil, he relents of the disaster (vv. 7–8); if he announces that he will build and plant a nation, and it does evil, he relents of the good (vv. 9–10). So he tells Judah that he is shaping disaster against it, like a potter at the wheel, while it can still be remade: return, every one, and amend your ways (v. 11). The people answer that it is hopeless and they will follow their own plans and the stubbornness of their evil hearts (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Warnings are conditional by design; they are offered so that they need not be carried out.

verseByVerse.quote: If at any time I declare concerning a nation or a kingdom, that I will pluck up and break down and destroy it, and if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it. And if at any time I declare concerning a nation or a kingdom that I will build and plant it, and if it does evil in my sight, not listening to my voice, then I will relent of the good that I had intended to do to it. Now, therefore, say to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: 'Thus says the LORD, Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way, and amend your ways and your deeds.' "But they say, 'That is in vain! We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s warnings of judgment and promises of blessing are conditional: when a nation turns from evil he relents of the disaster, and when it turns to evil he withdraws the good, so Judah is called to return, and answers that it is no use.

Pluck up and break down. This paragraph tells you how to read every threat in the prophetic books. The verbs are the ones from Jeremiah’s call (1:10), now shown to be conditional. A prophecy of judgment is not a weather forecast. It is a warning given so that it need not come true: God says what he intends to do so that the people will turn and he will not have to do it.

The case of Nineveh. Jonah is the case study. He preached that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown, with no conditions attached; the city repented; and “God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it” (Jonah 3:10). Jonah was furious precisely because he knew this principle in advance.

I will relent of the good. The rule runs the other way too, which is less often quoted. A promise of blessing is not a charm that survives rebellion. Judah’s whole delusion was that the promises to David and to Zion had made them permanently safe, whatever they did.

I am shaping disaster against you. The verb is a potter’s. The potter is at the wheel again, and what is taking form on it is judgment, announced while it is still soft, still capable of being collapsed and remade. Ezekiel puts God’s heart in it plainly: “I have no pleasure in the death of anyone”, so “turn, and live” (Ezekiel 18:32).

That is in vain! The answer chills, because it is not a denial. They do not say the message is false but hopeless, and then announce that they will do as they please anyway. Despair and defiance have arrived at the same place, as they often do. A person who says “I could never change” and a person who says “I will not change” end up doing exactly the same thing on Monday morning. The answer to both is the scene in the workshop: spoiled clay is not discarded but reworked, and by the potter’s hands, not its own. The call to return comes from the God who has just promised to relent when anyone turns.

Does God change his mind? “God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind” (Numbers 23:19). Scripture says he “relents” to describe his real response to repentance in human terms: his warnings are real, and when people turn, he does what he always purposed to do for those who turn. He is not surprised or moved as a man is; his unchanging character is the very reason he spares the penitent. A father who treated a repentant child like a defiant one would not be steadfast but indifferent.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Does the Snow of Lebanon Leave?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah’s forgetting of God is more unnatural than anything in creation, and it will end with God turning his back. God calls for a survey of the nations: who has ever heard of a people doing what virgin Israel has done (v. 13)? The snow on the mountains of Lebanon does not leave its crags, and the cold streams that flow from them do not run dry (v. 14), but God’s people have forgotten him, burned offerings to false gods, and stumbled off the ancient roads onto side tracks (v. 15). Their land will become a horror that passers-by hiss at (v. 16). God will scatter them like the east wind and, reversing the priestly blessing, show them his back, not his face, in the day of disaster (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Even the weather keeps faith better than this people; what nature does by nature they would not do by covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the LORD: Ask among the nations, Who has heard the like of this? The virgin Israel has done a very horrible thing. Does the snow of Lebanon leave the crags of Sirion? Do the mountain waters run dry, the cold flowing streams? But my people have forgotten me; they make offerings to false gods; they made them stumble in their ways, in the ancient roads, and to walk into side roads, not the highway, making their land a horror, a thing to be hissed at forever. Everyone who passes by it is horrified and shakes his head. Like the east wind I will scatter them before the enemy. I will show them my back, not my face, in the day of their calamity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mountain snow and cold streams keep faith with their maker, but God’s people have forgotten him for false gods, so their land will become a ruin people gape at, and God will turn his back on them in their disaster.

Who has heard the like of this? God calls for a survey again, as in 2:10: go and ask the pagans whether they have ever heard of a people abandoning its own God. The behaviour is not merely wrong; it is unprecedented.

Does the snow of Lebanon leave the crags of Sirion? Two questions from geography. The snow on the heights does not decide one year to be somewhere else; the cold streams that come off the mountains do not quit. Sirion is another name for Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9). As with the migrating birds that kept their calendar in chapter 8, creation does by instinct what Israel would not do by covenant.

In the ancient roads. The road image returns from 6:16, where they were told to ask for “the ancient paths”. Here the false gods have tripped them off the highway onto side tracks. Nobody plans to end up lost; they take a turning that looked reasonable.

A thing to be hissed at forever. The nation meant to make God known becomes a ruin travellers point at. Israel’s calling was to be a witness to God; she will be one either way, by her faithfulness or by her ruins.

Like the east wind. The east wind is the hot desert wind that strips a field. The last clause reverses the priestly blessing, “the LORD make his face to shine upon you” (Numbers 6:25): “I will show them my back, not my face”. The worst of the judgment is not the wind but the turned back. In Christ the face is turned toward us again, for God has shone “in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Uncertain wording. Two phrases in verse 14 are difficult in Hebrew, and the ESV marks both: “crags of Sirion” reads with a small change a word that is literally “of the field”, and the verb behind “run dry” normally means to be uprooted. The sense is still plain: mountain snow and streams are reliable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — Let Us Strike Him with the Tongue
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man who prayed for his people is repaid with a plot against his life, and he takes his case to God. The leaders reason that they still have priests for the law, sages for counsel and prophets for the word, so Jeremiah can be silenced without loss, and they agree to strike him with the tongue and ignore his words (v. 18). Jeremiah asks God to hear him and hear his accusers: should good be repaid with evil, when he stood before God to turn away his wrath from these very people (vv. 19–20)? Then he prays that the judgment already announced on the nation, famine, sword and bereavement, would fall on them, and that God would not forgive them but deal with them in his anger (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The man forbidden to defend himself hands everything to God, including a rage he does not disguise.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah, for the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, let us strike him with the tongue, and let us not pay attention to any of his words." Hear me, O LORD, and listen to the voice of my adversaries. Should good be repaid with evil? Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s religious leaders plot to discredit and silence Jeremiah, confident that their institutions will carry on without him, and he asks God to see that they are repaying with evil the man who prayed for them.

Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah. This is respectable religion defending itself: we still have priests for the law, sages for counsel and prophets for the word, so this one man can be removed without loss; the institution will carry on. Their slogan probably answers Jeremiah’s warnings that priest, prophet and wise man would all fail together (4:9; 8:8–10): the offices he condemned, they say, are in no danger at all. It is the argument every establishment makes against the person who says the establishment has gone wrong.

Let us strike him with the tongue. Not a knife, at this stage, but rumour, insinuation, official statements, the slow discrediting of a man. The psalm knows the method: those “who whet their tongues like swords, who aim bitter words like arrows, shooting from ambush at the blameless” (Psalm 64:3–4).

Should good be repaid with evil? He takes it to God and asks him to listen to both sides: hear me, and hear them. The question is the ache of the whole chapter.

To turn away your wrath from them. Here is what makes their plot so bitter. The prayers God had forbidden (7:16; 11:14; 14:11) were prayers for these very people. The man they are trying to kill has been standing between them and God’s wrath, and they never knew it.

The same plot against Christ. After Jesus raised Lazarus, the chief priests and Pharisees reasoned like Jeremiah’s enemies, to protect the nation and the holy place, and “from that day on they made plans to put him to death” (John 11:53). Jesus too was repaid evil for good, and he too stood between his people and God’s wrath, not only by praying but by dying; and “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore deliver up their children to famine; give them over to the power of the sword; let their wives become childless and widowed. May their men meet death by pestilence, their youths be struck down by the sword in battle. May a cry be heard from their houses, when you bring the plunderer suddenly upon them! For they have dug a pit to take me and laid snares for my feet. Yet you, O LORD, know all their plotting to kill me. Forgive not their iniquity, nor blot out their sin from your sight. Let them be overthrown before you; deal with them in the time of your anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of his strength, Jeremiah asks God to bring on his persecutors and their families the judgment already announced on the nation, and not to forgive them: an honest prayer that Scripture records, but does not hold up as a pattern for Christians. This is the hardest passage in the book to read as a Christian, and it should not be softened.

A prayer, not a plan. Several things need saying, none of them that this prayer is a model for ours. First, everything he wants done he asks God to do; he lifts no hand himself, and he goes on living among these people. People who do not pray their rage usually act on it.

The judgment already announced. Second, what he asks for is exactly the judgment God has already announced on the nation (14:12, 16). He is not inventing a punishment; he is asking God to do what he has said, and to do it now, because these men are murdering the messenger.

An honest record. Third, Scripture records it honestly without holding it up as a pattern. The Bible is an honest book about its heroes, and this is a man at the end of his strength, threatened by his own village, plotted against by the clergy, and forbidden to defend himself.

Forgive not their iniquity. This is the line no Christian can pray, and the reason is not that we are nicer than Jeremiah. It is that we stand on the other side of a cross where the one plotted against said, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34), the prayer this chapter could not reach. “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).

Vengeance handed over. Yet the instinct underneath is one the New Testament keeps: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). Jeremiah’s fury is handed over. That is not the last word on prayer, but it is far better than revenge.

Permission to be honest. What this passage gives a suffering believer is permission to be honest. God can be told the truth about what you feel toward people who have wrecked your life, and the telling is safer than the silence.

parallels.desc: Contrast: Christ prays for his killers

18.title: The Potter and the Clay
18.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 17 ended with the Sabbath sermon at the city gates and its two futures. Chapter 18 begins a new pair of acted lessons built on pottery: here a potter at his wheel, and in chapter 19 a clay flask smashed beyond repair.

The message. God is the potter and his people are clay in his hands: he has every right to reshape them, and he is the kind of craftsman who reworks spoiled clay rather than throwing it away. His warnings are therefore not fixed forecasts but real offers: if a nation turns, he relents of the disaster, and if it rebels, he withdraws the good. Judah hears the offer and answers that it is hopeless and they will do as they please, and the people turn on the prophet who prayed for them.

Why it was said. Judah believed that God’s promises to David and to Zion made it safe whatever it did, and that the priests, sages and prophets who told it so could not all be wrong (see the introduction). Jeremiah, the one voice saying otherwise, was becoming a target.

How the chapter makes its case. At the potter’s house Jeremiah watches a spoiled vessel reworked, and God asks whether he cannot do the same with Israel (vv. 1–6). Then the rule behind every prophecy: warnings and promises depend on a nation’s response, so Judah is called to return, and refuses (vv. 7–12). The refusal is unnatural: mountain snow and cold streams keep faith, but God’s people have forgotten him, and he will show them his back (vv. 13–17). Last, the leaders plot to silence Jeremiah, and he pours out to God a prayer against them that spares nothing (vv. 18–23).

Where it leads. First by the character of God revealed in Christ. The potter who reworks spoiled clay is the God who in Christ makes people new (2 Corinthians 5:17), not by their own effort but by his hands. Then by pattern. Jeremiah is plotted against by the religious leaders of Jerusalem, repaid evil for the good he did in praying for them; so was Jesus. But where Jeremiah, at the end of his strength, prayed “Forgive not their iniquity” (v. 23), Jesus prayed for his killers, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), and still intercedes for sinners.

For us. You are not your own maker, and that is good news: spoiled clay is safe in the potter’s hands. Do not answer God’s call with “It is no use” or “I will not”, which come to the same thing. And when you are repaid evil for good, tell God the truth about it, and leave judgment with him.
18.theology:
God has absolute right over his people as a potter over clay (vv. 5-6; Rom 9:21), and he is a potter who reworks spoiled clay rather than discarding it (v. 4). Prophecies of judgment and promises of blessing are conditional by design (vv. 7-10): warnings are given so that they need not be fulfilled, and promises do not shelter the unrepentant.

Despair and defiance end in the same conduct (v. 12). Opposition to God's word often comes from religious institutions defending themselves (v. 18). Jeremiah's prayer against his enemies hands his rage to God rather than acting on it (vv. 21-23).
18.examples: The chapter's central picture is a craftsman collapsing a spoiled pot and starting again with the same clay, and its sharpest irony is that the man they plotted to kill was the one who had been praying for them.

keyVerse.quote: O house of Israel, can I not do with you as this potter has done? declares the LORD. Behold, like the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel.
keyVerse.note: The scene at the wheel becomes a claim about God and his people. It is a claim of authority, for the clay does not tell the potter what to make, and of mercy, for this potter reworks spoiled clay instead of throwing it away. The rest of the chapter shows both: his freedom to relent or to judge, and Judah’s refusal to be reshaped.

18.reflection:
The potter reworks the spoiled vessel rather than throwing it away (v. 4). Where do you need to hear that God reshapes spoiled clay? How does it change things to know that the remaking is done by his hands rather than yours?

Verses 7–10 say God’s warnings and promises depend on a nation’s response. How should this shape the way we read the threats and promises of the prophets? Does it make God changeable? Why not?

“That is in vain! We will follow our own plans” (v. 12). Why do despair and defiance so often end in the same place? How would you answer someone who says, “I could never change”?

Jeremiah prays bitterly against those who plotted to kill him (vv. 19–23), while Jesus prayed for his killers. What can we learn from Jeremiah’s honesty with God, and why can Christians not simply copy his prayer?
