Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing such disaster upon this place that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle.<sup>4</sup>Because the people have forsaken me and have profaned this place by making offerings in it to other gods whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah have known; and because they have filled this place with the blood of innocents,<sup>5</sup>and have built the high places of Baal to burn their sons in the fire as burnt offerings to Baal, which I did not command or decree, nor did it come into my mind—<sup>6</sup>therefore, behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when this place shall no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter.<sup>7</sup>And in this place I will make void the plans of Judah and Jerusalem, and will cause their people to fall by the sword before their enemies, and by the hand of those who seek their life. I will give their dead bodies for food to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the earth.<sup>8</sup>And I will make this city a horror, a thing to be hissed at. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its wounds.<sup>9</sup>And I will make them eat the flesh of their sons and their daughters, and everyone shall eat the flesh of his neighbor in the siege and in the distress, with which their enemies and those who seek their life afflict them.'<sup>10</sup>"Then you shall break the flask in the sight of the men who go with you,<sup>11</sup>and shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel, so that it can never be mended. Men shall bury in Topheth because there will be no place else to bury.<sup>12</sup>Thus will I do to this place, declares the LORD, and to its inhabitants, making this city like Topheth.<sup>13</sup>The houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah— all the houses on whose roofs offerings have been offered to all the host of heaven, and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods—shall be defiled like the place of Topheth.'"<sup>14</sup>Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the court of the LORD's house and said to all the people:<sup>15</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, behold, I am bringing upon this city and upon all its towns all the disaster that I have pronounced against it, because they have stiffened their neck, refusing to hear my words."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Go to the Valley and Take Witnesses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends Jeremiah with witnesses to the very place of Judah’s worst sin, so that the sentence is heard where the crime was done. He is to buy a fired clay flask and take some of the elders of the people and of the priests to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, at the entrance of the Potsherd Gate (vv. 1–2). There he announces a disaster so shocking that every ear will tingle, the phrase once used of Eli’s house and of Manasseh’s Jerusalem (v. 3). The charge has three parts: they have forsaken God, profaned the place with offerings to new gods, and filled it with the blood of innocents (v. 4), burning their sons to Baal, something God never commanded and never even conceived (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The sermon is preached at the scene of the crime, with the establishment brought along as witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, "Go, buy a potter's earthenware flask, and take some of the elders of the people and some of the elders of the priests, and go out to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the entry of the Potsherd Gate, and proclaim there the words that I tell you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Jeremiah to take a fired clay flask and leading elders as witnesses out to the Valley of Hinnom, the place where children were burned, and to preach there.

A potter’s earthenware flask. Chapter 18 was clay on a wheel, soft and workable. Chapter 19 is a finished flask, fired hard in a kiln. The material has changed, and so has the message.

Some of the elders of the people. This time there is an audience: elders of the people and elders of the priests, civic and religious leadership together, men whose testimony cannot later be dismissed. Whatever happens, there will be witnesses.

The Valley of the Son of Hinnom. The location is chosen with terrible precision. The Valley of Hinnom, just south of the city, is where children were burned (7:31). He will preach about a smashed jar at the gate named for broken pots, in the valley where they burned their children.

Uncertain wording. The gate’s name occurs only here. It is most likely linked to the Hebrew word for a broken piece of pottery, though the King James Version took it as “the east gate”. Either way, it led out to the valley.
verseByVerse.note: The Potsherd Gate led out to the Valley of Hinnom.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing such disaster upon this place that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle. Because the people have forsaken me and have profaned this place by making offerings in it to other gods whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah have known; and because they have filled this place with the blood of innocents, and have built the high places of Baal to burn their sons in the fire as burnt offerings to Baal, which I did not command or decree, nor did it come into my mind—
verseByVerse.commentary:
God announces a disaster that will shock everyone who hears of it, because his people have abandoned him for new gods and burned their own children in the valley, a sacrifice he never commanded and that never even entered his mind.

The ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle. God used the phrase when he told the boy Samuel of the fall of Eli’s house, “at which the two ears of everyone who hears it will tingle” (1 Samuel 3:11), and again when he pronounced sentence on Jerusalem in Manasseh’s day: “such disaster that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle” (2 Kings 21:12). It means news so shocking that people flinch, and Jeremiah is announcing that the sentence passed under Manasseh has come due.

Because the people have forsaken me. The charge has three parts: forsaking God, profaning the place, and “the blood of innocents”. The gods are ones “whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah have known”: not ancient family loyalties but recent imports, and a nation that had the God of the exodus exchanged him for novelties.

To burn their sons in the fire. Then the specific horror, child sacrifice, with the same phrase as the temple sermon: “nor did it come into my mind” (7:31). God calls those children innocents; he saw every one of them, and their blood is precious in his sight.

Not in God’s name. A religion that burns children cannot claim any connection to him. When people do appalling things in God’s name, the question is whether he ever said it, and Scripture, not sincerity, is where that is settled.

The gods that still ask for children. Every reader recoils from this valley. But ask what Baal and Molech were thought to offer: rain, harvests, safety, a future for the family and the nation. Give the god what you love most, and he will secure what you want most. Idols always work that way. They begin by asking for a little and end by asking for everything, and they are hungriest for the people closest to us. We do not burn our children, but we can still lay them on altars: a childhood spent serving a parent’s ambition, a home given up for a career, a child made the proof that we are succeeding. Smaller fires, lit for the same reason. Here is the reversal. The one God who said a sacrifice like this had never even entered his mind is the God who “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32; see the note on Genesis 22:1–2). The idols take our children to secure our future. The living God gave his Son to secure ours, and that frees parents to love their children instead of using them.

Did God not foresee it? Of course he did; he knows all things (Psalm 139:4). “Nor did it come into my mind” means that such a thing never came from him: he never willed it or commanded it, and it is utterly foreign to his heart.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The valley of child sacrifice will become a valley of slaughter, and the city that offered its children will be reduced to horrors in the siege. God renames Topheth, the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, the Valley of Slaughter (v. 6). There he will pour out Judah’s plans like a jar’s contents and leave its fallen to the birds and beasts (v. 7). Jerusalem will become a ruin that passers-by hiss at, as was foretold when the temple was dedicated (v. 8). In the siege its people will eat the flesh of their own sons and daughters and of their neighbours, the worst of the covenant curses Moses had spelled out (v. 9). The sin of the valley comes back on the city in its own shape.
verseByVerse.theology: The valley where children were burned is renamed for what will be done in it.

verseByVerse.quote: therefore, behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when this place shall no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter. And in this place I will make void the plans of Judah and Jerusalem, and will cause their people to fall by the sword before their enemies, and by the hand of those who seek their life. I will give their dead bodies for food to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The valley where Judah sacrificed its children will be renamed for the slaughter of its people, and every plan of its leaders will be poured out on the ground like the contents of a jar.

The Valley of Slaughter. The new name of 7:32 is repeated on the spot. God renames the place for what will happen there; judgment is fitted to the crime so exactly that the map itself records it.

I will make void the plans. The flask in his hand gives the picture: plans poured out like the contents of a jar. In Hebrew you can hear the link: the jar is a baqbuq, and “make void” is baqqoti, perhaps even the sound of liquid gurgling out of a narrow neck. The psalm sets that against every human strategy: “The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples” (Psalm 33:10). Judah’s counsellors were clever. Cleverness against God is simply a longer route to the same valley.

From Hinnom to Gehenna. The Valley of Hinnom, where children were burned, gave its name to Gehenna, the word Jesus used for hell (Mark 9:43–47): a place of fire and judgment for those who reject God. The most loving person who ever lived spoke of it most often, as a warning given so that no one need go there.

Uncertain wording. The origin of the name Topheth is uncertain. It may be related to a word for a fireplace or hearth, and many scholars think its vowels were changed to echo the Hebrew word for “shame”.
verseByVerse.note: “Make void” (baqqoti) sounds like the word for the potter’s flask (baqbuq) Jeremiah is holding.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will make this city a horror, a thing to be hissed at. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its wounds. And I will make them eat the flesh of their sons and their daughters, and everyone shall eat the flesh of his neighbor in the siege and in the distress, with which their enemies and those who seek their life afflict them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem will become a ruin that makes travellers gasp, and in the siege its people will be driven to eat their own children: the covenant curse coming true, and their sin coming back on them in its own shape.

A thing to be hissed at. The city meant to be a light to the nations will make passers-by hiss, the sharp intake of breath travellers give at a ruin. And God had said so at the beginning. When Solomon dedicated the temple, the warning came with it: “this house will become a heap of ruins. Everyone passing by it will be astonished and will hiss”, and when they ask why, the answer will be, “Because they abandoned the LORD their God” (1 Kings 9:8–9). The hissing travellers of Jeremiah’s day fulfil a sentence spoken at the dedication service more than three centuries earlier.

The flesh of their sons and their daughters. Verse 9 is unbearable to read: in the siege people will eat their own children. And it happened. Lamentations, written over the ruins, records it: “The hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children” (Lamentations 4:10). It was the curse for breaking the covenant, which Moses had spelled out in almost the same words: “you shall eat the fruit of your womb, the flesh of your sons and daughters”, “in the siege and in the distress” (Deuteronomy 28:53).

The dreadful symmetry. They gave their children to the fire in this valley as an act of religion; in the siege they will eat them to stay alive. Sin runs its course to the end, and the end is always worse than the beginning promised.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–13 — So Will I Break This People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The breaking of the flask is God’s sentence acted out: what has been fired hard by long refusal will be smashed beyond human repair. Before the watching elders Jeremiah breaks the flask (v. 10) and declares that God will break the people and the city in the same way, so that it can never be mended; the dead will be buried in Topheth until there is no room left (v. 11). The whole city will become like Topheth, a defiled place of the dead (v. 12). Even the houses of Jerusalem and of its kings, where families burned offerings to the stars and poured drink offerings to other gods on their rooftops, will be as unclean as the valley of burning (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Yesterday's clay could be reworked; a fired flask smashed on the rocks cannot, and that is the point.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then you shall break the flask in the sight of the men who go with you, and shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel, so that it can never be mended. Men shall bury in Topheth because there will be no place else to bury. Thus will I do to this place, declares the LORD, and to its inhabitants, making this city like Topheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah smashes the fired flask before the witnesses: so God will break Jerusalem, past any human mending, and fill the valley with its dead.

Then you shall break the flask. The sermon becomes an action. In front of the elders he throws the jar down.

So that it can never be mended. Here is why the flask is fired and not wet. Soft clay can be collapsed and reworked (18:4); a kiln-hardened pot smashed on stones is finished. Put the two chapters together and you have the whole message. While the clay is soft, God says: return, and I will rework you. When it has been fired hard by years of refusal, there comes a moment when the pot is thrown down. The difference is not a change in God but a change in what the clay has become.

Like a potter’s vessel. Scripture uses this image for the judgment of God’s King too: “You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel” (Psalm 2:9), applied to the risen Christ in Revelation 2:27. And Lamentations mourns that the precious sons of Zion are “regarded as earthen pots, the work of a potter’s hands” (Lamentations 4:2).

Making this city like Topheth. The whole city will become what this valley was: a place of the dead, with graves dug until there is no room left.

Not beyond God’s repair. Yet the book that says “so that it can never be mended” also promises that the city will be rebuilt and even this valley made holy (31:38–40). What no human hand can repair, God does not patch either. He makes new: “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17). The gospel is not the mending of the broken flask. It is a new vessel from the same Potter.

The potter’s field. Matthew remembered this valley. The priests used Judas’s thirty pieces of silver to buy a potter’s field to bury strangers in, and Matthew says this fulfilled what was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet (Matthew 27:7–10). The words come mostly from Zechariah 11:12–13, which puzzles readers; the likeliest explanation is that Matthew joins Zechariah to Jeremiah’s potter, field and burial ground (here and 32:6–15) and names the greater prophet, as writers then commonly did. Tradition places that field in this very valley, bought with the price of the Lord’s betrayal.

verseByVerse.quote: The houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah— all the houses on whose roofs offerings have been offered to all the host of heaven, and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods—shall be defiled like the place of Topheth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the private homes of Jerusalem, where respectable families burned offerings to the stars on their rooftops, will be as defiled as the valley of burning.

On whose roofs offerings have been offered. Flat roofs were where families slept in summer and where, it turns out, they had been burning incense to the stars. It was household religion, conducted upstairs, in private, by respectable people. Worship of the sun, moon and stars had spread in Manasseh’s reign, probably under Assyrian influence (2 Kings 21:3–5). Josiah pulled down “the altars on the roof” (2 Kings 23:12), and since his death they had come back. Zephaniah, preaching in the same years, names “those who bow down on the roofs to the host of the heavens” (Zephaniah 1:5). What we worship in private, away from the temple and the crowd, is often the truest measure of what we love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–15 — From Topheth to the Temple Court
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah does not leave his message in the valley but carries it straight into the temple, because the root of everything is the people’s refusal to hear. Coming up from Topheth, where God had sent him, he stands in the court of the LORD’s house and speaks to all the people (v. 14). God is bringing on Jerusalem and all its towns every disaster he has announced, for one reason that lies behind the idolatry, the blood and the injustice: they have stiffened their necks and refused to hear his words (v. 15). It is the same place where the temple sermon of chapter 7 was preached, and the cost of saying it here follows at once, in the opening verses of chapter 20.
verseByVerse.theology: He carries the broken-flask message straight from Topheth into the temple courtyard, and it costs him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the court of the LORD's house and said to all the people: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, behold, I am bringing upon this city and upon all its towns all the disaster that I have pronounced against it, because they have stiffened their neck, refusing to hear my words."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah carries the sentence from the valley into the temple court, and names the root of all Judah’s sins: they have stiffened their necks and refused to hear God’s words.

In the court of the LORD’s house. He walks up out of the valley and straight into the temple courtyard, fresh from the broken flask, and preaches it again to the crowd. Nothing is toned down for the religious venue. This is the precinct of the temple sermon of chapter 7, he knows what it costs to say these things here, and the next chapter records the result: the chief officer of the temple has him beaten and put in the stocks overnight.

Refusing to hear my words. The reason is one clause. Not their idolatry, not the blood, not the injustice, but what lies behind all of them: the refusal to listen. That is the thread from chapter 7 to here. Everything in Jeremiah begins with hearing. The people who would not hear became people who could not (6:10), and that long refusal was the oven in which the flask was fired hard.

Stephen’s charge. Stephen used the same charge in the same city six centuries later, facing the council that was about to kill him: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you” (Acts 7:51). The neck stiffened against Jeremiah was still stiff against Christ’s witnesses. Yet a young man named Saul stood by at that stoning, and the risen Christ met him on the road and bent his neck by grace (Acts 7:58; 9:3–6). No refusal is beyond the reach of the one who calls.

19.title: The Broken Flask
19.overview:
Where we are. In chapter 18 Jeremiah watched soft clay reworked on the wheel, and Judah answered God’s call to return with “That is in vain!” (18:12). Chapter 19 is the second pottery lesson, and it moves from the workshop to the valley outside the walls where Judah burned its children. The story runs on into chapter 20.

The message. There comes a point when the clay is no longer soft. A people who have refused to hear God for generations, until they offered their own children to idols, will be broken like a fired clay flask smashed on the stones, beyond any human mending. God’s judgment fits the sin: the valley of their child sacrifice becomes the Valley of Slaughter, and the whole city becomes a place of the dead.

Why it was said. Child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom, promoted by Manasseh and stopped by Josiah, had returned, along with offerings to the stars on the rooftops of Jerusalem (see the introduction). The city still trusted its temple, and its leaders had just resolved to ignore Jeremiah (18:18).

How the chapter makes its case. Jeremiah buys a fired clay flask and leads elders of the people and of the priests out to the Valley of Hinnom by the Potsherd Gate (vv. 1–2). There he announces a disaster to make ears tingle, for the blood of innocents (vv. 3–5). The valley will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, Judah’s plans will be poured out, and the siege will bring horrors Moses had foretold (vv. 6–9). Then he smashes the flask before the witnesses: so God will break the city, and every house defiled by rooftop idolatry will be unclean like Topheth (vv. 10–13). Finally he carries the message straight into the temple court (vv. 14–15).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by promise. What is smashed cannot be mended by human hands, and the book that says so also promises that the city will be rebuilt and this very valley made holy (31:38–40). God does not repair the broken flask; in Christ he makes a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). The valley gave its name to Gehenna, the hell Jesus warned of, and by tradition held the potter’s field bought with the price of his betrayal (Matthew 27:7–10). The God who never willed the sacrifice of children gave his own Son, so that the judgment of this valley need not be ours.

For us. Hearts harden by long refusal, so hear God while the clay is soft. Watch for the modern altars on which we lay our children, and for the private, respectable idolatry of the rooftop. And bring what is broken beyond repair to the Potter who makes all things new.
19.theology:
God distances himself absolutely from atrocity done in his name: child sacrifice never came into his mind (v. 5; 7:31), and judgment is fitted to the sin (v. 6).

The soft clay of chapter 18 could be reworked; the fired flask of chapter 19 is broken beyond mending (vv. 10-11), and the difference lies not in God but in what long refusal has made of the people. What cannot be mended, God makes new (31:38-40). Private religion is not hidden from him (v. 13), and the root of every charge is the refusal to hear his words (v. 15).
19.examples: Jeremiah brings the elders along so that nobody can say later that it was not said, and empties the plans of the court like water from a jar. Then he walks from Topheth into the temple courtyard without softening a word.

keyVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter’s vessel, so that it can never be mended.
keyVerse.note: The smashed flask is the chapter’s whole message in one act. In chapter 18 the soft clay could be reworked; this flask has been fired hard by generations of refusal, and once broken it cannot be repaired. Only the God who makes all things new can answer it, not by mending the old vessel but by making a new one.

19.reflection:
Chapter 18 showed soft clay being reworked; chapter 19 shows a fired flask smashed beyond repair (v. 11). What does this contrast teach about the danger of putting off repentance? How do hearts become “fired hard”?

The people of Judah sacrificed their children to idols that promised them security and success (v. 5). In what ways can parents today sacrifice their children to their own ambitions or idols? How does the gospel free us to love our children instead of using them?

The rooftop worship of verse 13 was private religion practised by respectable people. What private idolatries might we keep in our homes while appearing faithful in public?

Jeremiah’s summary of the people’s sin is that they “stiffened their neck, refusing to hear my words” (v. 15). Why is refusing to listen so serious? What helps us to keep listening to God?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Beaten and Put in the Stocks
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first recorded violence against Jeremiah comes from the temple’s own officer, and God answers it by turning the persecutor’s power back on him. Pashhur the priest, chief officer of the temple, hears Jeremiah’s preaching, has him beaten and puts him in the stocks at the upper Benjamin Gate of the temple (vv. 1–2). When he is released the next day, Jeremiah gives him a new name from God: not Pashhur, but Terror on Every Side (v. 3). Pashhur will be a terror to himself and his friends and watch them fall, Judah and all its wealth will be handed to Babylon, and he and his household will die in exile, with the friends to whom he prophesied lies (vv. 4–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The first physical violence against Jeremiah is ordered by the man in charge of the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Pashhur the priest, the son of Immer, who was chief officer in the house of the LORD, heard Jeremiah prophesying these things. Then Pashhur beat Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the upper Benjamin Gate of the house of the LORD. The next day, when Pashhur released Jeremiah from the stocks, Jeremiah said to him, "The LORD does not call your name Pashhur, but Terror on Every Side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief officer of the temple has Jeremiah beaten and clamped in the stocks for his preaching, and when he is let out, Jeremiah gives him a new name from God: Terror on Every Side.

The first violence. Chapter 19 ended with Jeremiah preaching in the temple court. This is what happened next, the first recorded violence against him.

Pashhur the priest. The persecutor is not a mob or the palace, but a priest, “chief officer in the house of the LORD”, responsible for order in the temple. (He is not the Pashhur son of Malchiah who appears in 21:1 and 38:1.) He has the prophet beaten, probably flogged (the law set forty lashes as the limit, Deuteronomy 25:3), and clamped overnight in stocks. The word suggests the body twisted into a fixed, painful position, and it was done in a public gateway, where everyone going in to worship could see him.

Religious persecutors. Religious institutions can be the most efficient persecutors: they have authority, premises and the confidence of being on God’s side. Jesus himself was struck in the face by one of the high priest’s officers (John 18:22). The apostles were flogged by the council for preaching and left “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name” (Acts 5:41). Paul took the thirty-nine lashes five times (2 Corinthians 11:24). Hebrews sums up the line Jeremiah stands in: “Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment”, men “of whom the world was not worthy” (Hebrews 11:36, 38).

Terror on Every Side. The next day he comes out of the stocks stiff, bleeding and still preaching, and his first act is to rename his jailer. It is the phrase the book has used for the coming siege (6:25), and in a few verses it will be what his enemies whisper about him (v. 10). Pashhur will not merely witness the terror; he will be it, to himself and to everyone near him.
verseByVerse.note: “Terror on every side” (Magor-missabib) becomes Jeremiah’s nickname for Pashhur.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: Behold, I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends. They shall fall by the sword of their enemies while you look on. And I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon. He shall carry them captive to Babylon, and shall strike them down with the sword. Moreover, I will give all the wealth of the city, all its gains, all its prized belongings, and all the treasures of the kings of Judah into the hand of their enemies, who shall plunder them and seize them and carry them to Babylon. And you, Pashhur, and all who dwell in your house, shall go into captivity. To Babylon you shall go, and there you shall die, and there you shall be buried, you and all your friends, to whom you have prophesied falsely."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who used fear to silence God’s prophet will be consumed by fear himself, watch his friends die, and end his days in Babylon, because he comforted the people with lies.

A terror to yourself. A terrible sentence. The man who inflicted fear will be unable to escape it, because it is inside him. And he will watch his friends die: not spared, not blinded, but made to look on.

All the wealth of the city. Four words for what the city owned, wealth, gains, prized belongings and treasures, and one thing happens to all of it: God gives it into the hand of their enemies.

There you shall die. The sentence is personal: you will go, you will die there, you will be buried there. For a man whose identity was bound up with the temple in Jerusalem, dying in Babylon is the complete undoing of his life.

You have prophesied falsely. The last clause names the real crime. Not the beating, but the lies: Pashhur had been telling people what they wanted to hear, and the men who believed him will die in exile beside him. Comfortable preaching has casualties, and they include the preacher.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — A Fire Shut Up in My Bones
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the last of his confessions Jeremiah pours out his anguish to God, and finds that God’s word will not let him go. He accuses God of overpowering him into a calling that has made him a laughingstock, since every time he speaks he must cry “Violence and destruction!” (vv. 7–8). He resolves to stop, but the word becomes a fire shut up in his bones that he cannot hold in (v. 9). He hears whispering on every side, even from close friends waiting for him to stumble (v. 10). Yet with nothing changed he turns in faith: the LORD is with him as a dread warrior, he commits his cause to the God who sees the heart, and he sings praise to the one who rescues the needy (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Complaint, compulsion, confidence and praise in seven verses, all of them honest at once.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed. I have become a laughingstock all the day; everyone mocks me. For whenever I speak, I cry out, I shout, "Violence and destruction!" For the word of the LORD has become for me a reproach and derision all day long. If I say, "I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name," there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah complains that God overpowered him into a calling that has made him the city’s joke, yet when he tries to stop speaking, God’s word burns in his bones until he cannot hold it in.

You have deceived me. Straight from the stocks come some of the sharpest words in Scripture addressed to God. He does not mean that God lied. He means that when he was called he did not know what it would cost, that God overpowered his objections (“you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed”), and that the life he was drawn into has made him the joke of the city, every day, to everyone.

The Bible prints this. No editorial note corrects him, and no rebuke follows. God can be spoken to like this by a man at the end of his endurance, and the words are preserved in Scripture for every believer who has felt them and been afraid to say them.

A laughingstock all the day. Every time he speaks he announces catastrophe, and it has made him ridiculous. The word that was “a joy and the delight of my heart” (15:16) is now “a reproach and derision”. Both are true of the same word in the same man’s life.

I will not mention him. So he tries the obvious solution: resign, and never speak in God’s name again. And he cannot, because the word he has swallowed burns. God had told him that his words would be “a fire” in the prophet’s mouth (5:14), and later asks, “Is not my word like fire” (23:29).

A burning fire shut up in my bones. Few descriptions of a calling are so exact. He does not continue because he feels strong, or because it is going well, or because anyone thanks him. He continues because stopping is worse. Paul knew it (1 Corinthians 9:16), and so did the apostles before the council: “we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:20). Anyone who has said, “I cannot keep doing this,” and kept doing it, knows the fire.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “deceived” can mean to deceive, entice or persuade (it is used of seduction in Exodus 22:16), and translations vary. The same verb returns in verse 10, where his enemies hope he will be “deceived”. Either way, Jeremiah means that God drew him into a life he would not have chosen, and was too strong to resist.

verseByVerse.quote: For I hear many whispering. Terror is on every side! "Denounce him! Let us denounce him!" say all my close friends, watching for my fall. "Perhaps he will be deceived; then we can overcome him and take our revenge on him." But the LORD is with me as a dread warrior; therefore my persecutors will stumble; they will not overcome me. They will be greatly shamed, for they will not succeed. Their eternal dishonor will never be forgotten. O LORD of hosts, who tests the righteous, who sees the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause. Sing to the LORD; praise the LORD! For he has delivered the life of the needy from the hand of evildoers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surrounded by whispering enemies and treacherous friends, Jeremiah takes hold of God’s promise to be with him, commits his cause to God, and breaks into praise for the God who rescues the needy.

Terror is on every side! The phrase he gave Pashhur comes back at him as a nickname.

All my close friends. The worst detail is “all my close friends, watching for my fall”. Not enemies, but the men he ate with, hoping he will slip so they can be rid of him. The psalms know this pain (Psalm 31:13), and so did Jesus, at table with the twelve on the night Judas betrayed him.

As a dread warrior. Then, without transition, faith: the promise of 1:8 and 1:19, held onto in the dark and pictured as a champion standing at his shoulder. Nothing in his circumstances has changed between verse 10 and verse 11. The whispering continues. What has changed is what he is looking at.

To you have I committed my cause. Verse 12 repeats 11:20, and the ESV notes that “mind” is in Hebrew “kidneys”, the innermost self. The last clause is the discipline of his whole life: he hands his case over to God, and leaves vengeance with him (Romans 12:19). Christians, taught by Christ, pray both for justice and for their enemies: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).

Sing to the LORD. And he sings. In seven verses: you deceived me, I cannot stop, they are all against me, God is with me, sing to the LORD. That is not inconsistency; it is what a real prayer life looks like from inside a real crisis.
verseByVerse.note: “Mind” in v. 12 is literally “kidneys” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Straight after his song of praise, Jeremiah plunges into the darkest words in the book, and Scripture records them without tidying them. He curses the day he was born and asks that it never be blessed (v. 14). He curses the man who brought his father the glad news of a son, wishing on him the fate of the cities God overthrew without pity, because he did not kill him in the womb (vv. 15–17). The chapter ends with an unanswered question: why did he come out of the womb only to see toil and sorrow and to spend his days in shame (v. 18)? Job spoke the same way in his anguish. God gives no reply here, but he keeps the man, and goes on using him for decades.
verseByVerse.theology: The praise of verse 13 is followed immediately by the darkest words he ever speaks, and Scripture keeps both.

verseByVerse.quote: Cursed be the day on which I was born! The day when my mother bore me, let it not be blessed! Cursed be the man who brought the news to my father, "A son is born to you," making him very glad. Let that man be like the cities that the LORD overthrew without pity; let him hear a cry in the morning and an alarm at noon, because he did not kill me in the womb; so my mother would have been my grave, and her womb forever great. Why did I come out from the womb to see toil and sorrow, and spend my days in shame?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately after praising God, Jeremiah curses the day he was born and asks why he ever came out of the womb: honest despair that Scripture records without approving or condemning, and that God bore with in his servant.

Cursed be the day on which I was born! The order matters: verse 13 sings, verse 14 curses. Whoever assembled this chapter did not tidy it.

Not cursing God. He does not curse God, and he does not curse his mother. He curses a day, which cannot be harmed by it. It is the cry of someone who wants the fact of his own existence undone. Job did the same in the ashes: “Let the day perish on which I was born” (Job 3:3).

Cursed be the man who brought the news. Even the messenger who carried the happy news is cursed: the grief reaches back to the moment of gladness at his birth. The cities “that the LORD overthrew without pity” are Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24–25), the standing byword for total destruction.

Why did I come out from the womb? The chapter ends there: no answer, no divine reply, no resolution.

Despair, recorded. Several things should be said, gently. This is despair, and Scripture neither commends nor condemns it here; it records it. A man called before birth (1:5) now wishes that birth had never happened, and the book that contains this also contains 1:5. Both belong to the same life.

If you have felt this. You are not outside the company of God’s servants. Job said it, and Jeremiah, and neither was cast off. What God does with such words is keep them, and keep the man.

If the darkness goes further. Wishing you had never been born is not the same as wanting to end your life, and Jeremiah never took that step; he lived on, and God went on using him. But if your darkness has reached that point, do not carry it alone. Tell someone today: a pastor or biblical counsellor, a trusted friend, and see a doctor too, for the body can share in the darkness, and medical help is no failure of faith. If you are in danger, call the emergency services or a crisis line now, today. When Elijah asked to die, God sent him sleep and food before he sent him a word (1 Kings 19:4–8).

A greater prophet. There was a greater prophet who was also mocked all the day, “All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me” (Psalm 22:7), whose close friend betrayed him, whose soul was very sorrowful, even to death, and who asked for the cup to pass (Matthew 26:38–39). He did not curse the day he was born. On the cross he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), so that no one who trusts him will ever be forsaken. He was born for that day, and went through it, so that people who curse their own birthdays might be born again.

20.title: Terror on Every Side: The Prophet in the Stocks
20.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 19 ended with Jeremiah carrying the message of the smashed flask into the temple court. Chapter 20 tells what it cost him, and then gives the last and darkest of his “confessions”, the prayers in which he lays bare his struggle with his calling (11:18–12:6; 15:10–21; 17:14–18; 18:19–23). Chapter 21 moves on to the last years of Zedekiah.

The message. God’s word cannot be silenced, either by the priest who beats the prophet or by the prophet who wants to stop. The man who tries to shut Jeremiah up will himself be overtaken by the terror he denied; and Jeremiah, mocked, betrayed and longing to quit, finds the word burning in his bones until he must speak it. Faith and despair sit side by side in him, and God keeps him through both.

Why it was said. The temple’s own officials, confident that disaster would never come, used their authority to silence the one voice that told them the truth (see the introduction). His preaching had made him a joke in the city, and even his friends were waiting for him to fall.

How the chapter makes its case. Pashhur, the chief officer of the temple, has Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks; released the next day, Jeremiah renames him “Terror on Every Side” and announces that he and all Judah will go to Babylon (vv. 1–6). Then Jeremiah turns to God: you overpowered me, and your word has made me a laughingstock, yet when I try to hold it in, it burns like fire (vv. 7–9). His close friends whisper against him, but the LORD is with him like a mighty warrior, and he breaks into praise (vv. 10–13). At once he curses the day he was born (vv. 14–18). Scripture keeps both, and God keeps the man.

Where it leads. By pattern. Jeremiah is beaten on the orders of the temple authorities, mocked all day long, watched by close friends hoping for his fall, and still the word burns in him. Jesus walked the same road further: struck before the high priest, mocked by all who saw him, betrayed by a friend, sorrowful even to death. But he did not curse the day of his birth. He was born for the day of the cross, and there he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), so that those who trust him will never be forsaken.

For us. Faithfulness to God’s word may cost reputation, friendships and comfort; it is measured by obedience, not results. When you are at the end of your strength, you may tell God the truth, as Jeremiah did, and commit your cause to him. And if your own darkness grows deep, do not carry it alone.
20.theology:
Persecution of God's messengers often comes from religious authority (vv. 1-2; Acts 5:40-41), and false preaching destroys the preacher and those who believed him (v. 6).

Scripture keeps a servant's accusation that God overpowered him (v. 7) without rebuke: God can bear honest speech from exhausted people. A true calling continues not by enthusiasm but because the word burns if withheld (v. 9). Faith and despair occupy the same page (vv. 13-14), and Christ, mocked and betrayed by his friends (Ps 22:6-8; Matt 26:38), chose to be born for the suffering that made Jeremiah wish he had never been born.
20.examples: Jeremiah comes out of the stocks stiff and bleeding and preaches first. He tries to resign and finds he cannot, and he sees his close friends waiting for him to slip. The chapter sets praise in one verse and a cursed birthday in the next, with nothing tidied away.

keyVerse.quote: If I say, “I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name,” there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot.
keyVerse.note: This verse explains why Jeremiah kept preaching for forty years. It was not because he felt strong, or because anyone listened, or because he wanted to; he tried to stop, and God’s word would not let him. The word that the priest could not beat out of him burned within him, and it is the same word that still burns in the hearts of those to whom Christ opens the Scriptures (Luke 24:32).

20.reflection:
Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks by the chief officer of the temple (vv. 1–2). Why can religious people and institutions sometimes be the fiercest opponents of God’s word? How can we guard against that in ourselves and our churches?

Jeremiah tried to stop speaking God’s word, but it burned in his bones (v. 9). Have you ever wanted to give up on something God called you to do? What kept you going, or what could?

Within a few verses Jeremiah moves from complaint to praise to cursing the day he was born (vv. 7–18). What does it mean to you that Scripture records such honest and unresolved prayers? How might that shape the way you pray, and the way you care for others in darkness?

Jesus, the greater prophet, was mocked, betrayed and forsaken, but did not curse the day of his birth. How does his suffering speak to someone who feels as Jeremiah did in verses 14–18?

Perhaps the LORD will deal with us according to all his wonderful deeds and will make him withdraw from us."<sup>3</sup>Then Jeremiah said to them: "Thus you shall say to Zedekiah,<sup>4</sup>'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands and with which you are fighting against the king of Babylon and against the Chaldeans who are besieging you outside the walls. And I will bring them together into the midst of this city.<sup>5</sup>I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury and in great wrath.<sup>6</sup>And I will strike down the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast. He shall strike them down with the edge of the sword. He shall not pity them or spare them or have compassion.'<sup>8</sup>"And to this people you shall say: 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death.<sup>9</sup>He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who are besieging you shall live and shall have his life as a prize of war.<sup>10</sup>For I have set my face against this city for harm and not for good, declares the LORD: it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire.'<sup>11</sup>"And to the house of the king of Judah say, 'Hear the word of the LORD,<sup>12</sup>O house of David! Thus says the LORD: "'Execute justice in the morning, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed, lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of your evil deeds.'"<sup>13</sup>"Behold, I am against you, O inhabitant of the valley, O rock of the plain, declares the LORD; you who say, 'Who shall come down against us, or who shall enter our habitations?'<sup>14</sup>I will punish you according to the fruit of your deeds, declares the LORD; I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it shall devour all that is around her."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — I Myself Will Fight Against You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king who has ignored God for years asks for a miracle, and God answers that he is now fighting on the other side. Zedekiah’s envoys hope the LORD will act “according to all his wonderful deeds”, as he did when Assyria withdrew in Hezekiah’s day, but they say nothing of repentance (vv. 1–2). The answer reverses their hope: the defenders will be driven back inside the walls, God will fight the city with the outstretched hand and strong arm of the exodus, plague will strike, and the king and the survivors will be handed to a conqueror who will show no pity (vv. 3–7).
verseByVerse.theology: A king asks for a miracle like the old days and is told that the God of the exodus is now on the other side.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur the son of Malchiah and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, saying, "Inquire of the LORD for us, for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is making war against us. Perhaps the LORD will deal with us according to all his wonderful deeds and will make him withdraw from us." Then Jeremiah said to them: "Thus you shall say to Zedekiah, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands and with which you are fighting against the king of Babylon and against the Chaldeans who are besieging you outside the walls. And I will bring them together into the midst of this city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With Babylon at the walls, the king who ignored God’s prophet now asks him for a miracle, wanting Hezekiah’s rescue without Hezekiah’s repentance.

The setting. The book jumps forward nearly twenty years, to about 588 BC. Josiah and Jehoiakim are dead; Zedekiah is the last king of Judah, and Nebuchadnezzar’s army is outside the walls. This Pashhur is a different man from the priest who flogged Jeremiah in chapter 20.

Inquire of the LORD for us. For decades the palace has ignored, imprisoned and beaten this man. Now that the siege lines are up, the king sends an official delegation to ask him to pray.

According to all his wonderful deeds. The request is religious and hollow. They are thinking of the night the Assyrian army melted away outside these same walls in Hezekiah’s day (Isaiah 37:36), and they want it done again. There is no word of repentance. Prayer as a last-resort lever, offered by men who have not changed their minds about anything, is exactly what chapter 14 refused (14:11–12).

I will turn back the weapons of war. The answer is not merely no. God will turn back the weapons in their hands: the defenders will be driven back inside, and the fighting will end up in the streets instead of at the walls.
verseByVerse.note: From here on the Hebrew often spells Nebuchadnezzar as Nebuchadrezzar (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury and in great wrath. And I will strike down the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast. They shall die of a great pestilence. Afterward, declares the LORD, I will give Zedekiah king of Judah and his servants and the people in this city who survive the pestilence, sword, and famine into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of their enemies, into the hand of those who seek their lives. He shall strike them down with the edge of the sword. He shall not pity them or spare them or have compassion.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will fight against his own city with the arm that once rescued Israel from Egypt, and hand its king and survivors to a conqueror without pity.

With outstretched hand and strong arm. The sentence shocks because of where its words come from. The LORD brought Israel out of Egypt “with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm” (Deuteronomy 26:8), words recited at every Passover. Here the familiar pair is even turned round, outstretched hand and strong arm, and the arm is stretched out against them.

I myself will fight against you. The God who fought for them fights against them, with three words for his wrath piled up. Zedekiah asked for a repeat of the old wonders; he is told the old wonders are being reversed. There is no more sobering possibility in Scripture than this: to be on the wrong side of the God you claim as yours.

A great pestilence. In a besieged city, with the water fouled and the dead unburied, disease killed more than the swords did.

He shall not pity them. The king is named, and his fate is spelled out to his own messengers. The three refusals of mercy, no pity, no sparing, no compassion, were used of God in 13:14; here they describe the man he is handing them to. God says so in advance rather than letting them imagine a negotiated peace.

Where it leads. God’s wrath did one day fall on a son of David outside Jerusalem’s walls: not a faithless king but the faithful one, bearing what others deserved. Because it fell on him, God is never again against those who belong to him (Romans 8:31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — Life and Death Set Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sets before the people the choice Moses once set before Israel, life or death, but now the way of life is surrender. Whoever stays in the city will die by sword, famine and pestilence; whoever goes out to the Babylonians will keep his life, and nothing more, as a prize of war (vv. 8–9). The reason is that God has set his face against the city: it will be burned (v. 10). The city is lost, yet individuals inside it can still be saved, one at a time.
verseByVerse.theology: The way of life runs out through the gate of surrender, which is why the offer sounds like treason.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to this people you shall say: 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death. He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who are besieging you shall live and shall have his life as a prize of war. For I have set my face against this city for harm and not for good, declares the LORD: it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets before the people a choice of life or death, and the way of life is to walk out of the city and surrender to the Babylonians.

The way of life and the way of death. The words are Moses’ words. At the end of Deuteronomy he set the same choice before the nation: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19). Jesus put it as two gates and two roads, one wide and easy, one narrow and hard (Matthew 7:13–14).

He who goes out and surrenders. The startling thing is that the way of life is surrender. Walk out of the gate, hands empty, give yourself up to the enemy, and you will keep your life, though nothing else, as a prize of war, the way a soldier keeps his skin when everything else is lost.

Why they called him a traitor. This is the sermon that later gets Jeremiah thrown into a cistern for demoralising the troops (38:4). He tells a besieged city to give in because the siege is God’s judgment, and resisting it is resisting God.

Persons within the city. The city itself is not being saved. Individuals within it still can be, one at a time, by walking out. Judgment on a community and mercy to persons inside it are not contradictory, and this verse holds them together.

Losing life to save it. Jesus put the same paradox at the heart of following him: “whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel’s will save it” (Mark 8:35). The way of life still runs through surrender, now to a King who has gone through death himself and come out the other side.

A hard lesson. Sometimes the godly response to a disaster we have brought on ourselves is not to fight for the position we held but to surrender it and accept the loss. For the believer such discipline is a Father’s, not a sentence of rejection (Hebrews 12:6), and the life on the other side of it is real. Surrender looks like defeat and is the only way out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Execute Justice in the Morning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even with the enemy at the gate, God’s word to the palace is moral, not military: do justice first thing every morning and rescue the man who has been robbed, or God’s anger will burn unquenched (vv. 11–12). To a city that trusts its rocky heights and asks, “Who shall come down against us?”, God answers, “I am against you”, and promises to repay it by the fruit of its deeds with a fire in its forest of cedar (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Even at this hour the word to the palace is not military but moral: do justice before breakfast.

verseByVerse.quote: "And to the house of the king of Judah say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O house of David! Thus says the LORD: "'Execute justice in the morning, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed, lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of your evil deeds.'" "Behold, I am against you, O inhabitant of the valley, O rock of the plain, declares the LORD; you who say, 'Who shall come down against us, or who shall enter our habitations?' I will punish you according to the fruit of your deeds, declares the LORD; I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it shall devour all that is around her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the last hour God still tells the house of David to do justice first thing every morning, and tells the city that trusts its heights that he himself is against it.

Execute justice in the morning. With an army at the gates, the word to the royal household is about the courts. Kings and judges heard cases in the morning at the city gate (2 Samuel 15:2; compare Psalm 101:8), so the command is to make that daily sitting honest and to hold it before the day’s other business crowds it out.

Him who has been robbed. The concrete duty is named: deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. Not a statement about justice: the stolen thing returned to its owner.

How the house of David is judged. This is the measure by which the prophets judge the house of David: not the size of the army or the splendour of the temple, but whether a poor man who has been cheated can get a hearing before lunch. Two chapters on, God promises a son of David who will at last “execute justice and righteousness in the land” (23:5): the King this house never produced.

Who shall come down against us? Jerusalem sits on rock above its valleys, and confidence in that geography has become a slogan, asked as if it had no answer. God’s reply comes first, in the opening words of verse 13: I am against you. It is not the Babylonians who are coming down; it is God.

According to the fruit of your deeds. This is the harvest language of 17:10, where God searches the heart and gives each “according to the fruit of his deeds”. The forest where the fire is kindled is probably the cedar palaces of the royal quarter, which the next chapter addresses directly (22:6–7, 14). The chapter that began with a king asking for a miracle ends with God pointing at the palace and telling him where the fire will start.

Uncertain wording. O inhabitant of the valley, O rock of the plain is an unexpected way to address Jerusalem, which stands on hills, not in a valley or a plain. “Inhabitant” is feminine in Hebrew, the city personified, and “plain” may mean the level rock on which the city stood above its valleys; some take the title as ironic. The thrust is clear either way: the city that thinks its position puts it beyond reach.

21.title: The Way of Life and the Way of Death
21.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 21 jumps forward nearly twenty years from the stocks and lament of chapter 20 to about 588 BC. Babylon’s army is at the walls of Jerusalem, and Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, sends to the prophet his predecessors ignored. It opens a collection of words about the kings and prophets of Judah that runs to chapter 24.

The message. Religion cannot be used as a lever on God by people who will not turn to him. The king asks for a miracle like the old days and is told that God himself is now fighting against the city. Yet even at this hour there is a way of life, though it runs through surrender, and the house of David is still told what God wants from it: justice for the robbed.

Why it was said. Jerusalem trusted its walls, its rock and its history of rescue, as in Hezekiah’s day, and Zedekiah wavered between Babylon and Egypt without ever obeying the prophet (see the introduction). The city needed to hear that the siege was God’s judgment, not bad luck to be prayed away.

How the chapter makes its case. The king’s delegation asks for a repeat of God’s wonders, and God answers that he will turn their weapons back and fight against them with the arm that once freed Israel from Egypt (vv. 1–7). To the people he sets the way of life and the way of death: stay and die, go out and surrender and live (vv. 8–10). To the royal house comes the old charter, do justice in the morning, and to the city that thinks itself unreachable, “I am against you” (vv. 11–14).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes and by pattern. The house of David is told to execute justice and cannot; two chapters later God promises a Branch who “shall execute justice and righteousness in the land” (23:5), and that King is Jesus. And the way of life that ran out through the city gate takes a new shape in him: “Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). He bore the wrath this city faced, and life is found by going out to him and giving ourselves up.

For us. God is not a lever we pull in emergencies; prayer that wants rescue without repentance has misunderstood him. Sometimes the way of life is to stop defending what we have lost and surrender to God’s discipline. And the Christian’s first daily business, like the king’s, includes justice and mercy for the people nobody else will help.
21.theology:
Prayer used as a last-resort lever by people unwilling to repent is refused (vv. 1-2; compare 14:11-12), and God may turn the language of redemption against his own people: the outstretched arm that freed Israel now fights them (v. 5).

The choice of Deuteronomy is set again, but the way of life now runs through surrender (vv. 8-9; Deut 30:15-19), and judgment on a community and mercy to individuals within it stand together. The first duty of God's appointed king is justice for the robbed and oppressed (v. 12), the duty fulfilled at last by the righteous Branch (23:5).
21.examples: After twenty years of ignoring the prophet, the palace sends an official delegation when the siege lines go up, wanting Hezekiah's outcome without Hezekiah's humble trust. The answer turns their slogan, Who shall come down against us?, into God's own reply: I am against you.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death.
keyVerse.note: The words are Moses’ words (Deuteronomy 30:19), but the way of life now runs out through the city gate in surrender to the enemy God has sent. The verse holds the chapter together: judgment on the city is certain, yet mercy is still offered to every person in it who will stop resisting God.

21.reflection:
Zedekiah wanted God to act “according to all his wonderful deeds” without any change of heart (v. 2). When are we tempted to treat prayer as an emergency lever rather than a turning to God?

The way of life was to go out and surrender (v. 9). Have you known a time when giving something up to God’s discipline proved to be the way of life? How does Mark 8:35 shape that for a Christian?

With an enemy at the gates, God’s word to the king was “Execute justice in the morning” (v. 12). What would it look like for us, our church or our workplace to put justice for the wronged at the start of the day’s business?

The city asked, “Who shall come down against us?” (v. 13). What are the walls we trust to keep trouble out, and how does Christ, who suffered outside the gate, give a better security?

22.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Go down to the house of the king of Judah and speak there this word,<sup>2</sup>and say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David, you, and your servants, and your people who enter these gates.<sup>3</sup>Thus says the LORD: Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place.<sup>4</sup>For if you will indeed obey this word, then there shall enter the gates of this house kings who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people.<sup>5</sup>But if you will not obey these words, I swear by myself, declares the LORD, that this house shall become a desolation.<sup>6</sup>For thus says the LORD concerning the house of the king of Judah: "'You are like Gilead to me, like the summit of Lebanon, yet surely I will make you a desert, an uninhabited city.<sup>7</sup>I will prepare destroyers against you, each with his weapons, and they shall cut down your choicest cedars and cast them into the fire.<sup>8</sup>"'And many nations will pass by this city, and every man will say to his neighbor, "Why has the LORD dealt thus with this great city?"<sup>9</sup>And they will answer, "Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and worshiped other gods and served them."'"<sup>10</sup>Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away, for he shall return no more to see his native land.<sup>11</sup>For thus says the LORD concerning Shallum the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned instead of Josiah his father, and who went away from this place: "He shall return here no more,<sup>12</sup>but in the place where they have carried him captive, there shall he die, and he shall never see this land again."<sup>13</sup>"Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms by injustice, who makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages,<sup>14</sup>who says, 'I will build myself a great house with spacious upper rooms,' who cuts out windows for it, paneling it with cedar and painting it with vermilion.<sup>15</sup>Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? Then it was well with him.<sup>16</sup>He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the LORD.<sup>17</sup>But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence."<sup>18</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, my brother!' or 'Ah, sister!' They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, lord!' or 'Ah, his majesty!'<sup>19</sup>With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem."<sup>20</sup>"Go up to Lebanon, and cry out, and lift up your voice in Bashan; cry out from Abarim, for all your lovers are destroyed.<sup>21</sup>I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, 'I will not listen.' This has been your way from your youth, that you have not obeyed my voice.<sup>22</sup>The wind shall shepherd all your shepherds, and your lovers shall go into captivity; then you will be ashamed and confounded because of all your evil.<sup>23</sup>O inhabitant of Lebanon, nested among the cedars, how you will be pitied when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor!"<sup>24</sup>"As I live, declares the LORD, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off<sup>25</sup>and give you into the hand of those who seek your life, into the hand of those of whom you are afraid, even into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of the Chaldeans.<sup>26</sup>I will hurl you and the mother who bore you into another country, where you were not born, and there you shall die.<sup>27</sup>But to the land to which they will long to return, there they shall not return."<sup>28</sup>Is this man Coniah a despised, broken pot, a vessel no one cares for? Why are he and his children hurled and cast into a land that they do not know?<sup>29</sup>O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD!<sup>30</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not succeed in his days, for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Do Justice, or This House Becomes a Desolation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The throne of David exists for justice, and a royal house that refuses it will be destroyed. Jeremiah preaches at the palace gate to the king, his officials and the people (vv. 1–2), and gives them the charter of the monarchy: rescue the robbed, protect the alien, the fatherless and the widow, and shed no innocent blood (v. 3). God swears by himself that obedience will keep David’s line riding through these gates, and refusal will make the palace a desolation (vv. 4–5). Its cedars will be cut down for fuel (vv. 6–7), and passing nations will be told that the city fell because it forsook the covenant (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The throne is held on terms, and the terms are the treatment of people who cannot defend themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Go down to the house of the king of Judah and speak there this word, and say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David, you, and your servants, and your people who enter these gates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah is sent to preach at the palace gate to the king, his officials and the people together, and to measure them all by what David’s throne was for.

Go down to the house of the king. The prophet is sent to the palace and told to preach at the gate, as he did in the temple sermon (7:2) and the Sabbath sermon (17:19). He addresses the king, the civil service and the public together, because all three are implicated in how a country is run.

Who sits on the throne of David. The title matters. Everything that follows is measured against what that throne was for.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king’s job, in God’s own words, is to rescue the robbed and protect the defenceless: the alien, the fatherless and the widow.

Do justice and righteousness. The royal job description is strikingly concrete: deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed: get the stolen thing back. And protect the same three groups God names every time, the immigrant, the orphan and the widow, the people with no family power to protect them. This is not a political programme read back into Scripture; it is the charter of Israel’s monarchy, and the prophets judge every king by it.

The ideal king. The psalm of the ideal king says the same, and the church has long heard Christ in it: “May he defend the cause of the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor!” (Psalm 72:4), because “he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper”, and “precious is their blood in his sight” (Psalm 72:12, 14). The job description Jehoiakim ignored is the one the true Son of David fulfils.

Does this apply to immigrants today? It commands God’s people to do justice to the vulnerable: the resident alien, the fatherless, the widow. Christians must treat foreigners with love and justice (Matthew 25:35); how a nation sets its laws of entry is for governments to decide justly.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you will indeed obey this word, then there shall enter the gates of this house kings who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people. But if you will not obey these words, I swear by myself, declares the LORD, that this house shall become a desolation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God swears by himself that obedience will keep David’s line on the throne and disobedience will empty the palace.

If you will indeed obey this word. The same two futures as chapter 17 (17:24–27), and the same door: obedience keeps the dynasty riding through these gates; refusal empties the palace. The promise to David was never a licence for his descendants to behave as they liked.

I swear by myself. There is nothing higher to swear by. Hebrews notes the same oath when God promised Abraham: “since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself” (Hebrews 6:13). The oath that guarantees God’s promises guarantees his threats too. Both rest on God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD concerning the house of the king of Judah: "'You are like Gilead to me, like the summit of Lebanon, yet surely I will make you a desert, an uninhabited city. I will prepare destroyers against you, each with his weapons, and they shall cut down your choicest cedars and cast them into the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The royal palace, as grand and green as a forest of cedar, will be cut down and burned like firewood.

Like Gilead to me. The palace is compared to the grandest landscapes the region knew: the wooded highlands of Gilead, the cedar summits of Lebanon. It is the building itself, panelled with imported cedar, and the dynasty as everyone saw it: solid, green, permanent.

The House of the Forest of Lebanon. The image fits the building exactly. Solomon’s great hall was called by a forest’s name: “He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon”, “built on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars” (1 Kings 7:2). When God says like the summit of Lebanon and your choicest cedars, he is describing the royal complex itself, a manufactured forest.

I will prepare destroyers against you. The forest becomes a logging camp: God lines up his woodcutters, and the cedars the king was so proud of will be firewood. Anything built to show that we are here to stay is, in the end, fuel.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that an uninhabited city is in Hebrew “cities”. The sense is the same either way: what looked like a forest becomes desert.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And many nations will pass by this city, and every man will say to his neighbor, "Why has the LORD dealt thus with this great city?" And they will answer, "Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and worshiped other gods and served them."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruins of Jerusalem will preach a true sermon to the nations: the city fell because it forsook the covenant.

Why has the LORD dealt thus with this great city? Travellers will ask, and the answer will be accurate: not bad luck or Babylon’s gods, but a broken covenant. Israel was called to make God known among the nations. She does it here, from the rubble, and the sermon is true.

Scripted long before. Moses had told Israel what the nations would say over its ruins: “Why has the LORD done thus to this land?”, and the reply, “It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers” (Deuteronomy 29:24–25). Jeremiah’s hearers were watching Deuteronomy come true in their own streets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Woe to Him Who Builds by Unrighteousness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two sons of Josiah show what happens to kings who forget what the throne is for. Shallum, deported to Egypt, should be mourned more than his dead father, for he will never come home (vv. 10–12). Jehoiakim builds himself a great cedar palace with unpaid labour (vv. 13–14), and God sets him beside Josiah, who ate and drank and did justice, judged the cause of the poor, and so knew God (vv. 15–16). Jehoiakim has eyes only for dishonest gain, innocent blood and oppression (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Knowing God is defined, in God's own words, as judging the cause of the poor and needy.

verseByVerse.quote: Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away, for he shall return no more to see his native land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not weep for Josiah, who died at home; weep for his son, who is being taken away never to return.

Weep not for him who is dead. The dead man is Josiah, killed at Megiddo in 609 BC, and the whole country mourned him (2 Chronicles 35:24–25). God says: stop weeping for the king who died in his own land and weep for the one being marched away alive, his son Shallum (v. 11).

Worse than dying at home. There are worse things than dying at home. Josiah was spared what is coming (2 Kings 22:20); his son was not.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD concerning Shallum the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned instead of Josiah his father, and who went away from this place: "He shall return here no more, but in the place where they have carried him captive, there shall he die, and he shall never see this land again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shallum, the son who succeeded Josiah, will die in exile and never see his land again, and history confirms it.

Shallum the son of Josiah. Shallum is Jehoahaz, who reigned three months before Pharaoh Neco deposed him. The history confirms the sentence exactly: Neco “took Jehoahaz away, and he came to Egypt and died there” (2 Kings 23:34). Of the kings named in this chapter, he and Coniah both end their lives in a foreign country.

He shall return here no more. Twice in one sentence: He shall return here no more, and he shall never see this land again. Exile is not only punishment; it is the specific loss of home.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms by injustice, who makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages, who says, 'I will build myself a great house with spacious upper rooms,' who cuts out windows for it, paneling it with cedar and painting it with vermilion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to Jehoiakim, who builds himself a showpiece palace by forced, unpaid labour while his people are already being squeezed.

Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness. Now Jehoiakim, and the charge is unpaid labour: he makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages. The country was already being squeezed. Pharaoh Neco had put Jehoiakim on the throne and laid a heavy tribute on the land, which Jehoiakim raised by taxing “the people of the land” (2 Kings 23:33–35). The palace went up while his subjects were paying for his overlord.

What the law required. The law was emphatic: “The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night until the morning” (Leviticus 19:13), and “You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets (for he is poor and counts on it), lest he cry against you to the LORD” (Deuteronomy 24:15). James says the cry is heard: “the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you” (James 5:4). God notices payroll. Habakkuk pronounced the same woe on the same kind of builder: “Woe to him who gets evil gain for his house, to set his nest on high, to be safe from the reach of harm!” (Habakkuk 2:9).

I will build myself a great house. In the king’s own voice the details read like an advertisement: spacious upper rooms, large windows, cedar panelling, expensive red paint.

The house that says who I am.
