In 1899 the economist Thorstein Veblen coined the phrase “conspicuous consumption” for spending whose real purpose is to be seen: goods bought less for use than to display standing. Jehoiakim’s vermilion paint is that, and our version is everywhere: the extension, the car on the drive, the holiday photographs posted so that others will know. Underneath lies a question of identity: if the house is impressive, then perhaps I am somebody. But a self built from display has to be kept up for ever, and someone else usually pays for it, as Jehoiakim’s unpaid neighbour did. Scripture is not against pleasure; Josiah ate and drank and God commends him (v. 15). What finally ends the competition is a King who had “nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20) and who now says, “In my Father’s house are many rooms” (John 14:2). Someone whose standing is given, and whose house is being prepared for him, can stop painting the walls to prove a point.
verseByVerse.note: Jehoiakim built a lavish palace with forced labor.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? Then it was well with him. He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Kingship is not proved by building in cedar but by doing justice for the poor, and that, God says, is what it means to know him.

Do you think you are a king because you compete in cedar? Kingship is not a building project or a standard of living. Josiah is held up, and the description is ordinary. He ate and drank, enjoyed his life, and God does not fault him for it; and he did justice and righteousness. Twice comes the refrain: it was well with him, and then it was well.

Is not this to know me? This should stop every religious reader. God defines the knowledge of himself by the treatment of the poor. Not instead of worship, prayer or doctrine (this book has spent twenty chapters on idolatry), but as inseparable from them. A man who defends the cause of people who cannot pay him knows God; a man who does not, whatever else he knows, does not know him.

The least of these. The Lord makes the connection personal at the last judgment. The King says to those who fed the hungry and visited the prisoner, “as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40). And it is that King, not Josiah and not us, who has kept this charter perfectly. Those whose neglect of the poor is forgiven for his sake are given his Spirit, who turns eyes and heart from dishonest gain toward the neighbour (Galatians 5:22).

What this looks like. Jehoiakim was a king, but the New Testament carries the principle to every believer: “Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27). Pay people properly. If you employ anyone, a cleaner, a builder, a junior colleague, pay a fair wage and pay it on time; this woe began with unpaid wages (v. 13). Learn one name. Get to know one person who cannot repay you: the widow on your street, the asylum seeker who has started coming to church, the family your church supports through the food bank. Take up a cause, not just a feeling. Josiah judged the cause of the poor and needy: help someone fill in the benefits form, go with them to the housing office, write the letter they cannot write. Put it in the diary. Give it a regular slot, as you would a prayer meeting, because God counts it as knowing him. And we do it as people whose own cause was taken up when we had nothing to plead: “You have taken up my cause, O Lord; you have redeemed my life” (Lamentations 3:58). In Christ he has done exactly that for us.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoiakim’s inner life has narrowed to one thing, dishonest gain, and it spills out into bloodshed and oppression.

Eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain. Attention and affection are fixed on one desire, and it runs outward into blood. Scripture records one of them: the prophet Uriah, hunted down in Egypt and struck down with the sword at Jehoiakim’s command (26:20–23).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — The Burial of a Donkey
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king who built a monument will have no funeral, and the city that would not listen in its good years will cry out in vain. No one will mourn Jehoiakim as brother or as lord; he will be buried like a donkey, dragged out and dumped beyond the gates (vv. 18–19). Jerusalem is told to climb the heights and cry, because her foreign allies are destroyed; God spoke to her in her prosperity, and she would not listen (vv. 20–21). Her leaders will be scattered like chaff on the wind, and the city nested among cedars will writhe like a woman in labour (vv. 22–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The king who built himself a cedar palace is dragged out of the city gate like a dead animal.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, my brother!' or 'Ah, sister!' They shall not lament for him, saying, 'Ah, lord!' or 'Ah, his majesty!' With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king who built himself a monument will die unmourned and be thrown out of the city like a dead donkey.

They shall not lament for him. Nobody will mourn him as family (Ah, my brother!), and nobody will mourn him as king (Ah, lord!). The man who spent his reign building a monument will get no ceremony at all.

With the burial of a donkey. A dead donkey is dragged and dumped outside the city, and so will the king be. Set it beside the cedar and the vermilion: he built a house to be remembered by, and has no grave anyone would visit. The sentence is repeated after he burned Jeremiah’s scroll, in even starker terms: “his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night” (36:30).

Did he have a donkey’s burial? Kings says Jehoiakim “slept with his fathers” (2 Kings 24:6). That phrase means simply that he died; it says nothing of honourable burial. Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar bound him in chains to take him to Babylon (2 Chronicles 36:6), but not that he arrived. Scripture does not say how Jeremiah’s word was carried out; many think he died around the start of the siege in 598 BC and that his body was thrown out unburied.

verseByVerse.quote: "Go up to Lebanon, and cry out, and lift up your voice in Bashan; cry out from Abarim, for all your lovers are destroyed. I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, 'I will not listen.' This has been your way from your youth, that you have not obeyed my voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem is told to cry from every mountain, because her allies are gone and she refused to listen when times were good.

Go up to Lebanon, and cry out. The city is told to climb the heights in every direction and shout: north to Lebanon, north-east to Bashan, south-east to Abarim, the mountains of Moab. Everywhere the news is the same. All your lovers are destroyed: the foreign allies Judah has courted since chapter 2 are gone.

I spoke to you in your prosperity. God spoke while things were going well, when listening would have cost nothing and prevented everything. Good times are when warnings are cheapest to heed and hardest to hear. And it was no lapse: This has been your way from your youth.

The complacency of fools. Proverbs says how it happens: “the complacency of fools destroys them” (Proverbs 1:32). Jesus told of a rich man talking to his own soul in his prosperity, “Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry”, until God said, “Fool! This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:19–20).

verseByVerse.quote: The wind shall shepherd all your shepherds, and your lovers shall go into captivity; then you will be ashamed and confounded because of all your evil. O inhabitant of Lebanon, nested among the cedars, how you will be pitied when pangs come upon you, pain as of a woman in labor!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s leaders will be blown away like chaff, and the city that felt safe among its cedars will cry out like a woman in labour.

The wind shall shepherd all your shepherds. A bitter wordplay: the shepherds who were supposed to lead the flock will themselves be herded, and by the wind. Their foreign lovers will go into captivity with them.

Nested among the cedars. The city, comfortable, elevated and expensively furnished in its cedar palaces, will cry out like a woman in labour. Height and cedar were supposed to keep trouble out. They only made the fall longer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — The Signet Ring Torn Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even the king God called his signet ring is not exempt from judgment. Coniah (Jehoiachin) will be torn off God’s hand and handed to Nebuchadnezzar (vv. 24–25); he and his mother will be hurled into a foreign land and die there, longing for home (vv. 26–27). The prophet asks, almost in pity, whether this young king is a broken pot no one wants, and summons the land to listen (vv. 28–29). Then the sentence: write him down as childless, for none of his offspring will sit on David’s throne (v. 30). The promise to David seems to end here, and the next chapter answers it.
verseByVerse.theology: The signet ring of the house of David is pulled off and thrown away, and the line looks finished.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I live, declares the LORD, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off
verseByVerse.commentary:
Coniah, though he were as close to God as a signet ring on his right hand, will be torn off.

Coniah the son of Jehoiakim. Coniah is Jehoiachin, eighteen years old, three months on the throne, deported to Babylon in 597 BC.

The signet ring on my right hand. A signet ring was a king’s identity: it carried his seal, went everywhere with him and was never taken off. To call the Davidic king the signet on God’s right hand is to say he is God’s own authority displayed in the world.

Yet I would tear you off. The verb is violent. Even so intimate a symbol of the covenant with David is not immune when the man wearing it is faithless.

Textual note. Kings gives his age as eighteen (2 Kings 24:8); most Hebrew copies of Chronicles read eight (2 Chronicles 36:9), very likely a copying slip, since some ancient copies there read eighteen.
verseByVerse.note: Coniah is Jehoiachin (Jeconiah).

verseByVerse.quote: and give you into the hand of those who seek your life, into the hand of those of whom you are afraid, even into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of the Chaldeans. I will hurl you and the mother who bore you into another country, where you were not born, and there you shall die. But to the land to which they will long to return, there they shall not return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The young king and his mother will be handed over to the Babylonians he fears and will die in exile, longing for a home they will never see.

Into the hand. Four times into the hand, and the last phrase is the ache of every exile: the land to which they will long to return. They will have the longing, but not the return.

The mother who bore you. His mother, Nehushta, goes with him, as 13:18 said she would (2 Kings 24:8, 15).

Not forgotten. His release to eat at the king’s table is the note on which the book of Kings closes (2 Kings 25:27–30), a flicker of light at the end of that history, and this book records it too: “in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin”, Evil-merodach “graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison” (52:31). The ring was torn off; the man was not forgotten.

verseByVerse.quote: Is this man Coniah a despised, broken pot, a vessel no one cares for? Why are he and his children hurled and cast into a land that they do not know? O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Coniah is thrown away like a broken pot, and the prophet asks why with something close to pity, then summons the land to hear God’s sentence.

A despised, broken pot. The question echoes the broken flask of chapter 19. A smashed pot is swept up and thrown out without a thought, and that is what happened to the king: a vessel no one cares for.

Why are he and his children hurled? The tone is almost pity: even under judgment, God does not describe the ruin of a young king without feeling. Many Christians have heard in despised an echo of the King who later came through this very line: “He was despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3).

O land, land, land. Three times, like a herald in the street. The land itself is summoned to hear what is about to be said about the house of David.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not succeed in his days, for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No descendant of Coniah will reign on David’s throne, yet God keeps his promise to David through this very line, in Christ.

Write this man down as childless. Enter it in the record: childless. He had sons (1 Chronicles 3:17), but for the purposes of the throne the line stops here. No descendant of Jehoiachin reigned in Jerusalem. That looks like the end of the promise to David, and for centuries the question stood unanswered.

Zerubbabel the signet. Two things happen afterwards, and they must be held together. First, Haggai takes this very image and gives it back. To Zerubbabel, Jehoiachin’s grandson, God says, “I will take you, O Zerubbabel my servant”, and “make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you” (Haggai 2:23). The ring torn off is put back on.

Through Jechoniah to Christ. Second, Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy that runs straight through this name: “Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon”, and then “Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel” (Matthew 1:11–12), and on to Joseph, the husband of Mary.

Heir without the curse. The line that carried the throne also carried the curse, and the King who finally sat on David’s throne came into that family as its legal heir without being physically descended from Jeconiah. What God said stands, and what God promised stands, and the gospel is how both are true at once.

How can Jesus be Jeconiah’s heir? God said none of Jeconiah’s offspring would sit on David’s throne, yet Matthew traces Jesus through him (Matthew 1:11–12). Jesus was Jeconiah’s heir through Joseph, his legal father, but not his physical descendant; Luke traces his descent through Nathan, another son of David (Luke 3:31). The throne passed to a Son of David by another branch. Luke’s list also names a Shealtiel and a Zerubbabel (Luke 3:27); whether they are the same men as Matthew’s, and how the two lists fit together there, is debated.
verseByVerse.note: No son of Jehoiachin reigned; on Jesus' descent, see the question above.

22.title: The House of David on Trial
22.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 21 ended with God pointing at the palace; chapter 22 goes in. Jeremiah is sent down to the king’s house, and the chapter then gathers his words about the last kings of Judah in order: Shallum, Jehoiakim and Coniah.

The message. A king is measured by one thing: whether he does justice and righteousness for those who cannot defend themselves. That is what David’s throne was for, and that, God says, is what it is to know him. Kings who build their own monuments on the backs of the poor will lose everything, and even God’s signet ring can be torn off. The throne of David is left empty, waiting for the King God himself will raise up.

Why it was said. Judah’s kings had treated the promise to David as a guarantee that their house would stand whatever they did. After Josiah’s death the throne passed through a son deported to Egypt, a son who built a palace with forced labour, and a grandson taken to Babylon (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. At the palace gate Jeremiah preaches the royal charter: rescue the robbed and protect the alien, the fatherless and the widow (vv. 1–3). Refusal will turn the cedar palace into firewood and a ruin that explains itself to the nations (vv. 4–9). Shallum will never come home (vv. 10–12). Jehoiakim, who builds his house with unpaid labour, is set beside his father Josiah, who judged the cause of the poor: “Is not this to know me?” He will have the burial of a donkey, and the city that would not listen in its prosperity will cry out from the mountains (vv. 13–23). Coniah, God’s signet ring, is torn off, hurled into exile and written down as childless (vv. 24–30).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. The chapter leaves David’s throne empty, and the next one fills it with “a righteous Branch” who “shall execute justice and righteousness in the land” (23:5). Jesus is that King, and the charter Jehoiakim despised is the one he kept: he had “nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20), and he came for the poor. The signet torn from Coniah was given back to his grandson Zerubbabel (Haggai 2:23), and Matthew traces the royal line through this very name to Jesus (Matthew 1:11–12), who sits on David’s throne without the curse.

For us. Knowing God is never separate from how we treat people who cannot repay us, and that includes paying people properly and on time. Status built on display has to be kept up for ever; standing given by Christ does not. And no privilege, office or family name protects anyone who refuses to listen while things are going well.
22.theology:
The Davidic throne is held on covenant terms, and the test is justice for those who cannot defend themselves (vv. 3-5). God defines the knowledge of himself by the judging of the cause of the poor and needy (v. 16), not as a substitute for true worship but inseparable from it.

God speaks to people in their prosperity, when heeding him is cheapest (v. 21), and grandeur built on injustice ends as firewood and an unmourned burial (vv. 7, 19). Not even the signet ring of David's house is immune (v. 24), yet God gives the signet back to Zerubbabel (Hag 2:23), and the throne passes to Christ: the curse stands and the promise is kept.
22.examples: The chapter judges a king by whether a robbed man can get his property back, and sets cedar panelling and vermilion paint, paid for with wages never handed over, beside a dead donkey dragged out of the gate as the state funeral. It ends with a signet ring torn off a king's hand and, in Haggai, put back on his grandson's.

keyVerse.quote: He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the LORD.
keyVerse.note: Set between Jehoiakim’s cedar palace and his donkey’s burial, this verse tells us what a king is for and what knowing God looks like. It defines the knowledge of God not apart from worship but never apart from justice for those who cannot repay, the charter only Christ, the true Son of David, has perfectly kept.

22.reflection:
The king’s charter was to rescue the robbed and protect the alien, the fatherless and the widow (v. 3). Who are the most defenceless people in our town or church, and what would it look like to take up their cause?

“Is not this to know me?” (v. 16). Why does God tie knowing him so closely to how we treat the poor? How does this guard against both a cold orthodoxy and a gospel-less activism?

Jehoiakim competed in cedar (v. 15). Where are we tempted to build our identity on display, and how does the standing Christ gives free us from it?

God spoke to Judah “in your prosperity”, but they would not listen (v. 21). What warnings are easiest to ignore when life is going well? How does God keep his promise to David through Coniah’s line, and what does that teach us about his faithfulness?

23.text: <sup>1</sup>"Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!" declares the LORD.<sup>2</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the shepherds who care for my people: "You have scattered my flock and have driven them away, and you have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you for your evil deeds, declares the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Then I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and I will bring them back to their fold, and they shall be fruitful and multiply.<sup>4</sup>I will set shepherds over them who will care for them, and they shall fear no more, nor be dismayed, neither shall any be missing, declares the LORD.<sup>5</sup>"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.<sup>6</sup>In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is the name by which he will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'<sup>7</sup>"Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they shall no longer say, 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt,'<sup>8</sup>but 'As the LORD lives who brought up and led the offspring of the house of Israel out of the north country and out of all the countries where he had driven them.' Then they shall dwell in their own land."<sup>9</sup>Concerning the prophets: My heart is broken within me; all my bones shake; I am like a drunken man, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD and because of his holy words.<sup>10</sup>For the land is full of adulterers; because of the curse the land mourns, and the pastures of the wilderness are dried up. Their course is evil, and their might is not right.<sup>11</sup>"Both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in my house I have found their evil, declares the LORD.<sup>12</sup>Therefore their way shall be to them like slippery paths in the darkness, into which they shall be driven and fall, for I will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment, declares the LORD.<sup>13</sup>In the prophets of Samaria I saw an unsavory thing: they prophesied by Baal and led my people Israel astray.<sup>14</sup>But in the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: they commit adultery and walk in lies; they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil; all of them have become like Sodom to me, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah."<sup>15</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the prophets: "Behold, I will feed them with bitter food and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land."<sup>16</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you, filling you with vain hopes. They speak visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD.<sup>17</sup>They say continually to those who despise the word of the LORD, 'It shall be well with you'; and to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come upon you.'"<sup>18</sup>For who among them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and to hear his word, or who has paid attention to his word and listened?<sup>19</sup>Behold, the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked.<sup>20</sup>The anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly.<sup>21</sup>"I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied.<sup>22</sup>But if they had stood in my council, then they would have proclaimed my words to my people, and they would have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their deeds.<sup>23</sup>"Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far away?<sup>24</sup>Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the LORD. Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD.<sup>25</sup>I have heard what the prophets have said who prophesy lies in my name, saying, 'I have dreamed, I have dreamed!'<sup>26</sup>How long shall there be lies in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies, and who prophesy the deceit of their own heart,<sup>27</sup>who think to make my people forget my name by their dreams that they tell one another, even as their fathers forgot my name for Baal?<sup>28</sup>Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream, but let him who has my word speak my word faithfully. What has straw in common with wheat? declares the LORD.<sup>29</sup>Is not my word like fire, declares the LORD, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?<sup>30</sup>Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who steal my words from one another.<sup>31</sup>Behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who use their tongues and declare, 'declares the LORD.'<sup>32</sup>Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams, declares the LORD, and who tell them and lead my people astray by their lies and their recklessness, when I did not send them or charge them. So they do not profit this people at all, declares the LORD.<sup>33</sup>"When one of this people, or a prophet or a priest asks you, 'What is the burden of the LORD?' you shall say to them, 'You are the burden, and I will cast you off, declares the LORD.'<sup>34</sup>And as for the prophet, priest, or one of the people who says, 'The burden of the LORD,' I will punish that man and his household.<sup>35</sup>Thus shall you say, every one to his neighbor and every one to his brother, 'What has the LORD answered?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?'<sup>36</sup>But 'the burden of the LORD' you shall mention no more, for the burden is every man's own word, and you pervert the words of the living God, the LORD of hosts, our God.<sup>37</sup>Thus you shall say to the prophet, 'What has the LORD answered you?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?'<sup>38</sup>But if you say, 'The burden of the LORD,' thus says the LORD, 'Because you have said these words, "The burden of the LORD," when I sent to you, saying, "You shall not say, 'The burden of the LORD,'"<sup>39</sup>therefore, behold, I will surely lift you up and cast you away from my presence, you and the city that I gave to you and your fathers.<sup>40</sup>And I will bring upon you everlasting reproach and perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten.'"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where Judah’s shepherds have failed, God promises to gather his flock himself and to give it a righteous King. Woe to the leaders who destroyed and scattered God’s sheep: he will attend to them for their evil, bring back the remnant, and set over them shepherds who will care for them, so that none are missing (vv. 1–4). He will raise up for David a righteous Branch who will reign wisely and do justice, and his name will be “The LORD is our righteousness” (vv. 5–6). Then God will be known by a rescue greater than the exodus (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Against every failed shepherd God sets one King who will do what the house of David was given the throne to do.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!" declares the LORD. Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the shepherds who care for my people: "You have scattered my flock and have driven them away, and you have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you for your evil deeds, declares the LORD. Then I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and I will bring them back to their fold, and they shall be fruitful and multiply. I will set shepherds over them who will care for them, and they shall fear no more, nor be dismayed, neither shall any be missing, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God condemns the leaders who scattered his flock and promises to gather the sheep himself and give them shepherds who will care for every one.

Woe to the shepherds. The shepherds are the kings and leaders of chapter 22, and the charge is precise. They did not merely fail to gather; they destroy and scatter. Bad leadership is not neutral. And the flock was never theirs: these are the sheep of my pasture. They mishandled someone else’s property, and the owner was watching.

I will attend to you. There is a grim play on words. They did not attend to the flock, so God will attend to them, in judgment. Anyone with pastoral responsibility should feel the weight of it: the opposite of caring for people is not cruelty but inattention, and God treats inattention as an evil deed. The one safe place for a shepherd who has failed is under the good Shepherd, who laid down his life for sheep and shepherds alike.

I will gather the remnant of my flock. Now God takes the job himself. Ezekiel puts it even more strongly: “Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out” (Ezekiel 34:11). When human shepherds fail, God does not abandon the flock; he comes for them personally.

I will set shepherds over them. Then he gives them shepherds again, a promise fulfilled in the pastors and teachers Christ gives his church, and finally in “the chief Shepherd” himself (1 Peter 5:4). Success is measured as a shepherd measures it: neither shall any be missing. Every sheep is accounted for.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land. In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is the name by which he will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will raise up from David’s fallen line a righteous King who will do what no king of Judah did, and his name declares that he is his people’s righteousness.

The answer to chapter 22. Chapter 22 ended with the royal line written down as childless. Here is the answer, and the timing is deliberate.

A righteous Branch. The Branch is a shoot growing from a stump: a tree cut down to the ground, and one living green shoot coming up out of it. Isaiah had used the picture: “There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit” (Isaiah 11:1). The dynasty is a felled tree; God will grow a king out of the stump.

Execute justice and righteousness in the land. What he will do is exactly what chapter 22 demanded and no king delivered (22:3, 15). The job description is unchanged; at last there is someone to fill it.

The LORD is our righteousness. This name is the summit of the book so far. The king reigning as Jeremiah spoke was Zedekiah, whose own name means “the LORD is righteous”: a weak, faithless man whose reign ended in fire. The coming King will be everything he was not, and his name is not about himself at all: our righteousness. It is a statement about his people’s standing. He is called what they receive. His righteousness is reckoned as theirs, credited to them as if they had lived his life, which is why they are saved and dwell securely in his days rather than in their own.

What the New Testament says. The New Testament does not quote these verses, but it says in plain prose what they promise. “The righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law”, “through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe” (Romans 3:21–22). Christ “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Everything Jeremiah has exposed, the deceitful heart, the leopard’s spots, the sin engraved with an iron pen, requires a righteousness from outside. Here is his name.

Everyone has a righteousness project. Few modern people use the word righteousness, but almost all of us are working at it. We want to be on the right side of history, a good parent, an ethical shopper, the reasonable one in the argument. Much public life is now a contest of moral standing, in which the surest way to feel righteous is to find someone less righteous and say so loudly. Religious people do it with rules and attendance; secular people do it with causes and opinions. The project is the same: to be my own justification. And it is exhausting, because the verdict is never final and someone is always ready to reopen the case. That is why this name is such a surprise. It does not say, the LORD rewards our righteousness, or, the LORD helps us become righteous. It says the King is our righteousness. The verdict is settled by someone else’s life. A person who has received that can stop defending himself, can admit he was wrong without his whole world shaking, and can give others the mercy he no longer has to earn.

The name given to Jerusalem. Later in this book the same name is given to Jerusalem (33:16): the people are called by their King’s name, because what he is, they are counted to be in him. Hebrew names often made a statement about God, as Zedekiah’s did, so the name need not by itself call the Branch the LORD; yet many Christians have seen here a hint of what the New Testament makes plain, that the King who is our righteousness is himself God come in the flesh.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish readers have always taken the righteous Branch as the Messiah, the King of David’s line still to come: the Targum renders Branch here as Messiah, and the Talmud (Bava Batra 75b) counts the Messiah among those called by the name of God, citing this verse. Most Jewish interpreters take the name as a sentence praising God, not a claim that the King is divine. On the King himself the two readings agree. This commentary sees him in Jesus, descended from David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3), in whom God’s righteousness is given to his people (1 Corinthians 1:30).
verseByVerse.note: The “righteous Branch” is the Messiah; his name, “The LORD is our righteousness,” plays on King Zedekiah’s name (“the LORD is righteous”).

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they shall no longer say, 'As the LORD lives who brought up the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt,' but 'As the LORD lives who brought up and led the offspring of the house of Israel out of the north country and out of all the countries where he had driven them.' Then they shall dwell in their own land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rescue God promises with the righteous King will be so great that it will replace the exodus as the deed by which he is known.

The days are coming. The new-exodus oath of 16:14–15 is repeated, and its position here is the point: it comes immediately after the righteous Branch. The greater rescue and the greater King belong together. Once Israel swore by the God who brought them out of Egypt; then they will swear by the God who brought them home from every land.

A modest return. The return from Babylon, when it came, was modest: some fifty thousand people (Ezra 2:64–65), a small temple, no king. The oath was not yet fully kept. It is kept in Christ’s rescue of his people from a deeper exile than Babylon, the exile of sin and death.

Where Christians differ. All agree that the first fulfilment was the return from Babylon. Dispensationalists look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel; faithful Christians differ here.

This commentary’s view. In this chapter the promise is tied to the Branch, and its scope is his: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. It is fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered sheep from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Romans 11:26), and it will be complete in the new creation.

Textual note. The ESV notes a small textual difference in verse 8. The substance is unaffected: the God who is bringing them home will be known by that, as he was once known by the Red Sea.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Both Prophet and Priest Are Ungodly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The corruption of God’s people starts with those who speak for him. Jeremiah is shattered by God’s holy words, while the land is full of adultery and lies under the covenant curse (vv. 9–10). Prophet and priest alike are ungodly, even in the temple, and their path will be slippery and dark (vv. 11–12). Samaria’s prophets openly served Baal; Jerusalem’s prophets are worse, living immorally and strengthening evildoers so that no one repents, until the city is like Sodom. God will give them bitter food, because ungodliness has spread from them through the land (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Preaching that comforts people in their sin is not a minor failure; it is the source from which a nation's ungodliness spreads.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning the prophets: My heart is broken within me; all my bones shake; I am like a drunken man, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD and because of his holy words. For the land is full of adulterers; because of the curse the land mourns, and the pastures of the wilderness are dried up. Their course is evil, and their might is not right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah is shattered by the holiness of God’s word, while the land around him is full of unfaithfulness and the powerful use their strength for evil.

Concerning the prophets. The heading opens a collection that runs to the end of the chapter. Having dealt with the kings, God now turns to the preachers.

My heart is broken within me. Before he says a word against the false prophets, Jeremiah describes what God’s word does to him: heart broken, bones shaking, unsteady on his feet like a drunk. Not because of the opposition, but because of the LORD and because of his holy words. That is the contrast the whole section turns on: a man wrecked by handling the word of God, about to describe men who handle it lightly and sleep well. Anyone who teaches Scripture might ask which of the two he more resembles.

The land is full of adulterers. It is literal (verse 14 will say the prophets themselves commit adultery), and it is also spiritual: a nation unfaithful to the God it was bound to by covenant, as a wife to her husband. The two are rarely separate for long.

Because of the curse the land mourns. The drought is read for what it is: the curse written into the covenant long before, “the heavens over your head shall be bronze” and “The LORD will make the rain of your land powder” (Deuteronomy 28:23–24). The pastures are dying because the people broke faith, and the ground itself is pictured grieving. Sin is never as private as it feels; a nation’s unfaithfulness reaches its fields.

Their might is not right. Then the verdict on the powerful. They hold the influence in the land and use it wrongly, and strength that has lost its moral right is simply force.

verseByVerse.quote: "Both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in my house I have found their evil, declares the LORD. Therefore their way shall be to them like slippery paths in the darkness, into which they shall be driven and fall, for I will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prophets and priests, who should have kept each other honest, are corrupt together even in the temple, and they will slip and fall in the dark.

Both prophet and priest are ungodly. These two offices should have checked each other: the priest teaching the law that had been given, the prophet bringing the word God was speaking now. Instead they agreed, and when those meant to correct one another join in the same wrong, nobody is left to raise the alarm.

Even in my house. Not only in the streets and the high places, but inside the temple, among the men conducting the worship. Corruption at the centre of religion is worse than corruption outside it, because there is nowhere left for a seeker to go.

Like slippery paths in the darkness. Men who gave others no light will walk in the dark on wet stone. A psalmist once envied men like these until he went into the sanctuary and saw their end: “Truly you set them in slippery places; you make them fall to ruin” (Psalm 73:18). The false prophets looked as though they stood on the firmest ground in Jerusalem: the pulpit, the temple, the favour of the court. They were on a wet slope in the dark, and they were being driven.

The year of their punishment. The date is already set. Judgment is not improvised when patience runs out. It is on the calendar.

verseByVerse.quote: In the prophets of Samaria I saw an unsavory thing: they prophesied by Baal and led my people Israel astray. But in the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: they commit adultery and walk in lies; they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil; all of them have become like Sodom to me, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah." Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the prophets: "Behold, I will feed them with bitter food and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s prophets are worse than the pagan prophets of Samaria, because they use God’s name to make sinners comfortable, and so they have made the city like Sodom.

In the prophets of Samaria. Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom destroyed a century before, had prophets who openly served Baal. God calls that an unsavory thing: repellent, but at least undisguised. The men in Jerusalem, who preach in the name of the LORD, are worse: a horrible thing. Their private lives are corrupt and their public message is false, and the two are connected.

They strengthen the hands of evildoers. The phrase to weigh is so that no one turns from his evil. That is the effect of their preaching, the exact opposite of a prophet’s job. A man goes to worship intending to break with something, hears that God is fine with it, and goes home confirmed in it. Judged by outcome rather than intention, that is more destructive than Baal worship, because it uses God’s own name to do it.

Like Sodom to me. No Jerusalemite could hear this calmly. Isaiah had already addressed the city’s leaders that way: “Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom!” (Isaiah 1:10). Ezekiel names Sodom’s guilt: “pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49). The likeness is not only in sexual sin. It is a comfortable city that has lost the capacity to be shocked. Sodom had no prophets; Jerusalem had prophets, and they made it Sodom.

I will feed them with bitter food. The bitter food and poisoned water of 9:15 are now served to the preachers, and the reason names them as the source: ungodliness did not seep up from the people to the pulpit; it flowed out from the pulpit into the country.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — Visions of Their Own Minds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells his people not to listen to prophets who speak their own minds, and gives the tests that expose them. They fill people with vain hopes, promising peace to those who despise God’s word (vv. 16–17). None has stood in the council of the LORD; meanwhile his storm is already breaking on the wicked, and later they will understand (vv. 18–20). God did not send them, and the proof is that they did not turn anyone from evil (vv. 21–22). The God who fills heaven and earth sees every secret place (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology: The test of preaching is not sincerity or eloquence but whether it comes from God and turns people from evil.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you, filling you with vain hopes. They speak visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD. They say continually to those who despise the word of the LORD, 'It shall be well with you'; and to everyone who stubbornly follows his own heart, they say, 'No disaster shall come upon you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells his people not to listen to prophets whose comforting words come from their own minds, because false hope steals the time to repent.

Do not listen. This is a direct instruction to the congregation. Hearers are responsible for what they sit under.

Filling you with vain hopes. Hope is a gift; false hope is a cruelty, because it uses up the time a person had to repent. A doctor who tells a man with a treatable illness that nothing is wrong has not been kind to him.

Visions of their own minds. The source is named again (14:14). This is not plain lying; these men very likely believed their own material. Sincerity is not the test; where the message comes from is: not from the mouth of the LORD.

It shall be well with you. Look at the audiences: people who despise the word of the LORD and people who stubbornly follow their own hearts. To exactly those people they say, It shall be well with you, and they say it continually. Chapter 28 shows the message preached in the temple itself: Hananiah promising that within two years the exiles and the temple vessels would be home (28:2–4).

Itching ears. Paul saw the same market forming: “the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions” (2 Timothy 4:3). False prophets are not only a supply problem. There is always demand.

A God who only says nice things. The sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton, in Soul Searching (2005), gave a name to the faith they found among many American teenagers and their parents: Moralistic Therapeutic Deism. God wants people to be nice, wants them to feel good about themselves, and otherwise stays out of the way until he is needed. It is an exact description of It shall be well with you. Such a God is very pleasant, and useless when it matters, because a God who never warns cannot really rescue, and a God who never names sin cannot really forgive it. False comfort feels kind and leaves people alone with what they have refused to face. The true word says the disaster is real, and then shows the one on whom it fell. The false prophets said, No disaster shall come upon you. In Christ God says something deeper: the disaster came, and it came upon him. Peace built on that is not a vain hope.

How do I know whom to listen to? The voices now come by podcast and feed as well as from the pulpit, and the command still stands. Check the source. Does the speaker open the Bible and let it speak, or use a verse as a launch pad for his own ideas? Be like the Bereans, “examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so” (Acts 17:11). Notice what it does to you. Does it ever confront your sin, or only reassure? Teaching that says It shall be well with you to everyone, whatever they do, fails the test of verse 22. Watch where it points. Do you come away thinking more about Christ and his cross, or about the teacher, your success and your feelings? Choose a church, not just content. Sit under a pastor who knows you and can be questioned, and keep your diet of online teaching smaller than your diet of Scripture itself. And the safeguard is not finally your cleverness. The Good Shepherd says, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27); he keeps his own by his word.

verseByVerse.quote: For who among them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and to hear his word, or who has paid attention to his word and listened? Behold, the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked. The anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false prophets have never stood in God’s council to hear his word, and while they promise fair weather, his storm is already breaking on the wicked.

Who among them has stood in the council of the LORD? A true prophet has stood where God’s decisions are made and has listened. These men never went in, which is why they can only report their own minds. Scripture lets us glimpse that room. When four hundred court prophets told King Ahab to go up to battle and triumph, one man stood apart and said, “I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right hand and on his left” (1 Kings 22:19). Micaiah had been in the council; the four hundred had only been in the palace. Amos states the principle: “the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7).

Paid attention to his word and listened. Count the words for receiving in the question: stood, see, hear, paid attention, listened. Five of them before a single word about speaking. A preacher is first a listener, and a man who speaks more than he listens has reversed the order God requires.

Behold, the storm of the LORD! While they promise fair weather, the storm is already moving. These two verses return almost word for word in the Book of Consolation (30:23–24). There they guard the promise, reminding the restored that God’s anger against evil has not been cancelled; here they are aimed at the men who said no disaster would come. It is the same storm. What differs is whether a person is sheltered from it.

The intents of his heart. The anger is not a mood. It will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart: a settled purpose, terrifying for those who oppose it and steadying for those who trust that he will carry out his purposes of mercy just as surely.

In the latter days. The last line is honest about timing: In the latter days you will understand it clearly. Some things only make sense afterwards, and the people telling you otherwise now will not be there to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: "I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied. But if they had stood in my council, then they would have proclaimed my words to my people, and they would have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God did not send these busy prophets, and the proof is that their preaching never turned anyone from evil.

I did not send the prophets, yet they ran. God flatly denies two things: he did not send them, and he did not speak to them. Yet they ran, and they prophesied. Zeal and output are not evidence of a call. It is possible to be extremely busy in ministry that God never commissioned.

The practical test. Here is a wonderfully usable test: preaching that comes from God turns people from evil. Not that everyone repents; Jeremiah’s own ministry is proof that faithful preaching can be widely rejected. But the aim and tendency of the word is to turn people, and a message whose effect is to leave everyone exactly as they were, comfortable and unchallenged, has already told you where it came from. Deuteronomy gave a test by fulfilment (Deuteronomy 18:21–22); Jeremiah adds a test by fruit.

From their evil way. The turning is concrete: from their evil way, and from the evil of their deeds, the direction of a life and the particular things done in it. God’s word does not stop at general improvement; it names the road and the acts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far away? Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the LORD. Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is not a small local deity who can be quoted freely; he is near and far, he fills heaven and earth, and no one can hide from him.

Am I a God at hand? The false prophets behave as though God were at hand in the smallest sense: a local deity, resident in the temple precinct, near enough to be managed and too small to see what went on in their houses. A god like that can be quoted freely, because he will not object. God insists he is also a God far away: above, beyond, not contained by the building or by anyone’s theology of it. They wanted a God close enough to use and not great enough to fear.

Near and far together. Scripture holds both truths together, in a particular order: “I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit” (Isaiah 57:15). God is near because he chooses to come near, not because he is small, and the ones he comes near to are the humble, not the men using his name.

Can a man hide himself in secret places? Think of what was being done in secret in this chapter: adultery behind closed doors (v. 14), dreams rehearsed in private and passed off in public (v. 25). The question answers itself. “No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account” (Hebrews 4:13).

Do I not fill heaven and earth? This is not a picture of a very large being in a very large room. It means there is no location without him: no study, no bedroom, no pulpit, no private thought.

Where shall I flee? The psalm turns the same truth into comfort: “Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence?” (Psalm 139:7). Paul told pagans in Athens that “he is actually not far from each one of us” (Acts 17:27). To a liar it is terror; to a child it is home. The God who sees the unconfessed sin also sees the faithfulness nobody else noticed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word is as different from human dreams as wheat is from straw, and he is against those who confuse them. He has heard prophets claiming dreams in his name, dreams that make his people forget his name as their fathers did through Baal (vv. 25–27). Let the dreamer tell his dream, but let the one who has God’s word speak it faithfully, for that word is like fire and like a hammer that shatters rock (vv. 28–29). Three times God says he is against the prophets: those who steal words from one another, those who stamp their own words “declares the LORD”, and those who lead his people astray by lying dreams (vv. 30–32).
verseByVerse.theology: Dreams and God's word are not two grades of the same thing; they are straw and wheat.

verseByVerse.quote: I have heard what the prophets have said who prophesy lies in my name, saying, 'I have dreamed, I have dreamed!' How long shall there be lies in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies, and who prophesy the deceit of their own heart, who think to make my people forget my name by their dreams that they tell one another, even as their fathers forgot my name for Baal?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophets’ claimed dreams come from their own deceitful hearts, and they make God’s people forget his name as surely as Baal worship did.

I have dreamed, I have dreamed! The God who fills heaven and earth has been listening to the sermons. The repetition mimics them: the excited claim of a private revelation that cannot be checked. God traces it to its source, the deceitful heart of 17:9: the deceit is in the prophets’ own hearts, and they are its first victims. How long? is the voice of patience nearing its end.

Who think to make my people forget my name. Their dreams have the same effect as Baal did: they make people forget God’s name. Ministry that draws attention to the minister’s experiences is not neutral; it crowds out the name it claims to serve. The grandfathers forgot God by bowing to an idol; the grandsons forget him by listening to dreams told in his name. The method differs and the result is the same: idolatry does not require a statue.

Does God give dreams and visions today? He spoke by dreams and visions when Scripture was being given; now he has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and his word is complete. A dream may stir the conscience, but no believer should treat one as a word from God. “Let him who has my word speak my word faithfully” (v. 28).

Where Christians differ. Many continuationist Christians believe God still guides by dreams, always to be tested by Scripture.

This commentary’s view. This commentary is cessationist, holding that nothing received today adds to the finished word, and it honours brothers who see it differently.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream, but let him who has my word speak my word faithfully. What has straw in common with wheat? declares the LORD. Is not my word like fire, declares the LORD, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dreams may be told as dreams, but God’s word must be delivered faithfully, for it is as different from human ideas as wheat from straw, and it burns and breaks like fire and a hammer.

Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream. The ruling is not that dreams must be suppressed. Tell the dream, and call it a dream. What is forbidden is passing it off as the word of God.

Speak my word faithfully. The requirement laid on the one who has God’s word is a single word: faithfully. Not originally, not impressively, not with fresh angles. A messenger’s whole excellence is delivering the message as it was given.

What has straw in common with wheat? Both come off the same field; one feeds people and one does not. Preaching that is mostly the preacher’s own material may be pleasant, but nobody lives on straw.

Like fire, and like a hammer. Here is what the real thing does. It burns, as it burned in Jeremiah’s bones when he tried to keep silent (20:9); and it breaks rock, which is the only hope for a people whose faces are harder than rock (5:3). If preaching never burns or breaks anything, the problem may not be the congregation. Yet the power is not the preacher’s to produce: the word does its work in the hands of the Spirit, which is why a preacher’s first task is to deliver it faithfully and pray.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who steal my words from one another. Behold, I am against the prophets, declares the LORD, who use their tongues and declare, 'declares the LORD.' Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams, declares the LORD, and who tell them and lead my people astray by their lies and their recklessness, when I did not send them or charge them. So they do not profit this people at all, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is against three kinds of false prophet, the borrowers, the formula-users and the reckless, and for all their activity they help no one.

I am against the prophets. Three times God says it, and each names a different fraud.

Who steal my words from one another. The first is plagiarism. Having nothing from God themselves, they recycle each other’s material. A prophetic culture can run for years on borrowed phrases with no fresh dealing with God behind any of it.

Who use their tongues. The second is the formula. They have learned the phrase that makes speech sound authoritative and attach it to their own opinions: they use their tongues and say, declares the LORD. Every generation has its version, a tone of voice, a way of quoting, a confident “God told me”, by which personal judgment is given divine weight.

They do not profit this people at all. The third is recklessness: not only malice but carelessness with other people’s souls. And the verdict is quietly devastating: all that ministry, and nobody was helped.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–40 — The Burden of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A mocking catchphrase for God’s word is banned and turned back on those who use it. People and prophets had begun asking Jeremiah, “What is the burden of the LORD?”, treating his message as a tiresome weight. God answers that they are the burden, and he will cast them off (v. 33). The phrase is to be dropped; they are to ask instead, “What has the LORD answered?” (vv. 34–37). Those who keep saying it after being told not to will be lifted up and thrown away, with the city, under a shame that will never be forgotten (vv. 38–40).
verseByVerse.theology: A reverent-sounding phrase had become a joke about God's word, and God takes the joke away.

verseByVerse.quote: "When one of this people, or a prophet or a priest asks you, 'What is the burden of the LORD?' you shall say to them, 'You are the burden, and I will cast you off, declares the LORD.' And as for the prophet, priest, or one of the people who says, 'The burden of the LORD,' I will punish that man and his household. Thus shall you say, every one to his neighbor and every one to his brother, 'What has the LORD answered?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?' But 'the burden of the LORD' you shall mention no more, for the burden is every man's own word, and you pervert the words of the living God, the LORD of hosts, our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People mocked God’s word as “the burden of the LORD”, so God tells them they are the burden he will cast off, and bans the phrase.

What is the burden of the LORD? The section turns on a word. The burden of the LORD was a way of speaking about a prophet’s message, and a burden is also a load. People had started asking Jeremiah, with a smirk, what today’s burden was, treating God’s word as a heavy, tiresome thing and the prophet as the man who carries it round.

You are the burden. God takes the joke and returns it: You are the burden, and I will cast you off. You think my word is a weight? You are the weight, and I am putting it down.

You shall mention no more. The phrase is banned, and the ban reaches everyone, prophet, priest, ordinary citizen and his household, because an attitude to God’s word is taught at home before it is voiced in public. God legislates against a piece of religious slang because of the contempt packed into it.

What has the LORD answered? He gives them the replacement wording, humble and expectant: not, what is today’s burden, but what has God said. The change of phrase is a change of attitude. And the correction happens every one to his neighbor and every one to his brother, in ordinary conversation. The way believers talk to each other about God’s word, flippant or expectant, weary or hungry, shapes how they receive it.

The burden is every man’s own word. Here is the heart of it: everyone had made his own opinion the word from God. And the charge is the gravest in the chapter, you pervert the words of the living God, twisting them until they say something else. Weigh the three titles stacked at the end: the living God, not a dead text to be joked about; the LORD of hosts, the commander of heaven’s armies; our God, the one who belongs to these very people. They were bending the words of someone alive, powerful, and theirs.

Textual note. The ESV notes a textual variation in the question of verse 33, but the wordplay is plain enough.
verseByVerse.note: A pun: “burden” and “oracle” are the same Hebrew word (massa).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus you shall say to the prophet, 'What has the LORD answered you?' or 'What has the LORD spoken?' But if you say, 'The burden of the LORD,' thus says the LORD, 'Because you have said these words, "The burden of the LORD," when I sent to you, saying, "You shall not say, 'The burden of the LORD,'" therefore, behold, I will surely lift you up and cast you away from my presence, you and the city that I gave to you and your fathers. And I will bring upon you everlasting reproach and perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who keep mocking God’s word after being told to stop will be lifted up like a load and thrown away, under a shame that will never be forgotten.

When I sent to you. The instruction is repeated, now addressed to how people speak to the prophet himself, and the case against them is built like a legal charge. They were told plainly not to say it. They said it anyway. That moves the offence from contempt to defiance, and verse 38 records the command in God’s own voice so that no one can plead ignorance.

I will surely lift you up. The sentence uses their own word against them one last time: they called God’s message a burden, so he will lift them up like a load and put it down outside. What is cast away with them is a gift: the city that I gave to you and your fathers. Everything they had came from the God they were mocking.

Which shall not be forgotten. If God will “surely forget” them (see below), their shame shall not be forgotten. Set that beside the promise eight chapters later: “I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more” (31:34). Those are the only two outcomes Scripture offers. In the new covenant God forgets the sin and keeps the person. Outside it, he lets go of the person and the shame is never forgotten.

The two belong together. The chapter that gave us the most beautiful name in the book, The LORD is our righteousness, ends with everlasting reproach for those who made his word a joke. The King who is our righteousness is the Word made flesh, and how people handle the word is finally how they handle him.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that I will surely lift you up may be rendered “surely forget you”. The Hebrew verbs for lifting and forgetting sound almost alike, and either reading lands: they could not stop saying the word, and God will stop remembering them.

23.title: The Righteous Branch: The LORD Is Our Righteousness
23.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 22 judged Judah’s kings one by one and ended with the royal line written down as childless. Chapter 23 completes the collection begun in chapter 21: the answer to the empty throne, then God’s case against the preachers.

The message. When the shepherds of God’s people fail, God himself will gather his flock and raise up a righteous King from David’s line, whose name is “The LORD is our righteousness”. Meanwhile the deadliest danger to the people is not a foreign army but false preaching: men who speak their own dreams in God’s name and tell sinners all will be well. God’s word is not like their words; it is fire and a hammer, and it turns people from evil.

Why it was said. Judah’s kings had scattered the flock, and its prophets and priests were promising peace on the eve of disaster, strengthening the hands of evildoers (see the introduction). People mocked Jeremiah’s warnings as “the burden of the LORD”.

How the chapter makes its case. Woe to the shepherds; God will gather the remnant himself and give them true shepherds (vv. 1–4). He will raise up for David a righteous Branch, named “The LORD is our righteousness” (vv. 5–6), and his rescue will outshine the exodus (vv. 7–8). Then the prophets: Jeremiah trembles at God’s holy words, while prophet and priest are ungodly even in the temple, worse than Samaria’s (vv. 9–15). They speak visions of their own minds, never having stood in God’s council; if they had, they would have turned the people from evil (vv. 16–22). The God who fills heaven and earth sees them (vv. 23–24). Their dreams are straw beside the wheat of his word, and he is against them (vv. 25–32). Finally the mocking phrase “the burden of the LORD” is banned and turned back on those who use it (vv. 33–40).

Where it leads. By direct promise. The righteous Branch is Jesus, the Son of David who does what no king of Judah did, and whose name tells us what he gives: his righteousness is counted as ours (1 Corinthians 1:30; 2 Corinthians 5:21). He is also the Good Shepherd who gathers the scattered flock himself (John 10:11, 16), and the true Prophet who stood in the Father’s council and spoke only what he was given: “the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment” (John 12:49).

For us. No one can be righteous enough before God, and no one needs to be: the King is our righteousness. That frees us to listen to preaching that confronts us rather than flatters us, and to test every voice, however confident, by the written word. And it calls everyone who teaches Scripture to tremble at it, as Jeremiah did, and to speak it faithfully.
23.theology:
Leaders are accountable for a flock that belongs to God, and when shepherds fail, God gathers his people himself and gives them true shepherds under the chief Shepherd (vv. 1-4; John 10:11). The righteous Branch is the King who does what David's house failed to do, and his name declares what his people receive: his righteousness counted as theirs (vv. 5-6).

False prophecy is sincere and energetic, but it comes from the prophet’s own mind (vv. 16, 21), and is tested by its origin and its fruit: God's word turns people from evil (v. 22; Deut 18:20-22). God is near because he chooses to come near to the humble, not because he is small enough to be managed (vv. 23-24). And there are only two ways to be forgotten by God: in the new covenant he remembers the sin no more and keeps the person (31:34); for those who make his word a joke he lets go of the person, and the shame is never forgotten (vv. 39-40).
23.examples: The chapter's images are memorable: a shoot growing out of a stump that everyone had written off, preachers recycling each other's material with nothing fresh from God, and straw and wheat off the same field, of which only one feeds people. Its sharpest warning is the churchgoer who comes intending to break with a sin and goes home confirmed in it.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land. In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is the name by which he will be called: ‘The LORD is our righteousness.’
keyVerse.note: After a chapter that wrote David’s line down as childless and before a long indictment of false shepherds and prophets, God promises the King who will do what none of them did. His name is the gospel in miniature: the King himself is his people’s righteousness, fulfilled in Jesus, who “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

23.reflection:
God holds the shepherds responsible for scattering his flock and treats inattention as an evil deed (vv. 1–2). Whom has God given you to care for, and who might be “missing” from your attention?

The King’s name is “The LORD is our righteousness” (v. 6). In what ways do we still try to be our own righteousness, and what changes when we believe that the verdict has been settled by Christ’s life?

The false prophets said, “It shall be well with you” to those who despised God’s word (v. 17), and turned no one from evil (v. 22). How can we tell whether the teaching we listen to is from God? What should we do if it never confronts us?

God’s word is like fire and like a hammer (v. 29), and Jeremiah trembled at it (v. 9). How do we fall into treating the Bible as a “burden” (vv. 33–36), and how can we help one another ask, “What has the LORD spoken?”

24.text: <sup>1</sup>After Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken into exile from Jerusalem Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with the officials of Judah, the craftsmen, and the metal workers, and had brought them to Babylon, the LORD showed me this vision: behold, two baskets of figs placed before the temple of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>One basket had very good figs, like first-ripe figs, but the other basket had very bad figs, so bad that they could not be eaten.<sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to me, "What do you see, Jeremiah?" I said, "Figs, the good figs very good, and the bad figs very bad, so bad that they cannot be eaten."<sup>4</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>5</sup>"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans.<sup>6</sup>I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them back to this land. I will build them up, and not tear them down; I will plant them, and not pluck them up.<sup>7</sup>I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD, and they shall be my people and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart.<sup>8</sup>"But thus says the LORD: Like the bad figs that are so bad they cannot be eaten, so will I treat Zedekiah the king of Judah, his officials, the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this land, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse in all the places where I shall drive them.<sup>10</sup>And I will send sword, famine, and pestilence upon them, until they shall be utterly destroyed from the land that I gave to them and their fathers."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Two Baskets Before the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives Jeremiah a vision that will overturn what Jerusalem believes about who is favoured. It comes after Nebuchadnezzar has taken King Jeconiah, the officials and the skilled workers to Babylon in 597 BC, leaving the city standing with Zedekiah on the throne (v. 1). Before the temple stand two baskets: one of first-ripe figs, the best of the crop, and one of figs so rotten they cannot be eaten (v. 2). As at his call, God asks, “What do you see, Jeremiah?”, and Jeremiah simply describes the two baskets, very good and very bad, with nothing in between (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: Two baskets at the temple door, and the sorting is not the one anybody in Jerusalem would have made.

verseByVerse.quote: After Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken into exile from Jerusalem Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with the officials of Judah, the craftsmen, and the metal workers, and had brought them to Babylon, the LORD showed me this vision: behold, two baskets of figs placed before the temple of the LORD. One basket had very good figs, like first-ripe figs, but the other basket had very bad figs, so bad that they could not be eaten. And the LORD said to me, "What do you see, Jeremiah?" I said, "Figs, the good figs very good, and the bad figs very bad, so bad that they cannot be eaten."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the first deportation, God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs before the temple, one excellent and one rotten, to overturn Jerusalem’s belief that those left behind were the favoured ones.

The setting. The date fixes everything. This is after 597 BC, when Babylon took the young king Jeconiah, the Coniah of chapter 22, with the court, the skilled workers and the metalworkers. Jerusalem is still standing with Zedekiah on the throne.

We are the survivors. That situation produced a very natural way of thinking in the city: God has judged those people and spared us. The deportees must have been the sinners. We are the survivors, we still have the temple, and that proves whose side God is on.

Before the temple of the LORD. So the vision is set before the temple, the very place where that view was preached, and it is a picture of the harvest offering: two baskets of figs brought to God’s house.

So bad that they could not be eaten. First-ripe figs, picked in early summer, were a delicacy, the best of the crop. The other basket is not mediocre fruit but rotten. There is no middle category anywhere in this chapter.

What do you see, Jeremiah? The question is the one from the almond branch and the boiling pot (1:11, 13). God’s method with this prophet is to make him look at something ordinary and say what is there, and then to tell him what it means. Jeremiah’s answer is simply accurate and commits him to nothing, which is why God’s explanation comes as such a shock.
verseByVerse.note: Jeconiah (v. 1), Jehoiachin and Coniah (22:24) are three forms of the same young king's name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–7 — The Good Figs: the Exiles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The good figs are the exiles in Babylon, and their future rests on God’s grace, not their merit. God himself sent them away, and he will regard them as good (vv. 4–5). He will set his eyes on them for good and bring them back; he will build and plant them, the constructive verbs of Jeremiah’s call, and not tear them down or pluck them up (v. 6). Above all he will give them a heart to know him, so that they will be his people and he their God, and they will return to him with their whole heart (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The people who lost everything are the good figs, and God promises to give them the one thing they cannot give themselves: a heart to know him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans. I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them back to this land. I will build them up, and not tear them down; I will plant them, and not pluck them up. I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD, and they shall be my people and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The exiles in Babylon are the good figs, not because they were better people but because God has chosen to set his eyes on them, bring them home and give them a new heart.

Like these good figs. The good figs are the people in Babylon, which reverses everything Jerusalem believed. The men in chains, who lost their homes, their positions and their temple, are the first-ripe fruit. And note whom I have sent away: God, not Nebuchadnezzar, sent them. Their deportation was not abandonment but transplanting.

Were the exiles better people? Not by nature: Ezekiel, who lived among them, called them a rebellious house (Ezekiel 2:5). They are good figs because God says I will regard them so and sets his eyes on them for good. The difference lies in his choosing and his gift, not in their merit.

Why do we read suffering as a verdict? Circumstances are not a scoreboard. The social psychologist Melvin Lerner called the instinct behind it the belief in a just world: the deep assumption that people get what they deserve, so that when disaster strikes someone, we half-assume they earned it. It is comforting, because it means that if I am careful, it will not happen to me. Modern spirituality has its own version in karma, and the people left in Jerusalem had theirs: the deportees must have been the sinners. God overturns both the moralist, who reads every loss as punishment, and the cynic, who concludes that there is no justice at all (see the note on Job 1:20–22). The people whose lives look broken may be the ones God has his eye on, and those still holding the property may be the rotten basket.

The clearest case. By the reckoning of a just world, the man dying on the cross was plainly cursed. In fact he was the beloved Son, bearing a curse that belonged to others. Once you have seen that, you can never again read a life’s worth off its circumstances, your own or anyone else’s.

I will build them up. Listen to the verbs: build, plant, and the refusal of tear down and pluck up.
