They are four of the six verbs of Jeremiah’s call (1:10), and here the two constructive ones stand on their own, with the destructive pair expressly set aside. Ruin is not the last word of this ministry, and the exiles are where the building starts.

A heart to know me. Here is the promise the whole book has been driving toward. Chapter 13 asked whether a leopard could change its spots; chapter 17 said the heart is deceitful and desperately sick. The answer is not better instruction: I will give them a heart to know me. God gives what he requires. Ezekiel says the same: “I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 11:19). And the covenant promise follows, as it always does: they shall be my people and I will be their God.

With their whole heart. Notice the order in the last clause. Because he gives the heart, they shall return to me with their whole heart. Their wholehearted return is real, and it is the fruit of his gift rather than the price of it. That is the shape of the new covenant in 31:31–34, and of every conversion since. Paul calls believers a letter from Christ, written “with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3): the heart God promised the exiles is given by Christ through his Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — The Bad Figs: Those Who Remain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bad figs are those who thought themselves spared: King Zedekiah, his officials, the people left in Jerusalem, and those who had gone to Egypt (v. 8). Far from being favoured, they will become a horror and a byword, a taunt and a curse among all the kingdoms wherever God drives them (v. 9). Sword, famine and pestilence will pursue them until they are gone from the land that God had given to them and their fathers (v. 10). Being spared for a time proves nothing about God’s verdict.
verseByVerse.theology: Keeping your place in the land turns out to prove nothing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "But thus says the LORD: Like the bad figs that are so bad they cannot be eaten, so will I treat Zedekiah the king of Judah, his officials, the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this land, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt. I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse in all the places where I shall drive them. And I will send sword, famine, and pestilence upon them, until they shall be utterly destroyed from the land that I gave to them and their fathers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who stayed in Jerusalem or fled to Egypt, thinking themselves spared, are the rotten figs, and they will be scattered in disgrace and destroyed from the land.

Like the bad figs. The bad figs are the people still at home with the king, the officials and the temple, plus those in Egypt, probably Judeans who had gone there rather than submit to Babylon. They took their houses, jobs and worship as evidence of God’s approval. God calls them uneatable fruit. Being spared a disaster that fell on others proves nothing about your standing with God, and it is most dangerous when it is taken as his verdict in your favour.

A reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse. Verse 9 piles up words for public disgrace. The nation called to make God’s name known among the nations becomes the story other nations tell as a warning.

The land that I gave to them. Verse 10 brings the book’s familiar threefold sentence of sword, famine and pestilence, and the sting is in the last clause. The possession they trusted in is what they lose, because it was always a gift, never something they had earned. Ten verses overturn a whole way of reading what happens to us; anyone tempted to measure God’s favour by his circumstances should read them twice.

Textual note. The ESV notes a small textual difficulty in the opening phrase of verse 9.

24.title: Two Baskets of Figs
24.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 24 closes the collection on Judah’s kings and prophets (chapters 21–24). It is dated soon after 597 BC, when King Jeconiah, the Coniah of chapter 22, was taken to Babylon with the court and the craftsmen, while Zedekiah reigned over those left behind.

The message. Circumstances are not God’s verdict. Those left in Jerusalem thought survival proved God’s favour and exile proved his rejection, but God says the reverse: the exiles are the good figs he will bring back, build up and give a new heart, and those who stayed are the rotten fruit. His favour rests on his own choosing and gift, not on how a person’s life looks.

Why it was said. After the first deportation, the people in Jerusalem looked at the empty houses of the exiles and concluded that the sinners had been removed and the faithful spared, with the temple still standing to prove it (see the introduction). Zedekiah’s court took its survival as a reason to keep resisting Babylon and ignoring the prophet.

How the chapter makes its case. God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs before the temple, one of first-ripe figs and one too rotten to eat, and asks him what he sees (vv. 1–3). The good figs are the exiles: God sent them away, will set his eyes on them for good, bring them back, build and plant them, and give them a heart to know him (vv. 4–7). The bad figs are Zedekiah, his officials, those who remain in the land and those in Egypt: they will become a byword among the nations and be consumed by sword, famine and pestilence (vv. 8–10).

Where it leads. By covenant promise and by the need it exposes. Exile cannot change a heart any more than the temple could, so God promises to give what he requires: “a heart to know me” (v. 7), the gift at the centre of the new covenant (31:31–34), which Christ sealed in his blood and gives by his Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:3). And the chapter’s lesson reaches its clearest case at the cross, where a man who looked cursed, cast out and destroyed was the beloved Son, bearing a curse that belonged to others.

For us. Do not read God’s favour off anyone’s circumstances, your own included: comfort is not approval, and loss is not rejection. For believers in exile, through illness, failure or grief, God’s eyes are set on them for good. And a heart that truly returns to God is his gift, so ask him for it.
24.theology:
God's favour is not read off circumstances: the difference between the baskets lies in his choosing, not in anyone's merit (vv. 5, 8).

And God gives what he demands. The heart that 17:9 called deceitful, and that 13:23 said could no more change itself than a leopard its spots, he will replace with a heart to know him (v. 7), as Ezekiel 11:19-20 also promises and the new covenant of 31:31-34 will spell out.
24.examples: The chapter warns anyone who reads his own survival, or his comfortable circumstances, as God's verdict in his favour. And it comforts anyone whose life has been uprooted: God calls the deportation transplanting, promises building and planting with no tearing down attached, and gives the very heart he asks for.

keyVerse.quote: I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD, and they shall be my people and I will be their God, for they shall return to me with their whole heart.
keyVerse.note: This is what makes the exiles good figs: not their merit but God’s promise to give them the heart he requires. It anticipates the new covenant of 31:31–34, and it shows the order of grace: their wholehearted return is the fruit of his gift, not the price of it, and Christ now gives that heart by his Spirit.

24.reflection:
The people left in Jerusalem took their survival as proof of God’s favour (vv. 1–3). Where are we tempted to read God’s approval or disapproval from circumstances, our own or other people’s?

God says of the exiles, “I will set my eyes on them for good” (v. 6). How might this comfort a believer whose life has been uprooted by illness, loss or failure?

The exiles were not better people; God chose them and gave them a new heart (v. 7). How does this guard us against both pride and despair? How does the cross show that circumstances are not God’s verdict?

“They shall return to me with their whole heart” because God gives the heart (v. 7). What difference does it make to pray for ourselves and others, knowing that a changed heart is God’s gift?

25.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah (that was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon),<sup>2</sup>which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem:<sup>3</sup>"For twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, to this day, the word of the LORD has come to me, and I have spoken persistently to you, but you have not listened.<sup>4</sup>You have neither listened nor inclined your ears to hear, although the LORD persistently sent to you all his servants the prophets,<sup>5</sup>saying, 'Turn now, every one of you, from his evil way and evil deeds, and dwell upon the land that the LORD has given to you and your fathers from of old and forever.<sup>6</sup>Do not go after other gods to serve and worship them, or provoke me to anger with the work of your hands. Then I will do you no harm.'<sup>7</sup>Yet you have not listened to me, declares the LORD, that you might provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own harm.<sup>8</sup>"Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: Because you have not obeyed my words,<sup>9</sup>behold, I will send for all the tribes of the north, declares the LORD, and for Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring them against this land and its inhabitants, and against all these surrounding nations. I will devote them to destruction, and make them a horror, a hissing, and an everlasting desolation.<sup>10</sup>Moreover, I will banish from them the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp.<sup>11</sup>This whole land shall become a ruin and a waste, and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.<sup>12</sup>Then after seventy years are completed, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their iniquity, declares the LORD, making the land an everlasting waste.<sup>13</sup>I will bring upon that land all the words that I have uttered against it, everything written in this book, which Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.<sup>14</sup>For many nations and great kings shall make slaves even of them, and I will recompense them according to their deeds and the work of their hands."<sup>15</sup>Thus the LORD, the God of Israel, said to me: "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it.<sup>16</sup>They shall drink and stagger and be crazed because of the sword that I am sending among them."<sup>17</sup>So I took the cup from the LORD's hand, and made all the nations to whom the LORD sent me drink it:<sup>18</sup>Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, its kings and officials, to make them a desolation and a waste, a hissing and a curse, as at this day;<sup>19</sup>Pharaoh king of Egypt, his servants, his officials, all his people,<sup>20</sup>and all the mixed tribes among them; all the kings of the land of Uz and all the kings of the land of the Philistines (Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod);<sup>21</sup>Edom, Moab, and the sons of Ammon;<sup>22</sup>all the kings of Tyre, all the kings of Sidon, and the kings of the coastland across the sea;<sup>23</sup>Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who cut the corners of their hair;<sup>24</sup>all the kings of Arabia and all the kings of the mixed tribes who dwell in the desert;<sup>25</sup>all the kings of Zimri, all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of Media;<sup>26</sup>all the kings of the north, far and near, one after another, and all the kingdoms of the world that are on the face of the earth. You shall not go unpunished, for I am summoning a sword against all the inhabitants of the earth, declares the LORD of hosts.'<sup>30</sup>"You, therefore, shall prophesy against them all these words, and say to them: "'The LORD will roar from on high, and from his holy habitation utter his voice; he will roar mightily against his fold, and shout, like those who tread grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth.<sup>31</sup>The clamor will resound to the ends of the earth, for the LORD has an indictment against the nations; he is entering into judgment with all flesh, and the wicked he will put to the sword, declares the LORD.'<sup>32</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: Behold, disaster is going forth from nation to nation, and a great tempest is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth!<sup>33</sup>"And those pierced by the LORD on that day shall extend from one end of the earth to the other. verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s patience is measured in messengers, and Judah has refused them all. In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the year Babylon took control of the region, Jeremiah looks back over twenty-three years of preaching that met no response (vv. 1–3). He was not alone: God had persistently sent prophet after prophet with one simple message, turn from evil, do not serve other gods, and you may stay in the land, with the promise, “Then I will do you no harm” (vv. 4–6). The verdict is short: they did not listen, and the harm they chose is their own (v. 7). The disaster that follows was avoidable to the end.
verseByVerse.theology: Twenty-three years of preaching, summarised by the prophet himself in one word: unheard.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah (that was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon), which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem: "For twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, to this day, the word of the LORD has come to me, and I have spoken persistently to you, but you have not listened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In 605 BC, the year Babylon became master of the world, Jeremiah looks back on twenty-three years of faithful preaching that no one heeded.

In the fourth year of Jehoiakim. This is the year Babylon beat Egypt at Carchemish (46:2) and the year of the scroll in chapter 36. The world has just changed shape, and Jeremiah has been preaching into it for over two decades.

The first year of Nebuchadnezzar. The double date marks a shift in whose calendar counts: Judah’s years are now measured beside Babylon’s. In these years Nebuchadnezzar came against Jerusalem and took the first captives, among them a young man named Daniel. Daniel’s book dates it “In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim” (Daniel 1:1), probably counting the Babylonian way, which did not number a king’s first part-year. While Jeremiah preached this sermon, the exile had already begun.

For twenty-three years … you have not listened. He counts from his call in Josiah’s thirteenth year (1:2) to this day, and sums up the whole period in one clause. Twenty-three years of costly, unpopular work with no visible result: if ministry is measured by response, this is a failed career, and in chapter 20 the man himself would have said so. What God asked of him was faithfulness, and he was persistent for as long as it took. Paul names the only measure that applies: “it is required of stewards that they be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2). Not successful, not popular, not effective by any visible count.

Measured by the numbers. We live under dashboards: sales, followers, grades, attendance, steps. The historian Jerry Muller, in The Tyranny of Metrics (2018), argued that when counting becomes the goal, people work for the number instead of the thing it was meant to measure, and the work quietly bends out of shape. Churches feel this as much as companies. By any dashboard Jeremiah’s ministry was a disaster, and if our worth is our output, a life like his is wasted, and so, in our worst moments, are ours. Scripture’s measure is not lower but higher, because it sees what numbers cannot. Jesus’ own ministry ended, by the count, with a handful of women at a cross and his friends in hiding; the Father’s verdict on that work was resurrection. Those joined to him are measured by the same kind of judgment, given by grace: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little” (Matthew 25:21).

verseByVerse.quote: You have neither listened nor inclined your ears to hear, although the LORD persistently sent to you all his servants the prophets, saying, 'Turn now, every one of you, from his evil way and evil deeds, and dwell upon the land that the LORD has given to you and your fathers from of old and forever. Do not go after other gods to serve and worship them, or provoke me to anger with the work of your hands. Then I will do you no harm.' Yet you have not listened to me, declares the LORD, that you might provoke me to anger with the work of your hands to your own harm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For centuries God sent prophet after prophet with one simple offer, turn and stay, and the people refused it to their own harm.

All his servants the prophets. Jeremiah was not alone: God persistently sent prophets over centuries (7:25). The same word is used of God’s sending and of Jeremiah’s speaking. Patience is measured here in messengers.

Turn now, every one of you. The whole prophetic message in three sentences: turn, do not serve other gods, and you may stay in the land. The offer at the end is startling in its simplicity: “Then I will do you no harm.” It is mercy held out, not a price set. Everything that follows in this chapter was avoidable to the last week.

To your own harm. As in 7:19, those who provoke God hurt themselves, not him. Sin presents itself as gain and always sends its bill to the sinner.

The message outlived them. After the exile, Zechariah opened his ministry by quoting it to the returning generation: “Do not be like your fathers, to whom the former prophets cried out, ‘Thus says the LORD of hosts, Return from your evil ways and from your evil deeds.’ But they did not hear or pay attention to me” (Zechariah 1:4). The sermon Judah refused became the warning its grandchildren were raised on.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because Judah would not listen, God will send for Babylon, and he will also set a limit to Babylon. He summons Nebuchadnezzar, calling him “my servant”, and pronounces over his own land the sentence of destruction once spoken over Canaan (vv. 8–9). The ordinary sounds of home, the wedding, the mill and the lamp, will fall silent, and the nations will serve Babylon seventy years (vv. 10–11). Then the servant will be judged for its own iniquity, by everything written in this book against the nations, and enslaved in turn (vv. 12–14). History is neither out of control nor endless.
verseByVerse.theology: The empire that executes the judgment is called God's servant, and is given a term that expires.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts: Because you have not obeyed my words, behold, I will send for all the tribes of the north, declares the LORD, and for Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring them against this land and its inhabitants, and against all these surrounding nations. I will devote them to destruction, and make them a horror, a hissing, and an everlasting desolation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself summons Babylon against his people, calls its pagan king “my servant”, and hands Judah over to the destruction once pronounced on Canaan.

I will send for all the tribes of the north. God summons the invader like a master calling a servant into the room. The “north” is the direction from which the enemy of chapter 1 was always coming (1:13–15).

Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant. A pagan emperor who worshipped Marduk and will burn God’s temple is called God’s servant. He does not know it or intend it, and he will be judged for how he does it (v. 12), yet he is the instrument in God’s hand. That is a hard and necessary doctrine: God governs the powers that hurt his people. It does not make their cruelty less guilty, but it does mean history is not out of control.

I will devote them to destruction. One phrase turns the conquest inside out. The Hebrew word (herem) means handing something over wholly to God, usually for destruction, as a judgment from which no one may profit. It was spoken over Jericho: “And the city and all that is within it shall be devoted to the LORD for destruction” (Joshua 6:17). Now it is pronounced over Israel’s own land. The people who entered Canaan under that word will leave it under the same word.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, I will banish from them the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the grinding of the millstones and the light of the lamp. This whole land shall become a ruin and a waste, and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment will silence the ordinary sounds of home, and it will last seventy years: long enough that most will never return, but with an end set by God.

The voice of mirth. The refrain of 7:34 and 16:9 returns with two homely details added: the sound of the hand-mill grinding grain at dawn (see millstone), and the little oil lamp left burning at night in every house. Breakfast being made, a light left on: that is what judgment takes away, not first the palaces and armies, but the kitchen and the lamp.

The fall of the last Babylon. John hears this list again, almost item for item, at the fall of the world city that set itself against God: “the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more, and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more” (Revelation 18:22–23). What Jerusalem suffered becomes the pattern for the judgment of the world.

Seventy years. The number that shaped the next century of faith is a sentence with an end date. Daniel was reading this verse in Babylon when he understood that the time was nearly up and began to pray (Daniel 9:2), and the Chronicler says the land kept its Sabbaths “to fulfill seventy years” (2 Chronicles 36:21). God times his judgments, and he does not forget the people under them. For anyone in a season that seems to have no end, the One who set the length of the night has also set the morning.

Seventy weeks. Daniel’s prayer over this number was answered by stretching it: “Seventy weeks” of years, leading to “an anointed one” (Daniel 9:24–26). This commentary reads that prophecy as fulfilled in Christ’s first coming (see the notes on Daniel 9), who brought the deeper return from exile that Babylon’s fall only began. The details are debated; the direction is not.

How are the seventy years counted? The dates are approximate, and careful readers count in more than one way. From Babylon’s rise over the region (about 609–605 BC) to its fall to Cyrus in 539 BC is roughly seventy years, which fits the wording here: “these nations shall serve the king of Babylon”. From the first deportation (605 BC) to the first return (about 538 BC) is nearer sixty-seven. From the temple’s burning (586 BC) to its rebuilding (516 BC) is almost exactly seventy (compare Zechariah 1:12). Seventy is also the span of a human life (Psalm 90:10), so the number may be partly a round one: long enough that most who went would not come back.
verseByVerse.note: The Chronicler ties the seventy years to the Sabbath years the land had been denied (2 Chr 36:21), echoing the warning of Leviticus 26:34-35.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after seventy years are completed, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their iniquity, declares the LORD, making the land an everlasting waste. I will bring upon that land all the words that I have uttered against it, everything written in this book, which Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the seventy years are over, God will judge Babylon too, for being useful to God is no excuse for cruelty.

I will punish the king of Babylon. The servant is judged too. Babylon’s brutality was freely chosen, and no one may plead that he was only the rod in God’s hand; he answers for the blows he chose to strike. The point is made in 10:25 and worked out at length in chapters 50 and 51.

Everything written in this book. A glimpse of the book itself: there is a written collection, and God treats what is written in it as what he will do. The scroll is not a record of opinions but a list of what God has decided. The phrase which Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations points to the oracles against Egypt, Moab, Edom, Babylon and the rest, gathered near the book’s end (chapters 46–51), and treats them as already on file.

Textual note. In the shorter ancient Greek form of Jeremiah (see the introduction), the oracles against the nations stand here, straight after “everything written in this book”, instead of near the end of the book (chapters 46–51). English Bibles follow the Hebrew order, and the message is the same in both.

verseByVerse.quote: For many nations and great kings shall make slaves even of them, and I will recompense them according to their deeds and the work of their hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The empire that enslaved nations will itself be enslaved, repaid by the one standard God uses for everyone.

According to their deeds. The phrase that has run through the book about Judah, repaid according to the work of their hands, now applies to the empire. God has one standard, and Paul states it as the rule of the final judgment: “He will render to each one according to his works” (Romans 2:6).

Many nations and great kings. It happened as described. On the night Babylon fell, the writing on the wall was read to its king: “your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians” (Daniel 5:28). The empire that enslaved nations was handed to others by the same God who had handed nations to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–29 — The Cup of the Wine of Wrath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s wrath is a cup that every nation must drink, and it is handed first to his own city. Jeremiah takes the cup of the wine of wrath from the LORD’s hand and carries it, in vision, to the nations (vv. 15–17). The order is the message: Jerusalem and Judah first, then Egypt, the Philistine cities, Edom, Moab and Ammon, the Phoenician ports, the desert tribes and the eastern empires, and Babylon last of all (vv. 18–26). Any who refuse are told, “You must drink!” (vv. 27–28). The reason is unanswerable: if God begins with the city called by his name, no one else will go unpunished (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: God's own city drinks first, which settles for ever the question of whether he judges by favouritism.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus the LORD, the God of Israel, said to me: "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it. They shall drink and stagger and be crazed because of the sword that I am sending among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s judgment is pictured as a cup of strong wine that the nations must drink, the cup Jesus would one day take from his Father’s hand.

This cup of the wine of wrath. A new vision, and an image with a long future in Scripture. Everyone knows what strong drink does: it takes away balance, judgment and dignity, and the drinker cannot stop what happens next. God’s wrath is pictured not as a fit of temper but as a measured draught a nation must drink to the bottom. Whether Jeremiah carried a real cup or saw this only in vision, the text does not say; either way the nations “drink” it in the sword (v. 16).

The cup through Scripture. “For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed”, and “all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs” (Psalm 75:8). Isaiah speaks of Jerusalem having drunk “the cup of staggering” (Isaiah 51:17). Habakkuk warns Babylon, “The cup in the LORD’s right hand will come around to you” (Habakkuk 2:16). Revelation says the worshipper of the beast “will drink the wine of God’s wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger” (Revelation 14:10).

Let this cup pass from me. Then, in a garden, a man knelt and prayed, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). He knew exactly which cup it was, and he drank it to the dregs so that his people would never have to.

verseByVerse.quote: So I took the cup from the LORD's hand, and made all the nations to whom the LORD sent me drink it: Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, its kings and officials, to make them a desolation and a waste, a hissing and a curse, as at this day;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cup goes first to Jerusalem, and the prophet who loved the city has to hand it to his own people.

Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. The order of the list is itself the message. Jerusalem drinks first: not Egypt, not Babylon, but the city with the temple in it (v. 29).

As at this day. The phrase suggests the words were written down when the ruin had already begun, by the prophet or his scribe, as the curse was visibly coming true.

To his own city first. Jeremiah had to carry the cup to his neighbours, his relatives and the king he served under, and there is no sign that he took any pleasure in it. The man who wept over Jerusalem was the one told to hand it the cup, as a greater prophet would one day weep over the same city while announcing its fall (Luke 19:41–44).

verseByVerse.quote: Pharaoh king of Egypt, his servants, his officials, all his people, and all the mixed tribes among them; all the kings of the land of Uz and all the kings of the land of the Philistines (Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod); Edom, Moab, and the sons of Ammon; all the kings of Tyre, all the kings of Sidon, and the kings of the coastland across the sea; Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who cut the corners of their hair; all the kings of Arabia and all the kings of the mixed tribes who dwell in the desert; all the kings of Zimri, all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of Media; all the kings of the north, far and near, one after another, and all the kingdoms of the world that are on the face of the earth. And after them the king of Babylon shall drink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No nation, region or religion is beyond the reach of God’s judgment, and mighty Babylon, called here by a code name, drinks last.

The nations in rings. The list moves outward from Judah: Egypt to the south, the Philistine cities on the coast, Israel’s relatives east of the Jordan (Edom, Moab and Ammon), the Phoenician ports of Tyre and Sidon, the desert tribes of Arabia, the eastern empires of Elam and Media, and finally “all the kingdoms of the world that are on the face of the earth”.

The land of Uz. Two names stand out. The land of Uz is where Job lived (Job 1:1): the land of the righteous sufferer is under the same cup. And all who cut the corners of their hair are desert peoples marked by a custom Israel was forbidden (Leviticus 19:27; compare 9:26). No culture or region is outside this sentence. Paul’s summary is the same: “so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God” (Romans 3:19).

After them the king of Babylon shall drink. Babylon comes last. The Hebrew calls it Sheshach, a code name made by an ancient letter cipher. At the height of its power, the empire handing the cup to everyone else has its name written in cipher and placed at the end of the queue.

Uncertain wording. Zimri (v. 25) is not otherwise known as a nation. Some link it with Zimran, one of Abraham’s sons by Keturah (Genesis 25:2), whose descendants lived in Arabia; others suspect a coded name like Sheshach. Placed beside Elam and Media, it was evidently a people of the east. The point is unaffected: every king on earth drinks.
verseByVerse.note: Sheshach is formed by an ancient letter cipher that swaps the alphabet end for end, so that the consonants of Babel become those of Sheshach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink, be drunk and vomit, fall and rise no more, because of the sword that I am sending among you.' "And if they refuse to accept the cup from your hand to drink, then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts: You must drink!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proud empires end up like drunks in the street, and refusing the cup is not an option.

Drink, be drunk and vomit. The language is deliberately undignified; Scripture strips the glamour off power on purpose. Empires that thought themselves eternal are pictured as a drunk in the street, sick, on the ground, unable to get up. Kingdoms whose armies emptied cities end the verse in their own vomit.

You must drink! Refusal is anticipated and overruled. Nobody escapes God’s judgment by declining to acknowledge it, any more than a man escapes a court by refusing the summons.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, I begin to work disaster at the city that is called by my name, and shall you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, for I am summoning a sword against all the inhabitants of the earth, declares the LORD of hosts.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment begins with the people who bear God’s name, so no one else can hope to escape it.

At the city that is called by my name. Here is the logic of the whole chapter, and it runs the way people least expect: privilege brings judgment first. If God does not spare the place where he put his own name, on what basis would anyone else be spared? Amos said it: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you” (Amos 3:2). Peter says it to the church: “For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God?” (1 Peter 4:17).

Responsibility, not immunity. Closeness to God is not immunity. It is responsibility, and it means the searchlight starts at home: with the church before the culture, and with my own heart before my neighbour’s.

Mercy begins there too. Read the other way, the argument is the church’s hope. If judgment begins at God’s house, so does mercy. The one who drank the cup did it outside the walls of that same city, and it was from Jerusalem that forgiveness was first preached to the nations (Luke 24:47).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–38 — The LORD Will Roar from on High
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The judgment of Judah opens out into the judgment of the world, and those who led the flock have nowhere to hide. The LORD roars like a lion from his holy habitation and shouts like a man treading grapes, for he has a legal case against the nations and enters into judgment with all flesh (vv. 30–31). Disaster passes from nation to nation like a storm, and the slain lie unburied across the earth (vv. 32–33). The shepherds, the kings and rulers, are told to wail and roll in ashes, for there is no refuge left and their peaceful pastures are laid waste by the lion that has left its lair (vv. 34–38).
verseByVerse.theology: The local catastrophe opens out into a universal one: God has a case against the whole world.

verseByVerse.quote: "You, therefore, shall prophesy against them all these words, and say to them: "'The LORD will roar from on high, and from his holy habitation utter his voice; he will roar mightily against his fold, and shout, like those who tread grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth. The clamor will resound to the ends of the earth, for the LORD has an indictment against the nations; he is entering into judgment with all flesh, and the wicked he will put to the sword, declares the LORD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of Judah is the judge of the whole earth, and he comes against all flesh with a lion’s roar and a legal case.

The LORD will roar from on high. Two sounds. The first is a lion’s roar, the way prophets describe God going out to judgment. The roar is borrowed from Amos: “The LORD roars from Zion and utters his voice from Jerusalem; the pastures of the shepherds mourn” (Amos 1:2). But here it roars first against his fold, and the shepherds’ pastures mourn again at the end of this chapter (vv. 36–37).

Like those who tread grapes. The second sound is stranger and more chilling. The shout of men treading grapes in the winepress was a work song, the noise of harvest celebration. God is pictured shouting it over the nations, and what is being crushed is not fruit. Revelation takes the image to its end: the angel gathers the grape harvest of the earth “and threw it into the great winepress of the wrath of God” (Revelation 14:19).

The LORD has an indictment against the nations. Then a legal word: God has a case with charges. This is not rage but a court sitting, and the defendant is all flesh. Everything local in the book, a small kingdom, a siege, a temple, opens here into something universal. Isaiah uses the same courtroom language for the last day: “For by fire will the LORD enter into judgment, and by his sword, with all flesh; and those slain by the LORD shall be many” (Isaiah 66:16). What Jeremiah announces over the nations of his day is a foretaste of that final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: Behold, disaster is going forth from nation to nation, and a great tempest is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth! "And those pierced by the LORD on that day shall extend from one end of the earth to the other. They shall not be lamented, or gathered, or buried; they shall be dung on the surface of the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment sweeps across the earth like a storm, and the dead lie unmourned and unburied.

Disaster is going forth from nation to nation. Disaster spreads like weather, moving from country to country, a great tempest stirred up from the ends of the earth.

They shall not be lamented. The phrase from 8:2 and 16:4 returns on a global scale, with the same three denials: no mourning, no gathering, no burial. The Bible refuses to make judgment sound tidy, and it is this horror that makes the gospel’s rescue so great.

verseByVerse.quote: "Wail, you shepherds, and cry out, and roll in ashes, you lords of the flock, for the days of your slaughter and dispersion have come, and you shall fall like a choice vessel. No refuge will remain for the shepherds, nor escape for the lords of the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rulers who fed on the flock are told to mourn for themselves, for their refuges and escape routes have run out.

Wail, you shepherds. The shepherds of chapter 23, the kings and leaders, are now told to mourn for themselves. Roll in ashes is the grief of people with nothing left.

You shall fall like a choice vessel. The comparison recalls the broken flask of chapter 19. Not a cheap pot but a good one, the sort a household is proud of, and it shatters exactly the same way. Those who had refuges and escape routes, position, money and foreign contacts, find they have run out.

I will rescue my sheep. Ezekiel heard God say the same to the same class of men, and add a promise: “Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep at their hand”, and “I will rescue my sheep from their mouths” (Ezekiel 34:10). When the shepherds fall, the sheep are not abandoned. God takes the flock back into his own hands, and later in that chapter promises to set over it one shepherd, “my servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23): Jesus, the good shepherd.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice—the cry of the shepherds, and the wail of the lords of the flock! For the LORD is laying waste their pasture, and the peaceful folds are devastated because of the fierce anger of the LORD. Like a lion he has left his lair, for their land has become a waste because of the sword of the oppressor, and because of his fierce anger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with the cry of shepherds whose peaceful pastures are destroyed, as God comes out like a lion through the swords of an invading army.

The peaceful folds are devastated. You hear it before you see it: a voice, a cry, a wail. What is destroyed is named with an aching phrase, the peaceful folds, the quiet places where sheep were safe. The lion is out of the thicket, as in 4:7, and two causes are named in one breath: the sword of the oppressor and his fierce anger. A human army and God’s anger are at work in one event, which is how this whole book reads history.

A shepherd who stood between. The chapter ends with shepherds who have no refuge and a flock with no fold. The gospel does not answer that the roar was empty, but that it fell on a shepherd who stood between it and the sheep: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

Textual note. Most Hebrew manuscripts read the anger of the oppressor; some read the sword of the oppressor, the phrase used in 46:16 and 50:16, and the ESV follows them. Either way the oppressor is Babylon, and behind it the fierce anger of the LORD.

25.title: Seventy Years and the Cup of Wrath
25.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 25 closes the first great part of the book, the long case against Judah that began in chapter 2. After the Zedekiah chapters (21–24) it steps back to 605 BC, the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the year Babylon beat Egypt at Carchemish and became master of the region (see the introduction). It is the hinge between the prophet’s warnings and the story of his conflicts that follows.

The message. God’s patience is long, but it has an end, and so does his judgment. Judah refused twenty-three years of warning, so Babylon will come as God’s servant, for seventy years and no longer. Yet the God of Judah is the judge of all the earth: the cup of his wrath passes from Jerusalem to every nation, and Babylon drinks last. Nobody is exempt, and those nearest to God are judged first.

Why it was said. Judah treated Babylon as a political problem to be managed, and the small kingdoms around it thought themselves masters of their own fate. In the year the world changed shape, God tells them who has changed it, why, and for how long.

How the chapter makes its case. Jeremiah sums up twenty-three years of his own preaching and centuries of prophets: the call was always to turn, and Judah would not listen (vv. 1–7). So God will send for Nebuchadnezzar, “my servant”, silence the land’s joy and give the nations to Babylon for seventy years, after which Babylon itself will be repaid (vv. 8–14). Then Jeremiah is handed the cup of the wine of wrath: Jerusalem drinks first, the kingdoms around it after, and Babylon last, and none may refuse (vv. 15–29). Finally the LORD roars from on high with an indictment against all flesh, and the shepherds are told to wail, for no refuge is left (vv. 30–38).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the cup. The chapter holds no promise of a Messiah, but it gives the image Jesus took for his own death. In Gethsemane he prayed, “let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39), and he knew which cup he meant: the wrath every nation in this list must drink. He drank it so that those who trust him never will. The chapter also exposes the need: “all flesh” stands under indictment, Israel first (v. 31; Romans 3:19). And the seventy years point forward by promise, for Daniel read them and was told of a greater deliverance (Daniel 9:2, 24–26).

For us. Faithfulness, not visible success, is what God asks of his servants. Judgment begins at the household of God, so the church examines itself before it points at the world. God sets limits to the dark seasons of his people. And there is a cup none of us could drink, which Christ has already drained.
25.theology:
The chapter holds together three truths that people find hard to keep together. God governs even the empires that punish his people, and still holds them answerable for their cruelty (vv. 9, 12-14). His judgments are timed and limited, which gave the exiles something to hold on to (v. 11). And judgment begins with those nearest to him (v. 29), because nearness to God is responsibility, not immunity.

Over all of it stands the cup of wrath (vv. 15-28), the cup that Christ asked might pass from him in Gethsemane and then drank for his people.
25.examples:
A minister whose life's work looks fruitless may take heart from a prophet whose twenty-three years were summed up as unheard, and who was still counted faithful.

Judgment, in this chapter, takes away first not palaces but the millstone at dawn and the lamp at night; and the cup handed round the nations is the one Christ accepted in Gethsemane and drained at the cross.

keyVerse.quote: Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it.
keyVerse.note: The cup holds the chapter together: Judah’s judgment opens into the judgment of every nation, starting with the city called by God’s name and ending with Babylon. It is also the image Jesus took for his own death, when he asked in Gethsemane that “this cup” might pass from him and then drank it for his people.

25.reflection:
Jeremiah preached for twenty-three years and “you have not listened” (v. 3). How does 1 Corinthians 4:2 change the way we measure our own service, and where are we tempted to measure ourselves by visible results?

God calls Nebuchadnezzar “my servant” (v. 9) and then judges him for his cruelty (v. 12). How does it help to know that God rules even the powers that hurt his people, without excusing them?

Judgment begins “at the city that is called by my name” (v. 29; compare 1 Peter 4:17). What would it look like for our church, and for each of us, to let the searchlight start at home?

Read Matthew 26:39 beside verses 15–16. What does it mean to you that Jesus took this cup and drank it, and how should it shape the way we speak to others about God’s judgment?

And all the people gathered around Jeremiah in the house of the LORD.<sup>10</sup>When the officials of Judah heard these things, they came up from the king's house to the house of the LORD and took their seat in the entry of the New Gate of the house of the LORD.<sup>11</sup>Then the priests and the prophets said to the officials and to all the people, "This man deserves the sentence of death, because he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your own ears."<sup>12</sup>Then Jeremiah spoke to all the officials and all the people, saying, "The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and this city all the words you have heard.<sup>13</sup>Now therefore mend your ways and your deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God, and the LORD will relent of the disaster that he has pronounced against you.<sup>14</sup>But as for me, behold, I am in your hands. Do with me as seems good and right to you.<sup>15</sup>Only know for certain that if you put me to death, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves and upon this city and its inhabitants, for in truth the LORD sent me to you to speak all these words in your ears."<sup>16</sup>Then the officials and all the people said to the priests and the prophets, "This man does not deserve the sentence of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God."<sup>17</sup>And certain of the elders of the land arose and spoke to all the assembled people, saying,<sup>18</sup>"Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and said to all the people of Judah: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, "'Zion shall be plowed as a field; Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the house a wooded height.'<sup>19</sup>Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him to death? Did he not fear the LORD and entreat the favor of the LORD, and did not the LORD relent of the disaster that he had pronounced against them? But we are about to bring great disaster upon ourselves."<sup>20</sup>There was another man who prophesied in the name of the LORD, Uriah the son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim. He prophesied against this city and against this land in words like those of Jeremiah.<sup>21</sup>And when King Jehoiakim, with all his warriors and all the officials, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death. But when Uriah heard of it, he was afraid and fled and escaped to Egypt.<sup>22</sup>Then King Jehoiakim sent to Egypt certain men, Elnathan the son of Achbor and others with him,<sup>23</sup>and they took Uriah from Egypt and brought him to King Jehoiakim, who struck him down with the sword and dumped his dead body into the burial place of the common people.<sup>24</sup>But the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah so that he was not given over to the people to be put to death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Do Not Hold Back a Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends his prophet to say everything he is given, because the warning itself is mercy. At the start of Jehoiakim’s reign, with crowds from every town in Judah filling the temple court, Jeremiah is told not to hold back a word (vv. 1–2). The aim is not to condemn but to rescue: “It may be they will listen”, and if they turn, God will relent of the disaster (v. 3). But if they will not listen to his law and his prophets, he will make this house like Shiloh, the first sanctuary he let fall into ruins, and Jerusalem a curse among the nations instead of a blessing (vv. 4–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The sermon that could save them is the sermon that will cost the preacher his life.

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the LORD: "Thus says the LORD: Stand in the court of the LORD's house, and speak to all the cities of Judah that come to worship in the house of the LORD all the words that I command you to speak to them; do not hold back a word. It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster that I intend to do to them because of their evil deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends Jeremiah to the crowded temple with orders to say everything, because the warning is God’s own offer of mercy.

In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim. About 609 BC. Josiah is dead, killed at Megiddo, and his son Jehoiakim is on the throne. The reform that cleaned out the shrines is unravelling. Jeremiah is sent into the temple courtyard at a festival season, when worshippers from every town in Judah are streaming in. This is the occasion of the temple sermon of chapter 7.

Do not hold back a word. This is the clause that makes the chapter dangerous. God knows which sentences his preacher will want to leave out. It is always possible to give a congregation ninety per cent of a message and keep back the ten that would cost something; nobody is told what was cut, and the hard line simply does not get said.

It may be they will listen. Here is why the words must not be trimmed. The sermon is not a formality before a verdict already decided; it is God’s own attempt to avoid the verdict, on the terms he gave at the potter’s house: the moment a nation turns, he relents of the disaster (18:7–8). The trimmed sermon is the cruel one, because it withholds the very warning that could have saved them.

Does God change his mind? “God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind” (Numbers 23:19). Scripture says he “relents” to describe his real response to repentance in human terms: his warnings are real, and when people turn, he does what he always purposed to do for those who turn (18:7–10). He is not surprised or moved like a man; his unchanging character is the very reason he spares the penitent.
verseByVerse.note: This chapter tells what happened after the temple sermon recorded in chapter 7.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: If you will not listen to me, to walk in my law that I have set before you, and to listen to the words of my servants the prophets whom I send to you urgently, though you have not listened, then I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse for all the nations of the earth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the people refuse God’s word, he will let his own temple fall as he once let Shiloh fall, for he is not the prisoner of any building.

I will make this house like Shiloh. One word does the damage, and it is a place name. Shiloh was where the tabernacle stood for generations: “Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first” (7:12). It was no rival or pagan shrine but the place God himself had chosen. Then Israel carried the ark into battle as a lucky charm, and the day ended with thirty thousand dead and the news that “the ark of God was captured” (1 Samuel 4:11). A dying mother named her baby Ichabod and said, “The glory has departed from Israel” (1 Samuel 4:22). By Jeremiah’s day Shiloh was a ruin people could walk to and look at.

Not weak, but free. The claim is not that God is weak but that he is free. He is not a tenant of any building, and he has already once let his own house be levelled rather than let his name be used as a charm by people who would not obey him.

A curse for all the nations of the earth. The promise to Abraham is reversed. Through his family all the nations were to be blessed (Genesis 12:3); now Jerusalem becomes a byword for a curse. Privilege abused does not merely lose its blessing. It turns into a curse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — You Shall Die: The Prophet on Trial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The preacher is put on trial, and he uses the trial to preach again. The priests, the prophets and the people seize Jeremiah as soon as he finishes and demand his death, quoting his words exactly (vv. 7–9). The royal officials come up from the palace and sit as a court in the New Gate, and the religious leaders present their case: he has prophesied against this city (vv. 10–11). Jeremiah retracts nothing. He says again that the LORD sent him, calls his judges to mend their ways while God may still relent, puts himself in their hands, and warns them that killing him would bring innocent blood on the city (vv. 12–15).
verseByVerse.theology: He answers a death sentence by offering his judges the mercy they are refusing.

verseByVerse.quote: The priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the LORD. And when Jeremiah had finished speaking all that the LORD had commanded him to speak to all the people, then the priests and the prophets and all the people laid hold of him, saying, "You shall die! Why have you prophesied in the name of the LORD, saying, 'This house shall be like Shiloh, and this city shall be desolate, without inhabitant'?" And all the people gathered around Jeremiah in the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The religious leaders want the preacher dead for exactly what he said, and they seize him in the house of God.

The priests and the prophets. Consider who seizes him. Not idolaters or a street mob, but the clergy: men whose livelihood was bound up with the building he had said could fall, laying hands on God’s messenger inside it. Nothing in this scene is irreligious. It is a religious riot, and the sentence, “You shall die!”, comes before he is off the step.

They quote him correctly. That detail removes the usual excuse. This was not a misunderstanding to be cleared up with a better explanation; they heard him exactly and wanted him dead for what he had actually said. Offence at the message is not always a failure of communication.

Another trial. Six centuries later two witnesses would stand in another trial and repeat another saying about the temple: “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to rebuild it in three days’” (Matthew 26:61). In this city, a word against the house is the charge that gets a prophet killed.

verseByVerse.quote: When the officials of Judah heard these things, they came up from the king's house to the house of the LORD and took their seat in the entry of the New Gate of the house of the LORD. Then the priests and the prophets said to the officials and to all the people, "This man deserves the sentence of death, because he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your own ears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God protects his prophet through ordinary justice: the officials turn a lynching into a trial, though the only evidence is the sermon itself.

When the officials of Judah heard. The civil officials walk up from the palace and take their seats in the gateway where cases were heard, and the mob has to become a prosecution. That is a mercy, and it comes in an ordinary way, through men doing their jobs properly.

As you have heard with your own ears. The charge is capital and the evidence is the sermon. No witnesses are needed, because everyone heard it. The prosecution’s whole case is that the defendant said what God told him to say.

No lie needed. Set that beside the other trial, where the council “were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death” (Matthew 26:59), and could not find any that agreed. Jeremiah’s accusers needed no lies; Jesus’ judges could not convict him without them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah spoke to all the officials and all the people, saying, "The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and this city all the words you have heard. Now therefore mend your ways and your deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God, and the LORD will relent of the disaster that he has pronounced against you. But as for me, behold, I am in your hands. Do with me as seems good and right to you. Only know for certain that if you put me to death, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves and upon this city and its inhabitants, for in truth the LORD sent me to you to speak all these words in your ears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On trial for his life, Jeremiah repeats the message, offers his judges mercy, entrusts himself to them and warns them of innocent blood.

The LORD sent me. His defence opens by repeating the offence. No softening, no plea of being quoted out of context: he says it again before the court with his life at stake.

Mend your ways and your deeds. Then, astonishingly, he preaches to his judges and offers them the way out. He is not fighting for an acquittal; he is still doing the job he was arrested for. A man with nothing left to protect can afford to love his judges.

Behold, I am in your hands. No bargaining and no bravado. He neither threatens them with God nor pleads, but simply puts himself in their hands. That composure is not a matter of temperament; it comes from being certain who sent him. Christ promised the same help to his witnesses on trial: the Spirit of their Father would speak through them (Matthew 10:19–20).

Innocent blood. Even the warning is for their sake, not his, and another court would one day hear it and wave it away. A governor washed his hands and said, “I am innocent of this man’s blood; see to it yourselves”, and the crowd answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!” (Matthew 27:24–25). Jeremiah’s judges heeded the warning. The others took the blood, and the mercy of God is that the blood they called down on themselves is the only blood in the world that could wash them. Peter preached exactly that to the same city seven weeks later (Acts 2:36–38).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The court acquits the prophet on the right ground: he has spoken in the name of the LORD (v. 16). Then some of the elders give the verdict weight from history. A century earlier Micah of Moresheth had said Zion would be ploughed like a field, and King Hezekiah did not kill him but feared the LORD and sought his favour, and God relented (vv. 17–19). The precedent cuts both ways: it shows how to respond to a hard word, and it warns that to silence this prophet would be to bring disaster on themselves. Scripture remembered in time saves a life.
verseByVerse.theology: Someone in the room had read the prophets and could remember how a king ought to answer one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officials and all the people said to the priests and the prophets, "This man does not deserve the sentence of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God." And certain of the elders of the land arose and spoke to all the assembled people, saying, "Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and said to all the people of Judah: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, "'Zion shall be plowed as a field; Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins, and the mountain of the house a wooded height.' Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him to death? Did he not fear the LORD and entreat the favor of the LORD, and did not the LORD relent of the disaster that he had pronounced against them? But we are about to bring great disaster upon ourselves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The court acquits Jeremiah because he spoke in God’s name, and the elders confirm it from Scripture: King Hezekiah once heeded a word like this, and the city was spared.

This man does not deserve the sentence of death. The verdict turns on the right test: has he spoken in the name of the LORD? Not whether he is popular, good for morale or kind to the city’s confidence.

Micah of Moresheth prophesied. The elders save his life with a quotation. A century earlier a country prophet, Micah, had said the same unthinkable thing about the same city, and his words were on record; we still read them at Micah 3:12. Someone in that assembly knew his Scriptures well enough to see that the intolerable sermon had a precedent. This is one of the rare places where one prophet is quoted by name in another’s book.

The verse before it. The verse just before names the confidence Micah was demolishing: “Is not the LORD in the midst of us? No disaster shall come upon us” (Micah 3:11). That was the belief in the room in Jeremiah’s day too. It had learned nothing in a century.

Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him to death? Three questions and a conclusion that applies the old case to the hearers. Hezekiah heard his city sentenced to rubble and sought God’s face, and the city stood. Kill this preacher, the elders say, and the disaster we fear is one we will have brought on ourselves.

How to hear a hard word. Hezekiah is the model for every hearer: not to silence the messenger, but to fear the LORD and seek his favour. Repentance is always the right response to a true warning, and it is never too late while God is still speaking.
verseByVerse.note: It is rare for one prophet to be quoted by name in another prophet's book; here a sermon from Micah 3:12 saves a man's life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–24 — Uriah, and the Hand of Ahikam
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter refuses a tidy ending. Uriah of Kiriath-jearim preached the same message as Jeremiah, fled to Egypt in fear, and was brought back by the king’s men, executed and thrown into a common grave (vv. 20–23). Jeremiah survives, not because he was more faithful, but because one man, Ahikam son of Shaphan, stood with him (v. 24). God’s servants are not promised safety, and God often protects them through ordinary people willing to pay a price. The last words, that Jeremiah was not given over to be killed, leave room for one who would be.
verseByVerse.theology: Two faithful prophets, one buried in a common grave and one spared, and God was not absent from either.

verseByVerse.quote: There was another man who prophesied in the name of the LORD, Uriah the son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim. He prophesied against this city and against this land in words like those of Jeremiah. And when King Jehoiakim, with all his warriors and all the officials, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death. But when Uriah heard of it, he was afraid and fled and escaped to Egypt. Then King Jehoiakim sent to Egypt certain men, Elnathan the son of Achbor and others with him, and they took Uriah from Egypt and brought him to King Jehoiakim, who struck him down with the sword and dumped his dead body into the burial place of the common people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another prophet who preached the same word was hunted down and killed, for faithfulness is not a guarantee of survival.

There was another man. The narrator adds a second case, and it comforts nobody. Uriah came from Kiriath-jearim, the town where the ark had once rested for twenty years (1 Samuel 7:1–2).

He was afraid and fled. Uriah preached the same message and ran for his life. He was afraid is not written as an accusation. Jeremiah himself had begged to stop (20:9), and the man who never bolted had no room to despise the man who did.

King Jehoiakim sent to Egypt. Jehoiakim would not spend an hour listening to a prophet, but he would fund an expedition to silence one. He could reach into Egypt because Pharaoh Neco had put him on the throne (2 Kings 23:34); a vassal could probably ask his overlord to hand back a fugitive. The body went into the burial place of the common people, a last insult to a man of God. Strikingly, the officer sent, Elnathan son of Achbor, appears again in 36:25 urging the king not to burn Jeremiah’s scroll: people are rarely all one thing.

Why this paragraph is here. Because the Bible refuses to sell faithfulness as a survival strategy. Two men preached the same word from the same God in the same decade. One was acquitted and one was murdered, and the difference was not the quality of their obedience. Some “escaped the edge of the sword” and some “were killed with the sword”, and Hebrews 11 puts both in the same roll of honour (Hebrews 11:34, 37).

verseByVerse.quote: But the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah so that he was not given over to the people to be put to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah lives because one man of standing stood by him, and so the chapter points, by contrast, to the Prophet whom no one protected.

Ahikam the son of Shaphan. Ahikam’s father was Shaphan the scribe, who read the rediscovered book of the law aloud to Josiah (2 Kings 22:10), and Ahikam himself was one of the men Josiah sent to inquire of the LORD (2 Kings 22:12). This family appears at the turning points of the story, on the right side each time, and Ahikam’s son Gedaliah will be the governor who shelters Jeremiah after the city falls (chapters 39–41). Generations of quiet faithfulness turn out to hold up a great deal.

God’s care through human hands. The verse does not say that God protected Jeremiah, though he did. It says the hand of Ahikam was with him. God’s care in this chapter works through officials who held a proper court, elders who remembered a text, and one man with standing who used it. God’s care for his servants is very often somebody’s decision to stand next to them when it is expensive. That role is open to any believer: to stand beside the pastor under attack, the colleague who told the truth, the Christian on trial for his faith, and to spend what standing we have for them, as people for whom Christ stood when it cost him everything.

Not given over to the people. The chapter leaves a shadow across the page. Another prophet stood in that temple, spoke the same kind of word about the same house and was tried by the same kind of court, and when the moment came there was no Ahikam. The officials did not acquit him, no elder rose with a precedent, and his own people asked for a murderer instead. He was given over. The high priest had already explained the arithmetic, truer than he knew: “it is better for you that one man should die for the people” (John 11:50). Jeremiah was spared by a friendly hand; Jesus was handed over by his Father’s (Acts 2:23; Romans 8:32), and that is why anyone reading this has a hope beyond a fair trial.
verseByVerse.note: Ahikam's son Gedaliah, and Jeremiah's shelter with him after the fall of the city, appear in chapters 39 to 41.

26.title: The Trial of Jeremiah
26.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 26 opens the third part of the book, the prophet in conflict (chapters 26–29), and moves from sermons to story. It goes back to about 609 BC, the start of Jehoiakim’s reign, and tells what happened after the temple sermon of chapter 7: the preacher was put on trial for his life.

The message. God’s word must be spoken whole, because the whole of it is mercy: the warning is God’s own attempt to avoid the judgment. Those who hear it are on trial more than the preacher is. And God keeps his servants as he wills, sometimes through a just court and one brave friend, sometimes not at all in this life, but never because their faithfulness was greater or less.

Why it was said. Judah believed the temple made Jerusalem safe (7:4), and its priests and prophets defended that belief. The account showed later readers, in exile, that the city had been warned in full, had been offered mercy even at the trial, and had killed one prophet and only narrowly spared another (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God sends Jeremiah to the temple court with orders not to hold back a word, in the hope that the people will turn: if not, this house will become like Shiloh (vv. 1–6). The priests and prophets seize him, and the officials hold a trial in the New Gate, where Jeremiah retracts nothing, calls his judges to repent and warns them of innocent blood (vv. 7–15). The officials acquit him, and elders back the verdict with the case of Micah and Hezekiah (vv. 16–19). But Uriah, who preached the same word, was hunted down in Egypt and killed, and Jeremiah lives only because Ahikam’s hand was with him (vv. 20–24).

Where it leads. By pattern. Six centuries later another prophet spoke in this temple against this house, was seized by its priests, accused of threatening it (Matthew 26:61), and tried before a governor who washed his hands of “this man’s blood” (Matthew 27:24). But where Jeremiah was “not given over to the people to be put to death” (v. 24), Jesus was given over, by his own people, by Pilate and finally by his Father (Acts 2:23; Romans 8:32). The parallel turns at the end into a contrast, and that contrast is the gospel: Jeremiah was spared by a friend’s hand so that he could keep preaching; Jesus was not spared so that we could be.

For us. Preach and hear the whole word, for the trimmed sermon is the cruel one. Faithfulness is no guarantee of safety, as Uriah’s grave shows, but it is never wasted. And most of us are asked to be Ahikam: to stand beside those who tell the truth when it costs us something, as Christ stood for us.
26.theology:
The warning is the mercy: God sends the sermon so that he may relent, which is why no word may be held back (vv. 2-3). And he is not the tenant of his own house; Shiloh proves he will let a sanctuary fall rather than be used as a charm (v. 6).

Opposition to God's word is often religious, sincere and accurate in what it quotes (vv. 8-9). Faithfulness is not a survival strategy: Uriah and Jeremiah preached the same word, and only one was spared (vv. 20-24).

The whole trial foreshadows another in the same city, the trial of Jesus, where no friendly hand intervened.
26.examples:
Any preacher knows the temptation to give a congregation the ninety percent of a message that costs nothing. This chapter shows what the other ten percent can cost, and why it must still be said.

It also shows how God usually protects his servants: through officials who keep proper procedure, an elder who remembers his Bible, and one person with standing who decides to stand next to you when it is expensive.

keyVerse.quote: Now therefore mend your ways and your deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God, and the LORD will relent of the disaster that he has pronounced against you.
keyVerse.note: On trial for his life, Jeremiah does not defend himself but offers his judges mercy. The verse shows the heart of the whole chapter: God’s warnings are real, but their aim is repentance, and the door stays open even while his messenger is in the dock.

26.reflection:
God told Jeremiah, “do not hold back a word” (v. 2), and explained why: “It may be they will listen” (v. 3). Why is a trimmed message unloving, and where are we tempted to leave out the costly ten per cent?

Jeremiah’s accusers were priests and prophets, and they quoted him correctly (vv. 8–11). What does this teach about religious people and hard truths, and how should we respond when God’s word offends us?

Jeremiah was spared and Uriah was killed for the same message (vv. 20–24). How does Hebrews 11 help us hold God’s care and the reality of costly faithfulness together?

Jeremiah lived because “the hand of Ahikam” was with him, while Jesus was handed over with no one to stand for him. Whom could you stand beside at some cost, and how does Christ’s being given over for you make that possible?
