Then many nations and great kings shall make him their slave.<sup>8</sup>"'"But if any nation or kingdom will not serve this Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and put its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, I will punish that nation with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence, declares the LORD, until I have consumed it by his hand.<sup>9</sup>So do not listen to your prophets, your diviners, your dreamers, your fortune-tellers, or your sorcerers, who are saying to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon.'<sup>10</sup>For it is a lie that they are prophesying to you, with the result that you will be removed far from your land, and I will drive you out, and you will perish.<sup>11</sup>But any nation that will bring its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him, I will leave on its own land, to work it and dwell there, declares the LORD."'"<sup>12</sup>To Zedekiah king of Judah I spoke in like manner: "Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people and live.<sup>13</sup>Why will you and your people die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, as the LORD has spoken concerning any nation that will not serve the king of Babylon?<sup>14</sup>Do not listen to the words of the prophets who are saying to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon,' for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you.<sup>15</sup>I have not sent them, declares the LORD, but they are prophesying falsely in my name, with the result that I will drive you out and you will perish, you and the prophets who are prophesying to you."<sup>16</sup>Then I spoke to the priests and to all this people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who are prophesying to you, saying, 'Behold, the vessels of the LORD's house will now shortly be brought back from Babylon,' for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you.<sup>17</sup>Do not listen to them; serve the king of Babylon and live. Why should this city become a desolation?<sup>18</sup>If they are prophets, and if the word of the LORD is with them, then let them intercede with the LORD of hosts, that the vessels that are left in the house of the LORD, in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem may not go to Babylon.<sup>19</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the pillars, the sea, the stands, and the rest of the vessels that are left in this city,<sup>20</sup>which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon did not take away, when he took into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem—<sup>21</sup>thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning the vessels that are left in the house of the LORD, in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem:<sup>22</sup>They shall be carried to Babylon and remain there until the day when I visit them, declares the LORD. Then I will bring them back and restore them to this place."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Straps, Yoke-Bars, and the Owner of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before God speaks about politics, he speaks about who owns the world. Early in Zedekiah’s reign, with envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon in Jerusalem to plan a revolt, Jeremiah is told to make an ox’s yoke, wear it, and send a message home with the conspirators themselves (vv. 1–3). The message begins with creation: the LORD made the earth, its people and animals, and gives it to whomever he pleases (vv. 4–5). He has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar, “my servant”, for three generations, and then Babylon’s own time will come (vv. 6–7). The power over them is real, and it is temporary.
verseByVerse.theology: The empire everyone was plotting against is on a lease, and the landlord is the one who made the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD. Thus the LORD said to me: "Make yourself straps and yoke-bars, and put them on your neck. Send word to the king of Edom, the king of Moab, the king of the sons of Ammon, the king of Tyre, and the king of Sidon by the hand of the envoys who have come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Jeremiah to wear an ox’s yoke and send it as a message to the kings plotting revolt, carrying the humiliation himself before he asks them to accept it.

The setting. Zedekiah is Babylon’s appointee, put on the throne after Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) was carried off in 597 BC, and the small nations around Judah are testing whether a coalition could throw off the empire. The scene is about 594 BC (compare 28:1).

Make yourself straps and yoke-bars. God’s instruction is not to write a letter but to get dressed: to build the wooden bars that go over an ox’s neck, with leather straps to hold them, and wear them. Jeremiah walks the streets of Jerusalem harnessed like an ox, and he was still wearing the yoke when Hananiah broke it (28:10).

A message you can see. He has done this before: the ruined loincloth (13:1–11) and the smashed flask (19:1–13). A message you can see is harder to forget and harder to argue with, and this one puts the humiliation on the messenger first. Before he asks five kings to accept a yoke, he carries one himself.

By the hand of the envoys. The postal arrangements are ironic. The ambassadors have gathered to organise a revolt, and God uses the conspirators’ own delegation to carry his instruction home. The summit called to plan resistance leaves with a word from the God of Israel in its diplomatic bag.

Textual note. Most Hebrew manuscripts read “Jehoiakim” in verse 1, probably a copyist’s slip carried over from 26:1; some manuscripts read “Zedekiah”, and the ESV follows them. The scene itself is unmistakably Zedekiah’s: his envoys, his court, his crisis (vv. 3, 12; 28:1).
verseByVerse.note: The yoke stayed on Jeremiah's neck for some time: in 28:10 he is still wearing it when Hananiah breaks it.

verseByVerse.quote: Give them this charge for their masters: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: This is what you shall say to your masters: "It is I who by my great power and my outstretched arm have made the earth, with the men and animals that are on the earth, and I give it to whomever it seems right to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who made the earth owns it and gives it to whomever he chooses, and pagan kings must hear that first.

Creation first. These are pagan courts with their own gods, and the God of Israel does not ask for a hearing. Before a word about politics, he states who made the ground they are standing on.

I give it to whomever it seems right to me. Ownership follows from making. The one who made the earth and everything walking on it is entitled to say who holds which part of it, and nothing in that sentence submits itself to a vote.

My great power and my outstretched arm. This is exodus language, the vocabulary of the night Israel came out of Egypt, now used about the God of a small, defeated country and addressed to the powers of the region. Nebuchadnezzar himself would be brought to confess it, after hearing that “the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will” (Daniel 4:25; compare 4:34–35).

No authority except from God. Paul draws the line that reaches every government since: “there is no authority except from God” (Romans 13:1). No regime, however it came to power and however it behaves, holds anything it was not handed, and it will answer for how it used it.

Must Christians submit to any government? Judah was told to submit to Babylon because God had given Nebuchadnezzar the kingdom, and said so through his prophet. Christians are to honour and obey rulers in all lawful things (Romans 13:1–7), but never to obey a command to sin: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29), as Daniel and his friends showed under the same Babylon (Daniel 3; 6).

verseByVerse.quote: Now I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, my servant, and I have given him also the beasts of the field to serve him. All the nations shall serve him and his son and his grandson, until the time of his own land comes. Then many nations and great kings shall make him their slave.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has given the world to Nebuchadnezzar as his servant, but only for a set time; the power over them is real, and it is temporary.

My servant. Two words that would have stopped the room. The title belongs to Moses, to David, to the prophets, and it is given here to an idolatrous king who worships Marduk and will burn God’s temple. He is not called righteous or godly; he is called useful. God uses men who do not know they are being used, and he still calls them to account afterwards (25:12). The book has said it before (25:9), and the shock has not worn off.

The beasts of the field. Even the animals are included, echoing the dominion given to humanity at creation (Genesis 1:28): for this season, the whole sphere is placed under Babylon’s hand.

Until the time of his own land comes. Then the time limit is read out: three generations, and then Babylon’s turn to be conquered, when “many nations and great kings shall make him their slave”. The empire that looks permanent has an expiry date written into the very message announcing its power.

The double comfort. Here is the comfort of this chapter for anyone living under something they cannot change. The power over you is real, and it is temporary, and both are God’s doing. To submit to it is not to say it has the last word. It is to say that God has.

Who are the son and grandson? Nebuchadnezzar’s son Evil-merodach succeeded him (52:31), and after a few short reigns Babylon fell in 539 BC under Nabonidus and his son Belshazzar, who reigned alongside him (Daniel 5). They were probably not Nebuchadnezzar’s descendants by blood, though Daniel 5 calls him Belshazzar’s “father” in the ancient sense of predecessor. The phrase most likely means a span of about three generations, and Babylon’s empire did not outlast it: it fell some sixty-six years after Nebuchadnezzar came to the throne.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Submission to God’s appointed yoke is the way of life, and the voices that promise freedom are lying. Any nation that refuses to serve Babylon will be punished with sword, famine and pestilence; any that bows its neck will stay on its own land (vv. 8, 11). So the nations must ignore their prophets, diviners, dreamers and sorcerers, whose comfortable lie will end in exile (vv. 9–10). Zedekiah hears exactly the same terms, with no discount for being God’s covenant people: serve and live. God asks why he would choose to die, and disowns the prophets who use his name for a message he never sent (vv. 12–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Submission is the way to live, and the comforting sermon is the one that kills.

verseByVerse.quote: "'"But if any nation or kingdom will not serve this Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and put its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, I will punish that nation with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence, declares the LORD, until I have consumed it by his hand. So do not listen to your prophets, your diviners, your dreamers, your fortune-tellers, or your sorcerers, who are saying to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon.' For it is a lie that they are prophesying to you, with the result that you will be removed far from your land, and I will drive you out, and you will perish. But any nation that will bring its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him, I will leave on its own land, to work it and dwell there, declares the LORD."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refusing Babylon’s yoke means refusing the God who laid it, so the prophets who promise freedom are leading their nations to ruin, while submission keeps them on their land.

I will punish that nation. The threefold sentence of this book, sword, famine and pestilence, falls on the nations for a political decision, because the political decision is a religious one. Refusing the yoke means refusing the hand that placed it.

Do not listen to your prophets. Verse 9 lists five kinds of religious professional, and every one was predicting what the king wanted to hear. Independence sells. It always has, in every court and every pulpit, and the market for it does not care whether it is true.

The anatomy of a comfortable lie. Trace the chain in verse 10: they prophesy, you believe, you resist, you are driven out, you perish. The falsehood does not stay in the sermon. It ends up costing the land and the lives of the people who found it encouraging.

The mercy inside the sentence. Accept the yoke and you keep your fields, your house and your ordinary life. That is more than justice required.

verseByVerse.quote: To Zedekiah king of Judah I spoke in like manner: "Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people and live. Why will you and your people die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, as the LORD has spoken concerning any nation that will not serve the king of Babylon? Do not listen to the words of the prophets who are saying to you, 'You shall not serve the king of Babylon,' for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you. I have not sent them, declares the LORD, but they are prophesying falsely in my name, with the result that I will drive you out and you will perish, you and the prophets who are prophesying to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah gets the same terms as the pagan nations, serve and live, from a God who pleads with the king not to choose death and disowns the prophets who say otherwise.

Bring your necks under the yoke. Judah receives the same word as Moab, with no easier terms for being God’s covenant people. It has the temple, the promises and the line of David, and the instruction is identical: bend your neck and live.

Why will you and your people die? This is not a taunt but the question of a God who does not want this, reasoning with a man about to walk off a cliff (compare Ezekiel 18:31–32).

I have not sent them. The disowning is total. They used the name, the formulas and probably the same solemn voice, and the God they invoked had no part in it.

You and the prophets. And they go down with their congregation. A preacher who tells people what they want does not escape the wreck he talked them into. In the next chapter one of them, Hananiah, will snap the yoke off Jeremiah’s neck (28:10–11), promising the vessels back within two years (28:3), and he will be dead before the year is out (28:17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — The Test of a Prophet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The popular sermon in Jerusalem was that the temple vessels taken to Babylon would soon be brought back. Jeremiah calls it a lie and pleads again, “serve the king of Babylon and live” (vv. 16–17). Then he sets a test instead of an argument: if these men truly have the word of the LORD, let them do what true prophets do and intercede, praying that the treasures still left in Jerusalem are not taken too (v. 18). For God has already spoken about the great bronze pillars, the sea and the stands, the landmarks everyone thought would always be there (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: A true prophet prays; a false one predicts, and the test is whether he will get on his knees.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I spoke to the priests and to all this people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who are prophesying to you, saying, 'Behold, the vessels of the LORD's house will now shortly be brought back from Babylon,' for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you. Do not listen to them; serve the king of Babylon and live. Why should this city become a desolation? If they are prophets, and if the word of the LORD is with them, then let them intercede with the LORD of hosts, that the vessels that are left in the house of the LORD, in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem may not go to Babylon. For thus says the LORD of hosts concerning the pillars, the sea, the stands, and the rest of the vessels that are left in this city,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise that the temple treasures would soon come back was a lie; a true prophet would be praying that what was left would not be taken too.

The vessels of the LORD’s house. The popular sermon had found a good subject. Nebuchadnezzar had already carried off temple treasure, first under Jehoiakim, “with some of the vessels of the house of God”, as Daniel puts it (Daniel 1:2), and again with Jeconiah (2 Kings 24:13). The promise going round Jerusalem was that the gold would be back shortly: restoration without repentance, and soon.

Serve the king of Babylon and live. Once more God pleads and offers life. He argues for the city’s survival while the popular prophets march it toward ruin.

Let them intercede with the LORD of hosts. Here is the test, and it is a beautiful one. If these men have God’s ear, let them use it: stop forecasting and start praying. Intercession is the work of a true prophet (Abraham for Sodom, Moses on the mountain, Samuel for Israel), and a man who only ever announces good outcomes has never once had to plead for one.

The pillars, the sea, the stands. The inventory is deliberate. The bronze pillars Jachin and Boaz, the great bronze basin called the sea and the wheeled stands (1 Kings 7:15–39) were the immovable landmarks of Solomon’s temple, the things a Jerusalemite would point to as proof that some things never change. They are on the removal list, and Jeremiah 52:17 records them broken up and carried off.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — Until the Day When I Visit Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Both easy positions are wrong: the vessels will not return soon, and they are not lost for ever. Everything Nebuchadnezzar left behind when he took Jeconiah and the nobles into exile will be carried to Babylon as well (vv. 20–21). There it will remain “until the day when I visit them, declares the LORD”, and then God himself will bring it back and restore it to its place (v. 22). The timing belongs to God, not to the optimists. Decades later Cyrus sent the vessels home, counted out piece by piece, just as God had said.
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is not that nothing will be lost, but that God knows the day he will come for what is his.

verseByVerse.quote: which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon did not take away, when he took into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem— thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning the vessels that are left in the house of the LORD, in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem: They shall be carried to Babylon and remain there until the day when I visit them, declares the LORD. Then I will bring them back and restore them to this place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is left will go to Babylon too, but not for ever: God himself will bring the vessels back on his own day.

They shall be carried to Babylon. What survived the first deportation will not survive the second. The comfort people drew from the leftovers was misplaced: the pillars still standing proved only that God’s judgment was not yet finished.

Neither optimism nor despair. The chapter refuses both easy positions. The optimists said the vessels would be home within two years, and they were wrong. Those watching the bronze loaded onto carts would have said it was gone for good, and they were wrong too.

Until the day when I visit them. God keeps the date himself: not two years, not never, but his day. And it came. Decades later a Persian king who had never read this page gave the order: “Cyrus the king also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem” (Ezra 1:7), and they were counted out piece by piece to a prince of Judah. God had said the bowls were coming back, and the bowls came back.

A yoke taken up. Yet the chapter’s abiding image is a yoke on a prophet’s shoulders, and it does not rest until another Prophet takes it up. He told the truth about a temple’s fall and was killed for it. He stood before a governor and said what Jeremiah said to the nations: “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). And having borne the weight that breaks men, he says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden”, and, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:28–29). Babylon’s yoke bought survival in a ruined land. His yoke is easy, his burden is light, and it carries you home.

27.title: The Yoke of Babylon
27.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 27 moves on some fifteen years from the trial of chapter 26 to about 594 BC, early in the reign of Zedekiah, Babylon’s appointee after Jehoiachin was carried off in 597 BC. Envoys from five neighbouring kings are in Jerusalem to plan a revolt, and Jeremiah walks into the summit wearing an ox’s yoke. Chapters 27–29 form one story about true and false prophecy in Zedekiah’s early years.

The message. The God who made the earth gives it to whom he pleases, and for now he has given it to Babylon. To bow under the yoke he has laid on them is life; to refuse it, on the advice of prophets who promise freedom and a quick return of what was lost, is death. Yet the yoke has a time limit, and what God takes away he will bring back on his own day.

Why it was said. After the first deportation Judah and its neighbours were restless, and Jerusalem’s prophets were promising that the exiles and the temple treasures would soon return (see the introduction). The nations needed to hear who really ruled the world, and Judah needed to hear that rebellion against Babylon was rebellion against God’s discipline.

How the chapter makes its case. Jeremiah makes a yoke, puts it on, and sends a message home with the envoys (vv. 1–3). To their kings: the Creator has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar, “my servant”, until Babylon’s own time comes (vv. 4–7); serve and stay on your land, refuse and perish, and do not believe your diviners (vv. 8–11). To Zedekiah: the same terms, and the prophets promising independence are not sent by God (vv. 12–15). To the priests and people: the temple vessels will not come back shortly; what is left will go too, and remain in Babylon until the day God visits them and brings them home (vv. 16–22).

Where it leads. By God’s character and by pattern. The chapter shows a God who rules every empire and keeps his own timetable for restoration, and the vessels did come back under Cyrus (Ezra 1:7). But its central image is the yoke on the prophet’s neck. Jesus told the governor of another empire that he would have no authority “unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11), bore the heaviest yoke of all, and then offered his own: “Take my yoke upon you … and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).

For us. Distrust the message that promises escape from God’s discipline without repentance, however religious it sounds. Some burdens are God’s, to be borne in faith until he lifts them. And the deepest freedom is not having no yoke, but taking Christ’s.
27.theology:
God's right over the nations rests on creation: he made the earth and gives it to whom he pleases (v. 5). So a pagan emperor can be called his servant without being called godly, and Babylon's lease has its end written into the same message that announces its power (vv. 6-7).

Even the judgment comes with a way through it: those who accept the yoke stay on their land (v. 11). The false prophet flatters and predicts good things; the true one prays for the people (v. 18). And God keeps the date of his own restoration, neither two years nor never, but the day when he visits (v. 22).
27.examples:
A prophet walks through the city in an ox's harness, and a conspiracy's own ambassadors carry God's message home. The scene is a reminder that no summit or strategy is beyond the reach of God's word.

The test of verse 18 still searches anyone who speaks for God: does he only forecast good outcomes, or does he get on his knees and plead for them?

keyVerse.quote: Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people and live.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on the yoke: refusing it, on the word of prophets who promise freedom, leads to death, while bowing to the discipline God has laid on his people leads to life. It is a hard word, but it is God pleading for life, and it prepares for the greater call of Christ, “Take my yoke upon you” (Matthew 11:29).

27.reflection:
God begins his message to the pagan kings with creation: “It is I who … have made the earth” (v. 5). How does knowing who owns the world change the way we view governments, powers and events that frighten us?

Judah was told to accept Babylon’s yoke as God’s discipline (vv. 11–12), yet Christians are also told to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). How do we tell the difference between a burden to bear in faith and a command we must refuse?

The false prophets promised that what was lost would be back “shortly” (v. 16). What comfortable messages today promise escape from hardship without repentance, and why are they so attractive?

Jeremiah wore a yoke as a sign of judgment; Jesus says, “Take my yoke upon you” (Matthew 11:29). What is the difference between the two, and what would it mean for you to take up Christ’s yoke this week?

28.text: <sup>1</sup>In that same year, at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fifth month of the fourth year, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet from Gibeon, spoke to me in the house of the LORD, in the presence of the priests and all the people, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.<sup>3</sup>Within two years I will bring back to this place all the vessels of the LORD's house, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took away from this place and carried to Babylon.<sup>4</sup>I will also bring back to this place Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the exiles from Judah who went to Babylon, declares the LORD, for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon."<sup>5</sup>Then the prophet Jeremiah spoke to Hananiah the prophet in the presence of the priests and all the people who were standing in the house of the LORD,<sup>6</sup>and the prophet Jeremiah said, "Amen! May the LORD do so; may the LORD make the words that you have prophesied come true, and bring back to this place from Babylon the vessels of the house of the LORD, and all the exiles.<sup>7</sup>Yet hear now this word that I speak in your hearing and in the hearing of all the people.<sup>8</sup>The prophets who preceded you and me from ancient times prophesied war, famine, and pestilence against many countries and great kingdoms.<sup>9</sup>As for the prophet who prophesies peace, when the word of that prophet comes to pass, then it will be known that the LORD has truly sent the prophet."<sup>10</sup>Then the prophet Hananiah took the yoke-bars from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke them.<sup>11</sup>And Hananiah spoke in the presence of all the people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: Even so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all the nations within two years." But Jeremiah the prophet went his way.<sup>12</sup>Sometime after the prophet Hananiah had broken the yoke-bars from off the neck of Jeremiah the prophet, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>13</sup>"Go, tell Hananiah, 'Thus says the LORD: You have broken wooden bars, but you have made in their place bars of iron.<sup>14</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have put upon the neck of all these nations an iron yoke to serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and they shall serve him, for I have given to him even the beasts of the field.'"<sup>15</sup>And Jeremiah the prophet said to the prophet Hananiah, "Listen, Hananiah, the LORD has not sent you, and you have made this people trust in a lie.<sup>16</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will remove you from the face of the earth. This year you shall die, because you have uttered rebellion against the LORD.'"<sup>17</sup>In that same year, in the seventh month, the prophet Hananiah died.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — I Have Broken the Yoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: False prophecy can carry every mark of the real thing and still be a lie. In the temple, before the priests and all the people, Hananiah son of Azzur, from the priestly town of Gibeon, speaks in the full prophetic formula: “Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel.” His message is the exact reverse of Jeremiah’s: Babylon’s yoke is already broken, and within two years the temple vessels, King Jeconiah and all the exiles will be home (vv. 1–4). It is generous, specific and confident. It asks no repentance at all, and it contradicts what God has just said through the man standing there in a yoke.
verseByVerse.theology: Every word of the packaging is correct, and the contents are a lie.

verseByVerse.quote: In that same year, at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fifth month of the fourth year, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet from Gibeon, spoke to me in the house of the LORD, in the presence of the priests and all the people, saying, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon. Within two years I will bring back to this place all the vessels of the LORD's house, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took away from this place and carried to Babylon. I will also bring back to this place Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the exiles from Judah who went to Babylon, declares the LORD, for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hananiah, with every outward mark of a true prophet, announces in God’s name the exact reverse of what God has said: Babylon’s yoke is broken, and everything lost will be back within two years.

In that same year. About 594 BC, the year of the envoys’ summit (27:3). The timing helps explain why Hananiah was believed. The Babylonian Chronicle records a revolt inside Babylon itself in 595 to 594 BC, and envoys were in Jerusalem planning a coalition, so the empire may well have looked shaky.

Hananiah the son of Azzur. Everything about the scene looks official. A named man from a known priestly town stands in the temple, with the clergy and the congregation as his audience, using the full formula: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel. If you were grading the delivery you would give him full marks.

I have broken the yoke. The content is the exact reverse of what God had just said through the man wearing the yoke: not a shading of it or a softer version, but I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon, spoken in the first person as God’s own speech. Two men in one city, both saying “thus says the LORD”, are saying opposite things.

Within two years. The lie is generous. The gold comes home, the deportees come home, the rightful king comes home, all inside two years: soon enough to plan for, but not so soon as to be tested next week. Nothing is asked of anybody: no repentance, no change, no turning, simply a reversal handed over by God to people who had earned nothing. That is the shape false comfort always takes. It offers everything the true word offers, minus the repentance, and on a shorter timetable.

Uncertain wording. At the beginning of the reign and in the fifth month of the fourth year sound contradictory. The first phrase probably means the earlier part of Zedekiah’s eleven-year reign, as in 27:1; the ancient Greek translation simply reads in the fourth year. Either way the date is about 594 BC.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Amen, and Yet Hear This Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A true messenger longs for good news and still will not say what God has not said. Jeremiah’s first reply is a prayer: “Amen! May the LORD do so” (vv. 5–6). He takes no pleasure in the coming ruin. Then comes the “yet” (v. 7). The prophets God sent across the centuries mostly warned comfortable nations of war, famine and pestilence (v. 8), so the prophet of peace carries the burden of proof: he is shown to be sent only when his word comes to pass, as the law itself requires (v. 9; Deuteronomy 18:22). Jeremiah appeals not to a better vision but to the record and to Scripture.
verseByVerse.theology: A man who wants the comfortable message to be true, and will not say it is.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the prophet Jeremiah spoke to Hananiah the prophet in the presence of the priests and all the people who were standing in the house of the LORD, and the prophet Jeremiah said, "Amen! May the LORD do so; may the LORD make the words that you have prophesied come true, and bring back to this place from Babylon the vessels of the house of the LORD, and all the exiles. Yet hear now this word that I speak in your hearing and in the hearing of all the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah’s first word is a heartfelt amen, for he longs for the good news to be true; but wishing it true does not let him say that it is.

Amen! May the LORD do so. Of all the things a man in his position might have said, he says amen, and that one word shows what kind of man Jeremiah was. He had been called a traitor for decades, mocked, beaten, put in the stocks and tried for his life, and when a rival announces that the whole burden is lifted, his first instinct is to wish it were so. He takes no relish in the bad news and has no investment in being proved right.

A mark of a true messenger. That is one of the surest marks of a true messenger. A man who enjoys announcing judgment has stopped loving the people he announces it to, and his relish already gives a false picture of the God who sent the message. Jeremiah’s tears run through this whole book for exactly this reason: he never wanted a word of it to be true.

Yet hear now this word. Then comes the yet. Wishing the promise were true does not allow him to say that it is. He says what he wishes were true and then what is, in public, before the same crowd, without pretending the two are the same thing.

verseByVerse.quote: The prophets who preceded you and me from ancient times prophesied war, famine, and pestilence against many countries and great kingdoms. As for the prophet who prophesies peace, when the word of that prophet comes to pass, then it will be known that the LORD has truly sent the prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
History and the law both put the burden of proof on the prophet of easy peace: let his word come true before anyone rests on it.

The prophets who preceded you and me. The argument is historical, and disarmingly modest. Jeremiah claims no superior experience or better vision; he points at the record. Look at the men God has actually sent across the centuries, he says, and see what they mostly had to say to comfortable nations. It was not congratulation.

When the word of that prophet comes to pass. So the burden of proof falls on the preacher of peace, and the test is the plain one from the law: “when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken” (Deuteronomy 18:22). Waiting to see is not scepticism here; it is obedience to an explicit instruction.

A second test. The law adds a second test, so that the first is never used alone. A sign can come true and the man still be false, if what he teaches leads you away from God: “you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or that dreamer of dreams” (Deuteronomy 13:3). A prophet is judged by both tests together, which is why the Lord’s own summary is “You will recognize them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:16). And the same chapter of the law that gives the test also promises the Prophet who would pass it perfectly: “I will put my words in his mouth” (Deuteronomy 18:18).

What it does not mean. A gloomy message does not prove a prophet true. Scripture is full of promise, and Jeremiah himself will write chapters 30 to 33. The point is narrower: a message which asks nothing of its hearers and confirms what they already want has very little precedent among the men God commissioned.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Defying God’s word does not break it; it makes it heavier. Hananiah answers argument with theatre: he snaps the yoke-bars off Jeremiah’s neck before the crowd and declares that Babylon’s yoke will break the same way within two years (vv. 10–11). Jeremiah, with no word from God, simply goes his way, publicly beaten. Sometime later the answer comes (vv. 12–14): Hananiah has broken wooden bars, but in their place he has made bars of iron. God has put an iron yoke on all these nations and given Nebuchadnezzar even the beasts of the field. The sign was broken; the sentence it stood for was not.
verseByVerse.theology: Breaking the sign does not cancel the sentence; it only exchanges wood for iron.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the prophet Hananiah took the yoke-bars from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke them. And Hananiah spoke in the presence of all the people, saying, "Thus says the LORD: Even so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all the nations within two years." But Jeremiah the prophet went his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hananiah answers argument with theatre, snapping the yoke off Jeremiah’s neck, and Jeremiah, having no word from God, walks away in silence.

Hananiah took the yoke-bars. He does not answer the argument; he performs. It is superb staging: walk up to the old man in the harness, snap the bars off his neck in front of the crowd, and let the sound of splitting wood be the sermon. Prophecy with props was a known technique (another court prophet once “made for himself horns of iron” to promise a king victory, 1 Kings 22:11), and it works on a crowd, because people remember an action when they have forgotten an argument. Hananiah has even stolen Jeremiah’s own method. The yoke, the loincloth, the smashed flask were all visual sermons; now one is turned against the man who wore it, and the audience goes home having watched Babylon’s power break in the temple courtyard.

But Jeremiah the prophet went his way. That short phrase teaches as much as anything here. He does not shout, produce a second yoke or defend his reputation. He has no word from God about this, so he says nothing, and walks out of the temple publicly humiliated.

Silence, not weakness. Silence like that is the discipline of a man who will not manufacture a message to win an argument. He would rather lose the room than invent a sentence God had not given him, and he is willing to look beaten for as long as God leaves him without an answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Sometime after the prophet Hananiah had broken the yoke-bars from off the neck of Jeremiah the prophet, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Go, tell Hananiah, 'Thus says the LORD: You have broken wooden bars, but you have made in their place bars of iron. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: I have put upon the neck of all these nations an iron yoke to serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and they shall serve him, for I have given to him even the beasts of the field.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s answer comes later, and it is devastatingly brief: defying his word does not break it but makes it heavier, for the wooden bars are exchanged for iron.

Sometime after. Not that hour, and not while the crowd was still there to see him vindicated. God’s servant had to carry the defeat for a while before he was given anything to say, and the delay was not neglect. Vindication on Hananiah’s schedule would have been a smaller thing than vindication on God’s.

Bars of iron. The gesture worked: the wood really did break. It simply had no authority over the thing the wood stood for, and all Hananiah achieved by snapping the sign was to exchange it for a harder one. The iron yoke is the covenant curse itself: “he will put a yoke of iron on your neck until he has destroyed you” (Deuteronomy 28:48). The principle reaches far past this courtyard. A word from God is not disarmed by being defied, and sin’s consequences are not escaped by defying the warning; they grow heavier.

Even the beasts of the field. The terms of chapter 27 are restated with the metal upgraded, and the closing phrase shows the scale of the claim (compare 27:6). Even the wild animals are assigned to Nebuchadnezzar. A God who allocates the beasts of the field is not negotiating about the borders of Judah.

Your truth and my truth. Two men stand in the same courtyard, both sincere, both saying Thus says the LORD, and saying opposite things. The modern instinct is to call it a draw: he has his truth and Jeremiah has his, and who are we to judge? It sounds humble, and it is often meant kindly. But Babylon did not consult anyone’s truth; the iron yoke came whatever the crowd preferred to believe. Some things are true whether or not we like them, and there is a strange cruelty in a tolerance that will not tell a man the bridge is out. The phrase “my truth” turns truth into a possession, something I hold and you cannot touch. Scripture treats truth as something that holds us, and in the end as someone. Jesus did not say that he had a truth for those who liked it. He said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). That is a hard claim, because it will not go away when it is disbelieved. It is also the best news in the world, because the truth that will not bend is the one who bore the yoke for us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–17 — You Have Made This People Trust in a Lie
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word proves itself, and the false prophet falls under the sentence the law laid down. Jeremiah tells Hananiah to his face that the LORD has not sent him, and names the real damage: “you have made this people trust in a lie” (v. 15). Because he has spoken rebellion against the LORD, he will die this very year (v. 16; Deuteronomy 18:20). The chapter closes in one flat line: in the seventh month, two months after his promise of two years, Hananiah was dead (v. 17). The test Jeremiah had set the crowd was answered sooner than anyone expected, and in a way no one had imagined.
verseByVerse.theology: He had two years to be proved right and was given two months.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jeremiah the prophet said to the prophet Hananiah, "Listen, Hananiah, the LORD has not sent you, and you have made this people trust in a lie. Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will remove you from the face of the earth. This year you shall die, because you have uttered rebellion against the LORD.'" In that same year, in the seventh month, the prophet Hananiah died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah exposes Hananiah as unsent and pronounces the law’s sentence on him, and within two months it falls.

The LORD has not sent you. Two charges, and the second is the graver. First, the man had no commission, whatever he sincerely believed. This is the book’s standing verdict on the professionals: “I did not send the prophets, yet they ran” (23:21).

You have made this people trust in a lie. The damage is not to Jeremiah, and it is not chiefly Hananiah’s private guilt. A whole congregation has been persuaded to rest its weight on something that will not hold it, and they will still be resting on it when the Babylonians come. False comfort is not harmless over-optimism; it is a floor built over a hole. The same book says it of the same trade: “They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace” (6:14).

This year you shall die. The sentence is the law’s own, written centuries earlier for precisely this case: “the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him to speak … that same prophet shall die” (Deuteronomy 18:20). And the charge is named exactly: not error, not enthusiasm, but rebellion against the LORD. Speaking for God without being sent is treated as an act of war against him.

In the seventh month. The end is told in one flat line. Hananiah had promised two years, and he died in the seventh month, two months after he spoke. The proof Jeremiah had told the crowd to wait for arrived quickly: not the failure of the two-year promise, but the death of the man who made it.

The Prophet who was sent. Beyond the two men in the temple stands a third. Hananiah died because he spoke a word God had not given him. Jesus is the Prophet who spoke nothing except what the Father gave him (John 12:49), who went his way in silence when he was contradicted, and who was put to death all the same. Hananiah died for his own lie; Jesus died for ours, and the iron yoke our lies keep forging was laid on his shoulders, so that the yoke now offered to us is the one he calls easy (Matthew 11:30).

A warning that has not expired. “There will be false teachers among you” (2 Peter 2:1), and their message still has the same shape: full assurance, no repentance, a short timetable. Measure every preacher, however gifted, by both of the law’s tests: does his word prove true, and does it lead you to the LORD?

Should false teachers be put to death today? No. Here God himself carries out the sentence; Jeremiah lays no hand on Hananiah. The church bears no sword: it answers false teaching by refuting it from Scripture, warning, and finally refusing fellowship to those who will not turn (Titus 1:9–11; 3:10; 2 John 10), while praying that God may grant them repentance (2 Timothy 2:25).
verseByVerse.note: Gibeon, Hananiah's home town (v. 1), was one of the cities given to the priests, the descendants of Aaron (Josh 21:17).

28.title: Hananiah Breaks the Yoke
28.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 28 continues the story of chapter 27 in the same year, about 594 BC, early in Zedekiah’s reign. Jeremiah is still wearing the ox’s yoke he put on to tell the envoys of five kingdoms, and Judah’s own king, to serve Babylon. Now a rival prophet answers him in the temple.

The message. Two men stand in God’s house, both saying “Thus says the LORD”, and they say opposite things. God settles it: the comforting word that asks no repentance is a lie, however official it sounds, and defying his true word does not break it but makes it heavier. A people’s life hangs on which voice it trusts.

Why it was said. Judah longed to hear that the deportation of 597 BC would soon be undone (see the introduction), and with unrest inside Babylon itself, the empire looked shaky. Hananiah told them exactly what they wanted to hear; Jeremiah had to tell them it was not true, and how to tell the difference.

How the chapter makes its case. Hananiah, with every mark of a prophet, announces that Babylon’s yoke is broken and that the vessels, King Jeconiah and the exiles will be home within two years (vv. 1–4). Jeremiah answers with a heartfelt amen, then with the law’s test: the prophet of peace is proved sent only when his word comes true (vv. 5–9). Hananiah breaks the yoke-bars off Jeremiah’s neck, and Jeremiah walks away in silence until God answers: wood has been exchanged for iron (vv. 10–14). Finally Jeremiah tells Hananiah that the LORD has not sent him and that he will die that year, and two months later he is dead (vv. 15–17).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. The law that gives the test of a prophet (Deuteronomy 18:20–22) also promises a Prophet like Moses: “I will put my words in his mouth” (Deuteronomy 18:18), and the apostles proclaimed Jesus as that Prophet (Acts 3:22–26). Hananiah spoke what God had not given him and died for his own lie. Jesus spoke only what the Father gave him (John 12:49), was silent before those who contradicted him, and died for our lies. The iron yoke our rebellion deserved he bore, and the yoke he offers instead is easy (Matthew 11:30).

For us. Test what you hear by Scripture, not by how confident or official it sounds, and be wary of any message that promises God’s blessing without repentance. If you must speak hard truth, learn from Jeremiah’s amen: long for the good news, and still do not pretend. And if you are publicly beaten for telling the truth, you may walk away and wait, for God answers in his time.
28.theology:
The right words in the right place guarantee nothing: Hananiah has the prophet’s formula, the temple and the confidence, and God did not send him (vv. 1-2, 15). False comfort offers everything the true word offers, minus repentance and on a shorter timetable, and its real victims are the people who rest their weight on it.

The true messenger takes no pleasure in judgment (v. 6), tests every word both by whether it comes true and by whether it is faithful to God (vv. 8-9), and can bear public silence while he waits for God's answer (vv. 11-12). And defiance does not cancel God's decree; it hardens it (v. 13).
28.examples:
Hananiah would get full marks for delivery, and he promised everything restored with nothing asked of anybody. That is still the shape of the most attractive false teaching.

Jeremiah's amen is a model for anyone who must bring hard news: wish with all your heart that the comfortable message were true, and still do not say that it is. And his walk out of the temple, beaten and silent, is a comfort to anyone who must wait for God to answer for them.

keyVerse.quote: Listen, Hananiah, the LORD has not sent you, and you have made this people trust in a lie.
keyVerse.note: This verse names both what was wrong with Hananiah and why it mattered. He spoke without being sent, and the cost fell on the people who rested their lives on his comfortable word. It is the chapter’s answer to its own question, which voice to trust, and a standing warning to every preacher and every hearer.

28.reflection:
Hananiah had the right place, the right formula and a confident manner (vv. 1–4), yet God had not sent him. What makes a message sound authoritative to us, and how can we test it by Scripture rather than by its packaging?

Hananiah’s promise asked nothing of anyone and came on a short timetable. Where do you see the same shape of comfort without repentance today, in the church or in your own heart?

Jeremiah prayed “Amen! May the LORD do so” (v. 6) over a promise he could not endorse, and then told the truth. What does his example teach us about bringing hard news to people we love?

Jeremiah walked away beaten and silent until God gave him a word (vv. 11–12), and Jesus too was silent before his accusers. When have you needed to wait rather than defend yourself, and what helps you trust God with the outcome?
