Babylon: "The LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire,"<sup>23</sup>because they have done an outrageous thing in Israel, they have committed adultery with their neighbors' wives, and they have spoken in my name lying words that I did not command them. I am the one who knows, and I am witness, declares the LORD.'"<sup>24</sup>To Shemaiah of Nehelam you shall say:<sup>25</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have sent letters in your name to all the people who are in Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests, saying,<sup>26</sup>'The LORD has made you priest instead of Jehoiada the priest, to have charge in the house of the LORD over every madman who prophesies, to put him in the stocks and neck irons.<sup>27</sup>Now why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth who is prophesying to you?<sup>28</sup>For he has sent to us in Babylon, saying, "Your exile will be long; build houses and live in them, and plant gardens and eat their produce."'"<sup>29</sup>Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the hearing of Jeremiah the prophet.<sup>30</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>31</sup>"Send to all the exiles, saying, 'Thus says the LORD concerning Shemaiah of Nehelam: Because Shemaiah had prophesied to you when I did not send him, and has made you trust in a lie,<sup>32</sup>therefore thus says the LORD: Behold, I will punish Shemaiah of Nehelam and his descendants. He shall not have anyone living among this people, and he shall not see the good that I will do to my people, declares the LORD, for he has spoken rebellion against the LORD.'"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people are to settle in Babylon and seek its good, because God himself sent them there. Jeremiah writes from Jerusalem to the deportees of 597 BC, and his letter travels with King Zedekiah’s embassy to Nebuchadnezzar, carried by a son of Shaphan, the family that had protected him (vv. 1–3). God names himself as the one who sent them into exile, and tells them to live: build houses, plant gardens, marry and raise children, and increase rather than dwindle (vv. 4–6). Then comes the command no one expected: seek the welfare of the enemy’s city and pray for it, because their own welfare is bound up in it (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Settle down in the place of judgment, and pray for the good of the city that carried you off.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the surviving elders of the exiles, and to the priests, the prophets, and all the people, whom Nebuchadnezzar had taken into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon. This was after King Jeconiah and the queen mother, the eunuchs, the officials of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the metal workers had departed from Jerusalem. The letter was sent by the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. It said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah sends God’s word by letter to the exiles in Babylon, and God uses a king’s embassy and a faithful family to deliver it.

Prophecy by post. This time the word comes as a letter: not a sermon in a courtyard or a sign acted out in the street, but a document carried well over a thousand kilometres and read aloud to people the prophet would never see again.

The surviving elders. One word carries a weight of grief: they are written to as survivors. These are the deportees of 597 BC, the good figs of chapter 24, whom Nebuchadnezzar had taken away: the king and his mother, the officials, the skilled and the well-connected, whose absence gutted the city. Now they were living in settlements along the irrigation canals of Babylonia, trying to work out what God was doing.

By the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan. The postal arrangements matter, because God keeps using them. Zedekiah is sending an official delegation to his overlord, and Jeremiah’s letter travels with it. The embassy’s purpose is not stated; it was probably sent to assure Nebuchadnezzar of Zedekiah’s loyalty, perhaps after the plotting with neighbouring kings in chapter 27, which would date the letter to about 594 BC. One courier is a son of Shaphan, the family whose member Ahikam had saved Jeremiah’s life (26:24). A royal errand and a faithful family together carry God’s word into exile, and none of the officials involved had any idea they were doing it.
verseByVerse.note: The other courier, Gemariah son of Hilkiah (v. 3), may have been a son of the high priest who found the book of the law in Josiah's day (2 Kgs 22:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom I have sent into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon: Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters; take wives for your sons, and give your daughters in marriage, that they may bear sons and daughters; multiply there, and do not decrease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God, who sent his people into exile, tells them to settle down and live full lives in Babylon, because the exile will be long and his purpose for them goes on there.

Whom I have sent into exile. Before a single instruction, God corrects the record. Nebuchadnezzar’s army marched them out; God says he sent them. The empire was the instrument, and the hand on it was his. That one clause changes what exile is. If Babylon is an accident of politics, the exiles are simply unlucky, and their only sane response is to wait for better luck. If God sent them, Babylon is an assignment, and there is something to do there.

Build houses and live in them. The most ordinary commands imaginable are, in that setting, radical. Build a house, not a tent. Plant a garden, which means staying long enough to eat the fruit. Marry, and marry off your children, which means accepting that your grandchildren will be born in Babylon.

Neither false hope nor despair. Every one of those instructions kills the hope the exiles were nursing, that this would soon be over. And every one rules out the opposite error, despair: refusing to live because life is not what you wanted. God does not tell them to like Babylon. He tells them to live, and to put down roots where his providence, not their own choice, has placed them.

Multiply there, and do not decrease. This echoes God’s first command to mankind, “Be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:28). His purpose for his people is not put on hold while the exile lasts; it continues in captivity.

verseByVerse.quote: But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells his captive people to work and pray for the good of the enemy city that holds them, because their own good is bound up with it.

The welfare of the city where I have sent you. Babylon had besieged Jerusalem, stripped the temple, taken their king and marched them across a desert; Psalm 137 is the honest sound of a heart in that city. Into that, God says: work for its good. Welfare is shalom, the whole flourishing of a place, its peace, safety and prosperity together. They are not merely to tolerate Babylon or keep out of trouble in it, but to seek its good actively.

Pray to the LORD on its behalf. Here is the Old Testament seed of the Lord’s hard command to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44). It is asked not of a victorious nation being magnanimous but of prisoners of war, about their captors’ capital. No prisoner can produce that love by willpower; it grows from the kindness of the God who says, “I know the plans I have for you” (v. 11), and for the Christian it is the Spirit’s own fruit (Galatians 5:22).

In its welfare you will find your welfare. God ties their good to the good of the pagan city. There is no separate, sealed-off prosperity for the people of God while the place around them rots.

Christians as exiles. Peter writes to Christians in just these terms, as “elect exiles of the dispersion” (1 Peter 1:1), “sojourners and exiles” who are to “keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable” (1 Peter 2:11–12). The church is not to sulk in the culture or dissolve into it. Our “citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20), and for that very reason we seek the welfare of the city we are passing through. Timothy Keller often pointed out that Christians should neither withdraw from their city nor be absorbed by it, but serve it sacrificially as people with another home. That is what Christ did: he wept over the city that would reject him (Luke 19:41) and suffered outside its gate to make a people his own (Hebrews 13:12). We seek our city’s welfare because he sought ours.

How do I seek the welfare of my city? Start where God has sent you, which may be a town you did not choose or a street you hope to leave. Pray for it by name: the council, the head teacher, the hospital and the people on your road, as Paul urges prayer “for kings and all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:2). Do your work well. Honest accounts, prepared lessons, a boiler properly fixed: ordinary work is part of a city’s flourishing. Be a neighbour. Learn names, take in the parcel, sit with the lonely man at the bus stop, turn up to the residents’ meeting. Give beyond the church. Support the food bank or the school reading scheme, not only causes that benefit Christians.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Seventy Years, and the Plans I Have for You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The exile will be long, but it is held inside God’s good purpose. The prophets and diviners among the exiles, dreaming the dreams their hearers wanted, were promising a quick return; God says he did not send them (vv. 8–9). The truth is harder and better: after seventy years for Babylon he will visit them and keep his promise to bring them home, for his plans for them are for welfare and not for evil, to give them a future and a hope (vv. 10–11). Then they will call on him and he will hear; they will seek him with all their heart and find him, and he will gather them from everywhere they were scattered (vv. 12–14).
verseByVerse.theology: A promise most of its first readers would die before seeing, and it was still the best news in Babylon.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Do not let your prophets and your diviners who are among you deceive you, and do not listen to the dreams that they dream, for it is a lie that they are prophesying to you in my name; I did not send them, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God warns the exiles not to believe the prophets among them who promise a quick return: he did not send them, and their message is a lie.

Your prophets and your diviners who are among you. The false prophets were not left behind in Jerusalem. They were deported too, and they set up shop in the settlements with the same product: it will be over soon.

The dreams that they dream. The ESV’s note sharpens the accusation: the Hebrew reads “your dreams, which you cause to dream”. It is the people who cause the prophets to dream what they want to hear. The congregation supplies the longing; the preacher manufactures the vision to match. That is how the trade has always worked.

I did not send them. The verdict of chapters 27 and 28 is now posted to Babylon. Distance changed nothing. Wherever God’s people are scattered, someone will be telling them what they want to hear in God’s name, and the test does not change either.

Why the lie is cruel. If you believe the exile is nearly over, you will not build a house, plant a garden or raise a family. You will sit on your luggage for seventy years and waste your one life waiting for a journey home that is not coming.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you, and I will fulfill to you my promise and bring you back to this place. For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The exile will last seventy years, longer than most of its first hearers would live, but God has set its limit, and his settled purpose for his people through it is their good, a future and a hope.

When seventy years are completed for Babylon. The number is brutal and kind at once. The old men weeping by the canals would die in Babylon; their grandchildren would make the journey home. God does not soften that. The figure measures Babylon’s dominion, from its rise over the region about 609–605 BC to its fall in 539 BC, with the first exiles going home about 538 BC: roughly seventy years, a round number rather than a stopwatch.

I will visit you, and I will fulfill to you my promise. But God sets a limit, and a sentence with an end is a different thing from a sentence without one. Decades later Daniel sat with this very page open, having “perceived in the books the number of years that, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, must pass before the end of the desolations of Jerusalem, namely, seventy years” (Daniel 9:2), and began to pray. The Chronicler records the outcome in the driest terms: it happened “to fulfill the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah” (2 Chronicles 36:21).

For I know the plans I have for you. This verse turns up on mugs and graduation cards, and its setting is a prison camp. It was given to people whose city had been stripped and whose king was in chains, whose temple would burn within a decade, and who were being told to unpack. That makes it stronger, not weaker. Welfare is the word of verse 7 again, shalom (the ESV notes that it may be read “peace”): God’s settled intention toward this people is their whole flourishing, and he pursues it through seventy years of Babylon, not in spite of them. A future and a hope is not the absence of exile; it is God’s guarantee that exile is not the end of the story he is telling.

Is this promise to me? Read it in two steps. First, it was a promise to a people, the exiles as a whole, about a national return. It does not promise any one person health, wealth, a career or a quick end to trouble, and many who first heard it died in Babylon still trusting it. Second, in Christ it does reach us, for all God’s promises “find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20), and “for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28), even through exile. The God who planned welfare for exiles has given us “a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3), and his plans for us include discipline, suffering and waiting (Romans 8:17–18). The future and the hope are finally God himself and the new creation, not a better year. If you are in a hard place now, this verse does not promise it will end soon; it promises that God has not stopped meaning you good in it.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 10-14 echo Moses' promise to a scattered people in Deuteronomy 30:1-5: when they return to the LORD with all their heart, he will gather them from wherever he has driven them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will call upon me and come and pray to me, and I will hear you. You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart. I will be found by you, declares the LORD, and I will restore your fortunes and gather you from all the nations and all the places where I have driven you, declares the LORD, and I will bring you back to the place from which I sent you into exile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The exile will end as God’s people pray and seek him with all their heart, and God promises both that they will seek him and that he will be found.

Then you will call upon me and come and pray to me. Restoration comes not through a rebellion, a lobbying campaign or a change in Babylonian politics, but through prayer: a people on their knees in a foreign country, calling on a God whose temple lay far away across the desert. And God announces what they will do before they do it. The seeking is promised, not merely demanded, the same grace as the heart he pledged to give them in the vision of the figs (24:7): God supplies the very response he requires.

You will seek me and find me. The words come from Moses, spoken over the exile centuries before it happened: “you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 4:29). And the Lord Jesus gives the same invitation in its plainest form: “seek, and you will find” (Matthew 7:7).

When you seek me with all your heart. The half-hearted search is the one that fails, and not for lack of effort: a man who wants God as one item among several has not yet wanted God. Yet no one seeks with a perfectly whole heart, and the promise finally rests on the God who gives the heart, and who came in Christ “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

I will be found by you. God is not hiding. The exile never made him unreachable, and the gathering will reach every place they were scattered to: the God who sent them away will bring them back to the place he sent them from.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — The Vile Figs Left Behind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The relatives the exiles envied are not the fortunate ones. The exiles boasted that God had raised up prophets for them in Babylon, and they looked back to Jerusalem, where a son of David still reigned and their kinsmen still lived (v. 15). God answers that those left behind face sword, famine and pestilence: they are the rotten figs of chapter 24, and they will be scattered and become a byword among the nations (vv. 16–18). The reason is plain: they would not listen to the prophets God persistently sent (v. 19). The ones who lost everything are the objects of God’s good intentions.
verseByVerse.theology: Those who stayed in Jerusalem kept nothing in the end; the ones in chains were the good figs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Because you have said, 'The LORD has raised up prophets for us in Babylon,' thus says the LORD concerning the king who sits on the throne of David, and concerning all the people who dwell in this city, your kinsmen who did not go out with you into exile: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, behold, I am sending on them sword, famine, and pestilence, and I will make them like vile figs that are so rotten they cannot be eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The relatives in Jerusalem whom the exiles envy are not the blessed ones: God will send disaster on them, for they are the rotten figs.

The LORD has raised up prophets for us in Babylon. The exiles had a comparison running in their heads, and it was eating them. Our relatives are still at home, they thought, with the city, the temple and a son of David on the throne, and our prophets tell us we will soon join them. God answers the comparison directly, and your kinsmen who did not go out with you into exile names the envy precisely.

Like vile figs. Here is the image of the two baskets of figs. Jerusalem had been told it face to face (“like the bad figs that are so bad they cannot be eaten”, 24:8), and now it is written to the good figs in Babylon, so that the exiles can stop envying the wrong people.

A hard comfort. The comfort is real, if uncomfortable. The ones who look blessed are not; the ones who lost everything are the objects of God’s good intentions. That is hard to receive without bitterness, and the letter has already told them how: build, plant, pray for Babylon. Envy dies in a garden you are actually tending.

verseByVerse.quote: I will pursue them with sword, famine, and pestilence, and will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a curse, a terror, a hissing, and a reproach among all the nations where I have driven them, because they did not pay attention to my words, declares the LORD, that I persistently sent to you by my servants the prophets, but you would not listen, declares the LORD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment will pursue those left in Jerusalem wherever they go, because for years they refused to listen to the prophets God kept sending.

I will pursue them. This is not a disaster they can outrun by staying put, which was the whole basis of their confidence. Judgment follows them into every country it drives them to.

A curse, a terror, a hissing, and a reproach. The tragedy is that this is the nation appointed to make God’s name known among those same nations. They will still show the nations something about God, but now it is his judgment and not his blessing.

That I persistently sent to you. The reason is not obscure, and there is no hidden motive to puzzle over: they did not pay attention to my words. Decades of prophets were sent again and again to a city that had every chance to listen and used none of them. Judgment in this book always arrives late, after a long patience that has been ignored, and that is why it can be announced without apology.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God names the liars and exposes their lives. Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah were prophesying a lie to the exiles in God’s name (vv. 20–21). Nebuchadnezzar will execute them, roasting them in the fire, and their names will become a curse among the exiles (v. 22). Two crimes stand together: adultery with their neighbours’ wives, and lying words spoken in God’s name; and God, who saw what was done in secret, is the witness (v. 23). False teaching and a false life are seldom far apart.
verseByVerse.theology: God never judged the private life and the preaching separately.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, all you exiles whom I sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon: 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, who are prophesying a lie to you in my name: Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall strike them down before your eyes. Because of them this curse shall be used by all the exiles from Judah in Babylon: "The LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire," because they have done an outrageous thing in Israel, they have committed adultery with their neighbors' wives, and they have spoken in my name lying words that I did not command them. I am the one who knows, and I am witness, declares the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names two lying prophets among the exiles, foretells their execution by Nebuchadnezzar, and exposes the adultery that went with their lies, for he saw it all.

Concerning Ahab the son of Kolaiah. The letter does not deal in generalities about false teaching; it names the men doing it, because the exiles had to know whose meetings to stop attending.

He shall strike them down before your eyes. Nebuchadnezzar will execute them, probably because preaching a quick return home amounted to stirring up revolt against Babylon. He thought he was protecting his empire; God claims the sentence as his own.

Whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire. Their names become a proverb for a horrible death. Burning was a known Babylonian punishment (Hammurabi’s laws prescribe it for several crimes, and Daniel’s friends faced the furnace, Daniel 3:6), and the Hebrew carries a grim pun: the word for curse (qelalah) echoes the verb roasted (qalah). Men who had built careers on telling people what they wanted became the byword the same people used when they cursed.

An outrageous thing in Israel. Two charges stand in one sentence, and Scripture will not separate them: adultery with their neighbours’ wives, and lying in God’s name. The man who is willing to invent a message is the same man who is willing to break a marriage; a life that reshapes God’s word to suit itself will use other people to suit itself too.

I am the one who knows, and I am witness. The quietest and most searching line in the chapter. They had done it where no one saw. Someone saw.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Opposing God’s word shuts a man out of God’s good. Shemaiah of Nehelam, an exile, writes in his own name to the priest Zephaniah in Jerusalem, reminding him of his duty to put every “madman” who prophesies in the stocks, and asking why Jeremiah has not been silenced (vv. 24–28). His evidence is the letter’s gentlest lines: the exile will be long, so build and plant. Zephaniah reads the letter to Jeremiah instead (v. 29). God answers that Shemaiah, whom he never sent, made the people trust in a lie, so neither he nor his descendants will see the good God will do for his people (vv. 30–32).
verseByVerse.theology: He campaigned against the promise of restoration, and was excluded from it.

verseByVerse.quote: To Shemaiah of Nehelam you shall say: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have sent letters in your name to all the people who are in Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests, saying, 'The LORD has made you priest instead of Jehoiada the priest, to have charge in the house of the LORD over every madman who prophesies, to put him in the stocks and neck irons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shemaiah, an exile who rejects Jeremiah’s letter, writes in his own name to the temple authorities, demanding that Jeremiah be locked in the stocks as a madman.

You have sent letters in your name. Jeremiah’s letter provoked a reply, and the reply went over his head, to the temple authorities in Jerusalem. The phrase in your name sums up the charge against him: Jeremiah writes in the name of the LORD of hosts; Shemaiah writes in his own, and still expects the weight of God behind it.

Every madman who prophesies. He reminds the priest of his job description, which includes policing anyone who prophesies, and supplies the label in advance. Call the man unbalanced and you need not answer him; it saves the trouble of weighing whether what he said was true. The same label was later fixed on Jesus: “He has a demon, and is insane” (John 10:20).

The stocks and neck irons. Jeremiah had been in the stocks before, at the hands of Pashhur (20:2). Shemaiah knows exactly what he is asking for, and he asks from a safe distance, in a letter, with his own name on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth who is prophesying to you? For he has sent to us in Babylon, saying, "Your exile will be long; build houses and live in them, and plant gardens and eat their produce."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shemaiah’s whole case against Jeremiah is that he told the exiles the truth: the exile will be long, so settle down.

Why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth? The question is meant to shame the priest into acting, the standard move of a man who wants someone silenced and would rather another hand did it. And the address is a sneer: not the prophet, not the man God sent, but a villager from a small place whose own townsmen had once plotted to kill him (11:21). Reduce a man to the village he comes from and you need not reckon with his message.

Your exile will be long. Notice what finally provoked the campaign. It was not a threat or a curse. Shemaiah quotes back, accurately, the gentlest sentences in the letter: build houses, plant gardens. The intolerable part was what they implied, a long exile, which destroyed the hope he was selling. People will forgive a preacher a great deal sooner than they will forgive him for taking away a comfortable expectation, and the offence here is not harshness but realism about how long the trouble will last.

verseByVerse.quote: Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the hearing of Jeremiah the prophet. Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Send to all the exiles, saying, 'Thus says the LORD concerning Shemaiah of Nehelam: Because Shemaiah had prophesied to you when I did not send him, and has made you trust in a lie, therefore thus says the LORD: Behold, I will punish Shemaiah of Nehelam and his descendants. He shall not have anyone living among this people, and he shall not see the good that I will do to my people, declares the LORD, for he has spoken rebellion against the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priest quietly shows the letter to Jeremiah, and God sentences Shemaiah to be shut out of the good he will do for his people, the very good Shemaiah had argued away.

Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the hearing of Jeremiah. One sentence holds a quiet mercy. The priest who was being urged to put Jeremiah in irons took the letter to him and read it to him instead. Nothing is said of his motives. But this is how God has been protecting his prophet all along: Ahikam’s hand at the trial, the officials who convened a proper court, and now a temple official who declines to act on a poisonous letter.

Has made you trust in a lie. The two charges are Hananiah’s, in the same words: not sent, and has made you trust in a lie (28:15). The offence is never merely that the man was wrong. It is that people rested their weight on what he said.

He shall not see the good that I will do to my people. The sentence fits the crime with terrible precision. Shemaiah campaigned against the letter that promised a future and a hope, and he is left outside it. The penalty reaches his family too: he shall not have anyone living among this people means that no descendant of his would be among those who came home.

The good that I will do. Yet the sentence assumes something, and it is the chapter’s last word: there is good that God will do for his people. The letter that began by telling prisoners to unpack ends by taking that good for granted as the settled future of a battered congregation. God had sent them into exile and would visit them there, and the visiting was not finished at Cyrus’s decree. When John the Baptist was born, his father sang that God “has visited and redeemed his people” (Luke 1:68): the Lord himself came into the far country, sought the welfare of the city that would kill him, and prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 19:41–42; 23:34). Every exile who builds, plants and prays for the place God has put him is living on the strength of that.

29.title: The Letter to the Exiles
29.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 27 and 28 showed Jeremiah in Jerusalem wearing an ox’s yoke and contradicted by Hananiah, who promised that the exiles of 597 BC would be home within two years. Chapter 29 turns to those exiles, through a letter Jeremiah sends them in Babylon and the angry reply it provoked.

The message. Your exile is not an accident but an assignment: God himself sent you to Babylon, so do not sit on your luggage waiting for a quick return. Build, plant, marry and seek the welfare of the city that holds you, for the exile will be long, but God’s plans for you are for good, and he will be found by those who seek him with all their heart. The comfortable voices that promise otherwise are lying in his name.

Why it was said. The deportees of 597 BC, King Jeconiah, the officials and the craftsmen (see the introduction), were living in settlements in Babylonia while prophets among them promised an early homecoming, and they envied the relatives still in Jerusalem with its temple and its king (vv. 8–9, 15–16).

How the chapter makes its case. The letter and its couriers (vv. 1–3). Settle and seek Babylon’s welfare, because God sent you there (vv. 4–7). Do not believe the dreamers (vv. 8–9): the truth is seventy years and then a homecoming, for God’s plans are for welfare, and his people will seek him and find him (vv. 10–14). The relatives you envy are the rotten figs, facing sword, famine and pestilence because they would not listen (vv. 15–19). Two named liars in Babylon will be executed by Nebuchadnezzar (vv. 20–23). And Shemaiah, who demands that Jeremiah be put in the stocks, is shut out of the good God will do for his people (vv. 24–32).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the character of God. God’s people living as exiles, seeking the good of a city that is not their home, becomes the shape of the church’s life: Peter writes to Christians as “elect exiles” (1 Peter 1:1). And the God who promised to visit the exiles came in person. Zechariah sang that God “has visited and redeemed his people” (Luke 1:68), and Jesus wept over the city that would reject him. The future and the hope promised here are finally found in him, for all God’s promises “find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

For us. If you are somewhere you would never have chosen, God may have put you there with work to do. Do not waste your life waiting for it to end, and do not despair in it: put down roots, pray for your neighbours and your town, and refuse the voices that promise an easy way out. The God who planned good for exiles has not stopped meaning you good.
29.theology:
Exile is an assignment, not an accident: because God sent them, Babylon becomes a place with work to do in it (vv. 4, 7). So God's people seek the welfare of the city that holds them and pray for it, which is still the church's calling as exiles in this world.

God's good purpose does not mean no hardship; he firmly intends their good and brings it about through the hardship. The plans for welfare were sent to exiles with seventy years of captivity ahead. And grace comes before their seeking: God announces that they will seek him, and promises to be found (vv. 10-14).

False comfort costs the hearer his life, not just his theology (vv. 8-9), and a man’s preaching and his private life are judged together by the God who is witness to both (v. 23).
29.examples:
Building a house and planting a garden in a place you did not choose is an act of faith: it means accepting God's timetable and refusing both false hope and despair. So is praying for the good of the city that carried you off.

The best-loved verse of the chapter, often printed on mugs and cards, was first posted to a prison camp. Read there, it is not a promise of a better year but of a God who has not stopped meaning his people good.

keyVerse.quote: For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.
keyVerse.note: The whole letter rests on this verse. God tells exiles to unpack, seek Babylon’s good and wait seventy years because his intention toward them, through the exile and not merely after it, is their good. Spoken to a people, many of whom would die before the return, it promises not an easy year but a God who has not stopped meaning his people good, a promise that finds its Yes in Christ.

29.reflection:
God says that he himself sent the exiles to Babylon (vv. 4, 7). How does believing that God has placed you where you are change the way you live in a job, a town or a situation you did not choose?

God tells the exiles to seek the welfare of the city that had conquered them and to pray for it (v. 7). What would seeking the good of your own town or street look like this month, and who in it is hardest for you to pray for?

Jeremiah 29:11 is often quoted on its own. How does reading it alongside seventy years of exile (v. 10) and the call to seek God with all your heart (v. 13) change what it promises, and what it does not?

The false prophets told people what they wanted to hear, and Jeremiah was attacked for saying the trouble would be long (vv. 8–9, 28). Why are comfortable messages so attractive, and how can we help one another receive hard truth from God’s word?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Book, and a Day Like No Other
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s promises are written down for the people who will need them most, and they begin with honest terror. Jeremiah is told to write in a book all the words God has spoken, because days are coming when he will restore the fortunes of both Israel and Judah and bring them back to the land they will possess (vv. 1–3). Before the comfort comes the cry: panic and no peace, soldiers doubled over like women in labour, every face pale (vv. 4–6). It is a day so great there is none like it, a time of distress for Jacob, “yet he shall be saved out of it” (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The worst day in the story, and the promise of rescue is welded to it in the same sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you. For behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will restore the fortunes of my people, Israel and Judah, says the LORD, and I will bring them back to the land that I gave to their fathers, and they shall take possession of it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Jeremiah to write his promises in a book, because they are for a future generation: he will restore both halves of his broken people to their land.

Write in a book. After some forty years of preaching in the open air, Jeremiah is told to write it down. Spoken words reach the people in front of you; a book reaches those not yet born. What follows in chapters 30 to 33 is largely promise, and promise needs to outlive the preacher: the generation that would need these pages most would read them in Babylon, decades after Jeremiah was dead. It is also how we have them. A man in a besieged city can speak to the exiles, and to us, because God told him to write.

Israel and Judah. Israel, the northern kingdom, had been gone since 722 BC, deported by Assyria, its people scattered and assumed lost. Judah is about to follow. God names both halves of a broken nation and says he will restore the fortunes of both. The tribes nobody could find were still on God’s list, and the promise is specific: they shall take possession of it, not to visit but to hold. Remember that whenever something seems too far gone.

How is this return fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. But the promises reach beyond any return to territory: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. They are fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), and they will be complete in the new creation. On either reading below, Jewish people are saved as everyone is, by faith in Jesus their Messiah.

Where Christians differ: the land and Israel’s future. Dispensationalists look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel; they answer that promises made to Israel by name should be kept to Israel by name, and they deserve a careful hearing. Reformed Christians themselves differ over whether Romans 11:26 foretells a large-scale turning of Jewish people to Christ before the end, as many Puritans believed, or the full number of the elect from Israel saved through history. This commentary’s view: the land promises widen in Christ to the whole renewed earth (Romans 4:13; Matthew 5:5), because the New Testament treats them that way; and Paul most naturally looks for a great turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:26), within the one people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the words that the LORD spoke concerning Israel and Judah: "Thus says the LORD: We have heard a cry of panic, of terror, and no peace. Ask now, and see, can a man bear a child? Why then do I see every man with his hands on his stomach like a woman in labor? Why has every face turned pale?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Book of Consolation opens not with comfort but with screaming: God describes the coming terror honestly, as strong men left as helpless as women in labour.

A cry of panic, of terror, and no peace. Before any comfort is offered, the trouble is described honestly, and no peace lands on the exact word the false prophets had been handing out for chapters. They said peace; God reports panic. Real comfort never begins by understating the situation.

Can a man bear a child? The image is deliberately grotesque, the strongest picture of helplessness available. Soldiers, the men who were supposed to defend the city, are doubled over, hands on their stomachs, in the posture of a woman in labour. Something is happening to them that they can neither stop nor escape. Yet labour is not an image of pointless agony. It is pain with an outcome, terrible and productive at once, which is exactly what this day will turn out to be for Jacob.

verseByVerse.quote: Alas! That day is so great there is none like it; it is a time of distress for Jacob; yet he shall be saved out of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of distress will be like no other, and Jacob will be saved not from it but out of it. The whole book is in this one verse.

That day is so great there is none like it. It is beyond anything in the nation’s memory, and the prophets use this language for the day of the LORD itself: “A day of wrath is that day, a day of distress and anguish, a day of ruin and devastation” (Zephaniah 1:15).

A time of distress for Jacob. Jacob and Israel are paired as two names for the nation (v. 10), but Jacob may also recall the schemer who limped away from a night of wrestling with God. The distress is his, and it is deserved.

Yet he shall be saved out of it. Here is the hinge of the chapter, one word: yet. He is not spared the day or diverted around it, but saved out of the middle of it. God does not promise his people an easier day than the one that is coming. He promises that the day will not have the last word on them.

Where Christians differ: is this “the time of Jacob’s trouble” (as older translations put it), the future Great Tribulation? Dispensationalists read it so, as a seven-year period of distress for the Jewish nation before Christ returns. This commentary’s view: in context it is the terror of the Babylonian conquest (vv. 5–6), followed by rescue (vv. 8–9) under David their king, fulfilled in Christ. The Lord Jesus uses the same kind of language for the end, “then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now” (Matthew 24:21), so the verse looks at Babylon and beyond it; faithful readers differ on how far.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — Fear Not, Jacob My Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s rescue means a change of master, and his discipline never becomes destruction. In that day God will break the yoke from his people’s neck and burst their bonds, and foreigners will no longer enslave them (v. 8). Instead they will serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom God will raise up (v. 9). So Jacob, God’s servant, need not fear: God will save him from far away, bring his offspring back, and give him quiet and ease (v. 10). The reason is God’s presence, “I am with you to save you”, and his covenant: he will make a full end of the nations, but not of Israel, whom he will discipline in just measure (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The yoke this book has spent chapters fastening on is broken by the same hand that fastened it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall come to pass in that day, declares the LORD of hosts, that I will break his yoke from off your neck, and I will burst your bonds, and foreigners shall no more make a servant of him. But they shall serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself will break the yoke of foreign rule, and his freed people will serve him and the King from David’s line whom he will raise up.

I will break his yoke from off your neck. The yoke is back: the wood Jeremiah wore through the streets, the iron God said would replace it when Hananiah snapped the bars (28:10–14). Now the hand that put it on takes it off. Hananiah broke a yoke and died for it; God breaks this one himself. That is the whole difference between rebellion and redemption. The same yoke, removed by the wrong hand at the wrong time, is a lie; removed by God in his day, it is salvation.

But they shall serve the LORD their God. Freedom here does not mean serving no one; it means a change of master. They stop serving foreigners and start serving God, and a king.

David their king, whom I will raise up for them. David had been dead nearly four hundred years. The promise is of a David God will raise up, and the other prophets say it in the same terms: “I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23); the people will “seek the LORD their God, and David their king” in the latter days (Hosea 3:5). When it finally happened, Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, sang that God “has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David” (Luke 1:69).

Uncertain wording. The pronouns in verse 8 shift (his yoke, your neck, a servant of him), as often in Hebrew poetry, and the closing clause may also be rendered “serve him”, as the ESV notes. The sense is not in doubt: Israel will no longer be at the disposal of foreign masters.
verseByVerse.note: Ezekiel also calls the coming king simply “David”, and says he will be their prince for ever (Ezek 37:24-25).

verseByVerse.quote: "Then fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares the LORD, nor be dismayed, O Israel; for behold, I will save you from far away, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob shall return and have quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid. For I am with you to save you, declares the LORD; I will make a full end of all the nations among whom I scattered you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells his people not to fear, because he is with them to save them: he will discipline them as a father, but he will never make an end of them.

Fear not, O Jacob my servant. After the labour pains and the pale faces come two words, and the title attached is tender. This is the nation whose guilt is called great and whose sins are called flagrant a few verses later, addressed by God as his servant. The relationship is not suspended while the discipline runs.

Quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid. The promise is domestic and small-scale, which is what frightened people actually need. It is not empire, and not revenge, but sleep without fear.

I am with you to save you. The ground of the comfort is a person: not better circumstances, not a shorter exile, but his presence.

Of you I will not make a full end. Here is a distinction the whole Bible runs on. The nations get a full end; his people do not. The difference is not that Judah sinned less, for the next verses say her guilt is great. The difference is the covenant, God’s own promise binding him to this people.

I will discipline you in just measure. The last clause refuses to make that soft: I will by no means leave you unpunished. God’s people are not exempt from discipline; they are exempt from destruction. In just measure means the chastening is measured by a father, not unleashed by an enemy, and that is why sin in a believer’s life is dealt with rather than overlooked.

How do I “fear not”? Fear is not beaten by ordering yourself to stop feeling it. God does not say “fear not” and leave it there; he gives a reason, for I am with you to save you, so take the fear to the reason. Name it. At 2 a.m. tell God exactly what you are afraid of: the scan result, the redundancy letter, the child who will not speak to you. Set a promise against it. “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you” (Psalm 56:3): the psalm assumes the fear will come, and tells you where to put your weight when it does. Look at the cross, not the odds. “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). A God who has done that will not abandon you halfway. Do the next faithful thing. Make the phone call, keep the appointment, tell the truth in the meeting. You may meet discipline on the way; you will not meet a full end. In Christ, “I am with you” has a name, and he has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — No Healing for You, and I Will Heal You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wound God inflicted is beyond every human cure, and God himself will heal it. He pronounces the diagnosis: the hurt is incurable, there is no advocate, no medicine, no healing, and the allies Judah courted have forgotten her (vv. 12–14). The blow is his own, “the blow of an enemy”, because her guilt is great and her sins flagrant, and her cries change nothing (vv. 14–15). Then comes a “therefore” no one could predict: those who devoured her will be devoured, and God will restore her health and heal her wounds, because her enemies called her the outcast for whom no one cares (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: God pronounces the case terminal, and then heals it, for no reason found in the patient.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: Your hurt is incurable, and your wound is grievous. There is none to uphold your cause, no medicine for your wound, no healing for you. All your lovers have forgotten you; they care nothing for you; for I have dealt you the blow of an enemy, the punishment of a merciless foe, because your guilt is great, because your sins are flagrant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God pronounces his people’s wound incurable and the blow his own, sent because their guilt is great. No human remedy can touch it.

No medicine for your wound, no healing for you. Read the list of what is unavailable: no advocate, no medicine, no healing. Earlier Jeremiah had asked, “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there?” (8:22), and here is the answer, from God himself. Nothing in the pharmacy touches this. This is the honesty that makes the gospel possible. Until a man believes his condition is beyond treatment, every offer of grace sounds like an optional extra. Judah’s problem was never that she lacked good advice.

All your lovers have forgotten you. The lovers are the allies she courted instead of trusting God: Egypt, Assyria, the alliances that chapter 2 pictures as love affairs. They have moved on, as such lovers do.

I have dealt you the blow of an enemy. Then the hardest sentence. It was not Babylon’s blow but God’s, delivered with the force of a merciless foe. He does not hide behind the army he used or blame the politics of the day. The reason is stated without embarrassment, because your guilt is great, because your sins are flagrant, and a God who names the cause is a God who can be reasoned with about a cure.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you cry out over your hurt? Your pain is incurable. Because your guilt is great, because your sins are flagrant, I have done these things to you. Therefore all who devour you shall be devoured, and all your foes, every one of them, shall go into captivity; those who plunder you shall be plundered, and all who prey on you I will make a prey. For I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal, declares the LORD, because they have called you an outcast: 'It is Zion, for whom no one cares!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
With nothing changed in his guilty people, God turns on their enemies and promises to heal the wound no one else could, because the world had written Zion off.

Why do you cry out over your hurt? The question has an edge. Why cry out, as though this were unjust or unforeseen? She had been told, persistently, for forty years.

Therefore all who devour you shall be devoured. Therefore is the last word anyone would expect after that accusation. By ordinary moral reasoning it does not follow: your guilt is great, your sins are flagrant, therefore your enemies will be destroyed. Nothing in the patient has changed between verse 15 and verse 16. And the instruments God used are themselves judged: being used by God did not make Babylon innocent, a lesson the empire would learn when its own seventy years ran out.

Your wounds I will heal. The incurable is cured, by the only physician who was ever going to do it. And the stated reason is striking: not her repentance, not her improvement, but the contempt of her enemies. They said, It is Zion, for whom no one cares! God will not leave that sentence standing about his own people.

How the wound is healed. How God heals a wound he inflicted, without pretending the guilt away, is the question this chapter raises and does not answer. The answer comes from the wounds of another: “he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). The blow of an enemy fell, in the end, on him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — The Prince Who Dares Draw Near
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will rebuild his people’s life, and at its centre will be a ruler who can come near to him. The tents of Jacob will be restored, the city rebuilt on its mound, and songs of thanksgiving will rise from people who will no longer be few or small (vv. 18–19). Their children and congregation will be established before God, and their oppressors punished (v. 20). Their prince will be one of themselves, and God will bring him near, for no one would dare of himself to approach God (v. 21). All of it serves the covenant promise: “you shall be my people, and I will be your God” (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: One of their own, brought near by God to do what no one would dare attempt on his own account.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD: Behold, I will restore the fortunes of the tents of Jacob and have compassion on his dwellings; the city shall be rebuilt on its mound, and the palace shall stand where it used to be. Out of them shall come songs of thanksgiving, and the voices of those who celebrate. I will multiply them, and they shall not be few; I will make them honored, and they shall not be small.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will have compassion on the ruins and rebuild his people’s life on the old site, filling it with thanksgiving and multiplying those who feared they would dwindle away.

The city shall be rebuilt on its mound. The promise is specific and unglamorous: tents, dwellings, a city rebuilt on its mound, the same rubble heap on the old site. Ancient cities were rebuilt layer upon layer on their own ruins, and God promises not a better location but this one, restored.

Have compassion on his dwellings. The word governing it all is compassion. The God who dealt the blow of an enemy has compassion on the houses of the people he struck, a combination only the cross finally explains.

Songs of thanksgiving. For chapters the sound has been mourning, lament and the cry of panic; now the noise coming out of the ruins is thanksgiving and celebration.

I will multiply them, and they shall not be few. Each promise is stated both ways: multiplied and not be few, honoured and not be small. God answers their fear of dwindling away directly. The few who are left, who felt like nothing, are told they will not stay few.

verseByVerse.quote: Their children shall be as they were of old, and their congregation shall be established before me, and I will punish all who oppress them. Their prince shall be one of themselves; their ruler shall come out from their midst; I will make him draw near, and he shall approach me, for who would dare of himself to approach me? declares the LORD. And you shall be my people, and I will be your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises a ruler from among his own people whom he himself will bring near to his presence, where no one dares come of himself, and through him the covenant will stand: you shall be my people.

Their children shall be as they were of old. The restoration reaches backwards, repairing what the generations had lost, and creates a congregation established before me: a worshipping people who can come before God again.

Their prince shall be one of themselves. Here is the summit of the chapter. The ruler will not be a foreign governor but one of their own, and his defining act is not military or administrative. It is priestly: I will make him draw near, and he shall approach me.

Who would dare of himself to approach me? The question stops every religious project in its tracks. Nobody. That is the honest answer, and Israel’s whole system of temple curtains and courts, with one entrance a year by the high priest alone on the Day of Atonement, existed to say so. A prince who is both from among the people and able to approach God is a figure the Old Testament keeps sketching and never produces.

He dared, and takes us in with him. Hebrews does not quote this verse, but it names the figure: “since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near” (Hebrews 10:19–22). One of ourselves, brought near by God, he “is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him” (Hebrews 7:25). Nobody would dare of himself. He dared, and takes us in with him.

You shall be my people, and I will be your God. Then comes the covenant sentence, the thing all of it was for. It is not real estate or independence but belonging, and it is still being spoken at the end of the Bible: “they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3).

Why we no longer tremble. Most people today who believe in God at all assume he can be approached on any terms: warm, informal and above all safe. Who would dare? sounds like a relic of a more fearful age. Yet the age that lost the fear of God has hardly lost fear; it has moved it onto the economy, the climate and the opinions of strangers. Annie Dillard once wrote that if churchgoers grasped the power they so casually invoke, they would come in crash helmets and the ushers would hand out life preservers. The Bible will not let us have it either way. The moralist approaches God on the strength of his own record, and the casual modern on the strength of God’s niceness, and both assume a right to walk in. Nobody has one. But the answer is not to stay outside trembling. It is the Prince who dared, and who went in by way of a cross, so that we may now “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16): with confidence, because of him, and still with awe, because “our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29).

Uncertain wording. Who would dare of himself renders a compressed Hebrew idiom, literally something like “who is he who would pledge his heart to approach me?”: who would stake his very life on coming near? The general sense is clear; the exact force of the idiom is debated, but it underlines the danger of approaching God uninvited.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–24 — The Storm of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The promise of healing does not cancel God’s judgment on evil. The storm of the LORD goes out, a whirling tempest that will burst on the head of the wicked (v. 23). His fierce anger will not turn back until he has carried out all he intends, and the people are told that they will understand this in the latter days (v. 24). The comfort of the chapter is for people rescued from something real, and the same resolve that drives the storm stands behind every promise.
verseByVerse.theology: Comfort that has a storm at the end of it is the only kind worth having.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold the storm of the LORD! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked. The fierce anger of the LORD will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intentions of his mind. In the latter days you will understand this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter of comfort ends with God’s storm on the wicked, because his healing never means that evil stops mattering, and his purpose will be understood later.

Behold the storm of the LORD! After all that comfort, a storm. It reads like an intrusion until you notice what it protects. A promise of restoration that quietly dropped the subject of judgment would be a promise that evil simply stops mattering. Instead the chapter that healed an incurable wound insists in its last breath that wrath has gone forth and will burst upon the head of the wicked. The comfort is for people who needed rescuing from something real.

Words heard before. These lines are almost exactly those of 23:19–20, where the storm was aimed at the prophets who promised peace. Repeated here, at the close of a chapter of promises, they mark the difference between God’s comfort and the cheap peace those prophets sold.

Will not turn back. God’s anger is not a temper that flares and cools; it is a purpose he carries through until he has executed and accomplished the intentions of his mind. That is a fearful sentence about the wicked and a steadying one about everything else God intends, since the same resolve stands behind the promises in this chapter.

In the latter days you will understand this. The last line is a hand on the shoulder of anyone reading too early. Not now. The generation holding this book in Babylon could not see how a wound God inflicted could be a wound God heals, or how a prince could walk in where nobody dares. Later, they would. We read it on the far side of a cross, where the storm and the healing turn out to have met in one place.

30.title: Write It in a Book: The Healing of an Incurable Wound
30.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 29 told the exiles to settle in Babylon for seventy years. Now the book turns almost wholly to hope: chapters 30 to 33 are often called the Book of Consolation, and chapter 30 opens it with a command to write these promises down.

The message. The wound is real and so is the healing, and both come from God’s hand. A day of distress like no other is coming on Jacob, deserved and beyond human remedy, yet he will be saved out of it. The God who struck the blow will heal the wound, break the yoke, raise up David their king and bring near a prince who dares approach him, so that the covenant stands: “you shall be my people, and I will be your God” (v. 22).

Why it was said. Judah was about to lose city, temple and king, and the north had been lost for over a century (see the introduction). A people facing the worst day in their history needed a written hope, honest about the disaster, that they could carry into exile and read when the preacher was gone.

How the chapter makes its case. The words are to be written, because God will restore both Israel and Judah (vv. 1–3). First the terror, strong men doubled over like women in labour, yet Jacob shall be saved out of it (vv. 4–7). God will break the yoke and raise up David their king; so fear not, for he disciplines in just measure but makes no full end of his people (vv. 8–11). The wound is incurable and the blow his own (vv. 12–15), and then, with nothing changed in the patient, he promises to heal it (vv. 16–17). The city will ring with song, and a prince from among them will be brought near to God (vv. 18–22). The storm of his wrath on the wicked closes the chapter (vv. 23–24).

Where it leads. By promise and by the need it exposes. God promises “David their king, whom I will raise up” (v. 9), and at John the Baptist’s birth his father sang that God “has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David” (Luke 1:69). The prince who is one of the people yet brought near to God (v. 21) is the priest-king Jesus, who “is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him” (Hebrews 7:25). And the incurable wound exposes a need only he meets: the blow fell on him, and “with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).

For us. God does not promise his people an easier day than the one coming; he promises that it will not have the last word. His discipline is a Father’s and never ends in destruction. No one may walk into his presence on his own record, but in Christ, the Prince who dared, we may draw near with confidence and still with awe.
30.theology:
God does not promise his people an easier day than the one coming, but that the day will not have the last word (v. 7). Because of his covenant they are exempt from destruction, never from discipline, and the discipline is measured out as a father measures it (v. 11).

He himself declares the wound incurable and then heals it, for the sake of his own honour and not for anything in the patient (vv. 12-17); and the one who will draw near to God for his people is one of themselves, brought near by God (v. 21). The storm at the end guards the healing at the centre: comfort that dropped the subject of wrath would mean evil no longer mattered (vv. 23-24).
30.examples:
The Book of Consolation opens with screaming, and that is a lesson for anyone who comforts the suffering: real comfort never begins by understating the trouble.

For frightened people the promise is small and domestic: not empire or revenge, but quiet, ease and sleep without fear, grounded in a person: I am with you to save you.

keyVerse.quote: Alas! That day is so great there is none like it; it is a time of distress for Jacob; yet he shall be saved out of it.
keyVerse.note: The chapter turns on the word “yet”. God does not hide the coming disaster or promise his people a way around it, but he promises to save them out of the middle of it. Every comfort that follows, the broken yoke, the healed wound and the prince who draws near, unpacks that one word.

30.reflection:
The Book of Consolation begins with a cry of panic and “no peace” (vv. 5–7). Why does true comfort start by telling the truth about the trouble, and how can we comfort others in the same way?

God promises to discipline his people “in just measure” but never to make “a full end” of them (v. 11). How does knowing the difference between a Father’s discipline and an enemy’s destruction change how you read hard times in your own life?

God calls the wound incurable and then says, “your wounds I will heal” (vv. 12–17). Where have you tried to treat sin or guilt with your own remedies, and what does Isaiah 53:5 say about how God heals it?

“Who would dare of himself to approach me?” (v. 21). How do Christ’s priestly work and Hebrews 10:19–22 shape the way you come to God in prayer, with both confidence and awe?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Loved with an Everlasting Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s everlasting love is the ground of a joyful homecoming. He will be the God of all the clans of Israel, including the tribes long scattered, because he has loved them “with an everlasting love” and so kept faith with them (vv. 1–3). Therefore the ruined nation will be built again: tambourines and dancing, vineyards on the hills of Samaria, and northern watchmen calling their people to worship in Zion (vv. 4–6). God will gather them from the ends of the earth, the blind, the lame and women in labour among them, leading them weeping by brooks of water as a father and shepherd who ransomed them (vv. 7–11). They will be radiant over his goodness, and he will turn their mourning into joy (vv. 12–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything promised here rests on a love that started before the ruin and did not depend on it ending.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time, declares the LORD, I will be the God of all the clans of Israel, and they shall be my people." Thus says the LORD: "The people who survived the sword found grace in the wilderness; when Israel sought for rest, the LORD appeared to him from far away. I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will be the God of every scattered tribe, because he has loved his people with an everlasting love, and that love, not their record, is why he keeps faith with them.

All the clans of Israel. The chapter opens with the promise the whole Bible is driving at, that God will be their God and they will be his people, and it is made to all the clans: the ten tribes lost to Assyria more than a century before, written off by everyone as gone, included by name.

Found grace in the wilderness. The picture reaches back to the exodus: survivors of the sword, out in the desert, finding grace there. That was the pattern once and it will be again. God meets his people in the wilderness, not after they have got themselves home. And he appeared to him from far away: the distance is crossed from God’s side.

I have loved you with an everlasting love. Here is the ground of everything that follows, and it is nothing in them. A love with no beginning cannot have been started by anything Israel did, and a love with no end cannot be stopped by anything Israel did either. It was not switched on by her obedience in the wilderness and it was not switched off by her adultery in Canaan.

Therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you. His love is the cause and his faithfulness the result. He keeps on with this people because he loved them first, which is the only explanation the Bible ever gives for why any of us are still here.

Textual note. The ESV notes that where the main text reads that the LORD appeared to him from far away, following the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation), the Hebrew reads “me”. Either way the meaning stands: God appears, and comes the distance himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I will build you, and you shall be built, O virgin Israel! Again you shall adorn yourself with tambourines and shall go forth in the dance of the merrymakers. Again you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria; the planters shall plant and shall enjoy the fruit. For there shall be a day when watchmen will call in the hill country of Ephraim: 'Arise, and let us go up to Zion, to the LORD our God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will build his ruined people again, to joy and dancing, to vineyards that take years to bear, and to a reunited worship in Zion.

Again I will build you. Three times in two verses comes the word again: built again, dancing again, planting again. It is chosen to comfort, because the fear of a ruined people is not that God is unable but that the good days are simply over.

O virgin Israel! Consider what he calls her: the nation this book has called a prostitute, a faithless wife, a camel in heat. The name is not a polite fiction; it is what God intends to make her, and he uses the future name now.

In the dance of the merrymakers. The restoration is not solemn. It is tambourines and dancing, the noise of a village wedding.

Plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria. Samaria is the old northern capital, the heartland of the tribes everyone had given up on, and the promise is of vineyards there: a crop that takes years to bear, planted by people who expect to be around to drink the wine. The covenant curse, that they would plant vineyards and others would enjoy the fruit (Deuteronomy 28:30), is lifted.

Let us go up to Zion. Then the most unlikely sentence yet. Ephraim was northern territory, where rival shrines had stood for two centuries so that nobody would go up to Zion; now its watchmen call their own people to worship in Jerusalem. The division that split the kingdom is healed from the northern side.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: "Sing aloud with gladness for Jacob, and raise shouts for the chief of the nations; proclaim, give praise, and say, 'O LORD, save your people, the remnant of Israel.' Behold, I will bring them from the north country and gather them from the farthest parts of the earth, among them the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and she who is in labor, together; a great company, they shall return here. With weeping they shall come, and with pleas for mercy I will lead them back, I will make them walk by brooks of water, in a straight path in which they shall not stumble, for I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will gather his people from the ends of the earth and lead them home gently, the weakest included, because he is their father.

Sing aloud with gladness for Jacob. They are told to sing the rescue before it happens, and to pray for it in the same breath: O LORD, save your people. Praise and asking are not two separate steps here; the certainty of the promise is what makes the asking confident.

The blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and she who is in labor. Consider who is on this march: not the fit and the useful, but the four groups any commander would leave behind, because a column moves at the pace of its slowest member. God lists them deliberately. A rescue that quietly loses the weak on the road is not the rescue he is describing; nobody here is expendable, and the party travels at the speed of the woman in labour.

With weeping they shall come. They come home crying. The tears are not a failure of faith but the sound of repentance, and God leads a weeping people gently, by brooks of water, on a straight path chosen so that they will not stumble.

I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn. The reason is family. Ephraim, of all names, the tribe that led the rebellion and the shorthand for everything that went wrong in the north, is called the firstborn son.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear the word of the LORD, O nations, and declare it in the coastlands far away; say, 'He who scattered Israel will gather him, and will keep him as a shepherd keeps his flock.' For the LORD has ransomed Jacob and has redeemed him from hands too strong for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations must hear that the God who scattered Israel will gather and keep his people, for he has ransomed them from a power too strong for them.

Hear the word of the LORD, O nations. The nations are called as witnesses. They had watched the scattering and drawn the obvious conclusion, that Israel’s God was weak or finished, and now they are told to publish the correction as far as the coastlands reach.

He who scattered Israel will gather him. The sentence holds both halves together without flinching. No rival power scattered them. The scatterer and the gatherer are the same person, and the hand that drove the flock apart is the hand that will keep it, as a shepherd keeps his flock (see shepherds and sheepfolds).

The LORD has ransomed Jacob and has redeemed him. Two words of rescue: ransomed, the price paid to set a slave free, and redeemed, a kinsman buying back a relative or his land. And a phrase explains why it had to be God’s work: from hands too strong for him. Jacob was not held by something he could have shaken off with more effort. Babylon was stronger than him, and so was the sin that put him there. That is why, throughout this chapter, it is always God who acts: I will build, I will gather, I will lead, I have ransomed.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall come and sing aloud on the height of Zion, and they shall be radiant over the goodness of the LORD, over the grain, the wine, and the oil, and over the young of the flock and the herd; their life shall be like a watered garden, and they shall languish no more. Then shall the young women rejoice in the dance, and the young men and the old shall be merry. I will turn their mourning into joy; I will comfort them, and give them gladness for sorrow. I will feast the soul of the priests with abundance, and my people shall be satisfied with my goodness, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The redeemed will be radiant over God’s goodness, in plenty and in joy, as he turns their very mourning into gladness and satisfies them with himself.

Radiant over the goodness of the LORD. Their faces shine, and what they shine about is named: grain, wine, oil, lambs, calves. It is ordinary provision, received as goodness from a person.

Like a watered garden. The image would land hard on people who knew what a dry season did to a field. Everything in this book about drought, cracked cisterns and withered pasture is reversed in four words.

The young women rejoice in the dance. Three generations dance in the same sentence: girls, young men and the old. The community that lost its future is given one with children in it.

I will turn their mourning into joy. The verb is turn. God does not merely replace the mourning with joy once it has run its course; he turns the thing itself. The grief is not deleted from their history; it is changed into gladness, which is a harder and better promise.

My people shall be satisfied with my goodness. This book opened with people digging broken cisterns that could hold no water, having forsaken the fountain (2:13). Here the thirst is finally met, and met with God’s own goodness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — Rachel's Tears and Ephraim's Return
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God hears the grief of his people and the prayer of the penitent, and answers both with mercy. A voice is heard in Ramah: Rachel weeping for her children, refusing comfort, and God answers not with a rebuke but with a promise that her children will come back (vv. 15–17). He has overheard Ephraim confessing that he was like an untrained calf and praying, “bring me back that I may be restored”, and he answers with a father’s yearning: “I will surely have mercy on him” (vv. 18–20). So Israel, the wavering daughter, is to mark the road home, for God has created a new thing on the earth (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: God overhears a prayer for the very turning he commands, and answers it with yearning.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping. Rachel is weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more." Thus says the LORD: "Keep your voice from weeping, and your eyes from tears, for there is a reward for your work, declares the LORD, and they shall come back from the land of the enemy. There is hope for your future, declares the LORD, and your children shall come back to their own country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God hears Rachel weeping for her lost children and answers her grief not with a rebuke but with a promise: they will come back.

A voice is heard in Ramah. In the middle of the singing, someone is crying, and God stops the chapter to listen.

Rachel is weeping for her children. Rachel is Jacob’s beloved wife, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and her tomb was remembered in Benjamin’s territory (1 Samuel 10:2). Ramah, a few miles north of Jerusalem, is where the deportees were later gathered in chains before the march to Babylon (40:1). So the poem pictures the long-dead mother of the tribes watching her descendants marched past her grave, and weeping.

She refuses to be comforted. She is not rebuked for it. Some griefs should not be hurried into comfort. Parents who have buried a child may take that as permission: God does not hurry their tears, and he answers them, as he does here, with a promise rather than a lecture.

They shall come back from the land of the enemy. God does not answer the tears with an explanation but with a fact. When he tells her to keep her voice from weeping, it is because he has news for her, not because her grief was wrong. And he calls her grief your work, with a reward attached: the years of weeping over lost children are counted as labour that will be paid. There is hope for your future is said to a woman in a graveyard, which is where that sentence is needed most.

Matthew hears it again. Matthew heard this verse again on a night in Bethlehem when Herod’s soldiers came for the children: “A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more” (Matthew 2:18).
