The mothers of Bethlehem wept while the child who would one day wipe away every tear was carried to safety in Egypt.

How does Herod’s slaughter “fulfil” this? Jeremiah pictures Rachel weeping for her children going into exile, with God’s promise that they will return (vv. 16–17). Matthew sees the same grief at Bethlehem and the same hope: the Child who escaped would bring the true return from exile (Matthew 2:17–18). Scripture links Rachel’s tomb both with the road to Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19) and with Benjamin’s territory (1 Samuel 10:2); Ramah and Bethlehem both lie a few miles from Jerusalem, and Matthew’s point is the pattern, not the map. “Fulfil” here means that the exile’s grief, and its promised end, reach their full meaning in Jesus’ story.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah himself was later released from his chains at Ramah, where the captives were gathered for Babylon (40:1).

verseByVerse.quote: I have heard Ephraim grieving, 'You have disciplined me, and I was disciplined, like an untrained calf; bring me back that I may be restored, for you are the LORD my God. For after I had turned away, I relented, and after I was instructed, I struck my thigh; I was ashamed, and I was confounded, because I bore the disgrace of my youth.' Is Ephraim my dear son? Is he my darling child? For as often as I speak against him, I do remember him still. Therefore my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy on him, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has overheard Ephraim confessing his sin and asking to be brought back, and he answers with a father’s aching love and a promise of mercy.

I have heard Ephraim grieving. God has been listening to his son talk to himself. The image Ephraim reaches for is honest: like an untrained calf, a young animal that fights the yoke and has to be broken to be any use. He does not dispute the discipline or ask for it to stop.

Bring me back that I may be restored. Here is the prayer at the heart of all true conversion. He asks God to do the turning, knowing he cannot return by his own strength. This is the answer to the question the book pressed when it asked whether a leopard can change its spots (13:23): the return God commands is the return God must give.

I struck my thigh. Striking the thigh is a gesture of grief at oneself. The order matters: the turning came first, then the instruction, then the shame. Deep sorrow over sin often comes last, not first; the shame here is the fruit of being brought back, not the price paid for it.

Is Ephraim my dear son? God answers with two questions, and answers them by the way he asks them. Even while pronouncing judgment, as often as I speak against him, he never stopped remembering him.

My heart yearns for him. The Hebrew speaks literally of the inward parts, the bowels, stirred for him: the physical seat of feeling, the churn you feel in your stomach over someone you love. This is not mild, distant goodwill. It is a father who cannot get his son out of his mind, the father of the parable running down the road to the son who was “still a long way off” (Luke 15:20).

Uncertain wording. After I had turned away, I relented renders a Hebrew phrase, literally “after my turning, I repented”, that can mean either turning away from God or being turned back to him. The ESV takes it as straying followed by repentance; others read it as the turning God gave in answer to the prayer of verse 18, followed by sorrow. Either way, repentance and shame follow God’s work rather than earning it.
verseByVerse.note: Hosea heard the same struggle in God's heart over Ephraim: My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender (Hos 11:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "Set up road markers for yourself; make yourself guideposts; consider well the highway, the road by which you went. Return, O virgin Israel, return to these your cities. How long will you waver, O faithless daughter? For the LORD has created a new thing on the earth: a woman encircles a man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells his wavering people to mark the road home as they go into exile, because he is about to do something new that only he can create.

Set up road markers for yourself. Here is a practical instruction for people about to be marched away: mark the route. Pile the stones, note the landmarks, pay attention to the road you are being taken along, because you are coming back down it. It is a strange comfort, to plan the journey home while still going out, and it treats the promise as solid enough to plan a route by.

How long will you waver, O faithless daughter? The rebuke is gentle and impatient at once. The wavering is the old habit of trying to keep both God and the other things they trusted.

The LORD has created a new thing on the earth. Created is the verb Genesis uses when God makes the heavens and the earth. Something is coming that reverses the expected order, and it will be God’s own creation rather than Israel’s achievement. That is the direction the whole chapter runs: the faithless daughter will be made new by an act of creation, not by finally pulling herself together.

Uncertain wording. A woman encircles a man has long puzzled readers, and it is better to say so: the words are plain and the sense is not. The likeliest meaning is that Israel, the faithless daughter, will at last embrace and cling to her LORD; others suggest a reversal of roles in a land so safe that women protect men. Some early Christians saw the virgin conceiving a son, but that reads more into the words than they say.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–30 — Watching to Build and to Plant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who watched over the tearing down will watch over the building and planting. The old blessing on Jerusalem will be heard again, town and country will live together, and God will satisfy the weary and replenish every languishing soul, a vision so sweet that the prophet wakes from it refreshed (vv. 23–26). God will resow the land with people and animals, and watch over the rebuilding as carefully as he watched over the ruin (vv. 27–28). The sour-grapes proverb, which blamed the fathers for the children’s suffering, will be retired: each will answer for his own sin (vv. 29–30).
verseByVerse.theology: The same watchfulness that pulled the nation down is now set to building it.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Once more they shall use these words in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I restore their fortunes: "'The LORD bless you, O habitation of righteousness, O holy hill!' And Judah and all its cities shall dwell there together, and the farmers and those who wander with their flocks. For I will satisfy the weary soul, and every languishing soul I will replenish." At this I awoke and looked, and my sleep was pleasant to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will make Jerusalem a home of righteousness again and refresh every weary soul, and the prophet wakes from this vision with the only sweet sleep the book records.

O habitation of righteousness, O holy hill! An old blessing comes back into everyday use, the sort of thing neighbours say to each other in the street. And the name it gives Jerusalem is what the city had stopped being.

The farmers and those who wander with their flocks. Ordinary society is knitted back together: settled farmers and wandering herdsmen living in the same land without preying on each other.

I will satisfy the weary soul. Two words for exhaustion, weary and languishing, and two promises, to satisfy and to replenish. This is the pastoral centre of the chapter for anyone reading it tired. The Lord Jesus makes the same offer: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

At this I awoke and looked, and my sleep was pleasant to me. Here the prophet himself appears, waking up. Think what his nights had been: the boiling pot, the drought, the broken flask, the trial for his life, the stocks, the day he cursed his own birth. Now, after being shown all this, he records that his sleep had been sweet. It is the only moment of personal comfort he is given in the entire book, and it comes from having seen what God intends to do.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and the seed of beast. And it shall come to pass that as I have watched over them to pluck up and break down, to overthrow, destroy, and bring harm, so I will watch over them to build and to plant, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who carefully watched over his people’s demolition will watch just as carefully over their rebuilding.

I will sow the house of Israel. The emptied land is resown, and the metaphor is agricultural: God scatters people across it as a farmer scatters grain. Both houses come back, with their livestock, a country coming back to life down to its herds.

To pluck up and break down … to build and to plant. These are the words of Jeremiah’s calling forty years earlier (1:10). For four decades he has been announcing the tearing down, and here the building and planting finally get their turn. The repeated word is watched over: God was not careless in the demolition and will not be casual in the rebuilding. The ruin was never a loss of control, and the restoration will not be left to chance. For a man who had spent his life announcing the tearing down, it must have been something to be told that he had always been serving the building and the planting.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days they shall no longer say: "'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge.' But everyone shall die for his own iniquity. Each man who eats sour grapes, his teeth shall be set on edge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one will be able to blame his ancestors for his sin any longer: each will answer to God for himself, and that is the doorway to a personal new beginning.

The fathers have eaten sour grapes. The proverb was the popular theology of a defeated generation, and it was a complaint: our grandfathers sinned and we are the ones with our teeth on edge. There was truth in it, because consequences do run downhill through families and nations, but as they used it, it said that nothing they did mattered either way. Ezekiel was told to stop the same saying among the exiles: “this proverb shall no more be used by you in Israel” (Ezekiel 18:3).

Everyone shall die for his own iniquity. The answer is not that inherited consequence is a myth. It is that no one will be able to hide behind it: each person is dealt with by God directly, for what he himself has done.

Just before the new covenant. That sounds severe until you see where it sits. It comes immediately before the new covenant, where God deals with each person individually in mercy, writing on this heart, knowing this man, forgetting these sins. The end of hiding behind your ancestors is also the end of being trapped by them.

Isn’t everyone simply a product of their past? The sour-grapes proverb has a modern edition. The biologist Robert Sapolsky argued in Determined (2023) that free will is an illusion: every choice is the sum of genes, hormones, childhood and culture, so nobody truly deserves praise or blame. Everyday speech says something gentler: I am like this because of how I was raised. There is real truth in it, and Scripture itself traces how sin runs down the generations. But notice the cost. If no one is answerable, no one can be forgiven either, because there is nothing to forgive, and change becomes only a change of causes. The fatalist explains the prisoner and then leaves him in the cell. God is more radical than either the moralist, who says try harder, or the fatalist, who says you cannot help it. He holds each person answerable, and then offers each a new beginning that no family history can block: “you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises a new covenant that does what the old one could not. It will be made with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, unlike the covenant made when he took their fathers by the hand out of Egypt, which they broke though he was their husband (vv. 31–32). In the new covenant he will put his law within them and write it on their hearts; he will be their God and they his people; every member, from the least to the greatest, will know him; and underneath it all, he will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more (vv. 33–34).
verseByVerse.theology: The law moves from tablets to hearts, and the sins move out of God's memory.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, my covenant that they broke, though I was their husband, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises a new covenant, not a repair of the old one that Israel broke though he had been a faithful husband to them.

A new covenant. This is the sentence the rest of the Bible is built on, and the phrase new covenant appears nowhere else in the Old Testament: this is where it is given. Consider who says it and when. A prophet in a doomed city, watching the old arrangement collapse, announces that God’s answer is not a repair but something new, and it is promised to the same two houses that had just finished breaking the old one.

The day when I took them by the hand. The tenderness of the memory is startling: like a father teaching a child to walk, God led them out of Egypt. That is how he remembers the exodus.

My covenant that they broke, though I was their husband. The failure is stated without excuse, followed by words that carry the ache of the whole book (see weddings and betrothal). The problem with the old covenant was never its terms, which were holy, or its giver. One party to a marriage kept the vows and the other did not. Hebrews quotes this passage at length and draws the conclusion: God “finds fault with them” (Hebrews 8:8), not with the covenant. A law written on stone can tell you what to do but cannot make you want to do it.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish readers hear this as God’s promise to renew, not replace, the covenant of Sinai: the same Torah, written no longer only on stone but on Israel’s heart, so that the people at last keep it. Many place its fulfilment in the days of the Messiah, and note that it is made with Israel and Judah. This commentary agrees that the law is not changed but written within, and that the promise belongs to Israel. It reads it as begun in Jesus, who called the cup “the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20), and as opened to Gentiles grafted into Israel’s olive tree (Romans 11:17).

Where Christians differ: is the new covenant with Israel or with the church? It is promised to the house of Israel and the house of Judah, and dispensationalists hold that it awaits fulfilment with national Israel. Many dispensationalists today agree that the church already shares in its blessings through Christ, while still expecting a future fulfilment for national Israel; faithful Christians differ on that second part. This commentary’s view: Jesus established it in his blood at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews applies this passage to the church (Hebrews 8:6–13). It is made with the true Israel, Jews and Gentiles who believe in Christ (Galatians 6:16; Romans 11:17), because the New Testament applies the whole promise, forgiveness and the law on the heart, to every believer now (Hebrews 10:15–18).
verseByVerse.note: Hebrews quotes verses 31-34 in full (Heb 8:8-12), the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, and returns to them in 10:16-17.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no longer shall each one teach his neighbor and each his brother, saying, 'Know the LORD,' for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the new covenant God writes his law on his people’s hearts, makes every member truly know him, and forgives their sin so completely that he remembers it no more.

I will put my law within them. The law does not change. The place where it is written does. The old covenant put God’s commands on tablets outside the man, where they instructed him and condemned him and could not help him. The new one writes the same law on their hearts, which answers exactly the diagnosis this book has made for thirty chapters: sin engraved on the tablet of the heart (17:1), a heart deceitful above all things (17:9), a people who could no more change than a leopard its spots (13:23). If the problem is the heart, only a new heart is a solution. Paul saw it happen in his converts: “a letter from Christ … written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3).

Duty or desire? Our culture is torn between two ways of being good. One says morality is duty: rules you keep whether you feel like it or not. The other says the only authentic life flows from your own desires, and any rule imposed from outside is a kind of violence against the self. The first produces people who are upright and joyless; the second, people who are free and adrift. The new covenant overturns both. It does not abolish the law to liberate the heart, nor set the law against the heart to tame it. It writes the law on the heart, so that what God commands and what we want begin to be the same thing. Augustine put the result in a famous sentence: “Love, and do what you will.” He did not mean that love excuses anything, but that a remade heart wants what God wants. Only one person has ever lived like that completely, and the psalm puts it on his lips: “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8; Hebrews 10:5–7). The new covenant is his Spirit, writing that same delight in us.

They shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest. Under the old arrangement the covenant community was a mixed body, including circumcised men who did not know God at all, which is why they had to be told to know him. In the new one, membership and knowing God are the same thing. Teaching does not end, but nobody inside this covenant needs to be introduced to its God: the child and the scholar stand on the same footing.

What it means to know the LORD. We use know in two ways. I know who the prime minister is; I know my wife. The first is information; the second is a relationship, and the new covenant promises the second. To know the LORD is not merely to hold correct opinions about him but to be on speaking terms with him, trusting and trusted; the Hebrew uses the same word for the closeness of husband and wife. Timothy Keller often pointed out that a real relationship needs a God who can contradict you: a God who only ever agrees with you is not a person you know but an idea you are managing. So knowing him starts where this verse starts, with God speaking and God forgiving. Jesus said, “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3), and Paul corrects himself in mid-sentence: “now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God” (Galatians 4:9). He knew us first. So when a passage of his word cuts across what you wanted, do not explain it away. Take it as the sign that you are dealing with someone real, and answer him.

For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more. The foundation comes last, introduced with for, because it is the reason the rest is possible. Not overlook, not suspend: God puts his people’s sin out of his own memory. It cost him everything to be able to say it. On the last night, holding a cup, the Lord told his friends what would make this covenant new in fact and not only in promise: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). Hebrews, having quoted these verses twice, rests the whole assurance of a Christian on the final clause: “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more” (Hebrews 10:17).

Where Christians differ: if all in the new covenant know the LORD, what of a church with unbelievers in it? Paedobaptists, with the Westminster Confession, read the covenants as more continuous: the covenant community, like Israel, includes the children of believers, and some who do not truly know God. Presbyterian and other paedobaptist brothers hold this view from Scripture with equal seriousness. This commentary’s view: this verse marks the difference between the covenants. In the new, every member knows the Lord, so the church should receive by baptism those who profess faith, though no church can see hearts perfectly. That is the view of the 1689 London Baptist Confession, which this commentary follows.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 35–40 — As Fixed as the Sunrise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God stakes the future of his people on the order of creation and the immensity of the heavens. The LORD who gives the sun by day and fixes the moon and stars by night says that only if that order fails will Israel’s offspring cease to be a nation before him (vv. 35–36), and only if the heavens could be measured would he cast them off for all they have done (v. 37). Then the city is surveyed for rebuilding, its measuring line going out farther than before, and even the valley of the dead bodies and the ashes becomes sacred to the LORD, never to be uprooted again (vv. 38–40).
verseByVerse.theology: The valley where they burned their children is the last plot of land God claims as holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, who gives the sun for light by day and the fixed order of the moon and the stars for light by night, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar— the LORD of hosts is his name: "If this fixed order departs from before me, declares the LORD, then shall the offspring of Israel cease from being a nation before me forever." Thus says the LORD: "If the heavens above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth below can be explored, then I will cast off all the offspring of Israel for all that they have done, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God stakes the future of his people on the fixed order of the heavens: as surely as the sun rises, he will not cast them off, whatever they have done.

Who gives the sun for light by day. Before the guarantee come the credentials. The God about to make a promise is the one who runs the sun, the moon, the stars and the tides.

If this fixed order departs from before me. The logic is simple: only if sun, moon and stars leave their order will Israel cease to be a nation before God. Her future is as secure as sunrise, and anyone doubting it may test it against the evidence every morning. And this is said of a nation that was, at that moment, being dismantled. Nothing in its circumstances suggested it would survive; it was staked on the constancy of the God who keeps the moon in its course.

If the heavens above can be measured. The second guarantee rests on immensity rather than regularity: only if someone could measure the sky and explore the foundations of the earth would God cast Israel off. No one can.

For all that they have done. The last clause is honest. God does not minimise the record. The guilt is real and it is not the deciding factor, because the question was never whether they deserved to be cast off.

Where Christians differ: does this guarantee ethnic Israel’s future as a nation? It promises that God will never cast off the offspring of Israel, and Paul says the same: “God has not rejected his people” (Romans 11:2). Christian Zionists and many dispensationalists see the modern State of Israel as a fulfilment of such promises. This commentary’s view: the promise here is God’s faithfulness to save, not a guarantee of a modern state or territory. On the most natural reading Paul looks for a great turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:26), and Jewish people remain “beloved for the sake of their forefathers” (Romans 11:28), to be loved and prayed for.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when the city shall be rebuilt for the LORD from the Tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate. And the measuring line shall go out farther, straight to the hill Gareb, and shall then turn to Goah. The whole valley of the dead bodies and the ashes, and all the fields as far as the brook Kidron, to the corner of the Horse Gate toward the east, shall be sacred to the LORD. It shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rebuilt city will be bigger than the old and wholly holy, taking in even its most defiled ground, and it will never be uprooted again.

From the Tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate. The chapter ends with a survey. Named towers, named gates and a measuring line pulled across specific hills give the promise as a plan an engineer could work from. The Tower of Hananel stood at the north-east of the city wall (Nehemiah 3:1; 12:39) and the Corner Gate probably at the north-west (2 Kings 14:13), so the survey begins along the northern wall; that tower was among the first stretches of wall rebuilt after the return (Nehemiah 3:1). And the line goes out farther: the picture seems to be of a city larger than the one about to be destroyed.

The whole valley of the dead bodies and the ashes. Of every acre God could have chosen for the last word of this chapter, he takes the worst. This is most likely the ravine below the city, the Valley of Hinnom, where Jeremiah had stood with a clay flask and called it the Valley of Slaughter, where they had burned their own children to Baal (19:5–6). It was the most defiled ground in Israel, and its name became the New Testament’s word for hell. That valley, God says, shall be sacred to the LORD.

What the new covenant does. The book that began by measuring a nation’s guilt ends this chapter by measuring a city that includes its own worst place inside the holy ground. This is what the new covenant does. It does not quarantine the shameful part of the record and build around it; it takes the ash heap into the city and calls it holy, and fixes the boundary with a promise that has no expiry: It shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever. The words of tearing down from Jeremiah’s calling are used one last time, now to say what will never happen again.

Uncertain wording. The hill Gareb and the place Goah are mentioned nowhere else and can no longer be located, though the survey seems to continue round the city before reaching the Kidron valley and the Horse Gate on the east. The identification of the valley of the dead bodies and the ashes with the Valley of Hinnom is likely but not certain.

31.title: The New Covenant
31.overview:
Where we are. This is the heart of the Book of Consolation (chapters 30–33). Chapter 30 promised that the God who wounded his people would heal them; chapter 31 takes the promise further than any page in the Old Testament, to a new covenant.

The message. God’s love for his people is everlasting, older than their failure and stronger than their sin, so he will bring them home, the weakest included, and turn their mourning into joy. And because the old covenant failed through their hearts, not its terms, he will make a new one: his law written on their hearts, every member knowing him, and their sin remembered no more. That promise is as fixed as the sunrise.

Why it was said. It was spoken to a nation being dismantled: the north long scattered, Jerusalem about to fall, and a people whose heart, as this book has shown, could no more change than a leopard its spots (13:23; see the introduction). Their ruin needed not a repair but a new beginning only God could make.

How the chapter makes its case. Everything rests on “an everlasting love” (vv. 1–3): so God will rebuild the nation with dancing and vineyards and gather it from the ends of the earth, the blind and the lame among them (vv. 4–14). Rachel weeps for her lost children and is promised their return; Ephraim pleads to be brought back, and God’s heart yearns for him (vv. 15–22). The God who watched over the tearing down will watch over the building and planting (vv. 23–30). Then the new covenant: the law on the heart, all knowing God, sin remembered no more (vv. 31–34). Israel’s future is staked on the heavens, and the rebuilt city takes in even the valley of the dead as holy ground (vv. 35–40).

Where it leads. By covenant, and directly. On the night he was betrayed Jesus took the cup and said, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews quotes this passage as fulfilled in him (Hebrews 8:8–12; 10:15–18). The forgiveness at its foundation was paid for at the cross, and the law is written on the heart by his Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:3). By pattern too: Matthew hears Rachel weeping again at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18), where the child who would bring the true return from exile was carried to safety.

For us. You were loved before you failed, and nothing in your record can end an everlasting love. God does not leave the weak behind on the road home, and he hears the prayer “bring me back”. In Christ he has written his law on your heart and forgotten your sins, so you may know him, not merely about him, and come to want what he wants.
31.theology:
Everything here rests on an everlasting love. Israel's obedience did not start it and her sin cannot end it, and God keeps faith with her because he loved her first (v. 3). The scatterer and the gatherer are the same person, and the rescue had to be his because Jacob was held by hands too strong for him (vv. 10-11).

Even repentance is asked for as a gift (v. 18). The new covenant differs from the old not in its law but in where the law is written, and its foundation is forgiveness: God puts his people's sin out of his own memory (vv. 33-34). And grace claims the worst ground, taking the valley of the dead inside the holy city for ever (v. 40).
31.examples:
To people who think the good days are over, God says again, three times. To a nation he had called faithless he gives her future name, virgin Israel. And he sets the pace of the journey home by the woman in labour, so that nobody is left on the road.

To a weeping mother he speaks of hope; to a son ashamed of himself he shows a father who cannot get him out of his mind; and to all of us he promises a law written inside us and sins put out of his memory.

keyVerse.quote: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
keyVerse.note: This is the Old Testament’s only use of the phrase “new covenant”, and its centre. The law does not change; the place where it is written does, answering the book’s diagnosis of a hopelessly sinful heart with a heart remade by God. Jesus took these words onto his lips at the Last Supper and sealed them with his blood.

31.reflection:
God says, “I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you” (v. 3). How does it change your view of your own failures to know that God’s love did not begin with your good behaviour and will not end with your bad?

The march home includes “the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and she who is in labor” (v. 8), and Rachel is not rebuked for refusing comfort (v. 15). What do these verses teach about how our church should treat the weak and the grieving?

Ephraim prays, “bring me back that I may be restored” (v. 18). Why must God do the turning, and how does that shape the way we pray for ourselves and for others who have wandered?

In the new covenant God writes his law on our hearts and remembers our sin no more (vv. 33–34). Where do you still treat God’s commands as outside rules rather than desires he is writing within you, and how does his forgiveness free you to change?

32.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar.<sup>2</sup>At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the guard that was in the palace of the king of Judah.<sup>3</sup>For Zedekiah king of Judah had imprisoned him, saying, "Why do you prophesy and say, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall capture it;<sup>4</sup>Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him face to face and see him eye to eye.<sup>5</sup>And he shall take Zedekiah to Babylon, and there he shall remain until I visit him, declares the LORD. Though you fight against the Chaldeans, you shall not succeed'?"<sup>6</sup>Jeremiah said, "The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>7</sup>Behold, Hanamel the son of Shallum your uncle will come to you and say, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth, for the right of redemption by purchase is yours.'<sup>8</sup>Then Hanamel my cousin came to me in the court of the guard, in accordance with the word of the LORD, and said to me, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for the right of possession and redemption is yours; buy it for yourself.' Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>"And I bought the field at Anathoth from Hanamel my cousin, and weighed out the money to him, seventeen shekels of silver.<sup>10</sup>I signed the deed, sealed it, got witnesses, and weighed the money on scales.<sup>11</sup>Then I took the sealed deed of purchase, containing the terms and conditions and the open copy.<sup>12</sup>And I gave the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah son of Mahseiah, in the presence of Hanamel my cousin, in the presence of the witnesses who signed the deed of purchase, and in the presence of all the Judeans who were sitting in the court of the guard.<sup>13</sup>I charged Baruch in their presence, saying,<sup>14</sup>'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Take these deeds, both this sealed deed of purchase and this open deed, and put them in an earthenware vessel, that they may last for a long time.<sup>15</sup>For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land.'<sup>16</sup>"After I had given the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed to the LORD, saying:<sup>17</sup>'Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm! Nothing is too hard for you.<sup>18</sup>You show steadfast love to thousands, but you repay the guilt of fathers to their children after them, O great and mighty God, whose name is the LORD of hosts,<sup>19</sup>great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of man, rewarding each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.<sup>20</sup>You have shown signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and to this day in Israel and among all mankind, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day.<sup>21</sup>You brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and outstretched arm, and with great terror.<sup>22</sup>And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>23</sup>And they entered and took possession of it. But they did not obey your voice or walk in your law. They did nothing of all you commanded them to do. Therefore you have made all this disaster come upon them.<sup>24</sup>Behold, the siege mounds have come up to the city to take it, and because of sword and famine and pestilence the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans who are fighting against it. What you spoke has come to pass, and behold, you see it.<sup>25</sup>Yet you, O Lord GOD, have said to me, "Buy the field for money and get witnesses"—though the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans.'"<sup>26</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>27</sup>"Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too hard for me?<sup>28</sup>Therefore, thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hands of the Chaldeans and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall capture it.<sup>29</sup>The Chaldeans who are fighting against this city shall come and set this city on fire and burn it, with the houses on whose roofs offerings have been made to Baal and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods, to provoke me to anger.<sup>30</sup>For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth. The children of Israel have done nothing but provoke me to anger by the work of their hands, declares the LORD.<sup>31</sup>This city has aroused my anger and wrath, from the day it was built to this day, so that I will remove it from my sight<sup>32</sup>because of all the evil of the children of Israel and the children of Judah that they did to provoke me to anger— their kings and their officials, their priests and their prophets, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.<sup>33</sup>They have turned to me their back and not their face. And though I have taught them persistently, they have not listened to receive instruction.<sup>34</sup>They set up their abominations in the house that is called by my name, to defile it.<sup>35</sup>They built the high places of Baal in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to offer up their sons and daughters to Molech, though I did not command them, nor did it enter into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin.<sup>36</sup>"Now therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning this city of which you say, 'It is given into the hand of the king of Babylon by sword, by famine, and by pestilence':<sup>37</sup>Behold, I will gather them from all the countries to which I drove them in my anger and my wrath and in great indignation. I will bring them back to this place, and I will make them dwell in safety.<sup>38</sup>And they shall be my people, and I will be their God.<sup>39</sup>I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever, for their own good and the good of their children after them.<sup>40</sup>I will make with them an everlasting covenant, that I will not turn away from doing good to them. And I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me.<sup>41</sup>I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will plant them in this land in faithfulness, with all my heart and all my soul.<sup>42</sup>"For thus says the LORD: Just as I have brought all this great disaster upon this people, so I will bring upon them all the good that I promise them.<sup>43</sup>Fields shall be bought in this land of which you are saying, 'It is a desolation, without man or beast; it is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.'<sup>44</sup>Fields shall be bought for money, and deeds shall be signed and sealed and witnessed, in the land of Benjamin, in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, in the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb; for I will restore their fortunes, declares the LORD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — A Field Bought in a Besieged City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A prisoner buys a field in a country under sentence, because God has promised the land a future. The scene is set with care: the Babylonian army is round Jerusalem, and Zedekiah has shut Jeremiah in the court of the guard for saying the city will fall (vv. 1–5). God tells him his cousin Hanamel will come and offer him the family field at Anathoth, and Hanamel does (vv. 6–8). Jeremiah pays seventeen shekels, signs, seals and witnesses the deed, and has both copies stored in a clay jar to last a long time (vv. 9–14). Then God gives the meaning: houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: A prisoner buys real estate in a country that is about to be confiscated, and has the paperwork witnessed.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar. At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the guard that was in the palace of the king of Judah. For Zedekiah king of Judah had imprisoned him, saying, "Why do you prophesy and say, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall capture it; Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him face to face and see him eye to eye. And he shall take Zedekiah to Babylon, and there he shall remain until I visit him, declares the LORD. Though you fight against the Chaldeans, you shall not succeed'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that follows came in the darkest hour: Babylon at the walls, and God’s prophet in jail for saying so. Everything in the chapter depends on fixing this setting first.

In the tenth year of Zedekiah. It is 588 or 587 BC, the year before the city fell. The Babylonian army is camped round the walls and food is running out. Jeremiah is under arrest in the palace compound. Chapters 37 and 38 tell how he came there: arrested at the city gate as a supposed deserter during a lull in the siege, beaten, kept in a cellar, then moved to this courtyard by the king (37:11–21). It is an unpromising moment for a property transaction.

Why do you prophesy? The king’s question is almost plaintive. He does not ask whether it is true, but why Jeremiah keeps saying it. Zedekiah spends this whole book half-believing Jeremiah and never acting on it, and here he jails the man rather than answer him.

See him eye to eye. This was fulfilled with terrible precision. Zedekiah was brought before Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, watched his sons killed, and was then blinded (52:9–11). He saw the king of Babylon eye to eye, and the last thing those eyes saw was his own sons dying.

Until I visit him. Even here the wording is open. In this book God’s visiting can mean coming in judgment or in mercy; it is the same verb that carried the promise to the exiles (29:10). Scripture does not tell us which Zedekiah met; it records only that he died a prisoner in Babylon (52:11).
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 37 and 38 tell how Jeremiah came to be confined in the court of the guard.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah said, "The word of the LORD came to me: Behold, Hanamel the son of Shallum your uncle will come to you and say, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth, for the right of redemption by purchase is yours.' Then Hanamel my cousin came to me in the court of the guard, in accordance with the word of the LORD, and said to me, 'Buy my field that is at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for the right of possession and redemption is yours; buy it for yourself.' Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Jeremiah in advance that his cousin will offer him the family field, and when Hanamel walks in and says exactly that, Jeremiah knows the purchase is God’s command.

Hanamel the son of Shallum your uncle will come to you. God tells him what is about to happen, and it is nothing spectacular: a relative is going to turn up with a business proposition.

The right of redemption by purchase is yours. When an Israelite fell into poverty and had to sell family land, the nearest kinsman had the right and duty to buy it, keeping the inheritance in the family: “his nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what his brother has sold” (Leviticus 25:25). It is what Boaz did at the town gate, calling the elders to witness that he had bought the inheritance of a dead man to keep his name alive (Ruth 4:9–10).

Buy my field that is at Anathoth. Hanamel’s motive is easy to guess and not held against him. Anathoth lay about three miles north-east of Jerusalem, in country the Babylonians already held. The field was worthless and he wanted out. In business terms he was selling a loss, and God had told his prophet to be the buyer.

Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD. The confirmation came by no vision or voice. It came when a cousin walked into the guardhouse and said what God had said he would say. God often confirms his word through the ordinary run of events.

A picture of Christ. Christians have long heard in this law a picture of Christ, though Jeremiah does not draw it. The redeemer had to be a near kinsman, and the Son of God became our brother, sharing our flesh and blood “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death” (Hebrews 2:14), and buying back an inheritance we had lost and could never recover.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I bought the field at Anathoth from Hanamel my cousin, and weighed out the money to him, seventeen shekels of silver. I signed the deed, sealed it, got witnesses, and weighed the money on scales. Then I took the sealed deed of purchase, containing the terms and conditions and the open copy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah really paid, with full legal formality, for land he would never use: faith acting on God’s word with silver and signatures.

Seventeen shekels of silver. He paid. That is the whole force of the sign: real silver, seventeen shekels, recorded exactly, as a man records a sum he has genuinely parted with. Faith here is not a feeling about the future. It is money leaving a purse for land the buyer will never walk on, in a district under enemy control, paid by a man who had just been told the country was finished.

I signed the deed, sealed it, got witnesses, and weighed the money. Each of the four verbs is ordinary legal procedure for selling land, the silver weighed on scales because coins were not yet in use. God’s prophet does not make a gesture; he completes a binding sale with the correct formalities in front of observers. There is something bracing in that: an extravagant act of hope carried out with paperwork. Faith that expects God to keep his word will generally look like something concrete and slightly inconvenient rather than an inspiring mood.

The sealed deed of purchase … and the open copy. Two documents were made, as was standard practice: a sealed copy that could not be tampered with, and an open copy for consultation. Both are kept, because the sale is meant to be checked generations later by people who will need to know exactly where the boundary ran.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “containing the terms and conditions” (v. 11) is two legal words, literally “the commandment and the statutes”, and their exact sense here is not known. They most likely refer to the terms of the sale written in the deed, as the ESV takes them; some think they describe the sealed copy itself or the legal form it followed. The point is clear either way: the sale was done properly.
verseByVerse.note: Seventeen shekels was about 7 ounces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: And I gave the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah son of Mahseiah, in the presence of Hanamel my cousin, in the presence of the witnesses who signed the deed of purchase, and in the presence of all the Judeans who were sitting in the court of the guard. I charged Baruch in their presence, saying, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Take these deeds, both this sealed deed of purchase and this open deed, and put them in an earthenware vessel, that they may last for a long time. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The deeds are stored in a jar to last for decades, and God explains the sign: normal life will one day return to this land.

Baruch the son of Neriah. Here Baruch appears, the scribe who will write this book at Jeremiah’s dictation (36:4). Note the audience: the cousin, the witnesses, and “all the Judeans who were sitting in the court of the guard”, a yard full of prisoners and hangers-on watching a man buy a field he could not reach. The sign was public on purpose. In a city where everyone was calculating how long the food would last, here was a man behaving as though there would be a Judah in which to own land.

Put them in an earthenware vessel. The deeds go into a clay jar “that they may last for a long time”, which quietly admits how long this will take. Jeremiah will never use the field himself; the jar is for somebody’s grandchildren. Sealed pottery is how the ancient world kept what mattered, and how the Dead Sea Scrolls survived two thousand years in the same region. Hope with a long timescale needs a container.

Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land. The interpretation is given after the act, not before it. The point of the purchase was never the field but this sentence: markets open, families buying property, ordinary life restored in the country whose destruction had just been guaranteed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–25 — Nothing Is Too Hard for You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah has obeyed; now he prays, and his prayer is a pattern for faithful bewilderment. He begins with the Creator, for whom nothing is too hard (vv. 16–17), and with God’s own description of himself: steadfast love, real justice, wisdom, power and eyes that see everything (vv. 18–19). He recites the exodus and the gift of the land (vv. 20–22), agrees without complaint that Judah’s disobedience has brought the disaster now visible from the window (vv. 23–24), and only then lays his question down, half-finished: yet you told me to buy a field (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: He obeyed first and asked his question afterwards, which is the right order.

verseByVerse.quote: "After I had given the deed of purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed to the LORD, saying: 'Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm! Nothing is too hard for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having obeyed without understanding, Jeremiah takes his confusion to God, and starts not with the problem but with the Creator for whom nothing is too hard.

After I had given the deed of purchase. The order matters. He obeyed, completed the sale, filed the deeds, and then prayed about it. The obedience did not wait for the explanation.

Ah, Lord GOD! The prayer opens with a sigh, the sound of a man who has done something he does not understand and has come to talk about it.

Nothing is too hard for you. Before any question he states what he knows: God made the heavens and the earth. That is the right foundation for a confused prayer. He begins with the Creator, and the problem is measured against him rather than the other way round.

Borrowed words. When Sarah laughed behind a tent flap at the idea of a baby, the LORD said to Abraham, “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14). The same truth was told to a girl in Nazareth in the plainest form: “For nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). A barren womb, a doomed city, a virgin: the question turns up wherever God’s promise looks physically ridiculous, and it was answered for good when God raised his Son from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: You show steadfast love to thousands, but you repay the guilt of fathers to their children after them, O great and mighty God, whose name is the LORD of hosts, great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of man, rewarding each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah prays God’s own self-description back to him, love and justice, wisdom and power, eyes that miss nothing, without editing out the parts that hurt.

You show steadfast love to thousands, but you repay the guilt of fathers. He holds together two things we find easier to separate. The words come from the moment God proclaimed his name to Moses: “keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children” (Exodus 34:7). He does not trim them to make the prayer more comfortable. Praying honestly means praying to the God who is actually there, including the justice now battering his city. And note the proportion: love reaches thousands, the visiting of guilt three or four generations. Even in the verse that warns, mercy is the larger number.

Great in counsel and mighty in deed. God both knows what he is doing and is able to do it, the two things a man in a besieged city most needs to believe. Wisdom without power would be tragic; power without wisdom would be terrifying.

Whose eyes are open to all the ways of the children of man. Nothing in the siege, the guardhouse or the conduct of the men who put him there is unobserved.

According to the fruit of his deeds. God had already said this of himself: “I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds” (17:10). When a situation makes no sense, the safest way to pray is often not with a theory but with what God has said.

Does God punish children for their fathers’ guilt, when 31:30 says each dies for his own sin? Each is judged for his own guilt; but sin’s consequences fall on families, and children who continue in their fathers’ sin share their judgment (Exodus 20:5, “of those who hate me”).

verseByVerse.quote: You have shown signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and to this day in Israel and among all mankind, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day. You brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and outstretched arm, and with great terror. And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah reasons from what God has done, the exodus and the gift of the land, and so lays bare the painful contradiction: the land God swore to give is about to be taken away.

Signs and wonders in the land of Egypt. The prayer turns to history, where Israel always went for confidence. He does not reason from his circumstances to God’s character, but from what God has already done. This is not nostalgia. It is how a believer talks himself into hope: God has done the impossible before, with witnesses, and the record is public.

With a strong hand and outstretched arm. So a prisoner recites the exodus during a siege. “Outstretched arm” is the phrase he has just used of creation (v. 17): the arm that made the world is the arm that emptied Egypt, and it has not grown weaker.

Which you swore to their fathers. The land was a gift and an oath, and that is what makes the moment so painful to pray about. The field he has just bought is part of a gift God swore to give, and it is about to be taken away. He lays that contradiction before God rather than resolving it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And they entered and took possession of it. But they did not obey your voice or walk in your law. They did nothing of all you commanded them to do. Therefore you have made all this disaster come upon them. Behold, the siege mounds have come up to the city to take it, and because of sword and famine and pestilence the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans who are fighting against it. What you spoke has come to pass, and behold, you see it. Yet you, O Lord GOD, have said to me, "Buy the field for money and get witnesses"—though the city is given into the hands of the Chaldeans.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah agrees that the disaster is just, describes the siege outside the window, and then sets God’s command beside it, unresolved: yet you told me to buy a field.

They did nothing of all you commanded them to do. The prophet’s prayer contains no defence of his people, and the disaster is traced to its author without complaint: “you have made all this disaster come upon them.” He is not asking God to be fair. He agrees with the verdict, which is the only honest place to pray from.

Behold, the siege mounds have come up to the city. He describes what is out of the window: earth ramps rising against the wall, sword, famine and pestilence arriving as the book had warned, and a flat acknowledgement, “What you spoke has come to pass.” He had been called a traitor for forty years for saying this, and there is no note of triumph in it at all.

Yet you, O Lord GOD, have said to me, “Buy the field.” There is the question, and it is left unfinished. Everything you said would happen is happening, yet you told me to buy a field. He does not accuse God, and he does not pretend to understand. He sets the command beside the circumstances and leaves both in God’s hands. That is what faithful bewilderment sounds like, and it is open to anyone who has obeyed something he could not explain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–35 — Is Anything Too Hard for Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers bewilderment by handing the prophet’s own confession back to him, and then by refusing to soften the facts. “Is anything too hard for me?” (vv. 26–27). Yes, the city will be burned, with the very roofs where offerings were poured to Baal (vv. 28–29). The indictment is complete: evil from the nation’s youth and from the day the city was built, shared by kings, priests, prophets and people alike (vv. 30–32), a people who turned their backs on a patient teacher, defiled his house and burned their children in the valley below the city (vv. 33–35).
verseByVerse.theology: The same question stands over both the judgment and the promise.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too hard for me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers Jeremiah’s confession by turning it into a question: if nothing is too hard for the God of all flesh, then a field bought in a doomed land is no contradiction.

Is anything too hard for me? God answers the prayer by quoting it. Jeremiah had said, “Nothing is too hard for you”; God replies, “Is anything too hard for me?” It is the gentlest possible correction, and a real one. The prophet had stated the doctrine and then laid a difficulty beside it as though the two might not fit. God takes his own confession and makes it the answer. What we mostly need in bewilderment is not new information but the application of what we already say we believe.

The God of all flesh. The title is exact for the occasion. He is not the God of Judah only, whose reach ends at a besieged wall, but of every living thing: the Babylonian army, the cousin selling a field, and the generations who will one day open a clay jar.

Zechariah heard it too. After the exile, when the few who had returned thought the promised restoration too great to believe, God asked through Zechariah, “If it is marvelous in the sight of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my sight?” (Zechariah 8:6). What looks impossible to people standing in rubble does not look impossible from where God stands.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hands of the Chaldeans and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall capture it. The Chaldeans who are fighting against this city shall come and set this city on fire and burn it, with the houses on whose roofs offerings have been made to Baal and drink offerings have been poured out to other gods, to provoke me to anger. For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have done nothing but evil in my sight from their youth. The children of Israel have done nothing but provoke me to anger by the work of their hands, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not answer the hard question by softening the facts: the city will fall and burn, homes and all, because its sin is real.

I am giving this city into the hands of the Chaldeans. The first thing God says after “Is anything too hard for me?” is that the city will fall. The comfort will come, but not at the cost of the truth.

The houses on whose roofs offerings have been made to Baal. The detail is precise and damning. Flat roofs were where families sat in the evening, and they had been using them as private altars. Those same houses are named as fuel.

Nothing but evil in my sight from their youth. The verdict has nothing good to say, and it matters that it comes here, in a chapter of promise. The restoration a few verses on will not rest on finding the nation better than it seemed. The record is read out at full severity first.

verseByVerse.quote: This city has aroused my anger and wrath, from the day it was built to this day, so that I will remove it from my sight because of all the evil of the children of Israel and the children of Judah that they did to provoke me to anger— their kings and their officials, their priests and their prophets, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem has provoked God from its foundation, and every class shares the guilt, so whatever God does next will be grace from the ground up.

From the day it was built. Not since Manasseh, not since the monarchy went bad, but from the beginning. God’s review of Jerusalem finds no golden age to appeal to, and that clears away any idea that the restoration is a return to an earlier, purer city. There was never one. Ezekiel said it more bluntly: “Your origin and your birth are of the land of the Canaanites; your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite” (Ezekiel 16:3). Jerusalem had been a pagan city before David took it, and it never fully stopped being one.

Their kings and their officials. The list runs from the palace to the street: kings, officials, priests, prophets, the men of Judah, the people of Jerusalem. No class is exempt, and nobody is left to blame the others.

The golden age that never was. Almost every movement runs on a story about a golden age. For some it lies behind us: the country before it was spoiled, the church before it lost its way, the family as it used to be. For others it lies ahead, in the just society we will build once the old one is cleared away. Both stories name the villains and promise that, with the right people in charge, paradise can be recovered or constructed (on politics as a substitute religion, see the note on Acts 17:6–7). God’s review of Jerusalem pulls the ground from under both. That is not cynicism but the lifting of a burden. If no generation is the golden one, then no generation, ours included, has to be idolised or demonised, and no programme has to carry the weight of salvation. The hope of Scripture is a city God builds himself. The patriarchs “desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16), and its gate was opened by a King who was led out of the old city to die.

verseByVerse.quote: They have turned to me their back and not their face. And though I have taught them persistently, they have not listened to receive instruction. They set up their abominations in the house that is called by my name, to defile it. They built the high places of Baal in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to offer up their sons and daughters to Molech, though I did not command them, nor did it enter into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heart of the charge is a people who turned their backs on a patient Teacher, defiled his house, and burned their own children, something God never commanded or wanted.

Their back and not their face. The image is domestic and wounding: not argument or rival theology, but the posture of someone who has decided not to look at you.

Though I have taught them persistently. The adverb of this whole book (7:13, 25). God is the long-suffering teacher, sending prophet after prophet into a classroom whose pupils face the wall.

Their abominations in the house that is called by my name. They set up idols inside the temple. The building existed to display his name and was used to insult it.

To offer up their sons and daughters to Molech. The charges end with the worst: the high places in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, below the city, where they burned their children (7:31; 19:5). And God adds a clause about himself that is almost unbearable to read: “nor did it enter into my mind.” Whatever the worshippers told themselves about devotion and cost, God disowns the whole idea.

The same valley made holy. This valley is very likely the ground God promised in 31:40 would be “sacred to the LORD.” The place named here as the lowest point of Judah’s guilt is named there as holy, and between the two stands everything the gospel has to do. The gospel did it outside the walls of this city, where the Son was given up by his Father, not as a child sacrificed to an idol, but as the one offering that ends all others.

Does “nor did it enter into my mind” mean God did not foresee child sacrifice? No; he knows all things (Psalm 139:4). It means that such a thing never came from him: he never willed or commanded it, and it is utterly foreign to his heart.

Uncertain wording. Molech is usually taken as the name of a god, and the ESV reads it so. Some scholars think the Hebrew word first named a kind of sacrifice rather than a deity, so that the phrase would mean offered as a molek sacrifice. The evidence is debated. Either way the meaning is not in doubt: children were burned in worship, and God calls it an abomination.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–41 — One Heart and One Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the full indictment, God’s “therefore” introduces not punishment but promise, and the promise is all his own work. He will gather the people he drove away and bring them home in safety (vv. 36–37), and the covenant sentence stands: they shall be his people and he their God (v. 38). He will give them one heart and one way, make an everlasting covenant that he will never stop doing them good, and put his fear in their hearts so that they never turn from him (vv. 39–40). And he will do it gladly, with all his heart and all his soul (v. 41).
verseByVerse.theology: God himself keeps his people faithful, as he requires, and says he will enjoy doing it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning this city of which you say, 'It is given into the hand of the king of Babylon by sword, by famine, and by pestilence': Behold, I will gather them from all the countries to which I drove them in my anger and my wrath and in great indignation. I will bring them back to this place, and I will make them dwell in safety. And they shall be my people, and I will be their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the full list of Judah’s sins, God’s “therefore” introduces not punishment but promise: he will gather the people he drove out, and they will be his.

Now therefore. Two words carry the weight of the chapter. Read what precedes them: evil from the beginning, every class guilty, children burned in the valley, the city removed from God’s sight. A “therefore” after that should introduce the punishment. Instead it introduces the promise. There is no logic by which verse 37 follows verse 35 except the logic of grace.

I will gather them from all the countries to which I drove them. The same hand is at both ends: he drove them, and he will gather them. The anger was real (God does not now call the exile a misunderstanding), and it is the same God who ends it.

They shall be my people, and I will be their God. The covenant sentence comes again, and here it answers everything in the indictment. These are not a people who deserve him, but a people who are his. Hosea gave the same promise to a people named for their rejection: “And I will say to Not My People, ‘You are my people’; and he shall say, ‘You are my God’” (Hosea 2:23). Peter applies it to Gentile believers who had never belonged to Israel at all: “Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy” (1 Peter 2:10). The sentence spoken to exiles in a doomed city is spoken over every believer in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever, for their own good and the good of their children after them. I will make with them an everlasting covenant, that I will not turn away from doing good to them. And I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me. I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will plant them in this land in faithfulness, with all my heart and all my soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to give his people an undivided heart and to bind himself to them in an everlasting covenant that he will keep from both sides, and he says he will do it with joy.

One heart and one way. The gift is a heart, as throughout this book: the heart to know him (24:7), the law written within (31:33), and here one heart and one way. Ezekiel was given almost the same words: “And I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them” (Ezekiel 11:19). A divided heart was Judah’s disease, wavering between the LORD and Baal, the temple and the roof altar. The cure is not more willpower but an undivided heart, given.

An everlasting covenant … that they may not turn from me. There are two guarantees, one on each side. God will not turn away from doing them good, and, the astonishing half, he will put his fear in their hearts so that they do not turn away from him. The covenant is secured at both ends by the same Person. Hebrews names its price: God brought again from the dead “our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant” (Hebrews 13:20). This is why Christians can hope to persevere: not because their grip is strong, but because God has promised to keep them holding on (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6).

I will rejoice in doing them good. God speaks of his own feelings. He will do it “with all my heart and all my soul”: the words Israel was commanded to use of loving him (Deuteronomy 6:5), turned round and spoken by God about blessing them. This is not a God who forgives reluctantly and blesses grudgingly. Zephaniah saw the same: “he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing” (Zephaniah 3:17).

Where Christians differ: can a true believer finally fall away? Arminian Christians hold that a genuine believer can turn from Christ and be lost, and point to the warning passages (Hebrews 6:4–6). Reformed Christians hold that those God has truly saved are kept by his power and will never finally perish. This commentary’s view: verse 40 is one of the clearest promises behind the Reformed view: God undertakes not only to keep doing his people good but to keep them from turning from him. The warnings are real and are among the means he uses to keep them; those who finally fall away shared the church’s outward blessings but were never made new.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 42–44 — Deeds Signed and Sealed Again
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The good God promises is as certain as the disaster he brought, and it will look like ordinary life restored. Just as every threat came true, so will every promise (v. 42). In the land everyone calls a desolation, fields will be bought for money and deeds signed, sealed and witnessed, district by district across the country, because God will restore their fortunes (vv. 43–44). Jeremiah’s single purchase in the prison yard turns out to be the first entry in a register that God will reopen.
verseByVerse.theology: The land registry will reopen, district by district, and that is the shape the hope takes.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD: Just as I have brought all this great disaster upon this people, so I will bring upon them all the good that I promise them. Fields shall be bought in this land of which you are saying, 'It is a desolation, without man or beast; it is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.' Fields shall be bought for money, and deeds shall be signed and sealed and witnessed, in the land of Benjamin, in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, in the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb; for I will restore their fortunes, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good God promises is as sure as the disaster he has brought, and it will look like ordinary business restored across the whole land.

Just as I have brought all this great disaster. They had just seen every threat land: siege mounds, famine, the city given over. Very well, says God: that same reliability is now working for you. The accuracy of the judgment is the evidence for the promise. A God whose warnings come true is a God whose assurances can be relied on, and the logic runs the way Paul’s does when he argues from the greater gift to the lesser (Romans 8:32).

It is a desolation, without man or beast. God quotes the pessimism of the moment exactly and does not dispute it; that is what the land is about to become. And in that land, fields will be bought.

Deeds shall be signed and sealed and witnessed. The chapter ends in a solicitor’s office, with the vocabulary of verse 10. Jeremiah’s private transaction in a prison yard turns out to be the first entry in a register that will reopen across six named districts: Benjamin, the area round Jerusalem, the cities of Judah, the hill country, the Shephelah (the western foothills) and the Negeb (the dry south).

Hope past our own lifetime. This hope is described not as a vision or a feeling but as ordinary people doing ordinary business in a country God had promised to empty and then promised to fill. And the man who bought the first field never saw it. He paid seventeen shekels, filed the deeds in a jar, and died elsewhere: the pattern for every believer who has acted on a promise whose fulfilment lay beyond his own life (Hebrews 11:13).

32.title: The Field at Anathoth
32.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 30 and 31 promised healing, return and a new covenant. Chapter 32 brings those promises down to earth, in a prison yard, in the last year before Jerusalem fell. It is the one long story inside the Book of Consolation (chapters 30 to 33).

The message. God’s promise of a future is so sure that his prophet can put money on it while the city burns. Judgment is coming and it is fully deserved, yet nothing is too hard for the LORD: the God who drove his people out will gather them, give them one heart, bind himself to them in an everlasting covenant, and rejoice in doing them good. As surely as the disaster came, the good will come.

Why it was said. The Babylonian army was round the walls, food was running out, and Jeremiah had been jailed for saying the city would fall (see the introduction). Everyone could see the end; no one could see past it. God gave his people an act they could watch and a promise they could keep in a jar.

How the chapter makes its case. A prisoner buys a field: Hanamel comes as God said he would, and Jeremiah pays, signs, seals and stores the deeds, because houses and fields will again be bought in this land (vv. 1–15). Then he prays, confessing that nothing is too hard for God, reciting the exodus, agreeing with the verdict on Judah, and laying down his bewilderment: yet you told me to buy a field (vv. 16–25). God hands his confession back as a question, “Is anything too hard for me?”, and confirms that the city will burn for a record of evil running back to its foundation (vv. 26–35). Then comes the great “Now therefore”: gathering, one heart, an everlasting covenant, God’s whole-hearted joy in doing them good (vv. 36–41). The chapter ends where it began, with deeds signed and sealed across the land (vv. 42–44).

Where it leads. By promise, and by pattern. The everlasting covenant God promises here is the one Hebrews says was sealed by “the blood of the eternal covenant” (Hebrews 13:20), when the great Shepherd was led out of this same city to die and raised from the dead. The God for whom nothing is too hard said the same to Mary (Luke 1:37), and proved it at an empty tomb. And the kinsman who pays to buy back a lost inheritance is a picture Christians have long seen fulfilled in Christ, who became our brother to redeem what we had lost, though Jeremiah does not draw the picture himself.

For us. Faith in God’s promises usually looks like something concrete and slightly costly done now, for a future we may not live to see. When God’s command and our circumstances seem to contradict each other, we may bring both to him honestly, beginning with what we know of him. And our hope does not rest on our record being better than it looks, but on a God who has bound himself to do us good, with all his heart.
32.theology:
Faith acts before it understands: Jeremiah completed a binding purchase and asked his question afterwards (vv. 9-10, 25). And God answers bewilderment not with new information but by applying what the believer already confesses (vv. 17, 27).

Grace does not depend on finding the record better than it looked. The charges are read out in full, and then comes the therefore that introduces the promise (vv. 30-37). The covenant is secured at both ends by God, who will not turn from doing his people good and will keep them from turning from him; and he does it gladly, with all his heart and soul (vv. 39-41).
32.examples:
A prisoner buys farmland in a country under sentence, weighs out seventeen shekels in front of witnesses, and seals the deeds in a clay jar for somebody's grandchildren. Hope that trusts God's word usually looks like something concrete and slightly inconvenient.

When a command makes no sense, Jeremiah's prayer is a pattern: begin with who God is, recite what he has done, agree with his verdict, and then lay the question honestly before him.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too hard for me?
keyVerse.note: This is God’s answer to the whole chapter’s tension between a doomed city and a field bought for the future. He hands Jeremiah’s own confession (v. 17) back to him as a question, and everything that follows, the gathering, the one heart and the everlasting covenant, is the outworking of it.

32.reflection:
Jeremiah paid real silver for a field he would never use, because God had promised the land a future (vv. 9–15). What would it look like for you to act on one of God’s promises in a concrete and slightly costly way this week?
