Jeremiah obeyed first and prayed about his confusion afterwards, beginning with who God is (vv. 16–25). How could his prayer shape the way you pray when God’s word and your circumstances seem to pull in different directions?

The promise of verses 36–41 follows the full list of Judah’s sins with “Now therefore.” Why does it matter that God’s grace does not depend on our record turning out better than it looked?

God promises to put his fear in his people’s hearts so that they do not turn from him, and to do them good “with all my heart and all my soul” (vv. 40–41). How does this change the way you think about your own perseverance, and about how God feels towards you in Christ?

They shall fear and tremble because of all the good and all the prosperity I provide for it.<sup>10</sup>"Thus says the LORD: In this place of which you say, 'It is a waste without man or beast,' in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate, without man or inhabitant or beast, there shall be heard again<sup>11</sup>the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voices of those who sing, as they bring thank offerings to the house of the LORD: "'Give thanks to the LORD of hosts, for the LORD is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!' For I will restore the fortunes of the land as at first, says the LORD.<sup>12</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: In this place that is waste, without man or beast, and in all of its cities, there shall again be habitations of shepherds resting their flocks.<sup>13</sup>In the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb, in the land of Benjamin, the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, flocks shall again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says the LORD.<sup>14</sup>"Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will fulfill the promise I made to the house of Israel and the house of Judah.<sup>15</sup>In those days and at that time I will cause a righteous Branch to spring up for David, and he shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.<sup>16</sup>In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely. And this is the name by which it will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.'<sup>17</sup>"For thus says the LORD: David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel,<sup>18</sup>and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to make sacrifices forever."<sup>19</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>20</sup>"Thus says the LORD: If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night will not come at their appointed time,<sup>21</sup>then also my covenant with David my servant may be broken, so that he shall not have a son to reign on his throne, and my covenant with the Levitical priests my ministers.<sup>22</sup>As the host of heaven cannot be numbered and the sands of the sea cannot be measured, so I will multiply the offspring of David my servant, and the Levitical priests who minister to me."<sup>23</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>24</sup>"Have you not observed that these people are saying, 'The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight.<sup>25</sup>Thus says the LORD: If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth,<sup>26</sup>then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant and will not choose one of his offspring to rule over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s first answer to a prisoner in a doomed city is an invitation and a promise of healing that rests on forgiveness. The word comes a second time, while Jeremiah is still shut up, and invites him to call and be told great and hidden things (vv. 1–3). God does not soften the present: the houses torn down for barricades will be filled with the dead, because he has hidden his face from the city for its evil (vv. 4–5). Then, about the same city, he promises health, healing and restoration for both Judah and Israel, built on the cleansing and forgiveness of all their guilt (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology: God answers a man in prison by offering to tell him things he could not have worked out.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah a second time, while he was still shut up in the court of the guard: "Thus says the LORD who made the earth, the LORD who formed it to establish it— the LORD is his name: Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To a prisoner whose circumstances have not changed at all, God gives not release but a further word, and an invitation to ask for more: call to me, and I will tell you what you could never find out.

A second time … while he was still shut up. God had not finished speaking after the field was bought, and the prophet is no closer to release. Nothing has improved between chapter 32 and chapter 33; what arrives instead is more revelation. God’s answer to a faithful man in a bad situation is often not a change of situation but a further word about himself.

The LORD who made the earth, the LORD who formed it to establish it. Before the promise, the credentials: the Creator built the earth to stand. A God who makes things in order to make them last is the ground of everything promised in this chapter.

Call to me and I will answer you. Consider who is invited: a prisoner whose preaching has failed by every visible measure, who has just spent silver on a field he will never see, and whose last prayer was bewildered (32:16–25). God’s reply to that prayer is to invite more of them, not a rebuke for asking but an offer. What is promised is knowledge: “great and hidden things that you have not known.” The Hebrew word behind “hidden” usually means fortified or inaccessible, things walled off from human discovery. God’s purposes will not be worked out by looking at the siege ramps. They have to be told, and they are told to people who ask.

How do I call to him? Jeremiah is the pattern, because this invitation answers a prayer that was honest and confused. Bring the bewilderment as it is. He began, “Ah, Lord GOD!” and said plainly that buying the field made no sense to him (32:17, 24–25). You may tell God that the diagnosis, the stalled career or the wandering child makes no sense to you. Ask to know him, not only to escape. The promise is great and hidden things, so pray, “Show me what you are doing, and who you are in this,” and then open the Scriptures, where he has told them. Keep calling from the same cell. The answer came while Jeremiah was still shut up; do not wait for things to change before you pray again. Come through the Son. We call with more confidence than Jeremiah could, because Christ has opened the way: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). The Father is not irritated by the asking; he “gives generously to all without reproach” (James 1:5).

Is this a promise of private revelation? It was God’s word to Jeremiah, promising the restoration that follows. Believers today are given God’s great and hidden things in the gospel, revealed in Scripture (1 Corinthians 2:9–10; Colossians 1:26).

Textual note. The ESV notes that its wording in verse 2 follows the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, where the Hebrew simply has “it”. The sense, a Creator who makes things to last, is the same either way.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning the houses of this city and the houses of the kings of Judah that were torn down to make a defense against the siege mounds and against the sword: They are coming in to fight against the Chaldeans and to fill them with the dead bodies of men whom I shall strike down in my anger and my wrath, for I have hidden my face from this city because of all their evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city is pulling down its own houses to plug the walls, but the barricades will only fill with the dead, because the real cause of the collapse is that God has turned his face away.

Torn down to make a defense against the siege mounds. A city in its last weeks: they are pulling down their own homes, royal buildings included, for stone and timber to block the breaches where the Babylonian ramps come up to the wall. That is what the end looks like in practice: dismantling your own house to slow the enemy for another day, every resource turned to a defence that cannot hold.

To fill them with the dead bodies of men. The improvised barricades become the morgue. The stones pulled from bedrooms end up packed with the bodies of the men who stacked them.

I have hidden my face from this city because of all their evil. Underneath the military facts is the theological one, and it is the real cause. Not siege engineering, not the balance of power, but the averted face of God. The worst thing that can happen to a people is not that their walls fail but that God looks away, and this verse names that as the reason the walls fail at all. It is also why the gospel’s greatest gift is a face turned back towards us: “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 5 is compressed, and it is not clear who “they” are. The ESV takes it of the defenders coming out to fight, with the torn-down houses (its footnote says) filled with the dead. Some read it of the Chaldeans coming in to fight. The overall sense is not in doubt: the defence will fail, and the dead will lie in the ruins of the homes pulled down to build it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal them and reveal to them abundance of prosperity and security. I will restore the fortunes of Judah and the fortunes of Israel, and rebuild them as they were at first. I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me, and I will forgive all the guilt of their sin and rebellion against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same breath, about the same doomed city, God promises healing, restoration and, beneath it all, the complete forgiveness and cleansing of their guilt.

Behold, I will bring to it health and healing. The same “Behold” that introduced barricades full of corpses now introduces healing. This is the wound of chapter 30, which God called incurable, with no medicine and no healing (30:12–13), and here is the physician arriving. Nothing has changed in the patient. What changes is that God announces he will do it himself.

The fortunes of Judah and the fortunes of Israel. Both houses again, the northern kingdom included well over a century after it vanished, and “as they were at first”, with the damage of the centuries undone.

I will cleanse them … and I will forgive all the guilt. Under the health and security lies this foundation: the guilt has to go, and the sentence says it twice, with “all” both times. Cleansing and forgiveness are not quite the same, and both are needed. Forgiveness deals with the record; cleansing deals with the stain. A pardoned man who still feels filthy has only half of what God promises here, and the New Testament joins the two: “he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Their sin and rebellion against me. The offence is named for what it is, sin against me, twice. Judah’s problem was never merely social collapse or bad policy. It was personal, and so is the remedy: God himself takes the guilt away, which is why a believer who has failed comes back by confession rather than by first making himself clean (Psalm 32:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — The Voice of the Bridegroom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The forgiven city will be filled again with the most ordinary sounds of happiness, and its joy will make the nations tremble at God’s goodness. Jerusalem will become a name of joy and praise before the nations (v. 9). In the place everyone calls a waste, the voices God had silenced, bridegroom and bride, mirth and gladness, will be heard again, with worshippers singing that the LORD is good and his steadfast love endures for ever (vv. 10–11). Shepherds will rest their flocks and count them under their hand in every district of the land (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Weddings, singing and a shepherd counting sheep: the restoration measured in ordinary noise.

verseByVerse.quote: And this city shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and a glory before all the nations of the earth who shall hear of all the good that I do for them. They shall fear and tremble because of all the good and all the prosperity I provide for it. "Thus says the LORD: In this place of which you say, 'It is a waste without man or beast,' in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem that are desolate, without man or inhabitant or beast, there shall be heard again the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voices of those who sing, as they bring thank offerings to the house of the LORD: "'Give thanks to the LORD of hosts, for the LORD is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!' For I will restore the fortunes of the land as at first, says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city God forgives will become his joy and the nations’ wonder, and the sounds he silenced in judgment, weddings and songs of thanksgiving, will be heard in its streets again.

A name of joy, a praise and a glory. The city that had become a curse and a byword among the nations becomes God’s joy, and what changes her name is not her own strength but what God does for her.

They shall fear and tremble because of all the good. The nations tremble, not at judgment but at goodness. God’s generosity is itself awe-inspiring. Grace on that scale is not a comfortable thing to watch.

It is a waste without man or beast. God quotes the pessimism word for word, as in the previous chapter (32:43), and grants every word of it. The place is a waste. Then: “there shall be heard again.”

The voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride. Earlier in this book God had silenced exactly these sounds, promising to take away the voice of mirth and the voice of the bridegroom and bride (7:34; 16:9). Now he gives them back in the same words: weddings in the streets, singing, people walking up to the temple with thank offerings.

Give thanks to the LORD of hosts. The song is the one Israel had always sung, the refrain of Psalm 136: “Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever” (Psalm 136:1). It is sung by people who have watched the worst happen. They are not singing that nothing bad occurred; they are singing that his steadfast love outlasted it.

What steadfast love means. Steadfast love translates the Hebrew hesed, and English needs two words for it because one will not do. It is love that has bound itself by promise: not a feeling that rises and falls with how lovable we are, but loyalty that keeps going when the other side has given it every reason to stop. The people singing are the ones who broke the covenant; the love bringing them home is the love that would not break it from his side. When God passed before Moses he named himself “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6), and John, describing the Son, seems to echo that pair: “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). So on the day your own record makes you doubt your welcome, do not look for the answer in yourself. Say the refrain out loud anyway. It was written for people who had failed. See Steadfast Love.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: In this place that is waste, without man or beast, and in all of its cities, there shall again be habitations of shepherds resting their flocks. In the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the Shephelah, and in the cities of the Negeb, in the land of Benjamin, the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, flocks shall again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The emptied countryside will be peaceful farmland again, with shepherds settled and flocks counted in every district.

Habitations of shepherds resting their flocks. After the weddings, the sheep. The promise keeps getting more ordinary: shepherds with somewhere to settle, flocks lying down in country that had been emptied.

In the cities of the hill country. The same six districts as the land-registry promise at the end of chapter 32 (32:44), listed again. God maps his promises.

Under the hands of the one who counts them. The closing image is a man counting sheep as they file past under his hand. It is the smallest detail in the chapter and one of the most reassuring: flocks numerous enough to need counting, a shepherd unhurried enough to count them, and peace enough in the countryside for both. Nothing dramatic, just a working farm in a land God had promised to empty and then promised to fill. Christians will think of the good Shepherd who knows his own by name and loses none of them (John 10:3, 28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — A Righteous Branch, and a Name for the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will keep his old promise of a righteous King, and the King’s righteousness will become his people’s name. The days are coming when God fulfils the promise made to Israel and Judah (v. 14): a righteous Branch will spring up for David and do justice and righteousness in the land (v. 15). The name given to the king in 23:6, “The LORD is our righteousness”, is now given to the city he saves (v. 16). And David will never lack a man to sit on the throne (v. 17), the promise of 2 Samuel 7 restated at the moment of its apparent collapse.
verseByVerse.theology: The king's own name is handed to the people who live under him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will fulfill the promise I made to the house of Israel and the house of Judah. In those days and at that time I will cause a righteous Branch to spring up for David, and he shall execute justice and righteousness in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will keep his old promise to raise up a righteous King from David’s fallen house, a quiet shoot from a stump who will do the justice the kings never did.

I will fulfill the promise. God is not improvising a new plan to cope with the disaster; he is keeping an old word, and the disaster has not altered it. Ten chapters earlier, amid an indictment of worthless shepherds, he had said, “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land” (23:5). Now the same promise is repeated to a man in prison in a city about to fall.

A righteous Branch to spring up for David. The image is agricultural and deliberately humble. A branch is what sprouts from a stump, which is what the house of David was about to become, with Zedekiah blinded and his sons dead. Out of that stump, a shoot; and “spring up” is the language of something growing quietly rather than installed by force.

He shall execute justice and righteousness in the land. Not ceremony, not conquest: the two things chapter 22 said a king was for (22:3, 15), and that the actual kings never delivered.

The Branch has a name. The righteous Branch is Jesus, the Son of David (23:5–6). He is the one who did justice and righteousness perfectly, and he is “The LORD is our righteousness”, for Christ Jesus “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

Textual note. Verses 14 to 26 are absent from the ancient Greek translation of Jeremiah, which is shorter than the Hebrew in many places (see the introduction). They are part of the Hebrew text our Bibles follow, and they echo 23:5–6 closely.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely. And this is the name by which it will be called: 'The LORD is our righteousness.' "For thus says the LORD: David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The name that belonged to the King, “The LORD is our righteousness”, is now given to his people, a picture of justification; and David’s throne is promised a King for ever.

The LORD is our righteousness. Read this beside chapter 23 and one thing has changed, gloriously. There the name belonged to the king: “this is the name by which he will be called: ‘The LORD is our righteousness’” (23:6). Here it is given to the city.

A picture of justification. The king’s name has passed to his people, a picture of justification, in which God counts the king’s righteousness as theirs. His righteousness is not admired from a distance; the city carries it as its own name. Jerusalem is not renamed The City That Finally Got Its Act Together. It is called by his name, because the righteousness it lives on is his. That is the gospel for every reader who has not kept God’s law: Christ’s obedience is counted as ours (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Everyone is building a case. We tend to think the language of righteousness belongs to religious people. But watch any modern life and you will find someone assembling a defence: the CV, the curated feed, the causes we are seen to support, the reminders of how hard we work and how much we have given up. All of it is evidence for a verdict we badly want, that we are good, worthy, on the right side. The devout build the case out of prayers and attendance; the secular out of achievement and moral seriousness about the issues of the day. It is the same project, and it is exhausting, because the court never rises and the case is never closed. Jeremiah’s name for the city ends the trial from outside. The people do not earn righteousness; they are given a name and carry it as their own. Paul describes the relief of a man who stopped building: “not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ” (Philippians 3:9). Only someone whose case is already settled can afford to admit he was wrong.

David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne. This is the promise of 2 Samuel 7, restated at the moment of its apparent collapse: “your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16). Within months there would be no king in Jerusalem at all, and no son of David would sit on that throne again. The promise held anyway, and an angel told a girl in Nazareth how: “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — My Covenant with the Day and the Night
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God stakes the throne of David and the ministry of the priests on the regularity of the sunrise. The priests will never lack a man before him (v. 18). If anyone can break God’s covenant with day and night, then his covenant with David and with the Levitical priests may be broken too (vv. 19–21). And they will not merely survive but be multiplied beyond counting, in the very terms of the promise to Abraham, the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Anyone who wants the promise cancelled must first stop the sun.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to make sacrifices forever." The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises that a priest will never be lacking in his presence, a promise that ordinary priests who kept dying could not fulfil, and that Christ, the priest who lives for ever, does.

The Levitical priests shall never lack a man in my presence. Alongside the endless throne, an endless altar. The temple was little more than a year from being burned and its priesthood scattered, and God promises that there will never be a moment without a priest before him making offerings. Taken literally, that promise failed twice over: the sacrifices stopped in 586 BC, resumed after the exile, and ended in AD 70, this time for good. So either the word was broken, or it was pointing at a priesthood that does not depend on mortal men.

Hebrews explains. Hebrews takes the second view, and shows what was always wrong with the Levitical arrangement: “The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:23–24). Israel needed a succession of priests because each one kept dying. A priest who does not die needs no successor, and there has not been an hour since the cross when God has lacked a man in his presence, because “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah. A new word begins in verse 19, and even its opening says something in a chapter about permanence. God keeps speaking to this prisoner, paragraph after paragraph, while the city burns down around him.

Where Christians differ: will the Levitical priests and sacrifices be restored literally? Many dispensationalists expect them in a future millennial temple, with sacrifices as memorials. This commentary’s view: the New Testament never expects a rebuilt temple or renewed sacrifice. The promise is kept in Christ, who is both King of David’s line and the high priest who offered one sacrifice for ever (Hebrews 7:24–27; 10:12), and in his people, “a royal priesthood” offering spiritual sacrifices (1 Peter 2:5, 9). Hebrews says Christ’s one offering has made the old sacrifices obsolete (Hebrews 8:13; 10:18), so a return to animal sacrifice would look backward rather than forward.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD: If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night will not come at their appointed time, then also my covenant with David my servant may be broken, so that he shall not have a son to reign on his throne, and my covenant with the Levitical priests my ministers. As the host of heaven cannot be numbered and the sands of the sea cannot be measured, so I will multiply the offspring of David my servant, and the Levitical priests who minister to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God stakes his covenant with David and the priests on the sunrise: as long as day follows night, it stands, and the line will not merely survive but multiply beyond counting.

If you can break my covenant with the day. God offers a test anybody can attempt: stop tomorrow morning from arriving. Calling the sunrise a covenant is a striking way to describe creation’s regularity. Day and night are not mere physics; they are God keeping an appointment he made, every evening and every morning, without fail, in front of everyone (Genesis 8:22). Only if someone could stop them would God’s covenant with David be broken; until then, the matter is closed.

Better evidence than his eyes. The man hearing this could see the Babylonian army from the courtyard. His eyes told him the line of David was finished. God does not dispute the evidence of his eyes; he gives him better evidence, available every morning.

So I will multiply the offspring of David my servant. Not merely preserved but multiplied, in the terms of the oath to Abraham: “I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore” (Genesis 22:17). That is a royal family and a priesthood beyond counting, spoken over a dynasty about to lose its last king. It is hard to read it, this side of the cross, without thinking of a kingdom of priests too many to number, from every tribe and tongue, gathered round David’s greater Son (Revelation 5:9–10; 7:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — The Two Clans He Chose
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the public rumour that he has rejected his people exactly as he answered his prophet’s private doubt: by pointing to the fixed order of heaven and earth. People were saying that the LORD had rejected the two clans he chose, and despising his people as no nation at all (vv. 23–24). As surely as day and night keep their appointed times, God will not reject the offspring of Jacob and David (vv. 25–26). And the Book of Consolation ends not with an argument won but with mercy: “I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them” (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: The rumour was that God had finished with them; the reply ends in mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Have you not observed that these people are saying, 'The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight. Thus says the LORD: If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant and will not choose one of his offspring to rule over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the rumour that he has rejected his people by pointing again at the sky, and the Book of Consolation ends with mercy.

The LORD has rejected the two clans that he chose. God has been listening to the talk, and he repeats it back. Israel and Judah both seemed finished, and the conclusion was drawn everywhere that God had changed his mind about the people he chose.

No longer a nation in their sight. The consequence is public: his people are despised. When God’s people are visibly defeated, the watching world does not usually conclude that God is disciplining them. It concludes that he has dropped them, or was never there.

If I have not established my covenant with day and night. The same argument as before, now aimed at the rumour rather than the prophet’s doubt. God answers gossip about his faithfulness as he answered his servant’s confusion, by pointing at the sky.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The name-stacking is deliberate: Jacob, David, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob again. Every layer of the promise is named, so that rejecting this people would mean breaking all of it at once (compare Romans 11:1–2, 28–29).

And will have mercy on them. So the Book of Consolation ends, not with an argument won but with mercy. Weigh where these four chapters have come from: a man in custody, in a city eating itself, under a king who would be blinded, about a temple that would be ash within months. And they contain the new covenant, the everlasting love, the sins remembered no more, the healed wound, the field bought in faith, the Branch, and this last word of mercy. The circumstances never improved while he wrote. The revelation simply got better.

The answer to the invitation. That is the answer to the invitation at the head of the chapter. He called, and God told him great and hidden things he had not known, and the greatest of them was a name he would not live to hear anyone use, given first to a king and then handed to his people: “The LORD is our righteousness.”

33.title: Call to Me and I Will Answer You
33.overview:
Where we are. Jeremiah is still a prisoner in the court of the guard, the field at Anathoth bought and its deeds sealed in a jar (chapter 32). The siege is closing in. This chapter closes the Book of Consolation (chapters 30 to 33) with a second word to the same prisoner.

The message. God’s promises are as certain as tomorrow’s sunrise. He invites his servant to call on him, and answers with what no one could have worked out from the siege ramps: he will heal and forgive a city about to die, fill its silent streets with weddings and thanksgiving, and raise up a righteous Branch for David whose name, “The LORD is our righteousness”, his people will wear as their own. Throne and priesthood will never fail, because God keeps his covenant with day and night.

Why it was said. Within months Jerusalem would have no king, no temple and no priesthood, and people were already saying that God had rejected the two clans he chose (v. 24; see the introduction). A prophet, a city and the scattered exiles all needed to know whether God’s promises to David and to Israel had died with the city.

How the chapter makes its case. God invites the imprisoned prophet to call and be told great and hidden things (vv. 1–3). He does not hide the present: houses torn down for barricades will fill with the dead, because he has hidden his face (vv. 4–5). Then comes healing resting on full forgiveness (vv. 6–8), and a city become a joy, with the voices of bridegroom and bride and the song of thanksgiving back in its streets and shepherds counting flocks across the land (vv. 9–13). The righteous Branch of chapter 23 returns, and now the city bears his name (vv. 14–16). David will never lack a man on the throne nor the priests a man before God, as surely as day follows night (vv. 17–22). The rumour that God has rejected his people is answered the same way, and the Book of Consolation ends in mercy (vv. 23–26).

Where it leads. By promise, plainly. The righteous Branch is Jesus, the Son of David, to whom God gave “the throne of his father David” and a kingdom with no end (Luke 1:32–33). He is the priest who “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25), so that God has never lacked a man in his presence. And the name passing from king to people is the gospel itself: Christ Jesus “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

For us. God’s answer to a faithful believer in an unchanged trouble is often a deeper knowledge of himself, and he invites us to ask for it. Our standing before him rests not on a case we build but on a name we are given, Christ’s righteousness counted as ours. And when our own eyes say God has finished with his people, every sunrise says otherwise.
33.theology: The chapter turns on two things God gives a prisoner in place of release: a further word about himself, and an invitation to ask for more. Its promises rest on forgiveness that deals with both the record and the stain of sin (v. 8), and they reach their height when the name of the king, The LORD is our righteousness, is given to his people (v. 16; 23:6). That pictures justification, the king’s righteousness counted as his people’s, and it is fulfilled in the Son of David whose kingdom has no end and the priest who always lives to intercede (Luke 1:32-33; Heb 7:23-25). God answers both private doubt and public rumour the same way, by pointing at the sunrise he keeps as a covenant (vv. 20, 25).
33.examples: A family dismantling its own bedroom to plug a breach in the wall for one more day is what verse 4 describes, and it is a picture of every defence that cannot hold once God has hidden his face. Against it stand the smallest images of hope in the chapter: wedding songs back in streets God had silenced, and a shepherd unhurried enough to count his sheep. And when doubt says God has finished with his people, the chapter's own answer is still available to anyone: stop tomorrow morning from arriving, and then we will talk.

keyVerse.quote: In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely. And this is the name by which it will be called: ‘The LORD is our righteousness.’
keyVerse.note: In 23:6 this name belonged to the righteous King; here it is given to the people he saves. It is the great and hidden thing promised in verse 3, a picture of justification: the righteousness of Christ, the Branch of David, counted as his people’s own.

33.reflection:
God’s answer to Jeremiah, still in prison, was not release but an invitation: “Call to me and I will answer you” (v. 3). What situation in your life has not changed, and how might you pray about it, asking to know God and not only to escape?

God promises both to forgive and to cleanse (v. 8). Why do we need both, and how does 1 John 1:9 help someone who feels forgiven on paper but still stained?

The king’s name, “The LORD is our righteousness”, is given to his people (v. 16; 23:6). Where are you tempted to build your own case for being good enough, and what changes when you rest on Christ’s righteousness instead?

God points to the sunrise as proof that his promises stand (vv. 20–26). How could tomorrow morning become a reminder of his faithfulness when circumstances say he has forgotten his people?

Their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth.<sup>21</sup>And Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials I will give into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives, into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you.<sup>22</sup>Behold, I will command, declares the LORD, and will bring them back to this city. And they will fight against it and take it and burn it with fire. I will make the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Zedekiah the truth about his future, the hard part and the merciful part together, while the last fortresses of Judah are falling. The empire’s whole army is at the walls (v. 1). Jeremiah is sent to the king in person: the city will burn, and Zedekiah will be captured, will meet the king of Babylon eye to eye and go to Babylon (vv. 2–3). Yet he will not die by the sword but in peace, mourned with royal spices and lament, because God has spoken (vv. 4–5). Jeremiah delivers it all while only Lachish and Azekah still hold out (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: A promise of an honourable funeral, offered to a king who will be blinded first.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army and all the kingdoms of the earth under his dominion and all the peoples were fighting against Jerusalem and all of its cities: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Go and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am giving this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire. You shall not escape from his hand but shall surely be captured and delivered into his hand. You shall see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face. And you shall go to Babylon.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the whole empire at the walls, God sends Jeremiah to tell the king to his face that the city will burn and he himself will be taken to Babylon.

All the kingdoms of the earth under his dominion. The scale is spelled out to make the odds plain: not merely Babylon but every vassal nation in the empire, conscripted into the siege lines. Jerusalem is facing the known world.

Go and speak to Zedekiah. Not a written note but face to face, with the man who had already imprisoned him for saying this (32:3).

You shall see the king of Babylon eye to eye. The phrase had been used of this king before (32:4), and its fulfilment was exact in a way nobody would have wanted. Zedekiah was brought before Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, made to watch his sons executed, and then blinded (39:6–7). He did meet him eye to eye, and it was the last thing he ever saw. God’s words come true in their detail, and the detail is not always the comfort we imagined when we heard them.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet hear the word of the LORD, O Zedekiah king of Judah! Thus says the LORD concerning you: 'You shall not die by the sword. You shall die in peace. And as spices were burned for your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so people shall burn spices for you and lament for you, saying, "Alas, lord!"' For I have spoken the word, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in the sentence, God holds back a kindness for a weak and faithless king: he will not die by the sword, but in peace, and be mourned as a king.

Yet hear the word of the LORD, O Zedekiah king of Judah! After the sentence, a concession, addressed to him personally by name and title, with an urgency that reads almost like pleading.

As spices were burned for your fathers. What is offered is a decent death and a proper funeral: the royal spices, the formal lament, the cry “Alas, lord!” that had been denied to Jehoiakim, who was promised the burial of a donkey (22:18–19).

You shall die in peace. It is a strange mercy. Zedekiah will lose his city, his sons and his sight, and yet he is told he will die in peace, with mourners. Weigh it against the alternative he was courting, and against what his brother received, and it is real. God keeps a kindness back even for him.

For I have spoken the word. The guarantee is the one attached to every threat in this book. The promise of the funeral rests on exactly the same authority as the promise of the fire.

Where Christians differ: did this promise fail? Zedekiah was promised to die “in peace”, yet he was blinded and died in prison (52:11). Some interpreters take the promise as conditional on his obeying (vv. 2–5; 38:17–18): he refused, and so lost it. Others read “in peace” as meaning not by the sword, with mourning rites, which he may have received in Babylon. This commentary’s view: the second reading is more likely, since verse 5 contrasts his death with the sword and speaks of the mourning itself; but the appeal, “Yet hear the word of the LORD”, also shows how much more he could have had if he had listened.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah, in Jerusalem, when the army of the king of Babylon was fighting against Jerusalem and against all the cities of Judah that were left, Lachish and Azekah, for these were the only fortified cities of Judah that remained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah delivers the whole message, fire and funeral alike, as the last fortresses of Judah are falling one by one.

Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words. He delivered the concession and the sentence without editing either half to suit the audience: the same obedience as chapter 26, not holding back a word (26:2).

Lachish and Azekah. Two names date the scene precisely. They were the last strongpoints in the Judean lowlands, and archaeologists digging at Lachish found in a guardroom a group of ostraca, letters written on pottery by officers in these final months. One of them reports that the writer could no longer see the signals of Azekah, which many take to mean that Azekah had already fallen. The kingdom has been reduced to a capital and two garrisons, the beacons are going out one by one, and in that atmosphere the king of Judah decides to do something religious.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — The Proclamation and the Reversal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah’s one act of real obedience in these last months is reversed as soon as it stops being useful, and God calls that profaning his name. King and people covenant to free every Hebrew slave, they obey, and then they take them back into bondage (vv. 8–11). God answers from the exodus: he brought their fathers out of the house of slavery and commanded release in the seventh year, but they would not listen (vv. 12–14). Now this generation had repented and done right before him in his house, and then turned round and profaned his name by re-enslaving those they had freed (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The reform lasted exactly as long as the siege did.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to make a proclamation of liberty to them, that everyone should set free his Hebrew slaves, male and female, so that no one should enslave a Jew, his brother. And they obeyed, all the officials and all the people who had entered into the covenant that everyone would set free his slave, male or female, so that they would not be enslaved again. They obeyed and set them free. But afterward they turned around and took back the male and female slaves they had set free, and brought them into subjection as slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under the pressure of the siege, Judah formally freed its Hebrew slaves, a real act of obedience, and then took them back.

So that no one should enslave a Jew, his brother. For one moment, Judah does the right thing. This is a genuine reform, formally covenanted, and its wording is beautiful. The word “brother” is the argument: a fellow Israelite is not labour to be owned; he is family.

Why they did it. The motive was very probably the siege. With the enemy at the wall, freeing slaves put more men on the ramparts and fewer mouths in private households, and a public act of obedience might move God to relent. Repentance under pressure is still repentance, and God takes it at face value in verse 15.

They obeyed and set them free. “They obeyed,” says the narrator, twice, in a book where nobody obeys anything. For a short while in the last months of Judah, the law of Moses was actually kept in Jerusalem.

But afterward they turned around and took back. Men and women who had walked out of their owners’ houses, perhaps found family and started to plan a life, were rounded up and put back. Somebody had to go and fetch them. It is one thing never to free a slave; it is another to free him, watch him taste it, and then take it back.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I myself made a covenant with your fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, saying, 'At the end of seven years each of you must set free the fellow Hebrew who has been sold to you and has served you six years; you must set him free from your service.' But your fathers did not listen to me or incline their ears to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers as the One who brought Israel out of the house of slavery and commanded that no Hebrew be held for more than six years, a law their fathers had ignored for generations.

Out of the house of slavery. God’s answer begins with the exodus, and the phrase cuts deepest. He is talking to slave-owners who have just re-enslaved their brothers, and he names himself as the God who empties houses of slavery. Everything Israel possessed came out of that rescue; the law of release was the shape of life for people God had already freed. To hold a fellow Hebrew in bondage contradicted the event that made them a people at all.

At the end of seven years. The law is Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12: six years of service, release in the seventh, “he shall go out free, for nothing” (Exodus 21:2). It was not an obscure statute but one of the first ordinances given after Sinai, designed so that poverty could never become a permanent status in Israel (see Sabbath year). “At the end of seven years” means in the seventh year, after six of service; the two counts agree.

But your fathers did not listen to me. The law had been ignored for centuries. Zedekiah’s proclamation was not an innovation but the overdue obedience of generations, which makes its reversal worse. They restored a law their ancestors had let lapse, and then let it lapse again almost at once.

Why did God’s law allow Hebrews to be held as slaves at all? What it regulated was mostly debt-service: a man too poor to pay what he owed sold his labour for a limited term, and the law hedged it round with protections: release in the seventh year, gifts to start again (Deuteronomy 15:13–14), no ruling with harshness (Leviticus 25:43), and death for kidnapping a man to sell him (Exodus 21:16). That is far from the race-based slavery of later centuries. The law did allow foreigners to be held longer (Leviticus 25:44–46), a concession to a hard world which the gospel undoes by making slave and free one family in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Philemon 16).

verseByVerse.quote: You recently repented and did what was right in my eyes by proclaiming liberty, each to his neighbor, and you made a covenant before me in the house that is called by my name, but then you turned around and profaned my name when each of you took back his male and female slaves, whom you had set free according to their desire, and you brought them into subjection to be your slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God credits their repentance as real, and then charges them with profaning his name, because they took back in his presence what they had promised before him.

You recently repented and did what was right in my eyes. God gives them full credit. He does not dismiss the reform as insincere theatre, even though the timing was self-interested. It was right, and he says so.

In the house that is called by my name. The covenant was made in the temple, with God as witness to a promise about other people’s freedom.

You turned around and profaned my name. Not merely broke a promise, not merely wronged the poor, but dragged God’s reputation through it, because his name had been invoked over the transaction. That is what makes a broken religious commitment different in kind from a broken private one: when a vow made before God is reversed, the watching world learns something false about God.

According to their desire. The small phrase says much. The freed slaves wanted their freedom. The masters knew it, and took it away anyway.

The freedom we keep for ourselves. It is easy to look down on the slave-owners of Jerusalem. Ours is a culture that prizes freedom above almost everything, and slavery appals us. Yet the 2022 global estimates published by the International Labour Organization and its partners put the number of people in forced labour or forced marriage today at about fifty million, and some of what forced labour makes ends up in our shops at prices we enjoy. The masters in this chapter were not monsters. They had grown used to an arrangement that kept their households comfortable, and when the emergency passed, comfort won. That is the idol beneath the scene: not cruelty but convenience, which will quietly accept someone else’s chains rather than suffer inconvenience of its own. The moralist answers with outrage at other people’s sins; the cynic shrugs that this is how the world works. The gospel goes deeper than either, because it shows us a Lord who gave up his own freedom for ours: he “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). People set free at that cost cannot be indifferent to who else is still bound.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The punishment is built from Judah’s own word and Judah’s own ceremony. Because they would not proclaim liberty to their brothers, God proclaims liberty to the sword, pestilence and famine, and makes them a horror to the nations (v. 17). They had ratified the covenant by cutting a calf in two and walking between the halves, invoking that fate on themselves if they broke it. Now God will make the covenant-breakers like the calf, and the list of who walked between the pieces runs from officials and priests to all the people of the land (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: They walked between the halves of a dead animal to seal their promise, and became the animal.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, thus says the LORD: You have not obeyed me by proclaiming liberty, every one to his brother and to his neighbor; behold, I proclaim to you liberty to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine, declares the LORD. I will make you a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth. And the men who transgressed my covenant and did not keep the terms of the covenant that they made before me, I will make them like the calf that they cut in two and passed between its parts— the officials of Judah, the officials of Jerusalem, the eunuchs, the priests, and all the people of the land who passed between the parts of the calf.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God turns Judah’s own word and own ritual against them: they refused liberty to their brothers, so he releases the sword on them, and makes them like the calf they cut in two when they swore.

I proclaim to you liberty to the sword. God takes their word and turns it round, in one of the grimmest lines in Scripture. The sword, pestilence and famine that have stalked this book are released into the city like slaves let out of a house: the only emancipation Jerusalem will get, because it refused the one it had promised. Refuse to release, and something else gets released.

The calf that they cut in two and passed between its parts. Now we learn how the ceremony was done. They had cut a calf in half, laid the halves apart, and walked between them, in the oldest and most graphic form of covenant-making, whose meaning was unmistakable: may this be done to me if I break my word. The list names everyone who took that walk, from officials and priests to all the people of the land, and the sentence is simply that what they swore should happen to them will happen.

The ceremony of Genesis 15. Abram cut the animals and laid the halves against each other (Genesis 15:10), and then, in the dark, “a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces” (Genesis 15:17). God walked the path alone, as many read it, taking the curse of the covenant on himself while Abram slept.

Towards the gospel. Here the chapter turns towards the gospel, because there are only two ways the curse of a broken covenant can fall. It can fall on the one who broke it, as here. Or it can fall on someone who walks the bloody path alone in the dark on his behalf, which is what God did for Abram, and what he did at the cross for covenant-breakers who have taken back every freedom they ever promised: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

Textual note. The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks the words “them like”: it says more bluntly that God will make the men the calf.
verseByVerse.note: The rite lies behind the Hebrew idiom for making a covenant, which is literally to “cut” one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — The Army That Withdrew Will Return
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The detail that explains the whole chapter comes last: the army had withdrawn, and God will command it back. The covenant-breakers will be given to their enemies and left unburied (v. 20). Zedekiah and his officials will be handed to the Babylonian army “which has withdrawn from you” (v. 21), the moment when the pressure lifted and the slaves were taken back. God will order that army to return, take the city and burn it, and leave the towns of Judah desolate (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The relief that made them confident enough to re-enslave their brothers was temporary.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will give them into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives. Their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth. And Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials I will give into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their lives, into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you. Behold, I will command, declares the LORD, and will bring them back to this city. And they will fight against it and take it and burn it with fire. I will make the cities of Judah a desolation without inhabitant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The covenant-breakers will lie unburied, and the army whose withdrawal tempted them to take back their slaves will return at God’s command and burn the city.

Food for the birds of the air. No burial. The men who had denied their brothers a life will be denied a grave, left in the open for scavengers, the ancient world’s picture of total disgrace. Set it beside verse 5, where the king is promised spices and mourners: God treats people differently, and not according to rank, for the officials of verse 19 are among the unburied.

Which has withdrawn from you. The siege had lifted. Egypt had marched north, Nebuchadnezzar pulled back to deal with it (37:5), and suddenly the pressure was off. That is when the slaves were taken back. The covenant had been made when the ramps were rising; it was revoked when the dust cleared and the fields were safe to work again.

Religion while frightened. It is a devastating diagnosis of a certain kind of religion: sincere while frightened, and no longer required once the danger passes. The vow made in the hospital corridor, forgotten in the car park. Peter described where the pattern ends: “the last state has become worse for them than the first” (2 Peter 2:20).

In practice. Most believers have made a promise to God in a hard week: to give, to forgive, to pray, to stop something. When the pressure lifts, take that promise out and look at it again. “When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it” (Ecclesiastes 5:4). If it was rash, say so to him honestly rather than letting it quietly lapse; if it was right, keep it now that keeping it costs more, especially when it concerns other people, as Judah’s promise concerned real men and women. The point is not to earn favour with kept vows but to honour the name spoken over them, the name of the God who freed you.

Behold, I will command. God recalls the army. Nebuchadnezzar will think he is choosing his moment, and he will be answering an order he never heard.

Liberty, lost and fulfilled. The chapter leaves the word “liberty” ringing. Judah proclaimed it, took it back, and lost everything. The Hebrew word here is the word for the release of the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25:10), and Isaiah used it of the anointed one’s mission (Isaiah 61:1). Centuries later a man stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth, read that the Spirit of the Lord had anointed him “to proclaim liberty to the captives”, and told the room it was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:18–21). He proclaimed it and did not take it back. “For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery” (Galatians 5:1), the one warning this chapter exists to give. Christ gives the freedom, and his Spirit, not our nerve under pressure, keeps us in it (Galatians 5:16).

34.title: Liberty Proclaimed and Taken Back
34.overview:
Where we are. The Book of Consolation (chapters 30 to 33) is over, and the book returns to the last months of the siege. Chapters 34 to 39 tell how Jerusalem fell, and this chapter, set when only Lachish and Azekah still held out, shows why.

The message. A promise made to God in a crisis and taken back when the crisis passes profanes his name, and it brings on the breaker the very curse he invoked. Judah freed its slaves under the pressure of the siege, and God credited it as real repentance; then, when the Babylonians withdrew, the masters took their brothers back into bondage. So God gives them the only “liberty” they have left: liberty to the sword, pestilence and famine.

Why it was said. Judah had ignored God’s law of release for generations (v. 14), and even Josiah’s reform had never reached the people’s hearts (see the introduction). Their religion had become something to reach for when frightened and drop when safe. The chapter explains to the people of the siege, and to the exiles who read it later, that the city did not fall by accident or because God failed, but because his people broke the covenant they had sworn before him.

How the chapter makes its case. Jeremiah brings Zedekiah a word that gives and takes at once: capture and exile, yet a death in peace with royal mourning (vv. 1–7). Then the real story: king and people covenant in the temple to free their Hebrew slaves, they obey, and afterwards they take them back (vv. 8–11). God answers from the exodus and the law of release (vv. 12–14): they repented and did right, and then profaned his name (vv. 15–16). So he proclaims liberty to the sword, and makes the covenant-breakers like the calf they cut in two and walked between (vv. 17–19). The army that withdrew will return at his command, and the city will burn (vv. 20–22).

Where it leads. By covenant, and by the need it exposes. The calf cut in two shows that the curse of a broken covenant must fall on someone: on the breaker, as here, or on a substitute. In Genesis 15 God himself, as many read it, passed alone between the pieces, and at the cross “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). And the word Judah proclaimed and took back, liberty, is the word Jesus read in Nazareth when he came “to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Luke 4:18). He proclaimed it and never took it back.

For us. Promises made to God in a hard week should be looked at again when the pressure lifts, and kept, especially when they concern other people. Our religion is tested less in the crisis than when the danger has passed. And people set free at the cost of Christ’s own freedom cannot be indifferent to anyone still in chains.
34.theology: God credits repentance honestly, even when it comes under pressure (v. 15), but a vow made in his name and then reversed profanes that name (v. 16), and a religion that lasts only while the danger lasts is exposed the moment the siege lifts (v. 21). The punishment matches the sin: refuse to release, and God releases sword, famine and pestilence instead. Above all, the chapter shows that the curse of a broken covenant falls either on the breaker or on a substitute. The covenant-breakers are made like the calf they cut in two and walked between (v. 18); God walked that path alone for Abram in the dark (Gen 15:17), and Christ bore the curse at the cross (Gal 3:13). Liberty proclaimed and withdrawn by Judah is proclaimed and never withdrawn by him (Luke 4:18; Gal 5:1).
34.examples: Somebody had to go and fetch the freed slaves back, and that small detail is the measure of the chapter: freedom given, tasted, and taken from people who plainly wanted it. The same pattern shows in the promise made to God in a hospital corridor and forgotten in the car park, and in any kindness that lasts only as long as we feel we need God's help.

keyVerse.quote: Therefore, thus says the LORD: You have not obeyed me by proclaiming liberty, every one to his brother and to his neighbor; behold, I proclaim to you liberty to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine, declares the LORD.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter is gathered into one bitter play on the word “liberty”. Judah proclaimed release to its slaves and took it back, so God proclaims a release of judgment on Judah. The same word, the word of the Jubilee, is the one Jesus read in Nazareth when he came to proclaim a liberty he never withdraws (Luke 4:18).

34.reflection:
Judah freed its slaves when the city was under siege and took them back when the army withdrew (vv. 8–11, 21). Have you made promises to God in a hard time that you have quietly let lapse since? What would it mean to look at them again honestly?

God calls the reversal profaning his name (v. 16). Why does breaking a promise made before God, or in his name, do particular damage to how others see him?

The covenant-breakers walked between the halves of a calf, calling the curse on themselves (vv. 18–19). How do Genesis 15:17 and Galatians 3:13 show what God did with that curse for those who trust Christ?

The masters were moved less by cruelty than by convenience. Where might our comfort depend on other people’s lack of freedom today, and how should those Christ has set free respond?
