We have no vineyard or field or seed,<sup>10</sup>but we have lived in tents and have obeyed and done all that Jonadab our father commanded us.<sup>11</sup>But when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against the land, we said, 'Come, and let us go to Jerusalem for fear of the army of the Chaldeans and the army of the Syrians.' So we are living in Jerusalem."<sup>12</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>13</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Go and say to the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? declares the LORD.<sup>14</sup>The command that Jonadab the son of Rechab gave to his sons, to drink no wine, has been kept, and they drink none to this day, for they have obeyed their father's command. I have spoken to you persistently, but you have not listened to me.<sup>15</sup>I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, sending them persistently, saying, 'Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds, and do not go after other gods to serve them, and then you shall dwell in the land that I gave to you and your fathers.' But you did not incline your ear or listen to me.<sup>16</sup>The sons of Jonadab the son of Rechab have kept the command that their father gave them, but this people has not obeyed me.<sup>17</sup>Therefore, thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing upon Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, because I have spoken to them and they have not listened, I have called to them and they have not answered."<sup>18</sup>But to the house of the Rechabites Jeremiah said, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you have obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his precepts and done all that he commanded you,<sup>19</sup>therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Wine Set Before the Rechabites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God stages a scene in the temple with Judah as its audience: wine set before a family who never drink it. In Jehoiakim’s reign Jeremiah is told to bring the Rechabite clan into one of the temple chambers and offer them wine (vv. 1–2). He brings the whole household into a room the narrator locates precisely, next to the officials’ chamber, sets out pitchers full of wine and cups, and says, “Drink wine” (vv. 3–5). Every pressure in the scene runs one way: a sacred place, a man of God as host, and a direct invitation.
verseByVerse.theology: A prophet sets out drinks in the temple and presses them on men he knows will refuse.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "Go to the house of the Rechabites and speak with them and bring them to the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers; then offer them wine to drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Jeremiah to stage a scene in the temple, offering wine to a clan who never drink it, as a living sermon for Judah.

In the days of Jehoiakim. The date takes us back. Jehoiakim died in about 598 BC, and the raiders named in verse 11 (compare 2 Kings 24:2) probably place this episode in his last years, some ten years before the siege chapters on either side of it. The book is arranged by theme here rather than by calendar. Beside the broken covenant of chapter 34, where men who promised obedience to God went back on it almost at once, stand men who never promised God anything and have kept their word for generations.

Then offer them wine to drink. It is one of the strangest commands given to any prophet: fetch a particular family, take them into the temple, and put wine in front of them. God knows exactly what will happen. This is not a test of the Rechabites, who are in no danger of failing it, but a piece of theatre with an audience in mind, and the audience is Judah. Jeremiah has smashed a flask and worn a yoke; now the visual aid is a group of tent-dwellers who never touch wine, and a tray of drinks.
verseByVerse.note: Jonadab appears in 2 Kings 10:15-16; the clan's tents and abstinence are explained in verses 6 to 10 below.

verseByVerse.quote: So I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, son of Habazziniah and his brothers and all his sons and the whole house of the Rechabites. I brought them to the house of the LORD into the chamber of the sons of Hanan the son of Igdaliah, the man of God, which was near the chamber of the officials, above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, keeper of the threshold. Then I set before the Rechabites pitchers full of wine, and cups, and I said to them, "Drink wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah brings the whole clan into a named room in the temple and sets out full pitchers, so that every pressure of place, host and invitation pushes them to drink.

Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah. Names, and a whole household: brothers, sons, the entire clan. Their head’s father happens to share the prophet’s name, a coincidence the narrator lets stand.

Who were they? Descendants of Jonadab son of Rechab, who appears once elsewhere in Scripture, riding in Jehu’s chariot during the purge of Baal worship. Jehu asked him, “Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?” and then said, “Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD” (2 Kings 10:15–16). The family’s founder was a man known for his allegiance, about two and a half centuries before this scene.

The chamber of the sons of Hanan. The address is given with a surveyor’s precision: whose room, next to which, above which. This happened somewhere real, with officials in the adjoining rooms who could look in.

Pitchers full of wine, and cups. Not a token glass, but a table laid properly, with a prophet of the LORD in the temple of the LORD telling them to help themselves. Every pressure runs one way. The setting is sacred, the host is a man of God, the invitation is direct, and refusing would look rude and possibly impious.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — We Will Drink No Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Rechabites refuse at once, and their reason is simply obedience to their father. Jonadab son of Rechab commanded them never to drink wine, build houses, sow seed or plant vineyards, but to live in tents all their days (vv. 6–7). The whole family, wives, sons and daughters, has obeyed in everything, at the cost of never owning land (vv. 8–10). They volunteer the one exception honestly: when Nebuchadnezzar invaded, they took refuge in Jerusalem, which is why they are living in the city now (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Two and a half centuries of obedience to a man none of them had ever met.

verseByVerse.quote: But they answered, "We will drink no wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, 'You shall not drink wine, neither you nor your sons forever. You shall not build a house; you shall not sow seed; you shall not plant or have a vineyard; but you shall live in tents all your days, that you may live many days in the land where you sojourn.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Rechabites refuse without hesitation, for one reason only: their father told them not to drink wine, and to live as strangers in tents.

We will drink no wine, for Jonadab … commanded us. They do not hesitate or argue; they simply cite their father. What they do not say matters. They do not claim wine is evil, or that God forbade it, or that they are holier for abstaining. Their obedience needs no justification beyond the person who gave the command.

You shall live in tents all your days. The rule is wider than drink: no houses, no crops, no vineyards, tents only. It is a deliberate refusal of settled life, and the likeliest reason is spiritual. Canaanite religion was bound up with agriculture, with Baal as the god of rain and harvest, and a family that owned no fields had less to be tempted by. The tents kept them strangers.

That you may live many days in the land where you sojourn. Even the word “sojourn” concedes that the land was not theirs. The Rechabites were resident aliens who had made peace with never settling down.

A family rule, not God’s law. God nowhere commanded this. It is a family rule, not a law of Moses. Scripture does record a God-given abstinence, “the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD”, in which a man “shall separate himself from wine and strong drink” (Numbers 6:2–3), but that was voluntary, usually temporary, and instituted by God. Nothing here is held up as a standard for Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, in all that he commanded us, to drink no wine all our days, ourselves, our wives, our sons, or our daughters, and not to build houses to dwell in. We have no vineyard or field or seed, but we have lived in tents and have obeyed and done all that Jonadab our father commanded us. But when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against the land, we said, 'Come, and let us go to Jerusalem for fear of the army of the Chaldeans and the army of the Syrians.' So we are living in Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole family has kept the rule for generations at real cost, and they honestly admit the one exception: war drove them inside the city walls.

Ourselves, our wives, our sons, or our daughters. The report covers everybody. This was not one impressive individual but a culture, handed down until it was simply how the family lived.

We have no vineyard or field or seed. And it cost them. This is a statement of poverty. Generation after generation watched their neighbours plant, harvest, build and inherit, and stayed in tents.

We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab. “Obeyed” is the word the whole chapter turns on. In a book where Judah has obeyed nothing, here is a family whose summary of two and a half centuries is: we did what we were told.

So we are living in Jerusalem. They volunteer the exception, which is the most attractive thing about them. They are not in a tent as they speak but inside city walls, because an army was in the countryside. They do not pretend otherwise, and God does not reproach them. Their obedience was intelligent rather than wooden: the rule existed to keep them separate from Canaan’s settled religion, not to get them killed by Babylonian cavalry. That distinction, between the purpose of a command and its letter, is one that Judah’s own worshippers in the temple had never learned to make.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Will You Not Receive Instruction?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the sermon the scene was staged for: if a family can keep a man’s command for centuries, Judah has no excuse for ignoring God’s. God asks whether they will not receive instruction (v. 13). Jonadab’s command has been kept to this day, but God has spoken persistently and Judah has not listened (v. 14). He sent prophet after prophet with a reasonable message, turn from evil and keep the land, and they would not incline their ear (v. 15). The sons of Jonadab obeyed their father; this people has not obeyed God, and so all the disaster he pronounced will come, because he spoke and called and they neither listened nor answered (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: A dead man's house rule was kept for centuries; the living God's word was not kept for a generation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Go and say to the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? declares the LORD. The command that Jonadab the son of Rechab gave to his sons, to drink no wine, has been kept, and they drink none to this day, for they have obeyed their father's command. I have spoken to you persistently, but you have not listened to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a family can keep a dead man’s rule about wine for centuries, Judah cannot plead that obeying the living God was too hard: what it lacked was not ability but willingness.

Will you not receive instruction and listen to my words? The sermon begins, and the Rechabites were never the subject; they were the exhibit. The question is put to Judah with the tray of untouched wine still in the room.

They drink none to this day. On one side: a command from a man long dead, about a matter of no moral weight, with no penalty attached, kept for eight or nine generations. On the other: the word of the living God, on matters of life and death, backed by every warning and every mercy, delivered persistently by prophet after prophet, and ignored. The argument is not that the Rechabites were righteous, but that Judah cannot plead difficulty. Obedience across centuries is evidently possible, because a family of nomads managed it over wine. What Judah lacked was not capacity but willingness, and the untouched pitchers proved it in front of witnesses.

The obedient Son. The scene leaves a question over the whole Old Testament: will anyone ever answer God’s voice with a whole heart? The New Testament’s answer is the Son. Jesus could say, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), and “he learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), all the way to the cross. The Rechabites kept a father’s rule about wine; Christ kept his Father’s whole will, and “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).

How do I listen to his words? Judah heard the prophets for years and listened to none of them. Listening, in this chapter, means letting the word decide what you do. Give it a fixed place. The Rechabites kept their rule every day; give Scripture a regular time, before the phone and the news, not whenever there is room. Read for a reply. Ask of each passage what God is saying about himself, and what one thing he is telling you to stop, start or trust today. Answer the first time. When a verse touches the sharp remark you made at work or the money you have been holding back, act that day; the danger here is the habit of hearing without moving (James 1:22). Listen with others. Sit under preaching, and let a friend ask what you are doing about it (Hebrews 3:13). And listen as a child, not a slave. Christ has already given the Father the whole obedience Judah withheld, and his voice now comes to us as a shepherd’s: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27).

verseByVerse.quote: I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, sending them persistently, saying, 'Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds, and do not go after other gods to serve them, and then you shall dwell in the land that I gave to you and your fathers.' But you did not incline your ear or listen to me. The sons of Jonadab the son of Rechab have kept the command that their father gave them, but this people has not obeyed me. Therefore, thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing upon Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, because I have spoken to them and they have not listened, I have called to them and they have not answered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God asked less of Judah than Jonadab asked of his sons, and offered more, yet they never answered him, so the disaster he warned of will come.

Turn now every one of you from his evil way, and amend your deeds. The message had been reasonable: not tents or abstinence, but turning from evil, with the promise of keeping the land attached. God asked less of Judah than Jonadab asked of his sons, and offered more for compliance.

Sending them persistently. “Persistently” appears a second time in three verses (v. 14). This is the sorrow of the whole book: God as the sender who will not stop sending.

This people has not obeyed me. The charge is not that they failed to keep a code, but that they did not obey him. Disobedience in this book is always personal. God does not list idols or injustices here, though the book has catalogued both. He kept speaking and calling, and they never replied: “I have spoken to them and they have not listened, I have called to them and they have not answered” (v. 17). Two attempts, two silences. Behind it stands a God who, after centuries of being ignored, is still the one doing the talking.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–19 — Never Lack a Man to Stand Before Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with a blessing on the family that served as God’s illustration. Jeremiah tells the Rechabites that because they obeyed their father in everything (v. 18), Jonadab son of Rechab will never lack a man to stand before God (v. 19). It is the very formula God used two chapters earlier of David’s throne and Levi’s priests (33:17–18), now given to a household of outsiders, while the insiders are told their city will burn.
verseByVerse.theology: The same promise given to David's throne and Levi's altar, handed to a clan from outside the tribes.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the house of the Rechabites Jeremiah said, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you have obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his precepts and done all that he commanded you, therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God blesses the Rechabites with the promise he gave to David’s throne and Levi’s priests, a lasting place before him, given to outsiders while insiders lose theirs.

But to the house of the Rechabites. Before the chapter closes God speaks to the Rechabites themselves, who until now have served only as an illustration, beginning with a full recital of what they did right.

Shall never lack a man. Weigh that promise against the one given two chapters earlier: “David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne”, and the Levitical priests “shall never lack a man in my presence” (33:17–18). The formula is identical, and here it is given to a clan that was not one of the twelve tribes at all, most likely a family of Kenite outsiders (1 Chronicles 2:55), attached to Israel but not descended from Jacob.

To stand before me. This is priestly language, the posture of a servant in the sanctuary. Outsiders are promised a permanent place in God’s presence in the same breath that insiders are told their city will burn. The book has been moving this way for a while, and it is where the gospel goes: in Christ, people who were once “strangers to the covenants of promise” become “fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:12, 19).

What the tents preached. Their tents had been preaching all along. Abraham lived the same way, “living in tents with Isaac and Jacob”, because “he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:9–10). Men who refused to build houses were saying, for two hundred and fifty years, that they were not home yet.

What this chapter does not teach. It is not a call to give up wine or to live in tents. God never issued the Rechabite rule, and the Lord himself warned against treating human tradition as divine command: “So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God” (Matthew 15:6). He came eating and drinking and was slandered for it, while John came “eating no bread and drinking no wine” and was called demon-possessed (Luke 7:33–34): the same crowd finding fault either way. “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17).

The question the pitchers ask. The pitchers were only ever a mirror, and their question was never about wine: he has spoken to you persistently; have you answered? The same God who kept calling Judah still calls the one who has not answered, not to be scolded but to come home, and the Spirit he gives is what turns a deaf ear into a listening one (Ezekiel 36:27).

Where Christians differ: should Christians drink alcohol at all? Some, especially in the temperance tradition, urge total abstinence, sometimes citing the Rechabites, and some argue that biblical wine was unfermented. This commentary’s view: wine is God’s gift and Jesus made real wine (John 2:1–11); moderate drinking is Christian liberty, drunkenness is forbidden (Ephesians 5:18), and love gladly abstains for the sake of a weaker brother or sister (Romans 14:21). The Rechabites are praised for faithfulness to their father’s word, not for abstinence as such, and a Christian who chooses to abstain, for his own sake or someone else’s, does well.

35.title: The Rechabites
35.overview:
Where we are. The book steps back about ten years from the siege, to the last years of King Jehoiakim. It is placed beside chapter 34 by theme, not by date: there, men who swore obedience to God went back on it almost at once; here, a family that never promised God anything has kept its word for generations.

The message. Judah has no excuse. A clan kept a dead ancestor’s house rule for two and a half centuries at real cost, while God’s own people would not listen to the living God who spoke to them again and again, asking less and offering more. So the disaster he has pronounced will come; and the outsiders who obeyed are promised a permanent place before him.

Why it was said. Judah had heard prophet after prophet for decades and answered none of them (see the introduction). God gave them a picture they could not argue with: the problem was not that obedience was too hard, but that they did not want to obey.

How the chapter makes its case. God tells Jeremiah to bring the Rechabites into a temple chamber and set wine before them (vv. 1–5). They refuse without hesitation, citing their father Jonadab’s rule of no wine, no houses, no fields and tents only, with one honest exception: the flight into Jerusalem from the Babylonian army (vv. 6–11). Then comes the sermon the scene was staged for: a man’s command to his sons has been kept, but God has spoken persistently and Judah has not listened, so the disaster comes (vv. 12–17). The chapter ends with a blessing on the Rechabites: Jonadab will never lack a man to stand before God (vv. 18–19).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by pattern. Judah’s deafness leaves a question over the whole Old Testament: will anyone ever answer God’s voice with a whole heart? The answer is the Son, who could say, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), and by whose obedience “the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). And outsiders given a lasting place before God, while insiders lose theirs, is the direction the gospel takes, as those once “strangers to the covenants of promise” become “members of the household of God” in Christ (Ephesians 2:12, 19).

For us. We often keep family customs, routines and habits with perfect discipline while leaving God’s plain word unanswered. The chapter asks one question: he has spoken to you persistently; have you answered? And since Christ has already given the Father the obedience we withheld, we answer not as slaves earning a place, but as children called home.
35.theology: The chapter makes a comparison; it does not lay down a rule. God never gave the Rechabite rule, and it is held up as an example of constancy, not as a standard of holiness (Matt 15:6; Rom 14:17). Its point is that Judah cannot plead difficulty: God asked less of them than Jonadab asked of his sons, and offered more. Disobedience is personal; God spoke and called, and they neither listened nor answered. And the outsiders are given the promise made to David's throne and Levi's altar, never to lack a man to stand before God, while the insiders are told their city will burn, which is the direction the gospel takes (Eph 2:12, 19).
35.examples: The scene is a mirror held up to anyone who keeps a family custom, a sports routine or a work habit with perfect discipline while leaving God's plain word unanswered. The Rechabites' tents also have something to say: like Abraham's, they told the neighbours for two hundred and fifty years that this family was not home yet (Heb 11:9-10).

keyVerse.quote: The command that Jonadab the son of Rechab gave to his sons, to drink no wine, has been kept, and they drink none to this day, for they have obeyed their father’s command. I have spoken to you persistently, but you have not listened to me.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter is this comparison. A dead man’s rule about wine has been kept for generations, while the living God’s persistent word has been ignored. It removes Judah’s excuse: the problem was never that obedience was impossible, only that they would not listen.

35.reflection:
The Rechabites kept their father’s rule for about two and a half centuries at real cost (vv. 6–10). What customs, routines or habits do you keep faithfully, and how does that compare with the way you respond to God’s word?

The Rechabites took refuge in Jerusalem without abandoning their purpose (v. 11). How can we tell the difference between the purpose of a command and its letter, and why does it matter?

God says, “I have called to them and they have not answered” (v. 17). What has God been saying to you through Scripture lately that you have heard but not yet acted on?

Outsiders with no tribal claim are promised a lasting place before God (v. 19). How does Ephesians 2:12–19 help you see yourself in that promise, and how should it shape the way we welcome outsiders into the church?

You shall read them also in the hearing of all the men of Judah who come out of their cities.<sup>7</sup>It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the LORD, and that every one will turn from his evil way, for great is the anger and wrath that the LORD has pronounced against this people."<sup>8</sup>And Baruch the son of Neriah did all that Jeremiah the prophet ordered him about reading from the scroll the words of the LORD in the LORD's house.<sup>9</sup>In the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem proclaimed a fast before the LORD.<sup>10</sup>Then, in the hearing of all the people, Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the scroll, in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the secretary, which was in the upper court, at the entry of the New Gate of the LORD's house.<sup>11</sup>When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, heard all the words of the LORD from the scroll,<sup>12</sup>he went down to the king's house, into the secretary's chamber, and all the officials were sitting there: Elishama the secretary, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the officials.<sup>13</sup>And Micaiah told them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the scroll in the hearing of the people.<sup>14</sup>Then all the officials sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, son of Shelemiah, son of Cushi, to say to Baruch, "Take in your hand the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come." So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand and came to them.<sup>15</sup>And they said to him, "Sit down and read it." So Baruch read it to them.<sup>16</sup>When they heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear.
