Was it at his dictation?"<sup>18</sup>Baruch answered them, "He dictated all these words to me, while I wrote them with ink on the scroll."<sup>19</sup>Then the officials said to Baruch, "Go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are."<sup>20</sup>So they went into the court to the king, having put the scroll in the chamber of Elishama the secretary, and they reported all the words to the king.<sup>21</sup>Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the secretary. And Jehudi read it to the king and all the officials who stood beside the king.<sup>22</sup>It was the ninth month, and the king was sitting in the winter house, and there was a fire burning in the fire pot before him.<sup>23</sup>As Jehudi read three or four columns, the king would cut them off with a knife and throw them into the fire in the fire pot, until the entire scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the fire pot.<sup>24</sup>Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments.<sup>25</sup>Even when Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, he would not listen to them.<sup>26</sup>And the king commanded Jerahmeel the king's son and Seraiah the son of Azriel and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel to seize Baruch the secretary and Jeremiah the prophet, but the LORD hid them.<sup>27</sup>Now after the king had burned the scroll with the words that Baruch wrote at Jeremiah's dictation, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:<sup>28</sup>"Take another scroll and write on it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned.<sup>29</sup>And concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, 'Thus says the LORD, You have burned this scroll, saying, "Why have you written in it that the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land, and will cut off from it man and beast?"<sup>30</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He shall have none to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night.<sup>31</sup>And I will punish him and his offspring and his servants for their iniquity. I will bring upon them and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem and upon the people of Judah all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, but they would not hear.'"<sup>32</sup>Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote on it at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Write It on a Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has his word written down so that it can still reach people who will not hear the man who speaks it, and he does it in hope. In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the year Babylon rose to power, Jeremiah is told to write on a scroll everything God has said to him over twenty-three years (vv. 1–2). The purpose is stated twice, by God and then by Jeremiah: “it may be” that they will turn and be forgiven (vv. 3, 7). Jeremiah dictates and Baruch writes, and because the prophet is banned from the temple, the scribe must take the scroll there and read it on a fast day to the crowds from the whole country (vv. 4–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Twenty-three years of sermons copied out, on the chance that somebody might still repent.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Take a scroll and write on it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel and Judah and all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah until today. It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the disaster that I intend to do to them, so that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God had his warnings written down not to build a case against Judah but to give them one more chance to turn and be forgiven.

In the fourth year of Jehoiakim. That is 605 BC, the year Nebuchadnezzar beat Egypt at Carchemish and became the power every nation in the region had to reckon with (see the introduction). At that turning point of history, God tells Jeremiah to make a book.

From the days of Josiah until today. Jeremiah had begun in Josiah’s thirteenth year (1:2), so this is twenty-three years of preaching (25:3) collected into one document: the sermons nobody acted on, gathered up and written down.

It may be. These words should govern how the whole book is read. The scroll is not an archive, or evidence for the prosecution; it is an attempt. The aim is that they might turn, and the goal beyond that is forgiveness: “that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.” Every threat in the collection exists to make the pardon possible.

A sincere offer. God knows the end, but he speaks to people as responsible beings, and his call to repent is real. His foreknowledge never makes the offer insincere.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah's call had come in Josiah's thirteenth year, 627 BC (1:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote on a scroll at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD that he had spoken to him. And Jeremiah ordered Baruch, saying, "I am banned from going to the house of the LORD,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word moves from the prophet’s voice onto the page, so that it can go where the banned prophet cannot.

At the dictation of Jeremiah. Jeremiah spoke and Baruch wrote on the scroll, and the word passed from air into text, where it could be carried, copied, read in rooms the prophet could not enter, and outlive him. This chapter is the Bible describing its own making.

I am banned from going to the house of the LORD. Probably since the temple sermon and trial of chapter 26, or the night in the stocks of chapter 20. The man with the message cannot reach the place where the crowds are, and God’s response is not to remove the obstacle but to route around it: if the preacher is banned, send the book.
verseByVerse.note: Baruch was Jeremiah’s scribe and friend.

verseByVerse.quote: so you are to go, and on a day of fasting in the hearing of all the people in the LORD's house you shall read the words of the LORD from the scroll that you have written at my dictation. You shall read them also in the hearing of all the men of Judah who come out of their cities. It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the LORD, and that every one will turn from his evil way, for great is the anger and wrath that the LORD has pronounced against this people." And Baruch the son of Neriah did all that Jeremiah the prophet ordered him about reading from the scroll the words of the LORD in the LORD's house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baruch is sent to read the scroll in public on a fast day, holding out judgment and hope together, and he does it.

On a day of fasting. The plan is strategic: a fast day, when the temple is full and the mood already serious, and an audience that includes country people up from the towns. One reading will reach as many as possible.

What is asked of Baruch. He is to stand in the temple and read aloud a document predicting national ruin, in the name of a man the king has banned, to a crowd that has beaten and imprisoned that man before. The scribe takes the prophet’s risk, though God had called Jeremiah to this work and not him.

It may be that their plea for mercy will come before the LORD. “It may be” a second time, now on Jeremiah’s own lips. He had no illusions left about his audience, and he still would not close the door. In the same breath he announces the sentence: “great is the anger and wrath.” Faithful preaching does both, because the severity is what makes the appeal urgent.

Baruch … did all that Jeremiah the prophet ordered him. Quiet obedience at real cost. A short chapter dated to this same year lets us see what it cost him inside (45:1–5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — Read It to the Officials
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word read aloud divides its hearers, and some begin to take it seriously. Baruch reads the scroll to the people on a fast day, from the room of Gemariah, a son of Shaphan (vv. 9–10). Gemariah’s son Micaiah carries the news to the king’s officials (vv. 11–13), who send for Baruch, hear the whole scroll and turn to one another in fear (vv. 14–16). They resolve that the king must hear it, check carefully that the words really came from Jeremiah (vv. 17–18), and, knowing their king, tell Baruch and Jeremiah to hide where no one can find them (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The civil servants were frightened by the book, and warned the men who wrote it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem proclaimed a fast before the LORD. Then, in the hearing of all the people, Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the scroll, in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the secretary, which was in the upper court, at the entry of the New Gate of the LORD's house. When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, heard all the words of the LORD from the scroll,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A year later, on a national fast day, Baruch reads the scroll from a friendly family’s room in the temple, and a young man takes the words seriously.

In the ninth month. A year has passed since the command: the scroll took time to write, and the right day had to come. The ninth month fell around December (see The Jewish calendar). The fast was probably called because of Babylon: in that same winter of 604 BC, Babylonian records say, Nebuchadnezzar’s army captured Ashkelon on the coast. Fear makes people religious, as chapter 34 showed.

The chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan. Shaphan was the royal secretary who had read the newly found Book of the Law to Josiah (2 Kings 22:8–10), and his family keeps turning up on the right side of this story, as Ahikam did when he saved Jeremiah’s life (26:24). Somebody sympathetic lent Baruch a room. A clay seal impression reading “Gemaryahu son of Shaphan” was found in excavations in the City of David in the 1980s; many think it belonged to this very man, though that cannot be proved.

At the entry of the New Gate. This is where the officials had sat as a court and acquitted Jeremiah (26:10). The book is read at the spot where its author was once tried.

Micaiah the son of Gemariah, son of Shaphan. Three generations of one family are named, and the young man who hears the reading does not shrug it off. He goes to tell the government.

verseByVerse.quote: he went down to the king's house, into the secretary's chamber, and all the officials were sitting there: Elishama the secretary, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the officials. And Micaiah told them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the scroll in the hearing of the people. Then all the officials sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, son of Shelemiah, son of Cushi, to say to Baruch, "Take in your hand the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come." So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand and came to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The report goes straight to the king’s senior officials, and they send for Baruch and the scroll itself.

All the officials were sitting there. A cabinet meeting, its members listed by name. These lists are not padding; they are the marks of eyewitness testimony.

Elnathan the son of Achbor. One name should stop us. Elnathan is the man Jehoiakim sent to Egypt to bring back the prophet Uriah, who was then executed (26:22–23). In a few verses he will be one of three men urging the king not to burn this scroll. People are not always consistent, and God uses them at the point where they are willing.

Took the scroll in his hand and came to them. Summoned by the government, Baruch goes, carrying the evidence against himself in his own hand. He could have hidden it or left it behind; he brings it because he was asked for it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to him, "Sit down and read it." So Baruch read it to them. When they heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear. And they said to Baruch, "We must report all these words to the king." Then they asked Baruch, "Tell us, please, how did you write all these words? Was it at his dictation?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officials hear the whole scroll and are shaken, and they rightly decide that the king must hear it.

Sit down and read it. They want the whole thing, not a summary, and they give the scribe a chair: the second public reading of the day.

They turned one to another in fear. This is the reaction the book has waited twenty-three years to record. Not agreement necessarily, not repentance yet, but men visibly shaken, looking at each other because it is too much to absorb alone.

We must report all these words to the king. They are not trying to suppress the document; they are officials doing their job well, and God’s word is making its way up through a bureaucracy.

How did you write all these words? The question of serious men. They want to know where it came from: is this really Jeremiah’s, and how did it reach the page?

verseByVerse.quote: Baruch answered them, "He dictated all these words to me, while I wrote them with ink on the scroll." Then the officials said to Baruch, "Go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baruch explains that the words are Jeremiah’s, written exactly as he dictated them, and the officials, knowing their king, tell both men to hide.

He dictated all these words to me. The answer is unglamorous and precise: he spoke, I wrote, with ink. There is a doctrine in that sentence. The words are God’s, given to a prophet, spoken to a scribe and fixed in ink by an ordinary man doing careful work, and the humanity of the process takes nothing away from the divinity of the words. “All Scripture is breathed out by God” (2 Timothy 3:16), and this chapter shows what that looked like from the inside: a voice, a pen, a bottle of ink, a long labour.

Go and hide, you and Jeremiah. They know their king. Before they walk into his presence, they tell the two men to disappear properly, “let no one know where you are”, so that no official under pressure can give them away. It is a small act of courage from men with careers to protect, and God’s care for his servants keeps arriving in this book through people who decide to act decently at some cost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — A Knife and a Fire Pot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king hears every word of God and destroys it, and God protects his servants from him. Jehoiakim insists on having the scroll itself read to him as he sits by the fire in his winter house (vv. 20–22). As each few columns are read he cuts them off with a knife and throws them into the fire, until the whole scroll is gone, and neither he nor his servants show any fear or grief (vv. 23–24). Three officials plead with him, and he will not listen. He orders the arrest of Baruch and Jeremiah, but the LORD hides them (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology: He listened to three or four columns at a time, and only long enough to know what to cut off.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went into the court to the king, having put the scroll in the chamber of Elishama the secretary, and they reported all the words to the king. Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the secretary. And Jehudi read it to the king and all the officials who stood beside the king. It was the ninth month, and the king was sitting in the winter house, and there was a fire burning in the fire pot before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king insists on hearing the scroll itself, and the narrator sets the scene: a winter room, a fire, and the word of God unrolled before him.

Having put the scroll in the chamber of Elishama. They leave the scroll in a side room, perhaps hoping a spoken report would do and the document itself might survive.

The king sent Jehudi to get the scroll. Jehoiakim will not have it second-hand. The officials “stood beside the king” while he sat: everyone else on their feet, the king in his chair by the fire.

A fire burning in the fire pot before him. The scene is set with a novelist’s economy: the ninth month, around December, the winter house, a brazier of coals at the king’s feet, and a man standing before him unrolling the word of God. The narrator lets us see the fire before the king uses it.

verseByVerse.quote: As Jehudi read three or four columns, the king would cut them off with a knife and throw them into the fire in the fire pot, until the entire scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the fire pot. Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoiakim heard every word and calmly destroyed it, piece by piece, without fear and without grief: the exact opposite of his father Josiah.

The king would cut them off with a knife. The wording describes something done again and again. This was not one hot-blooded gesture but a routine kept up the length of a long document: listen to three or four columns, slice them off, feed them to the coals, listen again. The Hebrew calls it a scribe’s knife, the penknife used to trim pens and cut sheets: the tool for making books, turned to unmaking one. He heard every word and destroyed each section as soon as he had heard it. That kind of attention is worse than not listening at all: the deliberate, unhurried disposal of God’s word by a man warm and comfortable in his winter room.

Yet neither the king nor any of his servants … was afraid. Set this against the officials in Elishama’s chamber, who “turned one to another in fear” (v. 16). The same words, the opposite response.

Nor did they tear their garments. Tearing one’s clothes was the sign of grief and repentance (see Mourning Customs). Some eighteen years earlier a scroll had been found in this same temple and read to King Josiah, and “when the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes” (2 Kings 22:11). That tearing began the last reformation Judah ever had. Josiah tore his robe at the word of God; his son took a knife to the word of God and kept his robe intact. The two men are father and son, the two scrolls were read in the same city, and everything that follows in the history of Judah runs out of that difference.

In practice. Few readers take a knife to a Bible, but the same thing can be done quietly: skipping the passages that unsettle us, reading with our conclusions already fixed, or hearing a sermon only to decide which parts to discard. Josiah’s way is open to anyone. When a passage finds you out, stop there, admit to God that it is true, and ask what he wants changed, without dread, because the word that exposes was given “that I may forgive” (v. 3).

Uncertain wording. “Columns” translates a Hebrew word that normally means “doors”, used in the Bible only here for part of a scroll, so its exact sense is not certain. Most take it of the columns of writing, which stood side by side along a scroll like a row of door panels; some think of the separate sheets stitched together to make it. The picture is the same either way: the king destroyed the scroll section by section as he heard it.

verseByVerse.quote: Even when Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, he would not listen to them. And the king commanded Jerahmeel the king's son and Seraiah the son of Azriel and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel to seize Baruch the secretary and Jeremiah the prophet, but the LORD hid them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king overrules his own advisers and orders the arrest of Baruch and Jeremiah, but the LORD hides them.

Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah urged the king. Three men are named so that we know somebody in that room tried: Elnathan, who had once been the instrument of a prophet’s death; Delaiah; and Gemariah, in whose son’s hearing the scroll had first been read.

He would not listen to them. The verdict of the whole book, applied here to a man refusing not a prophet but his own advisers. By now Jehoiakim will not hear God, will not hear Jeremiah, and will not hear the officials he appointed.

To seize Baruch the secretary and Jeremiah the prophet. Burning the book is not enough; he wants the men. A royal prince and two officers are sent to find them, with the same energy that once sent an extradition party to Egypt after Uriah.

But the LORD hid them. No angel, no miracle described, no method given. The officials had said “go and hide”; the narrator says God hid them. Both are true, and that is usually how providence looks: sensible advice taken, a friend’s back room, and behind it all a hand the searchers never see.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word of God survives the fire, and the man who burned it falls under it. God’s response to the burning is simply to have the scroll written again (vv. 27–28). He quotes back the king’s real objection, the prediction that Babylon would come (v. 29), and pronounces sentence: no heir of Jehoiakim will sit on David’s throne, his body will lie unburied in heat and frost, and every threatened disaster will come, because they would not hear (vv. 30–31). Jeremiah and Baruch rewrite the whole scroll, and many similar words are added: the king could not even make the book shorter (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: The book came back longer than the one he burned.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after the king had burned the scroll with the words that Baruch wrote at Jeremiah's dictation, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: "Take another scroll and write on it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned. And concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, 'Thus says the LORD, You have burned this scroll, saying, "Why have you written in it that the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land, and will cut off from it man and beast?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king burned the scroll, so God simply tells Jeremiah to write it again, and names what the king really objected to.

Take another scroll. The king destroys the words, and the word comes again. That sequence is the point of the chapter, and the narrator does not even pause over it. The instruction is almost dismissive in its simplicity: write it again.

You have burned this scroll. God quotes the king’s objection back at him, and it was specific. Not the moral demands, not the charges of injustice, but the prediction about Babylon. He burned the scroll because of its politics. Burning a forecast does not change the weather.

The word cannot be burned. A book can be burned; the word it carries cannot. “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:8), and the Lord Jesus said the same of his own words: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35). Peter quotes Isaiah’s line and then says what that enduring word is: “And this word is the good news that was preached to you” (1 Peter 1:25). Every regime that has since burned Bibles has done what Jehoiakim did in a warm room in winter, with the same result.

So he came back from the grave. The pattern reached its end in Jesus. The God who spoke “at many times and in many ways” by the prophets has “in these last days” spoken “to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2), and Jesus told the parable of the vineyard owner who sent servant after servant and at last his beloved son, whom the tenants killed (Mark 12:1–8). The rulers of his day dealt with God’s final word as Jehoiakim dealt with the scroll: they heard him out, and then got rid of him. And as the scroll came back, so he came back from the grave, and the message they tried to silence went out to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He shall have none to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night. And I will punish him and his offspring and his servants for their iniquity. I will bring upon them and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem and upon the people of Judah all the disaster that I have pronounced against them, but they would not hear.'" Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote on it at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king who burned the word is sentenced by it, and the scroll is written again, longer than before.

The heat by day and the frost by night. The sentence answers the crime in kind. He fed the scroll to the fire in his warm room; his own body will lie out in the open, in the heat of the day and the frost of the night.

He shall have none to sit on the throne of David. Both parts of the sentence had been announced before. Jeremiah had already said of this king, “With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried, dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem” (22:19), and of his son Coniah that “none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David” (22:30). His son Jehoiachin reigned three months and was deported, and no son of his ever sat on that throne.

But they would not hear. The epitaph of the whole reign. Everything else in the verse is consequence; this is the cause.

Then Jeremiah took another scroll. So they sat down and did it all over again: the same long labour, voice and pen and ink, with a price now on both their heads.

And many similar words were added to them. The quiet triumph of the chapter. The second edition was longer. Everything Jehoiakim had cut off came back, and more with it, including the sentence on his own corpse, which exists only because he burned the first one. He could not even succeed in making the book shorter.

How then is Jesus David’s heir? Matthew’s genealogy runs through Jeconiah, that is Jehoiachin (Matthew 1:11–12). The sentence meant that no son of this line would reign on David’s throne in Jerusalem, and none ever did. But God had not abandoned David: he had already promised a righteous Branch who would reign (23:5–6; 33:15), and Jesus, David’s son through Joseph as his legal father, reigns not from Jehoiakim’s palace but from the right hand of God (Acts 2:30–36).

The book we are reading. What Jehoiakim held in his hands that December was the book we are reading. It survived him, outlasted his dynasty and Babylon, and is still read aloud in rooms full of people, which is what it was written for in the first place: “it may be” that someone will hear, and turn, and be forgiven.

Did he have a donkey’s burial? Kings says only that Jehoiakim “slept with his fathers” (2 Kings 24:6), a phrase that means simply that he died and says nothing of an honourable burial. He probably died in late 598 BC, as the Babylonian army closed in. Chronicles adds that Nebuchadnezzar bound him in chains to take him to Babylon (2 Chronicles 36:6), which may never have been carried out. Scripture does not describe what was done with his body, but this commentary takes Jeremiah’s word as fulfilled.

36.title: The Scroll Burned and Rewritten
36.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 36 steps back from the siege years of chapters 32 to 34 to 605 BC, the fourth year of Jehoiakim. It opens the account of what Jeremiah suffered for God’s word (chapters 36 to 45), which closes in this same year with a word for Baruch, the scribe of this chapter (45:1).

The message. God’s word is given so that sinners may turn and be forgiven, and it cannot be destroyed. A king may cut it up and burn it, but the word comes back with more added, and the man who burned it is judged by it. The question is never whether God’s word will survive us, but whether we will tremble at it and turn.

Why it was said. Babylon had just beaten Egypt at Carchemish and become master of the region, and Jehoiakim, a king who had already hunted down and killed a prophet (26:20–23), ruled a nation that had ignored Jeremiah for twenty-three years (see the introduction). The scroll was God’s appeal in a form they could not shout down, and its story told later readers in exile why the disaster had come.

How the chapter makes its case. God tells Jeremiah to write down every word he has spoken, because “it may be” that Judah will turn and be forgiven (vv. 1–8). Baruch reads it to the people and then to the king’s officials, who are shaken and tell both men to hide (vv. 9–19). The king has it read by his winter fire and cuts it into the flames column by column, unafraid; he orders the arrests, but the LORD hides his servants (vv. 20–26). God then sentences the king and has the scroll written again, with many words added (vv. 27–32).

Where it leads. By pattern, and in the character of God. The God who speaks again after his word is burned is the God who “in these last days … has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2). The rulers of Jesus’ day heard that final Word out and did away with him, as Jehoiakim did with the scroll; and as the scroll came back, he came back from the grave. The purpose God states here, “that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin” (v. 3), is the purpose for which Christ died.

For us. Each of us hears God’s word either as Josiah did, tearing his clothes, or as his son did, quietly discarding what he disliked. The word that exposes us is given to forgive us, so we can afford to let it find us out. And the Bible will outlast every fire lit against it, so every Baruch who copies, reads and carries it at some cost is doing work that lasts.
36.theology: God's purpose in writing down the threats is repentance and pardon, not record-keeping: it may be that they will turn. When the preacher is barred, God sends the book, and the word moves from air into ink so that it can enter rooms the prophet cannot and outlive the men who carry it (2 Tim 3:16). Attention is not obedience: Jehoiakim heard every column and destroyed each one, while his father Josiah had torn his clothes at a scroll. And a book can be burned, but the word cannot; it came back longer, as Jesus, God’s final Word, came back from the grave (Matt 24:35; Mark 12:1-8).
36.examples: The officials who warned Baruch and Jeremiah to hide had careers to protect, and still did what was decent; much of God's care for his servants in this book arrives that way. Jehoiakim's knife is the opposite: the reader who hears the Bible out, column by column, only to know which parts to cut away.

keyVerse.quote: It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the disaster that I intend to do to them, so that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.
keyVerse.note: This verse gives the purpose of the scroll, and of all Jeremiah’s warnings: not to condemn but to bring people to turn and be forgiven. It is what makes the burning in verse 23 so tragic, because what the king destroyed was an offer of pardon. The same purpose stands behind every hard word of Scripture, and it was fulfilled when Christ died for the forgiveness of sins.

36.reflection:
God had his warnings written down “that I may forgive” (v. 3). How does knowing the purpose behind God’s hard words change the way you hear them?

The officials turned to one another in fear; the king cut up the scroll and felt nothing (vv. 16, 23–24). What are the quieter ways we can do what Jehoiakim did, and what would Josiah’s response (2 Kings 22:11) look like for you this week?

Baruch wrote, read and carried a dangerous scroll, and the officials risked their careers to protect him. Where might God be asking you to take a small risk for the sake of his word or his people?

The burned scroll came back with more added (v. 32), and the rejected Son came back from the grave. How does that give you confidence when God’s word seems to be losing ground, in our culture or in your own family?

37.text: <sup>1</sup>Zedekiah the son of Josiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah, reigned instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim.<sup>2</sup>But neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listened to the words of the LORD that he spoke through Jeremiah the prophet.<sup>3</sup>King Zedekiah sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah, and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, to Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "Please pray for us to the LORD our God."<sup>4</sup>Now Jeremiah was still going in and out among the people, for he had not yet been put in prison.<sup>5</sup>The army of Pharaoh had come out of Egypt. And when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard news about them, they withdrew from Jerusalem.<sup>6</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet:<sup>7</sup>"Thus says the LORD, God of Israel: Thus shall you say to the king of Judah who sent you to me to inquire of me, 'Behold, Pharaoh's army that came to help you is about to return to Egypt, to its own land.<sup>8</sup>And the Chaldeans shall come back and fight against this city. They shall capture it and burn it with fire.<sup>9</sup>Thus says the LORD, Do not deceive yourselves, saying, "The Chaldeans will surely go away from us," for they will not go away.<sup>10</sup>For even if you should defeat the whole army of Chaldeans who are fighting against you, and there remained of them only wounded men, every man in his tent, they would rise up and burn this city with fire.'"<sup>11</sup>Now when the Chaldean army had withdrawn from Jerusalem at the approach of Pharaoh's army,<sup>12</sup>Jeremiah set out from Jerusalem to go to the land of Benjamin to receive his portion there among the people.<sup>13</sup>When he was at the Benjamin Gate, a sentry there named Irijah the son of Shelemiah, son of Hananiah, seized Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "You are deserting to the Chaldeans."<sup>14</sup>And Jeremiah said, "It is a lie; I am not deserting to the Chaldeans." But Irijah would not listen to him, and seized Jeremiah and brought him to the officials.<sup>15</sup>And the officials were enraged at Jeremiah, and they beat him and imprisoned him in the house of Jonathan the secretary, for it had been made a prison.<sup>16</sup>When Jeremiah had come to the dungeon cells and remained there many days,<sup>17</sup>King Zedekiah sent for him and received him. The king questioned him secretly in his house and said, "Is there any word from the LORD?" Jeremiah said, "There is." Then he said, "You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon."<sup>18</sup>Jeremiah also said to King Zedekiah, "What wrong have I done to you or your servants or this people, that you have put me in prison?<sup>19</sup>Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, 'The king of Babylon will not come against you and against this land'?<sup>20</sup>Now hear, please, O my lord the king: let my humble plea come before you and do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the secretary, lest I die there."<sup>21</sup>So King Zedekiah gave orders, and they committed Jeremiah to the court of the guard. And a loaf of bread was given him daily from the bakers' street, until all the bread of the city was gone. So Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king who will not obey God’s word still wants God’s help. Zedekiah owes his throne to Nebuchadnezzar, and neither he nor his officials nor the people listen to anything God says through Jeremiah (vv. 1–2). Yet he sends two men to ask the prophet to pray for them, at the very moment the Babylonian army has withdrawn from Jerusalem to meet an Egyptian force marching north (vv. 3–5). The relief looked like an answer, and prayer looked like a way to keep it coming. The narrator adds that Jeremiah was not yet in prison, warning us where the story is going (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: They will not hear a word he says, and they would like him to pray for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Zedekiah the son of Josiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah, reigned instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim. But neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listened to the words of the LORD that he spoke through Jeremiah the prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zedekiah is king only by a foreign emperor’s permission, and he, his officials and his people all refuse to listen to God.

Whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made king. Zedekiah is Josiah’s son, of David’s royal line, but he sits on the throne because Nebuchadnezzar put him there, in place of a nephew who was deported (2 Kings 24:15–17). He reigns by another king’s permission. That is the man the chapter shows us: a king with a title and no authority, frightened of his own officials, frightened of Babylon, and half-persuaded that Jeremiah is right.

Neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listened. Before a single event is narrated, the verdict is given, and it covers the whole society: king, civil service and ordinary people. Nobody listened. Put that beside what happens next and the chapter’s real subject appears: what religion looks like in people who have already decided not to obey.

verseByVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah, and Zephaniah the priest, the son of Maaseiah, to Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "Please pray for us to the LORD our God." Now Jeremiah was still going in and out among the people, for he had not yet been put in prison. The army of Pharaoh had come out of Egypt. And when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard news about them, they withdrew from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king who ignores God’s word asks God’s prophet to pray for him, just as the siege lifts.

Please pray for us to the LORD our God. A polite request for intercession, one verse after we are told this king listens to nothing the prophet says. They claim God as “the LORD our God” while ignoring his word. They want his power without his instruction, as if prayer were a service the prophet provides, detached from the message he brings.

Jehucal the son of Shelemiah, and Zephaniah the priest. Both messengers have histories. Zephaniah had come on this errand once before, when Zedekiah sent to say, “Inquire of the LORD for us” (21:2), and he was the priest who read Shemaiah’s hostile letter aloud to Jeremiah rather than act on it (29:29). Jehucal will shortly stand before the king demanding this prophet’s death, because “he is weakening the hands of the soldiers” (38:4). The man who carries the prayer request will call for the execution.

He had not yet been put in prison. The words quietly warn us of what is coming.

The army of Pharaoh had come out of Egypt. Here is why the palace suddenly wants prayer, and why it is about to stop wanting it. Pharaoh Hophra (almost certainly the king of 44:30) has marched north, Nebuchadnezzar has broken off the siege to deal with him, and the pressure is off. This is the withdrawal named in 34:21, “the army of the king of Babylon which has withdrawn from you”: the breathing space in which the slave-owners of Jerusalem fetched back the people they had just freed. The same lifted siege that produced the broken covenant produced this request for prayer.
verseByVerse.note: Hophra reigned in Egypt from 589 to 570 BC; his name appears in Scripture only at 44:30.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the request for prayer with the truth: the relief is temporary, and the city will still burn. Pharaoh’s army will go home, and the Chaldeans will come back, take Jerusalem and set it on fire (vv. 6–8). The people must not deceive themselves by reading the lifted siege as a rescue (v. 9). Even if they destroyed the whole Babylonian army and only wounded men were left in their tents, those men would get up and burn the city, because its fall is God’s decision, not a matter of military strength (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The outcome was never a military calculation, so a lifted siege proves nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet: "Thus says the LORD, God of Israel: Thus shall you say to the king of Judah who sent you to me to inquire of me, 'Behold, Pharaoh's army that came to help you is about to return to Egypt, to its own land. And the Chaldeans shall come back and fight against this city. They shall capture it and burn it with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the request for prayer with the truth: the Egyptian help will go home, and the Babylonians will come back and burn the city.

Pharaoh’s army that came to help you is about to return to Egypt. They asked for prayer; they get a word, and not the one they wanted. It begins by dismantling the very thing that had raised their spirits. The relieving army will not even be defeated in a great battle: the help everyone was counting on will simply turn round and leave.

An old sickness. Judah’s reliance on Egypt was nothing new. Isaiah had named it more than a century before: men who “set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh and to seek shelter in the shadow of Egypt”, of whom God said, “Therefore shall the protection of Pharaoh turn to your shame” (Isaiah 30:2–3).

They shall capture it and burn it with fire. Come back, capture, burn: the empty siege lines are a pause, not a deliverance, and God says so before anyone can conclude from the good news that he has rescued them.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, Do not deceive yourselves, saying, "The Chaldeans will surely go away from us," for they will not go away. For even if you should defeat the whole army of Chaldeans who are fighting against you, and there remained of them only wounded men, every man in his tent, they would rise up and burn this city with fire.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God forbids them to read the lifted siege as a rescue: the city’s fall is his decision, and nothing can overturn it.

Do not deceive yourselves. The command is about the inside of their heads. Nobody was lying to them here; they were doing it themselves, and with evidence: the army really had gone, the fields really were passable again, the relief was real. Self-deception rarely needs false facts; it only needs true facts read the way we want them read. God even supplies the sentence they were saying to each other, “The Chaldeans will surely go away from us”, and answers it directly: “for they will not go away.” He says hard things to people he means to save.

Only wounded men, every man in his tent. The picture is deliberately extreme. Suppose you won, and the entire Babylonian army lay wounded in their tents: those men would get up and burn Jerusalem anyway. This is not a comment on Babylonian toughness. The fall of this city is God’s decision, so no army can overturn it. This war was never going to be decided by military strength.

Shouldn’t I live by my own truth? We now speak easily of “my truth”, and there is something right in it: each of us has a story only we can tell. But the phrase slides from my experience to my reality, as if believing something hard enough could make it so. Jerusalem had its own truth: the Babylonians had gone, the fields were open, the worst was over. They had evidence, and they had each other, and none of it moved the army one mile. In The Brothers Karamazov Dostoevsky gives the old monk Zosima a warning about exactly this: above all, do not lie to yourself, because the one who listens to his own lie ends up unable to see any truth, in himself or around him. The deepest reason we lie to ourselves is that the truth about us is more than we can bear. That is why the gospel is the one safe place to stop pretending. It tells us the truth about ourselves at its worst, and then shows us a Saviour who knew all of it and came for us anyway: “you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:32).

How do I stop deceiving myself? The New Testament repeats the warning, because the heart has not changed: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). Notice the sentence you keep repeating. “It will blow over.” “Everyone does this.” “I can stop whenever I like.” Judah’s was “The Chaldeans will surely go away from us”; write yours down and hold it up against Scripture. Ask God to search you. Pray, “Search me, O God, and know my heart!” (Psalm 139:23), especially about the thing you least want to look at: the overdraft, the drinking, the friendship that has gone wrong. Let someone tell you the truth. Give one honest friend permission to say what they see, and do not argue the first time they do. Remember why you can afford to look. We deceive ourselves to escape a verdict. For those in Christ the verdict has already fallen, on him, so you can face the worst about yourself without being destroyed by it. The truth that exposes you is the same truth that forgives you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet who told the truth is treated as a traitor. During the lull Jeremiah sets out for the land of Benjamin on family business (vv. 11–12), and at the city gate a sentry seizes him, accusing him of deserting to the Chaldeans (v. 13). He denies it, truthfully, but no one listens. He is brought to the officials, who are furious, beat him and lock him in the underground cells of a secretary’s house turned into a prison, where he stays many days (vv. 14–16). Faithfulness has cost him his freedom and very nearly his life.
verseByVerse.theology: Forty years of being called a traitor, and when the charge is finally laid it is false.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Chaldean army had withdrawn from Jerusalem at the approach of Pharaoh's army, Jeremiah set out from Jerusalem to go to the land of Benjamin to receive his portion there among the people. When he was at the Benjamin Gate, a sentry there named Irijah the son of Shelemiah, son of Hananiah, seized Jeremiah the prophet, saying, "You are deserting to the Chaldeans." And Jeremiah said, "It is a lie; I am not deserting to the Chaldeans." But Irijah would not listen to him, and seized Jeremiah and brought him to the officials.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On an ordinary family errand during the lull, Jeremiah is arrested at the city gate on a false charge of deserting to the enemy.

To receive his portion there among the people. With the roads briefly open, the prophet sets out for his home district of Benjamin, where Anathoth lay, on family business to do with inherited land. Scripture does not say what, though it may have been the same property his cousin Hanamel would later offer him (32:6–9). It is an ordinary errand, and that is what makes what follows so bitter.

A sentry there named Irijah. A sentry with a name and a grandfather, doing what sentries do in a war, at a gate that led north into Benjamin. And the charge was not absurd on its face. Jeremiah had publicly advised the city to surrender, saying that whoever went out to the Chaldeans would live (21:9). A man with those views, walking out of the north gate during a lull, looked exactly like a defector.

It is a lie. The denial is blunt, and it is true. For nearly forty years he had been called a traitor for telling Judah what God said, and when an actual charge of treason was finally laid against him, it was false. He had urged surrender because God had spoken; he was not slipping away himself.

But Irijah would not listen to him. The phrase that echoes through the whole book, now from a soldier at a gate. Nobody in this chapter listens to anybody.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “to receive his portion there” is compressed, and its exact sense is uncertain. The verb has to do with dividing or sharing out. Most take it, as the ESV does, of receiving or settling a share of family property; older translations such as the King James Version render it “to separate himself” from the people. Either way, Jeremiah had a lawful reason to leave the city and was not deserting.

verseByVerse.quote: And the officials were enraged at Jeremiah, and they beat him and imprisoned him in the house of Jonathan the secretary, for it had been made a prison. When Jeremiah had come to the dungeon cells and remained there many days,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without a hearing, the officials beat Jeremiah and shut him in an underground prison for many days.

The officials were enraged at Jeremiah. These are not the officials of chapter 26 who convened a fair court, nor those of chapter 36 who trembled at the scroll and told Baruch to hide. Many of the old leaders had been deported with Jehoiachin in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:14). A different generation is in office now, and they are enraged.

They beat him and imprisoned him in the house of Jonathan the secretary. A private house has been converted into a jail. No trial is mentioned, no hearing, no examination of the sentry’s claim. The man who had just been asked to pray for the king is flogged by the king’s officials.

The dungeon cells … many days. Those two details are the whole cost of his obedience in this chapter. The narrator does not dwell on it and gives us no lament from the prophet. But this is the man who had said God’s word was a fire in his bones he could not hold in (20:9), and this is what speaking it out cost him: a cellar, for weeks, with no prospect of release and a fair expectation of dying there (v. 20).

Uncertain wording. “Dungeon cells” renders two Hebrew words, literally “the house of the pit” (the word used for a cistern) “and the vaults”. The second occurs only here, and no one is sure exactly what it describes: perhaps vaulted cells, perhaps rooms cut into the rock beneath the house. The sense is clear enough: an underground prison, dark and unhealthy, where a man could die.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–21 — Is There Any Word from the LORD?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king wants a different word and gets the same one, and God keeps his prophet alive. Zedekiah has Jeremiah brought to him secretly and asks whether there is any word from the LORD. There is: he will be handed over to the king of Babylon (v. 17). Only then does Jeremiah speak for himself, asking what wrong he has done and where the prophets of peace have gone (vv. 18–19), and humbly begging not to be sent back to die in the cellar (v. 20). The king moves him to the court of the guard with a daily loaf of bread, until the city’s bread runs out (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: He answers honestly first and asks for mercy second, in that order.

verseByVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent for him and received him. The king questioned him secretly in his house and said, "Is there any word from the LORD?" Jeremiah said, "There is." Then he said, "You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon." Jeremiah also said to King Zedekiah, "What wrong have I done to you or your servants or this people, that you have put me in prison? Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, 'The king of Babylon will not come against you and against this land'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
In secret the king asks for a word from God and receives the same word again; only then does Jeremiah plead his innocence.

The king questioned him secretly in his house. Everything about this interview is furtive. The king has the prophet brought up from the cells and questions him in private, because he dare not be seen consulting the man his officials have just beaten.

Is there any word from the LORD? One of the saddest questions in Scripture. He has heard the word for years, refused it, imprisoned the man who brought it, and now asks in a private room whether there is any more of it. He wants a different answer, and he asks the one person guaranteed not to give him one.

There is. Consider Jeremiah’s position. He stands before the only man who can release him, bruised from a beating, expecting to die in a cellar, and one softened sentence would have helped his case enormously. What he says is “There is”, and then the very sentence that put him where he is: “You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon.” No hedging, no trading. The message did not change because the prophet’s circumstances had.

What wrong have I done to you … ? Only after delivering the word does he speak for himself, and both questions are fair. The first is the protest of an innocent man. The second is unanswerable: where are the prophets who promised Babylon would never come? They had been believed and he had been beaten, and now the Babylonians were camped in the fields and the optimists had nothing to say.

Another prisoner, another ruler. Six hundred years later another prisoner stood before another frightened ruler who kept questioning him in private (John 19:8–11), and there the answer was different: “he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed” (Matthew 27:14). Jeremiah spoke the word and was spared; Jesus, the Word himself, was silent before his judge and was not spared, and it was for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Now hear, please, O my lord the king: let my humble plea come before you and do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the secretary, lest I die there." So King Zedekiah gave orders, and they committed Jeremiah to the court of the guard. And a loaf of bread was given him daily from the bakers' street, until all the bread of the city was gone. So Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah humbly asks not to be sent back to die, and the king moves him to the court of the guard, where God keeps him alive on a daily loaf.

Let my humble plea come before you. The iron prophet asks for something, courteously and without pretence. He does not ask for vindication, or for his accusers to be punished, or even for freedom. He asks not to be sent back to that cellar, and says plainly why: “lest I die there.” There is no false bravery in it. He was afraid of dying in a hole, he said so, and asking a weak king for a small mercy was not beneath him.

They committed Jeremiah to the court of the guard. The king does the one decent thing within his power: not release, for he has not the courage for that, but a transfer to the courtyard of the palace guard, and a daily loaf.

A loaf of bread was given him daily from the bakers’ street. Compare the rations another prophet was given for telling a king the truth: “Put this fellow in prison and feed him meager rations of bread and water” (1 Kings 22:27). Jeremiah gets a loaf a day from the bakers’ street, and it comes through the frightened man who had him beaten.

Until all the bread of the city was gone. The clause quietly measures the whole siege. His provision lasted exactly as long as there was any bread in Jerusalem to be had. God kept him alive on the last supplies of a starving city, one loaf at a time, in a courtyard. Jesus taught us to ask for bread a day at a time (Matthew 6:11), and this is what that prayer looks like answered in a siege.

The answer to his question. It was in that courtyard, on that bread, that Jeremiah bought the field at Anathoth and was given the promises of chapters 32 and 33. That is the answer to Zedekiah’s question, though he never grasped it. Was there any word from the LORD? There was: words given to a beaten man on a bread ration, about fields bought again and a righteous Branch for David.

37.title: Arrested at the Benjamin Gate
37.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 37 leaps forward from Jehoiakim’s scroll to the final siege under Zedekiah, around 588 BC. The Babylonians have briefly lifted the siege to meet an Egyptian army, and the chapter tells how Jeremiah came to be held in the court of the guard, where chapters 32 and 33 found him.

The message. People who will not obey God’s word may still want God’s help, but God will not be used. He tells them the truth: the relief is temporary, and the city will burn. His prophet suffers for saying it, yet the word does not bend to the prophet’s circumstances, and God keeps him alive. Self-deception cannot save anyone; only hearing God can.

Why it was said. Zedekiah was a king set up by Nebuchadnezzar who had rebelled against him, trusting Egypt (see the introduction). When Pharaoh’s army marched and the Babylonians withdrew, Jerusalem believed the danger had passed. For later readers in exile, the chapter shows that the city fell not for lack of warning, but because no one would listen.

How the chapter makes its case. Nobody listens (vv. 1–2), yet the king asks for prayer just as the siege lifts (vv. 3–5). God answers that Egypt will go home and the Chaldeans return; even wounded men would rise and burn the city (vv. 6–10). During the lull Jeremiah is arrested at the gate on a false charge of desertion, beaten and left in a cellar (vv. 11–16). The king fetches him secretly and asks for a word; Jeremiah gives the same word, protests his innocence, asks not to be sent back to die, and is kept in the court of the guard on a daily loaf until the bread runs out (vv. 17–21).

Where it leads. By pattern, and in the need it exposes. An innocent man, falsely charged with treason, beaten by officials and questioned in private by a frightened ruler: Jeremiah here foreshadows Jesus before Pilate (John 19:8–12). But Jeremiah spoke and was spared, while Jesus kept silence and was not spared, for us. And Zedekiah’s question, “Is there any word from the LORD?”, finds its final answer in the Word made flesh.

For us. It is possible to want God’s help while refusing his word, and to read good news as a way of avoiding repentance. The cure is to let God tell us the truth and believe it when it is unwelcome, knowing that in Christ the truth that exposes us also forgives us. And when faithfulness lands us in a hard place, God can keep us there, one day’s bread at a time.
37.theology: People who have already decided not to obey still want the benefits of prayer, claiming the LORD as our God while ignoring his word. Self-deception rarely needs false facts, only true facts read as we wish: the siege really had lifted, and the conclusion drawn from it was still a lie. Against this stands a prophet who will not trade the message for better treatment, yet is honest enough to ask for mercy and admit his fear. And God's provision can come through the hand of a frightened man who wronged you, and be exactly enough: a loaf a day, as long as the city had bread.
37.examples: Most of us know the pull of Zedekiah's position: asking God for help in a crisis while having decided in advance not to do what he says. And most of us know the relief that makes us read a lull as a deliverance. Jeremiah's plea not to be sent back to the cellar is a gift to anyone who has been ashamed of being afraid: the bravest prophet in the book asked a weak king for a small mercy, and God gave it through him.

keyVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent for him and received him. The king questioned him secretly in his house and said, “Is there any word from the LORD?” Jeremiah said, “There is.” Then he said, “You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon.”
keyVerse.note: This exchange is the heart of the chapter. A king who has refused God’s word for years still hopes for a different one, and a beaten prisoner who could have bought his freedom with a softer sentence gives him the same word unchanged. It shows both the folly of wanting God’s help without his truth and the faithfulness of a messenger who will not bend the message.

37.reflection:
Zedekiah asked for prayer while refusing to obey (vv. 2–3). In what ways can we want God’s help without wanting his word?

Jerusalem deceived itself with true facts read the way it wished (v. 9). What sentence do you tend to repeat to yourself to avoid something God has said, and how could others help you face it?

Jeremiah gave the king the same unwelcome word when a softer one might have freed him (v. 17). Where are you tempted to soften the truth to protect yourself, and what would faithfulness look like there?

God kept Jeremiah alive one loaf at a time, and Jesus kept silence before Pilate for our sake. How do these scenes help you trust God when faithfulness leaves you in a hard place?

He shall have his life as a prize of war, and live.<sup>3</sup>Thus says the LORD: This city shall surely be given into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon and be taken."<sup>4</sup>Then the officials said to the king, "Let this man be put to death, for he is weakening the hands of the soldiers who are left in this city, and the hands of all the people, by speaking such words to them. For this man is not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm."<sup>5</sup>King Zedekiah said, "Behold, he is in your hands, for the king can do nothing against you."<sup>6</sup>So they took Jeremiah and cast him into the cistern of Malchiah, the king's son, which was in the court of the guard, letting Jeremiah down by ropes. And there was no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud.<sup>7</sup>When Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch who was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah into the cistern—the king was sitting in the Benjamin Gate—<sup>8</sup>Ebed-melech went from the king's house and said to the king,<sup>9</sup>"My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they did to Jeremiah the prophet by casting him into the cistern, and he will die there of hunger, for there is no bread left in the city."<sup>10</sup>Then the king commanded Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, "Take thirty men with you from here, and lift Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies."<sup>11</sup>So Ebed-melech took the men with him and went to the house of the king, to a wardrobe in the storehouse, and took from there old rags and worn-out clothes, which he let down to Jeremiah in the cistern by ropes.<sup>12</sup>Then Ebed-melech the Ethiopian said to Jeremiah, "Put the rags and clothes between your armpits and the ropes." Jeremiah did so.<sup>13</sup>Then they drew Jeremiah up with ropes and lifted him out of the cistern.
