verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — He Is in Your Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who silence God’s word accuse its messenger of the harm they themselves are causing, and a weak king lets them. Four officials hear Jeremiah still telling the people that whoever stays in the city will die and whoever goes out to the Chaldeans will live, because the city will certainly be taken (vv. 1–3). They demand his death for weakening the soldiers’ will to fight, claiming that he seeks the people’s harm, not their welfare (v. 4). Zedekiah hands him over, saying the king can do nothing against them: a plea of powerlessness that the next scene proves false (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: A king who cannot say no, and hands over a man he believes to be a prophet.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Shephatiah the son of Mattan, Gedaliah the son of Pashhur, Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur the son of Malchiah heard the words that Jeremiah was saying to all the people: "Thus says the LORD: He who stays in this city shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence, but he who goes out to the Chaldeans shall live. He shall have his life as a prize of war, and live. Thus says the LORD: This city shall surely be given into the hand of the army of the king of Babylon and be taken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even as a prisoner Jeremiah keeps preaching God’s offer: stay and die, or go out and live, because the city will surely fall.

Jucal the son of Shelemiah. Four men, each named with his father, and one of them we have met. Jucal is the Jehucal who carried the king’s request for prayer to this same prophet (37:3). The man sent to ask for intercession now heads the party demanding an execution.

Saying to all the people. Jeremiah is confined to the court of the guard, and he is still preaching to all who will hear. A prison in the middle of the palace compound has become a pulpit.

He who goes out to the Chaldeans shall live. This is the word that made him hated, so it pays to be clear about what it offered. It was not propaganda for Babylon but an escape route: stay and die, go out and live, “and live” repeated as if to make sure nobody missed the offer inside the threat. It rests on the certainty that “this city shall surely be given”: that is why leaving it means life. Everything depends on whether what God has announced is true, which is exactly what his hearers would not believe.

His life as a prize of war. He will come out of the disaster alive, and his life is all he will carry off. The same phrase becomes God’s personal promise to Ebed-melech and to Baruch (39:18; 45:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officials said to the king, "Let this man be put to death, for he is weakening the hands of the soldiers who are left in this city, and the hands of all the people, by speaking such words to them. For this man is not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm." King Zedekiah said, "Behold, he is in your hands, for the king can do nothing against you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officials accuse the man who is trying to save the city of seeking its harm, and the king hands him over, pretending he has no choice.

He is weakening the hands of the soldiers. The charge is that he is damaging the soldiers’ will to fight, and on its own terms it is not stupid. A man telling the garrison that the city will fall and they should surrender is, militarily, a liability. Any war cabinet in history would have said the same.

Not seeking the welfare of this people, but their harm. But this last clause is the exact opposite of the truth. This is the prophet who had told the exiles to “seek the welfare of the city” and pray for it (29:7), who had pleaded with Judah for forty years to turn and live, and who was at that moment offering the only survivable course. The men marching the city into a furnace accused him of wanting its harm. That accusation has a long life: whoever tells an uncomfortable truth is charged with wishing the harm his warning is trying to prevent.

The king can do nothing against you. One of the most pitiful sentences in the book, and it is not true: he will overrule these same men almost at once when someone asks him to (v. 10). What he lacks is not authority but nerve. He hands over a man he believes to be a prophet, to men he is afraid of, and consoles himself with the fiction that he had no choice. “The fear of man lays a snare” (Proverbs 29:25).

Pilate did the same. Pilate would one day say it by washing his hands before the crowd. He knew the prisoner was innocent, and gave him up because the crowd was louder than his conscience (Matthew 27:24; John 19:12–16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Cast Into the Mud, and Lifted Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rescues his servant from the pit through an outsider who cares. The officials lower Jeremiah into a cistern with no water in it, only mud, and leave him to sink and starve (v. 6). Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian eunuch in the palace, goes straight to the king at the Benjamin Gate and says publicly that these men have done evil (vv. 7–9). The king who could do nothing now orders thirty men to the rescue (v. 10). Ebed-melech fetches old rags so the ropes will not cut, tells Jeremiah where to put them, and draws him out alive (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: A foreigner and a eunuch, thinking about how the ropes would cut.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took Jeremiah and cast him into the cistern of Malchiah, the king's son, which was in the court of the guard, letting Jeremiah down by ropes. And there was no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud. When Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch who was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah into the cistern—the king was sitting in the Benjamin Gate— Ebed-melech went from the king's house and said to the king,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officials lower Jeremiah into a muddy cistern to die, and the one man who moves to save him is a foreign servant of the palace.

The cistern of Malchiah. A cistern was a bottle-shaped pit cut into rock, narrow at the neck and wide below, made to hold rainwater. This one held no water, only mud. So they lowered him into a stone jar in the ground, in the dark, and he sank. There is no way out of such a hole without help from above: the walls curve inward and the floor gives way beneath you. They did not need to kill him; they only needed to leave him.

Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch. The rescuer is introduced with three details that in that society were all disqualifications: a foreigner, from Ethiopia (Cush, the land up the Nile beyond Egypt), and a eunuch, who under the law of Deuteronomy 23:1 could not enter the assembly of the LORD. Every Judean official in this chapter behaves badly. The one man who moves is an African court servant, and he moves at once: he heard, and he went. No committee, no delay. His name means “servant of the king”, and he proves a truer servant than any of the king’s officials.

A psalm’s picture of salvation. Hold the image, because a psalm turns it into the picture of salvation itself: “He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure” (Psalm 40:2). That is about to happen to Jeremiah, and it is what God does for sinners: not advice shouted down the shaft, but someone coming to haul us out.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word translated “eunuch” is used both of castrated men and, more broadly, of high court officials; Potiphar, a married man, is called by it (Genesis 39:1, “an officer of Pharaoh”). Which is meant here cannot be settled for certain. A foreign servant in the king’s household, where the royal women lived (v. 22), may well have been a eunuch in the literal sense, as the ESV takes it; but even if the word means only “official”, Ebed-melech remains an outsider in Judah who acted when its own leaders would not.
verseByVerse.note: Ebed-melech means “servant of the king”; he was a Cushite, from south of Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: "My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they did to Jeremiah the prophet by casting him into the cistern, and he will die there of hunger, for there is no bread left in the city." Then the king commanded Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, "Take thirty men with you from here, and lift Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ebed-melech tells the king to his face that the officials have done evil, and the king who could do nothing orders a rescue at once.

These men have done evil. He says it to the king’s face, in public at the Benjamin Gate, with the officials’ faction in power and his own position entirely dependent on royal favour.

There is no bread left in the city. He calls Jeremiah what the officials would not, “the prophet”, and his argument is practical and humane: the man will starve down there. The daily loaf of 37:21 has run out, which probably places this scene in the last weeks of the siege.

Take thirty men with you. Zedekiah, who had just said that the king can do nothing, immediately orders thirty men to the rescue. The king could act all along. The difference between a prophet dying in mud and a prophet drawn out of it was one man willing to speak up.

verseByVerse.quote: So Ebed-melech took the men with him and went to the house of the king, to a wardrobe in the storehouse, and took from there old rags and worn-out clothes, which he let down to Jeremiah in the cistern by ropes. Then Ebed-melech the Ethiopian said to Jeremiah, "Put the rags and clothes between your armpits and the ropes." Jeremiah did so. Then they drew Jeremiah up with ropes and lifted him out of the cistern. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ebed-melech draws Jeremiah out of the pit, and takes care that the rescue itself does not hurt him.

Old rags and worn-out clothes. He had his authority and thirty men, and before he pulled, he went looking for rags. He detoured to a palace storeroom, found old rags and worn-out clothes, and lowered them down the shaft first, because a man hauled out of a pit on bare ropes, by thirty men pulling hard, would have the rope cut into his armpits. He even tells the exhausted man below exactly where to put them.

Kindness over details. Scripture spends three verses on this. It could have said they pulled him out. Instead it records the wardrobe, the old clothes, the instruction about the armpits, because God takes notice of kindness that troubles itself over details. Anyone can want a man rescued. This is what it looks like to care whether the rescue hurts.

Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard. Out of the mud and back to the courtyard: still a prisoner, but alive and above ground.

Ebed-melech’s reward. When the city falls, God sends him a private word: “I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me” (39:18). The phrase offered to anyone who would leave the city is given personally to the man who pulled the prophet out, and the reason given is not his courage but his trust.

A promise for foreigners and eunuchs. Isaiah had made a promise for men in exactly his position: “let not the eunuch say, ‘Behold, I am a dry tree’”, for God would give such men “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters … an everlasting name that shall not be cut off” (Isaiah 56:3–5). A childless foreign servant has his name written in Scripture, remembered for one day’s decency, long after the officials who outranked him are recalled only as the men who did evil.

The promise comes true. On a desert road an Ethiopian court official, another eunuch from the same far country, was reading Isaiah’s servant song, heard that it spoke of Jesus, and was baptised (Acts 8:26–39). The outsider who pulled a prophet from a pit was a forerunner of a great company of outsiders welcomed into God’s household by Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even at the last hour God offers the king life, and the king refuses it for fear of being mocked. Zedekiah meets Jeremiah secretly at the temple and demands the whole truth; Jeremiah, knowing he will not listen, asks for his life to be guaranteed, and the king swears it (vv. 14–16). The offer is plain: surrender, and you, your house and the city will live; refuse, and the city will burn (vv. 17–18). The king fears the Judeans who have deserted (v. 19). Jeremiah answers that fear and shows him the shame refusal will bring: the women of the palace led out, mocking a king left stuck in the mud (vv. 20–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Obedience was offered to the end, and refused for fear of the wrong people.

verseByVerse.quote: King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah the prophet and received him at the third entrance of the temple of the LORD. The king said to Jeremiah, "I will ask you a question; hide nothing from me." Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "If I tell you, will you not surely put me to death? And if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me." Then King Zedekiah swore secretly to Jeremiah, "As the LORD lives, who made our souls, I will not put you to death or deliver you into the hand of these men who seek your life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king seeks the truth in secret, and Jeremiah, knowing he will not act on it, first asks for his life to be guaranteed.

At the third entrance of the temple of the LORD. Another secret meeting, at an entrance mentioned nowhere else and no longer identifiable, presumably a discreet one. The king who let him be thrown into a pit wants a private consultation, and opens with a demand for total honesty from a man he has failed to protect.

If I tell you, will you not surely put me to death? The prophet’s reply is two accusations, and both are accurate. The first is about his own safety: he had just been left to die and had every reason to expect it again. The second is sadder and sharper: “if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me.” He has read the man. There is no point advising someone who has already decided that advice will not move him, and Jeremiah says so before he speaks.

As the LORD lives, who made our souls. The oath is solemn and beautifully phrased, and it is sworn secretly. A king who dares not be seen keeping faith with a prophet swears by the God who made them both, in a side entrance, where nobody will hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, "Thus says the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel: If you will surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then your life shall be spared, and this city shall not be burned with fire, and you and your house shall live. But if you do not surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon, then this city shall be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and you shall not escape from their hand." King Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted to the Chaldeans, lest I be handed over to them and they deal cruelly with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God still offers the king his life and the city’s survival if he will surrender, and the king refuses for fear of being mocked.

If you will surrender to the officials of the king of Babylon. In the final weeks, with the walls about to break, God is still making an offer. Read what is on the table: the king’s life, his household, and “this city shall not be burned with fire.” Jerusalem could still have been spared; the temple need not have burned. Everything depended on one man walking out of a gate. Two roads are stated plainly, with nothing hidden, exactly as the king had asked. It is the shape of the whole book: repent and live, refuse and perish, with the choice genuinely open until the last hour.

I am afraid of the Judeans who have deserted. This is his answer to the offer of his city’s survival: he is worried about being mocked. The men who had already defected on Jeremiah’s advice would jeer at the king who arrived last. Weigh the calculation: Jerusalem burned, the temple destroyed, his sons killed, his own eyes put out, thousands dead of famine, because a frightened man could not bear the humiliation of walking out to people who had gone before him.

What fear of man does. Fear of man will accept enormous real disaster to avoid a small loss of face, and it always presents itself as prudence. Its cure is not a stronger nerve but a greater fear, of the LORD “who made our souls” and still holds out life; and God gives his people a spirit “not of fear but of power and love and self-control” (2 Timothy 1:7).

Was the fall certain? The city would certainly fall (v. 3), yet Zedekiah is told it need not burn. The fall was certain, but its manner depended on him: surrender, and the city and his household would be spared the fire. God’s warnings are real, and they call for a response.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah said, "You shall not be given to them. Obey now the voice of the LORD in what I say to you, and it shall be well with you, and your life shall be spared. But if you refuse to surrender, this is the vision which the LORD has shown to me: Behold, all the women left in the house of the king of Judah were being led out to the officials of the king of Babylon and were saying, "'Your trusted friends have deceived you and prevailed against you; now that your feet are sunk in the mud, they turn away from you.' All your wives and your sons shall be led out to the Chaldeans, and you yourself shall not escape from their hand, but shall be seized by the king of Babylon, and this city shall be burned with fire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah answers the king’s fear, pleads with him to obey, and shows him the shame that refusal will bring.

You shall not be given to them. The prophet answers the actual fear directly, then presses the one thing needed: “Obey now the voice of the LORD.” Note the pastoral patience of it. He does not lecture the king on cowardice. He removes the objection, promises that “it shall be well with you”, and asks for obedience today.

Now that your feet are sunk in the mud, they turn away from you. The vision is of the royal women marched out of the palace, and the words God gives them are a taunt in verse, the sort of thing that would be sung about him afterwards. The king who left a prophet to sink in mud will himself be stuck in it, abandoned by the officials he was too frightened to cross. Jeremiah was pulled out by a foreigner with rags; nobody will come down for Zedekiah.

Your trusted friends have deceived you. The Hebrew is literally “the men of your peace”, the men whose approval cost him his city. They will be the ones who “prevailed against you” and then walked away. The approval of men had been his idol, and this is what every idol does: it demands everything, and abandons you when you need it. A psalm uses the same phrase for the close friend who betrays (Psalm 41:9), words Jesus applied to Judas (John 13:18). Zedekiah was betrayed by the friends he chose over God; Jesus was betrayed by a friend he had chosen, and went on to die for those who deserted him.

All your wives and your sons shall be led out. The appeal ends with the list of what refusal will cost: wives, sons, his own capture, the city burned. Every item arrived exactly as stated (39:6–8).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king’s last concern is not his city but his secret. Zedekiah tells Jeremiah to keep their conversation hidden and gives him the words to say if the officials question him (vv. 24–26). They do question him, he answers as instructed, and they leave him alone because nobody overheard (v. 27). Jeremiah remains in the court of the guard until the day Jerusalem is taken (v. 28). The prophet who offered the city life outlives its refusal, while the king who could have saved it spends his last chance on keeping up appearances.
verseByVerse.theology: The king protected the secret of the conversation and not the city it was about.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, "Let no one know of these words, and you shall not die. If the officials hear that I have spoken with you and come to you and say to you, 'Tell us what you said to the king and what the king said to you; hide nothing from us and we will not put you to death,' then you shall say to them, 'I made a humble plea to the king that he would not send me back to the house of Jonathan to die there.'" Then all the officials came to Jeremiah and asked him, and he answered them as the king had instructed him. So they stopped speaking with him, for the conversation had not been overheard. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard until the day that Jerusalem was taken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king’s last concern is secrecy; Jeremiah keeps the secret without lying, and remains a prisoner until the city falls.

Let no one know of these words. The offer of life for his city has just been laid before him, along with the vision of his wives led away. His response is to worry about who might find out that they had spoken.

I made a humble plea to the king. He scripts the answer, and the line he supplies is a real one: the plea Jeremiah had made at their last meeting not to be sent back to the house of Jonathan to die there (37:20). The king tells him to give a true account of an earlier conversation instead of the subject of this one.

Hide nothing from us and we will not put you to death. The officials offer Jeremiah the same bargain the king just did: tell us everything and we will not kill you. Everyone in this palace bargains by threatening a man’s life. They came, exactly as the king predicted; Jeremiah answered as instructed, and the interrogation stopped because nobody could contradict him.

Until the day that Jerusalem was taken. He stayed in the courtyard while the food ran out, and the city fell around a man nobody would listen to.

Two figures side by side. Set the two figures of this chapter side by side. A king of David’s line, with armies, officials and the word of God delivered privately into his hand, who could do nothing; and an African servant with no rights at all, who heard about an injustice, walked to the gate, said so, fetched rags, and saved a prophet’s life. God’s verdict on them is recorded in the next chapter: one lost his sons, his sight and his city; the other was told, “because you have put your trust in me” (39:18).

The gospel in a cistern. The mud is the picture to keep: a man who could not climb out, and the ropes, padding and hands that came down for him (Psalm 40:2). That is the gospel in a cistern, with one difference. Christ did not only lower ropes; he came down himself, into death, to bring us up, and he was not ashamed to be seen doing it.

Was Jeremiah lying? He told the officials only what the king instructed, a true part of the conversation (compare 37:20), and withheld the rest. Withholding the truth from those who have no right to it, to protect life, is not the same as bearing false witness.

38.title: The Cistern and the Ethiopian
38.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 38 runs straight on from chapter 37, into the last weeks of the siege of Jerusalem. Jeremiah is held in the court of the guard but still preaching, and the city’s bread is running out.

The message. God’s word offers life even at the last hour, and what stands between people and that life is the fear of man. The powerful who silence the truth, and the king who lets them, are lost; a foreign servant with no standing, who trusts God and acts, is honoured. God draws his servant out of the pit, and his offer to the king stays open until the king himself refuses it.

Why it was said. The city was starving and its leaders were set on fighting on (see the introduction), so Jeremiah’s call to surrender sounded like treason. The chapter shows later readers why Jerusalem burned: not because God withheld mercy, but because a king feared his officials more than the LORD.

How the chapter makes its case. Officials demand Jeremiah’s death for weakening the army’s morale, and the king hands him over (vv. 1–5). Lowered into a muddy cistern to die, he is rescued by Ebed-melech, who confronts the king and draws him out with padded ropes (vv. 6–13). In a last secret meeting Jeremiah offers Zedekiah his life and the city’s survival if he will surrender; the king fears mockery, and the prophet describes the shame refusal will bring (vv. 14–23). The king’s final concern is secrecy, and Jeremiah remains a prisoner until the city falls (vv. 24–28).

Where it leads. By pattern. A righteous sufferer sinking in a pit and drawn up by hands from above is the picture Psalm 40 uses for salvation, and Christ did more than lower ropes: he went down into death himself to bring us up. A ruler who knows the prisoner is innocent and hands him over anyway foreshadows Pilate (Matthew 27:24). And the foreign eunuch honoured for his trust looks ahead to the Ethiopian official baptised into Christ (Acts 8:26–39).

For us. The fear of what others think can cost us everything God offers, and its cure is a greater fear, of the LORD who made our souls. Ebed-melech shows what trust in God looks like in practice: speaking up for the wronged at personal risk, and caring enough to pad the ropes. And no one is too far down for God to reach.
38.theology: Jeremiah was hated for telling the city to surrender, yet that message was a way of escape, and it stayed open until the final weeks. Fear of man is a snare that disguises itself as helplessness: the king who said he could do nothing ordered thirty men to the rescue the moment somebody asked him (Prov 29:25; John 19:12-16). God notices kindness that troubles itself over details, and he commends the outsider with no standing: a foreign eunuch is given a name in Scripture for his trust (Isa 56:3-5). And the mud is a picture of salvation, a pit with no way out but hands from above.
38.examples: A rescuer who stops to fetch rags so that the ropes will not cut is a model for every kind of practical care: the hospital visit, the meal left on a doorstep, the hard conversation with someone in power. And Zedekiah's choice, a city lost rather than face being laughed at, is a warning to anyone who knows what is right and fears the opinion of friends more than God.

keyVerse.quote: You shall not be given to them. Obey now the voice of the LORD in what I say to you, and it shall be well with you, and your life shall be spared.
keyVerse.note: Here, in the last weeks of the siege, is God’s final appeal to the last king of Judah, and it is an offer of life. Everything turned on one choice between the voice of the LORD and the fear of man, and Zedekiah chose wrongly. The verse shows that God’s judgment never comes without an open door, and that the door can be refused.

38.reflection:
The officials accused Jeremiah of seeking the people’s harm when he was offering them the only way to live (v. 4). Why are those who speak uncomfortable truths so often treated as enemies, and how should we respond when it happens to us?

Ebed-melech spoke up at personal risk, and then fetched rags so the ropes would not hurt (vv. 9–12). Who around you is “in the mud”, and what would both courage and careful kindness look like towards them?

Zedekiah lost his city because he was afraid of being mocked (v. 19). Where does the fear of what others think most shape your choices, and how does the fear of the LORD “who made our souls” (v. 16) free us from it?

Psalm 40:2 describes God drawing us up from the miry bog. How does Jeremiah’s rescue help you understand what Christ has done for you?
