And when they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, at Riblah, in the land of Hamath; and he passed sentence on him.<sup>6</sup>The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes, and the king of Babylon slaughtered all the nobles of Judah.<sup>7</sup>He put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.<sup>8</sup>The Chaldeans burned the king's house and the house of the people, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem.<sup>9</sup>Then Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, carried into exile to Babylon the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to him, and the people who remained.<sup>10</sup>Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left in the land of Judah some of the poor people who owned nothing, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.<sup>11</sup>Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon gave command concerning Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, saying,<sup>12</sup>"Take him, look after him well, and do him no harm, but deal with him as he tells you."<sup>13</sup>So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officers of the king of Babylon<sup>14</sup>sent and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard. They entrusted him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, that he should take him home. So he lived among the people.<sup>15</sup>The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard:<sup>16</sup>"Go, and say to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will fulfill my words against this city for harm and not for good, and they shall be accomplished before you on that day.<sup>17</sup>But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you shall not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid.<sup>18</sup>For I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me, declares the LORD.'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Breach Was Made in the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word against the city and its king comes true exactly. Nebuchadnezzar’s army besieges Jerusalem in the ninth year of Zedekiah, and in the eleventh year, a year and a half later, the wall is breached and Babylon’s officials take their seats in the gate (vv. 1–3). Zedekiah and his soldiers flee by night through a gate between the walls, heading for the Jordan valley, but are overtaken in the plains of Jericho (vv. 4–5). At Riblah Nebuchadnezzar passes sentence: the king’s sons and the nobles of Judah are killed before his eyes, and then his eyes are put out and he is bound for Babylon (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The last thing he ever saw was what his refusal cost his own children.

verseByVerse.quote: In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem and besieged it. In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month, a breach was made in the city. Then all the officials of the king of Babylon came and sat in the middle gate: Nergal-sar-ezer of Samgar, Nebu-sar-sekim the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, with all the rest of the officers of the king of Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a long siege the wall is breached and Babylon’s officials sit down in Jerusalem’s gate: the city has fallen, as God said it would.

In the ninth year of Zedekiah … in the eleventh year. Two dates, roughly January 588 BC and July 586 BC (some reckon a year earlier), with about a year and a half of siege between them. The narrator gives the siege no adjectives. Everything that happened inside those walls, the bread running out, the cistern, the last loaf from the bakers’ street, the horrors Lamentations records of starving families (Lamentations 4:4–10), sits compressed into the gap between one date and another.

A breach was made in the city. This is the sentence the whole book has been walking toward. Forty years of warning, and when it arrives it is reported like a line in a chronicle. For generations afterwards the people kept a fast in the fourth month to mourn it (Zechariah 8:19).

Sat in the middle gate. The names and titles are Babylonian. A clay tablet from Nebuchadnezzar’s reign names a chief official (the title Rab-saris) whose name is very like Nebu-sar-sekim’s. The first Nergal-sar-ezer is probably Neriglissar, Nebuchadnezzar’s son-in-law, who later seized the throne of Babylon.

The seat of justice. The gate was where Israel’s elders sat to judge, where Boaz called witnesses, where the officials had once acquitted Jeremiah. Now other men sit there, and their language is not Hebrew. The seat of justice in Jerusalem has changed occupants.

Uncertain wording. Rab-saris and Rab-mag are titles, not names: the first means something like “chief official”, and the second is a high court office whose exact sense is unknown. How the list should be divided is also uncertain. The ESV reads “Nergal-sar-ezer of Samgar”, taking Samgar as a place, while older translations such as the King James Version read “Samgarnebo” as a separate name; and the list does not quite match the officers named in verse 13. Where the middle gate stood is not known either. None of this affects the point.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah 52 and 2 Kings 25 give fuller accounts of the same events.

verseByVerse.quote: When Zedekiah king of Judah and all the soldiers saw them, they fled, going out of the city at night by way of the king's garden through the gate between the two walls; and they went toward the Arabah. But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. And when they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, at Riblah, in the land of Hamath; and he passed sentence on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king who would not walk out in obedience runs out in flight, and is caught.

They fled, going out of the city at night. He had been told, twice and plainly, that if he walked out to the Babylonians his life would be spared and the city would not burn (38:17). He would not do it in daylight as an act of obedience. So he goes out anyway: at night, by way of the king’s garden, through a gate between the walls, running for the Arabah, the Jordan valley. The feet that would not carry him out in surrender carry him out in flight. What obedience would have cost him was his dignity; what disobedience cost him is in the next three verses.

In the plains of Jericho. They catch him on the flat ground near Jericho, where Israel had first entered the land under Joshua. The story of the possession of Canaan ends where it began, with the last king of Judah taken prisoner. Years before, in Babylon, Ezekiel had acted out this very escape, digging through a wall at dusk with his baggage on his shoulder, as a sign of what the prince in Jerusalem would do (Ezekiel 12:3–13).

He passed sentence on him. He is brought to Riblah, on the Orontes river some two hundred miles north, where Nebuchadnezzar had his headquarters, to be judged as a vassal who had rebelled, because that is what he was: Nebuchadnezzar had put him on the throne and made him swear by God, and he had broken his oath (2 Chronicles 36:13).

verseByVerse.quote: The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes, and the king of Babylon slaughtered all the nobles of Judah. He put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zedekiah sees his sons killed and is then blinded: every word of God’s warning to him comes true.

Before his eyes. The order of events is deliberate: his sons are killed while he watches, as the parallel accounts also record (52:10; 2 Kings 25:7), and then he is blinded. God had told him, through the man he left in a cistern, “You shall see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face” (34:3), and that he would go to Babylon. Every clause came true, though not as he imagined. The last image his eyes ever held was his own children dying. They had done nothing; his fear of being laughed at had cost them everything, and the narrator records it without a word of comment, as if it were too heavy for one.

To take him to Babylon. Ezekiel had said the prince would be brought to Babylon, “yet he shall not see it, and he shall die there” (Ezekiel 12:13). Here is how both could be true: he was blinded at Riblah, then taken to Babylon, where he died. For years Zedekiah had treated his sentence as an opening offer to be bargained down; it was a plain statement of what would happen.

The promise of peace. Is anything left of the promise of 34:4–5, that he would not die by the sword but in peace, with spices burned for him and mourners to lament him? It is a thin mercy beside what he lost, but as far as we are told he died in prison in Babylon, not by the sword (52:11), and this commentary reads that as the promise kept, even to a king who had earned nothing.

The promise to David. What became of the promise that David would never lack a man to sit on the throne (33:17)? On this day the throne is empty and the king’s sons lie dead at Riblah. But David’s line survived in the exiled Jehoiachin (52:31–34), and the promise waited for the Branch. Six centuries later a son of David was crowned with thorns outside this same city, hailed in mockery as King of the Jews, and raised to the throne of his father David, of whose kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32–33).

Why would God allow children to be killed for their father’s sin? It is a terrible question, and the text does not soften the scene; Lamentations, traditionally Jeremiah’s own lament, weeps over the children fainting in the streets of this city (Lamentations 2:11). The cruelty was Nebuchadnezzar’s, and Scripture never calls it good. God foretold it and used it as judgment on a king who had broken a sworn oath (Ezekiel 17:15–19), and Babylon’s own cruelties would in turn be judged (25:12; 51:24).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The city is destroyed and its people deported, yet in the ruins the poor are given land. The Babylonians burn the palace and the houses and pull down the walls of Jerusalem (v. 8). Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, deports the rest of the population, both those who held out and those who had surrendered (v. 9). But he leaves behind some of the poorest, who had owned nothing, and gives them vineyards and fields (v. 10). People at the bottom of Judah’s society, so often wronged by its leaders, become landholders on the day the powerful lose everything.
verseByVerse.theology: The people with nothing to lose ended the day owning land.

verseByVerse.quote: The Chaldeans burned the king's house and the house of the people, and broke down the walls of Jerusalem. Then Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, carried into exile to Babylon the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to him, and the people who remained. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left in the land of Judah some of the poor people who owned nothing, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem is burned and its people deported, yet on the same day the poorest in the land are given vineyards and fields.

Broke down the walls of Jerusalem. The palace, the houses, the walls: everything Judah had trusted in, dynasty, city and defences, dismantled in one verse, exactly as the scroll Jehoiakim burned had said: “the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land” (36:29). The temple is not mentioned here. Chapter 52 supplies that detail (52:13), and perhaps this account cannot yet bring itself to say it.

Carried into exile to Babylon. Three groups, all deported: those who held out, those who had deserted, and the remainder. Even the deserters go, which shows that surrender was never a trick to avoid exile; it was the way to stay alive. Jeremiah had promised life as a prize of war, not a comfortable outcome.

The poor people who owned nothing. Then, in a chapter about catastrophe, the people left in the land are the poor who owned nothing, and a pagan general hands them vineyards and fields. The landless get land on the day the landowners lose everything. People who had been at the bottom of every list in Judah, freed and then re-enslaved by the officials of chapter 34, cheated of their wages by the king who built his palace without paying them (22:13), wake up as freeholders.

An exact reversal. Nobody planned this as justice. Nebuzaradan was solving an administrative problem: keep the countryside producing, and deport anyone who could organise a revolt. But the effect is a reversal so exact that it reads like a verdict. Mary sang of the same pattern at the coming of Christ: “he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate” (Luke 1:52). And the New Testament states as a principle what this verse only shows happening: “has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom” (James 2:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Deal With Him As He Tells You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet the city rejected is protected by the king who destroyed it. Nebuchadnezzar gives orders through Nebuzaradan that Jeremiah is to be looked after, done no harm, and treated as he himself asks (vv. 11–12). The senior Babylonian officers fetch him from the court of the guard and hand him to Gedaliah, son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan, from the family that had protected him before, to take him home (vv. 13–14). After the stocks, the cells, the cistern and the courtyard, Jeremiah lives free among his own people.
verseByVerse.theology: The emperor's standing order for one prisoner: do whatever he asks.

verseByVerse.quote: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon gave command concerning Jeremiah through Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, saying, "Take him, look after him well, and do him no harm, but deal with him as he tells you." So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-saris, Nergal-sar-ezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officers of the king of Babylon sent and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard. They entrusted him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, that he should take him home. So he lived among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pagan king who destroyed the city orders that the prophet it despised be cared for, and Jeremiah is handed to a friend.

Deal with him as he tells you. Nebuchadnezzar, the emperor of the known world, has one named prisoner on his mind. Weigh the irony without missing the providence. For forty years the rulers and priests of Judah imprisoned this man, beat him, banned him from the temple, burned his book and dropped him in a pit. The pagan king who destroyed the city gave orders that he was to be treated well and have his own way. Presumably they knew he had urged surrender and counted him useful. God’s protection of his servants routinely arrives through people acting for their own reasons.

Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan. The whole Babylonian high command fetches one old man out of a courtyard, and the man they entrust him to is a gift. Ahikam had protected him at a trial decades earlier (26:24); Ahikam’s son takes him home after the city falls. Shaphan’s family has turned up at every turning point of this book: reading the law to Josiah, lending Baruch a room, carrying the letter to the exiles (29:3), and now this. Faithfulness across generations does not make headlines, but it keeps quietly holding things up. Gedaliah’s own story continues in chapters 40 and 41.

So he lived among the people. After the stocks, the cells, the cistern and the court of the guard, the prophet ends the chapter a free man living among ordinary Judeans.

Chains at Ramah. Jeremiah was released into Gedaliah’s care here, but 40:1 finds him in chains at Ramah. He was most likely rounded up with the captives by mistake, then released again at Ramah when the commander recognised him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Because You Have Put Your Trust in Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God remembers, by name, the one man who trusted him. The chapter reaches back to the days when Jeremiah was still shut up in the court of the guard, for a word to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian (vv. 15–16). God does not promise that he will be spared the sight of the city’s fall; he will see it. But God will deliver him from the men he fears, and he will not fall by the sword but come through with his life (vv. 17–18). The reason is stated plainly: “because you have put your trust in me.”
verseByVerse.theology: The man who fetched the rags is told why he will live, and it is not because of the rags.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard: "Go, and say to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will fulfill my words against this city for harm and not for good, and they shall be accomplished before you on that day. But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you shall not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid. For I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me, declares the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the city fell, God promised the one man who had trusted him that he would come through alive, because he had trusted.

While he was shut up in the court of the guard. This word, given before the walls broke, is placed out of order so that we read it after the catastrophe it spoke of. It begins with the truth: “I will fulfill my words against this city for harm and not for good.” Ebed-melech will see the palace he served in burn. There is no promise that he will be spared the sight, only that he will come through it.

The men of whom you are afraid. God names the fear without rebuking it. Ebed-melech had walked up to the king at a public gate and accused powerful officials of evil, and he had been afraid of them ever since, as well he might be. Courage, in this book, is not the absence of fear. It is what Ebed-melech did while afraid, and God’s answer is not that his fear was foolish but that those men will never have him.

Your life as a prize of war. This is the phrase Jeremiah had proclaimed to the whole city: whoever goes out to the Chaldeans “shall have his life as a prize of war, and live” (38:2). What was offered publicly to everyone is now guaranteed personally to one man.

Because you have put your trust in me. Mark the reason God gives. Not because you rescued my prophet, not because you were brave or kind or fetched padding for the ropes, but because you trusted me. That verdict sorts everyone in the chapter. A king of David’s line, who had the promises, the temple and the prophet’s private counsel, lost his sons and his sight because he trusted the opinion of men he was afraid of. A foreign servant with no tribe, no children and no rights was saved because he trusted God, and his trust showed itself, as it always does, in what he did about a man sinking in mud.

Saved through faith. It is the ground on which any sinner is rescued: “by grace you have been saved through faith” (Ephesians 2:8), trusting the God who keeps his word, with a faith that then shows itself in love. God knew the name of the one servant in Jerusalem who believed him, and had a word addressed to him by name before the first stone came down.

Doesn’t it matter more how you live than what you believe? It is a widely shared conviction, and there is a fine instinct behind it. People have seen cruelty done by the doctrinally correct and kindness done by people with no creed at all, and they conclude that deeds are what count. This chapter seems to agree, until you look closely. The eunuch is the one who acted; the king is the one who talked. But God does not say “because you were brave”. He says “because you have put your trust in me”. Ebed-melech’s courage did not come from nowhere. He believed that the God of the prophet in the mud was real and would keep his word, and that belief sent him to the king at the gate. Zedekiah believed something too: that the officials and the crowd were more real than God, and his belief also showed itself in what he did. Everyone lives by a creed; the only question is whether it is true. The gospel does not make us choose between believing and doing. It gives us a God so trustworthy that trusting him at last makes cowards brave.

39.title: The City Falls
39.overview:
Where we are. After a siege of a year and a half, the moment the whole book has warned of arrives. Chapter 39 records the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC (told again more fully in chapter 52 and in 2 Kings 25), and what became of the people of chapters 37 and 38: the king, the prophet and the Ethiopian.

The message. Every word God spoke came true. The king who would not trust him lost everything, as he had been told; the poor received fields; the prophet the city despised was protected; and the one foreigner who trusted the LORD was saved. God’s judgment is certain, and so is his care for those who trust him.

Why it was said. The exiles needed to know that the catastrophe was neither chance nor the victory of Babylon’s gods, but the fulfilment of the LORD’s own word (see the introduction). If the threats came true to the letter, so would the promises of chapters 30 to 33.

How the chapter makes its case. The siege begins, and a year and a half later the wall is breached and Babylon’s officials sit in the gate (vv. 1–3). Zedekiah flees by night, is caught near Jericho, sees his sons killed at Riblah and is blinded (vv. 4–7). The city is burned and the people deported, but the poorest are given vineyards and fields (vv. 8–10). Nebuchadnezzar orders that Jeremiah be well treated, and he is entrusted to Gedaliah (vv. 11–14). Last comes a word from the siege: God will save Ebed-melech, because he trusted him (vv. 15–18).

Where it leads. By covenant and promise, and by the need it exposes. On this day David’s throne stood empty and his royal sons lay dead, and it seemed the covenant with David had failed. But God had promised a righteous Branch (23:5; 33:15), and six centuries later a son of David was crowned with thorns outside this city and raised to a throne that has no end (Luke 1:32–33). And the ground on which Ebed-melech was saved, “because you have put your trust in me”, is the ground on which any sinner is saved through faith in Christ.

For us. God’s warnings are not bluff, and refusing them costs more than we imagine; but neither are his promises, and he knows by name everyone who trusts him, even in a falling city. Such faith is never merely a private opinion: it shows itself, as Ebed-melech’s did, in what we do.
39.theology: God’s warnings state what will happen; they are not opening offers to be bargained down. Zedekiah treated the sentence as one, and every clause of it came true. Yet even here God's care shows. The landless are given land on the day the landowners lose everything, and the prophet whom Judah's rulers imprisoned is protected by a pagan emperor and taken home by a faithful family (Jas 2:5; Matt 5:5). And in the ruins, the one man promised his life is saved not for his bravery but for his trust, as every sinner is (Eph 2:8).
39.examples: Zedekiah walked out of the city in the end, by night and in flight, having refused to walk out by day in obedience. It is a picture worth keeping for anyone putting off a costly step God has made plain: delay does not usually spare us the step, only the blessing that went with it. Ebed-melech, frightened and faithful, is the other picture, and the more hopeful one.

keyVerse.quote: For I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me, declares the LORD.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter of fulfilled judgment, this promise stands out as fulfilled mercy. It sorts the whole story: the king who trusted men lost everything, and the foreign servant who trusted God was saved. It shows the ground on which God rescues anyone, not courage or merit but trust in him, a trust that had already shown itself in action.

39.reflection:
Zedekiah would not walk out in obedience, and ended up running out in flight (vv. 4–5; 38:17). Why is delayed or partial obedience so costly, and is there something God has made plain that you are putting off?

On the day the powerful lost everything, the poor were given fields (v. 10). What does this show about God’s concern for the poor, and how should it shape the way your church treats those with little?

Shaphan’s family kept quietly doing right across three generations, and in the end it was Gedaliah who took Jeremiah home (v. 14). What would faithfulness across generations look like in your family or church?

God saved Ebed-melech “because you have put your trust in me” (v. 18), and that trust had already shown itself in action. How does his story help you understand the relationship between faith and good works?

40.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD after Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had let him go from Ramah, when he took him bound in chains along with all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah who were being exiled to Babylon.<sup>2</sup>The captain of the guard took Jeremiah and said to him, "The LORD your God pronounced this disaster against this place.<sup>3</sup>The LORD has brought it about, and has done as he said. Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice, this thing has come upon you.<sup>4</sup>Now, behold, I release you today from the chains on your hands. If it seems good to you to come with me to Babylon, come, and I will look after you well, but if it seems wrong to you to come with me to Babylon, do not come. See, the whole land is before you; go wherever you think it good and right to go.<sup>5</sup>If you remain, then return to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon appointed governor of the cities of Judah, and dwell with him among the people. Or go wherever you think it right to go." So the captain of the guard gave him an allowance of food and a present, and let him go.<sup>6</sup>Then Jeremiah went to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah, and lived with him among the people who were left in the land.<sup>7</sup>When all the captains of the forces in the open country and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor in the land and had committed to him men, women, and children, those of the poorest of the land who had not been taken into exile to Babylon,<sup>8</sup>they went to Gedaliah at Mizpah— Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, Johanan the son of Kareah, Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, Jezaniah the son of the Maacathite, they and their men.<sup>9</sup>Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, swore to them and their men, saying, "Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you.<sup>10</sup>As for me, I will dwell at Mizpah, to represent you before the Chaldeans who will come to us. But as for you, gather wine and summer fruits and oil, and store them in your vessels, and dwell in your cities that you have taken."<sup>11</sup>Likewise, when all the Judeans who were in Moab and among the Ammonites and in Edom and in other lands heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as governor over them,<sup>12</sup>then all the Judeans returned from all the places to which they had been driven and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah. And they gathered wine and summer fruits in great abundance.<sup>13</sup>Now Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces in the open country came to Gedaliah at Mizpah<sup>14</sup>and said to him, "Do you know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take your life?" But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam would not believe them.<sup>15</sup>Then Johanan the son of Kareah spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah, "Please let me go and strike down Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and no one will know it. Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish?"<sup>16</sup>But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said to Johanan the son of Kareah, "You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking falsely of Ishmael."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Whole Land Is Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the remnant’s story begins, God vindicates his prophet and shows where Jeremiah’s heart lies. Found in chains among the deportees at Ramah, Jeremiah hears the Babylonian captain of the guard state his own message back to him: the LORD pronounced this disaster, brought it about and did as he said, because Judah sinned and would not obey his voice (vv. 1–3). Then the chains come off, and the old man is given a free choice between honour in Babylon and a ruined land (vv. 4–5). He goes to Gedaliah at Mizpah and stays among the poor who are left (v. 6): the prophet who had wept over this people for forty years will not leave them now that they are broken.
verseByVerse.theology: A pagan officer with better theology than Judah's kings, handing a prophet his freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD after Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had let him go from Ramah, when he took him bound in chains along with all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah who were being exiled to Babylon. The captain of the guard took Jeremiah and said to him, "The LORD your God pronounced this disaster against this place. The LORD has brought it about, and has done as he said. Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice, this thing has come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Freed from his chains at Ramah, Jeremiah hears a pagan general sum up his whole ministry: the LORD threatened this disaster, the LORD has done it, and Judah’s sin is the reason.

Bound in chains. Something has gone wrong between chapters, and the narrator does not hide it. The emperor had ordered that this man be looked after and given his own way (39:12), yet here he is bound in chains in a column of deportees at Ramah, the staging camp where the prisoners were mustered. Orders get lost, and God’s promises to his servants are not always administered smoothly by the people carrying them.

The word that came to Jeremiah. The heading promises a word from the LORD, yet no oracle follows at once. It probably introduces the whole story of the remnant that follows, in which the word of the LORD comes at last in 42:7.

Had let him go from Ramah. Ramah is where Rachel was heard weeping for her children (31:15). The prophet who wrote that verse now stands chained in the very place, among the people it was about. Matthew would hear that weeping again when Herod killed the children of Bethlehem (Matt 2:17-18), while the child Jesus, through whom the comfort promised to Rachel would come, was carried to safety.

The LORD your God pronounced this disaster. A Babylonian general, an idolater, summarises Jeremiah’s entire ministry in three sentences and gets it right. He says who did it: The LORD has brought it about. He says that God kept his word: has done as he said. He says why: Because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey his voice. Forty years of preaching that to Judah had earned the prophet a beating, a cistern and a burned scroll. The occupying officer worked it out from the outside, and said it to the one man in the country who had been saying it all along.

A warning for the church. It is a strange, bleak vindication. The nations understood what Judah would not, and there is a warning in that for anyone who has grown deaf inside the church while outsiders can see plainly what God is doing. Yet God still speaks, and those who have been deaf and turn to him are heard.
verseByVerse.note: Ramah lay about five miles north of Jerusalem, in the territory of Benjamin.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, behold, I release you today from the chains on your hands. If it seems good to you to come with me to Babylon, come, and I will look after you well, but if it seems wrong to you to come with me to Babylon, do not come. See, the whole land is before you; go wherever you think it good and right to go. If you remain, then return to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon appointed governor of the cities of Judah, and dwell with him among the people. Or go wherever you think it right to go." So the captain of the guard gave him an allowance of food and a present, and let him go. Then Jeremiah went to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah, and lived with him among the people who were left in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Offered honour in Babylon or a share in Judah’s ruin, Jeremiah chooses to stay with the poor of the land under Gedaliah at Mizpah.

I release you today. The chains come off, and the old man is handed something he has not had in decades: a choice. Babylon meant comfort, safety and status; the deportees included the skilled and the well-connected, and a prophet with a record of urging surrender would have been honoured there. Judah meant rubble, poverty and a wrecked community.

See, the whole land is before you. The phrase would echo for any Israelite: it is the language of Abraham offering Lot his choice of Canaan (Gen 13:9). Except that the land before Jeremiah now is ash.

An allowance of food and a present. Whatever the exact wording of the start of verse 5 (see the note below), the kindness is clear: rations and a gift, from the man who burned the temple, to the prophet who said it would burn.

Then Jeremiah went to Gedaliah. He stays. Mizpah, a Benjamite town a few miles north of the ruined capital, had become the seat of government; it was where Samuel had once gathered Israel to repent and judged the people (1 Sam 7:5-6).

Staying with the broken. It is one of the last great acts of his ministry. He had wept for this people for forty years while they hated him; now that they are broken and leaderless he will not leave them. A man who had every reason to shake the dust off his feet went and lived among them instead.

Christ became poor himself. It is a small picture of a far greater choice. The Son of God, who had every right to the glory of heaven, emptied himself and came to live among a ruined people (Phil 2:7), and he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Heb 2:11). Jeremiah stayed with the poor of Judah; Christ became poor himself, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor 8:9).

The career move nobody makes. Every modern life is expected to go up, and an offer like Nebuzaradan’s, a place in the capital with provisions and a hearing, is exactly what we are trained to accept. Turning it down to stay among the poor looks like a failure of ambition. Henri Nouwen, the Dutch priest and writer, gave up a teaching post at Harvard in the 1980s to live in a L’Arche community among people with severe learning disabilities, and he described the way of Jesus as downward mobility. He did not mean that poverty is holy or every ambition wrong, but that the love of God moves toward need rather than away from it, and that those who most resemble Christ are often walking the other way from the crowd. Jeremiah took the road to Mizpah. The Son of God came all the way down, and those who follow him find they have lost nothing: whoever loses his life for my sake will find it (Matt 16:25).

Textual note. The ESV notes that the opening of verse 5 follows the Syriac translation, because the Hebrew there is uncertain. The sense of the verse, an invitation to go back to Gedaliah if Jeremiah chooses to stay, is not in doubt.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Gather Wine and Summer Fruits
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After catastrophe, God’s mercy arrives in ordinary forms: a government, an oath of safety, and a harvest. The armed bands still at large in the countryside come in to Gedaliah at Mizpah, their commanders named one by one, the future assassin first (vv. 7–8). Gedaliah swears to them what Jeremiah had preached: do not be afraid, serve the king of Babylon, dwell in the land, and it shall be well with you; he will stand between them and the Chaldeans while they gather the harvest (vv. 9–10). Judeans scattered in Moab, Ammon and Edom hear the news and come home, and the year that saw Jerusalem burn yields wine and summer fruits in great abundance (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: A harvest in the year the city burned.

verseByVerse.quote: When all the captains of the forces in the open country and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor in the land and had committed to him men, women, and children, those of the poorest of the land who had not been taken into exile to Babylon, they went to Gedaliah at Mizpah— Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, Johanan the son of Kareah, Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, Jezaniah the son of the Maacathite, they and their men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The armed men still loose in the countryside come in to the new governor, among them both the man who will murder him and the man who will lead the remnant into Egypt.

Those of the poorest of the land. Judah is now a province run by a Judean governor, and its population is described without flattery: the poorest of the land. The people Nebuzaradan gave vineyards to (39:10) are the nation now.

All the captains of the forces in the open country. Out in the countryside are armed bands, officers whose units survived by staying out of the city. They come in when they hear there is a government again.

Ishmael the son of Nethaniah. The commanders are named. The first, Ishmael, will murder the governor within months; the second, Johanan the son of Kareah, will try to prevent it and then lead the survivors down to Egypt against God’s word (chapters 42–43). The narrator lists them without comment, the future assassin first, because at the time they all looked like loyal officers.
verseByVerse.note: Gedaliah ruled from Mizpah, north of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, swore to them and their men, saying, "Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be well with you. As for me, I will dwell at Mizpah, to represent you before the Chaldeans who will come to us. But as for you, gather wine and summer fruits and oil, and store them in your vessels, and dwell in your cities that you have taken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gedaliah’s first act as governor is to make Jeremiah’s preaching his policy: do not be afraid, serve Babylon, live in the land, and bring in the harvest.

Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Compare what the prophet had been saying for years: bring your neck under the yoke of Babylon and serve him and his people and live (27:12). Gedaliah says the same three things (do not be afraid, serve Babylon, dwell in the land) and adds an oath to guarantee them. This is what it looks like when someone finally believes the prophet, and it is no accident that the man doing it is Ahikam’s son. He grew up in a house where Jeremiah was taken seriously (26:24).

To represent you before the Chaldeans. He takes the unpleasant job himself, standing between his people and the occupiers, and gives everyone else the ordinary work: pick the grapes, gather the summer fruit, press the oil, fill the jars, live in your towns.

The way back. It is the same instruction God had sent to the exiles in Babylon: build houses, plant gardens, live (29:5). After catastrophe, the path back is not a grand project but harvest, storage and settled homes. Leaders who take the hard conversations on themselves and leave their people free to get on with ordinary faithful life are doing something very close to pastoral work.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, when all the Judeans who were in Moab and among the Ammonites and in Edom and in other lands heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as governor over them, then all the Judeans returned from all the places to which they had been driven and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah. And they gathered wine and summer fruits in great abundance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scattered Judeans come home from the nations around, and in the very year Jerusalem burned, God gives them a harvest in great abundance.

Heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant. Judeans had scattered into Moab, Ammon, Edom and further during the invasion. News reaches them that there is a remnant, a surviving group left in Judah, and a governor, and they come home.

In great abundance. It is a real mercy, though the book does not oversell it. With the temple gone and the king blinded, the vines and fruit trees of Judah bore heavily, and the returning refugees picked them. God had said he would gather his people from all the nations and all the places where I have driven you (29:14), and here is a first instalment, small enough to miss and real enough to eat.

What mercy looks like. Mercies after judgment often look like this: not a restored temple, but a good grape harvest and somewhere to put it, sent to people who had nothing in the very year they had least reason to expect it. Such mercies are easily despised because they are not the rescue we hoped for; they are given to be received with thanks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–16 — He Would Not Believe Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The new beginning is put at risk not by Babylon but by a warning refused. Johanan and the commanders bring Gedaliah specific intelligence: Baalis king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael to kill him; and Gedaliah will not believe them (vv. 13–14). Johanan presses the point in private, seeing clearly that the governor’s death would scatter the remnant, and offers to kill Ishmael secretly. Gedaliah rightly refuses the murder, but wrongly calls the warning false and takes no precautions at all (vv. 15–16). A good man’s generosity, applied where discernment was needed, leaves the door open for the next chapter’s sword.
verseByVerse.theology: A good man's refusal to think ill of anyone, and the remnant paid for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces in the open country came to Gedaliah at Mizpah and said to him, "Do you know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take your life?" But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam would not believe them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The commanders bring Gedaliah a true and specific warning that the king of Ammon has sent Ishmael to kill him, and the generous governor will not believe it.

Baalis the king of the Ammonites. The intelligence is specific: a named foreign king, a named agent, a named target. Baalis of Ammon wants the order Babylon has set up in Judah to collapse, and Ishmael, who (chapter 41 tells us) was of the royal family, has his own reason to resent a commoner governing Judah. The report is brought by several commanders together, not by one man with a grudge, and it was true.

But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam would not believe them. On this one sentence the future of the remnant turns. Why would he not believe it? Everything we know of him suggests a generous man: he had sheltered Jeremiah, he had sworn oaths of safety to these very officers, and his policy was trust and ordinary life. A man like that finds it hard to credit that someone who eats at his table is planning to kill him.

Charity without discernment. This is not the failure of a fool or a cynic, but a good man’s charity applied where discernment was needed, and Scripture does not praise it; it simply records what it cost. Refusing to think ill of anyone is not the same as wisdom, and leaders who will not hear a warning about a colleague can be as destructive as leaders who trust nobody.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Johanan the son of Kareah spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah, "Please let me go and strike down Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and no one will know it. Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans who are gathered about you would be scattered, and the remnant of Judah would perish?" But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said to Johanan the son of Kareah, "You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking falsely of Ishmael."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Johanan rightly sees that everything hangs on Gedaliah’s life and wrongly proposes a secret killing; Gedaliah rightly refuses the murder and wrongly dismisses the warning as a lie.

And no one will know it. Johanan tries again in private, and his proposal is ugly: a secret assassination to prevent an assassination. Gedaliah was right to refuse it. Nothing justifies killing a man on the strength of a report, however good, and a governor who had just sworn oaths of safety could hardly begin with a private murder.

The remnant of Judah would perish. Yet Johanan had seen further than anyone. He understood that everything now rested on one man’s survival: kill Gedaliah, and the harvest, the returning refugees and the whole fragile settlement come apart. He was exactly right about the danger and wrong about the remedy, as people often are when they see a danger clearly and reach for a sinful way to stop it.

You are speaking falsely of Ishmael. Gedaliah does not merely decline the murder; he calls the warning a lie. He could have refused the assassination and still taken precautions: kept Ishmael at a distance, declined to dine with him, posted a guard. Instead he accused the men telling him the truth of slander, and took no measures at all. Soon afterwards, in the seventh month, Ishmael came to Mizpah with ten men, and as they ate bread together there they rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword (41:1-2).

No rebuke, no eulogy. So the last good governor of Judah, from the house of Shaphan that had stood by the prophet, was murdered at his own table by a man he refused to suspect, and the remnant scattered exactly as Johanan had said. The book gives him neither rebuke nor eulogy. It simply records that he would not believe them, and lets the next chapter say what it cost.

How communities are lost. Judah’s story in the land ends not with a Babylonian army but with a dinner party and a sword: a sober word about how communities that survive catastrophe are usually lost, not to the great enemy outside but to one of their own, welcomed at the table, while a warning went unheeded.

40.title: Released at Ramah
40.overview:
Where we are. Jerusalem has fallen (chapter 39), and the book now follows the people left behind in the land (chapters 40 to 44). The story opens with Jeremiah himself, found in chains among the deportees at Ramah.

The message. After the judgment he had threatened, God gives what is left of his people a real new beginning: a freed prophet, a faithful governor, homes, and a harvest in great abundance. The word Jeremiah had preached for forty years, serve Babylon and live, is at last believed, and it bears fruit at once. But the mercy is fragile, and the chapter ends with a true warning dismissed as slander, a warning that will cost the remnant everything.

Why it was said. The first readers, in exile in Babylon or scattered in Egypt, needed to know why the hopeful start at Mizpah came to nothing (see the introduction). This chapter shows that God had not withheld mercy even in the year of ruin. It was lost from within.

How the chapter makes its case. A Babylonian commander frees Jeremiah and states the prophet’s message more plainly than Judah ever had: the LORD has done as he said, because you sinned (vv. 1–3). Offered comfort in Babylon, Jeremiah chooses to stay with the poor of the land under Gedaliah at Mizpah (vv. 4–6). Gedaliah makes Jeremiah’s preaching his policy, swearing to the scattered soldiers that serving Babylon will be well with them (vv. 7–10), and refugees come home to gather wine and summer fruits (vv. 11–12). Then Johanan brings a specific warning of a plot against the governor’s life, and Gedaliah calls it a lie (vv. 13–16).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Jeremiah’s choice to stay among a ruined people is a small picture of the Son of God, who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). And Gedaliah, the best governor the remnant could have had, could not keep even his own life. The people needed a Shepherd-King who is never taken by surprise, who knows the betrayer at his table, and who lays down his life for the sheep of his own accord (John 10:11, 18).

For us. God’s mercies after failure are often small and ordinary, a roof and a harvest, and they are to be received with thanks rather than despised for not being the restoration we wanted. Christ’s people are called to move toward the broken, as he did. And a warm heart needs a clear head: take a sober warning seriously, without slandering anyone and without reaching for a sinful remedy.
40.theology: An outsider can state plainly what those inside the covenant refuse to hear: a Babylonian officer summarised Jeremiah's whole message and got it right. Offered comfort in Babylon or ruin in Judah, the prophet chose his broken people, a small picture of the Son of God who became poor for us (2 Cor 8:9). After catastrophe, God's mercy often looks like a harvest and settled homes rather than a grand restoration. And the chapter ends with two warnings for leaders: refusing to think ill of anyone is not the same as wisdom, and a man can see a danger correctly and still propose a sinful way to stop it.
40.examples: Communities that survive a catastrophe are often lost not to the enemy outside but to trouble within, welcomed at the table while a warning goes unheeded. A church, a family or a business can learn from Gedaliah to take a sober warning seriously without slandering anyone, and from Johanan that seeing the danger clearly does not justify doing wrong to stop it.

keyVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah went to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah, and lived with him among the people who were left in the land.
keyVerse.note: Offered honour and safety in Babylon, the prophet who had warned this people for forty years chose to share their ruin. The verse gathers up the chapter’s mercy, a freed prophet, a faithful governor and a remnant given a new start, and it is a small picture of the Son of God, who left glory to live among a broken people and became poor for their sake (2 Corinthians 8:9).

40.reflection:
A Babylonian officer understood what Judah would not hear (vv. 2–3). Where might people outside the church see more clearly than we do what God is saying, and how should we respond when they do?

Jeremiah was offered comfort in Babylon and chose the ruined land and its poor (vv. 4–6). What would moving toward need rather than away from it look like for you or your church, and how does Christ’s becoming poor for us (2 Corinthians 8:9) shape that?

God’s mercy after judgment came as a harvest and settled homes rather than a restored temple (vv. 10–12). What ordinary mercies might you be overlooking because they are not the rescue you hoped for?

Gedaliah dismissed a true warning, and Johanan proposed a sinful remedy (vv. 13–16). How can a church, a family or a leader take warnings seriously without slander and without ungodly methods?

41.text: <sup>1</sup>In the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of the royal family, one of the chief officers of the king, came with ten men to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah. As they ate bread together there at Mizpah,<sup>2</sup>Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the ten men with him rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword, and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor in the land.<sup>3</sup>Ishmael also struck down all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean soldiers who happened to be there.<sup>4</sup>On the day after the murder of Gedaliah, before anyone knew of it,<sup>5</sup>eighty men arrived from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn, and their bodies gashed, bringing grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah came out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he came. As he met them, he said to them, "Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam."<sup>7</sup>When they came into the city, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the men with him slaughtered them and cast them into a cistern.<sup>8</sup>But there were ten men among them who said to Ishmael, "Do not put us to death, for we have stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey hidden in the fields." So he refrained and did not put them to death with their companions.<sup>9</sup>Now the cistern into which Ishmael had thrown all the bodies of the men whom he had struck down along with Gedaliah was the large cistern that King Asa had made for defense against Baasha king of Israel; Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.<sup>10</sup>Then Ishmael took captive all the rest of the people who were in Mizpah, the king's daughters and all the people who were left at Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. Ishmael the son of Nethaniah took them captive and set out to cross over to the Ammonites.<sup>11</sup>But when Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done,<sup>12</sup>they took all their men and went to fight against Ishmael the son of Nethaniah. They came upon him at the great pool that is in Gibeon.<sup>13</sup>And when all the people who were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him, they rejoiced.<sup>14</sup>So all the people whom Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah turned around and came back, and went to Johanan the son of Kareah.<sup>15</sup>But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites.<sup>16</sup>Then Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him took from Mizpah all the rest of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, after he had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam—soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs, whom Johanan brought back from Gibeon.<sup>17</sup>And they went and stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt<sup>18</sup>because of the Chaldeans. For they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — As They Ate Bread Together
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The remnant’s new beginning is destroyed from within, by a guest at the governor’s own table. In the seventh month Ishmael, a prince of the royal family and one of the king’s chief officers, comes to Mizpah with ten men and eats bread with Gedaliah (v. 1). Then they rise up and kill the governor Babylon had appointed (v. 2), and with him the Judeans at Mizpah and the Chaldean soldiers who happened to be there (v. 3). The warning Gedaliah called a lie (40:16) has come true, and by killing the Babylonian soldiers as well, Ishmael has made a reprisal certain.
verseByVerse.theology: A guest at the governor's table, with a sword under the meal.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of the royal family, one of the chief officers of the king, came with ten men to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, at Mizpah. As they ate bread together there at Mizpah, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the ten men with him rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword, and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor in the land. Ishmael also struck down all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean soldiers who happened to be there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prince of David’s house, received as a guest, murders the governor at his own table, and with him the Judeans and the Babylonian soldiers at Mizpah.

In the seventh month. Probably barely two months after the city fell (the year is not given), the assassin arrives. The fast of the seventh month that the Jews later kept (Zech 7:5; 8:19) is usually taken to remember this murder.

Of the royal family. Now we learn who he was: of the royal family, and one of the chief officers of the king. A prince of David’s line, while Gedaliah was a commoner appointed by Babylon. That is motive enough without Ammonite money.

As they ate bread together. What makes it more than politics is the setting: received as a guest, he drew his sword across the table. In the ancient world a shared meal was a bond. To eat a man’s bread was to place yourself under obligation to him, which is why a psalm reaches for exactly this image to describe the deepest wound there is: Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Psalm 41:9).

He passed him the bread anyway. The Lord took that verse onto his own lips in an upper room, of Judas, who sat at his table having already been paid to betray him: He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me (John 13:18). And there is a difference between the two tables that is the whole gospel. Gedaliah did not know, and had refused to be told. Jesus knew exactly who was reaching for the dish, and passed him the bread anyway.

Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan. The full genealogy is given as an epitaph. Shaphan read the law to Josiah; Ahikam’s hand saved Jeremiah’s life at his trial (26:24); Gedaliah took the prophet home when the city fell. Three generations of quiet faithfulness, and the line ends at a dinner table.

And the Chaldean soldiers. The Babylonian garrison dies too, and with it any hope that Babylon will treat this as an internal matter. Ishmael has not merely killed a governor; he has guaranteed a reprisal, and fear of it drives the next three chapters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — Eighty Pilgrims and a Cistern
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ishmael’s cruelty reaches beyond politics to the worshippers of God. The day after the murder, before anyone outside knows, eighty men arrive from the old northern towns of Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria, in mourning for Jerusalem and carrying offerings for the house of the LORD (vv. 4–5). Ishmael comes out weeping, invites them in the dead governor’s name, and slaughters them (vv. 6–7). Ten who promise him hidden stores of food are spared (v. 8), and the bodies fill the great cistern King Asa had made centuries earlier to keep Mizpah alive under siege (v. 9): counterfeit grief, murdered pilgrims, and a work of defence turned into a mass grave.
verseByVerse.theology: Grief counterfeited at the gate, and a reservoir built to save life packed with the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day after the murder of Gedaliah, before anyone knew of it, eighty men arrived from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn, and their bodies gashed, bringing grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day after the murder, eighty mourners from the old northern kingdom arrive with offerings for the house of the LORD, sincere in their grief and unaware of what has happened.

Before anyone knew of it. For one day Mizpah still looks like a working capital with a governor in it.

From Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria. These eighty men are among the saddest details in the book. They come from the old northern kingdom, whose people had been deported by Assyria well over a century before. Descendants of those left behind, they are still walking south with offerings for the God of Israel. They were probably heirs of Josiah’s reform, which had reached into the old northern territory and turned its worshippers toward Jerusalem (2 Kgs 23:15-20; 2 Chr 34:9). It was also the seventh month, the month of the Feast of Booths (Lev 23:34), which may explain the journey.

Their bodies gashed. They are in mourning for Jerusalem: beards shaved, clothes torn, bodies cut (see mourning customs). Two of those three were expressly forbidden: You shall not make any cuts on your body for the dead (Lev 19:28); You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead (Deut 14:1). Their grief was genuine, and their practice borrowed what the law forbade, learned from neighbours over generations without the law to correct it.

Grain offerings and incense to present at the temple of the LORD. They are carrying offerings to a temple that had been ash for perhaps two months. Either they had not heard, or they were going to the site anyway to lay offerings in the ruins.

Sincere but muddled. It would be easy, and wrong, to be superior about them. Eighty men walked thirty miles or more through occupied country, disfigured with grief, to bring flour and incense to a God whose house was rubble. Their theology was muddled and their hearts were not. God’s people are often more sincere than they are well taught, and the answer to that is teaching, not contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah came out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he came. As he met them, he said to them, "Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam." When they came into the city, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the men with him slaughtered them and cast them into a cistern.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ishmael uses counterfeit grief to lure the pilgrims inside, then slaughters them and throws their bodies into a cistern.

Weeping as he came. The tears were the trap: the one sure way into mourners’ confidence was shared grief. Then he invited them in the name of the man he had just killed: Come in to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam.

Hypocrisy as a tool. This is what hypocrisy is for. Not self-deception, but a tool: borrowing the forms of godliness and sorrow in order to get close enough to do harm. Wolves come in sheep’s clothing (Matt 7:15) because the clothing works.

Slaughtered them and cast them into a cistern. Eleven men killed seventy of the eighty pilgrims inside the walls, and the bodies went into a water pit (see cisterns). Each of them had a name and a home in the north, and had come to mourn; Scripture does not let them become a statistic, and neither should we.

Two cisterns. Hold this cistern beside the one three chapters earlier. Jeremiah had been lowered into a cistern with no water in the cistern, but only mud (38:6), and a foreigner came with ropes and old rags and drew him out. Here the same kind of pit hides a massacre. In one, a man is hauled up to live; in the other, seventy worshippers are thrown down. What differs is not the hole but the hand.

verseByVerse.quote: But there were ten men among them who said to Ishmael, "Do not put us to death, for we have stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey hidden in the fields." So he refrained and did not put them to death with their companions. Now the cistern into which Ishmael had thrown all the bodies of the men whom he had struck down along with Gedaliah was the large cistern that King Asa had made for defense against Baasha king of Israel; Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten men buy their lives with hidden food, and the dead fill the great cistern a godly king had made to keep Mizpah alive.

Hidden in the fields. Ten men live because they knew where food was buried in the open country, where it was safer than in a house. It shows what Ishmael valued: seventy murders were nothing to him, and a cache of grain was enough to stay his hand. Scripture records the ten men’s bargain, the kind famine forces on people, without praise or blame.

That King Asa had made for defense against Baasha king of Israel. The narrator stops to tell us who dug the hole. Three hundred years earlier King Asa had fortified Mizpah against the northern kingdom, carrying away the stones of Ramah to build it (1 Kgs 15:22). The cistern was part of that work: a reservoir to keep a garrison alive through a siege, engineering in the service of survival.

Filled it with the slain. And a prince of Asa’s own line filled it with the dead. Things built by good men to preserve life get used by later men for atrocity. Judah’s story is full of it: a temple built for God’s name used to house idols, a covenant ceremony used to seal a lie (34:18), and now a waterworks made into a grave.

Uncertain wording. Where the ESV says these men were struck down along with Gedaliah, its footnote gives the Hebrew as “by the hand of” Gedaliah, a compressed phrase. It most likely means the men killed with him, in his company or on his account, rather than men Gedaliah himself had killed. The general sense, that the cistern held the dead of the massacre, is clear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — Recovered at the Pool of Gibeon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For a moment the chapter turns toward rescue. Ishmael takes captive everyone left at Mizpah, the king’s daughters among them, people Nebuzaradan had entrusted to Gedaliah, and sets out for Ammon, the kingdom that had sent him (v. 10). Johanan, whose warning had been dismissed, hears of the evil and goes after him with his men (vv. 11–12). He catches up with Ishmael at the great pool of Gibeon, and the captives, seeing who has come, rejoice, turn round and walk over to him (vv. 13–14). No battle is described: people held by force simply leave as soon as there is somewhere to go.
verseByVerse.theology: The one glad moment in the chapter: prisoners seeing who has come for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ishmael took captive all the rest of the people who were in Mizpah, the king's daughters and all the people who were left at Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. Ishmael the son of Nethaniah took them captive and set out to cross over to the Ammonites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ishmael drives the whole remnant of Mizpah, the king’s daughters among them, toward Ammon, the kingdom that had sent him.

The king’s daughters. The whole remnant of Judah walks east in ropes, and it is a small shock to find the king’s daughters here. Zedekiah’s sons were killed at Riblah (39:6); his daughters, it seems, survived the fall of the city, were left behind as no threat to anybody, and are now being driven toward Ammon as spoil by a man of their own royal house.

Had committed to Gedaliah. They had been formally entrusted to Gedaliah by the captain of the guard, and the man who murdered him is now stealing them.

To cross over to the Ammonites. The destination is the point. Ishmael is taking them to the king who had sent him to do the killing (40:14). This may never have been a bid for the throne of Judah. It looks like a foreign operation, and the remnant were the payment.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done, they took all their men and went to fight against Ishmael the son of Nethaniah. They came upon him at the great pool that is in Gibeon. And when all the people who were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him, they rejoiced. So all the people whom Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah turned around and came back, and went to Johanan the son of Kareah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Johanan, whose warning had been dismissed, pursues the murderer, and at Gibeon the captives see their rescuers, rejoice, and walk free.

But. It is the first good word in the chapter. And it is Johanan, the man who brought the warning Gedaliah would not believe, who had asked leave to deal with Ishmael quietly and been told he was a liar (40:13-16). He had every excuse to say he had told them so. Instead he raised his men and went after the column. Being disbelieved is a real injury, and the test of a man is what he does for the people who dismissed him once they are in trouble. Johanan passes it.

The great pool that is in Gibeon. The place is named because everyone knew it: the great pool at Gibeon, where Joab’s and Abner’s men had once fought a murderous contest in David’s day (2 Sam 2:12-17).

They rejoiced. It is the only gladness in the chapter, the gladness of prisoners who look up and see who has come over the hill.

Turned around and came back. No battle is described. The hostages simply turned round and walked to the rescue party, and Ishmael’s operation collapsed. They had been with him only for the few miles from Mizpah, and their loyalty was never his: they were people, not cargo. People held by force can look as if they are willing, and the moment there is an alternative it becomes obvious where they stand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Intending to Go to Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rescue ends in flight, and fear sets the direction. Ishmael escapes to Ammon with eight men, unpunished as far as this book records (v. 15). Johanan gathers what is left of the people of God in the land, soldiers, women, children and eunuchs (v. 16), and leads them to Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, on the road south (v. 17). They mean to go on to Egypt, because they are afraid of the Chaldeans after the governor’s murder (v. 18). Their reasoning is understandable, and it points them toward the one country God had forbidden, which sets up their request for guidance in chapter 42.
verseByVerse.theology: Frightened people walking back toward the country God had brought them out of.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites. Then Johanan the son of Kareah and all the leaders of the forces with him took from Mizpah all the rest of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, after he had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam—soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs, whom Johanan brought back from Gibeon. And they went and stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt because of the Chaldeans. For they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The murderer escapes, and the frightened survivors camp near Bethlehem, intending to flee to Egypt for fear of Babylon’s reprisal.

Escaped from Johanan with eight men. He gets away to Ammon, where his paymaster is. He murdered a governor, seventy pilgrims and a garrison, and the chapter simply records that he escaped: no execution, no capture, no word of judgment pronounced over him in this book at all. Scripture is honest: wickedness often walks away from the scene, and justice is not always done before the story ends. What we are given instead is the assurance that the account is kept by the God who said I am the one who knows, and I am witness (29:23).

Soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs. Read the list slowly. This is what was left of the people of God in the land of promise: not a nation, but a column of survivors on a road, with their governor dead behind them.

Intending to go to Egypt. Their reasoning is not stupid: Babylon’s governor and soldiers have been murdered, and a reprisal is coming. But it points them in the one direction God had forbidden. Egypt is where the story of this people began, and the whole shape of their existence is that God brought them out of it. To walk back in is to undo the exodus.

For they were afraid of them. Fear is what does it. Not appetite, not idolatry in any obvious form, but fear with a plausible case attached. Gedaliah would not believe a warning and died of it; these men believe the evidence of their eyes and are about to make a worse mistake. Between trusting too easily and trusting only our own reckoning there is a third way, which is to ask God, and in the next chapter they do: that the LORD your God may show us the way we should go, and the thing that we should do (42:3). It is the right question, asked by men who have already decided the answer.

Near Bethlehem. The chapter’s last picture is a company of refugees encamped beside Bethlehem, facing south, afraid. That is where, six centuries later, the answer to all of it would be born (Mic 5:2; Matt 2:6): the true Shepherd of Israel, who would not run from danger but go to meet it for his sheep.

Uncertain wording. The name Geruth Chimham is not fully understood. Geruth occurs only here and is probably related to a word for lodging or staying as a guest, so the name may mean the lodging place of Chimham, a stopping place on the road south. Many connect it with the Chimham whom David took into his household (2 Sam 19:37-40), whose family may have held land near Bethlehem.

41.title: Murder at Mizpah
41.overview:
Where we are. Gedaliah has refused to believe the warning that Ishmael was sent to kill him (40:13–16). This chapter tells what that cost: the hopeful settlement at Mizpah, begun in mercy only weeks before, is destroyed from within.

The message. Judgment had not changed the heart of Judah. The same treachery, violence and contempt for God’s mercy that brought Jerusalem down now wreck the remnant, at the hands of a prince of David’s own house. A fresh start given by God is thrown away when hearts are unchanged, and the survivors end the chapter where fear always leads them: facing Egypt.

Why it was said. The exiles needed to know why Judah had no future in the land after the fall of Jerusalem, and the answer here is not Babylon’s cruelty but the remnant’s own sin. The murder of Gedaliah was remembered with a fast for generations afterwards (Zechariah 7:5; 8:19), and this chapter tells the story behind it (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Ishmael, of the royal family, kills Gedaliah while they eat bread together, and with him the Judeans and the Chaldean soldiers at Mizpah (vv. 1–3). The next day he weeps his way into the confidence of eighty pilgrims from the north, kills seventy of them and fills King Asa’s cistern with the bodies, sparing ten who buy their lives with hidden food (vv. 4–9). He drives the rest of Mizpah, the king’s daughters among them, toward Ammon (v. 10), until Johanan overtakes him at Gibeon and the captives walk free (vv. 11–14). Ishmael escapes, and the frightened survivors camp near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt (vv. 15–18).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. A guest who eats a good man’s bread and then strikes him is the betrayal the psalm laments, “Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9), words Jesus applied to Judas (John 13:18). But Jesus knew who was reaching for the dish and gave himself up anyway. And a prince of David’s line who murders and scatters shows how badly the people needed the true Son of David, the ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), who gathers the flock instead of scattering it and lays down his life for the sheep.

For us. A new start cannot change a heart; only the new covenant Christ made in his blood does that. The forms of grief and godliness can be borrowed to do harm, and sincere believers need teaching, not contempt. When wickedness seems to escape, God keeps the account. And fear with a sensible case attached is still fear: bring the decision to God before the bags are packed.
41.theology: This is the darkest chapter of the aftermath, and Scripture tells it without softening. Betrayal at the table is one of the deepest wounds there is, and the Lord himself bore it knowingly (John 13:18). Hypocrisy appears here not as self-deception but as a tool, tears used to get near enough to kill. Ishmael escapes unpunished in this chapter, and the reckoning is left to the God who is witness (29:23). And fear backed by sensible-sounding reasons is what turns God's people back toward Egypt, beside the town where the true Shepherd would one day be born (Matt 2:6).
41.examples: The eighty pilgrims carrying flour and incense to a temple of ashes are a reminder that God's people are often more sincere than well taught, and deserve teaching rather than contempt. And Johanan, who raised his men for the very people who had called him a liar, shows what to do with the injury of being disbelieved.

keyVerse.quote: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the ten men with him rose up and struck down Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, with the sword, and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor in the land.
keyVerse.note: One act of treachery at a shared meal undoes the fresh start God had given the remnant. The verse names the victim with his whole faithful family line and the authority that appointed him, so that the reader feels both the betrayal and the political disaster. Everything else in the chapter, the massacre, the captives and the flight toward Egypt, flows from this blow.

41.reflection:
Ishmael struck Gedaliah down while they ate bread together (vv. 1–2), and Jesus applied Psalm 41:9 to Judas at his own table (John 13:18). What does it mean to you that Jesus knowingly shared bread with his betrayer?

The pilgrims from the north were sincere but poorly taught, and Ishmael used counterfeit grief to deceive them (vv. 4–7). How can a church care well for people who are earnest but muddled, and guard against those who borrow the language of faith to do harm?

Ishmael escaped, and the chapter records no justice for him (v. 15). How does knowing God as the one who knows and is witness (29:23) help when wrongdoing seems to go unpunished?

The survivors were driven toward Egypt by fear with a sensible case attached (vv. 17–18). Where might fear be quietly setting your direction, and what would it look like to bring that decision to God before it is made?
