verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Whether It Is Good or Bad
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The request for guidance is flawless in form and hollow at heart. Everyone comes, from the commanders to the least of the people, and asks Jeremiah to plead with the LORD for the few who are left, that God would show them the way to go and the thing to do (vv. 1–3). Jeremiah agrees at once and promises to keep nothing back (v. 4). They answer with the most solemn oath available, calling on the LORD as a true and faithful witness against them, and pledging to obey his voice “whether it is good or bad” (vv. 5–6). Chapter 43 will show how long that pledge lasts.
verseByVerse.theology: A perfect prayer and a total oath, from people who have already decided where they are going.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the commanders of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, came near and said to Jeremiah the prophet, "Let our plea for mercy come before you, and pray to the LORD your God for us, for all this remnant— because we are left with but a few, as your eyes see us— that the LORD your God may show us the way we should go, and the thing that we should do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole remnant comes to Jeremiah with a model request for guidance, asking God to show them the way to go and what to do.

From the least to the greatest. Everyone comes. Not a delegation this time, but the commanders, the officers and all the people. After Mizpah there is nobody left who can afford to be indifferent.

Let our plea for mercy come before you. The request is beautifully put, and every part of it is right. They ask for prayer, they plead for mercy, they name their condition honestly, we are left with but a few, and they appeal to what the prophet can see with his own eyes.

The LORD your God. One phrase is a small warning light: your God, not ours. Zedekiah’s messengers had at least said the LORD our God (37:3); people who speak of God as someone else’s God are often keeping him at a distance in other ways too.

The way we should go, and the thing that we should do. It is the right question, and you could not improve on it as a prayer for guidance. The tragedy of the chapter is that it was asked by men with their bags already packed.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah the prophet said to them, "I have heard you. Behold, I will pray to the LORD your God according to your request, and whatever the LORD answers you I will tell you. I will keep nothing back from you." Then they said to Jeremiah, "May the LORD be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act according to all the word with which the LORD your God sends you to us. Whether it is good or bad, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God to whom we are sending you, that it may be well with us when we obey the voice of the LORD our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah promises to keep nothing back, and the people swear before God to obey whatever he says, whether it is good or bad.

I will keep nothing back from you. He agrees at once and makes one promise about himself, and forty years of ministry stand behind it. He had been beaten, put in the stocks, dropped in a cistern and had his book burned for keeping nothing back, and he was too old and too tested to start editing now. A preacher who tells his people in advance that he will not trim the answer has given them the most useful thing he has.

A true and faithful witness against us. Inviting God to witness against them is the most solemn commitment available. Whether it is good or bad: they foresee an unwelcome answer and pledge obedience anyway. And their wording has improved: twice now it is the LORD our God.

Hollow words. Every word is correct, and the whole thing is hollow, as chapter 43 will show as soon as the answer is given. There is a way of praying for guidance that is really a search for approval of a decision already made, and it can produce sincere-sounding oaths. The test of whether we meant whether it is good or bad comes only when the answer is bad.

How do I ask for guidance and mean it? Most of us have prayed their prayer, over a job offer, a move or a relationship we were already leaning into. Four marks of asking honestly. Name what you are hoping for. Tell God plainly which answer you want, so the wish is out in the open and not steering in the dark. Decide beforehand what would count as no. Settle what Scripture, a wise friend or a closed door would have to say for you to drop the plan, before you hear it. Ask someone who will keep nothing back. Find the person least likely to flatter you, and give them leave to say the unwelcome thing. Obey the part you already know. Most of God’s will is already written, and the remnant were told nothing here that Jeremiah had not been saying for years. None of this earns guidance. The Son prayed not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42) and obeyed when the answer was a cross; and the God who answered him works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Phil 2:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — If You Will Remain in This Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s answer is a gracious offer that turns on one condition: stay. After ten days of waiting the word comes, and Jeremiah gathers the whole people to hear it, reminding them that they sent him (vv. 7–9). If they remain in the land, God will build them up and not pull them down, plant them and not pluck them up, for he relents of the disaster (v. 10). He names their fear of the king of Babylon and answers it twice with his own presence: he is with them to save and deliver (v. 11). He will show them mercy, and so move the emperor to show mercy and let them stay at home (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Stay, and God will build and plant them, and deal with Nebuchadnezzar himself.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of ten days the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah. Then he summoned Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces who were with him, and all the people from the least to the greatest, and said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your plea for mercy before him:
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes the frightened people wait ten days for his answer, and Jeremiah delivers it to everyone who asked, reminding them that they sent him.

At the end of ten days. Ten days of nothing. God did not answer for a week and a half, with a frightened camp waiting outside and a Babylonian reprisal expected any day. Jeremiah could not produce an answer of his own, and had to go out each morning with nothing to report.

Why God delayed. God is not on call. He answers in his own time even when the request is urgent and the people genuinely afraid, and the delay is not indifference. Ten days also gave the remnant time to examine what they actually wanted, and gave the oath time to be more than a mood.

All the people from the least to the greatest. He calls the same crowd back, because the answer belongs to everyone who asked, not to the leadership alone. He will not tell the leaders first and let them decide what the people hear.

To whom you sent me. He begins by reminding them that this was their idea. Whatever follows, they asked for it.

verseByVerse.quote: If you will remain in this land, then I will build you up and not pull you down; I will plant you, and not pluck you up; for I relent of the disaster that I did to you. Do not fear the king of Babylon, of whom you are afraid. Do not fear him, declares the LORD, for I am with you, to save you and to deliver you from his hand. I will grant you mercy, that he may have mercy on you and let you remain in your own land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If they stay in the land, God promises to build and plant them, to be with them against the king they fear, and to turn even the emperor to mercy.

If you will remain in this land. The whole offer turns on one condition, and it is not a religious programme. It is geography: stay where God has put you.

I will build you up and not pull you down. These are the verbs of Jeremiah’s call. He was appointed to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant (1:10), and for forty years the first four had done the work. Here only the last two are used, with the destructive pair explicitly refused: built up and not pulled down, planted and not plucked up.

For I relent of the disaster that I did to you. The reason given is staggering. God speaks of turning from the harm with something like grief: not that he was wrong to send it, but that he takes no pleasure in it and is ready to deal kindly with them the moment they will stay put.

Do not fear the king of Babylon. God names the fear precisely and says do not fear twice, because a frightened man needs the sentence repeated. The reason he gives is not a change in Nebuchadnezzar’s plans but his own presence: for I am with you, to save you and to deliver you from his hand.

That he may have mercy on you. Follow the chain. God will show them mercy, and the effect will be that the emperor shows them mercy. God speaks of the attitude of the most powerful man alive as something he will change to keep a promise to a small band of refugees.

God with us. That promise of presence runs through the whole Bible, and it reaches its height in the child named Immanuel (which means, God with us) (Matt 1:23), who sent his frightened disciples out with the words I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt 28:20). The remedy for fear has always been a person, and in Christ that person has come.

Does God change his mind? God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind (Num 23:19). Scripture says he “relents” to describe his real response to repentance in human terms: his warnings are real, and when people turn, he does what he always purposed to do for those who turn (Jer 18:7–10). He is not surprised or moved like a man; his unchanging character is the very reason he spares the penitent.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The alternative is spelled out in the people’s own voice, and then turned inside out. If they say they will not remain, and that Egypt will give them what Judah cannot, no war, no trumpet, no hunger, they are disobeying the voice of the LORD (vv. 13–14). And their own reasons will undo them: if they set their faces toward Egypt, the sword they fear will overtake them there, and the famine they dread will follow close behind (vv. 15–16). All who go will die by sword, famine and pestilence, and the remnant will have no remnant or survivor (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The two things they were running from were waiting at the destination.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you say, 'We will not remain in this land,' disobeying the voice of the LORD your God and saying, 'No, we will go to the land of Egypt, where we shall not see war or hear the sound of the trumpet or be hungry for bread, and we will dwell there,' then hear the word of the LORD, O remnant of Judah. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: If you set your faces to enter Egypt and go to live there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God quotes in advance the people’s reasons for going to Egypt, peace and bread, and calls the decision what it is: disobedience, and a reversal of the exodus.

We will not remain in this land. God quotes the sentence before they say it, and labels it: saying it is disobeying the voice of the LORD your God. There will be no room afterwards to present the move as prudence rather than rebellion.

Or be hungry for bread. After a long siege, a murdered governor and a country of ashes, who would not want peace and bread? That is what makes the passage searching. The sin is not a craving for something wicked but for peace and bread in a place God had forbidden. And Egypt was the obvious refuge: the one great power still outside Babylon’s grip, whose army had once drawn the Chaldeans away from Jerusalem during the siege (37:5), and where Judeans already lived (24:8).

We will go to the land of Egypt. Egypt was forbidden by name. The law had said of the king that he must not cause the people to return to Egypt, because You shall never return that way again (Deut 17:16), and Isaiah had pronounced Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help (Isa 31:1). Egypt is the house of slavery they were brought out of. Walking back is not a change of address; it is a reversal of the exodus.

If you set your faces to enter Egypt. The phrase carries the whole problem. This is not drifting; it is a deliberate turning of the head in a chosen direction.

The god called safety. Few idols are harder to see than this one, because it does not look like an idol. It looks like common sense. Who could object to a family wanting to be out of danger and sure of the next meal? Yet much of modern life is quietly arranged around it: the job kept for its security long after it has hollowed us out, the risk never taken for a friend, the child shielded from every hardship until he can bear none. Augustine argued that sin is often not the love of bad things but the love of good things in the wrong order, so that a lesser good is given the place that belongs to God. Peace and bread are gifts. Made into the thing we must have at any cost, they become a master, and sooner or later every master demands obedience against God’s word. The remnant did not stop believing in God; they simply let fear decide. The gospel’s reversal is that real safety lies in walking toward the place God names, because the one who says I am with you walked into the worst danger of all for us, at the cross, and came out of the tomb alive.

verseByVerse.quote: then the sword that you fear shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine of which you are afraid shall follow close after you to Egypt, and there you shall die. All the men who set their faces to go to Egypt to live there shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence. They shall have no remnant or survivor from the disaster that I will bring upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sword and famine they are running from will be waiting for them in Egypt, and those who go will leave no survivors.

The sword that you fear shall overtake you there. The answer takes their two reasons and hands them back. They were going to Egypt to escape war and hunger. The sword they fear will overtake them there, and the famine they dread will follow close after them: two pursuers outrunning a column on the road.

Nowhere to run. There is no safe country. If God has sent the thing a man is fleeing, no distance will get him away from it, and the only refuge available was obedience in a ruined land. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death (Prov 14:12).

No remnant or survivor. The threefold sentence that runs through the whole book, sword, famine and pestilence, falls one last time, now on those who survived it, and the closing phrase is the bitterest in the chapter. These people are the remnant, the few survivors left; the word had been their identity and their comfort for two chapters. If they go down to Egypt, the remnant will have no remnant.

A door left open. Even this is not quite the last word. Two chapters later God allows that a few fugitives will get home (44:14, 28), and Scripture never closes the door on anyone who turns back from a wrong road: let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him (Isa 55:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — You Shall See This Place No More
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah ends by reading their hearts and their oath back to them. The wrath poured out on Jerusalem will be poured out on them in Egypt; they will become a curse and a taunt, and never see their land again (v. 18). The command is reduced to five plain words, “Do not go to Egypt”, and put formally on record before everyone (v. 19). They have already gone astray: they sent him to God swearing to do whatever God said, and now that they have the answer they have not obeyed it in anything (vv. 20–21). So they will die in the very place they long to go (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The oracle ends by naming where they will die: the place they want to go.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: As my anger and my wrath were poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so my wrath will be poured out on you when you go to Egypt. You shall become an execration, a horror, a curse, and a taunt. You shall see this place no more. The LORD has said to you, O remnant of Judah, 'Do not go to Egypt.' Know for a certainty that I have warned you this day
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wrath that fell on Jerusalem will follow them to Egypt, and Jeremiah puts the plain command, “Do not go to Egypt”, formally on record.

As my anger and my wrath were poured out. God compares what will happen to them in Egypt with what his anger did to Jerusalem, and that should have ended the discussion. They had just watched what that looked like; the smoke was barely gone.

An execration, a horror, a curse, and a taunt. Four words for their reputation, the kind of list already pronounced over the people of Jerusalem (29:18), now transferred to the refugees.

You shall see this place no more. A short sentence that would fall hardest on anyone who loved the country: go, and you will never come back.

Do not go to Egypt. The instruction is reduced to five words so that nobody can claim it was ambiguous.

Know for a certainty that I have warned you this day. Jeremiah puts his own testimony on record: the warning was given plainly, on a particular day, in front of everyone. A faithful minister makes sure that if his people go wrong they cannot say they were not told.

verseByVerse.quote: that you have gone astray at the cost of your lives. For you sent me to the LORD your God, saying, 'Pray for us to the LORD our God, and whatever the LORD our God says, declare to us and we will do it.' And I have this day declared it to you, but you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in anything that he sent me to tell you. Now therefore know for a certainty that you shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence in the place where you desire to go to live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their oath is read back to them as evidence: they asked for God’s word, swore to obey it, and have obeyed none of it, so they will die in the place they long to go.

You have gone astray at the cost of your lives. The wording stings: you have gone astray, already, before a single step south. God treats the decision as taken, because it was taken before they ever asked.

Whatever the LORD our God says. He quotes their promise exactly as they had worded it, calling him their own God: whatever the LORD our God says, declare to us and we will do it. The words are now evidence.

I have this day declared it to you. Jeremiah has kept his side exactly, nothing held back, and the charge against them is total: not obedient in anything. They received a specific, gracious answer to the exact question they had asked, and obeyed none of it.

In the place where you desire to go to live. The oracle ends on a phrase that diagnoses the whole human problem. That is where they will die: not in the place they feared, but in the place they wanted. The destination chosen for safety, bread and quiet turns out to be the grave, and it is chosen freely, with a warning ringing in their ears and an oath still warm on their lips.

Why this chapter matters. This is more than a piece of sixth-century politics. God gave them a plain word, named their fear, promised his presence, offered to build and plant them, and undertook to manage the emperor himself, and they preferred a country of their own choosing. The offer was If you will remain in this land, and remaining is generally harder than moving, because it requires trusting God rather than changing our circumstances.

Asking with the bags already packed. Every reader has asked for guidance with the bags already packed. The way back is not a better oath but the mercy this chapter itself offers, I relent of the disaster: Christ kept his Father’s word perfectly where we have not, and his obedience is counted as ours (Rom 5:19). And the Spirit he gives is what makes a frightened heart able to stay where God has put it and trust the One who says I am with you.

42.title: Whether It Is Good or Bad
42.overview:
Where we are. After Gedaliah’s murder the survivors are camped near Bethlehem, intending to go on to Egypt (41:17–18). Before they move, they ask Jeremiah to seek the LORD for them.

The message. God answers frightened people with a clear word, a gracious promise and a plain warning. Stay where he has put you, and he will build you up, be with you, and turn even the emperor’s heart; run to Egypt for safety, and the very things you fear will meet you there. The real question is not whether we ask God for guidance but whether we will obey it when it is not what we wanted.

Why it was said. The remnant was small, leaderless and terrified of a Babylonian reprisal, and Egypt, which Judah had long been tempted to trust (see the introduction), looked like the only safe place. For the exiles who read it later, the chapter shows that God offered the survivors a future in the land, and that they turned it down with their eyes open.

How the chapter makes its case. The whole people asks Jeremiah to pray and swears to obey God’s answer, “Whether it is good or bad” (vv. 1–6). After ten days the answer comes: if they remain, God will build and plant them, and they need not fear the king of Babylon, “for I am with you” (vv. 7–12). If they insist on Egypt for peace and bread, the sword and famine they fear will overtake them there (vv. 13–17). Jeremiah ends by exposing their hearts: they are already set on going, and they will die “in the place where you desire to go to live” (vv. 18–22).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by the need it exposes. The promise “I am with you, to save you and to deliver you” (v. 11) is the heart of God, and it took flesh in Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), who tells his frightened people, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20). And the remnant’s oath shows our need: we can promise total obedience and keep none of it. Christ asked his Father’s will and obeyed it when the answer was a cross (Luke 22:42), and by his obedience “the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).

For us. Ask for guidance honestly, ready for an answer you did not want. Much of God’s will is already plain; the hard part is often remaining where he has put us when every instinct says run. Fear is answered not by a safer place but by a Person who has promised to be with us, and who forgives those who have run.
42.theology: There is a way of asking for guidance that is really a search for approval of what we have already decided, and it can produce faultless prayers and sincere oaths; the test of whether it is good or bad comes only when the answer is bad. Against that stands a God who answers in his own time, who relents of disaster and takes no pleasure in it, and whose answer to fear is not a change in the enemy's plans but his own presence, fulfilled in Immanuel (Matt 1:23). The sin here is not appetite for evil but a craving for peace and bread in a place God forbade, and its end is death in the very place they wanted.
42.examples: Most of us have asked God for guidance with the bags already packed: praying over a move, a job or a relationship we have in fact already chosen. The chapter does not answer that with scorn but with an offer. God still says to the frightened, Do not fear, twice, because frightened people need it twice, and he promises to be with those who stay where he has put them.

keyVerse.quote: Do not fear the king of Babylon, of whom you are afraid. Do not fear him, declares the LORD, for I am with you, to save you and to deliver you from his hand.
keyVerse.note: Here is God’s answer to the fear that drives the whole story of the remnant. He names the fear exactly, forbids it twice, and meets it not with a safer place but with his own presence and saving power. The promise “I am with you” comes to its fullness in Christ, Immanuel, God with us (Matthew 1:23).

42.reflection:
The remnant’s request for guidance was flawless in its words, yet they had already decided (vv. 1–6). How can you tell whether you are seeking God’s will or seeking his approval for a decision already made?

God made Jeremiah and the people wait ten days for an answer (v. 7). What does waiting on God bring to the surface in us, and how have you seen him use delay?

God answered their fear of the king of Babylon with the promise of his presence (v. 11). What fear is shaping your choices at the moment, and how does Christ’s promise in Matthew 28:20 speak to it?

Egypt promised peace and bread (v. 14). What good things are you tempted to make into what you must have at any cost, and what would it mean for you to remain where God has put you?

43.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jeremiah finished speaking to all the people all these words of the LORD their God, with which the LORD their God had sent him to them,<sup>2</sup>Azariah the son of Hoshaiah and Johanan the son of Kareah and all the insolent men said to Jeremiah, "You are telling a lie. The LORD our God did not send you to say, 'Do not go to Egypt to live there,'<sup>3</sup>but Baruch the son of Neriah has set you against us, to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans, that they may kill us or take us into exile in Babylon."<sup>4</sup>So Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces and all the people did not obey the voice of the LORD, to remain in the land of Judah.<sup>5</sup>But Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces took all the remnant of Judah who had returned to live in the land of Judah from all the nations to which they had been driven—<sup>6</sup>the men, the women, the children, the princesses, and every person whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan; also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah.<sup>7</sup>And they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. And they arrived at Tahpanhes.<sup>8</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes:<sup>9</sup>"Take in your hands large stones and hide them in the mortar in the pavement that is at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah,<sup>10</sup>and say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne above these stones that I have hidden, and he will spread his royal canopy over them.<sup>11</sup>He shall come and strike the land of Egypt, giving over to the pestilence those who are doomed to the pestilence, to captivity those who are doomed to captivity, and to the sword those who are doomed to the sword.<sup>12</sup>I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and he shall burn them and carry them away captive. And he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin, and he shall go away from there in peace.<sup>13</sup>He shall break the obelisks of Heliopolis, which is in the land of Egypt, and the temples of the gods of Egypt he shall burn with fire.'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — You Are Telling a Lie
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An oath to obey “whether it is good or bad” lasts exactly as long as the answer is welcome. The narrator first insists that Jeremiah spoke all the words of the LORD their God, who had sent him (v. 1). Then Azariah, Johanan and all the insolent men call him a liar: the LORD did not send this word; Baruch has set him against them, to hand them over to the Chaldeans (vv. 2–3). So the commanders and the people refuse the command to remain in the land of Judah (v. 4), and gather up the whole remnant, even those who had only just come home from the nations where they had been driven (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: An oath to obey "whether it is good or bad" lasted exactly as long as the answer was welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jeremiah finished speaking to all the people all these words of the LORD their God, with which the LORD their God had sent him to them, Azariah the son of Hoshaiah and Johanan the son of Kareah and all the insolent men said to Jeremiah, "You are telling a lie. The LORD our God did not send you to say, 'Do not go to Egypt to live there,' but Baruch the son of Neriah has set you against us, to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans, that they may kill us or take us into exile in Babylon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as Jeremiah finishes, the leaders reject God’s answer by denying that it is God’s answer, and blame Baruch for turning the prophet against them.

All these words of the LORD their God. Before anyone speaks, the narrator sets the record straight: these were the words of the LORD their God, who had sent him with them.

You are telling a lie. Ten days they waited for this answer. They swore an oath to obey it whether it is good or bad (42:6). As soon as they hear it, they call the prophet a liar.

The LORD our God did not send you. They do not say the message is hard, or ask for time, or admit they are afraid. They say God did not send it. When obedience becomes unbearable, the tempting move is not open rebellion but deciding that the word was never really God’s. Then there is nothing left to obey.

Johanan the son of Kareah. Johanan is among them. The man who brought the true warning to Gedaliah and was called a liar for it (40:16) is now doing to Jeremiah exactly what was done to him.

Baruch the son of Neriah has set you against us. Then the conspiracy theory, aimed at the scribe: the old prophet is being used by his secretary, and the message is really Baruch’s plan to hand them over to Babylon. The charge need not deny that Jeremiah is godly; it need only say that someone else is steering him. Forty years of proven ministry were set aside with one accusation about the man holding the pen.

Explaining the speaker instead of answering him. Faced with a claim we dislike, we ask not whether it is true but where it came from: he only says that because of his upbringing, his class, his politics, his hurt. Motives do bend arguments, but C. S. Lewis noticed the trick and gave it a mocking name, Bulverism, after an imaginary inventor who discovered that you need not show a man is wrong if you assume he is and then explain how he came to be so silly. Lewis’s point was that it is a way of never having to think, and that it can be turned on anyone, including the person using it. The officers could not refute forty years of fulfilled warnings, so they explained them away, and it remains a favourite way to dodge a sermon. The gospel offers a better way to hear a hard word. If God has already told me the worst about myself at the cross, and loved me there, I no longer need to discredit the messenger in order to survive the message.

Textual note. Azariah the son of Hoshaiah is probably the Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah of 42:1; the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) reads Azariah in both places.

verseByVerse.quote: So Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces and all the people did not obey the voice of the LORD, to remain in the land of Judah. But Johanan the son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces took all the remnant of Judah who had returned to live in the land of Judah from all the nations to which they had been driven—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Calling God’s word a lie leads straight to disobeying it, and the leaders carry off even those whom God had just begun to gather home.

Did not obey the voice of the LORD. They had called it a lie; the narrator calls it what it is, and names the command they broke: to remain in the land of Judah. Nothing was required of them but to stay where God had put them and let him build and plant them there (42:10). The command came with the promise already attached.

Who had returned to live in the land of Judah. These were the people who had come home from Moab, Ammon and Edom when they heard there was a governor and a harvest (40:11-12). God had begun gathering them, in a small and real way, as he promised. Now they are taken out again by their own leaders, and the gathering is undone by the people it had gathered.
verseByVerse.note: From here to the end of chapter 44, Jeremiah's ministry takes place in Egypt.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The list of those who go down to Egypt is complete, and it ends with the two men who had told them not to go. Men, women, children, the princesses, everyone Nebuzaradan had left with Gedaliah, and last of all Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah, are taken on the road (v. 6). The narrator repeats the reason, that they did not obey the voice of the LORD, and records their arrival at Tahpanhes, a frontier town of the eastern Nile delta (v. 7). The people God had brought out of Egypt with a strong hand have walked back in of their own accord.
verseByVerse.theology: The two men who had told them not to go were carried along with them.

verseByVerse.quote: the men, the women, the children, the princesses, and every person whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan; also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah. And they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. And they arrived at Tahpanhes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole remnant goes down into Egypt, dragging along the two men who had warned against it, and the people God once brought out of Egypt walk back in.

The men, the women, the children, the princesses. The inventory is complete and heartbreaking: men, women, children, the royal daughters, and every person the Babylonians had entrusted to Gedaliah. Whatever was left of Judah in Judah is on this road.

Also Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch the son of Neriah. At the end of the list, as if incidental, come the two men just called a liar and a manipulator. Jeremiah had turned down Babylon to stay with these people (40:4-6), and this is what that choice cost him: the last journey of his life is a forced march into the one country his whole message had warned against, with men who had just disowned his ministry.

He goes with them. No lament or protest is recorded. He simply goes with them, which is the shape of his entire life: tied to a people who would not hear him and would not let him go. In that he is a faint likeness of the One who was numbered with the transgressors (Isa 53:12) and did not abandon the people who rejected him.

For they did not obey the voice of the LORD. The reason is stated a second time in four verses, so that no future reader mistakes this for an ordinary move to a new country.

They arrived at Tahpanhes. Tahpanhes was a frontier town in the eastern Nile delta, the first substantial place on the road in (compare 2:16). And the place itself tells the story: the people God took out of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm walked back in of their own accord.

What became of Jeremiah? Scripture does not say. He was last seen in Egypt, still preaching (chapter 44); later tradition, outside Scripture, says he died there, some accounts say at the hands of his own people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Egypt God speaks again, and the land the remnant chose as a refuge is shown to be under his rule. The word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes (v. 8). In full view of the men of Judah, he is to hide large stones in the mortar of the pavement at the entrance to Pharaoh’s palace (v. 9). Then the sign is explained: God will send for Nebuchadnezzar, “my servant”, and set his throne above those very stones, with the royal canopy spread over them (v. 10). The king they fled from will sit at the door of the king they fled to.
verseByVerse.theology: God lays a foundation in Pharaoh's forecourt for a throne that is coming whether Egypt likes it or not.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes: "Take in your hands large stones and hide them in the mortar in the pavement that is at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah, and say to them, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne above these stones that I have hidden, and he will spread his royal canopy over them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Egypt God speaks again, and through stones hidden at Pharaoh’s door he announces that the king the remnant fled from will set his throne on that very spot.

Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes. God speaks to him in Egypt, and that is not a small thing. Jeremiah had been dragged there by men who denied that God had sent him, and the word of the LORD arrives as it always had. He was disobedient in nothing, and God does not treat him as though he were. He remains a prophet, on the wrong side of a border he never wanted to cross.

Take in your hands large stones. One more acted sign, a message from God performed as well as spoken, and after the yoke, the flask and the field this one is characteristically odd: hide large stones in the mortar of the pavement at the entrance to Pharaoh’s palace, and do it in the sight of the men of Judah. An old man on his knees in a foreign forecourt, pushing stones into mortar while his countrymen watch. Within a day the stones will be invisible, which is the point: they are hidden, and they are still there.

I will set his throne above these stones. They came to Egypt to get away from Nebuchadnezzar, and God says he will set the man’s throne on this very pavement, with his royal canopy spread over the spot. The hidden stones are the foundation for a Babylonian throne in Pharaoh’s own doorway.

My servant. Once more the title appears that has run through this book (25:9; 27:6). The emperor is still an instrument, and the God who moves him is the God these refugees were running from: I will send and take him. You may cross a border to escape a man, and find that the One who commands him was waiting at the destination. There is no hiding place from providence.

Did Nebuchadnezzar invade Egypt? A fragmentary Babylonian tablet records a campaign against Egypt in his thirty-seventh year, about 568/567 BC, against Pharaoh Amasis. How far into Egypt he went is not known, but the record fits Jeremiah’s word (and Ezek 29:17-20), which this commentary takes as fulfilled.

Uncertain wording. The words rendered in the mortar in the pavement are rare: the first can mean mortar or clay, the second a brick kiln or brickwork (older translations have “in the clay in the brickkiln”). Most now take it as a brick-paved terrace at the entrance, a fitting place for a throne.
verseByVerse.note: Tahpanhes is usually identified with Tell Defenneh, where nineteenth-century excavators found a large brick platform in front of a fort; some linked it with this pavement, though that cannot be proved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–13 — As a Shepherd Cleans His Cloak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Egypt receives the same sentence as Judah, and its gods fare no better than the people who trusted them. Nebuchadnezzar will strike the land, giving each person over to pestilence, captivity or the sword as appointed (v. 11). God will kindle a fire in the temples of Egypt’s gods; the conqueror will burn them or carry them off, pick the land clean as a shepherd cleans his cloak, and go away in peace (v. 12). He will break the obelisks of Heliopolis, the city of the sun, and burn the temples of Egypt’s gods (v. 13). The refuge chosen against God’s word cannot protect even itself.
verseByVerse.theology: The refuge they chose receives the same sentence as the city they left.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall come and strike the land of Egypt, giving over to the pestilence those who are doomed to the pestilence, to captivity those who are doomed to captivity, and to the sword those who are doomed to the sword. I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt, and he shall burn them and carry them away captive. And he shall clean the land of Egypt as a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin, and he shall go away from there in peace. He shall break the obelisks of Heliopolis, which is in the land of Egypt, and the temples of the gods of Egypt he shall burn with fire.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt, the refuge they chose against God’s word, receives the same sentence as Judah: its land struck, its gods burned, its great obelisks broken.

He shall come and strike the land of Egypt. The judgments of pestilence, captivity and the sword follow them across the frontier, and the refuge turns out to be under the same verdict as the place they left.

I shall kindle a fire in the temples of the gods of Egypt. Note who lights the fire. God says he will do it, and Nebuchadnezzar will carry it out. The gods Judah had gone down to live among will be burned and carted off as loot by an army God sends.

As a shepherd cleans his cloak of vermin. Then an image of startling contempt: a shepherd sitting in the sun picking lice out of his coat and flicking them away. That is the sack of one of the great old civilisations, described as delousing a garment, and the shepherd walks off afterwards in peace, unhurried, having lost nothing.

He shall break the obelisks of Heliopolis. The Hebrew calls the city Beth-shemesh, house of the sun: Heliopolis, the sun-god’s city, whose stone pillars were among the most permanent objects in the world these people had fled into. Stone that had stood for a thousand years, broken.

What God has hidden. So the chapter ends where it began, with hidden stones and standing ones. The obelisks that looked eternal come down; the stones an old prophet pushed into mortar mark where an emperor’s throne will stand. What is visible is temporary, and what God has hidden is the thing that holds.

Out of Egypt I called my son. This is not the last word on Egypt in Scripture. Six centuries later an angel would tell a carpenter to take a child down into Egypt to keep him alive from a king who wanted him dead, and then to bring him home again, so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled: Out of Egypt I called my son (Matt 2:15; Hos 11:1). Judah went down to Egypt in disobedience and did not come back. The true Son went down in obedience, and came out, and made the road home for everyone who had taken the wrong one.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind clean ... of vermin usually means to wrap oneself in a garment, so older translations say the conqueror will “array himself with the land of Egypt, as a shepherd putteth on his garment” (KJV), wrapping himself in its spoil as easily as a shepherd throws on his cloak. The ESV takes it in a rarer sense, to pick clean. Either way, Egypt will be taken with ease.

43.title: Down Into Egypt
43.overview:
Where we are. Jeremiah has just given God’s answer to the remnant: stay in the land, and do not go to Egypt (chapter 42). This chapter records what they did with it, and how the story of Judah in its own land came to an end.

The message. People who will not obey God’s word usually end by saying it is not God’s word. The remnant call the prophet a liar, march the whole community back into Egypt, and find that the God they disobeyed is already there before them, Lord of the place they fled to. There is no hiding place from his word, and no safe refuge except obedience to him.

Why it was said. The first readers, scattered in Babylon and Egypt, needed to understand why Judah’s last survivors ended up in Egypt, the land of the old slavery, and why it was no safe haven (see the introduction). The chapter also shows that Jeremiah’s ministry did not end in silence: God was still speaking through him in Tahpanhes.

How the chapter makes its case. The leaders accuse Jeremiah of lying and blame Baruch for setting him against them (vv. 1–3). So they disobey, and take the whole remnant, even those who had come home from the nations, down to Egypt, with Jeremiah and Baruch carried along to Tahpanhes (vv. 4–7). There God tells Jeremiah to hide large stones at the entrance to Pharaoh’s palace: Nebuchadnezzar, God’s servant, will set his throne above them (vv. 8–10). He will strike Egypt, burn the temples of its gods, break its obelisks, and go away in peace (vv. 11–13).

Where it leads. By pattern, one that Matthew himself draws. Judah went down to Egypt in disobedience and did not come back. The child Jesus was taken down to Egypt in obedience to God’s word and brought out again, to fulfil the prophet’s words, “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Matthew 2:15). He is the true Son, who walked the road his people had ruined and made it a road home. And the faithful prophet, carried along among rebels and sharing their exile, points to the One who “was numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12).

For us. When God’s word cuts across our plans, the temptation is rarely open defiance. More often we explain it away, questioning the messenger, his motives or his advisers. We cannot outrun God, who is Lord of every place we flee to. But in Christ, who came up out of Egypt for us, even those who took the wrong road can come home.
43.theology:
The chapter shows how people refuse a word they cannot answer. They do not argue with it; they decide it is only a man’s word and explain where it came from (vv. 2-3). The sin itself is a failure to stay where God had put them, under a command that came with the promise already attached (42:10).

It also shows that there is no running from God's providence. The word reaches Jeremiah in a country he never chose, and the king the refugees fled is called God's servant and sent to the very door of their refuge (v. 10). Over it all stands the contrast the Gospels draw: Judah went down to Egypt in disobedience and never came back, but the true Son went down in obedience and was called out (Hos 11:1; Matt 2:15).
43.examples:
Think of someone who waits for counsel, promises in advance to take it, and then, once it is given, decides the adviser must have been got at by someone else. That is Johanan here: it is easier to blame the secretary than to obey the sermon.

Or think of an old man on his knees in a foreign forecourt, pressing stones into wet mortar while his countrymen watch. Within a day nothing can be seen. The thousand-year obelisks across the country look far more permanent, yet they are the things that fall, and the hidden stones are the things that hold.

keyVerse.quote: And they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of the LORD. And they arrived at Tahpanhes.
keyVerse.note: In one verse the exodus is run backwards: the people God brought out of Egypt walk back in. The narrator gives the reason a second time so that no reader mistakes it for an ordinary migration; it is disobedience, after an oath to obey. Matthew’s Gospel answers it with the Son who went down to Egypt in obedience and was called out again (Matthew 2:15).

43.reflection:
The leaders did not argue with God’s word; they said it was not God’s word, and blamed Baruch (vv. 2–3). In what ways are we tempted to discredit a messenger rather than face a hard message?

The leaders took back to Egypt even those whom God had just gathered home (v. 5). How can leaders undo what God is doing among his people, and how should that shape the way we pray for our own leaders?

Jeremiah was carried into Egypt against his will, yet the word of the LORD came to him there (vv. 6–8). How might that encourage someone who is in a place they did not choose because of other people’s decisions?

Judah went down to Egypt in disobedience; Jesus went down in obedience and came out again (Matthew 2:15). What does it mean for you that Christ made a road home for those who took the wrong one?

Behold, this day they are a desolation, and no one dwells in them,<sup>3</sup>because of the evil that they committed, provoking me to anger, in that they went to make offerings and serve other gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.<sup>4</sup>Yet I persistently sent to you all my servants the prophets, saying, 'Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate!'<sup>5</sup>But they did not listen or incline their ear, to turn from their evil and make no offerings to other gods.<sup>6</sup>Therefore my wrath and my anger were poured out and kindled in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, and they became a waste and a desolation, as at this day.<sup>7</sup>And now thus says the LORD God of hosts, the God of Israel: Why do you commit this great evil against yourselves, to cut off from you man and woman, infant and child, from the midst of Judah, leaving you no remnant?<sup>8</sup>Why do you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, making offerings to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to live, so that you may be cut off and become a curse and a taunt among all the nations of the earth?<sup>9</sup>Have you forgotten the evil of your fathers, the evil of the kings of Judah, the evil of their wives, your own evil, and the evil of your wives, which they committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?<sup>10</sup>They have not humbled themselves even to this day, nor have they feared, nor walked in my law and my statutes that I set before you and before your fathers.<sup>11</sup>"Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will set my face against you for harm, to cut off all Judah.<sup>12</sup>I will take the remnant of Judah who have set their faces to come to the land of Egypt to live, and they shall all be consumed. In the land of Egypt they shall fall; by the sword and by famine they shall be consumed. From the least to the greatest, they shall die by the sword and by famine, and they shall become an oath, a horror, a curse, and a taunt.<sup>13</sup>I will punish those who dwell in the land of Egypt, as I have punished Jerusalem, with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence,<sup>14</sup>so that none of the remnant of Judah who have come to live in the land of Egypt shall escape or survive or return to the land of Judah, to which they desire to return to dwell there. For they shall not return, except some fugitives."<sup>15</sup>Then all the men who knew that their wives had made offerings to other gods, and all the women who stood by, a great assembly, all the people who lived in Pathros in the land of Egypt, answered Jeremiah:<sup>16</sup>"As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you.<sup>17</sup>But we will do everything that we have vowed, make offerings to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as we did, both we and our fathers, our kings and our officials, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. For then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster.<sup>18</sup>But since we left off making offerings to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been consumed by the sword and by famine."<sup>19</sup>And the women said, "When we made offerings to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, was it without our husbands' approval that we made cakes for her bearing her image and poured out drink offerings to her?"<sup>20</sup>Then Jeremiah said to all the people, men and women, all the people who had given him this answer:<sup>21</sup>"As for the offerings that you offered in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, you and your fathers, your kings and your officials, and the people of the land, did not the LORD remember them?
