Then confirm your vows and perform your vows!<sup>26</sup>Therefore hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who dwell in the land of Egypt: Behold, I have sworn by my great name, says the LORD, that my name shall no more be invoked by the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt, saying, 'As the Lord GOD lives.'<sup>27</sup>Behold, I am watching over them for disaster and not for good. All the men of Judah who are in the land of Egypt shall be consumed by the sword and by famine, until there is an end of them.<sup>28</sup>And those who escape the sword shall return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, few in number; and all the remnant of Judah, who came to the land of Egypt to live, shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs.<sup>29</sup>This shall be the sign to you, declares the LORD, that I will punish you in this place, in order that you may know that my words will surely stand against you for harm:<sup>30</sup>Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and into the hand of those who seek his life, as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who was his enemy and sought his life."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — You Have Seen All the Disaster
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God begins with evidence no one can dispute: the ruin of Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which the refugees have seen with their own eyes. The word reaches Judeans now spread across Egypt, from the frontier to the far south (v. 1). God names the ruin as his own work and its cause as offerings to gods no one in Judah had ever known (vv. 2–3). He had pleaded with them persistently through his prophets, “do not do this abomination that I hate!” (v. 4), but they would not lean in to listen, so his anger was poured out and the land lies waste “as at this day” (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The argument opens with a ruin they had walked through themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Judeans who lived in the land of Egypt, at Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis, and in the land of Pathros, "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You have seen all the disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem and upon all the cities of Judah. Behold, this day they are a desolation, and no one dwells in them, because of the evil that they committed, provoking me to anger, in that they went to make offerings and serve other gods that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God opens his case with what the refugees have seen for themselves: Jerusalem lies in ruins, he brought the ruin, and the cause was their worship of gods that no one in Judah had ever known.

At Migdol, at Tahpanhes, at Memphis. The company that arrived together at Tahpanhes (43:7) has spread: north-east to Migdol on the frontier, south to Memphis, and up the Nile into Pathros, which is upper (southern) Egypt. They are settling in and making lives. A century or so later a Jewish garrison at Elephantine, far up the Nile in Pathros, had its own temple to the LORD, and its papyri suggest that other gods were honoured there beside him: the mixed worship this chapter confronts was slow to die.

You have seen. Not heard, not been told. These people had walked out through the rubble. Whatever else is arguable, the ruin is a fact in their own memories.

The disaster that I brought upon Jerusalem. God claims it. Babylon was only the instrument; the ruin was his doing.

Other gods that they knew not. The cause is idolatry, with a small devastating clause attached: gods “that they knew not, neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.” These were not ancestral deities with a long claim on the family but novelties picked up from neighbours, unknown to the generations that had seen God act. A nation abandoned the God who brought it out of Egypt for gods it had only recently met.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet I persistently sent to you all my servants the prophets, saying, 'Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate!' But they did not listen or incline their ear, to turn from their evil and make no offerings to other gods. Therefore my wrath and my anger were poured out and kindled in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, and they became a waste and a desolation, as at this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For centuries God pleaded with his people like someone trying to stop a loved one from destroying himself, and because they would not even lean in to listen, the ruin came.

Yet I persistently sent to you. The word that runs through the whole book appears again (7:25; 25:4), and this time with a cry that sounds like nothing else in Jeremiah.

Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate! That is not the language of a law code. It is the cry of someone trying to stop a person he loves from doing what will destroy them, and God puts it in his own mouth as the summary of four centuries of prophetic preaching: generation after generation of warning, distilled to a single “Oh”.

But they did not listen or incline their ear. Two verbs of refusal, and they are the epitaph of the kingdom. The second is worse than the first: to incline the ear is to lean in, and they would not even turn their heads toward it.

As at this day. The argument turns on this phrase. God is not asking them to accept a theory about judgment; he is pointing at a country they can still picture from where they stand, and asking them to read it correctly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Why Do You Commit This Great Evil Against Yourselves?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Their worship in Egypt is not only an offence against God but harm done to themselves. God asks why they are cutting off their own future, men, women and little children, by making offerings to other gods in the very land where they came for safety, so becoming a curse among the nations (vv. 7–8). Have they forgotten the evil of their fathers, their kings, the kings’ wives, themselves and their own wives (v. 9)? After everything, no one has humbled himself, feared God or walked in his law, “even to this day” (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: From God's side, sin is a wound the sinner opens in his own household.

verseByVerse.quote: And now thus says the LORD God of hosts, the God of Israel: Why do you commit this great evil against yourselves, to cut off from you man and woman, infant and child, from the midst of Judah, leaving you no remnant? Why do you provoke me to anger with the works of your hands, making offerings to other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to live, so that you may be cut off and become a curse and a taunt among all the nations of the earth? Have you forgotten the evil of your fathers, the evil of the kings of Judah, the evil of their wives, your own evil, and the evil of your wives, which they committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their idolatry, taken up again in Egypt, is a knife turned on themselves, and the guilt runs through every generation and every household in the assembly.

Against yourselves. It is the truest thing said about idolatry in the chapter. God has already said that it provokes him to anger; here he calls it self-mutilation, a knife taken to “man and woman, infant and child”, cutting away their own future. Sin is treason against God and self-destruction in the family, and the second is often what finally gets a person’s attention.

The works of your hands. They made the thing they worship. Paul describes the same exchange: they “exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals” (Romans 1:23).

Where you have come to live. They went to Egypt for safety and at once resumed the practice that had cost them their own country. A change of address does nothing to the heart that made the move.

Have you forgotten the evil of your fathers? Verse 9 lists the evil of five groups in one sentence: fathers, kings, royal wives, the hearers themselves, their own wives. Nobody in the assembly is outside it, and the wives are named twice, which prepares for verse 19.

Textual note. The ESV notes that where the English has “their wives” after the kings, the Hebrew reads “his wives”. Either way the list is comprehensive.

verseByVerse.quote: They have not humbled themselves even to this day, nor have they feared, nor walked in my law and my statutes that I set before you and before your fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After all they have seen, no one has humbled himself, feared God or kept his law: suffering on its own has not changed them.

Even to this day. Consider what “this day” contains: the city burned, the temple gone, the king blinded after watching his sons die, a long famine, a governor murdered at his table, seventy pilgrims thrown into a cistern, and a forced march into Egypt (chapters 39 to 43). If catastrophe by itself produced humility, these would be the humblest people alive.

They have not humbled themselves, nor have they feared. Suffering does not soften a heart on its own; it reveals what the heart already was. The same fire hardens clay and melts wax, and Judah in Egypt is the proof.

Nor walked in my law and my statutes. The third failure is the plainest: the law given to a people God had already brought out of Egypt, and nobody did it. No one ever has, fully: “Surely there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins” (Ecclesiastes 7:20). That is why this book’s hope rests on a new covenant with the law written on the heart (31:33), and on the one who walked in that law perfectly in our place, so that “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — They Shall All Be Consumed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who set their faces toward Egypt will find God’s face set against them. The remnant that chose Egypt over his word will be consumed there by sword and famine, from the least to the greatest, and become a byword (vv. 11–12). God will punish Egypt’s Judeans as he punished Jerusalem (v. 13). They came meaning to go home when the danger was past, but none will return, “except some fugitives” (v. 14): a remnant of the remnant, promised before the refusal is even spoken.
verseByVerse.theology: They wanted Egypt for a while and Judah in the end, and are told they will have neither.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will set my face against you for harm, to cut off all Judah. I will take the remnant of Judah who have set their faces to come to the land of Egypt to live, and they shall all be consumed. In the land of Egypt they shall fall; by the sword and by famine they shall be consumed. From the least to the greatest, they shall die by the sword and by famine, and they shall become an oath, a horror, a curse, and a taunt. I will punish those who dwell in the land of Egypt, as I have punished Jerusalem, with the sword, with famine, and with pestilence, so that none of the remnant of Judah who have come to live in the land of Egypt shall escape or survive or return to the land of Judah, to which they desire to return to dwell there. For they shall not return, except some fugitives."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who set their faces toward Egypt against God’s word will find his face set against them there, and only a handful of fugitives will ever see Judah again.

I will set my face against you. Earlier God had hidden his face from the city (33:5); here he turns it toward these people, and it is worse. An averted face means abandonment; a set face means deliberate opposition. The phrase answers theirs exactly: they “set their faces” toward Egypt (42:15, 17), and God sets his face against them. Two settings of the face in opposite directions, and only one of them can hold.

From the least to the greatest. This was the phrase used of the crowd that came asking for guidance and swore to obey (42:1, 8). The whole company that took the oath is the whole company under the sentence.

As I have punished Jerusalem. The comparison is the argument. They had seen what that looked like. Egypt will not be exempt.

To which they desire to return to dwell there. Here the hidden assumption of the migration is exposed in one clause. They never meant to stay in Egypt; the plan was to sit out the danger and go home afterwards: the reasoning of everyone who intends a short detour away from obedience and fully expects to come back.

Except some fugitives. They will not come back. Then, at the very end, three words refuse to close the door completely. A handful will straggle home. Even in this sentence God keeps a remnant of a remnant, and he says so before the chapter records the most direct refusal in the book.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — We Will Not Listen to You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Here the people stop pretending and refuse God’s word openly. A great assembly of men and women, knowing the word comes in the LORD’s name, says, “we will not listen to you” (vv. 15–16). They will keep their vows to the queen of heaven, because when they served her they had plenty, and since they stopped they have lacked everything (vv. 17–18). The women add that their husbands approved every cake and drink offering (v. 19). It is a careful reading of their own history, and it is exactly upside down.
verseByVerse.theology: They read the ruin of Jerusalem as evidence that they had not sinned enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the men who knew that their wives had made offerings to other gods, and all the women who stood by, a great assembly, all the people who lived in Pathros in the land of Egypt, answered Jeremiah: "As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you. But we will do everything that we have vowed, make offerings to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as we did, both we and our fathers, our kings and our officials, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. For then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole assembly, men and women together, knowingly refuses the LORD’s word and vows to go on serving the queen of heaven, because in her days they prospered.

A great assembly. The description is careful. The men “knew” what their wives were doing; the women stand by; it is a great assembly. This is not a faction muttering but a congregation, organised, with the households aligned.

We will not listen to you. For forty years this people had not listened, but they had always said something else: that Jeremiah was a traitor, or mad, or Baruch’s puppet, or not sent by the LORD (43:2–3). Here the pretence is dropped. They admit that the word was spoken “in the name of the LORD”, and refuse it anyway. It is one of the plainest sentences of unbelief in the Old Testament, and it is not the speech of ignorant people: they know what they are refusing, they mean it, and they say it together. Jesus told of citizens who said of their king, “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19:14), and he wept over the city that would say it of him (Luke 19:41).

The queen of heaven. A pagan goddess of fertility and provision, served with cakes and drink offerings. The cult was not new: decades earlier Jeremiah had described it in Jerusalem, “The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven” (7:18), a whole family working at it together, exactly as here.

We had plenty of food, and prospered. Their argument is economic. It is the reasoning of the unfaithful wife in Hosea, “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink” (Hosea 2:5), and God’s answer there is the answer here: “she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil” (Hosea 2:8).

The god of what works. The argument from prosperity would be at home on any self-help shelf. Do not ask whether a practice is true; ask whether it works: does it lower my stress, help my marriage, grow the business? Spirituality chosen by results is now the ordinary kind, and it can look humble because it makes no grand claims. But it puts us in charge. A god kept because he delivers is an employee, dismissed the day the results dip, which is exactly what these people say happened to the LORD under Josiah. And results are a poor judge: read over one generation, the evidence pointed them exactly the wrong way. The God of the Bible will not be hired on those terms. He gives bread to people who never thank him for it, and in the end he gave himself, in what looked by every measure of results like the greatest failure in history, a man dying on a Roman cross. That failure is the one thing that has worked for sinners ever since.

What it does not mean. Some Christians later gave the title “Queen of Heaven” to Mary. The title here belongs to a pagan goddess; Scripture gives it to no one, and offerings and prayers to anyone but God are forbidden.

Uncertain wording. Which goddess the “queen of heaven” was is not certain. She is most often identified with the Mesopotamian Ishtar, the Canaanite Astarte, or a blend of such goddesses, goddesses linked with the heavens, love and fertility. The chapter’s point does not depend on knowing which.
verseByVerse.note: This is the last time in the book that Jeremiah's hearers answer him, and their answer is the refusal itself.

verseByVerse.quote: But since we left off making offerings to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been consumed by the sword and by famine." And the women said, "When we made offerings to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, was it without our husbands' approval that we made cakes for her bearing her image and poured out drink offerings to her?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people read their history exactly upside down, blaming the disaster on the end of their idolatry, and the women add that their husbands approved every offering.

Since we left off making offerings. What they describe is most likely Josiah’s reformation (2 Kings 23). The idols were cleared out, the high places (the hilltop shrines) pulled down, and the queen of heaven’s cakes went off the family table; then came Josiah’s death at Megiddo, Egyptian rule, Babylon, the siege, the famine and the fall. They drew the obvious conclusion from the sequence: the trouble started when the reform did.

Right facts, wrong cause. The facts are right; cause and effect are the wrong way round, and so nearly right that it is frightening. There is a way of reading events that is careful, based on what really happened, and completely wrong, because it leaves out the four centuries of patience before the reform and the fact that the reform came too late and never reached the heart (3:10). People still argue this way: things went badly after I began to take God seriously, therefore taking God seriously was the mistake. The timeline is accurate and the verdict is a lie.

Was it without our husbands’ approval? Their point is legal. Under the law a husband who heard his wife’s vow and said nothing had confirmed it; only by opposing it on the day he heard could he annul it (Numbers 30:6–8). So: our husbands knew, and never once forbade us. That is unanswerable as far as it goes, and it indicts the men standing beside them, who had known all along (v. 15).

Shared blame. But they are not asking forgiveness or claiming they were pressured; they are establishing that the guilt is shared, as a reason to carry on. Spreading the blame feels like a defence, but it is a confession, and Jeremiah’s reply goes deliberately to “all the people, men and women” (v. 20).

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated “bearing her image” is a rare expression. It may mean that the cakes were shaped like the goddess or stamped with her image, or more generally that they were made to represent or honour her; moulds for cakes in the shape of a female figure have been found in the ancient Near East, which suits the ESV’s reading. Either way the cakes were acts of worship.

Textual note. The ESV notes that the words “And the women said” are supplied from the Syriac translation; in the Hebrew the speech simply continues. That the women are speaking is clear from what they say.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah answers their reading of history, and God answers their vow. The LORD remembered every offering made in Judah; their years of plenty were his patience, not his approval, and when he could bear it no longer the land became a desolation, because of the offerings, not because they stopped (vv. 20–23). Since they insist on their vows, he lets them keep them, and swears that his name will no more be on their lips in Egypt (vv. 24–26). He watches over them for disaster; the few who escape will know whose word stands, and Pharaoh Hophra’s fall will be the sign (vv. 27–30).
verseByVerse.theology: Two words have competed throughout this book, God’s and his opponents’, and the end shows which one holds.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeremiah said to all the people, men and women, all the people who had given him this answer: "As for the offerings that you offered in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, you and your fathers, your kings and your officials, and the people of the land, did not the LORD remember them? Did it not come into his mind? The LORD could no longer bear your evil deeds and the abominations that you committed. Therefore your land has become a desolation and a waste and a curse, without inhabitant, as it is this day. It is because you made offerings and because you sinned against the LORD and did not obey the voice of the LORD or walk in his law and in his statutes and in his testimonies that this disaster has happened to you, as at this day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah corrects their reading of history: God remembered every offering, their years of plenty were his patience, not his approval, and the disaster came because of the offerings, not because they stopped.

To all the people, men and women. He takes them at their word. They had argued that everybody was in it together, so he addresses everybody together.

Did not the LORD remember them? Two questions go straight at the hole in the argument. They had said that in the days of the cakes there was plenty and no disaster, as though God had not noticed. “Did it not come into his mind?”

Patience mistaken for approval. The years of prosperity were not evidence that God was pleased; they were the long stretch in which he sent prophet after prophet saying, “Oh, do not do this abomination that I hate!” (v. 4). Delay is not indifference, and every unpunished season is being remembered (compare Romans 2:4–5).

The LORD could no longer bear. The phrase implies that he had borne it a very long time, that there was a limit, and that the limit was reached. The desolation they keep pointing at is not the result of the reformation; it is the end of God’s forbearance with the very practice they have resumed. “It is because you made offerings”: the cause is stated outright, and the record is corrected.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeremiah said to all the people and all the women, "Hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who are in the land of Egypt. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: You and your wives have declared with your mouths, and have fulfilled it with your hands, saying, 'We will surely perform our vows that we have made, to make offerings to the queen of heaven and to pour out drink offerings to her.' Then confirm your vows and perform your vows! Therefore hear the word of the LORD, all you of Judah who dwell in the land of Egypt: Behold, I have sworn by my great name, says the LORD, that my name shall no more be invoked by the mouth of any man of Judah in all the land of Egypt, saying, 'As the Lord GOD lives.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since they insist on their vows, God lets them keep them, and swears that his name will no longer be on their lips in Egypt.

All you of Judah who are in the land of Egypt. The address almost defines what they have become: not Judah in Judah, but Judah in Egypt, a people identified by the place they should not be.

Then confirm your vows and perform your vows! God quotes their oath back to them and says: do it. There is no bluff in it. It is one of the most terrible things God says in the book, because it means he will no longer stand in their way. They have insisted long enough; he stops arguing and lets them keep what they chose. Scripture knows this judgment elsewhere, God giving people up to what they have chosen (Romans 1:24). It is not that he has grown indifferent, but that pleading has an end, and being left alone with what you insisted on is the worst thing a person can be given.

I have sworn by my great name. Here is the sentence: his name will never again be spoken by a Judean in Egypt. Weigh what is removed first: not their lives, but the words of their worship, the oath “As the Lord GOD lives”, the ordinary speech of a covenant people. They had gone on using his name while serving the queen of heaven, invoking him out of habit, and he will not have his name in their mouths on those terms. It is possible to lose the right to say God’s name while still saying it constantly.

For a tender conscience. Someone may fear that God has given them up like this. The fear itself is a good sign: those whom God has given up do not grieve over their sin or long for him. The door stays open for anyone who comes, for Christ has said, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am watching over them for disaster and not for good. All the men of Judah who are in the land of Egypt shall be consumed by the sword and by famine, until there is an end of them. And those who escape the sword shall return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, few in number; and all the remnant of Judah, who came to the land of Egypt to live, shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs. This shall be the sign to you, declares the LORD, that I will punish you in this place, in order that you may know that my words will surely stand against you for harm: Thus says the LORD, Behold, I will give Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and into the hand of those who seek his life, as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who was his enemy and sought his life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God watches over his word against them as carefully as he once watched over it to build, and the fall of Pharaoh Hophra will show whose word stands.

I am watching over them for disaster. The verb is the one from Jeremiah’s first vision, when God showed him an almond branch and said he was “watching over my word to perform it” (1:12). The same attentiveness that promised to build and plant (31:28) is here watching “for disaster and not for good”. It is the same eye, the same care, the same refusal to be distracted. His watchfulness is not automatically comfort; what it means for you depends on which side of his word you have placed yourself.

Few in number. A few will get home, the fugitives of verse 14, and the reason given for their survival is not comfort but demonstration: so that everyone “shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs.”

Whose word will stand. That is the question the whole book has asked since that first vision. Two words had been on offer in Jerusalem for forty years: Jeremiah’s and everybody else’s. Hananiah said two years (28:3); the queen of heaven’s devotees said prosperity; the prophets of peace said no disaster would come (23:17). Each of those words could be tested by what happened, and each failed.

Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt. The sign is aimed at what they trusted. Hophra, whose army had once marched north and lifted the siege of Jerusalem for a time (37:5), was the Pharaoh they relied on. He will go the way Zedekiah went, and the comparison is spelled out so nobody can miss it. History records it: Hophra (the Greeks called him Apries) lost his throne to his general Amasis after an army revolt in about 570 BC, and within a few years he was dead, most likely killed trying to win it back, “into the hand of those who seek his life”.

The last word to his people. So Jeremiah’s last recorded words to his own people end on a question rather than a curse, and the answer to it is the reason this book exists. Every word spoken against Jerusalem stood, and that means the other words stand too: the everlasting love, the law written on the heart, the sins remembered no more, the shepherd who gathers, the Branch called “The LORD is our righteousness” (23:6). The God who kept the hard half of his word to the letter has promised the rest, and every promise is kept in Christ: “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

44.title: We Will Not Listen to You
44.overview:
Where we are. Jerusalem has fallen, Gedaliah has been murdered, and the survivors, against God’s plain word, have dragged Jeremiah with them to Egypt (chapters 40 to 43). Chapter 44 is the last sermon of his we have, preached to Judeans now scattered across Egypt, and the people’s answer to it.

The message. Suffering on its own does not change a heart. These people have seen their city burned for worshipping other gods, and in Egypt they take up the same gods again and say to God’s prophet, “we will not listen to you.” God has watched over his word to bring the disaster, and he will watch over it still; the only question that matters is “whose word will stand, mine or theirs.”

Why it was said. The refugees had gone to Egypt for safety and bread, meaning to return home once the danger passed, and they had a ready explanation for the ruin: it came because Josiah’s reform stopped the offerings to the queen of heaven (see the introduction on Josiah and the last kings). The chapter answers that reading of history for them and for the exiles who would later read it.

How the chapter makes its case. God points to evidence they cannot deny: the ruined cities, the gods they turned to, the prophets he sent pleading, “do not do this abomination that I hate” (vv. 1–6). He asks why they are doing the same thing again, to their own harm, when no one has humbled himself even now (vv. 7–10), and he sentences the refuge to Jerusalem’s fate, except for a few fugitives (vv. 11–14). A great assembly of men and women refuses outright, arguing that they prospered while they served the queen of heaven (vv. 15–19). Jeremiah replies that the LORD remembered those offerings and could bear them no longer (vv. 20–23); God hands their vows back to them, removes his name from their lips, and gives Pharaoh Hophra’s fall as the sign of whose word stands (vv. 24–30).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the need it exposes, and by the character of God it shows. If the fall of a city cannot turn a heart, only a new heart will do, which is why this book’s hope rests on the new covenant (31:33) that Christ made in his blood. And the God who kept the hard half of his word to the letter is the God whose promises “find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). The refusal itself has a pattern: Jesus told of citizens who said, “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19:14), and then went to the cross for people like them.

For us. We too can read events upside down, blaming our troubles on the moment we began to take God seriously, or keep his name on our lips while our real trust lies elsewhere. The answer is not to wait for disaster to humble us but to come now to the Christ who never casts out anyone who comes to him.
44.theology:
The chapter is a study of how a people can see God's judgment with their own eyes and still read it upside down. Suffering did not humble them (v. 10); God's long patience was mistaken for approval (vv. 21-22); and an accurate timeline was turned into a false verdict, as though the trouble began when the idols were removed (v. 18; Hos 2:5, 8).

Against that stands the faithfulness of God's word. His watchfulness is not automatically comfort: the eye that watched to build and plant can watch for disaster (v. 27; 1:12; 31:28). Yet because every hard word against Jerusalem stood, the promises of the same book stand too.
44.examples:
Some people say that things went badly from the time they began to take God seriously, so taking God seriously must have been the mistake. The women of Judah argued exactly that, and the timeline they gave was accurate. What they left out was four centuries of God's patience, and the fact that the reform never reached their hearts.

Others keep using God's name as a habit while their real trust lies elsewhere, the way the refugees went on saying As the Lord GOD lives while baking cakes for the queen of heaven. The chapter warns that it is possible to lose the right to say God's name while still saying it every day.

keyVerse.quote: And those who escape the sword shall return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, few in number; and all the remnant of Judah, who came to the land of Egypt to live, shall know whose word will stand, mine or theirs.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter, and in a sense the whole book, comes down to this question: whose word will stand? The refugees trusted their own reading of events, their vows and Pharaoh; God’s word outlasted them all. Because his warnings stood to the letter, his promises of a new covenant and a righteous King will stand too, and they do in Christ.

44.reflection:
The refugees had seen Jerusalem burn, yet “they have not humbled themselves even to this day” (v. 10). Why does suffering harden some people and soften others? What does that tell us about what really changes a heart?

The people argued that things went wrong when they stopped serving the queen of heaven (vv. 17–18). Have you ever been tempted to read your own story that way, blaming hard times on taking God seriously? How does this chapter help you answer that thought?

God’s long patience was mistaken for approval (vv. 21–22). Where might we be treating God’s silence or delay as a sign that he does not mind?

The chapter ends with the question “whose word will stand, mine or theirs” (v. 28). How does the fact that God kept his hard words give you confidence in his promises in Christ?

45.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at the dictation of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to you, O Baruch:<sup>3</sup>You said, 'Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain. I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.'<sup>4</sup>Thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD: Behold, what I have built I am breaking down, and what I have planted I am plucking up—that is, the whole land.<sup>5</sup>And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh, declares the LORD. But I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who speaks to kings and empires has a private word for one weary scribe, and he begins by repeating Baruch’s own complaint. The word is dated to the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when Baruch wrote Jeremiah’s sermons in a book at his dictation (v. 1). It is addressed “to you, O Baruch” with the full solemnity of “Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel” (v. 2). Then God quotes him: “Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain. I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest” (v. 3). He has heard every word, and he does not rebuke it.
verseByVerse.theology: God repeats a tired man's private complaint to him, word for word, and it is not a rebuke.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch the son of Neriah, when he wrote these words in a book at the dictation of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, to you, O Baruch: You said, 'Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain. I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God speaks by name to one exhausted scribe, quoting his private complaint back to him without a word of reproach. The book keeps this word until now, so that Jeremiah’s words to his people end not with a nation’s refusal but with God bending down to one tired assistant.

In the fourth year of Jehoiakim. The date takes us back nearly twenty years, to the year Baruch wrote twenty-three years of sermons onto a scroll at Jeremiah’s dictation (36:2, 4) and watched the king cut it up and feed it to a brazier. Placed here, after the flight to Egypt, it reaches a man who has since lost far more.

To you, O Baruch. The solemn opening, “Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel”, which introduces oracles to kings, Babylon, Egypt and the nations, is used here to speak to a secretary, and by name. The God who commands the empires has a private message for the man holding the pen. That is a word for anyone who has served in a supporting role and wondered whether anyone noticed the work.

Woe is me! “The LORD has added sorrow to my pain”: Baruch is not blaming circumstances but God, openly. “I am weary with my groaning”: worn out by his own complaining, which is a particular kind of exhaustion.

What Baruch had lost. He had reason. He came from a prominent family (his brother Seraiah was a royal officer, 51:59; compare 32:12), and by attaching himself to Jeremiah he had chosen the losing side of every argument in Jerusalem. He saw his book burned, had to go into hiding (36:26), and was blamed as the sinister influence behind the prophet (43:3).

His master’s complaint too. Jeremiah had said the same kind of thing: “I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot” (20:9). Serving God faithfully does not exempt anyone from being worn out by it, and Scripture records the complaints of both men without embarrassment. God would rather hear our honest groaning than our silence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers Baruch’s grief with the truth about what he is doing, a call to let go, and a promise. The ruin all around is no accident: what God built he is breaking down, and what he planted he is plucking up (v. 4). In such a time Baruch must not seek great things for himself, for disaster is coming on all flesh (v. 5). But God gives him what a soldier carries off a lost battlefield: his life, as a prize of war, in every place he may go. The great things are not for him; he will live.
verseByVerse.theology: Baruch is promised no career, no safety and no acclaim, only his life, wherever he ends up.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus shall you say to him, Thus says the LORD: Behold, what I have built I am breaking down, and what I have planted I am plucking up—that is, the whole land. And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh, declares the LORD. But I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God shows Baruch that the ruin is his own deliberate work, tells him to give up seeking great things for himself in such a time, and promises him his life wherever he goes. He begins not by consoling him but by showing him the larger picture.

What I have built I am breaking down. Baruch’s own scroll had recorded Jeremiah’s commission, “to pluck up and to break down … to build and to plant” (1:10). Now God applies those verbs to himself. He is not losing; he is deliberately demolishing his own work. That puts Baruch’s grief in a different light: his pain was real, but the ruin around him had not got out of God’s control. God’s way with his weary servants is often this, not a rebuke but a clear-eyed account of what he is doing; Jeremiah himself had been answered the same way (12:5).

Do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not. The question goes straight to what was wrong, and it is asked without contempt. A man of his background, on the right side of the argument, might reasonably have looked for vindication and a future, and God names that hope and tells him to give it up. Not because ambition is always wicked, but because of the hour: this is not the time for building a career. And the command comes wrapped in a gift: the God who tells him to want less is about to give him his life.

For every Christian. The New Testament says it to everyone: “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (Matthew 6:33), for “the appointed time has grown very short” (1 Corinthians 7:29). A man who had thrown away far better prospects than Baruch’s put it plainly: “whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ” (Philippians 3:7). None of us lets go of great things for ourselves by resolve; the Spirit shows us Christ as worth more than they are. And the one who said “I do not seek my own glory” (John 8:50) has already done perfectly, in our place, what we do so poorly.

What this looks like. Seeking great things for yourself is rarely a grand plan. It is usually quieter: the promotion rehearsed in your head at night, the need to be credited in the meeting, the sense that after all you have given up you are owed a future. Letting it go looks ordinary. Name the great thing to God, the title, the house, the recognition, as Baruch’s was named for him. Do the unseen task well: Baruch wrote the whole scroll out again after the first was burned, and faithfulness in work nobody praises is the great thing given to most of us. Let someone else have the credit this week, and notice what it costs you. Hold your plans with an open hand, saying, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that” (James 4:15). We can do this without bitterness, because we have been given what Baruch was given and more: a life “hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3), which no war and no disappointment can take.

I will give you your life as a prize of war. Jeremiah had shouted this promise across Jerusalem: whoever goes out to the Chaldeans “shall have his life as a prize of war” (38:2). It was given personally to Ebed-melech, “because you have put your trust in me” (39:18). Now the scribe receives it. It is a soldier’s phrase, the one thing you carry off the field, and “in all places to which you may go” exactly suits a man about to be marched into Egypt against his will. God does not promise him a destination he would choose; he promises to keep him wherever he ends up.

What Baruch was given. So the last word to Baruch is: the great things are not for you, and you will live. And we can see what he was given instead of a career. He wrote the burned scroll again, longer (36:32), and much of what we have of Jeremiah, including the book in which the new covenant stands, probably came to us through his hand. It has outlasted Jehoiakim, Babylon and Egypt, and is read still.

A life no place can take. For a Christian the promise reaches further. Baruch was given his life in every place he might go; those who belong to Christ are given a life no place and no power can take. The one who laid down his life and took it up again says of his sheep, “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word behind “the whole land” at the end of verse 4 can mean either “land” or “earth”. The ESV takes it as the land of Judah, which God had planted; others read “the whole earth”, which would match “disaster upon all flesh” in verse 5 and the oracles against the nations that follow. Both readings fit; on either, the ruin is God’s own doing.

45.title: A Word for Baruch
45.overview:
Where we are. The story of Jerusalem’s end and the flight to Egypt is over, and the people have spoken their final refusal (chapter 44). Before the book turns to the nations (chapters 46 to 51), it pauses for five verses addressed to one man: Baruch, Jeremiah’s scribe. The word itself dates from nearly twenty years earlier, the year he first wrote the prophet’s sermons on the scroll that Jehoiakim burned (chapter 36).

The message. God hears the private complaint of his weary servant, and answers it not with a rebuke but with the truth: the ruin around him is God’s own deliberate work, so this is no time to seek great things for himself. Instead God gives him what no war can take away: his life, wherever he goes.

Why it was said. Baruch came from a prominent family and had tied his future to the most hated man in Jerusalem. He had watched his scroll burned and gone into hiding, and he would be blamed for the prophet’s message and taken to Egypt (43:3, 6). Placed here, his word speaks to every faithful servant, and every exile, who wonders whether their losses are noticed.

How the chapter makes its case. God speaks to the scribe by name and quotes his complaint back to him without reproach: “Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain” (vv. 1–3). Then he shows Baruch the larger picture: what God built he is breaking down, the whole land (v. 4). In that light he asks, “do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not”, and he promises Baruch his life as a prize of war in every place he may go (v. 5).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. Baruch is asked to give up great things for himself in a time of judgment; Christ, who had every claim to glory, did not seek his own glory (John 8:50) but “emptied himself” and went to a cross (Philippians 2:7). Baruch was promised his life in every place; those who belong to Christ are given eternal life, and “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

For us. God notices the tired servants in supporting roles, and he lets them speak honestly. He may ask us to lay down the great things we want for ourselves, but never without giving us something better: a life “hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3) that nothing can take.
45.theology:
God has private words for those who serve in supporting roles, and he uses their names (v. 2). Faithful service does not exempt anyone from exhaustion, and Scripture records Baruch's weariness, like his master's, without embarrassment (v. 3; 20:9).

God comforts Baruch here by showing him what God is doing, not by sympathy, and he answers his ambition not with shame but by telling him that this is not the hour for great things (vv. 4-5; Matt 6:33; 1 Cor 7:29-31; Phil 3:7). What he promises is not the destination his servant would choose but his keeping in every place the servant is taken (38:2; 39:18).
45.examples:
Picture a secretary who has spent twenty years writing down another man's unpopular words, watched the work cut up and burned, written it all out again, and been blamed for it by people who would not blame the prophet himself. Baruch's "woe is me" is the voice of every faithful assistant who has wondered whether anyone noticed.

God's reply is not a speech about his feelings. It tells him what God is doing, asks him to want less, and gives him one promise he can carry anywhere. Many weary Christians have found that the way through: not a better career, but the Lord's own company in the places they did not choose.

keyVerse.quote: And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh, declares the LORD. But I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go.
keyVerse.note: This verse holds the whole of God’s answer to Baruch: a gentle question that names the hope he must let go, the reason (God’s judgment is falling), and a gift far better than what he gives up. It speaks to every servant of God tempted to look for reward in this age, and it points to the life Christ gives, which no place and no power can take.

45.reflection:
Baruch’s complaint is quoted by God without rebuke (v. 3). What does that tell you about how God receives the honest groaning of his servants? Is there something you need to tell him plainly?

God answers Baruch by showing him what he is doing in the world (v. 4). How can seeing God’s larger purposes help us bear personal loss and disappointment?

“Do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not” (v. 5). What are the “great things” people around you, and you yourself, tend to seek? What would it look like to let them go in favour of faithfulness in unseen work?

Baruch was promised his life “in all places to which you may go.” How does the life Christ gives (John 10:28; Colossians 3:3) change the way you face uncertain places and futures?
