verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Rising Like the Nile, and Fallen at Carchemish
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first oracle against the nations shows Egypt’s great army, for all its noise and confidence, broken at Carchemish by the LORD’s own hand. A heading introduces the whole section on the nations and dates this poem to 605 BC, when Nebuchadnezzar defeated Pharaoh Neco by the Euphrates (vv. 1–2). The poem opens with battle orders and breaks off in panic, terror on every side, the swift and strong unable to escape (vv. 3–6). Egypt boasts that she will rise like the Nile and cover the earth (vv. 7–9), but the day is the LORD’s day of vengeance, a sacrifice by the river (v. 10), and no balm can heal her (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: An army dresses for victory on the very field where God is holding a sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations. About Egypt. Concerning the army of Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates at Carchemish and which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new section of the book begins, God’s words to the nations, and it opens with Egypt, defeated at Carchemish in the very year Baruch wrote the scroll. The God who judged his own people is no local god.

Concerning the nations. For forty-five chapters God has dealt chiefly with Judah; now six chapters widen the horizon to the whole world, as Jeremiah’s call had promised: “I appointed you a prophet to the nations” (1:5).

About Egypt. Egypt comes first, and for a reason. Pharaoh Neco (Neco II) had marched north in 609 BC to prop up the failing Assyrians, killing Josiah at Megiddo on the way (2 Kings 23:29). Egypt was the power Judah’s politicians kept looking to for rescue (2:18, 36; 37:5–7), so this oracle is aimed as much at Judah’s hopes as at Pharaoh.

In the fourth year of Jehoiakim. That is 605 BC, the year of the scroll (36:1). At Carchemish on the Euphrates, Nebuchadnezzar, then still Babylon’s crown prince, routed Neco’s army and drove it back toward Egypt. It was the battle that made Babylon master of the world.

Textual note. The ancient Greek translation places these oracles after 25:13, in a different order; our English Bibles follow the Hebrew (see the introduction).
verseByVerse.note: Carchemish stood at a crossing of the upper Euphrates, on today's border between Turkey and Syria.

verseByVerse.quote: "Prepare buckler and shield, and advance for battle! Harness the horses; mount, O horsemen! Take your stations with your helmets, polish your spears, put on your armor! Why have I seen it? They are dismayed and have turned backward. Their warriors are beaten down and have fled in haste; they look not back— terror on every side! declares the LORD. "The swift cannot flee away, nor the warrior escape; in the north by the river Euphrates they have stumbled and fallen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poem musters Egypt’s proud army and then, in mid-parade, shows it running in terror, because the battle belongs to the LORD.

Prepare buckler and shield. The poem opens inside the Egyptian camp, and the voice is a drill sergeant’s: shields up, horses harnessed, helmets on, spears polished. It is all noise and confidence, and the reader should suspect irony.

Why have I seen it? The poem breaks off in the middle of the parade. The armour has only just been polished, and already the soldiers are running, too frightened even to look back.

Terror on every side! Jeremiah had once worn this phrase as a nickname: it was what he cried and what his enemies called him (6:25; 20:3, 10). Now it is pronounced over the army Judah was trusting in.

The swift cannot flee away. Speed and strength, the two things a soldier relies on, both fail, as Amos had said they would on the day of judgment (Amos 2:14–15). “In the north by the river Euphrates” names the place exactly: Carchemish lay hundreds of miles from the Nile, at the far edge of Egypt’s reach. The word “stumbled” will return as the last word of the poem (v. 12).

verseByVerse.quote: "Who is this, rising like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge? Egypt rises like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge. He said, 'I will rise, I will cover the earth, I will destroy cities and their inhabitants.' Advance, O horses, and rage, O chariots! Let the warriors go out: men of Cush and Put who handle the shield, men of Lud, skilled in handling the bow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt boasts that she will rise like the Nile and cover the earth, but she has chosen a picture of something that always goes down again.

Rising like the Nile. The image is Egypt’s own. The Nile flood was the source of everything she had, and the boast borrows its language: “I will rise, I will cover the earth.” But the Nile rises every year and goes down every year. A power that compares itself to the flood has chosen a picture of something that subsides.

Advance, O horses, and rage, O chariots! The second poem follows the pattern of the first: boast and battle orders first (compare vv. 3–4), collapse after. The orders are probably ironic, a summons to the slaughter the next verse describes. The roll call is Egypt’s allied and hired troops: Cush is the upper Nile (Nubia), and Put and Lud peoples further afield.

Uncertain wording. Put is probably Libya, though some think of Punt on the Red Sea coast. Lud is probably the Lydians of Asia Minor, whose mercenaries served the pharaohs of this period, though some suggest an African people of similar name. Either way, an army of many nations.

verseByVerse.quote: That day is the day of the Lord GOD of hosts, a day of vengeance, to avenge himself on his foes. The sword shall devour and be sated and drink its fill of their blood. For the Lord GOD of hosts holds a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The battle at Carchemish is the LORD’s day of judgment, his settling of accounts with Egypt, and he calls it his sacrifice.

That day is the day of the Lord GOD of hosts. “The day of the LORD” is the prophets’ name for the time when God steps in to judge (Amos 5:18; Zephaniah 1:14–16). Here it is a dated battle in 605 BC: the day of the LORD arrives in particular days of history, each a foretaste of the last one. “A day of vengeance” is not spite but the settling of accounts by the rightful judge: “Vengeance is mine, and recompense” (Deuteronomy 32:35).

The Lord GOD of hosts holds a sacrifice. Egypt thought it was a campaign; God calls it a sacrifice, an act of his judgment, with himself as the one holding it. Isaiah had used the same terrible picture of a sword “sated with blood” at a sacrifice in Edom (Isaiah 34:6).

Is God bloodthirsty? The picture is meant to shock, but it is not delight in slaughter: “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11). It is the language of justice. Egypt had killed Josiah at Megiddo and ruled Judah by force (2 Kings 23:29–35), and the judge of all the earth does not let such things pass for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Go up to Gilead, and take balm, O virgin daughter of Egypt! In vain you have used many medicines; there is no healing for you. The nations have heard of your shame, and the earth is full of your cry; for warrior has stumbled against warrior; they have both fallen together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt, famed for her medicine, will find no cure for this wound, because unlike Judah she has no covenant God to heal what he has struck.

Go up to Gilead, and take balm. Egypt is told to fetch balm, a healing resin, from Gilead east of the Jordan, where it came from. Jeremiah had once asked over his own people, “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there?” (8:22). Judah’s wound was called incurable too (30:12), and then God said, “I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal” (30:17).

There is no healing for you. Here the sentence stops at the diagnosis. The difference between Judah and Egypt is not the severity of the wound. It is that one of them had a covenant, and a God who heals the wounds he inflicted. That is still the only hope of any sinner: not a better medicine, but the physician who came “not to call the righteous but sinners” (Mark 2:17).

Warrior has stumbled against warrior. The poem ends where the first one did (v. 6), with stumbling and falling: a rout so crowded that soldiers trip over one another in flight, and the hired troops of verse 9 go down with the Egyptians they were paid to protect. Egypt wanted to “cover the earth” (v. 8); instead “the earth is full of your cry”, and her shame is known to every nation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–19 — Noisy One Who Lets the Hour Go By
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sword Egypt hoped to escape will follow her home, into the very towns where Judah’s refugees had settled. The word is proclaimed in Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes (vv. 13–14). Egypt’s mighty fall because the LORD thrusts them down, and her hired soldiers head for their own lands (vv. 15–16). Pharaoh is renamed “Noisy one who lets the hour go by” (v. 17), while the true King, the LORD of hosts, swears by his life that the invader will come, as unmissable as a mountain (v. 18). Egypt must pack for exile (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The great power everyone trusted is renamed as all noise and no timing.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that the LORD spoke to Jeremiah the prophet about the coming of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to strike the land of Egypt: "Declare in Egypt, and proclaim in Migdol; proclaim in Memphis and Tahpanhes; say, 'Stand ready and be prepared, for the sword shall devour around you.' Why are your mighty ones face down? They do not stand because the LORD thrust them down. He made many stumble, and they fell, and they said one to another, 'Arise, and let us go back to our own people and to the land of our birth, because of the sword of the oppressor.' Call the name of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, 'Noisy one who lets the hour go by.' "As I live, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts, like Tabor among the mountains and like Carmel by the sea, shall one come. Prepare yourselves baggage for exile, O inhabitants of Egypt! For Memphis shall become a waste, a ruin, without inhabitant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sword is proclaimed in the very Egyptian towns where Judah’s refugees had fled from it, and Pharaoh, all noise and no timing, is set against the true King, the LORD of hosts.

Declare in Egypt, and proclaim in Migdol. Read the place names and remember who is living in them: Migdol, Memphis, Tahpanhes, the towns where the Judean refugees had settled (44:1). They fled there to escape the sword, and the sword is proclaimed over the streets they chose.

Because the LORD thrust them down. The cause is stated without decoration. Egypt’s champions do not stand, because God pushed them over.

Let us go back to our own people. Egypt’s army was full of foreign mercenaries, and here they break for home. Hired soldiers fight for pay and leave when the pay is not worth the risk: the lasting weakness of any strength that is merely bought.

Noisy one who lets the hour go by. Pharaoh is given a devastating nickname: all sound and no timing, a man who blusters while the moment passes him. The refugees had staked their lives on Pharaoh (44:30), and God gives him a name that says he will not turn up.

As I live, declares the King. In a chapter full of pharaohs and emperors, only one is called King, and he swears by his own life. Pharaoh is a noise that misses its moment; the King of all the armies of heaven and earth has never missed one. The invader will come “like Tabor among the mountains and like Carmel by the sea”: not a passing raid but something as fixed and unmissable as a mountain. So, “Prepare yourselves baggage for exile”: the country the refugees chose as a refuge is told to pack.

The LORD of hosts. The title runs through this book like a signature, and it is easy to read past it. Hosts means armies: the stars, the angels, every power in heaven and on earth, all under one command. Egypt’s hired soldiers turned and fled (v. 21); the armies of the LORD do not desert. Elisha’s frightened servant was shown them once, when “the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:17). When Isaiah heard the seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3), John tells us that he “saw his glory and spoke of him” (John 12:41), meaning Jesus. On the night he was arrested, the Lord of those armies said he could ask his Father for “more than twelve legions of angels” (Matthew 26:53), and did not ask, so that he could be taken in our place. When the news is loud with the powerful, pray the psalm the title belongs to: “The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress” (Psalm 46:7).

Uncertain wording. Verse 15 is difficult. The ESV notes that the Hebrew reads “He does not stand”, one champion rather than many. Some translations (the RSV, for example) divide the Hebrew letters differently and read, “Why has Apis fled?”, Apis being the sacred bull of Memphis, which would fit the judgment on Egypt’s gods (v. 25). Pharaoh’s nickname in verse 17 is a wordplay whose exact sense is debated, but the sense of empty bluster is clear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — A Beautiful Heifer and a Biting Fly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a series of belittling pictures, mighty Egypt is shown as helpless before the invader, yet God promises her a future beyond judgment. She is a beautiful heifer driven frantic by a biting fly; her hired troops are fattened calves who run (vv. 20–21); she slides away like a serpent while woodcutters, countless as locusts, fell her forest (vv. 22–24). The LORD will punish Amon of Thebes, Pharaoh, Egypt’s gods and all who trust in Pharaoh (vv. 25–26). Then comes one surprising word: “Afterward Egypt shall be inhabited as in the days of old.”
verseByVerse.theology: A superpower is reduced to livestock troubled by an insect, and is still given an afterward.

verseByVerse.quote: "A beautiful heifer is Egypt, but a biting fly from the north has come upon her. Even her hired soldiers in her midst are like fattened calves; yes, they have turned and fled together; they did not stand, for the day of their calamity has come upon them, the time of their punishment. "She makes a sound like a serpent gliding away; for her enemies march in force and come against her with axes like those who fell trees. They shall cut down her forest, declares the LORD, though it is impenetrable, because they are more numerous than locusts; they are without number. The daughter of Egypt shall be put to shame; she shall be delivered into the hand of a people from the north." The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, said: "Behold, I am bringing punishment upon Amon of Thebes, and Pharaoh and Egypt and her gods and her kings, upon Pharaoh and those who trust in him. I will deliver them into the hand of those who seek their life, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his officers. Afterward Egypt shall be inhabited as in the days of old, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sleek, mighty Egypt is shown in farmyard and forest pictures to be helpless before the invader, yet God, who judges her gods, promises her a future afterward.

A beautiful heifer is Egypt. The imagery is deliberately belittling: a sleek, well-fed heifer tormented by a biting fly. Anyone who has watched cattle in summer knows the picture: a huge animal made frantic by an insect it cannot reach.

Like fattened calves. Her professional soldiers are fattened calves: animals prepared for slaughter rather than for work.

Like a serpent gliding away. Three more pictures in quick succession: a snake hissing as it slides off through the grass, woodcutters swinging axes, and invaders more numerous than locusts. Egypt’s forest is called impenetrable, and it comes down anyway.

Amon of Thebes … her gods and her kings. The list reaches past the politics to the religion. Amon was the great god of Thebes, Egypt’s southern capital, honoured as king of the gods, so the sentence strikes first at the head of Egypt’s religion, as God had once judged “all the gods of Egypt” at the exodus (Exodus 12:12). Then it ends on a phrase aimed straight at the Judeans reading it: “those who trust in him.” They had trusted Pharaoh. They are on the list.

Afterward Egypt shall be inhabited. Then one word changes the mood. Egypt will be inhabited again, “as in the days of old”. This is not an oracle of annihilation: the God who judges the nations has a future for them beyond the judgment, a remarkable thing to say of Egypt, the house of slavery. It came in history as Egypt recovered under later rulers, and Isaiah looks further, to a day when the LORD will say, “Blessed be Egypt my people” (Isaiah 19:25). That hope began to be fulfilled when Egyptians heard the gospel at Pentecost (Acts 2:10).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “biting fly” (v. 20) occurs only here. “Gadfly” suits the picture of a heifer, and most modern translations take it so; the King James Version reads “destruction”. Either way, the enemy comes from the north.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–28 — But Fear Not, O Jacob My Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The oracle against Egypt ends with comfort for God’s own people, in words repeated from the Book of Consolation (30:10–11). Jacob, God’s servant, scattered even into Egypt, is told twice not to fear: God will save him from far away and bring his offspring home to quiet and ease (v. 27). The reason is God’s presence, “for I am with you”, and his covenant: he will make a full end of the nations, but never of his people. He will discipline them in just measure, as a father, not destroy them as an enemy (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The oracle against Egypt closes with the exact comfort once spoken to Jacob.

verseByVerse.quote: "But fear not, O Jacob my servant, nor be dismayed, O Israel, for behold, I will save you from far away, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob shall return and have quiet and ease, and none shall make him afraid. Fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares the LORD, for I am with you. I will make a full end of all the nations to which I have driven you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even as Egypt falls, God tells his scattered people not to fear: he is with them, and though he will discipline them, he will never make a full end of them.

Fear not, O Jacob my servant. These verses repeat 30:10–11 almost exactly. Think who first needed to hear it: Judeans living in Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes, just told that the sword would come to those streets. The same word that announces Egypt’s ruin turns to the exiles trapped inside it and calls them God’s servant, and the comfort rests on his presence: “for I am with you.”

But of you I will not make a full end. Here is the distinction the whole section rests on. The nations get a full end; Israel does not. The reason is not that Israel behaved better, which this book has spent forty-five chapters disproving. It is that God has bound himself to them by covenant, his sworn promise, and nothing else.

I will discipline you in just measure. Nor is the comfort soft. The same sentence promises discipline and adds, “I will by no means leave you unpunished.” This is a father’s measured hand, not an enemy’s, and the difference between being disciplined and being ended is the difference between belonging to him and not.

The full end fell on him. For those in Christ the line runs deeper. The full end their sin deserved was not simply cancelled; it was borne by the one who was “cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people” (Isaiah 53:8). What remains for God’s children is a Father’s discipline, never an enemy’s wrath, “For the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6; Romans 8:1). And the true Israel, God’s Son, once went down into Egypt himself, carried there as a refugee in obedience to God, so that the word might be fulfilled, “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Matthew 2:15).

Judgment not the last word. So the first oracle against the nations closes unexpectedly: Egypt is given an afterward, Israel a promise, both from the same God on the same page. Judgment is never the last word in this book, not even for Egypt, and never for the people he keeps.

46.title: Against Egypt
46.overview:
Where we are. The story of Judah’s end is over, and the book turns to the oracles “concerning the nations” (chapters 46 to 51). Egypt comes first: the power Judah’s kings kept leaning on, and the country where the last refugees, with Jeremiah among them, had just settled (chapters 43 and 44).

The message. The LORD of hosts, not Pharaoh, rules the nations. Egypt’s great army, rising like the Nile, will be broken at Carchemish and then pursued into Egypt itself, and nothing she trusts, her soldiers, her medicines or her gods, can heal her. Yet God’s judgment is not the last word: Egypt is promised an afterward, and his own scattered people are told not to fear, because he is with them and will never make a full end of them.

Why it was said. Judah’s politicians had looked to Egypt for rescue for a generation, and the refugees had fled there for safety (see the introduction on Carchemish and the last kings). The chapter tells them that the refuge they chose is under the same sword, and that their only security is the God who keeps covenant.

How the chapter makes its case. A heading opens the whole section and dates the first poem to Carchemish in 605 BC (vv. 1–2). The poem musters Egypt’s army and then breaks off as it runs (vv. 3–6); Egypt boasts of rising like the Nile, but the battle is the LORD’s day of vengeance and there is no healing for her (vv. 7–12). A second word carries Nebuchadnezzar into Egypt, to the very towns where the refugees lived: the mighty fall, the mercenaries flee, Pharaoh is renamed a noise that misses its moment, and the true King swears by his life (vv. 13–19). Egypt the sleek heifer is stung by a fly from the north, her forest felled, her gods punished; yet afterward she will be inhabited again (vv. 20–26). Last, God turns to Jacob his servant: fear not, for I am with you (vv. 27–28).

Where it leads. By the character of God, by covenant and by promise. The King “whose name is the LORD of hosts” (v. 18) is the Lord of glory who, on the night of his arrest, would not call on twelve legions of angels, so that he could be taken in our place (Matthew 26:53). The promise that God will not make a full end of his people rests on covenant alone, and in Christ the full end our sin deserved fell on him. Even Egypt’s afterward points forward, to Egyptians hearing the gospel at Pentecost (Acts 2:10). And the Son of God himself was once carried into Egypt as a refugee, in obedience, and called out of it again (Matthew 2:13–15).

For us. Every refuge but God eventually fails, however impressive it looks. Believers can face the noise of the powerful without fear, because the Lord of hosts is with us, and even his discipline is a Father’s, never an enemy’s.
46.theology:
The God who judged Judah is not a local deity, and the nations that boast of what they will do (I will rise, I will cover the earth) find that he calls their battle his own sacrifice, his act of judgment (vv. 8, 10). Yet his judgment of the nations is not annihilation; Egypt is given an afterward (v. 26).

The chapter also marks the difference between Judah and Egypt. Both are wounded, but only one has a covenant and a God who heals what he has struck (v. 11; 30:17). Israel is spared a full end by that covenant, not by better behaviour, and its discipline is a father's, measured and purposeful (vv. 27-28).
46.examples:
Any power can look like the Nile in flood, rising to cover the earth. Jeremiah shows the same army polishing its spears and then fleeing, and the Pharaoh everyone was relying on renamed "Noisy one who lets the hour go by." It is a sobering picture for anyone tempted to trust a government, an employer or a market more than God.

It is also a comfort for those who live inside a world under judgment. The Judeans in Migdol and Memphis heard the sword proclaimed over their own streets, and in the same breath heard God call them his servant and say, I am with you.

keyVerse.quote: Fear not, O Jacob my servant, declares the LORD, for I am with you. I will make a full end of all the nations to which I have driven you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter about the fall of the power everyone trusted, this verse tells God’s people where their safety lies: not in Egypt but in his presence and his covenant. It holds judgment and mercy together, a full end for the nations, measured discipline for his own, and it is fulfilled for believers in Christ, who bore the full end in their place.

46.reflection:
Egypt looked impressive, “rising like the Nile” (vv. 7–8), and Judah kept trusting her. What are the “Egypts” people turn to for security today? Why do they seem so convincing, and how does this chapter expose them?

Pharaoh is called “Noisy one who lets the hour go by” (v. 17), while the LORD swears, “As I live, declares the King” (v. 18). How does knowing that the LORD of hosts rules, the one who would not call twelve legions of angels to save himself (Matthew 26:53), help you face the loud powers of our day?

God promises Egypt an “afterward” (v. 26). What does this tell us about God’s purposes for the nations, and how should it shape the way we pray for nations hostile to the gospel?

“I will discipline you in just measure” (v. 28). How does it help to know the difference between a Father’s discipline and an enemy’s destruction when you are going through hard times?

47.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck down Gaza.<sup>2</sup>"Thus says the LORD: Behold, waters are rising out of the north, and shall become an overflowing torrent; they shall overflow the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it. Men shall cry out, and every inhabitant of the land shall wail.<sup>3</sup>At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his stallions, at the rushing of his chariots, at the rumbling of their wheels, the fathers look not back to their children, so feeble are their hands,<sup>4</sup>because of the day that is coming to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper that remains. For the LORD is destroying the Philistines, the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor.<sup>5</sup>Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon has perished. O remnant of their valley, how long will you gash yourselves?<sup>6</sup>Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet? Put yourself into your scabbard; rest and be still!<sup>7</sup>How can it be quiet when the LORD has given it a charge? Against Ashkelon and against the seashore he has appointed it."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Waters Rising Out of the North
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines, Israel’s ancient enemies, are about to be overwhelmed by an invader from the north, and the LORD himself is behind it. The word is dated by an Egyptian strike on Gaza (v. 1). The invader comes like rising waters that become an overflowing torrent, covering city and countryside, and the people wail (v. 2). The noise of hoofs and wheels is so terrible that fathers run without looking back for their children (v. 3). No help will come from Tyre and Sidon, for the LORD is destroying the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The flood comes out of the north, and fathers are too weak to turn round for their own children.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck down Gaza. "Thus says the LORD: Behold, waters are rising out of the north, and shall become an overflowing torrent; they shall overflow the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it. Men shall cry out, and every inhabitant of the land shall wail. At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his stallions, at the rushing of his chariots, at the rumbling of their wheels, the fathers look not back to their children, so feeble are their hands, because of the day that is coming to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper that remains. For the LORD is destroying the Philistines, the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Philistines, Israel’s old tormentors, will be swept away by an invader from the north like a flood, and the terror will be so great that fathers abandon their children, because the LORD is destroying them.

Concerning the Philistines. Seven verses for a people who had troubled Israel since the judges. Samson, Goliath, the ark carried into Ashdod, Saul’s body hung on the wall of Beth-shan: the Philistines are woven through the earlier history, and here they are dealt with in a single short poem. This oracle names no crime, but other prophets do: Amos charged Gaza with carrying whole communities into exile to be sold (Amos 1:6), and Ezekiel spoke of their “never-ending enmity” (Ezekiel 25:15).

Before Pharaoh struck down Gaza. The word is dated by an Egyptian attack on Gaza, which most likely belongs to the years around Carchemish (perhaps 609 or about 601 BC; the date is debated). The small nations on the coast road are in the great powers’ way.

Waters are rising out of the north. The direction is the one this book has used from the beginning. The boiling pot tilted from the north in chapter 1 (1:13–14), and the enemy from the north hung over Judah for twenty-five chapters. The same water that drowned Jerusalem now comes down the coast. A flood does not fight a city; it covers it, and there is nothing to fight back against.

So feeble are their hands. One image does more than any casualty figure: men running who do not turn round for their own sons and daughters, and the reason given is not cowardice but collapse. Scripture is not sneering. It is telling the truth about what overwhelming force does to ordinary people.

Every helper that remains. Their allies to the north, Tyre and Sidon, cannot help, because the same invader will reach them too.

The remnant of the coastland of Caphtor. Caphtor was the Philistines’ old homeland, named in the table of nations (Genesis 10:14; compare Amos 9:7), most likely Crete or the islands and coasts nearby. They were sea people who had arrived from elsewhere centuries before. God knows where every nation came from, and the word “remnant” quietly says that they are already the leftovers of something larger.
verseByVerse.note: Caphtor is probably Crete, the Philistines’ ancestral home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–7 — Sword of the LORD, How Long?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet grieves as the Philistine cities fall, and pleads with God’s sword to rest, but it cannot, because the LORD has given it a charge. Gaza shaves its head and Ashkelon is silenced; the survivors gash themselves in mourning (v. 5). Jeremiah cries, “Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet?” (v. 6). The answer is that the sword is under orders: the LORD has appointed it against Ashkelon and the seashore, and it will not rest until his purpose is done (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Someone begs the sword to stop, and is told who is holding it.

verseByVerse.quote: Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon has perished. O remnant of their valley, how long will you gash yourselves? Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet? Put yourself into your scabbard; rest and be still! How can it be quiet when the LORD has given it a charge? Against Ashkelon and against the seashore he has appointed it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the Philistine cities fall, the prophet grieves and begs God’s sword to rest, but it cannot, because the LORD has given it a charge: history is in his hands, not chance.

Baldness has come upon Gaza. Two of the five Philistine cities are named, and their mourning takes the forms these people used: heads shaved, bodies cut (see mourning customs). It is the practice the pilgrims from Shechem and Shiloh had followed before Ishmael met them on the road (41:5), and one Israel was expressly forbidden: “You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead” (Deuteronomy 14:1). So “how long will you gash yourselves?” is not mockery but a comment on futility: cutting yourself changes nothing. Babylon’s own chronicle records that Nebuchadnezzar took Ashkelon in 604 BC, plundered it and turned it into a heap of ruins.

Ah, sword of the LORD! The poet turns from the victims and speaks to the weapon, and the tone is not triumph but the cry of a man who has watched too much of this. Jeremiah had wept over his own people’s ruin (9:1), and he does not gloat over the ruin of Israel’s old enemies either. That rebukes anyone who speaks of God’s judgment coldly or with satisfaction. Anyone who can contemplate it without grief has not understood it.

How can it be quiet? The answer is not comfort: the sword cannot rest because it is under orders. God has “given it a charge” and “appointed it”, with a named target. So one of the shortest oracles in this section makes the point the whole section exists to make. History is not a series of accidents in which the strong happen to eat the weak. There is a sword, it is the LORD’s, and it moves when he gives it a charge and rests when he says so.

The sword is at rest. Standing where we do, there is more to say. A day came when the sword of the LORD was given a charge and did not fall on Ashkelon or on Judah. Zechariah had heard God say, “Awake, O sword, against my shepherd”, and Jesus took that verse to himself on the night he was betrayed (Zechariah 13:7; Matthew 26:31). The sword fell on a man who had asked in a garden that his cup might pass from him, and who then put himself in its way, so that for everyone who is his, the question “How long till you are quiet?” finally has its answer: the sword is at rest. And the peace reached even Philistia. An angel sent Philip down the road to Gaza, and afterwards he “found himself at Azotus”, the old Philistine city of Ashdod, and preached the gospel there (Acts 8:26, 40).

Uncertain wording. “O remnant of their valley” (v. 5) is a difficult phrase. The Hebrew “their valley” may mean the coastal plain; some translations (the RSV, for example), following the ancient Greek, read “O remnant of the Anakim”, the giant clan of whom some survived in Gaza and Ashdod (Joshua 11:22). The sense, the pitiful survivors of Philistia, is clear on any reading.

Textual note. The ESV notes that in verse 7 the Hebrew reads “you” where the English has “it”: the poet is still addressing the sword directly.

47.title: Against the Philistines
47.overview:
Where we are. After Egypt (chapter 46), the oracles against the nations move up the coast to the Philistines, Israel’s old enemies since the days of the judges. It is one of the shortest oracles in the book: seven verses for a people whose story runs through Samson, Goliath and Saul.

The message. The LORD rules the history of even the small nations on the coast road. The invader that sweeps over Philistia like a flood from the north is his sword, sent with his charge, and it will not rest until it has done what he appointed. Yet the prophet who announces it does not gloat: he grieves, even over Israel’s old enemies.

Why it was said. The Philistine cities lay on the road between Egypt and Babylon, and in Jeremiah’s day the great powers marched up and down it (see the introduction on Carchemish). Judah needed to know that these upheavals were not accidents in which the strong happen to eat the weak, but the work of the God who judges every nation.

How the chapter makes its case. The heading dates the word before an Egyptian attack on Gaza (v. 1). Waters rise out of the north and become a torrent; at the thunder of hoofs and chariot wheels fathers flee without turning back for their children, and every ally is cut off, because the LORD is destroying the Philistines (vv. 2–4). Gaza and Ashkelon mourn in the old pagan way (v. 5). Then the prophet cries to the sword of the LORD to go back into its scabbard, and is answered that it cannot, for the LORD has given it a charge (vv. 6–7).

Where it leads. By the character of God and by pattern. The sword of the LORD is not blind force; it moves at his command and rests when he says. And there came a day when God said, “Awake, O sword, against my shepherd” (Zechariah 13:7), and Jesus took those words to himself on the night he was betrayed (Matthew 26:31). The sword fell on him, so that for all who are his it is at rest. Then the gospel went down the road to Gaza and through Ashdod itself (Acts 8:26, 40): the old enemies were offered peace.

For us. No nation, however small or far from the headlines, is outside God’s rule. We should speak of his judgment as Jeremiah did, with grief and never with satisfaction, and point people to the one in whom the sword is sheathed.
47.theology:
The flood from the north that covered Judah now covers the coastal plain: God's instruments are not reserved for one nation, and he knows where every nation came from (vv. 2, 4; 1:13-15; Gen 10:14). History is not chaos; it runs under God’s orders. The sword moves when he gives it a charge and rests when he says so (v. 7; Isa 34:5-6).

Yet the prophet does not gloat. He tells the truth about what terror does to ordinary people and pities even Israel's old tormentors (vv. 3, 6). Anyone who can think about God's judgment without grief has not understood it.
47.examples:
When news comes of a war far away, it is easy to read it either as random chaos or as the deserved fall of people we never liked. Jeremiah refuses both. The sword is the LORD's and is under orders, and the man who announces it still cries out, "How long?"

The father fleeing without turning back for his children is not mocked. Scripture lets us see what overwhelming force does to people, so that we feel it before we analyse it.

keyVerse.quote: How can it be quiet when the LORD has given it a charge? Against Ashkelon and against the seashore he has appointed it.
keyVerse.note: This verse gives the meaning of the whole oracle, and of the oracles against the nations: the invader is the LORD’s sword, moving under his orders, not a blind force of history. The same truth comforts and humbles us, and it prepares for the day the sword was awakened against God’s own shepherd, so that it might rest for all who are his.

47.reflection:
The oracle shows fathers fleeing without looking back for their children (v. 3). Why do you think Scripture describes the human cost of judgment so vividly? How should that shape the way we think and speak about war and disaster?

Jeremiah cries, “Ah, sword of the LORD! How long till you are quiet?” (v. 6), even over Israel’s old enemies. How can we hold together a firm belief in God’s justice and real grief over those who face it?

The sword moves only when the LORD “has given it a charge” (v. 7). How does believing that God rules history, even among small nations, help you when the news seems chaotic?

The sword that might have fallen on us fell on Christ (Zechariah 13:7; Matthew 26:31), and the gospel later reached Gaza and Ashdod (Acts 8:26, 40). Who are the “old enemies” you find it hardest to imagine coming to Christ, and how might you pray for them?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moab’s fall is total, and its cause is a false trust. Town after town is named as it falls, Nebo, Kiriathaim, Heshbon, Horonaim, until “the renown of Moab is no more” and the cry of its children is heard on the roads of flight (vv. 1–5). The people are told to run, because they trusted in their works and their treasures, and their god Chemosh will be carried into exile with his own priests (vv. 6–7). No city escapes; Moab would need wings to get away (vv. 8–9). The section ends with a hard word to the army God is sending: his work is not to be done with slackness (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Moab's national god is carried off into exile alongside the clergy who served him.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Moab. Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Woe to Nebo, for it is laid waste! Kiriathaim is put to shame, it is taken; the fortress is put to shame and broken down; the renown of Moab is no more. In Heshbon they planned disaster against her: 'Come, let us cut her off from being a nation!' You also, O Madmen, shall be brought to silence; the sword shall pursue you. "A voice! A cry from Horonaim, 'Desolation and great destruction!' Moab is destroyed; her little ones have made a cry. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; for at the descent of Horonaim they have heard the distressed cry of destruction. Flee! Save yourselves! You will be like a juniper in the desert! For, because you trusted in your works and your treasures, you also shall be taken; and Chemosh shall go into exile with his priests and his officials. The destroyer shall come upon every city, and no city shall escape; the valley shall perish, and the plain shall be destroyed, as the LORD has spoken. "Give wings to Moab, for she would fly away; her cities shall become a desolation, with no inhabitant in them. "Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD with slackness, and cursed is he who keeps back his sword from bloodshed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab’s towns fall one after another and its god goes into exile, because Moab trusted in what it had made and saved rather than in the LORD.

Concerning Moab. Moab was the nation across the Dead Sea, close kin and old enemy. Genesis records the ugly beginning, when Lot’s daughter “bore a son and called his name Moab” (Genesis 19:37); from then on they are neighbours, sometimes allies, mostly trouble. Isaiah had preached against Moab a century earlier (Isaiah 15–16), and Jeremiah takes up many of his lines.

Woe to Nebo, for it is laid waste! The poem moves through real towns with markets and families, for judgment in Scripture is rarely abstract. It even plays on their names: in Hebrew, Heshbon sounds like “planned” and Madmen like “brought to silence”.

Her little ones have made a cry. The sound that carries is a child’s: the detail a prophet includes when he is not enjoying his subject.

At the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping. Isaiah had written the same scene, fugitives climbing the same road (Isaiah 15:5). Two prophets, the same hill, the same people stumbling up it.

You trusted in your works and your treasures. This is the indictment: what you have made and what you have saved. It is the most respectable idolatry there is, and it needs no shrine.

Chemosh shall go into exile. Then comes the picture that exposes it: “Chemosh shall go into exile with his priests and his officials.” The national god of Moab is deported. A god who has to be carried into captivity by the men who served him is not a god; he is luggage. Moab’s own monument, the Moabite Stone set up by King Mesha at Dibon about 840 BC, credits Chemosh with Moab’s victories over Israel and boasts of taking Nebo and dragging the vessels of the LORD before Chemosh. Jeremiah names the same god and the same towns.

Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD with slackness. This hard word is spoken to the Babylonian army God had sent to judge Moab: to do his work half-heartedly would be to defy him. Why would God command bloodshed? Because here he acts as judge of a nation whose guilt was full, and the army only carries out his sentence. It is no warrant for violence today, for the church does God’s work with other weapons (2 Corinthians 10:4); but work God assigns, whatever it is, is still not to be done with slackness. And the curse has already fallen elsewhere: Christ, who did his Father’s work perfectly, became “a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), and his Spirit makes us diligent in that work now.

Uncertain wording. In verse 6, “juniper” is spelled like the town Aroer (v. 19); it probably means a lonely desert shrub, though some read “like Aroer”. In verse 9, the word translated “wings” is rare and disputed (elsewhere it means a blossom or a gleaming plate; some suggest “salt”, sown on ruined land). “Wings” fits the line best: Moab would need to fly to escape.

Textual note. The ESV notes that the Hebrew of verse 5 reads ‘weeping goes up with weeping’, and that the ancient Greek translation has ‘heard the cry’, as in Isaiah 15:5. The meaning is not affected.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moab’s real danger was comfort. Like wine never poured off its sediment, Moab has been at ease from his youth, never carried into exile, and so never changed (v. 11). God will send pourers to empty the jars and smash them, and Moab will be as ashamed of Chemosh as Israel was of Bethel (vv. 12–13). The boast of mighty warriors is answered by slaughter, and the sentence is signed by “the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts” (vv. 14–16). The neighbours are told to lament the broken scepter, and Dibon and Aroer to come down from their glory and ask the refugees what has happened (vv. 17–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Wine left undisturbed keeps its taste; a nation never poured out keeps its sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moab has been at ease from his youth and has settled on his dregs; he has not been emptied from vessel to vessel, nor has he gone into exile; so his taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed. "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I shall send to him pourers who will pour him, and empty his vessels and break his jars in pieces. Then Moab shall be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, their confidence. "How do you say, 'We are heroes and mighty men of war'? The destroyer of Moab and his cities has come up, and the choicest of his young men have gone down to slaughter, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. The calamity of Moab is near at hand, and his affliction hastens swiftly. Grieve for him, all you who are around him, and all who know his name; say, 'How the mighty scepter is broken, the glorious staff.' "Come down from your glory, and sit on the parched ground, O inhabitant of Dibon! For the destroyer of Moab has come up against you; he has destroyed your strongholds. Stand by the way and watch, O inhabitant of Aroer! Ask him who flees and her who escapes; say, 'What has happened?' Moab is put to shame, for it is broken; wail and cry! Tell it beside the Arnon, that Moab is laid waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab’s real danger was a comfortable life that had never been shaken, and God will now shake it. Undisturbed ease had kept Moab exactly as it was, and that is not the same thing as God’s favour.

Settled on his dregs. The picture comes out of a winery. New wine was left to stand so the sediment, the dregs, would settle, and then it was poured off into another jar, and another, leaving the sediment behind. Wine that was never poured off kept its strength but also kept everything that should have been removed.

Moab has been at ease from his youth. That is Moab: never carried into exile, never poured out, and therefore never changed. “His taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed.” Judah had been poured from vessel to vessel until she hardly knew herself; Moab had been left alone on the shelf, and the text treats that as the worse condition. Comfort is not the same as God’s favour, and it can be the very reason a life never becomes anything different.

I shall send to him pourers. So God sends pourers. The pouring out that Moab never had is coming as an invasion, and this time the jars are broken as well as emptied.

Bethel, their confidence. Verse 13 is even-handed. The golden calf Jeroboam set up at Bethel is named in the same breath as Chemosh, and both are called “their confidence”. God does not flatter his own people by contrast.

We are heroes and mighty men of war. Moab’s boast is answered by events, and the oracle is signed “declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts.” In a section full of nations and kings, one King signs the oracles, and every throne stands or falls at his word.

How the mighty scepter is broken. The neighbours are told to mourn, and the words given them are not gloating: “How the mighty scepter is broken, the glorious staff.” Moab’s greatness is acknowledged in the act of lamenting its end. Dibon, the town where Mesha’s boastful monument stood, is told to “come down from your glory, and sit on the parched ground”.

Poured out for us. Scripture never tells us to go looking for suffering. It does tell us that God pours his people from jar to jar because he loves them too much to leave them on their dregs, and that his own Son “poured out his soul to death” for them (Isaiah 53:12), so that every pouring of theirs ends in joy.

The world that abolished discomfort. Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World (1932) imagines a society that has finally solved unhappiness. Everyone is comfortable, entertained and pleasantly drugged, and nobody is ever poured from vessel to vessel. Near the end a young man raised outside that world refuses it: “I don’t want comfort. I want God, I want poetry, I want real danger, I want freedom, I want goodness.” Huxley saw that a life arranged wholly around ease would cost almost everything that makes a person grow. Our age often wishes for his world: no friction, no waiting, no pain we cannot numb. Moab is the warning: left undisturbed, he stayed exactly himself.

Textual note. In verse 12 the ESV notes that the Hebrew reads ‘their’ where the English has “his” jars. The meaning is not affected.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–33 — He Magnified Himself Against the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The root of Moab’s guilt is named: he magnified himself against the LORD and made a joke of Israel. Judgment sweeps through a long roll-call of towns until Moab’s horn is cut off (vv. 21–25). Moab must drink the cup of wrath until he wallows in his vomit, because he wagged his head at Israel whenever she fell (vv. 26–27). He is told to hide like a dove in the cliffs, and his pride is piled up in five words, though his boasts are false (vv. 28–30). Then the voice pronouncing the sentence breaks into weeping, “Therefore I wail for Moab”, over vineyards stripped and winepresses where no one shouts for joy (vv. 31–33).
verseByVerse.theology: God pronounces the sentence and then weeps over the country he is sentencing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Judgment has come upon the tableland, upon Holon, and Jahzah, and Mephaath, and Dibon, and Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim, and Kiriathaim, and Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon, and Kerioth, and Bozrah, and all the cities of the land of Moab, far and near. The horn of Moab is cut off, and his arm is broken, declares the LORD. "Make him drunk, because he magnified himself against the LORD, so that Moab shall wallow in his vomit, and he too shall be held in derision. Was not Israel a derision to you? Was he found among thieves, that whenever you spoke of him you wagged your head? "Leave the cities, and dwell in the rock, O inhabitants of Moab! Be like the dove that nests in the sides of the mouth of a gorge. We have heard of the pride of Moab— he is very proud— of his loftiness, his pride, and his arrogance, and the haughtiness of his heart. I know his insolence, declares the LORD; his boasts are false, his deeds are false. Therefore I wail for Moab; I cry out for all Moab; for the men of Kir-hareseth I mourn. More than for Jazer I weep for you, O vine of Sibmah! Your branches passed over the sea, reached to the Sea of Jazer; on your summer fruits and your grapes the destroyer has fallen. Gladness and joy have been taken away from the fruitful land of Moab; I have made the wine cease from the winepresses; no one treads them with shouts of joy; the shouting is not the shout of joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab is judged above all because he magnified himself against the LORD and laughed at Israel’s fall, yet the God who pronounces the sentence weeps over it.

Judgment has come upon the tableland. Eleven towns in four verses, then “all the cities of the land of Moab, far and near.” The roll-call is slow on purpose: somebody knew these places.

He magnified himself against the LORD. The charge is stated at last, and it is not the towns or the treasure but this. The punishment fits the image of the chapter: the nation never poured out is now made to drink the cup of God’s wrath, which Moab was named among the nations to drink (25:15, 21), and it ends up wallowing in its own vomit. There is nothing dignified in the picture, which is the point about pride.

Was not Israel a derision to you? The specific offence is startling: Moab is judged for mockery. Whenever Israel was humbled, Moab laughed and “wagged your head”. Zephaniah records the same charge, “I have heard the taunts of Moab… how they have taunted my people”, and the sentence comes “in return for their pride” (Zephaniah 2:8, 10). Nor was it only talk: under Jehoiakim, Moabite raiding bands joined the attacks on Judah (2 Kings 24:2).

Be like the dove. The advice is to go and live like a dove in a cliff face, which is what people did when nothing was left. The gentleness of the image sits oddly beside the sentence, as though the one pronouncing it is watching a people he does not hate.

We have heard of the pride of Moab. Five words for the same thing are piled up: pride, loftiness, pride, arrogance, haughtiness. Underneath the noise is God’s own assessment: “his boasts are false, his deeds are false.” The swagger had nothing behind it, and God had always known.

Therefore I wail for Moab. Then, without warning, the voice breaks. After such a charge we expect “therefore” to introduce a punishment; it introduces tears. The God who has just catalogued Moab’s arrogance mourns for him by name, and for the men of one particular town.

Gladness and joy have been taken away. Moab was famous for its vineyards, and the picture is of harvest silenced. Treading grapes in the winepress was noisy work, done with singing. Now there is shouting, but it is the shout of battle, not of harvest joy.

I have made the wine cease. It is the LORD who says this. He is not grieving over something that happened to him; he has brought this judgment himself, and he grieves over it. Both are true at once, which is as close as the Old Testament comes to explaining the tears of God. The fuller explanation comes in person, when Jesus, who would bear judgment himself, wept over Jerusalem while he foretold its fall (Luke 19:41–44).

How we speak of another’s fall. God had sent the disaster on Judah himself, and he still holds the onlookers accountable for enjoying it. How we speak of another’s downfall is noticed. The answer is not a stricter tongue alone but a new heart: those who have been shown mercy at their own lowest point learn to weep with others at theirs.

Uncertain wording. No “Sea of Jazer” is known (v. 32). Isaiah’s form of the line has the vine reaching to Jazer and passing over the sea (Isaiah 16:8), probably the Dead Sea; the repeated word here may be a slip in copying, or a poetic name for a pool near Jazer. The picture is clear either way: Moab’s vines once spread far and wide.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–47 — My Heart Moans Like a Flute
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God grieves over the judgment he brings, no one escapes it, and yet his last word is mercy. The cry runs from town to town, the high places fall silent, and God’s heart moans like a funeral flute while Moab shaves its head and is broken like an unwanted jar (vv. 34–39). An eagle swoops, and terror, pit and snare leave no way out (vv. 40–44). Israel’s ancient victory song over Moab is sung once more (vv. 45–46). Then, after all of it: “Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days” (v. 47).
verseByVerse.theology: After forty-six verses of ruin comes one word: Yet.

verseByVerse.quote: "From the outcry at Heshbon even to Elealeh, as far as Jahaz they utter their voice, from Zoar to Horonaim and Eglath-shelishiyah. For the waters of Nimrim also have become desolate. And I will bring to an end in Moab, declares the LORD, him who offers sacrifice in the high place and makes offerings to his god. Therefore my heart moans for Moab like a flute, and my heart moans like a flute for the men of Kir-hareseth. Therefore the riches they gained have perished. "For every head is shaved and every beard cut off. On all the hands are gashes, and around the waist is sackcloth. On all the housetops of Moab and in the squares there is nothing but lamentation, for I have broken Moab like a vessel for which no one cares, declares the LORD. How it is broken! How they wail! How Moab has turned his back in shame! So Moab has become a derision and a horror to all that are around him." For thus says the LORD: "Behold, one shall fly swiftly like an eagle and spread his wings against Moab; the cities shall be taken and the strongholds seized. The heart of the warriors of Moab shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains; Moab shall be destroyed and be no longer a people, because he magnified himself against the LORD. Terror, pit, and snare are before you, O inhabitant of Moab! declares the LORD. He who flees from the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare. For I will bring these things upon Moab, the year of their punishment, declares the LORD. "In the shadow of Heshbon fugitives stop without strength, for fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the house of Sihon; it has destroyed the forehead of Moab, the crown of the sons of tumult. Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh are undone, for your sons have been taken captive, and your daughters into captivity. Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days, declares the LORD." Thus far is the judgment on Moab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s grief over Moab deepens, there is no escaping his judgment by running, and yet his last word to Moab is a promise of restoration.

Him who offers sacrifice in the high place. As the cry runs across the map, worship at the hilltop shrines stops, because there is nobody left to climb them.

My heart moans for Moab like a flute. Twice more comes the lament, now with an instrument. The flute was played at funerals, so God says his heart makes the sound of a funeral instrument over a pagan nation. Isaiah had written the same line with a different instrument, “my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth” (Isaiah 16:11), and named the same town. Two prophets, a century apart, were given the same grief.

Every head is shaved. These are the mourning customs we have met twice already in this book: shaved heads, cut beards, gashed hands, sackcloth (41:5; 47:5). And the vessel picture returns one last time, now not merely poured out but broken “like a vessel for which no one cares”.

Terror, pit, and snare. Three hazards in a row (vv. 43–44), arranged so that escaping one lands you in the next: a hunt from which nobody escapes by running faster.

Fire came out from Heshbon. Verses 45–46 are a quotation. When Israel first came through this territory, the old Amorite victory song ran: “For fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the city of Sihon… Woe to you, O Moab! You are undone, O people of Chemosh!” (Numbers 21:28–29). Jeremiah sings Moab’s ancient defeat song back over its final defeat; God has not forgotten the words.

The forehead of Moab. The same lines also echo Balaam’s oracle from those days, which promised that “a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; it shall crush the forehead of Moab” (Numbers 24:17). The King who was to rise from Israel would master Moab; verse 47 shows that he would also bring Moab home.

Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days. This is the phrase used of Israel herself (29:14; 30:3), and it is spoken over the people of Chemosh, the nation that wagged its head at Jerusalem’s funeral, the drunkard in his own vomit.

Ruth the Moabite. It had already begun, quietly. In the days of the judges a Moabite widow followed her mother-in-law home to Bethlehem and said that Israel’s God would be her God; the neighbourhood women named her son Obed, and “He was the father of Jesse, the father of David” (Ruth 4:17). The line that runs to the Messiah has Moab in it, and Matthew names Ruth in Jesus’ genealogy (Matthew 1:5).

Thus far is the judgment on Moab. The judgment reaches this far and no further, and the God who wailed over a pagan country while sentencing it had a latter-day mercy in mind for it all along.

How was the promise kept? Moab was subdued by Babylon, probably about 582 BC, and afterwards disappears as a nation, so the promise looks beyond its ruin. Isaiah’s oracle on Moab had already pointed to a throne established in steadfast love in the tent of David (Isaiah 16:5), and the apostles saw David’s fallen tent rebuilt as people from the nations were gathered to David’s greater Son (Acts 15:16–17).

Uncertain wording. “The sons of tumult” (v. 45) is a rare phrase; at the same point Balaam’s oracle has “the sons of Sheth” (Numbers 24:17), and Jeremiah may be playing on it. Either way it means Moab’s proud warriors.

Textual note. The ancient Greek translation of Jeremiah, shorter throughout, lacks verses 45–47. The ESV follows the Hebrew, which has them, and the hope they hold is taught in many other places.

48.title: Against Moab
48.overview:
Where we are. The oracles against the nations began with Egypt and Philistia (chapters 46 and 47). Now comes Moab, Israel’s close kin and old enemy across the Dead Sea, and its oracle is the longest in the series apart from Babylon’s.

The message. God judges pride wherever he finds it, including the quiet pride of a comfortable nation that trusts what it has made and laughs when a neighbour falls. Yet the God who sentences Moab weeps over it as he does so, and his last word is not ruin but “Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days” (v. 47).

Why it was said. Jeremiah was appointed “a prophet to the nations” (1:5), and these oracles were spoken mostly in Judah’s hearing (see the introduction). They told God’s people that the LORD rules every nation, not Israel only; that the neighbours who mocked them would answer to him, so Judah need neither take revenge nor lean on alliances; and that pride is judged wherever it is found, Judah’s included.

How the chapter makes its case. Town after town falls, and Chemosh goes into exile with his priests, because Moab trusted in its works and treasures (vv. 1–10). Its deeper trouble is undisturbed comfort: Moab has “settled on his dregs”, never poured from vessel to vessel, so God will send pourers (vv. 11–20). The root charge is that “he magnified himself against the LORD” and mocked Israel, and then, unexpectedly, the voice pronouncing sentence breaks into lament (vv. 21–33). The grief deepens, God’s heart moaning “like a flute”, and no one escapes by running; then a single word turns everything: “Yet” (vv. 34–47).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the character of God that Christ reveals, and by promise. The God who wails over a nation while judging it is seen fully in Jesus, who wept over Jerusalem as he foretold its fall (Luke 19:41–44). And the promise to Moab had already begun quietly in Ruth the Moabite, great-grandmother of David, whom Matthew names in Jesus’ family line (Matthew 1:5). It is fulfilled as people from every nation are gathered to David’s greater Son (Acts 15:16–17).

For us. Comfort is not the same as God’s favour, and a life never disturbed may be a life never changed. Moab’s respectable sins are ours too: trusting what we have built, and enjoying another’s fall. Yet the Judge of all the earth grieves even as he judges, and in Christ his last word to the nations is mercy.
48.theology:
Moab's sins are respectable ones: trust in its own works and treasures, the complacency of a life never disturbed, and the pleasure of watching a neighbour fall (vv. 7, 11, 27). God names all three, and does not flatter Israel by contrast; Israel’s false worship at Bethel is named beside Moab’s god Chemosh (v. 13).

The chapter's deepest note is the grief of the judge. The same God who pronounces the sentence wails over Moab and grieves over what he himself has done (vv. 31-36). And his last word over this pagan enemy is restoration, a mercy already foreshadowed in Ruth the Moabitess, who stands in the line of David and of Christ (v. 47; Ruth 4:17).
48.examples:
It is possible to live a life like wine left on the shelf: never shaken, never poured out, keeping both its strength and its sediment. Moab's comfort was not a sign of God's favour but the reason it never changed. Christians who have been "poured from vessel to vessel" by loss or upheaval can take heart that God's disturbing is often his kindness.

The chapter also warns against the pleasure of seeing someone else humbled. Moab wagged its head at Judah's funeral, and God remembered it, though he had sent Judah's disaster himself.

keyVerse.quote: Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days, declares the LORD.
keyVerse.note: After forty-six verses of ruin, one word turns the chapter: “Yet”. The judgment is real and deserved, but it is not God’s last word to Moab, and the promise had begun to be kept when a Moabite widow came to Bethlehem and became an ancestor of Christ. It holds out hope to every nation, and every person, that has magnified itself against the LORD.

48.reflection:
Moab “has been at ease from his youth” and so never changed (v. 11). How has God used unsettling times to change you? Where might comfort be keeping you exactly as you are?

Moab is judged for laughing whenever Israel fell (v. 27). Why does God take seriously the way we speak about other people’s downfall, even a deserved one? How does the gospel change the way we talk about those who fail?

God says “I wail for Moab” and “my heart moans for Moab like a flute” (vv. 31, 36) while he is judging Moab. What does this show you about his justice and his compassion, and where do we see both together in Jesus?

The chapter ends with “Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab” (v. 47), and Ruth the Moabite stands in Jesus’ family line. Who are you tempted to think is beyond God’s mercy?
