verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ammon will lose what it stole, because the land was Israel’s by God’s gift. When the northern tribes were carried off, Ammon moved into Gad’s towns as though Israel had no heirs (v. 1). So the battle cry will sound against Rabbah, the capital, and Israel will dispossess those who dispossessed him (v. 2). Ammon’s towns are told to wail, for their god Milcom will go into exile with his priests, as Chemosh did (v. 3), and the nation that trusted in its treasures and asked who could come against it will be driven out (vv. 4–5). Then, after five verses of ruin: “But afterward I will restore the fortunes of the Ammonites” (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Like Moab’s god Chemosh, Ammon’s god Milcom is carried off with his priests, and like Moab, Ammon is promised restoration after judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning the Ammonites. Thus says the LORD: "Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? Why then has Milcom dispossessed Gad, and his people settled in its cities? Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will cause the battle cry to be heard against Rabbah of the Ammonites; it shall become a desolate mound, and its villages shall be burned with fire; then Israel shall dispossess those who dispossessed him, says the LORD. "Wail, O Heshbon, for Ai is laid waste! Cry out, O daughters of Rabbah! Put on sackcloth, lament, and run to and fro among the hedges! For Milcom shall go into exile, with his priests and his officials. Why do you boast of your valleys, O faithless daughter, who trusted in her treasures, saying, 'Who will come against me?' Behold, I will bring terror upon you, declares the Lord GOD of hosts, from all who are around you, and you shall be driven out, every man straight before him, with none to gather the fugitives. "But afterward I will restore the fortunes of the Ammonites, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ammon had taken land God gave to Israel, so God will take Ammon’s land and its god; yet after the judgment he will restore Ammon.

Concerning the Ammonites. Ammon was Moab’s kinsman, descended from Lot’s other son, Ben-ammi (Genesis 19:38), and its territory lay east of the Jordan beside Gad’s. In Jeremiah’s own day the Ammonite king Baalis sent Ishmael to murder Gedaliah, and Ammon sheltered the assassin afterwards (40:14; 41:15).

Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? The charge is occupation. When Assyria deported the northern tribes, Ammon moved into Gad’s towns and stayed. But the tribe’s land still had an owner: it remained Israel’s inheritance from God.

Dispossess those who dispossessed him. Ammon took Gad’s land in the name of its god Milcom; the reversal is exact, and God defends the inheritance of a tribe already carried off for its own sins. When God disciplines his people, he does not hand their inheritance to anyone else.

Milcom shall go into exile. Moab’s god Chemosh received the same sentence (48:7). Two national gods are deported, and each needs its own priests to carry it.

Who will come against me? Good land, full treasuries, and the question every secure nation asks just before the answer arrives.

But afterward. Five verses of judgment, and then “afterward”: after the judgment God will restore them. It is the pattern of Moab’s “Yet” (48:47) and Egypt’s “Afterward” (46:26), and it marks this whole section. God’s last word to the nations around Israel is not extinction.

The heir. “Has he no heir?” has its last answer in Christ, “the heir of all things” (Hebrews 1:2). Those joined to him are “fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17), and no one can squat on their inheritance, which is kept in heaven for them (1 Peter 1:4).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “Milcom”, the Ammonite god, can also be read “their king” (vv. 1, 3); the Hebrew letters are the same, and either reading makes the same point. In verse 4 the ESV also notes that the Hebrew reads ‘boast of your valleys, your valley flows’, a compressed phrase that probably pictures well-watered, fruitful valleys. What is clear is the confidence they bred.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–22 — Though You Make Your Nest as High as the Eagle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Edom’s wisdom and fortresses cannot save her from the God who brings the proud down. Her famous counsel has vanished, and her neighbours are warned to hide (vv. 7–8). She will be stripped bare, yet God offers to keep her orphans and widows alive (vv. 9–11). If even those who did not deserve the cup must drink it, Edom will not escape (vv. 12–13). Though she nests as high as the eagle, God will bring her down and make her a ruin like Sodom (vv. 14–18). He comes like a lion from the Jordan, asking “who is like me?”, and the earth trembles at her fall (vv. 19–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Edom trusts a fortress in a cliff, and God asks who could ever call him to court.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Edom. Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Is wisdom no more in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent? Has their wisdom vanished? Flee, turn back, dwell in the depths, O inhabitants of Dedan! For I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time when I punish him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom, Esau’s nation and famous for its wisdom, did not see its own ruin coming; even its neighbours are warned before it is.

Concerning Edom. Edom is Esau, and the rivalry goes back to a womb: “Two nations are in your womb… the older shall serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23). Judah had a fresher grievance too: when Jerusalem fell, Edom cheered and joined in the plunder (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10–14).

Is wisdom no more in Teman? Edom was famous for its wise men, and the oracle asks where their wisdom has gone.

O inhabitants of Dedan! Dedan was an Arabian trading people to the south-east, whose caravans passed through Edom (Isaiah 21:13; Ezekiel 27:20). They are told to hide in the depths, probably caves or remote country, because “the calamity of Esau” is coming and anyone near him will be caught in it.
verseByVerse.note: Teman (v. 7) was a district of Edom named after a grandson of Esau (Gen 36:11) and famous for its wise men; Job's friend Eliphaz was a Temanite (Job 2:11).

verseByVerse.quote: If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings? If thieves came by night, would they not destroy only enough for themselves? But I have stripped Esau bare; I have uncovered his hiding places, and he is not able to conceal himself. His children are destroyed, and his brothers, and his neighbors; and he is no more. Leave your fatherless children; I will keep them alive; and let your widows trust in me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom will be stripped more bare than any harvest or robbery could leave it, and yet God offers to keep its orphans and widows alive.

If grape gatherers came to you. Harvesters always left gleanings (the law required it, Leviticus 19:10), and thieves take only what they can carry. Edom’s ruin will be worse than either: nothing left over, nothing overlooked.

I have uncovered his hiding places. Edom trusted its geography, the canyons and cliff fortresses of the region of Petra; but there is no terrain God does not know.

Leave your fatherless children. Then comes an extraordinary verse in the middle of a judgment oracle (v. 11). To an enemy nation being stripped bare, God says: leave your orphans with me, and let your widows trust me. The God who is “Father of the fatherless and protector of widows” (Psalm 68:5) is the same God even here. If he would care for Edom’s widows, no one who is alone and trusts him is beyond his care.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: "If those who did not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, will you go unpunished? You shall not go unpunished, but you must drink. For I have sworn by myself, declares the LORD, that Bozrah shall become a horror, a taunt, a waste, and a curse, and all her cities shall be perpetual wastes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God’s own people had to drink the cup of his wrath, guilty Edom cannot escape it. The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if even they, how much more you.

If those who did not deserve to drink the cup must drink it. This is the cup of wrath God handed round the nations beginning with Jerusalem (25:15–18). “Those who did not deserve to drink” probably means Judah: compared with Edom, God’s own people were the less deserving, and they drank anyway. How then shall Edom escape?

I have sworn by myself. God swears by himself because there is no one greater to swear by (Hebrews 6:13), binding himself to the sentence. Bozrah was Edom’s chief city in the northern highlands, probably modern Buseirah in Jordan. Four words pile up, “a horror, a taunt, a waste, and a curse”: Bozrah will become a name people use as a warning.

Did it happen? Edom faded as a nation after the Babylonian period; Arab peoples, later the Nabataeans, took over its land, and many Edomites moved into southern Judah, the later Idumea. From that Idumean stock came Herod the Great, who tried to kill the newborn King of the Jews.

The innocent drank the cup. The sentence reaches further than Edom, because there was one who truly did not deserve the cup and drank it to the bottom. In a garden he prayed, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). So verse 12 warns, and the cross comforts. If the innocent drank, the guilty cannot claim to be let off; and because the innocent drank, the guilty who hide in him need not drink it.

verseByVerse.quote: I have heard a message from the LORD, and an envoy has been sent among the nations: "Gather yourselves together and come against her, and rise up for battle! For behold, I will make you small among the nations, despised among mankind. The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart, you who live in the clefts of the rock, who hold the height of the hill. Though you make your nest as high as the eagle's, I will bring you down from there, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself raises the nations against Edom, and he will bring her proud heights low.

An envoy has been sent among the nations. Jeremiah hears the LORD’s message, and the picture is of a herald going round the nations to raise a coalition: “Gather yourselves together and come against her.” Behind the movements of armies stands God’s summons.

I will make you small among the nations. A people proud of being great and feared will be made small and “despised among mankind”.

You who live in the clefts of the rock. Obadiah has this passage almost word for word: “The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock… Though you soar aloft like the eagle, though your nest is set among the stars, from there I will bring you down” (Obadiah 3–4).

The horror you inspire has deceived you. Being feared had convinced them they were safe. A reputation for being dangerous is no defence against God, who “has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate” (Luke 1:52).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “the horror you inspire” occurs only here in the Old Testament; it comes from a root meaning to shudder, and probably means the dread Edom caused others, though some take it as the horrid idol Edom trusted. The ESV also notes that “the clefts of the rock” may be read ‘the clefts of Sela’, a place name in Edom, since sela is the Hebrew word for rock.

verseByVerse.quote: "Edom shall become a horror. Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its disasters. As when Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities were overthrown, says the LORD, no man shall dwell there, no man shall sojourn in her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom will become a ruin as complete as Sodom, where no one will live or even stop for the night.

Edom shall become a horror. The people who inspired horror (v. 16) become a sight that horrifies; the Hebrew words differ, but the reversal is plain. Passers-by “hiss”, a gesture of shock and contempt at a ruin, as Jeremiah had said they would over Jerusalem (19:8; compare 1 Kings 9:8).

As when Sodom and Gomorrah. Sodom, traditionally placed at the southern end of the Dead Sea on Edom’s doorstep, is Scripture’s standing example of a judgment so complete that nobody lives there again (Deuteronomy 29:23). “No man shall dwell there, no man shall sojourn in her”: not even a traveller will stop for the night. The same words are spoken over Hazor (v. 33) and over Babylon (50:40).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, like a lion coming up from the jungle of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make him run away from her. And I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me? Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Edom and the purposes that he has formed against the inhabitants of Teman: Even the little ones of the flock shall be dragged away. Surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can stand against God or call him to account, and his plan, not Edom’s wisdom, will stand.

Like a lion coming up from the jungle of the Jordan. The jungle of the Jordan was the dense thicket along the river, where lions lived (compare 12:5). God pictures himself as a lion bursting out on a well-watered pasture and scattering flock and shepherds alike. “I will appoint over her whomever I choose”: Edom’s future rulers are God’s appointment, not Edom’s. The same words are used of Babylon (50:44).

For who is like me? These three questions are the heart of the section, and the second is the sharpest: who could ever call him to court? The silence that follows answers every complaint that his judgments are unfair, for there is no higher court. That is not a refusal to hear our questions, since Jeremiah himself brought his complaints to God (12:1); it is a reminder of who the judge is.

The one no one can summon. There is a wonder here. The God whom no one can summon allowed himself, in his Son, to be summoned: Jesus stood silent before the high priest and before Pilate, condemned in the place of those who deserved the verdict (Mark 14:60–64).

Hear the plan that the LORD has made. Teman, proud of its counsel (v. 7), is told of a counsel it cannot match. Even “the little ones of the flock” are dragged away, and the fold itself is appalled. The wise men had plans; God has a plan, and only his stands (Proverbs 19:21).

verseByVerse.quote: At the sound of their fall the earth shall tremble; the sound of their cry shall be heard at the Red Sea. Behold, one shall mount up and fly swiftly like an eagle and spread his wings against Bozrah, and the heart of the warriors of Edom shall be in that day like the heart of a woman in her birth pains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom’s fall will be heard far and wide, and the eagle-high nation will be overtaken by an eagle.

At the sound of their fall the earth shall tremble. The crash of Edom is heard as far as the Red Sea, here its eastern arm, the Gulf of Aqaba, where Edom’s ports had stood (1 Kings 9:26).

One shall mount up and fly swiftly like an eagle. Edom had nested “as high as the eagle’s” (v. 16); now an eagle comes against her, the conqueror swooping on Bozrah. The same picture was used of Moab (48:40–41), with the same end: the warriors’ hearts become “like the heart of a woman in her birth pains”, helpless before what cannot be stopped. Height was Edom’s confidence, and God sends something that flies higher.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Neither an ancient capital nor the remotest desert camp lies beyond God’s reach. Damascus melts in panic and turns to flee, and her young men fall in her squares, though she is “the city of my joy” (vv. 23–27). Nebuchadnezzar is sent against Kedar and the settlements of Hazor: their tents, flocks and camels are taken, and the old cry “Terror on every side!” follows them into the desert (vv. 28–30). A nation at ease, with no gates or bars, that trusted in being out of everyone’s way, is scattered to every wind and left a haunt of jackals (vv. 31–33).
verseByVerse.theology: Walls are no defence, and having no walls at all is no defence either.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Damascus: "Hamath and Arpad are confounded, for they have heard bad news; they melt in fear, they are troubled like the sea that cannot be quiet. Damascus has become feeble, she turned to flee, and panic seized her; anguish and sorrows have taken hold of her, as of a woman in labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear spreads through Syria like a sea that cannot settle, and Damascus, once a proud capital, turns to flee.

Hamath and Arpad are confounded. Hamath and Arpad lay north of Damascus; the bad news reaches them first and the panic runs south. Assyria had boasted of taking both a century earlier (Isaiah 10:9; 36:19).

Like the sea that cannot be quiet. The picture is exact: like water that cannot stop moving, fear cannot settle or rest.

Damascus has become feeble. Damascus, the old capital of Aram that had fought Israel for generations, turns to flee, seized by pains “as of a woman in labor”.

verseByVerse.quote: How is the famous city not forsaken, the city of my joy? Therefore her young men shall fall in her squares, and all her soldiers shall be destroyed in that day, declares the LORD of hosts. And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Damascus, a famous city and a city delighted in, will fall, and its warriors will die in its squares because they stayed.

The city of my joy. As the verse stands, God seems to call a Gentile capital that (see the box below). Damascus was ancient and beautiful, and its maker takes pleasure in it even while pronouncing its fall: the God of Israel is not indifferent to the cities of the nations.

How is the famous city not forsaken. The line probably means: why did the people not abandon the city while they could? They stayed, and so (“therefore”, v. 26) “her young men shall fall in her squares”. The same words are spoken over Babylon (50:30): the fate of the small capitals is the fate of the great one.

The strongholds of Ben-hadad. Amos had said the same, naming the same dynasty: “I will send a fire upon the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the strongholds of Ben-hadad” (Amos 1:4). The two prophets agree because one God speaks through both.

Uncertain wording. Verse 25 is hard. It may mean that the people did not leave the city while they could, or the “not” may be taken as an exclamation, ‘How the famous city is forsaken!’ It is also not certain who says “my joy”: it may be God, or a citizen of Damascus lamenting the city he loved. Either way the fall of a beloved city is mourned, not gloated over.

verseByVerse.quote: Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck down. Thus says the LORD: "Rise up, advance against Kedar! Destroy the people of the east! Their tents and their flocks shall be taken, their curtains and all their goods; their camels shall be led away from them, and men shall cry to them: 'Terror on every side!' Flee, wander far away, dwell in the depths, O inhabitants of Hazor! declares the LORD. For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made a plan against you and formed a purpose against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word reaches the desert nomads as surely as the capitals, and Nebuchadnezzar’s raid on them is God’s plan carried out.

Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor. Now come the Arab tribes of the desert. This Hazor is not the old Canaanite city in Galilee but a cluster of desert settlements, which Nebuchadnezzar raided probably about 599 BC. The inventory changes accordingly: not walls and gates but tents, curtains, flocks and camels. God’s word names what the nomads actually own.

Terror on every side! The phrase that had been Jeremiah’s nickname (20:3, 10) and was pronounced over Egypt (46:5) is now shouted after camel herds.

Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made a plan against you. “The people of the east” is the old name for the desert tribes beyond the Jordan (Judges 6:3). They are told to “wander far away” and hide in the depths, as Dedan was (v. 8). Edom heard of “the plan that the LORD has made” (v. 20); here the plan is Nebuchadnezzar’s, but the LORD declares it, so the king’s scheme carries out God’s word.

verseByVerse.quote: "Rise up, advance against a nation at ease, that dwells securely, declares the LORD, that has no gates or bars, that dwells alone. Their camels shall become plunder, their herds of livestock a spoil. I will scatter to every wind those who cut the corners of their hair, and I will bring their calamity from every side of them, declares the LORD. Hazor shall become a haunt of jackals, an everlasting waste; no man shall dwell there; no man shall sojourn in her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A people who felt safe because no one noticed them find that remoteness cannot hide them from God.

That has no gates or bars. Hazor’s defence was that it had nothing worth attacking: no gates or bars, living alone out in the desert where armies do not go.

Those who cut the corners of their hair. This was a desert custom of trimming the hair at the temples, forbidden to Israel (Leviticus 19:27) and used by Jeremiah as a name for these tribes (9:26; 25:23). God will scatter them “to every wind” and bring calamity “from every side”: the people whose safety was distance will find no direction left to flee. And Hazor is given the sentence Jerusalem had been given: “a haunt of jackals” (9:11; 10:22).

Three false securities. Moab felt secure because he had never been disturbed (48:11), Edom because of her cliffs, these tribes because no one noticed them. All three fall: no walls, wealth or remoteness hide anyone from God, and “a nation at ease” is a warning in these chapters, not a compliment.

No promise for some. Egypt, Moab, Ammon and Elam are all promised restoration afterward; Damascus, Kedar and Hazor are not. God does not owe an explanation for the pattern, and the book does not offer one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rules even the farthest nation, and his last word to it is mercy. Early in Zedekiah’s reign the word comes concerning Elam, beyond Babylon (v. 34). God will break the famous bow that was the mainstay of its might, scatter its people to the four winds and send his fierce anger after them (vv. 35–37). He will set his own throne in Elam and remove its king and officials (v. 38). Then comes the last word of the chapter: “But in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam” (v. 39).
verseByVerse.theology: God sets his throne in the farthest country named, and then promises it a future.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning Elam, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah. Thus says the LORD of hosts: "Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the mainstay of their might. And I will bring upon Elam the four winds from the four quarters of heaven. And I will scatter them to all those winds, and there shall be no nation to which those driven out of Elam shall not come. I will terrify Elam before their enemies and before those who seek their life. I will bring disaster upon them, my fierce anger, declares the LORD. I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them, and I will set my throne in Elam and destroy their king and officials, declares the LORD. "But in the latter days I will restore the fortunes of Elam, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will break Elam’s famous strength and rule there himself, and then restore its fortunes.

Concerning Elam. Elam lay beyond Babylon, in what is now south-western Iran, one of the farthest nations named in the book: a country most Judeans would never see. The oracle is dated early in Zedekiah’s reign, about 597 BC.

I will break the bow of Elam. Their strength is named precisely: “the bow of Elam, the mainstay of their might.” Elamite archers were famous. God names what a nation is proud of before he breaks it.

I will set my throne in Elam. Not a garrison but a throne, in the most distant capital in the book: the LORD of hosts governs there, and its king holds his seat only by God’s leave. The risen Christ makes the same claim over every land: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18).

I will restore the fortunes of Elam. The chapter ends with a promise rather than a sentence. After Egypt (46:26), Moab (48:47) and Ammon (49:6), Elam is the fourth nation in these chapters told that judgment is not the end of its story.

Elamites at Pentecost. On the day of Pentecost, when the Spirit fell and the crowd heard the mighty works of God each in his own language, Luke’s list of the nations present begins, “Parthians and Medes and Elamites” (Acts 2:9). The restoration of Elam, promised through a prophet in a doomed city, turns up as men from Elam hearing the gospel in their own tongue.

49.title: Ammon, Edom, and the Nations Around
49.overview:
Where we are. After Egypt, Philistia and Moab (chapters 46 to 48), four shorter oracles sweep round the rest of Judah’s world: Ammon and Edom close at hand, Damascus to the north, the desert tribes to the east, and far-off Elam beyond Babylon. Babylon itself comes next (chapters 50 and 51).

The message. No corner of the world lies outside the LORD’s rule, and nothing a nation trusts, whether stolen land, famous wisdom, cliff fortresses, remoteness or a famous bow, can shelter it from him. “For who is like me? Who will summon me?” (v. 19). Yet even here, his last word to several of these nations is mercy.

Why it was said. These names were the map of Judah’s world, and several had wronged her: Ammon’s king sent the man who murdered Gedaliah (40:14), and Edom cheered when Jerusalem fell (Psalm 137:7). The oracles assured God’s people that their neighbours answered to their God, so they need neither take revenge nor trust in alliances (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Ammon, which took Gad’s land, will lose its own, and its god will go into exile, “But afterward” (vv. 1–6). Edom, proud of its wisdom and its cliffs, is stripped bare: if those who did not deserve the cup must drink it, Edom cannot escape, and though she nests as high as the eagle, God will bring her down (vv. 7–22). Damascus melts in panic, though she is called “the city of my joy” (vv. 23–27), and the desert tribes of Kedar and Hazor, at ease with no gates or bars, are scattered to every wind (vv. 28–33). Elam’s famous bow is broken and God sets his throne there; then he promises to restore its fortunes (vv. 34–39).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. The cup that “those who did not deserve” must drink (v. 12) was drunk at last by the only one who truly did not deserve it, when Jesus prayed in Gethsemane, “let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39), and then drank it, so that those who shelter in him need not. And the promise to Elam began to come true at Pentecost, when Elamites heard the mighty works of God in their own language (Acts 2:9–11).

For us. Pride still trusts the same things: what we have taken, what we know, how high we have built, how unnoticed we live. None of it hides anyone from God. But the Judge who asks “Who will summon me?” has drunk the cup himself, and he invites every nation to shelter in him.
49.theology:
No kind of security works against God, whether walls, wealth, a cliff, a fearsome reputation, or even having no gates at all (vv. 16, 31). He is the only judge, with no higher court to summon him (v. 19). Yet the same God tells a nation being stripped bare to leave its orphans with him (v. 11) and calls a Gentile capital the city of my joy (v. 25).

At the centre stands the cup. If those less deserving drank it, the guilty cannot claim to be let off; and because one wholly innocent drank it to the bottom, those who hide in him need not drink it (v. 12; 25:15-16; Matt 26:39).
49.examples:
Edom is the picture of a person whose safety lies in being feared: the sharp tongue, the reputation nobody wants to cross. The horror you inspire was exactly what deceived her. Hazor is the opposite, safe because no one notices her, and she falls too. Neither strength nor obscurity hides anyone from God.

Yet in the middle of Edom's sentence God says, leave your fatherless children with me. Even under judgment, the widow and the orphan can still be placed in his hands.

keyVerse.quote: For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me?
keyVerse.note: These three questions are the heart of the chapter, and they are asked again over Babylon (50:44). Every nation here trusted something, but no wisdom, height or distance can stand before the God who has no equal and answers to no higher court. The same God, in Christ, allowed himself to be summoned and judged in our place.

49.reflection:
Each nation in this chapter trusted something: stolen land (v. 1), its treasures (v. 4), its wisdom (v. 7), its height (v. 16), its remoteness (v. 31), its famous bow (v. 35). Which of these is closest to what people trust today, and what are you most tempted to rely on?

In the middle of Edom’s judgment God says, “Leave your fatherless children; I will keep them alive; and let your widows trust in me” (v. 11). What does this show you about God’s character, even when he judges? How might it comfort someone who is alone?

Read verse 12 beside Matthew 26:39. How does Jesus drinking the cup he did not deserve change the way we hear the warnings in this chapter?

Ammon and Elam are promised restoration, and Elamites were among those who heard the gospel at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). How should this shape the way we pray for the nations, including those hostile to Christ?

A sword against her warriors, that they may be destroyed!<sup>37</sup>A sword against her horses and against her chariots, and against all the foreign troops in her midst, that they may become women! A sword against all her treasures, that they may be plundered!<sup>38</sup>A drought against her waters, that they may be dried up! For it is a land of images, and they are mad over idols.<sup>39</sup>"Therefore wild beasts shall dwell with hyenas in Babylon, and ostriches shall dwell in her. She shall never again have people, nor be inhabited for all generations.<sup>40</sup>As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities, declares the LORD, so no man shall dwell there, and no son of man shall sojourn in her.<sup>41</sup>"Behold, a people comes from the north; a mighty nation and many kings are stirring from the farthest parts of the earth.<sup>42</sup>They lay hold of bow and spear; they are cruel and have no mercy. The sound of them is like the roaring of the sea; they ride on horses, arrayed as a man for battle against you, O daughter of Babylon!<sup>43</sup>"The king of Babylon heard the report of them, and his hands fell helpless; anguish seized him, pain as of a woman in labor.<sup>44</sup>"Behold, like a lion coming up from the thicket of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make them run away from her, and I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me?<sup>45</sup>Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Babylon, and the purposes that he has formed against the land of the Chaldeans: Surely the little ones of their flock shall be dragged away; surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate.<sup>46</sup>At the sound of the capture of Babylon the earth shall tremble, and her cry shall be heard among the nations."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Babylon Is Taken, Bel Is Put to Shame
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Babylon’s fall is news to be published everywhere, and in the same breath God’s scattered people come home. Babylon is taken and her gods, Bel and Merodach, are put to shame (v. 2) by a nation from the north, the phrase that had long threatened Judah, now turned on Babylon (v. 3). Israel and Judah come together, weeping, asking the way to Zion and seeking an everlasting covenant (vv. 4–5). They were lost sheep, led astray by their shepherds and devoured by enemies who said they were not guilty (vv. 6–7). Now they are told to flee Babylon, for God is stirring up great nations against her (vv. 8–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Babylon, the enemy from the north that Judah feared, now faces an enemy from the north herself.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that the LORD spoke concerning Babylon, concerning the land of the Chaldeans, by Jeremiah the prophet: "Declare among the nations and proclaim, set up a banner and proclaim, conceal it not, and say: 'Babylon is taken, Bel is put to shame, Merodach is dismayed. Her images are put to shame, her idols are dismayed.' "For out of the north a nation has come up against her, which shall make her land a desolation, and none shall dwell in it; both man and beast shall flee away. "In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, the people of Israel and the people of Judah shall come together, weeping as they come, and they shall seek the LORD their God. They shall ask the way to Zion, with faces turned toward it, saying, 'Come, let us join ourselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.' "My people have been lost sheep. Their shepherds have led them astray, turning them away on the mountains. From mountain to hill they have gone. They have forgotten their fold. All who found them have devoured them, and their enemies have said, 'We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the LORD, their habitation of righteousness, the LORD, the hope of their fathers.' "Flee from the midst of Babylon, and go out of the land of the Chaldeans, and be as male goats before the flock. For behold, I am stirring up and bringing against Babylon a gathering of great nations, from the north country. And they shall array themselves against her. From there she shall be taken. Their arrows are like a skilled warrior who does not return empty-handed. Chaldea shall be plundered; all who plunder her shall be sated, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon’s fall is announced, beginning with her gods, and with it comes the homecoming of God’s scattered people, weeping and seeking him.

The instrument on trial. God had called Nebuchadnezzar “my servant” three times and told the nations to bow to his yoke. These two chapters, a hundred and ten verses, are the longest oracle in the book, because they answer the hardest question Jeremiah’s hearers faced: had God simply gone over to Babylon’s side?

Bel is put to shame. The news is to be published, “conceal it not”, and what falls first is not the walls or the army but the gods, Bel and Merodach, two names for Babylon’s chief god Marduk. Isaiah had drawn the scene: “Bel bows down; Nebo stoops; their idols are on beasts and livestock; these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts” (Isaiah 46:1). These are gods that have to be carried to safety on pack animals.

Out of the north. Since chapter 1 that phrase has meant the enemy coming against Judah. Now it points at Babylon: she does not decide where judgment falls; God does.

The people of Israel and the people of Judah. In the middle of an oracle against an empire, both houses come home together: the northern tribes, scattered for more than a century, and Judah, in one company. They come weeping and asking directions: “They shall ask the way to Zion, with faces turned toward it.” People who had forgotten the road have to be told it, and their faces turn toward home before their feet arrive. The covenant they seek is the one promised in chapter 31, “an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten”, and it is asked for, not imposed. The God who scattered them has made them long for him.

My people have been lost sheep. God’s diagnosis does not begin with the sheep’s foolishness but with the shepherds, the kings, priests and prophets of chapter 23, who “scattered my flock” (23:2). Yet the sheep are still “my people”. Their enemies even knew the theology: “We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the LORD” (v. 7). They were right that Israel had sinned, and wrong that this made them innocent, as the rest of the chapter shows.

Flee from the midst of Babylon. The exiles are to “be as male goats before the flock”, the animals that push out first through the gate. The voice that once said build houses and plant gardens in Babylon (29:5) now says leave. Obedience does not mean always doing the same thing; it means doing what God says at each time, and the people who had settled in for seventy years had to be told when the seventy years were up. John hears the call again over a later Babylon: “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues” (Revelation 18:4).

The Shepherd who came for them. Isaiah puts the lost sheep and the remedy together: “All we like sheep have gone astray”, and “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). Jesus looked on the crowds as “sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36) and came as the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep.

When was this fulfilled? It began when exiles of both kingdoms came home under Cyrus, but the everlasting covenant they seek is the new covenant of 31:31–34, which Hebrews says Christ has brought in (Hebrews 8:6–13). In him the lost sheep of both houses, and of the nations too, become one flock under one shepherd (John 10:16).
verseByVerse.note: Bel (Marduk) and Merodach are names of Babylon’s chief god.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–20 — The Hammer Punished, the Flock Restored
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Babylon will be repaid for what she did, and Israel will be restored and forgiven. The plunderers who frolicked over God’s heritage will see their mother land made the last of the nations, a desert all who pass will hiss at (vv. 11–13). Archers are summoned because she has sinned against the LORD: do to her as she has done (vv. 14–16). Israel was a sheep mauled by two lions, Assyria and then Babylon, and Babylon’s king will be punished as Assyria’s was (vv. 17–18). Israel will graze in the good pastures again, and when God searches for its sin, none will be found, for he will pardon the remnant (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Instruments are not exempt. God punishes the hammer he swung.

verseByVerse.quote: "Though you rejoice, though you exult, O plunderers of my heritage, though you frolic like a heifer in the pasture, and neigh like stallions, your mother shall be utterly shamed, and she who bore you shall be disgraced. Behold, she shall be the last of the nations, a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert. Because of the wrath of the LORD she shall not be inhabited but shall be an utter desolation; everyone who passes by Babylon shall be appalled, and hiss because of all her wounds. Set yourselves in array against Babylon all around, all you who bend the bow; shoot at her, spare no arrows, for she has sinned against the LORD. Raise a shout against her all around; she has surrendered; her bulwarks have fallen; her walls are thrown down. For this is the vengeance of the LORD: take vengeance on her; do to her as she has done. Cut off from Babylon the sower, and the one who handles the sickle in time of harvest; because of the sword of the oppressor, every one shall turn to his own people, and every one shall flee to his own land. "Israel is a hunted sheep driven away by lions. First the king of Assyria devoured him, and now at last Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has gnawed his bones. Therefore, thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing punishment on the king of Babylon and his land, as I punished the king of Assyria. I will restore Israel to his pasture, and he shall feed on Carmel and in Bashan, and his desire shall be satisfied on the hills of Ephraim and in Gilead. In those days and in that time, declares the LORD, iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none, and sin in Judah, and none shall be found, for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon is punished for her own sin against the LORD, while Israel, mauled by two empires, is brought back to pasture and forgiven so completely that its sin cannot be found.

Though you frolic like a heifer in the pasture. Babylon is pictured as livestock kicking up its heels, cut down to size as Egypt was (a heifer troubled by a fly) and Moab (wine left on its dregs). The empire that was first among the nations will be “the last of the nations”, and its “mother”, the land itself, a desert.

She has sinned against the LORD. Here is the reason behind the whole chapter, and it answers the question of whether God has changed sides. Babylon is not punished for defeating Judah; that was God’s own doing. She is punished because “she has sinned against the LORD”, and the measure is “do to her as she has done”.

Accountable in God’s hand. An instrument used by God is still accountable for how it behaved in his hand. Babylon went beyond what God sent her to do: cruelty, pride, the temple burned, God’s heritage plundered for pleasure. Being useful to God is not the same as being righteous, and it excuses no one from judgment.

Israel is a hunted sheep driven away by lions. Two empires are pictured as two lions over one sheep. Assyria “devoured him”; Babylon “has gnawed his bones”, the second predator working over what the first left behind.

As I punished the king of Assyria. Assyria is the precedent. That empire had been God’s rod against the northern kingdom, and its capital Nineveh was destroyed in 612 BC, within living memory. Babylon can read her future in Assyria’s ruins, and so can every power that thinks it is the exception.

I will restore Israel to his pasture. The sheep get pasture again, and named pasture: Carmel, Bashan, Ephraim, Gilead, the best grazing country.

Sin in Judah, and none shall be found. Then comes a sentence that goes further than any restoration of land: “iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none.” Someone looks for the sin and does not find it, not because it was small, but because of the last clause: “for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant.” This is the promise of 31:34, that God will remember their sin no more, pictured as a search that comes back empty.

What it means for God to pardon. We tend to hear pardon as God being easygoing. This chapter will not let us think that, for in the same breath God says of Babylon, “Repay her according to her deeds” (v. 29). He shrugs at no one’s sin. Timothy Keller often pointed out that real forgiveness is never free: when someone wrongs you, either you make them pay or you absorb the cost yourself, and to forgive is to bear it. God’s pardon is like that. The debt did not vanish; it was carried, and the chapter names who carries it: “Their Redeemer is strong” (v. 34). That Redeemer came in person: “In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses” (Ephesians 1:7). So when an old failure rises at night and accuses you, do not argue that it was small. Tell it where it went. If it was laid on Christ, the search comes back empty. See Forgiveness.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hammer of the whole earth is broken because she fought against God. The attack is ordered on districts whose names mean double rebellion and punishment (vv. 21–22). Babylon, the hammer that smashed the nations, is caught in a snare she never saw (vv. 23–24). God opens his armoury, her granaries are broken open and her young warriors slaughtered (vv. 25–27). Refugees carry the news to Zion: this is vengeance for his temple (v. 28). The proud one who defied the Holy One of Israel falls with none to raise her (vv. 29–32), because, like Pharaoh, she held God’s people fast and refused to let them go (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: A district named Double Rebellion is caught in a snare it never saw.

verseByVerse.quote: "Go up against the land of Merathaim, and against the inhabitants of Pekod. Kill, and devote them to destruction, declares the LORD, and do all that I have commanded you. The noise of battle is in the land, and great destruction!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God orders the attack on Babylon, and the very names of her districts spell out her guilt and her sentence.

Against the land of Merathaim. These are two Babylonian districts, and the ESV explains why they are named: ‘Merathaim means double rebellion’ and ‘Pekod means punishment’. They are real places on the map whose names, heard in Hebrew, spell out the charge and the verdict.

The noise of battle is in the land. Like a shout from the field, the orders of verse 21 are already being carried out. “Do all that I have commanded you” makes the invader God’s servant, as Babylon had been; what God commands is as good as done.

Kill, and devote them to destruction. The Hebrew word, herem, means to hand something over wholly to God, here for destruction, as in the conquest of Canaan; the ESV explains it as set apart as an offering to the Lord for destruction. This old language of holy war is now turned on the empire that had carried out God’s own judgment.

What it does not mean. This is God’s sentence on an empire that had crushed nations, carried out by the armies he sent against it: a judgment of that moment, not a pattern for believers, whose King said his servants do not fight for his kingdom (John 18:36). The Judge of all the earth may end a guilty power; no Christian may take up that sword in his name.
verseByVerse.note: Pekod was an Aramean tribe east of the Tigris, known from Assyrian records; Merathaim, "land of bitter waters", was probably a name for southern Babylonia near the Gulf.

verseByVerse.quote: How the hammer of the whole earth is cut down and broken! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations! I set a snare for you and you were taken, O Babylon, and you did not know it; you were found and caught, because you opposed the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hammer God used to smash the nations is itself broken, caught in a trap she never saw because she was fighting God.

The hammer of the whole earth. Babylon’s oracle will say it more plainly still: “You are my hammer and weapon of war: with you I break nations in pieces” (51:20). A hammer is a tool, and a tool can be broken by the hand that used it.

You did not know it. The snare was set, sprung and closed while the empire went about its business. That is how judgment often comes to those who feel secure: the battle is lost before they notice. Belshazzar’s feast was going on the night the city fell (Daniel 5).

Because you opposed the LORD. Babylon thought she was fighting Judah, Egypt and the rest; in fact she had picked a fight with God. Whoever contends with God is caught in the end, as the snare catches the bird that never saw it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has opened his armory and brought out the weapons of his wrath, for the Lord GOD of hosts has a work to do in the land of the Chaldeans. Come against her from every quarter; open her granaries; pile her up like heaps of grain, and devote her to destruction; let nothing be left of her. Kill all her bulls; let them go down to the slaughter. Woe to them, for their day has come, the time of their punishment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brings out the nations as weapons from his armoury, and Babylon’s storehouses and warriors are given up to destruction.

The LORD has opened his armory. God keeps an armoury, and its weapons are nations. The invaders think they pursue their own ambitions; in fact God has brought them out, for he “has a work to do in the land of the Chaldeans”.

Open her granaries. Babylon’s storehouses, filled from the harvests and plunder of many nations, are broken open, and the city itself is piled up like heaps of grain. “Kill all her bulls” probably means her young warriors, pictured as bulls (compare Psalm 22:12; Isaiah 34:7), sent down to the slaughter. “Their day has come”: the day God had fixed (compare 46:10).

verseByVerse.quote: "A voice! They flee and escape from the land of Babylon, to declare in Zion the vengeance of the LORD our God, vengeance for his temple. "Summon archers against Babylon, all those who bend the bow. Encamp around her; let no one escape. Repay her according to her deeds; do to her according to all that she has done. For she has proudly defied the LORD, the Holy One of Israel. Therefore her young men shall fall in her squares, and all her soldiers shall be destroyed on that day, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
News reaches Zion that God has avenged his temple and repaid Babylon for her proud defiance of the Holy One of Israel.

They flee and escape from the land of Babylon. Refugees run the other way, out of Babylon toward Zion, carrying news, and the news has a specific object: “vengeance for his temple”. The burning of that building was not overlooked.

The Holy One of Israel. The charge is pride, and the title used is the one that ties God to his people. Babylon had defied not an abstract deity but the God of the people she had plundered.

Repay her according to her deeds. The principle is justice in kind: Babylon receives what she gave. Revelation takes up these words over the last Babylon, the world city that persecutes the saints (Revelation 18:6). Her young men falling in her squares (v. 30) is the sentence already pronounced on Damascus (49:26).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I am against you, O proud one, declares the Lord GOD of hosts, for your day has come, the time when I will punish you. The proud one shall stumble and fall, with none to raise him up, and I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it will devour all that is around him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets himself against Babylon, whom he names “proud one”, and she falls with no one to lift her up.

Behold, I am against you, O proud one. Babylon is now named by her sin: the Hebrew word for “proud one” stands as her name, like a title. “I am against you” is the most frightening thing God can say to anyone (compare 21:13; 51:25).

The proud one shall stumble and fall. Pride goes before a fall (Proverbs 16:18), and this fall has “none to raise him up”: no ally will lift her. The fire kindled in her cities answers the fire she set in Jerusalem (52:13). “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: The people of Israel are oppressed, and the people of Judah with them. All who took them captive have held them fast; they refuse to let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon, like Pharaoh, refuses to release God’s people, and so, like Pharaoh, she will meet their Redeemer.

The people of Israel are oppressed, and the people of Judah with them. Both kingdoms are named together, the north carried off by Assyria in 722 BC and the south by Babylon: the whole family of Jacob held fast by its captors (compare v. 17). It is the plain complaint of the oppressed, and God himself states it.

They refuse to let them go. Israelites would hear the exodus here: the Pharaoh who would not release God’s people, and the God who took them out anyway. Babylon has made herself a second Egypt, and the next verse gives God’s answer: “Their Redeemer is strong.”

A greater exodus. On the mountain of transfiguration Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31); Luke’s word is exodos. The exodus from Egypt and the return from Babylon both point to the release Christ won at the cross from a harder captivity than either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The captives have a strong Redeemer who takes up their case himself. Because he pleads their cause, the sword falls on everything Babylon trusted: officials and wise men, diviners and warriors, horses, treasures and the waters that fed her, for she is a land mad over idols (vv. 34–38). She will be left to wild beasts, like Sodom (vv. 39–40). The army from the north that once threatened Jerusalem now comes against the daughter of Babylon, and her king’s hands fall helpless (vv. 41–43). The questions once asked over Edom, “For who is like me?”, now silence even Babylon, and the earth trembles at her capture (vv. 44–46).
verseByVerse.theology: The captives do not have a lawyer; they have a Redeemer, and he takes the case himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause, that he may give rest to the earth, but unrest to the inhabitants of Babylon. "A sword against the Chaldeans, declares the LORD, and against the inhabitants of Babylon, and against her officials and her wise men! A sword against the diviners, that they may become fools! A sword against her warriors, that they may be destroyed! A sword against her horses and against her chariots, and against all the foreign troops in her midst, that they may become women! A sword against all her treasures, that they may be plundered! A drought against her waters, that they may be dried up! For it is a land of images, and they are mad over idols. "Therefore wild beasts shall dwell with hyenas in Babylon, and ostriches shall dwell in her. She shall never again have people, nor be inhabited for all generations. As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighboring cities, declares the LORD, so no man shall dwell there, and no son of man shall sojourn in her. "Behold, a people comes from the north; a mighty nation and many kings are stirring from the farthest parts of the earth. They lay hold of bow and spear; they are cruel and have no mercy. The sound of them is like the roaring of the sea; they ride on horses, arrayed as a man for battle against you, O daughter of Babylon! "The king of Babylon heard the report of them, and his hands fell helpless; anguish seized him, pain as of a woman in labor. "Behold, like a lion coming up from the thicket of the Jordan against a perennial pasture, I will suddenly make them run away from her, and I will appoint over her whomever I choose. For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me? Therefore hear the plan that the LORD has made against Babylon, and the purposes that he has formed against the land of the Chaldeans: Surely the little ones of their flock shall be dragged away; surely their fold shall be appalled at their fate. At the sound of the capture of Babylon the earth shall tremble, and her cry shall be heard among the nations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s strong Redeemer takes up their case himself, and the sword falls on everything Babylon trusted until she is silenced like Sodom.

Their Redeemer is strong. The Redeemer is the kinsman with the right and the duty to buy back what a relative had lost, as Boaz did for Naomi’s family and Jeremiah himself did for a field at Anathoth (32:7). The captives have no rights and no one to speak for them. What they have is a relative with the power to free them.

He will surely plead their cause. He does not send a lawyer; he takes the case. Isaiah names him in the same breath: “Our Redeemer… is the Holy One of Israel” (Isaiah 47:4).

A sword against the Chaldeans. Five swords and a drought are hammered out one after another, and the list is a catalogue of everything Babylon trusted: government, scholarship, divination, army, cavalry, treasury, and the canal system that made the land fertile. The diviners get a particular sentence, “that they may become fools”, and the diagnosis underneath it all is blunt: “they are mad over idols.” Not merely mistaken: mad.

As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. The picture is a ruin with animals in it, measured against the oldest ruin in Scripture (Genesis 19:24). John sees the same desolation over the last Babylon: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!… a haunt for every unclean bird” (Revelation 18:2).

His hands fell helpless. Verses 41–43 repeat, almost word for word, what Jeremiah once said of the northern army coming against Jerusalem (6:22–24), but “daughter of Zion” has become “daughter of Babylon”. The words once spoken over Jerusalem’s terror now fall on Babylon’s king, and every empire in this section ends in the same posture.

What shepherd can stand before me? Verses 44–46 repeat the words spoken over Edom a chapter earlier (49:19–21). The same three questions, “For who is like me? Who will summon me? What shepherd can stand before me?”, silence the greatest nation as they silenced a small one. “I will appoint over her whomever I choose”: within a lifetime the appointment was made, and his name was Cyrus.

The Redeemer became a kinsman. That Redeemer at last became a kinsman in the full sense. The Son of God was “born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Galatians 4:4–5), and he shared our flesh and blood to free those held in slavery all their lives (Hebrews 2:14–15). The captives’ powerful relative turned out to be the LORD himself, and the price was his own life.

For the first readers. For the exiles, the point was not the satisfaction of seeing an enemy fall. It was that the God who had used Babylon was not owned by Babylon: the seventy years had an end written into them, and the people asking the way to Zion had a Redeemer strong enough to plead their cause against the hammer of the whole earth.

Did this come true? Babylon surrendered to Cyrus in 539 BC with little fighting and stayed inhabited for centuries; it declined slowly, was damaged by later kings, and became the ruin it is today.

Where Christians differ. Because Babylon was not destroyed suddenly, some dispensational teachers expect a literal Babylon to be rebuilt in Iraq and destroyed at the end, fulfilling these chapters and Revelation 18 to the letter. Others hold that the prophecy was fulfilled in the city’s long decline into an empty ruin, and that Revelation takes up Babylon as a symbol.

This commentary’s view. Babylon fell as God said and became the desolate mound it is today; prophecy often compresses a long process into a single picture. In Revelation, Babylon is Rome in John’s day, standing for the proud and seductive world system of every age (see the notes on Revelation 17–18), and its fall is as certain as ancient Babylon’s.

Uncertain wording. In verse 38 the Hebrew consonants for “drought” also spell “sword”, so some read ‘A sword against her waters’; “drought” fits the drying waters, and the wordplay caps the list of swords. The word for “diviners” (v. 36) means empty talkers, probably a scornful name for Babylon’s omen-readers.

Textual note. The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks ‘in Babylon’ in verse 39; the words are supplied from the context.

50.title: Against Babylon
50.overview:
Where we are. The oracles against the nations end with the longest of all, against Babylon (chapters 50 and 51). For most of the book Babylon has been God’s instrument: Nebuchadnezzar was “my servant” (25:9; 27:6), and Judah was told to bow to his yoke. Now the instrument is put on trial.

The message. God has not gone over to Babylon’s side. The empire he used to judge his people answers for its own pride and cruelty, and it will fall; and its fall means freedom for a people he has not forgotten. Their Redeemer is strong, he pleads their cause himself, and he will pardon them so completely that their iniquity “shall be sought” and not found (v. 20).

Why it was said. The exiles in Babylon lived under an empire that seemed permanent, and many must have wondered whether God had abandoned them or changed sides (see the introduction on the seventy years). The chapter tells them that Babylon’s days are numbered, that the God who sent them into exile will bring them home, and that when the time comes they must leave.

How the chapter makes its case. Babylon is taken and her gods are shamed by a nation from the north, while Israel and Judah come home together, weeping and seeking an everlasting covenant (vv. 1–10). The plunderers who frolicked over God’s heritage will be made the last of the nations, while the sheep that two lions mauled is restored and pardoned (vv. 11–20). The hammer of the whole earth is broken in a snare she never saw, because she defied the Holy One of Israel and would not let his people go (vv. 21–33). Their Redeemer is strong: swords fall on everything Babylon trusted, and the questions once asked over Edom silence her too (vv. 34–46).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. The everlasting covenant the exiles seek (v. 5) is the new covenant of 31:31–34, which Christ made in his blood (Luke 22:20). The pardon that leaves sin unfound (v. 20) is the pardon he paid for, and the strong Redeemer who pleads their cause (v. 34) is the God who became our kinsman to buy us back (Galatians 4:4–5). In Revelation, Babylon’s fall becomes the pattern for the fall of every proud power that oppresses God’s people (Revelation 18).

For us. No empire, however permanent it looks, owns God or outlasts him, and being useful in his hand excuses no one. For those who belong to Christ, the chapter’s deepest comfort is verse 20: when an old sin rises to accuse, it is sought and not found, because our Redeemer is strong.
50.theology:
This chapter answers the question the exiles must have asked: had God simply changed sides? He had not. Babylon is judged not for defeating Judah, which was his own doing, but for her pride and cruelty in doing it. Being useful to God excuses no one from judgment, and he alone decides where judgment falls (vv. 3, 14-15, 23).

Through it all runs a promise for the scattered flock. God blames the shepherds before the sheep (v. 6), searches for his people's iniquity and finds none because he has pardoned them (v. 20; 31:34), and stands as their Redeemer, the kinsman who takes their case himself (v. 34).
50.examples:
Some of the strongest powers in history have believed they were the exception, the hammer and never the anvil. Jeremiah tells Babylon to read her future in Nineveh's ruins; she did not, and the city fell while the feast went on.

For the believer, the comfort is personal. Those who have no rights and no one to speak for them are not left to plead their own case. Their Redeemer is strong, and the price of their freedom was his own life.

keyVerse.quote: Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause, that he may give rest to the earth, but unrest to the inhabitants of Babylon.
keyVerse.note: The captives had no rights and no one to speak for them, but they had a kinsman with the right and the power to set them free, and he took up their case himself. That is why the empire falls and the exiles go home. The same Redeemer took our flesh and paid our ransom with his own life.

50.reflection:
Babylon had been God’s instrument, yet she is judged for the way she behaved (vv. 11–16, 29). What does this teach about the difference between being used by God and being right with God?

The exiles come home “weeping as they come”, asking “the way to Zion” (vv. 4–5). What part do sorrow and seeking play in coming back to God? Is there a road back you need to ask the way to?

Verse 20 says Israel’s sin will be sought and not found. How does the cross make that possible without God pretending that sin does not matter? How would believing it change the way you deal with old guilt?

“Their Redeemer is strong… He will surely plead their cause” (v. 34). Where do you, or someone you know, most need to hear that the Lord takes up the cause of those who cannot defend themselves?
