verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Golden Cup That Made the Earth Drunk
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has not forsaken his people, so the empire that holds them will fall. He stirs up a destroyer and sends winnowers against Babylon, sparing none of her army (vv. 1–4), for Israel and Judah are not forsaken, while Babylon is full of guilt (v. 5). The exiles must flee, because Babylon, the golden cup that made the nations drunk, has fallen, and the attempt to heal her has failed (vv. 6–10). The kings of the Medes are stirred up as vengeance for God’s temple, and the city that lives by many waters hears that its end has come (vv. 11–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Babylon was the cup that made the world drunk, but the LORD held her in his hand all along, and now he sets her down.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will stir up the spirit of a destroyer against Babylon, against the inhabitants of Leb-kamai, and I will send to Babylon winnowers, and they shall winnow her, and they shall empty her land, when they come against her from every side on the day of trouble. Let not the archer bend his bow, and let him not stand up in his armor. Spare not her young men; devote to destruction all her army. They shall fall down slain in the land of the Chaldeans, and wounded in her streets. For Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God, the LORD of hosts, but the land of the Chaldeans is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel. "Flee from the midst of Babylon; let every one save his life! Be not cut off in her punishment, for this is the time of the LORD's vengeance, the repayment he is rendering her. Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunken; the nations drank of her wine; therefore the nations went mad. Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been broken; wail for her! Take balm for her pain; perhaps she may be healed. We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed. Forsake her, and let us go each to his own country, for her judgment has reached up to heaven and has been lifted up even to the skies. The LORD has brought about our vindication; come, let us declare in Zion the work of the LORD our God. "Sharpen the arrows! Take up the shields! The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose concerning Babylon is to destroy it, for that is the vengeance of the LORD, the vengeance for his temple. "Set up a standard against the walls of Babylon; make the watch strong; set up watchmen; prepare the ambushes; for the LORD has both planned and done what he spoke concerning the inhabitants of Babylon. O you who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come; the thread of your life is cut. The LORD of hosts has sworn by himself: Surely I will fill you with men, as many as locusts, and they shall raise the shout of victory over you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will send the Medes against Babylon, the golden cup in his hand, because he has not forsaken his people, and Babylon is now past healing.

I will send to Babylon winnowers. Winnowers tossed threshed grain into the wind so the chaff blew away. God will do that to Babylon and “empty her land”, sparing none of her army.

Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God. Verse 5 is the pastoral heart of both chapters. It answers the question the exiles were actually asking, not ‘will Babylon fall?’ but ‘has God dropped us?’ They had every appearance of being forsaken, with the city gone, the temple burned and the king blinded, and the verse denies it flatly. This is God’s faithfulness at its most stubborn: he has disciplined them, scattered them and burned his own house, and he has not let go of them for an hour.

Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD’s hand. It is an image of terrible beauty. Babylon was genuinely magnificent, and she was in the LORD’s hand the whole time. He poured her out for the nations to drink, and the drinking drove them mad. Empires are intoxicating: their wealth, art and confidence go to the heads of everyone around them. But the cup never held itself up. John sees the great prostitute of the last Babylon holding “a golden cup full of abominations” (Revelation 17:4).

Take balm for her pain; perhaps she may be healed. Somebody fetches medicine for the empire that burned the temple. The balm of Gilead once longed for in Judah (8:22) and denied to Egypt (46:11) is brought to Babylon’s bedside, and the verdict is, “We would have healed Babylon, but she was not healed.” Judgment here is not pictured as eagerness to destroy; it comes after the cure has been tried and the patient is past healing.

The kings of the Medes. The nation God would use is named a generation before it arrived. Isaiah had said the same, “Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against them” (Isaiah 13:17), and Daniel records the night it happened: “And Darius the Mede received the kingdom” (Daniel 5:31).

The vengeance for his temple. The stated motive is a building. The house Solomon built and the Chaldeans burned is on the charge sheet: God does not shrug off what was done to the place where his name dwelt.

Forsaken in their place. “Not forsaken” was a promise God kept at great cost. On the cross Jesus cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), bearing the abandonment his people deserved, so that he can say to every one of them, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

Uncertain wording. “Leb-kamai” (v. 1) is a code name for Chaldea, made by reversing the Hebrew alphabet (see the note); why a cipher is used is not certain, since Babylon is named openly in the same verse, but read as it stands the name means something like ‘heart of those who rise against me’, which may be the point. The opening of verse 3 is hard in Hebrew: the same letters can be read ‘let not’ or ‘against’, so older translations have ‘Against him that bendeth let the archer bend his bow’; either way Babylon’s army is doomed. The word for “shields” in verse 11 is uncertain and may mean quivers. And “the thread of your life is cut” (v. 13) is literally ‘the cubit of your cutting off’, probably a weaver’s picture of cloth measured and cut from the loom (compare Isaiah 38:12).
verseByVerse.note: Leb-kamai is a code name for Chaldea (ESV note): read with the Hebrew alphabet reversed, it spells the word for Chaldeans.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Creator of all things stands against Babylon’s breathless idols, and Babylon herself was only his tool. A hymn praises the one who made the earth by his power and commands the weather (vv. 15–16); the idol-makers are put to shame by gods with no breath in them (vv. 17–18), while Israel’s portion is the Maker of all (v. 19). Babylon is told what she was: God’s hammer, with which he broke nations, armies and ordinary people in pieces (vv. 20–23). Now she will be repaid for the evil done in Zion and left a burnt mountain, not even good for building stone (vv. 24–26).
verseByVerse.theology: The tool is told what it was, just before it is put down.

verseByVerse.quote: "It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens. When he utters his voice there is a tumult of waters in the heavens, and he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who made the world and commands its weather stands behind his word against Babylon.

It is he who made the earth by his power. In the middle of a war oracle comes a hymn, the one sung earlier against the idols of Judah (10:12–16), repeated here against the idols of Babylon. Three of God’s qualities are named, power, wisdom and understanding, and then the weather is described as his work: mist raised from the ends of the earth, lightning made for the rain, and “the wind from his storehouses”, as though God keeps weather in a warehouse and brings out what the day requires.

Established the world by his wisdom. Babylon was famous for its learning: astronomy, omens, the reading of the stars. The hymn answers that the wisdom which set the world in place and stretched out the heavens is the LORD’s (compare Proverbs 3:19). Surrounded by the temples and lore of the greatest city on earth, the exiles are reminded who made the sky the Babylonians studied.

verseByVerse.quote: Every man is stupid and without knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols, for his images are false, and there is no breath in them. They are worthless, a work of delusion; at the time of their punishment they shall perish. Not like these is he who is the portion of Jacob, for he is the one who formed all things, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the LORD of hosts is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Idols are lifeless products of human skill that will perish with Babylon, but Israel’s portion is the living Creator, who has made Israel his own.

There is no breath in them. Against the Creator stands the craftsman. One brings forth the wind; the other brings forth a statue, and its fatal lack is named exactly. The God who breathed life into dust is set beside gods that cannot breathe at all.

Every man is stupid. This does not mean idol-makers lack skill; the goldsmith is very skilful. It means that skill without the knowledge of God ends by worshipping its own work, and is put to shame by it. Idols have their own day of judgment: when Babylon falls, her gods fall with her (50:2; 51:44, 47).

The portion of Jacob. Israel’s share, her allotted inheritance, is a person, and the sentence turns round and says Israel is his: “the tribe of his inheritance”. Each belongs to the other.

He is the one who formed all things. The one who formed all things has a name in the New Testament. John says of the Word who became flesh, “All things were made through him” (John 1:3, 14). The portion of Jacob, the Creator set against breathless idols, is the God who came to his people in Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "You are my hammer and weapon of war: with you I break nations in pieces; with you I destroy kingdoms; with you I break in pieces the horse and his rider; with you I break in pieces the chariot and the charioteer; with you I break in pieces man and woman; with you I break in pieces the old man and the youth; with you I break in pieces the young man and the young woman; with you I break in pieces the shepherd and his flock; with you I break in pieces the farmer and his team; with you I break in pieces governors and commanders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon was never a rival to God, only the hammer in his hand.

With you I break in pieces. Nine times in four verses comes the phrase, with the rhythm of a hammer, and the list moves from cavalry to civilians, from shepherds and ploughmen to the government. Read as a whole it is God’s own account of what Babylon was: “You are my hammer and weapon of war.” Not a rival kingdom he failed to stop, but an implement he swung. No power on earth, however crushing, acts outside his hand, and none who are used by him have anything to boast of.

Where Christians differ. Interpreters differ over who the hammer is. The verbs can be read as future, and some take the hammer to be Israel, or Cyrus, about to be swung against Babylon.

This commentary’s view. This commentary follows the many who take it of Babylon herself, since the next verse turns at once to repay her, and 50:23 has already called Babylon “the hammer of the whole earth”.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea before your very eyes for all the evil that they have done in Zion, declares the LORD. "Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain, declares the LORD, which destroys the whole earth; I will stretch out my hand against you, and roll you down from the crags, and make you a burnt mountain. No stone shall be taken from you for a corner and no stone for a foundation, but you shall be a perpetual waste, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hammer is accountable for what it did in Zion, and Babylon will become rubble too worthless to build with, while God builds on the stone he laid in Zion.

For all the evil that they have done in Zion. The tool went beyond what it was sent to do, and the repayment will happen “before your very eyes”, so the exiles will see it.

O destroying mountain. Babylon sat on a flat plain, so “destroying mountain” describes her towering power, not her landscape. Her sentence is to be rolled down from the crags and left “a burnt mountain”, a heap of burnt-out rubble.

No stone shall be taken from you for a corner. Ruined cities were quarries for the next builders. This rubble will not even be worth carting away.

No stone for a foundation. The contrast is with Zion, of which God had said, “Behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion, a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation” (Isaiah 28:16), and the apostles saw that stone in Christ (1 Peter 2:4–6). Babylon’s rubble will never be built into anything; the stone God laid in Zion carries a building that is still rising.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The empire collapses from within, and God answers his people’s complaint by taking up their cause. Peoples of the far north and the Medes are summoned, and the land trembles because the LORD’s purposes stand (vv. 27–29). Babylon’s warriors stop fighting, runners race to tell the king his city is taken, and she lies like a threshing floor before harvest (vv. 30–33). Zion describes how Nebuchadnezzar swallowed her and asks that her blood be on Babylon (vv. 34–35). God answers, “I will plead your cause”: he will dry up her waters, turn her into ruins and give her roaring lions a feast that ends in endless sleep (vv. 36–40).
verseByVerse.theology: The city is taken while the messengers are still running to say so.

verseByVerse.quote: "Set up a standard on the earth; blow the trumpet among the nations; prepare the nations for war against her; summon against her the kingdoms, Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz; appoint a marshal against her; bring up horses like bristling locusts. Prepare the nations for war against her, the kings of the Medes, with their governors and deputies, and every land under their dominion. The land trembles and writhes in pain, for the LORD's purposes against Babylon stand, to make the land of Babylon a desolation, without inhabitant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God musters nations from the far north against Babylon, because his purpose against her stands.

Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz. These are three little-known peoples of the northern highlands, in the region of modern Armenia, called up to join the attack. They had come under the power of the Medes, who are named next (v. 28; on the Medes see the note on vv. 1–14). The cavalry comes up like a bristling swarm of locusts, too many to count.

The LORD’s purposes against Babylon stand. The trumpet and the standard gather the nations, but the one who musters them is God. Verse 29 says why the land trembles: not because of the armies, but because his purposes stand. Human plans rise and fall; his counsel stands (Isaiah 46:10).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “bristling” is rare and its meaning uncertain; it may describe the spiky stage of a young locust, or locusts swarming thickly.

verseByVerse.quote: The warriors of Babylon have ceased fighting; they remain in their strongholds; their strength has failed; they have become women; her dwellings are on fire; her bars are broken. One runner runs to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to tell the king of Babylon that his city is taken on every side; the fords have been seized, the marshes are burned with fire, and the soldiers are in panic. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor at the time when it is trodden; yet a little while and the time of her harvest will come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon’s defence collapses from the inside, the news races to the king, and the city lies ready for God’s harvest of judgment.

The warriors of Babylon have ceased fighting. They have not been beaten in the field; they have stopped fighting and gone indoors, and then “their strength has failed”. The bars of the gates are broken and the houses are burning.

One runner runs to meet another. Couriers collide on the road, each carrying worse news to the palace. By the time the king is told, “his city is taken on every side”. Anyone who has watched an institution fail will recognise the picture, the messages arriving faster than the leadership can take them in.

The fords have been seized. Babylon’s defences were water: the Euphrates ran through the city, and canals and marshes surrounded it. Seize the crossings and burn the reed-beds, and the defence is gone. The Greek historian Herodotus later told how Cyrus’ army entered the city by lowering the river and marching in along its bed (compare v. 36).

Like a threshing floor at the time when it is trodden. A threshing floor was stamped hard and level before the harvest. The trampling Babylon now suffers prepares her for the harvest of judgment, when she will be threshed as she threshed others (compare the winnowers of v. 2). “Yet a little while”: the time is short, and it is fixed.

verseByVerse.quote: "Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon has devoured me; he has crushed me; he has made me an empty vessel; he has swallowed me like a monster; he has filled his stomach with my delicacies; he has rinsed me out. The violence done to me and to my kinsmen be upon Babylon," let the inhabitant of Zion say. "My blood be upon the inhabitants of Chaldea," let Jerusalem say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God lets Zion say plainly what Babylon did to her and hand the guilt over to him as judge.

He has rinsed me out. Zion is given a voice, and it is one of the most physical complaints in Scripture. Six verbs of being eaten: devoured, crushed, emptied, swallowed, gorged on, and then the last indignity, “he has rinsed me out”, like a jar licked clean and set aside.

Honest complaint. God lets his people say exactly how bad it was, and does not tell them to tone it down. For anyone who has been badly wronged, this is permission to name the harm honestly before God rather than pretend it was nothing.

My blood be upon the inhabitants of Chaldea. Zion asks that the guilt for the violence and bloodshed be laid where it belongs. This is not private revenge but an appeal to the judge, the same appeal the martyrs make in Revelation (Revelation 6:10), and it is left in God’s hands: “Vengeance is mine” (Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19). Telling God plainly what was done to us is part of how we leave it with him.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “he has rinsed me out” may be read ‘he has expelled me’; the rare verb can mean to wash out or to cast out, and either way it pictures Judah emptied and discarded.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will plead your cause and take vengeance for you. I will dry up her sea and make her fountain dry, and Babylon shall become a heap of ruins, the haunt of jackals, a horror and a hissing, without inhabitant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers his people’s complaint by becoming their advocate and giving Babylon the very sentence she gave Jerusalem.

I will plead your cause. The answer to Zion’s complaint is not a lecture but an advocate. Christians have the same answer in fuller form: “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1).

I will dry up her sea and make her fountain dry. Babylon lived by water, the Euphrates and its network of canals. Isaiah had put the same promise next to a name: God “says to the deep, ‘Be dry; I will dry up your rivers’” and “says of Cyrus, ‘He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose’” (Isaiah 44:27–28).

Babylon shall become a heap of ruins. Every phrase of verse 37 was first spoken over Jerusalem: “a heap of ruins, a lair of jackals” (9:11), “a horror, a hissing” (25:9, 18). The city that made Jerusalem a ruin is given Jerusalem’s sentence. That is how exactly God pleads his people’s cause.

verseByVerse.quote: "They shall roar together like lions; they shall growl like lions' cubs. While they are inflamed I will prepare them a feast and make them drunk, that they may become merry, then sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the LORD. I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams and male goats.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon’s rulers, roaring like lions over their prey, will be given a feast that ends in death, as happened on the night the city fell.

They shall roar together like lions. The Babylonians growl like lions over their prey, and the roar becomes the noise of their drinking party (v. 39). Then the picture turns: the lions are brought down “like lambs to the slaughter” (v. 40). The beasts of prey become the sacrificed flock, and “a perpetual sleep” is death, from which they will not wake.

While they are inflamed I will prepare them a feast. A feast, wine, merriment, and then sleep. Daniel 5 records the night: a banquet, the vessels of the temple used for drinking, writing on the wall, and “That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed” (Daniel 5:30). Babylon, who had made the nations drink, was handed a cup of her own.

Another lamb. Babylon’s lords go down like lambs to the slaughter against their will, under judgment. Another went “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7) of his own will, for the sins of others, and his death is the reason judgment need not be the end of anyone who trusts him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–53 — Go Out of the Midst of Her, My People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Babylon is taken, and God’s people are called to leave her and remember him. The city that was the praise of the whole earth is overwhelmed, and Bel is made to give back what he swallowed (vv. 41–44). God’s people must go out, and not lose heart at the years of rumour and upheaval that come first (vv. 45–46). When Babylon’s idols are judged, heaven and earth will sing, for she must fall for the slain of Israel (vv. 47–49). The survivors are told to remember the LORD from far away, though shame still covers them for the desecrated temple (vv. 50–51); however high Babylon climbs, God’s destroyers will reach her (vv. 52–53).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people are told to get out, and to take Jerusalem with them in their minds.

verseByVerse.quote: "How Babylon is taken, the praise of the whole earth seized! How Babylon has become a horror among the nations! The sea has come up on Babylon; she is covered with its tumultuous waves. Her cities have become a horror, a land of drought and a desert, a land in which no one dwells, and through which no son of man passes. And I will punish Bel in Babylon, and take out of his mouth what he has swallowed. The nations shall no longer flow to him; the wall of Babylon has fallen. "Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD! Let not your heart faint, and be not fearful at the report heard in the land, when a report comes in one year and afterward a report in another year, and violence is in the land, and ruler is against ruler. "Therefore, behold, the days are coming when I will punish the images of Babylon; her whole land shall be put to shame, and all her slain shall fall in the midst of her. Then the heavens and the earth, and all that is in them, shall sing for joy over Babylon, for the destroyers shall come against them out of the north, declares the LORD. Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel, just as for Babylon have fallen the slain of all the earth. "You who have escaped from the sword, go, do not stand still! Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind: 'We are put to shame, for we have heard reproach; dishonor has covered our face, for foreigners have come into the holy places of the LORD's house.' "Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will execute judgment upon her images, and through all her land the wounded shall groan. Though Babylon should mount up to heaven, and though she should fortify her strong height, yet destroyers would come from me against her, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon, the wonder of the world, is taken and her god made to give back what he swallowed; so God’s people must leave her, hold steady through years of rumour, and remember the LORD from far away.

How Babylon is taken, the praise of the whole earth seized! The ESV notes that the Hebrew here reads ‘Sheshach’, the code name for Babylon used in chapter 25, where Babylon drank last from the cup she had carried round (25:26). The code name returns for her funeral. “The praise of the whole earth” is not sarcasm: Babylon was admired everywhere, and the tone is astonishment rather than gloating.

I will punish Bel in Babylon. Bel had swallowed the offerings and tribute of the world, and the temple vessels of Jerusalem with them. God will reach into the idol’s mouth and “take out of his mouth what he has swallowed”, which is what happened when Cyrus counted the bowls back out to a prince of Judah (Ezra 1:7–8).

Go out of the midst of her, my people! The call to leave rests on verse 5: a people not forsaken by their God is being called home, not driven out. And pastoral care is attached. There will be years of rumour first, “a report comes in one year and afterward a report in another year”, with violence and “ruler is against ruler”, and God tells them in advance not to let their hearts faint at each new report. John hears the same summons over the last Babylon: “Come out of her, my people” (Revelation 18:4).

Shall sing for joy over Babylon. Creation sings: not human vindictiveness but the relief of a world that has been groaning, and the reason given is the dead: “Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel.” The psalmist by the canals had said it in grief, “O daughter of Babylon, doomed to be destroyed” (Psalm 137:8), and here God answers him.

Is it right to rejoice when a city falls? The joy here is at the end of oppression and at justice for the dead, and it belongs to God’s judgment, not to private revenge. Christians still pray for their enemies (Matthew 5:44) and leave vengeance with God (Romans 12:19); and they may rejoice, as heaven does in Revelation 19:1–2, when he puts an end to cruelty.

Remember the LORD from far away. Two instructions for survivors: remember the LORD, and “let Jerusalem come into your mind”, even while the shame of the desecrated temple still covers their faces (v. 51). Faith at a distance, with a city held in the memory, is how most of God’s people have lived ever since.

How do I remember the LORD from far away? The New Testament carries this over: Peter writes to Christians as “elect exiles of the dispersion” (1 Peter 1:1), and “here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come” (Hebrews 13:14). Remembering from far away is a habit more than a feeling. Keep a fixed time. Daniel, in Babylon itself, prayed three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10); give the Lord the first minutes of the day, before the news and the inbox. Keep the Lord’s Day with his people, the weekly reminder that you belong to another city. Let the other city shape the budget: give to the church and to the poor, because “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). Talk about home at the table, so your children inherit the memory. And remember why there is a home to remember: Christ has gone ahead to prepare a place for us and promised to come again and take us to himself (John 14:2–3).

Though Babylon should mount up to heaven. This is the old ambition of Babel, still running. Isaiah had put the boast in the first person, “I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high”, and given the answer: “But you are brought down to Sheol” (Isaiah 14:13–15). Height is no defence when the destroyers come “from me”.
verseByVerse.note: Sheshach is a code name for Babylon (ESV note), formed the same way by reversing the alphabet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God silences Babylon, and his word outlasts her. The roar of the great city is stilled, her warriors taken and her broad wall levelled, for the LORD is a God of recompense, and the nations have laboured only for fire (vv. 54–58). Then comes a final acted sign. Jeremiah writes the oracle in a book and gives it to Seraiah, Baruch’s brother, who is travelling with King Zedekiah to Babylon; there it is to be read aloud, tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates: “Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more” (vv. 59–64). Here the words of Jeremiah end.
verseByVerse.theology: A book weighted with a stone and dropped in a river serves as the closing sermon of Jeremiah's book.

verseByVerse.quote: "A voice! A cry from Babylon! The noise of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans! For the LORD is laying Babylon waste and stilling her mighty voice. Their waves roar like many waters; the noise of their voice is raised, for a destroyer has come upon her, upon Babylon; her warriors are taken; their bows are broken in pieces, for the LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay. I will make drunk her officials and her wise men, her governors, her commanders, and her warriors; they shall sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. "Thus says the LORD of hosts: The broad wall of Babylon shall be leveled to the ground, and her high gates shall be burned with fire. The peoples labor for nothing, and the nations weary themselves only for fire." The word that Jeremiah the prophet commanded Seraiah the son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, when he went with Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon, in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah was the quartermaster. Jeremiah wrote in a book all the disaster that should come upon Babylon, all these words that are written concerning Babylon. And Jeremiah said to Seraiah: "When you come to Babylon, see that you read all these words, and say, 'O LORD, you have said concerning this place that you will cut it off, so that nothing shall dwell in it, neither man nor beast, and it shall be desolate forever.' When you finish reading this book, tie a stone to it and cast it into the midst of the Euphrates, and say, 'Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more, because of the disaster that I am bringing upon her, and they shall become exhausted.'" Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God silences Babylon and levels everything built without him, and the word he spoke through Jeremiah, sunk in the Euphrates with a stone, outlasts the empire.

Stilling her mighty voice. A great city is a noise of markets, processions and crowds, and God turns it off.

The LORD is a God of recompense; he will surely repay. It is one of the plainest statements in Scripture that God repays evil, and it makes the rest of the book bearable. A world in which the hammer is never put down would be a world without justice.

The broad wall of Babylon. Babylon’s walls, which Greek writers said were wide enough to drive chariots along, come down.

The peoples labor for nothing. The last line of the oracle is an epitaph for every empire: “The peoples labor for nothing, and the nations weary themselves only for fire” (compare Habakkuk 2:13). Decades of forced labour hauled brick for gates that will only feed the fire. Whatever is built without God is built for burning.

Isn’t history moving forward? Most of us were raised on the story of progress: each generation wiser and kinder than the last. There is much to be thankful for, from anaesthetics to clean water. But the English philosopher John Gray, himself an atheist, has argued that faith in progress is Christian hope with God taken out, and that without God it is a myth: knowledge piles up, but human beings do not improve, and what one age gains another can lose. Babylon lived inside that myth. Her walls were a wonder of the world, and the verdict is that the nations weary themselves only for fire. Jeremiah does not answer the myth with despair but with a different story, in which history does move toward an end, though not by our momentum. The broad wall falls; the city that is coming is the one “whose designer and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:10), and it was secured not by the labour of the peoples but by the work of the one who said, “It is finished” (John 19:30).

Was Babylon really levelled? Not in 539 BC: Cyrus took it with little fighting, and it remained a great city for a time. But over the following centuries it declined until it became the empty mound it is today, as Jeremiah said (50:39–40). Prophecy often shows the end of a long process in a single picture.

Seraiah the son of Neriah. Seraiah was Baruch’s brother (32:12) and “the quartermaster”, a senior official travelling with the king to Babylon, probably in 594 or 593 BC. The family that gave Jeremiah his scribe also gave him a courier into the enemy capital.

Jeremiah wrote in a book. The man whose first scroll was burned writes again, and sends the book hundreds of miles to be read aloud in the city it condemns: a private reading, probably to nobody but God and one official standing by a river.

Tie a stone to it. This is the last acted sign recorded in the book, though it was performed years before he buried the stones at Tahpanhes (43:8–13). He had worn a yoke, smashed a flask, buried a loincloth and bought a field. Now, by proxy, a book is weighted with a stone and dropped into the Euphrates, and the words are spoken over the ripples: “Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more.” The closing words, “and they shall become exhausted”, repeat the end of verse 58, marking where the oracle itself ends.

A millstone into the sea. Some seven centuries later John saw a mighty angel throw a stone like a great millstone into the sea, saying, “So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more” (Revelation 18:21). The last book of the Bible repeats the gesture of a courier at a riverbank.

Thus far are the words of Jeremiah. Seven words close forty years. There is no account of his death, no grave, no scene of vindication; he is last seen in Egypt among people who would not hear him, and the book simply stops recording what he said.

What outlasted every power. What he said outlasted every power in it. Jehoiakim burned the first scroll, and within a few years his son lost the throne after three months; Babylon is a mound in the desert; and the words thrown into the Euphrates with a stone tied to them are still read. The man who asked God why he had ever been born (20:18) wrote the promise of the law written on the heart and sins remembered no more, and it is being read this morning in languages that did not exist when he dictated it, because the one who made that covenant in his blood has risen and reigns.

Textual note. In verse 59 the ancient Greek translation says Seraiah went ‘from’ Zedekiah, that is, sent by him, rather than “with” him. Either way he travelled on the king’s business.
verseByVerse.note: Zedekiah's journey to Babylon in his fourth year is not recorded elsewhere; it may have been to assure Nebuchadnezzar of his loyalty after the plotting of chapter 27.

51.title: A Stone in the Euphrates
51.overview:
Where we are. The oracle against Babylon that began in chapter 50 reaches its climax here, and with it the words of Jeremiah come to an end (v. 64). Only the historical appendix of chapter 52 follows.

The message. The God who made the heavens and the earth has not forsaken his people, and the empire that seemed to own the world was only a cup and a hammer in his hand. He will repay her, plead his people’s cause and call them out of her, and everything built without him, however magnificent, is built for the fire. His word, sunk in the Euphrates with a stone, will outlast Babylon.

Why it was said. The exiles lived surrounded by the splendour, gods and learning of the greatest city on earth, and by years of rumour and upheaval (v. 46). They needed to know that God had not let go of them (v. 5), that Babylon’s fall was fixed, and how to stay faithful far from Jerusalem until then (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God stirs up the Medes against Babylon, the golden cup in his hand, because Israel and Judah have not been forsaken; she is past healing (vv. 1–14). A hymn sets the Maker of all things against breathless idols, and Babylon learns she was only his hammer, to be repaid and left a burnt mountain (vv. 15–26). Nations are summoned, her defence collapses from inside, Zion pours out her complaint, and God answers, “I will plead your cause” (vv. 27–40). Babylon is taken, Bel is made to give back what he swallowed, and God’s people are called out and told to remember the LORD from far away (vv. 41–53). At last the broad wall falls, and Jeremiah’s scroll, read aloud in Babylon, is sunk in the Euphrates: “Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more” (vv. 54–64).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by pattern. The Creator of verse 19, “the one who formed all things”, is the Word through whom “All things were made” and who became flesh (John 1:3, 14). The God who has not forsaken his people kept that promise by letting his Son be forsaken in their place (Matthew 27:46). Babylon’s rubble is useless for a foundation (v. 26), but God has laid in Zion a tested cornerstone, Christ (1 Peter 2:6). And Revelation takes up this chapter’s last gestures, the call to come out of her (Revelation 18:4) and the stone thrown into the water (Revelation 18:21), for the final fall of every Babylon.

For us. Christians still live as exiles in cities that dazzle and do not last. Remember the Lord from far away, do not faint at every rumour, and do not spend your life on what will only feed the fire, but on the city whose builder is God.
51.theology:
The exiles' real question was not whether Babylon would fall but whether God had dropped them, and the answer is flat: they have not been forsaken (v. 5). The empire that looked like their master was a cup in his hand and a hammer he swung, accountable for the evil it did beyond what God sent it to do (vv. 7, 20, 24).

God's judgment is not eagerness to destroy; balm was offered first (v. 9). His people are allowed to say exactly how much they have suffered, and he answers as their advocate (vv. 34-36). Because he is a God of recompense, the hammer is not swung for ever (v. 56), and whatever is built without him is built for burning (v. 58).
51.examples:
Anyone who has watched an institution fail will know the picture of the runners: one messenger after another arriving with worse news, until the leadership learns the city is already taken. Pride rarely sees its fall coming.

For believers living far from home, the chapter gives two instructions that have shaped God's people ever since: Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind. Faith often lives at a distance, holding to a city it cannot yet see (Heb 11:16).

keyVerse.quote: For Israel and Judah have not been forsaken by their God, the LORD of hosts, but the land of the Chaldeans is full of guilt against the Holy One of Israel.
keyVerse.note: This is the pastoral heart of the oracle against Babylon. The city was gone, the temple burned and the people in exile, and every appearance said that God had dropped them; this verse denies it flatly. In Christ the promise holds for all his people, because he was forsaken so that they never will be.

51.reflection:
Verse 5 says Israel and Judah “have not been forsaken by their God” even after their city burned. When have you felt forsaken by God? How do this verse and the cross answer that fear?

Babylon was “a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunken” (v. 7). What in our own culture is beautiful and intoxicating in the same way? How can Christians enjoy what is good in it without being drunk on it?

God told the exiles, “Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come into your mind” (v. 50). What habits help you remember that you belong to another city?

“The peoples labor for nothing, and the nations weary themselves only for fire” (v. 58). What are you giving your life to that will last, and what may only be fuel for the fire?

And they went in the direction of the Arabah.<sup>8</sup>But the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, and all his army was scattered from him.<sup>9</sup>Then they captured the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and he passed sentence on him.<sup>10</sup>The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and also slaughtered all the officials of Judah at Riblah.<sup>11</sup>He put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him in chains, and the king of Babylon took him to Babylon, and put him in prison till the day of his death.<sup>12</sup>In the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month—that was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon—Nebuzaradan the captain of the bodyguard, who served the king of Babylon, entered Jerusalem.<sup>13</sup>And he burned the house of the LORD, and the king's house and all the houses of Jerusalem; every great house he burned down.<sup>14</sup>And all the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down all the walls around Jerusalem.<sup>15</sup>And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive some of the poorest of the people and the rest of the people who were left in the city and the deserters who had deserted to the king of Babylon, together with the rest of the artisans.<sup>16</sup>But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to be vinedressers and plowmen.<sup>17</sup>And the pillars of bronze that were in the house of the LORD, and the stands and the bronze sea that were in the house of the LORD, the Chaldeans broke in pieces, and carried all the bronze to Babylon.<sup>18</sup>And they took away the pots and the shovels and the snuffers and the basins and the dishes for incense and all the vessels of bronze used in the temple service;<sup>19</sup>also the small bowls and the fire pans and the basins and the pots and the lampstands and the dishes for incense and the bowls for drink offerings. What was of gold the captain of the guard took away as gold, and what was of silver, as silver.<sup>20</sup>As for the two pillars, the one sea, the twelve bronze bulls that were under the sea, and the stands, which Solomon the king had made for the house of the LORD, the bronze of all these things was beyond weight.<sup>21</sup>As for the pillars, the height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits, its circumference was twelve cubits, and its thickness was four fingers, and it was hollow.<sup>22</sup>On it was a capital of bronze. The height of the one capital was five cubits. A network and pomegranates, all of bronze, were around the capital. And the second pillar had the same, with pomegranates.<sup>23</sup>There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides; all the pomegranates were a hundred upon the network all around.<sup>24</sup>And the captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest and the three keepers of the threshold;<sup>25</sup>and from the city he took an officer who had been in command of the men of war, and seven men of the king's council, who were found in the city; and the secretary of the commander of the army, who mustered the people of the land; and sixty men of the people of the land, who were found in the midst of the city.<sup>26</sup>And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.<sup>27</sup>And the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was taken into exile out of its land.<sup>28</sup>This is the number of the people whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year, 3,023 Judeans;<sup>29</sup>in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar he carried away captive from Jerusalem 832 persons;<sup>30</sup>in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Judeans 745 persons; all the persons were 4,600.<sup>31</sup>And in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-fifth day of the month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the year that he began to reign, graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison.<sup>32</sup>And he spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat above the seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon.<sup>33</sup>So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. And every day of his life he dined regularly at the king's table,<sup>34</sup>and for his allowance, a regular allowance was given him by the king, according to his daily needs, until the day of his death, as long as he lived.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chronicle begins with the king, and the first cause it names is God. Zedekiah did evil like his brother Jehoiakim, and behind his rebellion stood the LORD’s anger casting his people out of his presence (vv. 1–3). Then the record turns to dates: the siege from the ninth year, the famine until there was no food, the breach in the wall and the flight by night towards the Arabah (vv. 4–7). The king is caught near Jericho and judged at Riblah. His sons are killed before his eyes, his eyes are put out, and he is kept in a Babylonian prison till the day of his death (vv. 8–11). Every detail fulfils what Jeremiah had warned.
verseByVerse.theology: After fifty-one chapters of warning, the fall is told as plain fact, and the facts prove Jeremiah right.

verseByVerse.quote: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. And he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that Jehoiakim had done. For because of the anger of the LORD it came to the point in Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon. And in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came with all his army against Jerusalem, and laid siege to it. And they built siegeworks all around it. So the city was besieged till the eleventh year of King Zedekiah. On the ninth day of the fourth month the famine was so severe in the city that there was no food for the people of the land. Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled and went out from the city by night by the way of a gate between the two walls, by the king's garden, and the Chaldeans were around the city. And they went in the direction of the Arabah. But the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, and all his army was scattered from him. Then they captured the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and he passed sentence on him. The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and also slaughtered all the officials of Judah at Riblah. He put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him in chains, and the king of Babylon took him to Babylon, and put him in prison till the day of his death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem fell exactly as Jeremiah had said, and the record insists that behind Babylon’s army stood the LORD himself, casting his people out of his presence. After fifty-one chapters of poetry, lament and tears, the book ends in the flat prose of a court chronicle, almost word for word with 2 Kings 24:18–25:30.

An appendix. Since chapter 51 closed with “Thus far are the words of Jeremiah” (51:64), this was probably added by another hand, many think Baruch’s, to show that every word had come true (see the introduction).

Jeremiah of Libnah. Not the prophet, but a namesake from the town of Libnah. Hamutal was also the mother of Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:31), so Zedekiah was full brother to the king carried off to Egypt (22:11–12).

He cast them out from his presence. Verse 3 gives two causes, and the order matters. What God did comes first, “he cast them out from his presence”, and only then what the king did, Zedekiah’s rebellion. The army is not the whole story.

In the ninth year of his reign. The dating is precise to the day, which is how you write about something you cannot forget. A siege of about a year and a half, roughly 588 to 586 BC, is summed up in one clause: “there was no food for the people of the land.” Jeremiah lived through it on a loaf a day until the bread ran out (37:21).

The army of the Chaldeans pursued the king. Told already in chapter 39, the capture is retold without a word of interpretation: no lament, no reproach, no reminder that he could have surrendered and lived (38:17).

Put him in prison till the day of his death. A detail chapter 39 and 2 Kings leave out. He had been promised death not by the sword but in peace (34:4–5), and this is what that mercy looked like: years in a Babylonian cell, blind, then a quiet end. God kept the promise exactly, in a shape nobody would have pictured. Remember the phrase; the chapter ends with it (v. 34).
verseByVerse.note: Chapter 52 closely follows 2 Kings 24:18–25:30.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–23 — He Burned the House of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The house Judah thought God would never give up is burned, and its treasures go exactly where God had said. A month after the breach Nebuzaradan burns the temple, the palace and every great house, breaks down the walls and deports the people, leaving only the poorest to tend vines and fields (vv. 12–16). Then comes a long inventory of the bronze: the pillars, the stands, the sea and the vessels of worship, broken up and carried to Babylon (vv. 17–19). Last, the measurements of Solomon’s two pillars are written down, down to the count of their pomegranates, as if someone could not bear to let their beauty be forgotten (vv. 20–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Someone lovingly records the temple’s beauty as it is broken up, and God has promised to bring it back (27:22).

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month—that was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon—Nebuzaradan the captain of the bodyguard, who served the king of Babylon, entered Jerusalem. And he burned the house of the LORD, and the king's house and all the houses of Jerusalem; every great house he burned down. And all the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down all the walls around Jerusalem. And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive some of the poorest of the people and the rest of the people who were left in the city and the deserters who had deserted to the king of Babylon, together with the rest of the artisans. But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to be vinedressers and plowmen. And the pillars of bronze that were in the house of the LORD, and the stands and the bronze sea that were in the house of the LORD, the Chaldeans broke in pieces, and carried all the bronze to Babylon. And they took away the pots and the shovels and the snuffers and the basins and the dishes for incense and all the vessels of bronze used in the temple service; also the small bowls and the fire pans and the basins and the pots and the lampstands and the dishes for incense and the bowls for drink offerings. What was of gold the captain of the guard took away as gold, and what was of silver, as silver. As for the two pillars, the one sea, the twelve bronze bulls that were under the sea, and the stands, which Solomon the king had made for the house of the LORD, the bronze of all these things was beyond weight. As for the pillars, the height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits, its circumference was twelve cubits, and its thickness was four fingers, and it was hollow. On it was a capital of bronze. The height of the one capital was five cubits. A network and pomegranates, all of bronze, were around the capital. And the second pillar had the same, with pomegranates. There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides; all the pomegranates were a hundred upon the network all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house Judah trusted to protect it was burned, and its bronze, the very items God had named years before, went to Babylon just as he had said.

He burned the house of the LORD. A month after the walls broke, the fire. Chapter 39 did not clearly name the temple (39:8); here it stands first. This was the house the people had trusted with a chant, “This is the temple of the LORD” (7:4), and God had warned he would make it like Shiloh (7:14).

On the tenth day of the month. Jeremiah dates the burning to the tenth day of the fifth month, 2 Kings to the seventh (2 Kings 25:8). Most likely the commander arrived on the seventh and burned it on the tenth. Jewish tradition still fasts on the ninth of Ab for this.

Some of the poorest of the land. The poorest are left with the vines and ploughs, as in 39:10: an administrative decision that reads like a verdict on the rich.

The pillars of bronze. These are the exact items God had named when the popular prophets promised the treasure back within two years: the pillars, the sea and the stands (27:19). They would stay in Babylon “until the day when I visit them” (27:22). Here they go, and the promise to bring them back goes with them.

Which Solomon the king had made. This bronze was nearly four centuries old, the work of Solomon (1 Kings 7:15–47), and now it is scrap metal, so much that it is “beyond weight”.

As for the pillars. Then comes the strangest passage in the chapter: the pillars Jachin and Boaz (1 Kings 7:21) measured in cubits (about 18 inches, or 45 centimetres), the bronze’s thickness in fingers, the pomegranates counted. Somebody wrote this down while they were being broken up and loaded onto carts. It is an act of love, recording a beautiful thing as it is destroyed so that it would not be as though it had never existed. Grief keeps inventories.

The true temple. The fire exposed what the chant of 7:4 had hidden: no building could guarantee God’s presence with a sinful people. Jesus spoke of another temple, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”, meaning his body (John 2:19–21). In him God dwells with his people in a house no army can burn.

Uncertain wording. In verse 20 the Hebrew lacks “the sea” (as the ESV notes) and, read literally, puts the bulls under the stands; they had carried the sea (1 Kings 7:25), and Ahaz had long since taken it off them (2 Kings 16:17), so the list may describe Solomon’s work as made. In verse 23 the word rendered “on the sides” is rare; probably 96 of the hundred pomegranates faced outward. And 2 Kings 25:17 gives the capital three cubits, not five (compare 1 Kings 7:16). None of this touches the point.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — So Judah Was Taken Into Exile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A nation ends in a headcount, yet the few who remain carry all God’s promises. The captain of the guard takes the chief priests, the doorkeepers, the commanders and counsellors, and sixty men of the people to Riblah, where they are executed (vv. 24–27). Then one flat sentence records the end the whole book had warned of: “So Judah was taken into exile out of its land.” The three deportations are counted, 4,600 in all, a number small enough to write in one line (vv. 28–30). Everything God had promised about restoration now rests on these few.
verseByVerse.theology: A nation's end is recorded as a headcount.

verseByVerse.quote: And the captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest and the three keepers of the threshold; and from the city he took an officer who had been in command of the men of war, and seven men of the king's council, who were found in the city; and the secretary of the commander of the army, who mustered the people of the land; and sixty men of the people of the land, who were found in the midst of the city. And Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. And the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was taken into exile out of its land. This is the number of the people whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year, 3,023 Judeans; in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar he carried away captive from Jerusalem 832 persons; in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Judeans 745 persons; all the persons were 4,600.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s leaders were executed and its people counted out of the land, so that a nation ended as a headcount; yet that small remnant carried every promise God had made.

Seraiah the chief priest. The leadership is collected by function: high priest, deputy, doorkeepers, commander, counsellors (five in 2 Kings 25:19), the conscription secretary and sixty ordinary men.

Zephaniah the second priest. One name is poignant. Zephaniah read Shemaiah’s hostile letter to Jeremiah instead of acting on it (29:29), and was twice sent to ask the prophet for prayer (21:1; 37:3). He was no enemy. He goes to Riblah with the rest.

So Judah was taken into exile out of its land. One sentence for the end of a nation, the sentence the book has warned of since the young Jeremiah was shown an almond branch: God watches over his word to perform it (1:11–12).

All the persons were 4,600. Three deportations, small in any reckoning, perhaps counting adult men or households. Do they contradict the ten thousand of 597 BC (2 Kings 24:14)? Probably not: this list dates by Nebuchadnezzar’s own years, one earlier than Kings (2 Kings 24:12; 25:8), and seems to count particular groups where Kings gives a round figure. The third deportation, about 582 BC, is recorded nowhere else; probably Babylon’s reprisal for Gedaliah’s murder (41:2–3), which the survivors had fled to Egypt to escape (41:18).

What a remnant looks like. A remnant, the few God keeps through judgment, looks like this on paper: a number low enough for one line. Every promise of restoration, the everlasting covenant, the Branch, the law written on the heart, now rested on 4,600 deportees and some vinedressers. Even the executed high priest’s line went on: his grandson Joshua came home as high priest (1 Chronicles 6:15; Ezra 3:2).

God’s purposes in small numbers. God’s purposes have often been carried by numbers that look like nothing. The narrowing went on until all of them rested on one Israelite, the Son of David alone at the cross; from him the remnant has grown into a multitude no one can number (Revelation 7:9). A small church or a lonely believer is not evidence that God has failed.

Textual note. The ancient Greek translation lacks verses 28–30 altogether.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book ends with grace. Thirty-seven years into his captivity Jehoiachin, the king of David’s line taken to Babylon in 597 BC, is released by the new king Evil-merodach (v. 31). He is spoken to kindly and given a seat above the other captive kings (v. 32). He takes off his prison garments and eats at the king’s table every day of his life, with an allowance for his daily needs until the day of his death (vv. 33–34). Nothing is said of his deserving it. The promise to David is still alive, and the closing scene is a small light pointing on to David’s greater Son.
verseByVerse.theology: The book of the weeping prophet ends with a pardoned son of David eating dinner.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-fifth day of the month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the year that he began to reign, graciously freed Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison. And he spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat above the seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon. So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. And every day of his life he dined regularly at the king's table, and for his allowance, a regular allowance was given him by the king, according to his daily needs, until the day of his death, as long as he lived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book ends with grace: after thirty-seven years in prison, David’s heir is lifted up, clothed and fed at a king’s table for life, a sign that God’s promise to David had not died. After everything, the book lifts.

Jehoiachin king of Judah. Thirty-seven years, to about 561 BC: most of a lifetime. He is the Coniah of chapter 22, carried off in 597 BC, of whom God said “Write this man down as childless” (22:30), and the good figs of chapter 24 went with him. He has been in a Babylonian prison ever since.

Graciously freed Jehoiachin. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is “lifted up the head of”, the idiom for Pharaoh restoring his cupbearer from prison (Genesis 40:13, 20): a face raised out of shame into favour. The lifter was Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk), Nebuchadnezzar’s son, who reigned about two years; a new king’s first year was a natural moment for a release. Babylonian ration tablets from years earlier list oil for Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and his sons.

Four pictures of grace. He is spoken to kindly, rare words from a foreign king to a king of Judah. He is given “a seat above the seats of the kings”, for no stated reason. He puts off his prison garments. And he eats at the king’s table “every day of his life”. David had once given Saul’s lame grandson Mephibosheth such a place (2 Samuel 9:13); now David’s heir receives it.

Until the day of his death. The chapter began with one king of Judah in prison “till the day of his death” (v. 11) and ends with another at the king’s table “until the day of his death”. Judgment first, grace last.

Nothing deserved. Jehoiachin had done what was evil (2 Kings 24:9), and a new emperor, for reasons of his own, raised his head, changed his clothes and sat him down to dinner. It is what happens to every sinner God pardons: brought out of a cell, robes exchanged, seated at a table, and fed daily for life.

David’s line alive. There is more here than a picture: the line of David is alive. The house that seemed finished has a living heir in Babylon, and Matthew’s genealogy runs through him: Jeconiah, and then the generations to Joseph the husband of Mary (Matthew 1:11–16). God had sworn that David’s throne would be established for ever (2 Samuel 7:16), and in a Babylonian prison that promise looked dead. This scene says it was not, and the angel’s word to Mary says where it was going: “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David … and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33).

According to his daily needs. The weeping prophet’s book ends with food for a pardoned king. No temple yet, no city, no Branch, but a son of David at a table with bread for each day; many readers hear in it the daily bread his greater Son taught us to ask for (Matthew 6:11).

Why the rest stands. Everything else here came true to the letter: the siege, the famine, the blinded king, the burned house. On the strength of that, the rest of what Jeremiah wrote stands: an everlasting love, a new heart that God himself gives, a righteous Branch, a city called “The LORD is our righteousness”, and sins that God has undertaken to remember no more.

What it does not mean. Not the restoration itself: Jehoiachin dies in Babylon, a foreign king’s dependant. The book closes with a small light, not the dawn, and teaches us to live on God’s promise while its fulfilment is out of sight.

How can Jesus descend from Jeconiah? God said none of Jeconiah’s offspring would sit on David’s throne (22:30), yet Matthew traces Jesus through him (Matthew 1:11–12). Jesus was Jeconiah’s heir through Joseph, his legal father, but not his physical descendant; Luke traces his descent through Nathan, another son of David (Luke 3:31), and many take that list as Mary’s line. Others add that God reversed the signet-ring sentence of 22:24 for Jeconiah’s grandson Zerubbabel (Haggai 2:23). Either way, the throne passed to a Son of David as God had promised.

52.title: A King at the Table
52.overview:
Where we are. The words of Jeremiah ended with Babylon sinking like a stone in the Euphrates, and the line “Thus far are the words of Jeremiah” (51:64). Chapter 52 is an appendix in the plain prose of a court record, closely matching the end of 2 Kings. It tells the fall of Jerusalem once more, already narrated in chapter 39, and then adds an ending no one in the burning city could have expected.

The message. Every word God spoke through Jeremiah came true, to the day, the weight of bronze and the number of captives. And because the judgment came exactly as he said, so will the mercy. The last scene is not the ashes of the temple but a son of David brought out of prison, clothed, and fed at a king’s table for life: God had not forgotten his promise to David.

Why it was said. The book’s first readers were exiles, asking whether the LORD had failed or had finished with them (see the introduction). This chapter answers both questions: the disaster was his word kept, not his weakness, and the royal line was still alive in Babylon.

How the chapter makes its case. First the king: Zedekiah’s evil reign, the siege and famine, his flight and capture, his sons killed before his eyes and his own eyes put out (vv. 1–11). Then the house: the temple burned, the walls broken, the people deported, and the bronze God had named years before carried to Babylon, down to the last pomegranate (vv. 12–23). Then the people: the leaders executed at Riblah and the exiles counted, 4,600 in all (vv. 24–30). Last, after thirty-seven years, Jehoiachin is released and given a seat of honour at the king’s table (vv. 31–34).

Where it leads. Chiefly by covenant and promise. God had sworn that David’s throne would be established for ever (2 Samuel 7:16), and in 586 BC that throne lay in ashes; the closing verses show the line surviving, and Matthew traces Jesus’ legal descent through this very king (Matthew 1:11–12). The scene is also a pattern of grace: an undeserving prisoner lifted up, his prison clothes exchanged, seated at the table and fed every day of his life, which is what God does in Christ for every sinner he pardons.

For us. The God whose warnings came true to the letter will keep his promises to the letter too, so we can trust him when his purposes look reduced to a number on a list. And whoever feels shut up in the prison of their own failure should look at the last verses: in Christ there is a table, a robe and daily bread for those who deserve none of it.
52.theology:
The appendix shows that God keeps his word exactly, though not always as we would picture it. God’s casting out of his people is named as the cause of the fall before Zedekiah’s rebellion (v. 3); Zedekiah's promised peaceful death meant years blind in a cell (v. 11; 34:4-5); and the temple vessels went to Babylon just as chapter 27 had said (27:19-22).

But the last word is grace. A remnant small enough to fit in one line carries all God's promises (v. 30), and a pardoned son of David sits at a king's table with nothing said about deserving it (vv. 31-34). The line of David is alive in Babylon and runs on to Christ (Matt 1:11-12).
52.examples:
When something precious is lost, people keep inventories: the photographs labelled, the recipes written down, the dates remembered. The clerk who counted the pomegranates on Solomon's pillars while they were broken up was doing the same thing, making sure that a beautiful thing would not vanish as though it had never been.

And when someone has spent years in the prison of their own failure, the end of this book is for them. Jehoiachin had done evil; a king lifted his head, changed his clothes and sat him down to dinner. That is what God does for every sinner he pardons.

keyVerse.quote: So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. And every day of his life he dined regularly at the king’s table
keyVerse.note: After fifty-one chapters of warning and a chapter of ruins, the book ends here, with David’s heir out of prison and fed at the king’s table. It shows that God’s judgment, however exact, was not his last word, and that his promise to David was still alive. It is also a picture of what grace does for any sinner: the prison clothes taken off, and a place at the table for life.

52.reflection:
Verse 3 names God’s anger as the cause of the fall before it names Zedekiah’s rebellion or Babylon’s army. Why does it matter to see God’s hand behind events, even painful ones, and how can we do that without becoming fatalistic or harsh?

Zedekiah’s promise of a peaceful death came true in a way no one would have pictured (v. 11; 34:4–5). Have you known God to keep a promise in a different shape from the one you expected? How does that help you read his promises now?

Someone carefully recorded the beauty of the temple’s pillars as they were broken up (vv. 21–23), and the total of exiles was only 4,600 (v. 30). How do we grieve what is lost without losing hope, and what encouragement is there here for small or struggling churches?

Jehoiachin did nothing to earn his release, his new clothes or his place at the table (vv. 31–34). In what ways is his story a picture of what God has done for you in Christ, and who in your life needs to hear that such grace is possible?
